and with the exact centre row) were checked for consistency with the exported data and logs only, not recomputed
independently; none is a converged solution of the discrete hydrostatic problem, these finite results do not
demonstrate convergence with resolution, and selection of c was not tested (a run with the map rebuilt from c was not
made). These computations do not establish existence of a hydrostatic solution, and a hydrostatic solution alone would
not give a profile of the original equations (3.72(e)). No computation at eps > 0 connecting these states to the
original problem was made. By 3.80, ten saved states of this item and of the same kind (listed there) satisfy the axis
equation on no nonempty open interval of y > 0. No candidate.

## 5. Explicit checks: rho_y(0), determination of c_l, scaling audit

- rho_y(0) != 0: no candidate. All retained computed forced and discrete states have a0 != 0 (the collapsed
  a0 = 0 states of 4.7 are discarded as spurious) (positive on sheet 1, negative on
  its beta < 0 continuation).
- Is c_l determined? Open. Proved: no point transformation changes c_l or a0 (3.13), and the residual scaling
  preserves both; hence two exact profiles with different c_l are never related by these maps. For trial densities the
  dilation also preserves a0 and c_l (3.5), so changes of a0 or c_l in a computation are not motion along it; this
  invariance does not show that the equation determines c_l. Proved as a conditional implication (3.27): for a smooth
  exact profile satisfying
  (H-dyn), whose augmented linearization is Fredholm of index 1 on a weighted Sobolev graph space with kernel equal to
  the scaling direction, c_l and a0 are locally determined. Proved under (H-dyn) alone (3.28): the Fredholm and index
  part of that hypothesis, at even integer orders above the threshold (with the far-field bounds of 3.23). Whether any
  profile satisfies (H-dyn) or the kernel hypothesis is unknown. In the planted test of Section 4.4 a single Newton recovery
  returns c_l; in the real problem there is no candidate on which to test it.
- Scaling audit: see 3.5, 3.6, 3.13 and 3.19. Treatment adopted: (i) reporting gauge L_K = 1 (valid for every exact
  profile of the primary class, since K != 0 by 3.6); (ii) inside solvers, any local slice transversal to the scaling
  generator e_sc is acceptable, with transversality checked, provided the slice functional is continuous in the
  topology used. The solvers of Section 4 fix one of two gauge functionals. In 4.1-4.6 it is the far-field angular
  mean of kappa, set equal to beta; with grid exponent p it is, up to the fixed factor L_g^{p-1}, the angular mean of
  Theta0(th)/sin th. In 4.7 it is the y-axis value K_g, which up to a fixed factor is K = lim_{y -> inf} y^{-p} rho(0,
  y) = Theta0(pi/2). Under rho_l = l rho(X/l) both scale as l^{1 - p}, so their derivatives along the scaling
  generator are (1 - p) beta and (1 - p) K_g, and a fixed nonzero value of either functional is reached by a positive
  dilation only from profiles whose functional has the same sign. The second is nonzero for every exact profile
  (K != 0 by 3.6). The first is nonzero only for profiles whose far-field angular mean is nonzero, which K != 0 does
  not imply, so the gauge of 4.1-4.6 reaches only such profiles (4.3). Each functional is a transversal slice where
  its derivative is nonzero and it is continuous (for example in weighted norms of weight exactly p in which the
  limits exist). The reporting length L_K is not continuous in weighted Holder norms of weight q > p: a function equal
  to r^p Theta0(th) for r > 2R and to 0 for r < R has such norms O(R^{p - q}) -> 0 while its axis coefficient stays K.
  So L_K = 1 is a reporting normalization only, not a slice in that topology; a0 and c_l are never normalized without
  loss of generality (c_l is a scanned parameter in forced problems and, in unforced ones, either fixed or solved for,
  as stated for each run). Fixing a Taylor coefficient such as b would be a valid local slice only where b != 0 and is
  therefore not used as a global normalization; the origin trace h_y(0) is not a slice at all (it vanishes on e_sc).
  (iii) Robustness of an endpoint under scaling: in a forced formulation with a fixed forcing width, a root is
  accepted only if the same c_l, the same a0 and the same scale-free quantities are obtained for several values of the
  scale parameter, and the rescaled state re-converges as an unforced solution after regridding (rationale in 3.19).
  The withdrawn branch of 4.6 failed this test. (iv) A beta-scan at fixed forcing width is equivalent to an eps-scan
  at fixed gauge (3.19); the large-beta behaviour of sheet 1 therefore corresponds to the concentrated-forcing limit
  of 4.5. Scale-invariant quantities there are c_l, mu, a0, Delta = mu/a0, b_cub L_K^2 and H_4 L_K^2; eps, beta, K,
  L_K and b_cub themselves are not invariant.

## 6. What prevents a decision

No identity found so far yields an automatic contradiction on the full class: the weighted identity 3.4, the Darcy
identity 3.16 and the label equation 3.15 all contain terms of undetermined sign. The strain constraint
c = 1 - c_l < 0 (3.2, 3.14) excludes restricted classes (3.14, 3.24) but not the primary class; the exclusion of
finite angular support (3.10) uses more than the sign of the strain. Shape classes on which the canonical inverse is
explicit are excluded by direct computation (finite angular support, 3.10; radial densities y f(r), 3.57(c);
elliptical shapes a0 y F(alpha x^2 + beta y^2) without any sign condition, 3.60); these arguments use the explicit
inverse and do not extend to general angular content. Finite Cartesian separation rank, also outside a disk, is
excluded through the far field alone (3.62), using only the convergence to the homogeneous far field, K != 0 and the
Holder continuity of Theta0 (3.6, 3.7); this says nothing about densities of infinite rank. Exterior solutions of P(d)
sigma = 0 for a nonzero linear differential operator P(d) with constant coefficients, and densities within o(r^p) of
them, are excluded by the same far-field information together with the smoothness of the far field off 0 (3.64).
Finite angular support outside a disc is excluded as well (3.66), by an expansion of rho outside the disc to every
depth in which the highest angular frequency grows along a cascade with nonvanishing coefficients; this uses the exact
transport outside the disc. The same expansion without any assumption on the angular support (3.67) shows that when
only the trace Theta0 is a trigonometric polynomial, rho still has nonzero modes of arbitrarily high frequency at
large radii, with the cascade coefficients as leading terms, and that for every exact profile the number of nonzero
angular modes on the circle of radius r tends to infinity as r -> inf; these are necessary conditions, they do not
give infinitely many modes on any one circle, and they say nothing about existence. For an arbitrary smooth trace the
construction still gives finite expansions of rho and U to every depth, with smooth angular coefficients, density
degrees p - k delta - 2l, the further velocity degrees -2m - 1, and no logarithm when delta is irrational (3.68); this
constrains far-field representations, identifies no necessarily nonzero coefficient beyond the leading one
P_p = Theta0 (nonzero for an exact profile, 3.7) and gives no convergence. Logarithms do occur: for the trace
Theta0 = A sin th with c_l = 3 or c_l = 5/2 the stream and the density have nonzero logarithmic terms at infinity
(3.69); such terms are compatible with smoothness and exclude no profile. The resonant coefficient that forces them
depends on arbitrarily high angular modes of the trace, keeps its sign under perturbations small in a strong weighted
norm, and vanishes for some positive two-mode traces (3.71). The transport identities obtained by integrating div(W
Phi(r, rho)) over the plane, for all compactly supported smooth weights Phi depending on r and rho, are equivalent to
the vanishing of the image of the measure E dX under X -> (r, rho(X)), where E is the residual; at regular levels this
is the vanishing of the conditional means of the residual on the level sets of rho on each circle. They force the
profile equation near 0, but each admissible power-weight identity of 3.70(iii) is satisfied by some smooth canonical
non-profile with psi_xy(0) = 1 - c_l. A single projection of transport does not bound the slope either: R_1 = 0
together with the one-sided sign, the centre normalization and the growth bound leaves a0 unbounded, already for
densities with two angular modes (3.61), while R_1 = R_3 = 0 bound a0 for these two modes (3.59(iv)); imposed only on
a disc, with a fifth mode outside it, the two projections and the one-sided sign do not bound a0 (3.63), and neither
do R_1 = ... = R_{2N-1} = 0 for any N >= 2, or exact transport, on a disc with q < 1 off 0 (3.65): these conditions on
a disc of radius R give no upper bound on a0 depending only on c_l and R. The energy identities for D^k rho (3.35)
give scale-invariant lower bounds on sup |grad rho| + sup |DU|, but no upper bound for exact profiles is known, so
they do not close either. The same holds for the weighted identities (3.42, 3.44): they bound sigma from below in
terms of c_l and a0, and under the extra strain cap sigma <= c_l - 1 they restrict a0 (3.46, 3.47: a0 >= 2 (2
c_l - 1) > 0 for every capped profile; the one-sided sign rho/(a0 y) <= 1 alone already excludes a flat h, 3.47(iv),
gives a0 >= 2 (2 c_l - 1) for 1 < c_l <= 5, 3.51, and together with q_th >= 0 on the first quadrant excludes every
profile, 3.53; for 1 < c_l <= 5 it forces the negative angular variation N(q) > pi/(16 A), 3.54), but no upper bound
on sigma is known for exact profiles. Approximate states do not transfer the cap to a limit without control: by 3.55
the cap passes to limits of near-capped states with common bounds, but C^1 convergence alone does not control the
strain. For large slopes the exact rescaling of 3.72(a) makes the slope an anisotropy parameter of the stream
equation. The question becomes a singular limit. Under uniform bounds on the rescaled density, its gradient and its
second xi-derivative, and C^2 convergence of the rescaled densities on compact sets, the canonical inverses converge
to the hydrostatic one (3.72(d)). On each fixed compact range of c_l, if the hydrostatic problem (3) of 3.72 (or, for
negative slopes, its signed analogue) had no solution with these bounds, the absolute slopes |a0| of profiles in that
range obeying such bounds with common constants and common local bounds on third derivatives would be bounded
(3.72(e)). On the axis the hydrostatic problem (3) of 3.72 selects neither the axis density nor c_lim, and three
natural forms are excluded (3.73). Every solution of (3) in the class of 3.73 has a continuous leading far-field
trace, no family of solutions has a regular expansion at c_lim = 1 under the hypotheses of 3.74(c), and no rule
selecting c_lim is known (3.74). Local real-analytic solutions from the bottom exist for every positive even analytic
bottom slope k with k(0) = 1, and their continuation to solutions with the bounds and the condition at infinity is not
controlled (3.75). For 1 < c_lim < 2 the first two compatibility conditions of a far-field expansion with smooth
angular coefficients give no sign obstruction for positive monotone traces (3.76). For every solution the limit of
V_2(xi, y) - V_2(0, y) as y -> inf is 0 whenever it exists, and C_p(Theta) = 0 (all c > 1), m_0 = 0 and C_d^- = 0
(c > 2) and B = 0 (c = 2, B as in 3.77(d)) are necessary for solutions with far-field expansions of the kinds stated
in 3.77, which are not known to hold for solutions (3.77). Formally, the leading inner problem of a near-axis layer of
width y^{(p + 1)/2} has exactly one solution for every value of C_p(Theta), with the nonzero leading layer excluded by
those expansions, and imposes no condition C_p(Theta) = 0, while its higher orders and its matching with the outer
region and the core are not constructed (3.78). For the signed problem of the negative slopes the corresponding
formally derived leading inner problem has no nonzero solution that is even and C^1 at the axis and has the required
behaviour at infinity, so at that order such a layer requires C_p(Theta) = 0 (3.79). The bounds of the class alone do
not suffice (3.72(c)), and neither the uniform bounds nor the hydrostatic problem is settled (the least-squares trial
states of 4.10 end in stalls or at iteration caps, at states that move under refinement, and by 3.80 no member of the
class of polynomial axis data of 3.80 with 1 < P < 27/2, which contains the axis data of ten of them, solves the axis
equation on a nonempty open interval of y > 0, which says nothing about limits as the degrees tend to infinity).

Numerical residuals cannot decide the question on their own: the explicit smooth non-profiles of 3.41 have pointwise
relative residuals at most (23/7)(c_l - 1), and those of 3.37(iii) have zero residual on arbitrarily large disks, so
small relative residuals near c_l = 1, or small residuals on bounded regions, do not by themselves certify proximity
to a profile (for the family of 3.41 the distance of 3.41(v) to every exact profile with the same c_l stays positive);
the dilation-invariant derivative residual of 3.40 separates the family of 3.41 from profiles.

The nonlocal term U[h] . grad rho of the linearization is of order zero; no compactness or smallness relative to the
transport part has been established in any norm used here, so standard perturbation arguments do not apply directly.
The energy matrix of 3.17 is positive at the source for a0 > -3 c_l, but its sign elsewhere is a property of the
unknown profile (the derivative decay at infinity is now available from 3.23), and positivity would control only
localized perturbations, not the c_l direction or the far-field data. For the functional-analytic route the
linearization is now proved Fredholm of index 1 with c_l free, under (H-dyn), on a weighted Sobolev graph space at
even integer orders above the threshold (3.28), using the far-field bounds proved from the equation (3.23). What
remains for local uniqueness modulo scaling: (H-dyn), which is equivalent to a strict sign condition on rho (3.22) and
is not known for an arbitrary exact profile; by 3.30 it is equivalent to rho_y(x, 0) != 0 on the x-axis and to the
absence of zeros of Theta0 in (0, pi), and a profile violating it would need a multiple or flat zero of Theta0 in (0,
pi) (3.34(e)); and the kernel hypothesis (the composition of 3.27 and 3.28, including the equal-weight step of A.3.27,
is settled in 3.52). Even then the result is local uniqueness modulo scaling, not existence or nonexistence.

At the source, when a0 > A (1 + alpha) - 1, the linearization with coefficients frozen at the source has homogeneous
modes of class C^{1,alpha} that are not C^2 at 0, for all but finitely many degrees in (1 + alpha,
min{2, a0 + 1 - (A - 1)(1 + alpha)}) (3.25(ii)), and for intervals of degrees in C^{m,alpha} when m + alpha < s_sup
(sharpness in the scope of 3.38). This is consistent with the observation that discretizations which do not impose
smoothness at the origin have non-smooth discrete solutions (4.2) and degenerate forced sheets (4.3(d), 4.6); it does
not by itself show that the nonlinear problem has non-smooth solution families. Numerically, along forced sheet 1, in
the parameter range where it is well conditioned, the concentrated-forcing continuation shows a scale-free cubic
coefficient growing in magnitude (4.5); neither convergence of these states nor the regularity of a limit is proved,
and a smooth exact profile, if one exists, has not been reached by the continuations performed. The formal reduction
of Section 7, item 6, is not a result.

## 7. Next steps (prioritized)

Priority (a judgement of the prospect of deciding the question for the primary class, not a result; the items keep
their numbers for reference): items 1, 7, 4, 2, 6 and 5, in this order. Item 1 searches the primary class directly;
item 7 has concrete analytic and numerical tests (3.72-3.80), with a bound on |a0| conditional on the nonexistence and
common-bound hypotheses of 3.72(e), and continuation to finite slopes still to be investigated if a solution of the
hydrostatic problem is found; item 4 concerns the hypotheses that would turn the conditional and subclass results into
statements on all profiles; item 2 requires a justified nonlinear expansion, and item 6 requires control of inner
layers beyond the conditional exclusion of the slow regime in 3.49(d); item 5 concerns the finite-regularity class and
cannot by itself decide the primary question. Items 3 and 8 are validation steps that apply, and take priority, as
soon as a forced root or a candidate appears.

1. Unforced discretizations that are smooth at the origin by construction (4.7). With the radial map rebuilt from the
   current c_l at every step (4.7(a)) the releases drift toward c_l = 1 or stop at the solver bound, with sampled
   relative far-field defects of order 1e-5 to 1e-2, or stall above 1 (for example near c_l = 1.0816, with sampled
   |R|/N_f around 2e-6 on the reported grids, 4.7(a)); the first task is to decide whether the residual tends to zero
   only as c_l -> 1 or at some c_l > 1, with a0/D tracked along the drift; an approach to the degenerate endpoint
   rho = a y, U = 0 (outside the class) is one possibility, but zero, non-affine or noncompact limiting behaviour is
   not excluded until a compactness or classification result excludes it (3.37(iv)). Earlier attempts collapsed to the
   spurious a0 = 0 state or stalled with the far-field exponent fixed at its starting value (4.7(a)). Next steps: a
   deflation of the a0 = 0 branch that keeps the full centre relation of 3.2-3.3, wider free-c_l searches with
   continuation in c_l (a nonzero gauge value already fixes a scaling slice, Section 5), a trust-region
   (Levenberg-Marquardt) solver in place of the Gauss-Newton steps with backtracking of 4.7, and, at fixed c_l, the
   cap diagnostics of 4.7 (sampled sigma - D, |grad rho|/|a0| - 1 and the sign of y H near 0) followed under
   refinement, since they bear on 3.46-3.47, 3.51 and 3.53. Report absolute residuals and the derivative residual
   eta_3 of 3.40 together with the relative ones (3.41). Far-field fits must allow the lower-order and logarithmic
   terms of 3.68: a trace proportional to sin th at c_l = 3 or 5/2 forces logarithms (3.69), while for other traces
   the coefficient that forces the first logarithm can vanish (3.71(c)) and depends on arbitrarily high modes
   (3.71(a)), so a value computed from a truncated trace needs a tail bound in the norm of 3.71(b). Diagnostic (not
   decisive): the decay of max |R|/N_f and the stability of (c_l, a0) as the basis grows (spectral decay with stable
   c_l would point to a smooth profile; algebraic decay or c_l drift would be consistent with non-smooth limits but is
   not evidence that a non-smooth nonlinear family exists; algebraic decay can also be produced by the
   compactification of the radial variable). Before conditioning studies, resolve the mechanism of the difference
   between the canonical evaluation and the evaluation using the interpolated stream in 4.7(c), and test exterior
   closure (4.8). Then measure conditioning between Gram matrices of norms above the threshold of 3.17 after
   projecting off the scaling direction, and test nondegeneracy (dimension of the near-kernel modulo scaling), which
   is the hypothesis of the conditional uniqueness statement of 3.27; a discrete near-kernel is meaningful only in
   specified norms and for a discretization that approximates the operator on its graph domain. A time-dependent route
   (proposal of the main analysis; the change of variables and the centre equations below were checked by the checker;
   runs of this route are reported in 4.9): with varrho(t, Z) = A(tau) rho(tau, Z/L(tau)), dtau/dt = A/L,
   c_w = -A_tau/A and c_x = -L_tau/L, the IPM equation becomes rho_tau = c_w rho - (c_x X + U) . grad rho, whose
   steady states with c_w > 0 and c_x/c_w > 1 give profiles rho/c_w with c_l = c_x/c_w (the setting requires c_l > 1).
   Keeping rho_y(0) = 1 fixes c_w = c_x + psi_xy(0); a steady state then has slope a0 = 1/c_w > 0, so this is a
   positive-slope search (rho_y(0) = -1 gives the negative slopes). One more scalar condition fixes the scaling:
   either c_x = C c_w with C fixed, which prescribes c_l = C, so that a steady state exists only if a profile with
   c_l = C does (a search at a prescribed exponent), or a fixed cubic coefficient e != 0 of rho(0, y), a gauge only
   where that coefficient does not vanish: with rho = y + b x^2 y + e y^3 + ... and psi = c x y + d x^3
   y + f x y^3 + ..., the centre equation is e_tau = -2 c_w e - f, so c_w = -f/(2e) (nothing guarantees c_w > 0 along
   the way). The physical time is finite if and only if int_0^inf exp(-int_0^s (c_x - c_w)) ds < inf; c_x > c_w at
   every time does not suffice (c_w = 1, c_x = 1 + 1/(1 + tau) gives infinite time). A radial map rebuilt during the
   run must include its chain-rule term. A trajectory converging to a steady state would give a candidate for the
   tests above; a run that does not converge is not evidence of nonexistence.
2. Along the computed families of non-smooth discrete states and of forced states in c_l (4.2, 4.5), extract the coefficient of the leading non-smooth origin
   term as a function of c_l and look for sign changes; smoother states could occur at isolated c_l where it vanishes
   (a heuristic, not a result). This requires first a correct description of the admissible singular terms: the mode
   statements of 3.25(ii) and 3.38 concern the linearization with coefficients frozen at the source of an unforced
   profile, their use for a nonlinear profile needs the expansion and termwise-inverse hypotheses of 3.38, and for
   forced states of finite width the origin matrix and the thresholds must be corrected as in 3.20.
3. For every root of a forced formulation: refinement invariance of (mu, a0, root), the scaling-robustness test of
   Section 5 (iii), and independent residual tables. A converged fifth-order difference quotient near the source is a
   diagnostic only (it can separate a large cubic jet from a fractional term of low order, but it cannot certify C^inf;
   for example y r^{9/2} passes it).
4. Analysis: decide (H-dyn), equivalently the strict sign condition of 3.22, for exact profiles. By 3.30 it suffices
   to show rho_y(x, 0) != 0 for all x, that is, to exclude a first axis zero of W_1(x, 0), which would be a saddle
   with d_x W_1 = -A/(m - 1) or a degenerate zero where rho is flat; equivalently (3.30(vii)) to show that Theta0 has
   no zero in (0, pi). An exact profile violating (H-dyn) would have a zero q of W with grad rho(q) = 0 and an
   escaping nodal trajectory in y > 0 along which grad rho = 0, hence a multiple or flat zero of Theta0 (3.30,
   3.34(b), (e)); for odd m it would change sign in y > 0. So it would suffice to show that interior zeros of Theta0
   are simple, or to exclude both the saddle resonances and the flat-zero alternative of 3.34(f) (conditional
   exclusions in 3.39). Numerically, the minimum of |Theta0| + |Theta0'| over [delta, pi - delta] (small delta > 0;
   near the endpoints Theta0 vanishes by parity) is the relevant diagnostic (it cannot certify the absence of a double
   zero). Decide the kernel hypothesis of 3.27 (for a candidate: the near-kernel dimension modulo scaling in the space
   of 3.28). Sign of a0 and the low-slope regime a0 <= A - 1 (where int rho_3 s^{-2} <= -a0/4 is forced; the sharpness
   statement 3.38 does not cover a0 <= A - 1; conditional low-slope statements are in 3.48); a rigorous version of the
   concentrated-forcing limit. Upper bounds on sup |grad rho| or sup |DU| for exact profiles, in terms of c_l, a0 and
   Theta0. Any upper bound below the energy lower bound of 3.35 on some range of parameters would be a partial
   nonexistence theorem. The higher-order and weighted forms examined so far (3.36) give no unconditional
   contradiction, and any such upper bound must use the equation (3.36, remarks: smooth non-profiles with the same
   origin and far-field data have arbitrarily large gradients). Proving the strain cap sigma <= c_l - 1 of 3.36(iii)
   in some range, or the remainder estimate that would give sigma >= c_l, would each give a partial result: by 3.46
   and 3.47 a capped profile has a0 >= (n - 1)(2 c_l - 1) >= 4 c_l - 2, where n >= 3 is the degree of the first
   nonzero homogeneous part of h = rho - a0 y, so an upper bound a0 < 4 c_l - 2 for capped profiles would exclude the
   capped subclass; the cap alone does not bound a0 (3.50(a)). Such an upper bound must be global: the endpoint
   a0 = 2(2 c_l - 1) is realized, with the cap, by exact local solutions, and every a0 > 4(c_l - 1) by capped
   canonical pairs exact on an arbitrarily large disc (3.50(c), (d)). With the one-sided sign rho/(a0 y) <= 1 in place
   of the cap, h is again not flat (3.47(iv)), and the jet bounds of 3.51 give a0 >= 2 (2 c_l - 1) when 1 < c_l <= 5;
   for c_l > 5 the sign-compatible leading jets allow a0 < 0, so a global argument is needed there. With q_th >= 0 in
   addition the one-sided sign excludes every profile (3.53). So for 1 < c_l <= 5 an upper bound a0 < 2 (2 c_l - 1)
   under the one-sided sign alone would exclude that subclass; by 3.50(a) such a bound must use transport globally. By
   3.54 it would suffice to show N(q) <= pi/(16 A) under q <= 1; the non-profiles of 3.54(c) satisfy this bound, so
   the exclusion in 3.54(a) uses transport essentially. The first-moment identity 3.56 is an explicit necessary
   condition at the first degree; it can sharpen the inequalities listed in 3.51(c) but is implied by the full leading
   equations together with the sign, and it does not bound a0 from above. The full family of first-sine-projection
   moment identities over all admissible weights is equivalent to the vanishing of the first sine projection R_1 of
   the residual, and adding it to the one-sided sign, the centre normalization and (T1) strictly restricts the class
   they define (3.57); it excludes the radial densities y f(r) but gives no upper bound on a0; whether a0 is bounded
   among exact profiles of the primary class is open. Under the one-sided sign, R_1 = 0 alone gives a0 >= 2 (2
   c_l - 1) when a0 > 0 and 1 < c_l <= 5, unless h is flat, and the flat case violates the strain cap (3.59(i), (ii));
   for densities with the modes 1 and 3 only, R_1 = R_3 = 0 bound a0 from above (3.59(iv)), while R_1 = 0 with the
   one-sided sign, the centre normalization and the growth bound does not, even for these two modes (3.61). If higher
   modes are allowed outside a disc, R_1 = R_3 = 0 on the disc with q < 1 off 0 do not bound a0 (3.63), nor do
   R_1 = ... = R_{2N-1} = 0 for any N >= 2, or exact transport, on the disc (3.65); whether the two projections at
   every radius bound a0 for general angular content is open (by 3.63 an argument for it must be global: the moment of
   the fifth density mode outside the disc enters the stream inside it as a harmonic term, the free datum H of A.3.63,
   which has to be controlled through the projections at all radii and the conditions at infinity), and the radial
   family of 3.58(ii) shows that R_1 = 0 with the one-sided sign and the strain cap does not force transport outside
   the smooth class. Without any sign condition, no exact profile has q = rho/(a0 y) constant on the ellipses alpha
   x^2 + beta y^2 = const (3.60), none has finite Cartesian separation rank on the upper half-plane, also outside a
   disk and in linear coordinates (3.62), none satisfies P(d) rho = 0 outside a compact set for a nonzero linear
   differential operator P(d) with constant coefficients (3.64), none has finitely many angular modes outside a disc
   (3.66), and for every exact profile the number of nonzero angular modes on the circle of radius r tends to
   infinity, with nonzero modes of arbitrarily high frequency at large radii when the trace is a trigonometric
   polynomial (3.67); whether some circle must carry infinitely many modes is open, and the example in A.3.67 shows
   that the asymptotics alone do not decide it.
5. Weak class: the compactness statement 3.25(iii) does not control differentiability or the slope of the limit at the
   origin; under its hypotheses, common C^{1,eta} bounds near 0 for some 0 < eta < 1 together with a_j -> a_* != 0
   would remove the strain-moment defect of 3.25(iv) and make the limit an exact profile of finite regularity (class
   P_{1,beta} of 3.25(i) for some beta > 0) with slope a_*.
6. Small c_l - 1 (formal; not a result of this report). Put D = c_l - 1, s = D log r, and assume rho = r[D h(s) sin
   th + D^2 sum_{j = 3, 5, ...} h_j(s) sin j th + ...] with slow-derivative bounds. The canonical inverse and
   transport then give, formally, h' = -h F and F' = h F/4 - h_3, where F = 1 - h/4 + int_s^inf h_3 (the local linear
   strain is D (F - 1)), together with equations for h_3, h_5, ..., which are not stated here. The unforced boundary
   conditions are h(-inf) = a0/D, F(-inf) = 0, h(+inf) = 0, F(+inf) = 1. Since s = D log r, a solution that approaches
   its values at s = -inf at the rate e^{lambda s} corresponds to an origin term r^{1 + lambda D}, which is not smooth
   when 0 < lambda D < 2; so, if these rates are of order one, a smooth profile with a0 = O(D) would have to leave
   this formal regime, for example through an inner layer at r = O(1). The energy bound of 3.35 makes part of this
   rigorous: an exact profile has sup |grad rho| + sup |DU| >= (2 c_l - 1)/C_*, so the slow regime cannot hold with
   uniformly O(D) gradients; under the explicit uniform bounds of 3.49(d) on h, H_j and their slow derivatives the
   gradients are O(D), so no exact family has that representation (3.49(d)). A rigorous version without them (an
   analysis of inner layers) would give a partial statement for c_l near 1 and small slope.
7. Large slopes (3.72-3.80). Decide whether the hydrostatic problem (3) of 3.72 has C^2 solutions with the bounds of
   3.72(d) for some c_lim > 1, and whether exact profiles with large slopes obey such bounds uniformly after the
   rescaling of 3.72(a). On each fixed compact range of c_l, nonexistence for (3) (for negative slopes, for the signed
   problem of 3.72(e)) together with common bounds and common local bounds on third derivatives would bound |a0|
   (3.72(e)); a solution of (3) would be a starting point for continuation to finite slopes in the parameter
   eps = 1/|a0|, in which the inverse is a singular perturbation (3.72(c)). By 3.73 the axis data are an
   infinite-dimensional family for each c, so the axis does not select c_lim, and the calculation of 3.73(c) gives no
   justification for constructing solutions by continuation in xi from the axis; it does not exclude such a
   construction. By 3.74 every solution has a continuous leading far-field trace, a regular expansion at c_lim = 1 is
   impossible under the hypotheses of 3.74(c), and, formally, a far-field expansion with coefficients C^1 near the
   vertical axis requires the finite part C_p(Theta) of 3.74(d) to vanish; if approximate solutions g_n with
   c_n -> c > 1 and d_y g_n(0) = 1 satisfy the three bounds with common constants and common local bounds on third
   derivatives and have residuals tending to zero on compact sets, a subsequence converges in C^2 on compact sets to a
   solution of the hydrostatic problem (3.74(e)), so establishing all these hypotheses for computed approximations
   would give a C^2 solution of the hydrostatic problem (not a profile of the class); whether c_lim is selected
   remains open. By 3.75 a solution that is real analytic near the bottom is determined there by its bottom slope k,
   so for such solutions the question is which k admit continuation to {y >= 0} with the bounds and h -> 0 as
   y -> inf; for solutions with g_y > 0 on {y >= 0} the representation (2) of 3.75 gives Z in terms of H, and a
   fixed-point formulation built on it has not been analysed. For 1 < c_lim < 2 the first two far-field compatibility
   conditions hold together for some positive monotone traces (3.76); the conditions at higher degrees have not been
   examined. By 3.77, C_p(Theta) = 0 for all c > 1, m_0 = C_d^- = 0 for c > 2 and B = 0, m_0 = C_0(f_0) for c = 2 (B
   and f_0 as in 3.77(d)) are necessary for solutions with far-field expansions of the kinds stated there, and
   g(xi, y) = G(y) + M(xi) y^{p - 1} + o(y^{p - 1}) with M(xi) != 0 is impossible in the class; whether solutions have
   such expansions, or angular layers of shrinking width near the vertical axis, is not decided; by 3.78 (formal) the
   leading inner problem of a near-axis layer of physical width y^{(p + 1)/2} has exactly one solution with the
   required behaviour at the axis and at infinity for every value of C_p(Theta), so it imposes no condition
   C_p(Theta) = 0, and it is not decided whether the higher inner orders (in which a coefficient vanishes for
   p = sqrt(5) - 2 and for p = (sqrt(17) - 3)/4), the nonlocal matching of the outer terms or the matching with the
   core impose C_p(Theta) = 0. For the signed problem of the negative slopes, 3.79 (a formal derivation, with a proved
   statement on the inner equations) gives C_p(Theta) = 0 at leading order for a near-axis layer of this width that is
   even and C^1 at the axis; layers of other widths and nonlinear inner balances are not excluded. As g solves the
   signed problem if and only if -g solves (3) of 3.72 with g_y(0) = -1, the first two termwise far-field conditions
   of the signed problem for 1 < c < 2 are again C_p(Theta) = 0 and C_d(f_d) = 0 of 3.76, and some positive monotone
   traces satisfy both (3.76(b), 3.79(d)); these are conditions on the trace, not an obstruction. For the computed
   states of 4.7(c), 2 A eps is near 1/2. The first least-squares trial states of the hydrostatic problem at c = 2 and
   3 end in Gauss-Newton stalls or at iteration caps without established convergence under refinement (at c = 2 the
   between-node maxima of |R_h|/N_f of the main computation in 1 <= r < 100 and in 100 <= r <= r_max decrease from
   96 x 24 through the continued 128 x 32 state and 160 x 40 to 192 x 48; from 192 x 48 to 224 x 56 the first of these
   maxima rises; the differences of states of successive sizes are not monotone in the size up to 224 x 56; the cubic
   coefficients, the centre defect and C_p have not settled; and at a far node of the 96 x 24 state near the xi-axis
   the checker's reconstruction of the solver's quadrature of the inverse differs from a refined one by order one in
   the velocity; angularly oversampled solves with a refined quadrature give states at the scaled distance 0.22 from
   the state of the standard quadrature at 128 x 32, with centre defects that decrease in magnitude over four sizes
   and cubic coefficients that have not settled; 4.10); exact solutions of the axis equation are excluded within the
   class of polynomial axis data of 3.80 except in the cases left undecided there (half-integer exponents P >= 27/2
   with a special root structure), so an exact solution, if one exists, has axis data (the axis density and d/dy
   V_2(0, y) together) outside that class or in one of those cases.
8. If a candidate appears: an a-posteriori (Newton-Kantorovich type) certification in the label formulation, which
   needs a computable bound on the inverse of the linearization modulo scaling in the weighted norms.

# Appendix A. Proofs

Standing conventions. Unless stated otherwise rho is an exact profile of the primary class P_inf with exponent gamma:
(c_l X + U) . grad rho = rho with c_l > 1, U the canonical velocity, psi the stream function odd in x and in y, W =
c_l X + U, Phi_t the flow of W and p = 1/c_l. (r, th) are polar coordinates, C denotes constants depending on the
profile, hat f(xi) = int f(X) e^{-i X . xi} dX, so that ||f||_2^2 = (2pi)^{-2} ||hat f||_2^2 and the inverse
transform carries the factor (2pi)^{-2}, and "(condensed)" marks a routine step written in compressed form. A.3.k
proves result 3.k, and "(outline)" marks an argument that is not a complete proof; the missing step is named there.
Section 3.31 has no appendix entries.

## A.3.1 Canonical inverse

Hypotheses: rho in P_inf; exactness is not used. (i) If U and U' are admissible, D = U - U' has div D = curl D = 0, so
Lap D1 = d_x div D - d_y curl D = 0 and Lap D2 = d_y div D + d_x curl D = 0. The gradient estimate |grad D_i(X)| <=
(2/R) sup_{B(X,R)} |D_i| = o(1) as R -> inf makes D constant, and D = 0 because D1 is odd in x and D2 is odd in y. The
strain k_s (-x, y) is excluded by U = o(|X|); a constant added to psi is excluded by the odd-odd normalization. (ii)
With G0 = -(1/2pi) log|Z| and g = d_x G0 = -(1/2pi) z1/|Z|^2, K = (-d_y g, d_x g) has div K = 0 and curl K = Lap g = 0
off 0. In distributions d_x d_y G0 = PV z1 z2/(pi |Z|^4) and d_x^2 G0 = PV (z1^2 - z2^2)/(2pi |Z|^4) - delta_0/2, so
for compactly supported rho, psi = G0 * d_x rho gives U1 = K1 * rho and U2 = K2 * rho - rho/2, with multipliers hat U1
= xi1 xi2 hat rho/|xi|^2 and hat U2 = -xi1^2 hat rho/|xi|^2. For growing rho these multipliers do not fix the action
at xi = 0, so the disk-truncated formula is the definition and the canonical law is verified directly. Convergence at
fixed X: near Y = X the principal value converges (K has zero circular mean, rho is Lipschitz); the bounded middle
region converges absolutely; on |Y| > 2|X| + 2 one may replace K(X - Y) by K(X - Y) - K(-Y), because K(-Y) rho(Y) is
odd under Y -> -Y and integrates to 0 over centred annuli, and |K(X - Y) - K(-Y)| <= C |X| |Y|^{-3} bounds the tail by
C |X| int_{2|X|}^inf s^{gamma-2} ds = C |X|^gamma. For a radial cutoff zeta = 1 on B(0, 2 R0), on B(0, R0) the part
from zeta rho is a classical potential (div = 0, curl = -d_x (zeta rho)) and the part from (1 - zeta) rho is smooth
with div = curl = 0. The parities follow from the symmetric disks (K1 is odd in each variable, K2 is even in each),
smoothness from Lap U1 = d_y d_x rho and Lap U2 = -d_x^2 rho, and (i) identifies the formula with the canonical
velocity. (iii) At |X| = r >= 1 the regions |Y - X| < r/2 (zero mean and |rho(Y) - rho(X)| <= C r^{gamma-1} |Y - X|),
{|Y| < 2r, |Y - X| >= r/2} and |Y| > 2r contribute C r^gamma, C r^{-2} r^gamma r^2 and C r^gamma, and |rho|/2 <= C
r^gamma.
(iv) The stream function (U = (-psi_y, psi_x), odd in x and in y) satisfies -Lap psi = d_x rho and |psi| <= C (1 +
r)^{1+gamma}. From d_x = cos th d_r - r^{-1} sin th d_th, the modes satisfy -(psi_n'' + psi_n'/r - 4n^2 psi_n/r^2) =
f_n with

    f_n = (1/2) (rho_{2n-1}' - (2n-1) rho_{2n-1}/r + rho_{2n+1}' + (2n+1) rho_{2n+1}/r).

The formula of 3.1(iv) is a solution, bounded at 0 and O(r^{1+gamma}) at infinity since |f_n| <= C r^{gamma-1}; the
difference a r^{2n} + b r^{-2n} has b = 0 by boundedness at 0 and a = 0 since 1 + gamma < 2n. Integration by parts (m
= 2n) gives the derivative-free form

    psi_n = (1/2) [ r^m int_r^inf s^{-m} rho_{m+1} ds - r^{-m} int_0^r s^m rho_{m-1} ds ].

The manufactured pair of 3.1 satisfies -Lap psi = d_x rho (exact symbolic check, accompanying artifacts); it and the
quadrature comparison test an implementation of (ii) and are not part of the proof.

## A.3.2 Strain identity and origin relation

The identity holds for every rho in P_inf. No quadratic monomial is even in x and odd in y, and no cubic monomial is
odd in both variables, so rho = a0 y + O(r^3), psi = c x y + O(r^4), psi_1 = (c/2) r^2 + O(r^4) and f_1 = O(r^2). In
3.1(iv) with n = 1 the first term is O(r^4) and the second is (r^2/4)(int_0^inf s^{-1} f_1 + O(r^2)), so c = (1/2)
int_0^inf s^{-1} f_1 ds. By the formula for f_1, s^{-1} f_1 = (1/2)(rho_1/s)' + (1/2) s^{-4} (s^3 rho_3)', and
int_0^inf s^{-4} (s^3 rho_3)' ds = [rho_3/s]_0^inf + 4 int_0^inf rho_3 s^{-2} ds. Since rho_1/s -> a0 at 0, rho_3 =
O(s^3) at 0 and rho_1, rho_3 = O(s^gamma) at infinity, c = (1/2)(-a0/2 + 2 int rho_3 s^{-2}) = -a0/4 + int_0^inf rho_3
s^{-2} ds. Checks: y e^{-r^2} has rho_1 = r e^{-r^2}, rho_3 = 0 and c = -1/4; (3x^2 y - y^3) e^{-r^2} = r^3 e^{-r^2}
sin 3th has a0 = 0 and c = int_0^inf r e^{-r^2} dr = 1/2. Origin relation (exact profile): U = (-c x, c y) + O(r^3),
so W = ((c_l - c) x, (c_l + c) y) + O(r^3) and the linear part of W . grad rho - rho is ((c_l + c) a0 - a0) y. Hence
c_l + c = 1, c = 1 - c_l < 0 and DW(0) = diag(A, 1).

## A.3.3 Cubic Taylor relations

With rho = a0 y + b x^2 y + e y^3 + O(r^5), psi = c x y + q1 x^3 y + q2 x y^3 + O(r^6), c_l - c = A and c_l + c = 1,
W1 = A x - q1 x^3 - 3 q2 x y^2 + O(r^5) and W2 = y + 3 q1 x^2 y + q2 y^3 + O(r^5). The cubic part of W . grad rho -
rho is (2Ab + 3 a0 q1) x^2 y + (2e + a0 q2) y^3, and the quadratic part of -Lap psi = d_x rho is -6 (q1 + q2) x y = 2b
x y. Hence q1 = -2Ab/(3 a0), q2 = -2e/a0 and q1 + q2 = -b/3, which give 6e = (a0 - 2A) b (T1) and
H_4 = q1 - q2 = (6e - 2Ab)/(3 a0) = (a0 - 4A) b/(3 a0). Global side: cos^3 th sin th = (2 sin 2th + sin 4th)/8 and cos
th sin^3 th = (2 sin 2th - sin 4th)/8, so the r^4 sin 4th coefficient of psi is H_4/8 (c x y contributes only to sin
2th). By 3.1(iv), psi_2 = (1/8)[r^{-4} int_0^r s^5 f_2 + r^4 int_r^inf s^{-3} f_2]. The sin 4th mode of d_x rho starts
at degree 4, so f_2 = O(r^4) at 0, and f_2 = O(r^{gamma-1}) at infinity, so int_0^inf s^{-3} f_2 ds converges
absolutely. In the bracket the first term is O(r^6) and the second is r^4 int_0^inf s^{-3} f_2 + O(r^6), so
psi_2 = (1/8) r^4 int_0^inf s^{-3} f_2 ds + O(r^6). Comparing r^4 coefficients, H_4/8 = (1/8) int_0^inf s^{-3} f_2 ds,
i.e. H_4 = int_0^inf s^{-3} f_2 ds (T2).

## A.3.4 Weighted identity

phi = r^{-3} sin 3th is harmonic on R^2 \ 0 with X . grad phi = -3 phi, so W . grad rho = rho and div W = 2 c_l give
div(rho phi W) = (1 + 2 c_l) rho phi + rho (c_l X . grad phi + U . grad phi) = (1 - c_l) rho phi + rho U . grad phi.
Integrate over eps < |X| < R. The outer flux is at most C R^gamma R^{-3} R R = C R^{gamma-1}. On the inner circle
(outer normal -e_r), rho = a0 r sin th + O(r^3) and W . e_r = r (A cos^2 th + sin^2 th) + O(r^3), so the flux with
normal +e_r tends to a0 int_0^{2pi} sin th sin 3th (A cos^2 th + sin^2 th) dth = a0 pi (A - 1)/4 = a0 pi (c_l - 1)/2,
by sin th sin 3th = (cos 2th - cos 4th)/2 and A cos^2 th + sin^2 th = (A + 1)/2 + ((A - 1)/2) cos 2th. Next, both area
integrals are taken over the annuli. Integrating first in th (circular cancellation), int_{eps<|X|<R} rho phi dX = pi
int_eps^R rho_3 r^{-2} dr; after this cancellation only the radial integral pi int_0^inf rho_3 r^{-2} dr converges
absolutely, since rho_3 = O(r^3) at 0 and rho_3 = O(r^gamma) at infinity with gamma < 1. The area integral of rho phi
itself is not absolutely convergent at 0: rho phi = a0 r^{-2} sin th sin 3th + O(1), and int_{eps<|X|<1} r^{-2} |sin
th sin 3th| dX grows like log(1/eps) when a0 != 0; so int rho phi dX means the circular limit lim_{eps -> 0}
int_{|X|>eps} rho phi dX, which equals pi int_0^inf rho_3 r^{-2} dr. At infinity |rho phi| <= C r^{gamma-3} and |rho
U . grad phi| <= C r^{2 gamma - 4} are integrable on |X| > 1, so R -> inf may be taken in each term for fixed eps.
Then let eps -> 0: the inner flux and the rho phi term converge, hence so does int_{|X|>eps} rho U . grad phi dX, and
the identity holds with this limit. Near 0, U = c (-x, y) + O(r^3), and -x d_x + y d_y = -r cos 2th d_r + sin 2th d_th
maps phi to 3 r^{-3} sin 5th, so rho U . grad phi = 3 a0 c r^{-2} sin th sin 5th + O(1): its circular mean is zero but
it is not absolutely integrable at 0, so the circular truncation is part of the statement. The flux constant and the
sin 5th identity are confirmed by an exact symbolic check (accompanying artifacts).

## A.3.5 Scaling freedom

Let rho_l(X) = l rho(X/l), psi_l = l^2 psi(X/l) and U_l = l U(X/l), l > 0. U_l is divergence free with curl U_l = -d_x
rho_l, has the parities and |U_l| <= C_l (1 + |X|)^gamma, so it is the canonical velocity of rho_l by 3.1(i), and -Lap
psi_l = d_x rho_l. Since grad rho_l(X) = (grad rho)(X/l), (c_l X + U_l) . grad rho_l - rho_l = l [(c_l Y + U(Y)) .
grad rho(Y) - rho(Y)] at Y = X/l: the equation is preserved and R_l(X) = l R(X/l). Every term of N_f and N_v
transforms in the same way, so R/N_f and R/N_v are invariant at corresponding points. Growth and smoothness are
preserved, D^j rho_l = l^{1-j}(D^j rho)(X/l), D^j psi_l = l^{2-j} (D^j psi)(X/l) and ||D^j rho_l||_q = l^{1-j+2/q}
||D^j rho||_q when finite. A Taylor coefficient of rho of degree 2j + 1 is multiplied by l^{-2j}, and a far-field term
K r^s Theta(th) becomes l^{1-s} K r^s Theta(th). Thus a0 and c_l are invariant, and e_sc = d/dl rho_l at l = 1 equals
rho - X . grad rho. Freeness: if rho_l = rho with l != 1, then also rho_{1/l} = rho, so we may take l > 1; then rho(X)
= l^k rho(X/l^k) for every k, the right side tends to grad rho(0) . X = a0 y, and rho = a0 y violates the growth bound
with gamma < 1.

## A.3.6 y-axis lemma and reporting gauge

On x = 0, psi = 0 (odd in x), so W1 = -psi_y = 0 and the equation reads v G' = G. By 3.2, v(0) = 0 and v'(0) = 1;
G'(0) = a0, and v, G are odd. Suppose y* > 0 is the first zero of v. On (0, y*), wherever G != 0, (log |G|)' = 1/v >
0; since |G| > 0 near 0+, |G| is positive and increasing on (0, y*), so |G(y*)| > 0, while v(y*) G'(y*) = 0 = G(y*), a
contradiction. Hence v > 0 on (0, inf), and G and G' = G/v have the sign of a0 there. By 3.1(iii), v = c_l y + U2(0,
y) with |U2| <= C (1 + y)^gamma, so v >= c_l y/2 for large y and 1/v - p/y = -U2/(c_l y v) = O(y^{gamma-2}).
Integrating (log |G|)' = 1/v from 1 gives G(y) = G(1) y^p exp(int_1^y (1/v - p/s) ds) = K y^p (1 + O(y^{gamma-1})),
with K as displayed in 3.6 (the integral converges at infinity), nonzero and of the sign of a0. Since |G(y)| <= C (1 +
y)^gamma, p <= gamma, i.e. c_l >= 1/gamma > 1. Under scaling G_l(y) = l G(y/l), so K_l = l^{1-p} K. As K/a0 > 0 and
c_l/(c_l - 1) = 1/(1 - p), L_K = (K/a0)^{1/(1-p)} is defined, (L_K)_l = l L_K, and l = 1/L_K is the only l with
(L_K)_l = 1.

## A.3.7 Far field

Up to the definition of Theta0 only smoothness, the parities, div W = 2 c_l, |U| <= C (1 + r)^gamma and exact
transport rho(Phi_t X) = e^t rho(X) are used (A.3.12 relies on this). Exact transport enters only through the formula
for r^{-p} rho along trajectories below, which is used again in steps (4), (5) and (7); the Jacobian identity uses
only div W = 2 c_l. Choose R0 >= 1 with V := W . e_r >= c_l r/2 on r >= R0, and put Q := W . e_th = U . e_th.
Trajectories cross circles outward, with dth/dr = Q/(r V) and th(R0, om) = om; let Dt := tau - p log(r/R0) =
int_{R0}^r (1/V - p/s) ds, where tau = int_{R0}^r ds/V is the travel time. Since |1/V - p/s| + |Q/(s V)| <= C
s^{gamma-2}, Dt -> Dt_inf(om) and th -> th_inf(om) uniformly at rate C r^{gamma-1}, and om -> th(r, om) is a
degree-one circle map, so each point with r > R0 lies on exactly one trajectory. Since rho(Phi_t X) = e^t rho(X),
r^{-p} rho(r, th(r, om)) = R0^{-p} e^{Dt} rho(R0, om) -> T_inf(om) := R0^{-p} e^{Dt_inf} rho(R0, om) uniformly, and
|rho| <= C (1 + r)^p. In polar form div W = d_r V + V/r + r^{-1} d_th Q = 2 c_l, so J := d_om th satisfies d_r log J =
d_th(Q/(r V)) = 2 c_l/V - 1/r - d_r log V(r, th(r, om)) along trajectories; with 2 c_l p = 2 this integrates exactly
to

    J(r, om) = R0 V(R0, om) e^{2 c_l tau} / (r V(r, th(r, om))) = r V(R0, om) e^{2 c_l Dt} / (R0 V(r, th(r, om))),

so J -> J_inf = V(R0, om) e^{2 c_l Dt_inf}/(c_l R0) > 0 uniformly. Hence th_inf is a C^1 circle diffeomorphism, Theta0
:= T_inf o th_inf^{-1} is continuous and sup_th |r^{-p} rho(r, th) - Theta0(th)| -> 0. On the y-axis Q = -W1 = 0, so
th(r, pi/2) = pi/2 and Theta0(pi/2) = lim r^{-p} G(r) = K.
Holder bounds, velocity limit and rate (0 < alpha < 1 fixed). (1, condensed) For R >= 1, rho^R(Z) := R^{-gamma}
rho(RZ) has |rho^R| <= C (1 + |Z|)^gamma and |grad rho^R| <= C |Z|^{gamma-1}, and u^R := R^{-gamma} U(R .) is its
kernel velocity. On 1/2 <= |Z| <= 2, u^R is log-Lipschitz uniformly in R: for |Z - Z'| = h < 1/8 and the common
displacement z = Z - Y = Z' - Y', |z| < 2h gives C h (zero mean), 2h <= |z| <= 1/4 gives C h log(1/h), and the regions
|Y| < 1/4 and |Y| > 4 (kernel difference C h |Y|^{-3}), the bounded remainder and the boundary layers give C h. (2)
Hence the angular seminorms on |X| = r satisfy [U . e_r]_alpha + [Q]_alpha <= C r^gamma, and [1/V - p/r]_alpha + [Q/(r
V)]_alpha <= C r^{gamma-2}. (3) By the identity for J, J and 1/J are bounded uniformly in r, so th(r, .) is uniformly
bi-Lipschitz. (4) |Dt(r, om) - Dt(r, om')| <= int_{R0}^r [1/V - p/s]_alpha |th(s, om) - th(s, om')|^alpha ds <=
C |om - om'|^alpha, so T_inf and Theta0 are C^alpha. (5) rho_R(Z) := R^{-p} rho(RZ) is uniformly C^alpha on each
annulus a <= |Z| <= b: angularly by (3) and (4); radially, F := r^{-p} rho along a trajectory has F' = r^{-p} rho
(1/V - p/r) = O(r^{gamma-2}), so |F(R s2) - F(R s1)| and the angle drift are at most C R^{gamma-1} (s2 - s1) <= C
|s2 - s1|. (6) U_R := R^{-p} U(R .) is the kernel velocity of rho_R, and rho_R -> rho_inf := |Z|^p Theta0(arg Z)
locally uniformly; let u_inf be the kernel velocity of rho_inf (A.3.1(ii) needs only the Holder bound, |rho_inf| <= C
|Z|^p and oddness). On 1/2 <= |Z| <= 2 split the kernel integral of rho_R - rho_inf into |Y - Z| < delta (C
delta^alpha by the zero mean), |Y| < delta' (C delta'^2), |Y| > M with the subtracted kernel (C M^{p-1}) and the rest
(which tends to 0). So U_R -> u_inf there, u_inf is homogeneous of degree p, and U = O(r^p). (7) The setup bounds then
improve to C s^{p-2}, so |Dt - Dt_inf| + |th - th_inf| <= C r^{p-1}, and with th = th(r, om), |r^{-p} rho(r, th) -
Theta0(th)| <= C |e^{Dt} - e^{Dt_inf}| + |Theta0(th_inf(om)) - Theta0(th)| <= C r^{p-1} + C r^{-alpha(1-p)}. Since p
<= gamma (A.3.6), U = O(r^p) improves the a priori exponent only if p < gamma, and the exponent p is attained only if
u_inf != 0. Differentiability of Theta0, DU -> 0 and a second asymptotic term are not obtained by this argument; they
follow from 3.23 and 3.32.

## A.3.8 Regularity of early numerical states

The saved states have the form rho = y w(r) kappa(r, th) with w = (1 + r^2/L_g^2)^{(gamma-1)/2} and L_g = 1 for every
state below (the form printed in 3.8), kappa = sum_{k<M} kappa_k(t(r)) cos(2k th), each kappa_k a polynomial of degree
N in t in [-1, 1], r = L_g (1 + t)/(1 - t)^q and q = 1/(1 - gamma); so t(0) = -1, t'(0) = 2^q/L_g != 0, and the
angular mean of kappa is kappa_0(t(r)). Lemma: if rho is C^2 at 0, then kappa_k'(-1) = 0 for every k, in particular
d/dr kappa_0(t(r)) = 0 at r = 0. Indeed w = 1 + O(r^2), so along rays rho = r sin th kappa(0, th) + r^2 sin th t'(0)
sum_k kappa_k'(-1) cos(2k th) + O(r^3); for C^2 rho the r^2 coefficient is the quadratic Taylor polynomial on the unit
circle, which vanishes because no quadratic monomial is even in x and odd in y, and the functions sin th cos(2k th)
are linearly independent. (A nonzero mean derivative is the coefficient of a term y r, which is not C^2.)
The Lemma is the proved part of 3.8. What follows is a numerical check: a recorded evaluation whose inputs (the saved
nodal values, among the accompanying artifacts) are not reproduced here, so it is not a self-contained proof.
Numerical check. The interpolant is defined by the saved nodal values at the Radau nodes t_j = -cos(2 pi j/(2N + 1)),
j = 0..N (t_0 = -1), and the angular nodes th_i = (i + 1/2) pi/(2M), i < M. Since sum_{i<M} cos(2k th_i) = 0 for 1 <=
k < 2M (for even k the geometric sum vanishes, for odd k it is purely imaginary), the arithmetic mean of the M nodal
values at t_j equals kappa_0(t_j) exactly; it is formed as an exact rational from the binary64 nodal values. Since
kappa_0 has degree N, it is the interpolant P_N of these N + 1 means, and P_N'(t_0) = sum_{j>=1}
(lam_j/lam_0)(P_N(t_j) - P_N(t_0))/(t_0 - t_j) with lam_j = 1/prod_{i != j}(t_j - t_i). This sum is evaluated in
256-bit ball arithmetic, with the nodes t_j enclosed as balls, and multiplied by 2^q/L_g, where q and L_g are the
stored binary64 values taken exactly: L_g = 1 for all four states, q = 0x1.7c8cdd70946bcp+4 (23.784390868916248...)
for (N, M) = (48, 12) and q = 0x1.7c8cdd70dee55p+4 (23.78439087...) for the other three. The evaluation was made
twice, by the checker and, from the same stored inputs, independently in the main analysis; the balls overlap and all
radii are below 1e-63. With decimal endpoints rounded outward, the enclosures are

    (N, M)      d/dr kappa_0(t(r)) at r = 0                     kappa_0'(-1)
    (48, 12)    [378733.03013903260915, 378733.03013903260916]  [0.026213082986050378844, 0.026213082986050378845]
    (96, 16)    [163912.83752126993653, 163912.83752126993654]  [0.011344827272179273224, 0.011344827272179273225]
    (192, 24)   [178529.74664225329925, 178529.74664225329926]  [0.012356500986931357761, 0.012356500986931357762]
    (256, 32)   [261571.08679002747628, 261571.08679002747629]  [0.018104004810751960225, 0.018104004810751960226]

Every interval excludes 0. If this evaluation is accepted, the Lemma shows that none of these four interpolants is C^2
at 0. Nothing follows for exact solutions, other states or limits.

## A.3.9 Formal jet resonances at the source

Setup. Let rho^(n) and psi^(n+1) be the homogeneous parts (n odd). By 3.2, c_l X + U^(1) = (A x, y), and the degree-n
parts of W . grad rho = rho and -Lap psi = d_x rho are

    (A x d_x + y d_y - 1) rho^(n) + a0 d_x psi^(n+1) = - sum U^(m) . grad rho^(m'),     -Lap psi^(n+1) = d_x rho^(n),

with U^(m) = (-d_y psi^(m+1), d_x psi^(m+1)) and the sum over odd m, m' in [3, n - 2] with m + m' = n + 1 (lower-order
data). The harmonic datum, the coefficient of r^{n+1} sin((n+1) th) in psi^(n+1), equals (1/(2(n+1))) int_0^inf s^{-n}
f_{(n+1)/2} ds by 3.1(iv), because f_{(n+1)/2} = O(r^{n+1}) at 0; for n = 3 this is (T2).
Square system. With n = 2k + 1, h := rho^(n) = sum_{j<=k} h_j x^{2j} y^{n-2j} and chi := psi^(n+1) = sum_{j<=k} g_j
x^{2j+1} y^{n-2j} there are 2k + 2 unknowns, against k + 1 transport equations (monomials x^{2j} y^{n-2j}), k Poisson
equations (x^{2j-1} y^{n-2j}, 1 <= j <= k) and the datum. The Poisson+datum block in g is a constant invertible
matrix: its kernel would be an odd-odd harmonic polynomial of degree n + 1, a multiple of Im z^{n+1}, with zero datum.
By the Schur complement the determinant is a nonzero constant times det M_n, where M_n is the transport matrix in h
after substitution of the zero-datum Poisson solution; it vanishes iff the homogeneous problem has a nonzero solution.
Homogeneous problem. ell_j := 2k + 2j(A - 1) > 0 is the eigenvalue of A x d_x + y d_y - 1 on x^{2j} y^{n-2j}.
Transport gives ell_j h_j + a0 (2j+1) g_j = 0 and Poisson gives -(2j(2j+1) g_j + (2k-2j+3)(2k-2j+2) g_{j-1}) = 2j h_j
(1 <= j <= k); eliminating h_j, (2k-2j+3)(2k-2j+2) g_{j-1} = 2j(2j+1)(a0/ell_j - 1) g_j, so

    g_j = C_{k,j} prod_{i=j+1}^k (a0/ell_i - 1) g_k,     C_{k,j} = (2k+1)!/((2j+1)! (2k-2j+1)!).

The sin((n+1) th) coefficient of cos^{2j+1} th sin^{n-2j} th is 2^{-2k-1} (-1)^{k-j}, so the zero datum reads
2^{-2k-1} g_k P_k(a0) = 0 with P_k(a0) := sum_{j=0}^k C_{k,j} prod_{i=j+1}^k (1 - a0/ell_i), and a nonzero solution
exists iff P_k(a0) = 0 (g_k = 0 forces every g_j and h_j to vanish). Here C_{k,0} = C_{k,k} = 1, C_{k,1} = k(2k+1)/3
and P_k(0) = (2k+2)^{-1} sum_j binom(2k+2, 2j+1) = 2^{2k+1}/(2k+2). For k = 1, 2, 3, P_1 = (4A - a0)/(2A), P_2 =
P5/(24A(A+1)) and P_3 = -P7/(24A(A+2)(2A+1)), with P5 = 3 a0^2 - (38A + 26) a0 + 128A(A + 1) and P7 = (a0 - 8A -
4)(a0^2 - (18A + 30) a0 + 96A^2 + 192A), the three displayed curves.
All degrees. Let k >= 2. If a0 < 0, every term of P_k is positive. If 0 <= a0 <= ell_2, every factor 1 - a0/ell_i with
i >= 2 is >= 0 (ell_i increases with i); the terms j = 0, 1 combine to prod_{i>=2} (1 - a0/ell_i) [1 - a0/ell_1 +
C_{k,1}] >= 0, since a0/ell_1 <= ell_2/ell_1 < 2 and C_{k,1} >= 10/3; the terms 2 <= j < k are >= 0, and the term j =
k equals 1. Hence P_k >= 1 for a0 <= ell_2, and every real resonance at degree n >= 5 has a0 > ell_2 = 4A + n - 5 >=
4A. With n = 3 (a0 = 4A): every resonance has a0 >= 4A, with equality only at n = 3, none has a0 <= 0, and for given
(A, a0) only degrees n < a0 - 4A + 5 can be resonant.
Weaker bound by recurrence (brief). Applying d_x to the homogeneous transport equation and using h_x = -Lap chi gives
(A x d_x + y d_y + A - 1) Lap chi - a0 chi_xx = 0. The operator has eigenvalue ell_j on x^{2j-1} y^{n-2j}, so with z_j
:= (-1)^j g_j

    (ell_j - a0) 2j(2j+1) z_j = ell_j (n-2j+2)(n-2j+1) z_{j-1}   (1 <= j <= k),     sum_j z_j = 0 (zero datum).

If a0 < ell_1 the z_j share one sign, so all vanish; if a0 = ell_1, then z_0 = 0 and z_1, ..., z_k share one sign, so
again all vanish. Then chi = 0, h = h_0 y^n and transport gives (n - 1) h_0 = 0. Hence a0 > ell_1 = n + 2A - 3. For 1
< A <= 3 this yields a0 >= 4A: with w := 4A - a0 >= 0, P5 = 24A(A + 1) + (14A + 26) w + 3 w^2 > 0; the quadratic
factor of P7 equals 40A^2 + 72A + (10A + 30) w + w^2 > 0 and its linear factor vanishes at 8A + 4 > 4A; and n + 2A - 3
>= 4A for n >= 9.
Matrices (a = a0). Rows are the coefficients of x^{2j} y^{n-2j} (j = 0, 1, ...) in the transport defect after
substitution of the zero-datum Poisson solution; columns are h_0, h_1, ... (h_0 y^n does not enter Poisson). Exact
symbolic check (accompanying artifacts):

    M3 = [[2, -a/6], [0, 2A - a/2]],                                                    det M3 = 4A - a,
    M5 = [[4, -13a/160, 3a/80], [0, 2A + 2 - 3a/16, -3a/8], [0, 3a/32, 4A - 13a/16]],    det M5 = P5/4,
    M7 = [[6, -5a/112, a/70, -a/112], [0, 2A + 4 - a/16, -3a/10, 3a/16],
          [0, 5a/48, 4A + 2 - a/2, -5a/16], [0, -a/48, a/10, 6A - 15a/16]],              det M7 = -3 P7/8.

Degree 3: g_1 = q1 and g_0 = q2, so q1 + q2 = -b/3 and q1 - q2 = H_4 give q1 = -b/6 + H_4/2, q2 = -b/6 - H_4/2, and
2Ab + 3 a0 q1 = 0 becomes b (a0 - 4A) = 3 a0 H_4. On a0 = 4A this forces H_4 = 0, and then e = Ab/3 and
q1 = q2 = -b/6. Off the curve |b| = 3 |a0| |H_4|/|a0 - 4A|. Both b (cubic coefficient of rho) and H_4 (quartic
coefficient of psi) scale as l^{-2}, so a statement about large b needs the normalization L_K = 1 and |H_4| bounded
below.

## A.3.10 No exact profile with finite angular support

Suppose rho_k = 0 at every r for all k > N, N odd and rho_N not identically zero, and put m = N + 1. Then f_n = 0 and,
by 3.1(iv), psi_n = 0 for n > m/2, and the derivative-free form gives the top stream mode P := psi_{m/2} = -(1/2)
r^{-m} I with I(r) := int_0^r s^m rho_N(s) ds, so P' = -m P/r - rho_N/2. In polar form U . grad rho = r^{-1} (psi_r
rho_th - psi_th rho_r), and c_l r rho_r - rho has no mode above N, so the sin((2N+1) th) coefficient of the equation
comes only from the two top modes: (1/(2r)) (N P' rho_N - m P rho_N') = 0. Substituting P' gives m I (rho_N' + N
rho_N/r) = N r^m rho_N^2. For J(t) := I(sqrt(2t)), J' = r^N rho_N and J'' = r^{N-1} (rho_N' + N rho_N/r), so m J J'' =
N J'^2. Writing J = +-F^m with F > 0 on a component of {J != 0} gives m^2 F^{2m-1} F'' = 0, so sgn(J) |J|^{1/m} is
affine there. A bounded component (t1, t2) has J(t1) = J(t2) = 0, which forces F = 0, impossible. On an unbounded
component |J| = c (t - t1)^m with c > 0, but |rho_N| <= C (1 + r)^gamma gives |J| <= C (1 + t)^{(N+2+gamma)/2} and
(N + 2 + gamma)/2 < N + 1 = m. Hence J = 0 and rho_N = 0, a contradiction. One cutoff N valid at all radii is assumed;
finite-mode approximations are not addressed.

## A.3.11 Local smooth-angular modes at the source

Let h = r^d Theta(th) with d > 1 non-integer and Theta smooth, even in x and odd in y. h is C^1, homogeneous and
tempered, so the equations hold in distributions on R^2, and FT(x_j d_j f) = -(hat f + xi_j d_{xi_j} hat f).
Uniqueness of chi: two homogeneous inverses of degree d + 1 differ by a function harmonic on R^2 \ 0 and homogeneous
of non-integer degree, i.e. r^{d+1} (c1 cos + c2 sin)((d+1) th), which is not 2pi-periodic unless it vanishes;
existence follows from the unique homogeneous extension of i xi1 hat h/|xi|^2 (degree -d-3, not an integer). On xi !=
0 the equation (A x d_x + y d_y - 1) h + a0 chi_x = 0 becomes (A xi1 d_xi1 + xi2 d_xi2 + A + 2 + a0 w1^2) hat h = 0, w
= xi/|xi|. Smoothness off 0: by Hecke-Bochner FT(r^d e^{ik th}) = (-i)^{|k|} 2^{d+2} pi Gamma((|k| + d +
2)/2)/Gamma((|k| - d)/2) |xi|^{-d-2} e^{ik arg xi}; for non-integer d the constant is nonzero and bounded above and
below by powers of |k|, so h -> hat h is injective and Theta is smooth iff hat h = |xi|^{-d-2} F(arg xi) with F
smooth. Quadrant solution: for xi1, xi2 > 0 write hat h = xi2^{-d-2} f(q), q = xi1/xi2; then (A - 1) q f' = (d - A -
a0 q^2/(1 + q^2)) f, so f = C q^u (1 + q^2)^{-a0/(2B)}, i.e. hat h = C |xi1|^u sgn(xi2) |xi2|^v |xi|^{-a0/B} with u =
(d - A)/B and v = (a0 + 2 - A(d + 1))/B, the same C in every quadrant by parity. If C = 0, hat h is supported at 0 and
h is a polynomial, impossible at non-integer degree. Smoothness across xi1 = 0 (even) and xi2 = 0 (odd) forces u = 2m,
v = 2n + 1 with integers m, n >= 0, i.e. d = A + 2m (A - 1) and a0 = A(d + 1) - 2 + (2n + 1)(A - 1) = (A - 1)(A + 3 +
2mA + 2n); the solution is unique up to C.
Sufficiency. Put s = d + 2m + 2n + 1 (non-integer, s + 2 = a0/B), h = d_x^{2m} d_y^{2n+1} r^s and chi = -d_x^{2m+1}
d_y^{2n+1} r^{s+2}/(s + 2)^2. Since Lap r^{s+2} = (s + 2)^2 r^s, -Lap chi = h_x. FT(r^s) = c(s) |xi|^{-s-2} with c(s)
!= 0 gives hat h = c' xi1^{2m} xi2^{2n+1} |xi|^{-a0/B}, which solves the Fourier equation off 0, so the defect (A x
d_x + y d_y - 1) h + a0 chi_x has transform supported at 0; it is then a polynomial homogeneous of non-integer degree
d, hence zero. For m = n = 0, after division by A + 1, this is h = y r^{A-1}, chi = -x y r^{A-1}/(A + 3), a0 = (A -
1)(A + 3). Both equations are confirmed for (A, m, n) = (3/2, 0, 0) and (5/4, 1, 1) by an exact symbolic check
(accompanying artifacts). References: Hormander, The Analysis of Linear Partial Differential Operators I, Sections 3.2
and 7.1. These are local homogeneous inverses, not canonical inverses of admissible global densities.

## A.3.12 Secondary branch

Hypotheses: an exact profile with the parities, smoothness and growth of P_inf, except that a0 may vanish. Jet: psi =
c x y + O(r^4) (no odd-odd cubic), so v(y) = W2(0, y) = (c_l + c) y + O(y^3) and G = a_k y^k + O(y^{k+2}); the y^k
terms of v G' = G (A.3.6) give k (c_l + c) = 1, so DW(0) = diag(c_l - c, c_l + c) = diag(2 c_l - 1/k, 1/k). Let P_d be
the lowest nonzero homogeneous part of rho. Since W - DW(0) X = O(r^3), the degree-d part of the equation is (DW(0) X)
. grad P_d = P_d, so each monomial x^i y^j of P_d (i even, j odd) has weight (2 c_l - 1/k) i + j/k = 1. For i >= 2 the
weight is at least 4 c_l - 1/k > 3, and for i = 0 it equals 1 only at j = k. Hence P_d = a_k y^k. Far field: if
rho(X0) != 0, then rho(Phi_t X0) = e^t rho(X0) along the global flow (|W| <= C (1 + r)), so the trajectory leaves
every compact set; it then lies on the trajectory th(r, om0) of A.3.7 for some om0, along which rho does not vanish,
so T_inf(om0) != 0 and Theta0 is not identically zero. Since |rho(r, th(r, om0))| ~ |T_inf(om0)| r^p and |rho| <= C
(1 + r)^gamma, p <= gamma. Under scaling Theta0 -> l^{1-p} Theta0 (as K in A.3.6), so S = ||Theta0||_{L^2(S^1)} > 0
scales as l^{1-p}, and l = S^{-1/(1-p)} gives the unique representative with S = 1. The case k = 1 is the primary
class and k >= 3 the secondary class. The jet statement needs a finite-order term of G: for example G = sgn(y)
exp(-1/y^2) solves v G' = G with v = y^3/2, so flat traces are compatible with the axis equation; they are not covered
by the jet statement, while the far-field statement covers them.

## A.3.13 Point symmetries (condensed)

Write F = M rho_x + N rho_y - rho with M = c_l x - psi_y, N = c_l y + psi_x, and E = Lap psi + rho_x. Infinitesimal
symmetries. Let Z = a1 d_x + a2 d_y + a3 d_rho + a4 d_psi + a5 d_cl with coefficients depending on (x, y, rho, psi,
c_l). Prolonging d_x c_l = d_y c_l = 0 gives a5 = a5(c_l). The conditions pr Z(F) = pr Z(E) = 0 on F = E = D_x F = D_y
F = 0 are split over the free jets; every admissible second jet is attained by a local analytic solution
(Cauchy-Kovalevskaya in y where N != 0, with data rho, psi, psi_y on a line), and N = 0 follows by continuity. (a) At
fixed first jet and psi Hessian the density Hessian can be varied by t (N^2, -MN, M^2); its coefficient in pr Z(E) is
(M^2 + N^2)(d_rho a4 - psi_x d_rho a1 - psi_y d_rho a2), so a1, a2, a4 do not depend on rho. (b) The trace-free part
of the psi Hessian is free, which gives d_psi a1 = d_psi a2 = 0 and the Cauchy-Riemann equations d_x a1 = d_y a2, d_y
a1 = -d_x a2. (c) Eliminating rho_y by F = 0 and splitting in psi_x, psi_y, rho_x gives d_x a2 = 0; so on each c_l
leaf a1 = k x + d1, a2 = k y + d2, a4 = n1 psi + b4(x, y) and a3 = (n1 - k) rho + b3(x, y), with constants k, n1, d1,
d2 and Lap b4 + d_x b3 = 0. (d) With T := n1 - 2k, pr Z(F) - (2 n1 - 3k) F is an affine function of (rho_x, rho_y,
psi_x, psi_y), containing T rho, that vanishes on {F = 0}; where rho != 0 this quadric (bilinear part psi_x rho_y -
psi_y rho_x) lies in no affine hyperplane, so b3 = 0, T = 0, d_y b4 = a5 x + c_l d1 and d_x b4 = -a5 y - c_l d2, and
mixed partials give a5 = 0. Hence a3 = k rho and a4 = 2k psi + c_l (d1 y - d2 x) + g, the four generators of 3.13,
with pr Z(F) = k F and pr Z(E) = 0.
Finite transformations. Let an invertible point transformation (x, y, rho, psi, c_l) -> (z1, z2, rho', psi', c_l') map
solutions to solutions. Splitting d_z c_l' = 0 over free first jets gives c_l' = C(c_l), so leaves map to leaves and
the symmetry algebras are conjugate. With Z_S the dilation, Z_x, Z_y the compensated translations and Z_0 = d_psi,
[Z_S, Z_x] = -Z_x, [Z_S, Z_y] = -Z_y, [Z_S, Z_0] = -2 Z_0 and [Z_x, Z_y] = -2 c_l Z_0, so the nilradical n = span(Z_x,
Z_y, Z_0), its derived algebra span(Z_0) and the class Z_S + n (ad Z_S = -I on n/[n, n]) are preserved. Hence Z_0 maps
to k1 Z_0' (k1 != 0), so z and rho' do not depend on psi and psi' = k1 psi + Hs(x, y, rho); n annihilates rho', so
rho' = f(rho), and Z_S -> Z_S' mod n' gives rho f' = f, f = m rho (m != 0); the images of Z_x, Z_y, Z_S give z = B X +
w rho + d with B invertible. The free density Hessian in the transformed Poisson equation gives d_rho Hs = (B^{-1} w)
. (k1 grad psi + grad_X Hs); replacing grad psi by grad psi + t grad rho preserves F, so (B^{-1} w) . grad rho = 0 on
an open set, whence w = 0 and d_rho Hs = 0. The free trace-free psi Hessian forces B^{-1} B^{-T} = s^{-2} I; the
remaining Poisson terms give Lap Hs = 0 and m B^{-1} e1 = k1 s^{-2} e1, so B = diag(a, s), a^2 = s^2 and k1 = m a. In
the transformed transport equation the free first jets give m = s and grad_z^perp Hs = (c_l - c_l') B X - c_l' d; this
field is divergence free, so c_l' = c_l, grad_z^perp Hs = -c_l d and Hs = c_l (d1 z2 - d2 z1) + g0. Conversely F' = s
F and E' = (s/a) E.
Class restriction. Write a = l sa and s = l ss with l > 0 and signs sa, ss. For d = 0 the parities give s rho(z1/a,
z2/s) = rho_l(z) and a s psi(z1/a, z2/s) = psi_l(z), so the reflections act trivially, and g0 = 0 by the odd-odd
normalization. For d != 0 the new velocity is U~(z) = B U(B^{-1}(z - d)) - c_l d; if U and U~ are both odd under X ->
-X, then with D0 := B^{-1} d, U(X + 2 D0) - U(X) = -2 c_l D0 for all X, so |U(2j D0)| >= 2j c_l |D0| - |U(0)|,
contradicting U = o(|X|). The effective action is the positive dilations of A.3.5, which preserve c_l and a0; for B =
I this is the translation identity printed in 3.13.

## A.3.14 Absolutely convergent strain formula and a sign restriction

In polar coordinates x y |X|^{-4} = sin(2th)/(2 r^2) and rho_x = sum_n f_n sin(2n th), so by Fubini (justified below)
(1/pi) int x y |X|^{-4} rho_x dX = (1/pi)(pi/2) int_0^inf f_1(r) dr/r = c (A.3.2), and c = 1 - c_l (3.2). This agrees
with d_x d_y G0 = x y/(pi r^4), which has no point-mass part; the modal route avoids convolving a growing density.
Integrability: rho_x is smooth and odd in x and in y, so rho_x = x y g(X) with g smooth (Hadamard), and the integrand
x^2 y^2 r^{-4} g is bounded near 0; at infinity |rho_x| <= C r^{gamma-1}, so the integrand is O(r^{gamma-3}),
integrable against r dr. The integrand is even in x and in y, so 4 times its integral over the open first quadrant
equals pi c < 0, and rho_x < 0 somewhere there. If a0 > 0, then for fixed y > 0, |rho(x, y)| <= int_0^y |rho_y(x, s)|
ds <= C y (1 + |x|)^{gamma-1} -> 0 as x -> inf while rho(0, y) = G(y) > 0 (A.3.6), so this case already follows from
the decay. If a0 < 0, rho < 0 on y > 0 and |rho| is nonincreasing in x > 0, then rho_x >= 0 in the first quadrant,
which is excluded. Nothing follows for general a0 < 0.

## A.3.15 Characteristic labels on the source basin

Local chart. Since rho_y(0) = a0 != 0, the implicit function theorem solves rho(x, y)/a0 = b near 0 as y = Y(x, b),
with Y smooth, even in x, odd in b and Y_b(0, 0) = 1. Set L_y = rho/a0 and L_x(x, Y(x, b)) := int_0^x Y_b(s, b) ds. In
the coordinates (x, b), d_y L_y = 1/Y_b and d_x L_x|_b = Y_b, so det D(L_x, L_y)/D(x, y) = 1; L_x is odd in x and even
in b, hence even in y, and DL(0) = I because rho = a0 y + O(r^3). Pushed field: the second component of DL W is W .
grad L_y = L_y; since det DL = 1, divergence is preserved, so the first component g1 satisfies d_{L_x} g1 = 2 c_l - 1
= A, i.e. g1 = A L_x + m0(L_y). The reflection x -> -x preserves W and L_y and reverses L_x, so g1 is odd in L_x and
m0 = 0. No non-resonance condition is used, so integer A is not exceptional.
Globalization. In the chart the label flow is (a, b) -> (a e^{At}, b e^t). Fix s0 so that Rs0 = {|a| < s0^A, |b| < s0}
lies in the chart image, and let N0 be its preimage, which is backward invariant. For X in B0, Phi_{-t} X is in N0 for
t >= t(X); set L(X) := diag(e^{At}, e^t) L(Phi_{-t} X), independent of t >= t(X). Then L is smooth on B0, W . grad L_x
= A L_x, W . grad L_y = L_y, L_y = rho/a0 (since rho(X) = e^t rho(Phi_{-t} X)), the parities persist, and det DL(X) =
e^{(A+1) t} det D Phi_{-t}(X) = e^{(A+1) t} e^{-2 c_l t} = 1. Injectivity: L(X) = L(X') gives L(Phi_{-t} X) =
L(Phi_{-t} X') in the chart for large t, so X = X'. Surjectivity: given (a, b), choose t with (a e^{-At}, b e^{-t}) in
Rs0, take its chart preimage X0 and set X = Phi_t X0 (the flow is complete since |W| <= C (1 + r)). So L : B0 -> R^2
is a diffeomorphism with Jacobian 1. Curl equation: from DL W = (A L_x, L_y) and det DL = 1, W = (A L_x d_y L_y - L_y
d_y L_x, -A L_x d_x L_y + L_y d_x L_x); differentiating gives curl W = L_y Lap L_x - A L_x Lap L_y - (A - 1) grad L_x
. grad L_y, and curl W = curl U = -rho_x = -a0 d_x L_y gives the stated equation. It must be read together with det DL
= 1, since div W computed from this formula is (A + 1) det DL.

## A.3.16 Weighted Darcy identity

Inputs: U = O(r^p) and rho = O(r^p) from 3.7. Since curl(-U - rho e_2) = -curl U - rho_x = 0, there is P with grad P =
-U - rho e_2 and P(0) = 0; it is even in x and in y, P = c x^2/2 - (c + a0) y^2/2 + O(r^4) at 0 and P = O(r^{1+p}) at
infinity. On Omega = {eps < r < R} let w = r^{-m}, so grad w = -m r^{-m-2} X, and let "bdy" denote the flux through
the boundary of Omega with outer normal n. Since div U = 0, int w |U|^2 = -bdy(w P U . n) - m int r^{-m-2} P U . X -
int w rho U2. Since W . grad(y rho) = (1 + c_l) y rho + rho U2 and div(w W) = (2 - m) c_l w - m r^{-m-2} U . X, int w
rho U2 = bdy(w y rho W . n) + [(m - 3) c_l - 1] int w y rho + m int r^{-m-2} y rho U . X. Combining,

    int w |U|^2 + [(m - 3) c_l - 1] int w y rho + m int r^{-m-2} (P + y rho)(U . X) = -bdy(w (P U . n + y rho W . n)).

Near 0 all three integrands are O(r^{2-m}) (U = O(r), y rho = O(r^2), P = O(r^2)), integrable iff m < 4; at infinity
they are O(r^{2p-m}), O(r^{1+p-m}) and O(r^{2p-m}), integrable iff m > p + 3 (note p + 3 > 2p + 2). The boundary terms
are O(eps^{4-m}) and O(R^{2p+2-m}) + O(R^{p+3-m}), and both tend to 0 for p + 3 < m < 4. As a check, at m = 4 the
coefficients of the logarithmic divergences at 0 sum to pi a0 (c_l - 1 + c) = 0 (exact symbolic check, accompanying
artifacts). If P(0) = P0 != 0, the extra term m P0 int r^{-m-2} U . X is not absolutely convergent at 0 (U . X =
O(r^2)), but int_0^{2pi} U . X dth is the flux of the divergence-free field U through the circle of radius r, hence 0,
so the term vanishes after circular truncation. No term involving U . X has a known sign.

## A.3.17 Linearization at an exact profile

Energy identity. Let Phi in C_c^inf(R^2) be odd in y and h = -Lap Phi. The field (-Phi_xy, Phi_xx) is compactly
supported and divergence free with curl = d_x Lap Phi = -d_x h, so by the argument of A.3.1(i) (decay in place of
parity) it is U[h], and psi[h] = Phi_x. With V = c_l X + U and div V = 2 c_l: int (V . grad h) Phi = -int h (2 c_l
Phi + V . grad Phi), int Lap Phi (V . grad Phi) = -int grad Phi^T DV grad Phi - int V . grad(|grad Phi|^2/2) and int V
. grad(|grad Phi|^2/2) = -c_l int |grad Phi|^2, which together give int (V . grad h) Phi = -2 c_l int |grad Phi|^2 -
int grad Phi^T sym(DU) grad Phi; next int (-h) Phi = -int |grad Phi|^2; finally U[h] . grad rho = Phi_xx rho_y -
Phi_xy rho_x = d_x(Phi_x rho_y) - d_y(Phi_x rho_x), so int (U[h] . grad rho) Phi = int (rho_x Phi_x Phi_y - rho_y
Phi_x^2). Summing gives -<L0 h, Phi> = int grad Phi^T M grad Phi with the stated M. At 0, sym DU = diag(c_l - 1, 1 -
c_l), rho_y = a0 and rho_x = 0, so M(0) = diag(3 c_l + a0, c_l + 2). Compact support is needed: Phi = y gives h = 0
with infinite right side. Conversely, for Phi = zeta(X) cos(Kx) with zeta in C_c^inf odd in y and supported near 0,
the right side is (K^2/2) int M_11 zeta^2 + o(K^2), so the sign of 3 c_l + a0 is detected. At infinity grad rho =
O(r^{gamma-1}) -> 0 already holds in the class; only DU -> 0 is missing.

Frozen identity. Let h be Schwartz, even in x and odd in y, with hat h supported away from 0; put H = hat h and Vf =
(A xi1, xi2). Then hat(Lf h) = -Vf . grad H - (A + 2 + a0 w1^2) H and Re int |xi|^{2s} (-Vf . grad H) conj(H) = (1/2)
int div(|xi|^{2s} Vf) |H|^2 = int [(A + 1)/2 + s Q] |xi|^{2s} |H|^2 with Q = A w1^2 + w2^2. (Here hat(x f) = i d_{xi1}
hat f and hat(d_x f) = i xi1 hat f, so hat(x d_x h) = -H - xi1 d_{xi1} H, and the nonlocal term has symbol a0 (i
xi1)^2/|xi|^2 = -a0 w1^2.) Hence Re int |xi|^{2s} hat(Lf h) conj(H) dxi = int [s Q - (A + 3)/2 - a0 w1^2] |xi|^{2s}
|H|^2 dxi. Under the standing convention Parseval reads <f, g> = (2pi)^{-2} int hat f conj(hat g) dxi, so Re <|D|^s Lf
h, |D|^s h> is (2pi)^{-2} times this integral and ||h||^2_{dot H^s} = (2pi)^{-2} int |xi|^{2s} |H|^2 dxi; this is the
identity of 3.17, with the same factor (2pi)^{-2} on both sides. With t = w1^2 in [0, 1] its coefficient is s - (A +
3)/2 + t (s (A - 1) - a0), affine in t, with minimum delta = min{s - (A + 3)/2, A s - a0 - (A + 3)/2}.

Necessity (condensed): if delta <= 0, take H = i times a
parity-symmetrized bump in a thin cone around the xi2-axis (t = 0) or the xi1-axis (t = 1), radially in an annulus;
the quotient tends to the endpoint value, so no positive constant works. The condition is therefore s > (A + 3)/2 and
s > ((A + 3)/2 + a0)/A; the max(a0, 0) of 3.17 is redundant, since for a0 < 0 the second bound follows from the first.
At s = 0 with a0 >= 0 the coefficient is <= -(A + 3)/2, so ||Lf h|| >= ((A + 3)/2) ||h||; the threshold concerns this
quadratic form only.

## A.3.18 Integer degrees in the local mode problem

Even d. The Hecke-Bochner constant is nonzero for odd k ((|k| - d)/2 is a half-integer), so off 0 the analysis of
A.3.11 applies: C = 0, or hat h = C |xi1|^{2m} sgn(xi2) |xi2|^{2n+1} |xi|^{-a0/B} on the lattice. If C = 0, h is a
homogeneous polynomial of even degree d, even in x and odd in y, hence 0. On the lattice the function off 0 has degree
-2 - d and its moments against xi1^i xi2^j, i + j = d, vanish because the integrand is odd in xi1 or in xi2, so it has
a homogeneous extension (Hormander, Thm 3.2.4), unique up to a polynomial of degree d with the parities of h,
which is 0. For chi (degree -3 - d) the moments of odd order d + 1 vanish by parity and there is no odd-odd polynomial
of odd degree d + 1, so chi is unique. Sufficiency is as in A.3.11, the defect being a homogeneous polynomial of
degree d with the parities of h, hence 0. Such h is not a polynomial, so, being homogeneous of integer degree, it is
not smooth at 0.
Odd d. The Hecke-Bochner constant now vanishes for odd |k| <= d (those modes are polynomials) and is nonzero for |k| >
d, so off 0 hat h again has the quadrant form and C = 0 unless (u, v) = (2m, 2n + 1). In that case test the identity
<hat h, (E - d) f> = 0 (E = xi . grad, valid for every distribution homogeneous of degree -d - 2) with f = xi2
|xi|^{d-1} q0(|xi|), where q0 in C_c^inf([0, inf)) equals 1 near 0 (f is smooth since d - 1 is even). Since (E - d) f
= xi2 |xi|^d q0'(|xi|) vanishes near 0, 0 = C (int_0^inf q0'(s) ds)(int_0^{2pi} cos^{2m} th sin^{2n+2} th dth) = -C
int_0^{2pi} cos^{2m} th sin^{2n+2} th dth, so C = 0. Hence hat h is supported at 0 and h is a homogeneous polynomial;
i xi1 hat h/|xi|^2 vanishes off 0, so chi is a polynomial, determined by -Lap chi = h_x up to multiples of Im z^{d+1}
(a free harmonic datum). This is the problem of A.3.9 with the datum free: with d = 2k + 1 it has k + 1 transport and
k Poisson equations, 2k + 1 in all, for the 2k + 2 coefficients of (h, chi), so nonzero polynomial pairs exist for
every (A, a0). Once the datum (the coefficient of r^{d+1} sin((d+1) th) in chi) is prescribed, the problem is the
square system of A.3.9 and the fixed-datum analysis of 3.9 applies unchanged: off the resonance curves of 3.9 the pair
is determined linearly by the datum (so it vanishes for zero datum), and on them a nonzero pair with zero datum
exists. The resonances of 3.9 therefore restrict the fixed-datum
problem only; they do not constrain the polynomial pairs of the datum-free problem.
C^3 statement. Hypotheses: rho in P_{3,0} (C^3 with the parities and growth of P_inf), exact, with canonical U. Since
-Lap psi = rho_x is C^2, psi is C^{3,alpha} near 0 for every alpha < 1, so W1 = A x + O(r^{2+alpha}) by parity, and
rho = a0 y + b x^2 y + e y^3 + o(r^3). Solving the equation for W2 = (rho - W1 rho_x)/rho_y gives W2 = y - (2Ab/a0)
x^2 y - (2e/a0) y^3 + o(r^3), and integrating psi_x = W2 - c_l y from x = 0 (psi(0, y) = 0, c = 1 - c_l) gives psi = c
x y + q1 x^3 y + q2 x y^3 + o(r^4) with q1 = -2Ab/(3 a0) and q2 = -2e/a0. Then psi_eps(X) := [psi(eps X) - c eps^2 x
y]/eps^4 -> q1 x^3 y + q2 x y^3 and -Lap psi_eps = eps^{-2} rho_x(eps X) -> 2b x y locally uniformly, so -6(q1 + q2) =
2b in distributions, and (T1) and H_4 = (a0 - 4A) b/(3 a0) follow without differentiating a Peano remainder. The sin
4th mode of rho_x is f_2 = o(r^2). As in A.3.3 (growth removes r^4 at infinity, and psi_2 = O(r^4) removes r^{-4} at
0), psi_2(r)/r^4 = (1/8)[r^{-8} int_0^r s^5 f_2 ds + int_r^inf s^{-3} f_2 ds], where the first term is o(1); since
psi_2/r^4 -> H_4/8, lim_{r -> 0} int_r^inf s^{-3} f_2 ds = H_4. Absolute convergence is not claimed, and the limit is
not a consequence of C^3 regularity alone: near 0, rho = a0 y + r^3 sin 5th/L with L = log(1/r) is C^3, but f_2 = 4
r^2/L + r^2/(2 L^2) and int s^{-3} f_2 diverges like 4 log L, so such a density is not an exact C^3 profile.

## A.3.19 Scaling structure of forced numerical formulations

Scaling. For rho_l(X) = l rho(X/l) with its canonical velocity (A.3.5), R[rho_l](X) = l R[rho](X/l), so R[rho] = mu y
