phi(|X|/eps) implies R[rho_l] = mu y phi(|X|/(l eps)): (rho, mu) at width eps maps to (rho_l, mu) at width l eps,
N(rho_l) = l^sigma N(rho), and l = eps'/eps gives the stated correspondence. For N = K, sigma = 1 - p (A.3.6). (i) If
mu = 0 the width is immaterial; rho*_l with l = (beta/N(rho*))^{1/sigma} (l > 0 iff beta N(rho*) > 0) has N(rho*_l) =
beta, and c_l, a0 and scale-free quantities are invariant (A.3.5).
(ii) Let beta -> (rho(beta), mu(beta)) be continuous on an interval I not containing 0 and parametrically locally
unique. The set Z0 = {beta in I : mu(beta) = 0} is closed in I by continuity. For beta0 in Z0, rho(beta0) is exact
with N(rho(beta0)) = beta0 != 0, and by (i) rho(beta0)_l with l = (beta/beta0)^{1/sigma} solves the problem at beta
with mu = 0. For beta near beta0 both this state (l near 1) and rho(beta) (continuity of the curve) lie in the
uniqueness neighbourhood, so they coincide and mu(beta) = 0. Hence Z0 is open, and Z0 is empty or I. In the example x
(x - (beta - 1)^2) = 0 every solution at fixed beta is isolated, but along the continuous branch x = (beta - 1)^2 the
unknown x (in the role of mu) vanishes only at beta = 1; no neighbourhood of x = 0 contains a unique solution for all
beta near 1, so (ii) does not apply.
(iii) For c_l X . grad rho - rho = mu y phi(|X|/eps), the difference D of two solutions smooth at 0 satisfies c_l X .
grad D = D, so D(tX) = t^p D(X); since D(0) = 0 and D is Lipschitz at 0, t^p |D(X)| <= C t |X| for small t, and D = 0
because p < 1. Existence: for rho = R(r) sin th, (r^{-p} R)' = (mu/c_l) r^{-p} phi(r/eps), which gives the displayed
formula, and with u = r v, rho = (mu/c_l) y int_0^1 v^{-p} Phi(r^2 v^2/eps^2) dv, where phi(t) = Phi(t^2) and Phi is
smooth because phi(|X|) is smooth and radial (Whitney's theorem on even functions). So rho is smooth and a0 = (mu/c_l)
int_0^1 v^{-p} dv = mu/(c_l - 1). For phi(t) = 1 + t the formula gives mu y/(c_l - 1) + mu y r/(eps (2 c_l - 1)),
which is not C^2 at 0 for mu != 0. Existence of a nonlinear small-amplitude branch is not proved.

## A.3.20 Origin structure of forced states

The forced equation is (c_l X + U) . grad rho - rho = mu y phi(|X|/eps) with the canonical U; put Delta := mu/a0. The
Taylor forms of A.3.3 hold (only the parities and the Poisson equation were used there): rho = a0 y + b x^2 y + e
y^3 + O(r^5), psi = c x y + q1 x^3 y + q2 x y^3 + O(r^6), and the degree-2 Poisson relation gives q1 + q2 = -b/3.
Linear order: W = ((c_l - c) x, (c_l + c) y) + O(r^3), so the linear part of the residual is ((c_l + c) a0 - a0) y,
and with phi(0) = 1 it equals mu y. Hence c_l + c = 1 + Delta and c_l - c = A - Delta, DW(0) = diag(A - Delta, 1 +
Delta), a hyperbolic source iff both entries are positive, i.e. -1 < Delta < A. Cubic order: phi(|X|/eps) = 1 - 2
r^2/eps^2 + O(r^4) for phi(t) = (1 + t^2)^{-2}, and with W1 = (A - Delta) x - q1 x^3 - 3 q2 x y^2 + O(r^5), W2 = (1 +
Delta) y + 3 q1 x^2 y + q2 y^3 + O(r^5), the x^2 y and y^3 coefficients give [2 (A - Delta) + (1 + Delta) - 1] b + 3
a0 q1 = (2A - Delta) b + 3 a0 q1 = -2 mu/eps^2 and (2 + 3 Delta) e + a0 q2 = -2 mu/eps^2. With H_4 = q1 - q2, q1 =
-b/6 + H_4/2, so the first relation reads (2A - Delta - a0/2) b + (3/2) a0 H_4 = -2 mu/eps^2; multiplying by -2 gives
b (a0 - 4A + 2 Delta) = 3 a0 H_4 + 4 mu/eps^2 (exact symbolic check, accompanying artifacts). Frozen coefficient: as
in A.3.17 with Vf = ((A - Delta) xi1, (1 + Delta) xi2), whose divergence is still A + 1 = 2 c_l, hat(Lf h) = -Vf .
grad H - (2 c_l + 1 + a0 w1^2) H and Re int |xi|^{2s} (-Vf . grad H) conj(H) = int [c_l + s ((A - Delta)
w1^2 + (1 + Delta) w2^2)] |xi|^{2s} |H|^2, so the coefficient is s [(A - Delta) w1^2 + (1 + Delta)
w2^2] - (1 + c_l) - a0 w1^2, affine in t = w1^2. Its endpoint values s (1 + Delta) - (1 + c_l) (t = 0) and s
(A - Delta) - (1 + c_l) - a0 (t = 1) are positive iff s exceeds the stated maximum when A - Delta > 0 and
1 + Delta > 0, and the concentration argument of A.3.17 shows that the condition is also necessary.

## A.3.21 Flow facts and axis identities

(i) At a zero z of W, rho(z) = W(z) . grad rho(z) = 0; at a local extremum X of rho, grad rho(X) = 0, so rho(X) = W .
grad rho(X) = 0. (ii) If a closed invariant Jordan curve bounded a region Omega (in particular for a periodic orbit),
Omega would be invariant, while |Phi_t Omega| = e^{2 c_l t} |Omega| by det D Phi_t = e^{2 c_l t}; impossible. With R
as in A.3.30(i), W points outward on |X| = r >= R, so a backward trajectory enters D_R and stays there, and a forward
trajectory starting outside D_R has radius growing at least like e^{c_l t/2}. (iii) d/dt rho(Phi_t X) = (W . grad
rho)(Phi_t X) = rho(Phi_t X), so rho(X) = e^t rho(Phi_{-t} X). On B0, backward orbits enter any neighbourhood of the
source, where (eigenvalues A and 1) |Phi_{-t} X| <= C e^{-lam t} for a fixed lam < 1 with 3 lam > 1; since rho = a0
y + O(r^3), e^t [rho - a0 y](Phi_{-t} X) = O(e^{(1 - 3 lam) t}) -> 0, so e^t y(Phi_{-t} X) converges to rho(X)/a0 =:
L_y(X). The half-planes y > 0, y < 0 and the axis are invariant, and near 0, L_y = y (1 + O(r^2)) has the sign of y;
by L_y(X) = e^t L_y(Phi_{-t} X) this holds on B0. (iv) On y = 0, W2 = 0 and rho = 0 (oddness), d_y W1 = 0 (W1 is even
in y) and d_y W2 = 2 c_l - w' (div W = 2 c_l). Differentiating W . grad rho = rho in y at y = 0 gives (2 c_l - w') g +
w g' = g, i.e. w g' = (w' - A) g, equivalently (w/g)' = A/g where g != 0. Since w/g -> 0 at 0 (w = A x + O(x^3), g(0)
= a0), w(x) = A g(x) int_0^x ds/g(s) > 0 on any (0, x] free of zeros of g. At a zero x2 of g of finite order m >= 1,
w(x2) = 0 (otherwise the ODE is nonsingular there and forces g = 0 near x2). Writing g = (x - x2)^m G1 with G1(x2) !=
0 and comparing the lowest-order terms of w (m G1 + (x - x2) G1') = (w' - A)(x - x2) G1 gives w'(x2) m = w'(x2) - A,
so m != 1, m >= 2 and w'(x2) = -A/(m - 1) < 0; DW(x2, 0) = diag(w'(x2), 2 c_l - w'(x2)) (W1 even and W2 odd in y), a
saddle. The last sentence is A.3.22.

## A.3.22 Dynamics and sign

(1) implies (3). Backward orbits are bounded (A.3.21(ii)), and by A.3.30(v) (whose proof uses only (i) of A.3.21 and
the potential) every backward limit point is a zero of W, hence 0; so every backward orbit tends to 0, B0 = R^2, and
rho = a0 L_y with L_y of the sign of y (A.3.21(iii)), which is (2). On the axis w > 0 for x > 0 (w = A x + O(x^3) near
0 and w has no positive zero), so w g' = (w' - A) g is a nonsingular linear equation on every [x', x''] in (0, inf); g
has the sign of a0 near 0, so g/a0 > 0 for all x (g is even). Forward escape: let V be a small sublevel set of the
Lyapunov form of the source (A.3.34(b), with B = diag(A, 1)); W points outward on its boundary, so no forward orbit
enters V from outside, and an orbit starting in V minus {0} leaves V for good. If a forward orbit of X != 0 were
bounded, its omega-limit set would be nonempty, compact and invariant, and the backward orbit of any of its points
tends to 0, so 0 would lie in the omega-limit set, which the previous sentence excludes. So every nonzero forward
orbit is unbounded and, once outside D_R, escapes.
(3) implies (2) trivially. (2) implies (1). A zero of W off the x-axis is a zero of rho with y != 0 (A.3.21(i)),
excluded by (2). On the axis w > 0 near 0+; at a first zero x1 > 0, w'(x1) <= 0 and DW(x1, 0) = diag(w'(x1), 2 c_l -
w'(x1)) with 2 c_l - w'(x1) >= 2 c_l > 1. For 1 < kk < 2 c_l - w'(x1), the strong unstable manifold tangent to e_2
(obtained by contraction in the norm sup_{t<=0} e^{-kk t} |.|; this includes w'(x1) = 0) contains points X with y != 0
and |Phi_t X - (x1, 0)| <= C e^{kk t} for t <= 0. As rho(x1, 0) = 0 and rho is Lipschitz, |rho(X)| = e^{-t} |rho(Phi_t
X)| <= C e^{(kk - 1) t} -> 0 as t -> -inf, so rho(X) = 0 with y != 0, contradicting (2). The weak condition rho a0 y
>= 0 does not exclude such nodal points, so it is not covered.

## A.3.23 Symbol bounds at infinity

The proof has a local theorem for the time-dependent IPM system (a), its application to the self-similar solution (b),
and the angular rate (c). Inputs from the class: U = O(r^p) and rho = O(r^p) (A.3.7, step 6), gamma >= p (A.3.6) and
|grad rho| <= C (1 + r)^{gamma-1}.
(a) Local theorem. Let D be a disk and (varrho, u) smooth on D x (t_*, 0) (smooth up to every closed time interval
ending before 0) with d_t varrho + u . grad varrho = 0, div u = 0, curl u = -d_1 varrho, sup_t (||varrho(t)||_inf +
||u(t)||_inf) < inf and int_{t_*}^0 ||grad varrho(t)||_{L^inf(D)} dt < inf. Then for every disk D' compactly inside D
and every k, all spatial derivatives of order <= k are bounded on D' uniformly as t -> 0. (Only spatial bounds: varrho
= 0, u = (sin(1/t), 0) satisfies the hypotheses without a velocity limit.) Inputs, with q = 4 and disks of radii in a
fixed compact interval: (E1) ||DF||_4 <= C (||div F||_4 + ||curl F||_4) for compactly supported F (Calderon-Zygmund,
Riesz multipliers of order 0), also after further derivatives; (E2) Morrey, [f]_{C^{1/2}} <= C ||Df||_4; (E3)
Gagliardo-Nirenberg, ||D^j f||_{4m/j} <= C ||f||_inf^{1-j/m} (||D^m f||_4 + ||f||_inf)^{j/m}; (E4) interior derivative
bounds for harmonic functions. All estimates are made at t < 0 on smooth functions.
Step 1 (outward coordinates). Centre D at 0 and put lambda = 1 + sqrt(-t), h = -lambda'/lambda > 0, R(Y, t) =
varrho(lambda Y, t), V(Y, t) = u(lambda Y, t), b = V/lambda + h Y and Omega = grad_Y^perp R. Then R_t + b . grad R =
0, div b = 2h, div V = 0, curl V = -Omega_2 and Omega_t + h Omega + b . grad Omega = lambda^{-1} DV Omega (by J M^T
J^{-1} = (tr M) I - M for the quarter turn J). With |V| <= M, b . Y >= lambda^{-1} |Y| (-M + |Y|/(2 sqrt(-t))) > 0 on
|Y| >= r_min for t near 0, so every radial nonincreasing cutoff psi supported there has b . grad psi <= 0. K(t) :=
||Omega(t)||_inf on the outer disk is integrable in t.
Step 2 (div-curl without a gradient norm in the remainder). For a cutoff psi with d = max(1, ||D psi||_inf) let T =
||psi^6 D^2 V||_4, B = ||psi^5 DV||_4, L = ||psi^4 V||_4. By (E1), T <= C ||psi^6 D Omega||_4 + C d B. One integration
by parts in int psi^20 |DV|^4 gives B^4 <= C L T B^2 + C d L B^3, so B <= C (L T)^{1/2} + C d L, and Young's
inequality gives ||psi^6 D^2 V||_4 <= C ||psi^6 D Omega||_4 + C d^2 ||psi^4 V||_4.
Step 3 (energy). F := D Omega satisfies F_t + b . grad F + 2h F = lambda^{-1} [DV F + (Omega . grad) DV - F DV].
Testing with psi^24 |F|^2 F, Z := ||psi^6 F||_4^4 satisfies Z' + 6h Z - int (b . grad psi^24) |F|^4 <= C
||DV||_{L^inf(supp psi)} Z + C K ||psi^6 D^2 V||_4 Z^{3/4}, where 6h = 4 (2h) - div b and the boundary term is >= 0.
Step 2 and Young's inequality (K kept outside) give Z' <= C (||DV||_{L^inf(supp psi)} + K) Z + C K d^8.
Step 4 (logarithmic bound with the radius loss recorded). Take radii r_m increasing to r_* with r_{m+1} - r_m = c
2^{-m}, radial nonincreasing cutoffs psi_m = 1 on B(r_m), supported in B(r_{m+1}), |D psi_m| <= C 2^m, and Z_m :=
||psi_m^6 D Omega||_4^4. Write V as the Biot-Savart field of a fixed cutoff of curl V plus a harmonic remainder; the
first is bounded by C K, the second and its derivative by C (||V||_inf + K) (E4). The derivative of the first is a
mean-zero kernel of degree -2 plus a bounded contact term. On |z| < delta_m (a small multiple of r_{m+2} - r_{m+1})
its density -Omega_2 has Holder seminorm H_m <= C ||D Omega||_{L^4(B(r_{m+2}))} <= C Z_{m+2}^{1/4} (E2). Subtracting
Omega_2(X) on circles centred at the query point X, |z| < eps contributes C H_m eps^{1/2} and eps < |z| < C
contributes C K log(C/eps). With eps = min(delta_m/2, (e + H_m)^{-2}, eps_0) this gives ||DV||_{L^inf(B(r_{m+1}))} <=
C (1 + K) [m + 1 + log(e + Z_{m+2})], with no log K and no L^inf bound for a Riesz transform.
Step 5 (nested inequalities). Insert Step 4 in Step 3 for psi_m and integrate from t0. With Y_m := e + Z_m + d0^{m+1}
(d0 absorbs m + 1 and the cutoff cost 2^{8m}) there are d > 1 and a = C (1 + K) integrable with Y_m(t) <= d^{m+1} +
int_{t0}^t a Y_m log Y_{m+2} ds. If X_m is the right side, beta_m := log X_m satisfies beta_m(t) <= (m + 1) log d +
int_{t0}^t a beta_{m+2} ds. Fix t < 0: smoothness on [t0, t] gives beta_m(s) <= C_t (m + 1) for s <= t, so N
iterations give beta_0(t) <= log d sum_{j<N} (2j + 1) A^j/j! + C_t (2N + 1) A^N/N! with A = int_{t0}^t a. Letting N ->
inf at fixed t gives beta_0(t) <= (1 + 2A) e^A log d, bounded as t -> 0 because A is (the limit in N is taken before t
-> 0). Hence D^2 R is bounded in L^4 on B(r_0), R is uniformly W^{2,4} and C^{1,1/2}, and by (E1) so is V on a smaller
disk.
Step 6 (higher orders). Induction on k >= 2, each time on fresh nested disks inside a disk where the order k - 1
bounds hold (finitely many shrinkings for each k). Differentiate the transport equation k times and test with |D^k
R|^2 D^k R on B(r_m): the boundary flux is >= 0 by Step 1, the dilation term (4k - 2) h is >= 0, and the commutator
sum_{i=1}^k binom(k, i) D^i V D^{k-i+1} R is bounded in L^4 by C_k (1 + ||D^k V||_4 + ||D^k R||_4) by (E3) with m
= k - 1 (the interpolation parameters (i-1)/(k-1) and (k-i)/(k-1) sum to 1 and the reciprocal exponents to 1/4). The
Biot-Savart field of chi_m curl V (chi_m = 1 between r_m and r_{m+1}, derivatives C_j delta_m^{-j}) gives ||D^k
V||_{L^4(B(r_m))} <= C_k ||D^k R||_{L^4(B(r_{m+1}))} + C_k D_k^m, the gap entering only lower-order terms. So E_m
:= 1 + ||D^k R||_{L^4(B(r_m))}^4 satisfies E_m' <= C_k (E_m + E_{m+1} + D_k^{4m}); after an integrating factor, F_m(t)
<= d^{m+1} + C int_{t0}^t F_{m+1} ds, and iteration at fixed t (remainder M_t (C (t - t0))^N/N! -> 0) gives F_m(t) <=
d^{m+1} e^{d C (t - t0)}, uniformly. Sobolev embedding completes (a).
(b) Application. Let tau = -t, alpha = 1/(c_l - 1), beta = c_l alpha, and varrho(t, Z) = alpha tau^alpha rho(Z
tau^{-beta}), u(t, Z) = alpha tau^alpha U(Z tau^{-beta}). With X = Z tau^{-beta}, alpha - beta = -1 and beta/alpha =
c_l, d_t varrho + u . grad varrho = alpha^2 tau^{alpha-1} [c_l X . grad rho + U . grad rho - rho] = 0, curl u = alpha
tau^{alpha-beta} curl U and d_1 varrho = alpha tau^{alpha-beta} rho_x, so (varrho, u) solves IPM. On a disk away from
Z = 0, alpha = beta p and |rho| + |U| <= C (1 + r)^p give |varrho| + |u| <= C, and |grad_Z varrho| <= C tau^{alpha -
beta gamma} = C tau^{-kappa} with kappa = (gamma - p)/(1 - p) in [0, 1), which is integrable. By (a) every D_Z^k
varrho and D_Z^k u is bounded on the annulus 1/2 <= |Z| <= 2 for small tau, and D_X^k rho(RZ) =
alpha^{-1} tau^{-alpha + k beta} D_Z^k varrho with R = tau^{-beta} gives |D^k rho| <= C_k R^{p-k} on |X| ~ R; likewise
for U. Smoothness on compact sets gives the bounds for all X.
(c) Write rho = r^p f(s, th), U = r^p v(s, th), s = log r. Since c_l p = 1, the equation becomes d_s f = -r^{p-1} (p
v_r f + v_th d_th f)/(c_l + r^{p-1} v_r), with denominator >= c_l/2 for large r; since d_th^j f = r^{-p} d_th^j rho
and |d_th^j rho| <= C_j sum_{i<=j} r^i |D^i rho| <= C_j r^p, the angular derivatives of f and v are bounded, so ||d_s
f||_{C^k(S^1)} <= C_k e^{-(1-p) s}. Integrating from s to infinity, f(s, .) converges in every C^k, the limit is
Theta0 (uniform convergence, 3.7), so Theta0 is C^inf and ||r^{-p} rho(r, .) - Theta0||_{C^k} <= C_k r^{p-1}. The
scaled velocities R^{-p} U(R .) converge uniformly on compact annuli (A.3.7, step 6) and are bounded in every C^k
there by (b), so they converge in every C^k. In particular grad rho, DU = O(r^{p-1}). The far-field bound U = O(r^p)
is used in (b) for the boundedness of u; uniform convergence of r^{-p} rho alone would not give it.

## A.3.24 Sign and size of the slope in monotone subclasses

Exact profiles of the primary class; q = rho/(a0 y) = G/a0 (rho = y G) is smooth with the parities, q(0) = 1 and q ->
0 uniformly at infinity (|rho| <= C (1 + r)^gamma and, near the x-axis, q = a0^{-1} int_0^1 rho_y(x, t y) dt with grad
rho -> 0); 3.23 supplies second-derivative bounds where needed. Q1 is the open first quadrant.
(i) By 3.14, c = (1/pi) int x y r^{-4} rho_x dX with rho_x = a0 y q_x; the integrand is even in x and in y, so c/a0 =
(4/pi) int_{Q1} x y^2 r^{-4} q_x dX. If q_x <= 0 on Q1 the right side is <= 0, and it is nonzero because c = 1 - c_l =
-D != 0; so it is negative and a0 = c/(c/a0) > 0.
(ii) V := y^2 X/r^4 = y^2 r^{-4} X has div V = X . grad(y^2 r^{-4}) + 2 y^2 r^{-4} = 0 (degree -2 homogeneity). On
{eps < r < R} intersect Q1, V . n = 0 on both axes (V1 = 0 at x = 0, V2 = 0 at y = 0), and V . e_r = sin^2 th / r, so
int div(q V) = int_0^{pi/2} q(R, th) sin^2 th dth - int_0^{pi/2} q(eps, th) sin^2 th dth -> -pi/4. Hence (4/pi)
int_{Q1} (x y^2 r^{-4} (-q_x) + y^3 r^{-4} (-q_y)) dX = 1, the integrals converging monotonically under both
monotonicity assumptions, i.e. 1 = S + T with S = -c/a0 = D/a0 (by (i)) and T >= 0. T = 0 would give q_y = 0 on Q1
and, letting y -> inf, q = 0, contradicting q(0) = 1; so T > 0, S < 1 and a0 > D. Sharpness: the formula of (i) holds
for any admissible density (3.14), and for q = F(alpha x^2 + beta y^2), q_x = 2 alpha x F', int_0^inf F'(r^2 m) r dr =
-1/(2m) with m = alpha cos^2 th + beta sin^2 th, so c/a0 = -(4 alpha/pi) int_0^{pi/2} cos^2 th sin^2 th/m dth =
-alpha/(sqrt(alpha) + sqrt(beta))^2 (the last integral is pi/(4 (sqrt(alpha) + sqrt(beta))^2)), which tends to -1 as
beta/alpha -> 0.
(iii) Below degree n = 2k + 1, rho^(m) = 0 for 3 <= m < n, and the degree-m transport equation reduces to a0 d_x
psi^(m+1) = 0, so psi^(m+1) = 0 (odd in x). At degree n all lower-order data vanish, so with h_j := a0 t_j (rho^(n) =
a0 y Q_{2k} = sum h_j x^{2j} y^{n-2j}) the transport and Poisson relations of A.3.9 hold with the harmonic datum
unrestricted: ell_j h_j + a0 (2j + 1) g_j = 0 and -(2j(2j+1) g_j + (2k-2j+3)(2k-2j+2) g_{j-1}) = 2j h_j, ell_j = d_j.
Eliminating g gives 2j (a0 - d_j) t_j = [(2k-2j+3)(2k-2j+2)/(2j-1)] d_{j-1} t_{j-1}. Since Q_{2k} is the leading part
of q - 1, q_y <= 0 and q_x <= 0 near 0 in Q1 give 2k t_0 y^{2k-1} = d_y Q_{2k}(0, y) <= 0 and 2 t_1 x y^{2k-2} +
O(x^3) = d_x Q_{2k} <= 0, so t_0, t_1 <= 0. If a0 < d_1, the j = 1 relation has left side >= 0 and right side <= 0
(d_0 = 2k > 0), so t_0 = t_1 = 0, and for j >= 2, a0 - d_j < 0 forces t_j = 0 inductively, contradicting Q_{2k} != 0.
Hence a0 >= d_1 = 2A + 2k - 2 >= 2A = 4 c_l - 2.
Flat germs (global non-profiles). (a) The family q_L of 3.37(iii). By dilation (A.3.5) take L = 1, so q_1 = a y
chi(r) + b r sin 3th eta(r) with b = (a/4 - D)/J. It is smooth, compactly supported and has the parities, so its
canonical velocity is the kernel velocity and the derivative-free form of A.3.1(iv) applies: psi_n = (1/2)[r^m
int_r^inf s^{-m} rho_{m+1} ds - r^{-m} int_0^r s^m rho_{m-1} ds], m = 2n. Here rho_1 = a r chi(r), rho_3 = b r eta(r)
and rho_k = 0 otherwise. For r < 1: n = 1 gives psi_1 = (1/2)[r^2 int_2^3 b s^{-1} eta(s) ds - r^{-2} int_0^r a s^3
ds] = (b J/2 - a/8) r^2 = -(D/2) r^2; n = 2 gives psi_2 = 0 (rho_5 = 0, and rho_3 = 0 on (0, 2)); n >= 3 gives psi_n
= 0. Hence psi = -(D/2) r^2 sin 2th = -D x y, U = (D x, -D y) and W = (A x, y) on B_1, and W . grad q_1 = a y = q_1
there. Being compactly supported, q_1 has no nonzero axis tail, so it is not a profile (3.6, 3.7). (b) A monotone
variant. For a0 > D let F(t) = 1 for t <= 1 and F(t) = exp(-(t - 1) exp(-1/(t - 1))) for t > 1; F is smooth (flat at t
= 1), nonincreasing and F(t) <= e^{2-t} (as e^{-v} >= 1 - v). Put rho = a0 y F(alpha x^2 + y^2) with sqrt(alpha) =
sqrt(D/a0)/(1 - sqrt(D/a0)), so q = F(alpha x^2 + y^2) has q_x <= 0 and q_y <= 0 on Q1, q = 1 near 0 (all Taylor
corrections vanish), and by the sharpness formula of (ii) (beta = 1) c/a0 = -alpha/(sqrt(alpha) + 1)^2 = -D/a0, i.e. c
= -D. Put r_1 = min(1, alpha^{-1/2}), so rho = a0 y on B_{r_1}. For r < r_1 and m = 2n >= 4: rho_{m-1} = 0 on (0, r),
and with Qa := alpha cos^2 th + sin^2 th the substitution u = s sqrt(Qa) gives int_r^inf s^{1-m} F(s^2 Qa) ds =
r^{2-m}/(m - 2) + Qa^{n-1} k_m with k_m a constant. The angular weight of rho_{m+1} is sin th sin((m+1) th) = (cos(m
th) - cos((m+2) th))/2, orthogonal both to constants and to Qa^{n-1}, a trigonometric polynomial of degree 2n - 2 =
m - 2. So psi_n = 0 on B_{r_1} for n >= 2, while psi_1 = (r^2/2)(int_0^inf s^{-2} rho_3 ds - a0/4) = (c/2) r^2 there
by 3.2, since rho_1 = a0 s and rho_3 = 0 on (0, r_1). Hence U = (D x, -D y) on B_{r_1} and W . grad rho = rho there,
while q -> 0 exponentially, so y^{-p} rho(0, y) -> 0, contradicting K != 0 (3.6): rho is not a profile. Both examples
have q = 1 near 0 (so the hypotheses of (iii) near 0 hold but its Taylor polynomial is constant), strain c = -D and
the exact equation near 0, and (b) also satisfies the global monotonicity of (i) and (ii) for every a0 > D; so no
argument that uses only the equation near 0, even together with that monotonicity, extends the bound of (iii) to
flat germs.
(iv) As in A.3.10, rho_3 = (4/pi) int_0^{pi/2} rho sin 3th dth, and sin 3th = sin th (4 cos^2 th - 1), so rho_3/a0 = r
E[q (4 cos^2 th - 1)] for the probability measure (4/pi) sin^2 th dth on [0, pi/2], under which E[cos^2 th] = 1/4;
hence rho_3/a0 = 4 r Cov(q(r, .), cos^2 th). With J := int_0^inf rho_3/(a0 r^2) dr, 3.2 gives -D = c = -a0/4 + a0 J,
i.e. a0 (1/4 - J) = D. If q_th >= 0, q(r, .) and cos^2 th are oppositely monotone, so Cov <= 0, with strict inequality
for some r unless q(r, .) is constant for all r, which (v) excludes; so J < 0, a0 = D/(1/4 - J) and 0 < a0 < 4D. If
q_th <= 0 and q_x <= 0, then a0 > 0 by (i), Cov >= 0 with strict inequality somewhere, J > 0, J < 1/4 and a0 =
D/(1/4 - J) > 4D. Combined with (iii), a0 >= 4 c_l - 2 = 4D + 2 contradicts a0 < 4D.
(v) rho = y f(r) = r f(r) sin th has only the sin th mode, which A.3.10 excludes.
The Gaussian non-profile. For rho = -y (1 + 4x^2) e^{-r^2}/100: 4 x^2 y = r^3 (sin th + sin 3th), so rho_1 = -(r +
r^3) e^{-r^2}/100, rho_3 = -r^3 e^{-r^2}/100, a0 = -1/100 and c = 1/400 - 1/200 = -1/400 (3.2); so c_l = 401/400 gives
c_l + c = 1, D = 1/400, and q = (1 + 4x^2) e^{-r^2} > 0.
Outward flow. With the standing convention, the transforms of e^{-x^2}, x^2 e^{-x^2} and y e^{-y^2} are sqrt(pi)
e^{-xi1^2/4}, sqrt(pi) (1/2 - xi1^2/4) e^{-xi1^2/4} and -i sqrt(pi) (xi2/2) e^{-xi2^2/4}, so hat rho(xi) = (i pi/200)
xi2 (3 - xi1^2) e^{-|xi|^2/4}. Since rho is a Schwartz function, U is its kernel velocity (A.3.1(ii)) and hat psi = i
xi1 hat rho/|xi|^2. With DU = [[-psi_xy, -psi_yy], [psi_xx, psi_xy]], hat(DU)(xi) = hat psi(xi) (xi2, -xi1)^T (xi1,
xi2), a rank-one matrix of operator norm |hat psi| |xi|^2 = |xi1| |hat rho|, which is integrable; so DU is the inverse
transform of hat(DU) and sup |DU|_op <= (2pi)^{-2} int |xi1| |hat rho| dxi = (2pi)^{-2} (pi/200) I1 I2 with I2 = int
|xi2| e^{-xi2^2/4} dxi2 = 4 and, by u = xi1^2/4 and (d/du)[(4u + 1) e^{-u}] = (3 - 4u) e^{-u}, I1 = int |xi1| |3 -
xi1^2| e^{-xi1^2/4} dxi1 = 4 [(4 e^{-3/4} - 1) + 4 e^{-3/4}] = 32 e^{-3/4} - 4. Hence sup |DU|_op <= (8 e^{-3/4} -
1)/(50 pi) = 0.01769... (the bound 17/(75 pi) = 0.0721... of the external audit is valid but weaker). U(0) = 0 by
parity, so |U(X)| <= 0.0177 |X| and X . W = c_l |X|^2 + X . U >= (401/400 - 0.0177) |X|^2 > 0 for X != 0.
Failure of 3.4. Here (1 - c_l) pi int_0^inf rho_3 r^{-2} dr = (-1/400) pi (-1/200) = pi/80000 and -a0 pi (c_l - 1)/2 =
pi/80000, so 3.4 would require J := lim_{eps -> 0} int_{|X|>eps} rho U . grad phi dX = 0 (for an exact profile J =
-pi D (D + a0/4), which vanishes here). In polar form U = (-(1/r) psi_th, psi_r) and grad phi = (-3 r^{-4} sin 3th, 3
r^{-4} cos 3th), so U . grad phi = 3 r^{-4} (cos 3th psi_r + r^{-1} sin 3th psi_th). The sin 2th and sin 4th modes of
d_x(-100 rho) are r^2 (3 - 2 r^2) e^{-r^2} and -r^4 e^{-r^2}, and the Green formula of 3.1(iv) gives, with t = r^2,
psi = -(P_2 sin 2th + P_4 sin 4th)/100 where

    P_2 = (t/2 + 3/4 + 3/(4t)) e^{-t} - 3/(4t) = r^2/8 - r^4/4 + O(r^6),
    P_4 = (t/4 + 3/4 + 3/(2t) + 3/(2t^2)) e^{-t} - 3/(2t^2) = -r^4/16 + r^6/20 + O(r^8)

(they solve the mode equations, are bounded at 0 and decay at infinity, so they are the canonical modes by A.3.1(iv)).
Inserting rho = rho_1 sin th + rho_3 sin 3th and integrating first over th, int_{|X|>eps} rho U . grad phi dX =
10^{-4} (3 pi/4) int_{eps^2}^inf F(t) dt with

    F(t) = (t/2 - 7/(2t) - 12/t^2 - 21/t^3 - 12/t^4) e^{-2t} + (-3/t^2 + 9/t^3 + 12/t^4) e^{-t},

which is bounded at 0 (F(0) = 1/2, the negative powers cancel) and decays exponentially, so the limit exists and J =
10^{-4} (3 pi/4) int_0^inf F dt. For Re z > -1 the integral int_0^inf t^z F(t) dt is analytic in z, and for Re z > 3
it equals the termwise sum of the values int_0^inf t^{z+k} e^{-a t} dt = Gamma(z + k + 1) a^{-z-k-1}; letting z -> 0
in that sum (the poles of the individual terms cancel) gives int_0^inf F dt = (11/2) log 2 - 83/24, so

    J = pi [(33/8) log 2 - 83/32]/10^4 = 8.3403667725...e-5 != 0.

The angular integration and the continuation were done by exact symbolic computation, and the value was confirmed by
radial quadrature (agreement to 11 digits) and by a two-dimensional quadrature on 1e-4 < r < 8 (relative difference
1.5e-8, of the size of the omitted disc r < 1e-4). So rho violates 3.4 by J; since 3.2 forces c_l = 1 - c = 401/400
for an exact profile, rho is not a profile at any c_l, although it has c_l + c = 1, q > 0 and X . W > 0 off 0.

## A.3.25 Finite-regularity variant

(i) (condensed). For rho in C^{1,alpha}_loc with the parities and growth, the construction of A.3.1 applies unchanged
(it uses only local integrability and the growth bound); localizing, the local part of psi solves -Lap psi = rho_x
with rho_x in C^alpha, so psi is C^{2,alpha}_loc by the Schauder estimate and U is C^{1,alpha}_loc, the separated part
being harmonic. The strain formula: rho = a0 y + O(r^{1+alpha}) and a0 y has no sin 3th mode, so rho_3 =
O(r^{1+alpha}) and rho_3 r^{-2} = O(r^{alpha-1}) is integrable at 0, while |rho_3| <= C r^gamma with gamma < 1 makes
it integrable at infinity; the derivation of 3.14 uses no second derivative. For an exact profile with a0 != 0, DU(0)
= diag(-c, c) and U(X) = DU(0) X + O(r^{1+alpha}), grad rho = a0 e_2 + O(r^alpha), so W . grad rho - rho = a0 (c_l +
c - 1) y + O(r^{1+alpha}), which forces c_l + c = 1 and DW(0) = diag(c_l - c, c_l + c) = diag(A, 1). The proof of
A.3.7 uses only first derivatives of rho and U along characteristics and the growth bound, so it applies as written.
The cubic relations of 3.3 involve third derivatives at 0, which need not exist.
(ii) Angular system. For H = r^d Theta(th) and chi = r^{d+1} Phi(th), x d_x = r cos^2 th d_r - sin th cos th d_th
gives (A x d_x + y d_y - 1) H = r^d [(d - 1 + (A - 1) d cos^2 th) Theta - (A - 1) sin th cos th Theta'], chi_x = r^d
[(d + 1) cos th Phi - sin th Phi'] and d_x H = r^{d-1} [d cos th Theta - sin th Theta'], so the frozen equation (V[H]
= grad^perp chi, V[H]_2 = chi_x) and -Lap chi = d_x H read

    (A - 1) sin th cos th Theta' = (d - 1 + (A - 1) d cos^2 th) Theta + a0 ((d + 1) cos th Phi - sin th Phi'),
    Phi'' + (d + 1)^2 Phi = sin th Theta' - d cos th Theta,

a first-order system Y' = M(th) Y for Y = (Theta, Phi, Phi'), analytic on (0, pi/2). The parities of H and chi (Theta
odd under th -> -th and even under th -> pi - th, Phi odd under both) are S: (Theta, Phi)(th) -> (-Theta, -Phi)(-th)
and T: (Theta, Phi)(th) -> (Theta, -Phi)(pi - th), and the system is equivariant under both. Near th = 0, M = R0/th +
(analytic) with R0 = [[kappa_x, a0 (d + 1)/(A - 1), 0], [0, 0, 0], [0, 0, 0]]; near th = pi/2, M = R1/(th - pi/2) +
(analytic) with R1 = (A - 1)^{-1} [[1 - d, 0, a0], [0, 0, 0], [1 - d, 0, a0]]. Both have rank one and eigenvalues {0,
0, kappa} (kappa_y = trace R1, with eigenvector (1, 0, 1)), and both are diagonalizable because kappa != 0. For
non-integer kappa no two eigenvalues differ by a positive integer, so (Coddington and Levinson, Theory of Ordinary
Differential Equations, Chapter 4) the solutions near an axis are the P(t) v with v in ker R, P analytic and P(0) = I
(t the signed distance to the axis), together with the multiples of |t|^kappa P(t) e, e the kappa-eigenvector. The
Phi-component of the latter is O(|t|^{kappa+1}), so l0(Y) := Phi(0+) and l1(Y) := Phi(pi/2-) are linear functionals on
the three-dimensional solution space on (0, pi/2), and l0 != 0 (the analytic solution with initial value (-a0 (d +
1)/(A d - 1), 1, 0) at th = 0 has l0 = 1). Admissibility: if l0(Y) = 0, the analytic part of Y at th = 0 has initial
value v in ker R0 with v_2 = 0, hence v = (0, 0, v_3), which S fixes, so it is S-invariant (S maps analytic solutions
to analytic solutions and acts on initial values by (Theta, Phi, Phi') -> (-Theta, -Phi, Phi')); the S-extension of Y
is then C^{1,alpha} in Theta and C^2 in Phi near 0, as Phi'' = -(d + 1)^2 Phi - d cos th Theta + sin th Theta' tends
to 0 there. If l0(Y) != 0, the odd extension of Phi is discontinuous. The same holds at pi/2 with T: l1(Y) = 0 forces
the analytic initial value to be a multiple of (a0, 0, d - 1), which T fixes, and Theta' and Phi'' tend to 0 at pi/2.
Near each axis Theta - (analytic part) = O(|t|^kappa) with derivative O(|t|^{kappa-1}), and kappa_x > d > q0
(kappa_x - d = (d - 1)/(A - 1)) and kappa_y > q0 (equivalent to d < a0 + 1 - (A - 1) q0), so the extended Theta is
C^{1,alpha} on the circle.
Existence. dim(ker l0 cap ker l1) >= 1; take Y != 0 there and extend it to the circle by S and T. Both equations hold
on the whole circle (they hold off the axes and all terms are continuous), H = r^d Theta is C^{1,alpha}_loc (grad H is
homogeneous of degree d - 1 > alpha with C^alpha angular part), and chi = r^{d+1} Phi is C^2 off 0 with grad chi =
O(r^d), so -Lap chi = d_x H in distributions on R^2 and grad^perp chi is the unique homogeneous inverse V[H] (A.3.11;
d + 1 is not an integer). Theta is not identically 0: otherwise the transport equation (a0 > A q0 - 1 > 0) gives
(d + 1) cos th Phi = sin th Phi', so Phi = C sin^{d+1} th, and the Poisson equation gives C (d + 1) d sin^{d-1} th =
0, so C = 0 and Y = 0. Since 1 < d < 2 and H != 0, H is not C^2 at 0 (a C^2 function homogeneous of degree d in (1, 2)
has continuous second derivatives homogeneous of negative degree, hence zero, so it is linear and therefore zero).
kappa_x is an integer only for d = ((A - 1) n + 1)/A and kappa_y only for d = a0 + 1 - (A - 1) n, finitely many d in
the bounded interval. At A = d = 3/2, a0 = 9/4 (kappa_x = 5/2, kappa_y = 7/2), Theta = sin th and Phi = -sin(2 th)/9,
i.e. H = y r^{1/2} and chi = -(2/9) x y r^{1/2}, solve both equations (the m = n = 0 member of A.3.11).
Superpositions. Let J = [d0, d1] be a closed interval of non-excluded d with d0 > q0 and kappa_x, kappa_y >= q0 + m on
J for some m > 0, on which dim(ker l0 cap ker l1) is constant. The Frobenius coefficients are given by a recursion
whose linear maps X -> X (R + n) - R X (n >= 1, eigenvalues n and n +- kappa) are invertible with inverses bounded
uniformly on J, and the majorant bounds are uniform, so P, the fractional solutions and (in the basis of initial
values at th = pi/4) l0 and l1 are analytic in d. If the dimension is 1, the cross product of the coefficient vectors
of l0 and l1 is an analytic nonvanishing choice of Y_d; if it is 2, the analytic solution with initial value (0, 0, 1)
at th = 0 is one. Then Theta_d != 0 for every d in J, and for b smooth on J with b(d0) != 0, H = int_J b(d) r^d
Theta_d dd and chi = int_J b(d) r^{d+1} Phi_d dd solve the frozen equation (V extended linearly), and H is
C^{1,alpha}_loc (the bounds are uniform on J). With lam = -log r and g(d) = b(d) Theta_d(th), integration by parts
gives int_J g(d) e^{-d lam} dd = r^{d0} [g(d0)/lam + O(lam^{-2})] uniformly in th, because d_d Theta_d is bounded (the
d-derivative of |t|^{kappa(d)} is kappa'(d) |t|^{kappa(d)} log|t|); so H = r^{d0} [b(d0) Theta_{d0}(th)/|log r| +
O(|log r|^{-2})] is not a pure power at leading order. Independence: if a finite sum of r^{d_k} Theta_k with distinct
d_k in (1, 2) is C^2 near 0, then on each ray it equals l(th) r + O(r^2), and comparing powers gives Theta_k = 0.
Finally y r^s/log(e/r) (0 < s < 1, r < 1) is C^{1,alpha} for alpha <= s and r^{-q} times it has no nonzero limit for
any q, so C^{1,alpha} regularity alone does not produce a homogeneous leading term. The residue matrices, the
equivariance, the Theta = 0 obstruction and the lattice pair are confirmed by an exact symbolic check, and the
matching by a numerical solution at (A, a0, d) = (3/2, 3, 1.7) and (5/4, 2, 1.55) (accompanying artifacts).
(iii) (condensed). The hypotheses include common bounds |rho_j| + (1 + r) |grad rho_j| <= C (1 + r)^gamma (value and
gradient growth), which give uniform Lipschitz bounds; Arzela-Ascoli and a diagonal extraction give locally uniform
convergence on R^2, C^{1,beta} convergence on compact subsets of R^2 \ {0} and weak-* convergence in W^{1,inf}_loc.
The canonical velocities converge locally uniformly: near a query point use the common Lipschitz estimate, on bounded
regions the uniform density convergence, and in the exterior the uniform tail of A.3.1 controlled by the common growth
bound. Since div W_j = 2 c_l, W_j . grad rho_j = div(rho_j W_j) - 2 c_l rho_j, and the forcing mu_j y phi(r/eps_j) has
L^1 norm O(|mu_j| eps_j^3) -> 0, the limit satisfies div(rho W) - 2 c_l rho - rho = 0 in distributions on all of R^2,
so no point source at 0. The tail passes to the limit: on the y-axis v_j G_j' = G_j + mu_j y phi(y/eps_j) (notation of
3.6, mu_j = a_j Delta_j bounded), and the integration of A.3.6 from a fixed Y0 with v_j >= c_l y/2 on y >= Y0 (common
growth bound) gives |y^{-p} G_j(y) - K| <= C y^{gamma-1} for y >= Y0 with C and Y0 independent of j (the forcing, at
most |mu_j| eps_j^4 y^{-3} on the axis, contributes C |mu_j| eps_j^4 y^{-3}); letting j -> inf and then y -> inf gives
lim y^{-p} G(y) = K.
(iv) For each j the strain formula gives c_j = -a_j/4 + int_0^delta rho_{j,3} r^{-2} dr + int_delta^inf rho_{j,3}
r^{-2} dr, and c_j = 1 - c_l + Delta_j -> 1 - c_l. The last integral converges to int_delta^inf rho_3 r^{-2} dr
(locally uniform convergence and the common growth bound). For the limit, c = -a/4 + int_0^inf rho_3 r^{-2} dr.
Subtracting and letting delta -> 0 gives the stated expression; if a != 0 the limit has c_l + c = 1 by (i), giving
(a_* - a)/4. Countertest: with z = X/eps, z_2 = (r/eps) sin th and 3 z_1^2 z_2 - z_2^3 = (r/eps)^3 sin 3th, so the
slope is m and int_0^inf rho_3 r^{-2} dr = (m/2) int_0^inf s e^{-s^2} ds = m/4, giving strain -m/4 + m/4 = 0; the
gradient is bounded uniformly in eps and every C^k norm on {r >= r0} is O(eps^N).
(v) Put rhot(Z) = rho_eps(eps Z)/eps and psit(Z) = psi_eps(eps Z)/eps^2. Since U(eps Z) = eps grad^perp psit(Z),
dividing the forced equation at X = eps Z by eps gives (c_l Z + grad^perp psit) . grad rhot - rhot = mu_eps Z_2
phi(|Z|), and -Lap psit = d_1 rhot. By hypothesis rhot = a Z_2 + C eps^s (F + f_eps) and psit = c Z_1 Z_2 + C eps^s
(G + g_eps) with f_eps -> 0 in C^3 and g_eps -> 0 in C^4 on compact sets. Linear order (A.3.20, which uses only first
derivatives at 0; a0_eps = d_2 rhot(0) = a + O(eps^s) != 0): Delta_eps = c_l + c_eps - 1 with c_eps = d_1 d_2 psit(0)
= c + C eps^s (c_F + o(1)); as c = 1 - c_l, Delta_eps = C c_F eps^s + o(eps^s) and mu_eps = a0_eps Delta_eps = a C c_F
eps^s + o(eps^s). Order eps^s: since c_l Z + grad^perp(c Z_1 Z_2) = (A Z_1, Z_2) and c_l + c = 1, the left side equals
C eps^s [(A Z_1 d_1 + Z_2 d_2 - 1)(F + f_eps) + a d_1 (G + g_eps)] + C^2 eps^{2s} grad^perp(G + g_eps) . grad(F +
f_eps); dividing by C eps^s and letting eps -> 0 locally uniformly gives (A x d_x + y d_y - 1) F + a G_x = a c_F Z_2
(1 + |Z|^2)^{-2}, and the Poisson relation gives -Lap G = F_x. Cubic order: rho_eps(X) = eps rhot(X/eps) gives b_eps =
(1/2) d_1^2 d_2 rho_eps(0) = eps^{-2} (1/2) d_1^2 d_2 rhot(0) = C b_F eps^{s-2} + o(eps^{s-2}) (C^3 convergence at 0;
a Z_2 has no cubic part), and in the same way the quartic Taylor coefficients of psi_eps are C eps^{s-2} times those
of G plus o(eps^{s-2}) (C^4 convergence), so H_eps = C H_F eps^{s-2} + o(eps^{s-2}). The cubic relation of A.3.20, b
(a0 - 4A + 2 Delta) = 3 a0 H_4 + 4 mu/eps^2 (it uses only the Taylor expansions of rho_eps to order 3 and of psi_eps
to order 4 at 0), multiplied by eps^{2-s}/C, reads (a - 4A) b_F + o(1) = 3 a H_F + 4 a c_F + o(1). Finally eps^2
b_eps/Delta_eps = (b_F + o(1))/(c_F + o(1)) -> b_F/c_F when c_F != 0; b_F != 0 makes the limit nonzero. The derivation
is complete; the expansions are hypotheses and are not proved for the computed branch. The order-eps^s algebra and the
scaling of the cubic relation are confirmed by an exact symbolic check (accompanying artifacts).

## A.3.26 Norm dependence of the linearized source operator

(i) Let h be smooth, compactly supported, with the parities. div(A x, y) = A + 1, so <(A x d_x + y d_y) h, h> = -((A +
1)/2) ||h||_2^2 and <L h, h> = -((A + 3)/2) ||h||_2^2 + a0 <U[h]_2, h>. The symbol of U_2 is -xi1^2/|xi|^2 (A.3.35),
so <U[h]_2, h> = -(2pi)^{-2} int xi1^2 |xi|^{-2} |hat h|^2 dxi <= 0, and for a0 >= 0, -<L h, h> >= ((A + 3)/2) ||h||_2^2;
Cauchy-Schwarz gives the bound. For the background operator L_b h = W_b . grad h - h + U[h] . grad rho_b, <W_b . grad
h, h> = -c_l ||h||^2 = -((A + 1)/2) ||h||^2, and U[h] . grad rho_b = a0 U[h]_2 + U[h] . O(r^2) with |<U[h] . O(r^2),
h>| <= C eps^2 ||U[h]||_2 ||h||_2 <= C eps^2 ||h||_2^2 for supp h in B_eps (||U[h]||_2 <= ||h||_2 by the same symbol
bound).
(ii) This is the Sobolev computation of A.3.17: the coefficient of |xi|^{2s} |H|^2 in the energy identity is affine in
t = w1^2 in [0, 1], with values s - (A + 3)/2 at t = 0 and A s - (A + 3)/2 - a0 at t = 1. If both have the same
nonzero sign the form is definite and Cauchy-Schwarz gives a lower bound; if they have opposite signs,
parity-symmetrized bumps in thin cones around the two axes, dilated to high frequency, give quotients tending to the
two endpoint values, so the identity decides nothing. At A = 3/2, a0 = 9/4, s = 3/2 the endpoints are -3/4 and -9/4,
so the coefficient is -3/4 - (3/2) w1^2.
(iii) Here ||h||_{C^{1,beta}} := sup |h| + sup |grad h| + [grad h]_beta on R^2, with beta = d - 1 in (0, 1) and
[.]_beta the Holder seminorm. At A = d, a0 = (d - 1)(d + 3) the lattice pair h = y r^{d-1}, chi = -x y r^{d-1}/(d + 3)
satisfies (d x d_x + y d_y - 1) h + a0 chi_x = 0 and -Lap chi = h_x off 0 (A.3.11 with m = n = 0; for d = 3/2 this is
the pair of A.3.25(ii)). Fix zeta in C_c^inf((1, 2)) with 0 <= zeta <= 1 and zeta = 1 on [5/4, 7/4], let s = -log r/T
and h_T = zeta(s) h, supported in e^{-2T} <= r <= e^{-T}. As h_T has compact support its canonical stream is psi_T =
G0 * d_x h_T (A.3.1(ii)); write psi_T = zeta(s) chi + g. Since zeta(s) chi has compact support, g = G0 * f_T with f_T
= d_x h_T + Lap(zeta(s) chi), and a direct computation (exact symbolic check, accompanying artifacts) gives

    L h_T = -(1/T) zeta'(s) h + a0 d_x g,
    f_T = (1/T) x y r^{d-3} [((d - 1)/(d + 3)) zeta'(s) - zeta''(s)/(T (d + 3))].

Lemma: if k = r^beta K(th, s) with |K| + |d_th K| + |d_s K| <= M, then [k]_beta <= C M for T >= 1. Indeed |grad k| <=
C M r^{beta-1}; for |Y| <= |X|, |k(X) - k(Y)| <= C M |X|^{beta-1} |X - Y| <= C M |X - Y|^beta if |X - Y| <= |X|/2 (the
segment stays in |Z| >= |X|/2), and |k(X) - k(Y)| <= 2 M |X|^beta <= 2^{1+beta} M |X - Y|^beta otherwise. grad h_T,
grad(zeta'(s) h) and T f_T are of this form with M independent of T. Hence [grad h_T]_beta <= C, sup |h_T| <= e^{-dT}
and sup |grad h_T| <= C e^{-(d-1)T}, while for X = (R, 0), Y = (0, R), R = e^{-3T/2} (where zeta(s) = 1 and grad h =
(0, R^{d-1}), (0, d R^{d-1})), [grad h_T]_beta >= (d - 1) R^{d-1}/(sqrt2 R)^beta = (d - 1) 2^{-beta/2}; so
||h_T||_{C^{1,beta}} is bounded above and below. For the residual: the Newtonian potential of a C^beta function f
supported in B_rho satisfies [D^2 (G0 * f)]_beta <= C [f]_beta on R^2 and sup_{B_{2 rho}} |D^2 (G0 * f)| <= C (sup
|f| + rho^beta [f]_beta) (Gilbarg and Trudinger, Elliptic Partial Differential Equations of Second Order, Lemma 4.4,
on balls of radius R -> inf and R = 2 rho). With rho = e^{-T}, [f_T]_beta <= C/T, sup |f_T| <= C e^{-(d-1)T}/T and
||f_T||_1 <= C e^{-(d+1)T}/T, this gives [grad d_x g]_beta <= C/T; |grad g| <= e^{-T} sup |f_T| <= C e^{-dT}/T (from
|grad G0 * f| <= (2pi)^{-1} int |f(Y)| |X - Y|^{-1} dY); |D^2 g| <= C e^{-(d-1)T}/T on B_{2 e^{-T}}, and |D^2 g(X)| <=
C ||f_T||_1 |X|^{-2} <= C e^{-(d-1)T}/T outside. With the explicit term, ||L h_T||_{C^{1,beta}} <= C/T. h_T vanishes
near 0 and outside a compact set, so its jets at 0 and its far-field amplitude vanish; it has only the sin th mode, so
rho_3 = 0 and the strain formula gives c = 0. (L and the seminorm [grad h]_beta commute with h(X) -> l^{-d} h(l X), so
for the seminorm alone the position of the support is immaterial; the support near 0 makes the sup terms small.)
(iv) Persistence. Let rho_b, W_b = c_l X + U_b be a background with the parities, U_b of class C^2 near 0, the same
source jet (DW_b(0) = diag(A, 1) and grad rho_b(0) = a0 e_2, with A = d and a0 = (d - 1)(d + 3)) and grad rho_b in
C^{1,beta}(R^2) with finite norm (for an exact smooth profile this follows from the bounds of 3.23), and let L_b h =
W_b . grad h - h + U[h] . grad rho_b. Then (L_b - L) h_T = E . grad h_T + U . B with E = W_b - (A x, y), U = U[h_T]
and B = grad rho_b - a0 e_2; E(0) = 0 and DE(0) = 0, B(0) = 0, and DB(0) = D^2 rho_b(0) = 0 by parity. Put delta =
e^{-T} and take T >= 5. First term: it is supported in B_delta, where |E| <= C r^2, |DE| <= C r, |D^2 E| <= C and |D^k
h_T| <= C r^{d-k} (k <= 3, uniformly in T), so V = grad(E . grad h_T) has sup |V| <= C delta^d, sup |DV| <= C
delta^{d-1} and [V]_beta <= (2 sup |V|)^{1-beta} (sup |DV|)^beta <= C delta; the first term is O(delta) in C^{1,beta}.
Second term: as in (iii), sup |U| <= C delta^d, sup |DU| <= C delta^{d-1} and [DU]_beta <= C [d_x h_T]_beta <= C, and
since U is a kernel homogeneous of degree -2 applied to h_T (A.3.1(ii)), |DU(X)| <= C delta^{d+2} |X|^{-3} and |D^2
U(X)| <= C delta^{d+2} |X|^{-4} for |X| >= 2 delta. Then sup |U . B| and sup |D(U . B)| are O(delta^beta), and [(DB)^T
U]_beta <= sup |DB| [U]_beta + [DB]_beta sup |U| = O(delta), using [U]_beta <= (2 sup |U|)^{1-beta} (sup |DU|)^beta <=
C delta. For (DU)^T B put eta = delta^{1/2} (so eta/4 >= 2 delta) and split |DU(X) B(X) - DU(Y) B(Y)| <= |DU(X) -
DU(Y)| |B(X)| + |DU(Y)| |B(X) - B(Y)|. The second part is at most C delta^{d-1} min(|X - Y|, 1) <= C delta^{d-1} |X -
Y|^beta. The first is at most C eta^{1+beta} |X - Y|^beta if |X| <= eta (|B(X)| <= C |X|^{1+beta}, as B(0) = 0, DB(0)
= 0 and DB is C^beta); at most 2 sup |DU| sup |B| <= C delta^{d-1} eta^{-beta} |X - Y|^beta if |X| > eta > 2 |Y| (then
|X - Y| > eta/2); and, if |X|, |Y| >= eta/2, at most C delta^{d+2} eta^{-4} |X - Y| when |X - Y| <= eta/4 (the segment
stays in |Z| >= eta/4) and C delta^{d+2} eta^{-3} otherwise, both at most C delta^{d+2} eta^{-3-beta} |X - Y|^beta.
Altogether ||(L_b - L) h_T||_{C^{1,beta}} <= C delta^{beta/2} = C e^{-beta T/2}, so ||L_b h_T||_{C^{1,beta}} <= C/T
and the quasimodes persist. A smaller Holder exponent for grad rho_b is not covered by this argument.
Distant quasimodes. Let ||h||_w := ||h||_{C^{k,alpha}(B_2)} + sup_{R >= 1} R^{-p} ||h(R X)||_{C^{k,alpha}(1 < |X| <
2)} (k >= 0, 0 < alpha < 1), let rho_b be smooth with the parities and supported in B_{R0} (its source data at 0 are
arbitrary), and let W_b, L_b be as above. For T >= 2 and ell >= 4 R0 + 2 put h = zeta(log(r/ell)/T) r^p sin th, with
zeta as in (iii), supported in ell e^T <= r <= ell e^{2T}. (a) For R with zeta = 1 on the whole annulus R < r < 2R
(possible as T >= 2), R^{-p} h(R X) = |X|^p sin th, and for every R the X-derivatives of zeta(log(R |X|/ell)/T) are
O(1/T), so ||h||_w is bounded above and below independently of T and ell. (b) (c_l X . grad - 1) h = (c_l/T)
zeta'(log(r/ell)/T) r^p sin th, of weighted norm O(1/T). (c) For |X| >= 2 R0, |D^j U_b(X)| <= C_j |X|^{-2-j} (a kernel
homogeneous of degree -2 applied to rho_b), so on the annuli meeting supp h, R^{-p} ||(U_b . grad h)(R
X)||_{C^{k,alpha}(1 < |X| < 2)} <= C R^{-3} <= C ell^{-3}. (d) U[h] . grad rho_b is supported in B_{R0}; U[h](0) = 0
by parity, and for |Z| <= ell/2 and j >= 1, |D^j U[h](Z)| <= C_j int_{|Y| >= ell} |Y|^{-2-j} |h(Y)| dY <= C_j
ell^{p-j} (p < 1), so ||U[h]||_{C^{k+1}(B_{2 R0})} <= C R0 ell^{p-1} and the weighted norm of U[h] . grad rho_b is at
most C ell^{p-1}. Choosing ell large for each T gives ||L_b h||_w <= C/T with ||h||_w bounded below, so source data
alone give no lower bound in this weight.

## A.3.27 Conditional local uniqueness modulo scaling (condensed)

Hypotheses as stated in 3.27. Slice. Let rho be an exact profile of the primary class (at c_l* + delta) with ||rho -
rho*||_{C^{s+1,alpha}_q} <= eps. With rho_l = l rho(X/l) (A.3.5), the map (l, rho) -> rho_l(X_0) - rho*(X_0) is C^1
near (1, rho*) and its l-derivative at (1, rho*) is e_sc(X_0) != 0, so for eps small there is a unique l near 1, |l -
1| <= C eps, with h := rho_l - rho* vanishing at X_0. Since rho*_l - rho* = O(|l - 1|) in C^{s+1,alpha}_q (rho* is
smooth with the symbol bounds of 3.23) and ||(rho - rho*)_l|| <= C ||rho - rho*||, ||h||_{C^{s+1,alpha}_q} <= C eps;
rho_l is again an exact profile at c_l* + delta (A.3.5). As q < nu, the weighted Holder space embeds in E (int^inf
r^{2q - 2nu} dr/r < inf on the cylinder), and the point evaluation at X_0 is continuous on E because s > 2.
Equation for h. Subtracting (c_l* X + U*) . grad rho* = rho* from ((c_l* + delta) X + U* + U[h]) . grad(rho* + h) =
rho* + h gives L(h, delta) = -(U[h] + delta X) . grad h. The right side lies in E with norm <= C
||h||_{C^{s+1,alpha}_q} (||h||_E + |delta|): grad h and its derivatives up to order s are bounded by C
||h||_{C^{s+1,alpha}_q} r^{q-1-k}, so multiplication by them maps the H^s and r^nu H^s_b parts of U[h] boundedly (U[h]
is controlled in these norms by ||h||_E, as in A.3.28), and |X| |D^k grad h| <= C r^{q-k} with q < 1 handles the delta
term. Hence also P0 h = L(h, delta) - M h - delta X . grad rho* is in E, so (h, delta) lies in X0 x R.
Inverse bound. L : X0 x R -> E is Fredholm of index 1 with kernel span{(e_sc, 0)}. The slice S = {(h, delta) : h(X_0)
= 0} is a closed subspace of codimension 1 not containing (e_sc, 0), so L restricted to S is Fredholm of index 0 and
injective, hence an isomorphism onto E: ||h||_{X0} + |delta| <= C_1 ||L(h, delta)||_E. Combining, ||h||_E + |delta| <=
C_1 C eps (||h||_E + |delta|), so for C_1 C eps < 1, h = 0 and delta = 0, i.e. rho = (rho*)_{1/l} and c_l = c_l*; a0
is scale invariant.
Equal weight (neighbourhood in C^{s+1,alpha}_nu). The argument above cannot be repeated verbatim with q = nu: the
embedding of C^{s+1,alpha}_nu into E fails (the exterior cutoff of r^nu sin th has annular C^{s+1,alpha} norms of
size 2^{nu j}, so its weighted square sum in E diverges), and so does the bound ||X . grad h||_E <= C ||h||. Instead,
fix bar_p with p* := 1/c_l* < bar_p < nu, and let rho be an exact profile with ||rho - rho*||_{C^{s+1,alpha}_nu} <=
eps. (1) The slope and the strain are continuous in C^{s+1,alpha}_nu: for f = d_x(rho - rho*), odd in x and in y, |f|
<= C ||rho - rho*|| |x| |y| near 0 and |f| <= C ||rho - rho*|| r^{nu-1} at infinity, so the formula c = (1/pi) int x y
r^{-4} rho_x dX of 3.14 converges absolutely for the difference and |c - c*| <= C eps. By 3.2 (a0 != 0 for eps small),
c_l = 1 - c, so |c_l - c_l*| <= C eps, p := 1/c_l < bar_p, and c_l stays in a compact subset of (1, inf). (2)
Uniform exterior upgrade (condensed). Since U is bounded on C^{s+1,alpha}_nu (the dyadic block argument of A.3.28
Step 1 with the local Holder estimate for order-zero singular integrals in place of the H^s one), |D^k U| <= C B
r^{nu-k} with B a bound for ||rho||_{C^{s+1,alpha}_nu}, so V = W . e_r >= c_l r/2 on r >= R0 with R0 depending only on
B. In t = log r the orbits satisfy dth/dt = Q/V and dtau/dt = r/V, and Q/V and r/V - p are O(e^{-(1-nu) t}) in
C^{s+1,alpha} on unit t-cylinders, with constants depending only on B. Differentiating the angular equation in the
initial angle beta, each derivative solves a linear equation whose coefficient d_th(Q/V) is integrable in t, plus
integrable lower-order terms; Gronwall's inequality bounds the angular flow maps beta -> th(t, beta), their inverses
th -> beta(t, th) and the correction H := tau - p (t - t0) in C^{s+1,alpha} uniformly in t (the first derivative is
the exponential of a bounded integral, hence bounded below). Exact transport gives rho(e^t, th) = e^{p (t - t0)}
e^{H(t, beta)} rho(e^{t0}, beta) with beta = beta(t, th), so ||rho(2^j .)||_{C^{s+1,alpha}(annulus)} <= C 2^{p j} <= C
2^{bar_p j}: ||rho||_{C^{s+1, alpha}_{bar_p}} is bounded uniformly over the neighbourhood. Let B0 be a common bound
for these norms, for rho* and for the dilations rho_l with |l - 1| small. (3) After the slice dilation as above, h =
rho_l - rho* has ||h||_{C^{s+1, alpha}_nu} <= C eps and ||h||_{C^{s+1,alpha}_{bar_p}} <= 2 B0, so a_j := ||h(2^j
.)||_{C^{s+1}(annulus)} <= min(C eps 2^{nu j}, 2 B0 2^{bar_p j}). Since ||(X . grad h)(2^j .)||_{H^s(annulus)} <= C
a_j, splitting the square sum of E at the first j with 2 B0 2^{-(nu - bar_p) j} <= C eps (about log(B0/eps)/(nu -
bar_p) terms of size (C eps)^2, then a geometric tail) gives

    ||h||_E + ||X . grad h||_E <= C eps sqrt(1 + log(B0/eps)) =: omega(eps) -> 0.

(4) The product estimate for U[h] . grad h used only an exponent < 1 (the factor 2^{-(1-nu) j} <= 1 on the j-th
annulus), so ||U[h] . grad h||_E <= C eps ||h||_E, while ||delta X . grad h||_E <= omega(eps) |delta|. With M bounded
on E and X . grad rho* in E, P0 h = L(h, delta) - M h - delta X . grad rho* is in E, so (h, delta) lies in X0 x R. (5)
The slice inverse bound gives ||h||_E + |delta| <= C_1 (C eps ||h||_E + omega(eps) |delta|), so h = 0 and delta = 0
once C_1 C eps < 1 and C_1 omega(eps) < 1. Hence the conclusion of 3.27 also holds in a small C^{s+1,alpha}_nu
neighbourhood. Nothing here gives the kernel hypothesis.

## A.3.28 Conditional Fredholm property of the linearization

Hypotheses as in 3.28; the symbol bounds of 3.23 are used throughout, (H-dyn) only in the escape weight and the index.
Put P_tau = P0 + tau M (0 <= tau <= 1), so L0 = P_1.
Step 1 (Hilbert realization, condensed). Use the complete metric g = b_g(r)^2 dX^2 (b_g = 1 for r <= 2, b_g = 1/r for
r >= 4), whose end is the flat cylinder t = log r, A_m = (1 - Lap_g)^m, a positive even-even weight w equivalent to
r^{-nu} with bounded covariant derivatives of log w, J h = A_m(w h) and ||h||_E = ||J h||_{L^2(g)}. On dyadic annuli
the cylinder chart is uniformly equivalent to rescaling X = 2^j Z, so this norm is equivalent to the weighted dyadic
H^s norm of 3.28. M is bounded on E: near-diagonal annulus pairs by the order-zero multipliers on H^s; for input
annulus k >= j + 3 (output j) the subtracted kernel K(X - Y) - K(-Y) (the odd input has zero integral against K(-Y))
gives the block bound C 2^{-(1-nu)(k-j)}; for j >= k + 3 subtracting K(X) gives C 2^{-(3+nu)(j-k)}; both sum since 0 <
nu < 1, and multiplication by grad rho = O(r^{p-1}) with all scaled derivatives (3.23) is bounded. With D_W = W . grad
and b0 = -1 - D_W log w, B_tau := J P_tau J^{-1} = T + C_tau with T = W . grad + (div_g W)/2 and C_tau = [A_m, D_W]
A_m^{-1} + A_m b0 A_m^{-1} + tau A_m w M w^{-1} A_m^{-1} - (div_g W)/2 bounded on L^2(g): [A_m, D_W] has order <= s
with bounded coefficients (the order s + 1 terms cancel), and W, div_g W and their covariant derivatives are bounded
by 3.23.
Step 2 (graph domain and adjoint domain). W is complete (|W| <= C (1 + r)), and Q_t f = J_t^{1/2} f o Phi_t (J_t the
density Jacobian) is a strongly continuous unitary group on L^2(g) whose generator is T on the maximal distributional
domain D(T): if v, Tv are in L^2 then Q_t v - v = int_0^t Q_s Tv ds weakly, hence strongly. T is skew-adjoint (both
lambda +- T are onto via the Laplace transforms of Q_{+-t}), and time-mollified smooth compactly supported functions
form a graph core. As C_tau is bounded, B_tau is closed with D(B_tau) = D(B_tau*) = D(T) and B_tau* = -T + C_tau*.
Hence X0 = {h in E : P0 h in E} = J^{-1} D(T) with an equivalent graph norm for every tau, and the parity-preserving
tests chi_R h (radial cutoffs with escaping transitions) converge to h in the graph norm, because P_tau(chi_R h) -
P_tau h = (chi_R - 1) P_tau h + (W . grad chi_R) h + tau (M(chi_R h) - chi_R M h), where W . grad chi_R is bounded
with its cylinder derivatives and supported where r is comparable to R, and M(chi_R h) - chi_R M h = M((chi_R - 1)
h) - (chi_R - 1) M h with M bounded on E. Compact-error lemma: if Re <B v, v> >= eps ||v||^2 -
||K v||^2 with K compact on tests, it extends to D(T) for B and for B* (Re <Tv, v> = 0), so ||v||^2 <= eps^{-2}
||Bv||^2 + (2/eps) ||K v||^2 for both, and B and B* have finite kernels and closed ranges (a normalized sequence with
Bv_n -> 0 has a convergent subsequence); B is Fredholm.
Step 3 (escape weight). Under (H-dyn) every trajectory from a small outward circle about 0 crosses a large outward
circle at a time that is continuous (transversality, no return) and hence bounded. For an even-even chi >= 0 supported
in a slightly enlarged annulus and equal to 1 on a prescribed transition annulus, F(X) := int_{-inf}^0 chi(Phi_t X) dt
is bounded, smooth, zero near 0, satisfies W . grad F = chi, and is constant along trajectories beyond supp chi; its
cylinder derivatives are bounded because the exterior angular ODE has coefficients with all cylinder derivatives
O(e^{-(1-p) t}) (3.23). Set w = e^{-M0 F} w0 with w0 = 1 near 0 and r^{-nu} near infinity; this adds M0 chi to -D_W
log w and keeps the norm equivalent.
Step 4 (local symbol and compact errors). For a compactly supported even-even cutoff zeta, the real part of zeta C_tau
zeta equals, modulo compact operators, sum_{i,j} R_i* zeta^2 (H_tau)_{ij} R_j with R_j the multiplier i xi_j/(1 +
|xi|^2)^{1/2} and H_tau = s sym DW + [s D_W log b_g - 1 - D_W log w - (div_g W)/2] I + tau [[-rho_y, rho_x/2],
[rho_x/2, 0]]. Indeed [-Lap, D_W] has principal part -2 (d_i W_j) d_i d_j and [b_g^{-s}, D_W] = s b_g^{-s} D_W log
b_g, so the degree-s numerator of [A_m, D_W] is s xi^T sym DW xi/|xi|^2 + s D_W log b_g, while M has symbols xi1
xi2/|xi|^2 and -xi1^2/|xi|^2 (3.1), which give the last matrix. The errors are compact by three facts; let f be smooth
with compact support (multiplication operator). (i) Let m be a symbol of order zero that is smooth on all of R^2,
|d^beta m(xi)| <= C_beta (1 + |xi|)^{-|beta|}; this covers R_j and the parts (1 - chi_0) m of the homogeneous symbols
of M, where chi_0 in C_c^inf is even-even and equals 1 near 0. Then [m(D), f] maps L^2 to H^1, so with compactly
supported output it is compact by Rellich. The output outside a large disk is small in Hilbert-Schmidt norm: the
kernel k_m satisfies |k_m(z)| <= C_N |z|^{-N} for |z| >= 1, because z^beta k_m is, up to a constant factor, the
inverse transform of d^beta m, which is integrable for |beta| = N > 2; for |X| > R and Y in supp f the operator kernel
is k_m(X - Y) f(Y), whose squared Hilbert-Schmidt norm is at most ||f||_2^2 int_{|z| > R - R_f} |z|^{-2N} dz -> 0 (R_f
the radius of supp f). This decay holds only for symbols smooth at xi = 0: the full homogeneous symbols xi1 xi2/|xi|^2
and -xi1^2/|xi|^2 have kernels decaying only like |z|^{-2}. (ii) Low frequencies. For a homogeneous symbol m0 of M the
remaining part chi_0 m0 is bounded with compact support, so k_lo, its inverse transform, lies in L^2 with ||k_lo||_2 =
(2pi)^{-1} ||chi_0 m0||_2 (standing convention). The operators (chi_0 m0)(D) f and f (chi_0 m0)(D) have kernels
k_lo(X - Y) f(Y) and f(X) k_lo(X - Y), each of Hilbert-Schmidt norm exactly ||k_lo||_2 ||f||_2 = (2pi)^{-1} ||chi_0
m0||_2 ||f||_2, so both, and hence their commutator, are Hilbert-Schmidt. With (i) applied to (1 - chi_0) m0, every
commutator [m0(D), f] is compact.
(iii) The parametrix b_g^s (1 - Lap)^{-m} inverts A_m locally modulo operators gaining s + 1 derivatives, and
separated input/output pieces of A_m^{-1} and of the canonical kernel are smoothing. All cutoffs are even-even, so the
parity sector is preserved; auxiliary multipliers act on full L^2. [C_tau, zeta] is compact: the compact-output part
by (i)-(iii), the far part by Step 5.
Step 5 (positivity). At the source b_g = w0 = 1, F = 0, sym DW = diag(A, 1), div_g W = 2 c_l and grad rho = (0, a0),
so H_tau(0) = diag(sA - 1 - c_l - tau a0, s - 1 - c_l), positive for all tau in [0, 1] exactly by s > max(1 + c_l,
(1 + c_l + max(a0, 0))/A); a margin persists on a small ball. On the end DW = c_l I + O(r^{p-1}), D_W log b_g = -c_l +
O(r^{p-1}), div_g W = O(r^{p-1}), D_W log w0 = -nu c_l + O(r^{p-1}) and grad rho = O(r^{p-1}), so H_tau = (c_l nu - 1)
I + O(r^{p-1}), positive since nu > p. In the cylinder c_l d_t commutes with A_m, the coefficients of [A_m, D_W], b0 -
(c_l nu - 1) and div_g W decay like e^{-(1-p) t} with derivatives, and the M term obeys the same bound, so ||1_{t>T0}
(C_tau - (c_l nu - 1) I)|| -> 0 as T0 -> inf (no commutator compactness is used here). Taking chi = 1 on the remaining
compact annulus and M0 large gives H_tau >= eps0 I everywhere, uniformly in tau.
Step 6 (Fredholm). With zeta0^2 + zeta1^2 = 1 (zeta0 compact, zeta1 on the far end), C_tau - zeta0 C_tau zeta0 - zeta1
C_tau zeta1 is compact; the end gives Re <C_tau zeta1 v, zeta1 v> >= ((c_l nu - 1)/2) ||zeta1 v||^2, and the compact
part gives eps0 ||zeta0 v||^2 modulo a compact form, by sum_j R_j* R_j = I - (1 - Lap)^{-1}. So Re <C_tau v, v> >= eps
||v||^2 - <|K0| v, v> with K0 compact self-adjoint, and Step 2 with K = |K0|^{1/2} shows every P_tau : X0 -> E is
Fredholm; tau -> P_tau is norm continuous on the fixed graph space (M is bounded on E), so the index is constant.
Step 7 (index at tau = 0, compatible data). J0 h := h_y(0) is continuous on E (s >= 4). For h in X0, differentiating W
. grad h - h at 0 with DW(0) = diag(A, 1) and parity gives d_y(P0 h)(0) = 0, so ran P0 lies in ker J0. Kernel: L_y =
rho/a0 is in E (3.23, nu > p) and P0 L_y = 0; if P0 h = 0, then g := h - (J0 h) L_y vanishes to second order at 0 and
g(X) = e^T g(Phi_{-T} X) = O(e^{(1 - 2 lam) T}) for any lam < 1 near 1, so g = 0 at every point (H-dyn); ker P0 =
span{rho}. Range: for f smooth, compactly supported, with the parities and f_y(0) = 0, f = O(r^3) and h(X) :=
int_{-inf}^0 e^{-t} f(Phi_t X) dt converges with all derivatives (derivatives of the backward source flow are O(e^{lam
t}), and terms with at most 3 outer derivatives are O(e^{3 lam t}), 3 lam > 1), solves P0 h = f, and outside supp f
solves the homogeneous equation, so it has the symbol bounds and lies in X0. Such f are dense in ker J0 (subtract J0
values times one fixed test with J0 = 1) and the range is closed, so ran P0 = ker J0, of codimension 1, and ind P0 =
1 - 1 = 0. For general f in ker J0, the restriction of P0 to {J0 h = 0} is a bounded bijection onto ker J0 with
bounded inverse S; for compatible approximants f_n -> f, |(f_n - f)(Z)| <= C ||f_n - f||_{C^2} |Z|^2 near 0 bounds the
backward tail by C ||f_n - f||_{C^2} int_T^inf e^{-(2 lam - 1) t} dt, so S f is the backward integral. Compatibility
is needed: for f = y zeta(r) (zeta = 1 near 0), f_y(0) = 1 and e^T y(Phi_{-T} X) has a nonzero limit on the y-axis
(W2(0, y) = y + O(y^3)), so the integral diverges there. Augmented map: X . grad rho is in E by 3.23, adding the
column delta X . grad rho raises the index by 1, and the scaling orbit gives (e_sc, 0) in the kernel (e_sc != 0 by
A.3.5). The derivative identity: d_y(X . grad rho)(0) = a0, and d_y(M h)(0) = d_y(U[h]1 rho_x + U[h]2 rho_y)(0) = a0
d_y U[h]2(0) = a0 psi[h]_xy(0) (rho_x = 0 on the y-axis, U[h]2 = psi[h]_x), which with d_y(P0 h)(0) = 0 gives the
stated formula.

## A.3.29 Differentiated transport

Differentiating W . grad h = h + g in x gives W . grad h_x = h_x + g_x - d_x W_1 h_x - d_x W_2 h_y. Where W_2 != 0,
h_y = (h + g - W_1 h_x)/W_2; substituting gives W . grad h_x = d h_x - (d_x W_2/W_2)(h + g) + g_x with d = 1 - d_x
W_1 + W_1 d_x W_2/W_2. Since W_2 is smooth and odd in y, W_2 = y b with b(x, y) = int_0^1 d_y W_2(x, t y) dt smooth,
and d_x W_2/W_2 = d_x b/b, so d = 1 - d_x W_1 + W_1 d_x b/b is smooth wherever b != 0. At 0, b(0) = d_y W_2(0) = 1 and
W_1(0) = 0, so d(0) = 1 - A = 2 - 2 c_l < 0 (DW(0) = diag(A, 1), 3.2). At infinity, 3.23 gives |D^k U| <= C r^{p-k}
for k = 1, 2. In |y| >= r/2, b = c_l + U_2/y = c_l + O(r^{p-1}) and d_x b = d_x U_2/y = O(r^{p-2}). In |x| >= sqrt(3)
r/2, the segment from (x, 0) to (x, y) stays at distance >= sqrt(3) r/2 from 0, so b = c_l + int_0^1 d_y U_2(x, t y)
dt = c_l + O(r^{p-1}) and d_x b = int_0^1 d_x d_y U_2(x, t y) dt = O(r^{p-2}). The two regions cover a neighbourhood
of infinity, and with d_x W_1 = c_l + O(r^{p-1}), |W_1| <= C r, d = 1 - c_l + O(r^{p-1}) uniformly. Coupled form:
grad(W . grad h) = DW^T grad h + D^2h W, so W . grad(grad h) = (I - DW^T) grad h + grad g holds wherever h, g are C^2,
with no division. Energy matrix: from A.3.17, M = (1 + 2 c_l) I + sym DU + [[rho_y, -rho_x/2], [-rho_x/2, 0]], and sym
DU = O(r^{p-1}), grad rho -> 0 (3.23), so M -> (1 + 2 c_l) I. At an interior zero X1 of b (W_2(X1) = 0 with y != 0)
no extension of d is claimed: if W_1 d_x b != 0 at X1, then |d| -> inf as X -> X1 along points with b != 0, by the
formula for d. No example of such a zero is given here, and nothing else uses one; the coupled form is the substitute
that holds without division.

## A.3.30 Trapped set and criteria for (H-dyn)

Inputs: A.3.2 (DW(0) = diag(A, 1)), 3.7 and 3.23 (U, rho = O(r^p) with symbol bounds; uniform smooth limit Theta0),
3.21(iv) (w g' = (w' - A) g on the axis). Neither finiteness nor isolation of Z is used.
(i) Choose R with W . X >= c_l r^2/2 on r >= R. The flow is complete (|W| <= C (1 + r)), D_R is backward invariant,
and K = intersection_{t>=0} Phi_{-t}(D_R): a trajectory that leaves D_R has radius growing at least exponentially and
never returns, and a forward-bounded one never leaves. K is compact, invariant, and connected as a nested intersection
of compact topological disks containing 0. Since det D Phi_t = e^{2 c_l t}, |K| = |Phi_t K| = e^{2 c_l t} |K|, so |K|
= 0. Every zero of W lies in K, and rho(Phi_t X) = e^t rho(X) is bounded for t >= 0 on K, so rho = 0 on K. Near 0, rho
= y G with G(0) = a0 != 0, so the nodal set there is the x-axis. On the axis w is odd, w'(0) = A > 0 and w > 0 for
large x; if x_* is the largest nonnegative root of w (x_* = 0 if w has no positive root; x_* is the b of 3.30 and
3.34), the scalar flow on the invariant axis gives K intersect {y = 0} = [-x_*, x_*] x {0}.
(v) curl(W + rho e_2) = curl U + rho_x = 0, so Pi(X) := int_0^1 (W + rho e_2)(tX) . X dt is smooth with grad Pi = W +
rho e_2 and Pi(0) = 0; since grad(c_l |X|^2/2 - P) = c_l X + U + rho e_2 for the pressure of 3.16, Pi = c_l |X|^2/2 -
P. Along trajectories dPi/dt = grad Pi . W = |W|^2 + rho W_2, which is |W|^2 where rho = 0. Backward orbits are
bounded (they enter D_R and stay), and on them |rho W_2| <= C e^t for t <= 0, so int_{-inf}^0 |W(Phi_t X)|^2 dt < inf;
as |W|^2 has bounded derivative along the orbit closure, |W(Phi_t X)| -> 0 as t -> -inf and every backward limit point
is a zero of W.
(iii) At a zero z, differentiating W . grad rho = rho gives DW(z)^T grad rho(z) = grad rho(z), and tr DW(z) = div W =
2 c_l. If grad rho(z) != 0, 1 is an eigenvalue and the other is 2 c_l - 1 = A. If grad rho(z) = 0, curl W(z) = curl
U(z) = -rho_x(z) = 0, so DW(z) is symmetric. The spectrum is real in both cases.
(ii) If w > 0 on x > 0, then x_* = 0 and, since the nodal set near 0 is the axis, 0 is an isolated point of the
connected set K, so K = {0}; every backward trajectory then converges to 0 by (v) and every nonzero point escapes,
which is (H-dyn). Conversely (H-dyn) excludes zeros of W other than 0, so w > 0 on x > 0 (its sign near 0). If w > 0
on x > 0, w g' = (w' - A) g is a nonsingular linear equation on each compact subinterval of (0, inf) and g(0) = a0 !=
0, so g != 0 (reflection covers x < 0). If g != 0 everywhere but w has a positive root, then at the first root x1,
w'(x1) <= 0, while the equation at x1 gives 0 = (w'(x1) - A) g(x1), i.e. w'(x1) = A > 0, a contradiction. With 3.22
this gives the stated equivalence with rho/(a0 y) > 0.
(iv) If (H-dyn) fails, x1 exists, g(x1) = 0 and lambda_- := w'(x1) <= 0. On the axis W1 is even and W2 odd in y, so
DW(x1, 0) = diag(lambda_-, lambda_+) with lambda_+ = 2 c_l - lambda_-. If lambda_- < 0, the solution to the left of x1
is g = C w exp(-A int_{x'}^x ds/w(s)), a smooth nonvanishing factor times (x1 - x)^{1 - A/lambda_-} with C != 0 (g(0)
!= 0); smoothness of g forces m := 1 - A/lambda_- to be an integer >= 2, so lambda_- = -A/(m - 1) and g vanishes to
order exactly m. The lowest homogeneous part R_k of rho at (x1, 0) satisfies (DW(x1, 0) Y) . grad R_k = R_k, so a
monomial Y1^n Y2^k' occurs only if n lambda_- + k' lambda_+ = 1: k' = 0 is impossible (lambda_- <= 0), k' = 1 gives n
= m, and k' >= 2 gives degree > m + 1; with the nonzero order-m coefficient of g, the leading term is C1 (x - x1)^m y,
C1 != 0. If lambda_- = 0 the eigenvalues 0 and 2 c_l give the polynomial eigenvalues 2 c_l k', never 1, so the first
jet vanishes and induction on the Taylor equation makes rho flat. If m is odd, g changes sign at x1, so a point just
above the axis to the right of x1 has rho/a0 < 0; it is not in K (rho != 0), so it escapes with scattering angle in
(0, pi) by (vi), Theta0/a0 < 0 there, while Theta0(pi/2) = K has the sign of a0 (A.3.6); Theta0 has a zero in (0, pi).
(vi) In the exterior, r' = c_l r + O(r^p) and dth/dr = U_th/(r (c_l r + U_r)) with all angular derivatives O(r^{p-2})
(3.23). So log r - c_l t and th converge, every escaping orbit crosses a fixed large circle |X| = R exactly once
(crossing angle th, time t), and Q = e^{c_l t} A_R(th) e^{i S_R(th)} with A_R(th) = R exp(int_R^inf U_r/(s (c_l s +
U_r)) ds) > 0 and S_R the limiting angular map, a circle diffeomorphism (its derivative is exp of an integrable
integral). All of this converges in every C^k, so Q is a smooth diffeomorphism from the complement of K onto R^2 minus
{0}. The axes are invariant, so S_R fixes 0, pi/2, pi and the open quadrants are preserved. Since c_l p = 1, the
far-field limit and transport give rho = |Q|^p Theta0(arg Q); hence escaping trajectories in y > 0 with rho = 0
correspond (up to time translation) to zeros of Theta0 in (0, pi).
(vii) If (H-dyn) holds, each point of y > 0 tends backward to 0 inside y > 0, where rho has the sign of a0 y, so
rho/a0 > 0 on y > 0; each angle in (0, pi) is the scattering angle of an escaping orbit (invert S_R), on which rho !=
0, so Theta0 has no zero there. Conversely assume Theta0 has no zero in (0, pi) (hence, by reflection, none in (pi, 2
pi)); then by (vi) every nodal point off the axis lies in K. Suppose K != {0}. By connectedness K contains points of
every small radius, which are nodal and hence on the axis, where Pi(x, 0) = A x^2/2 + O(x^4) > 0, so max_K Pi > 0. Let
q be a maximizer; dPi/dt = |W|^2 on K forces W(q) = 0, and q != 0. By (iii) DW(q) has real eigenvalues, the largest,
lambda_max, being >= c_l > 1; fix sigma with 1 < sigma < lambda_max and sigma not an eigenvalue of DW(q). The local
strong unstable manifold of q for the part of the spectrum above sigma (a local ODE fact needing only this spectral
gap, no hyperbolicity or isolation) contains points other than q, and for its points |Phi_{-T} X - q| <= C e^{-sigma
T} for T >= 0. Since rho(q) = 0 and rho is Lipschitz, |rho(X)| = e^{T} |rho(Phi_{-T} X)| <= C e^{(1 - sigma) T} -> 0
as T -> inf, so they are nodal, and Pi(X) - Pi(q) = int_{-inf}^0 |W(Phi_t X)|^2 dt > 0 off q. If q
is off the axis, such X near q stay in the open half-plane of q, so X lies in K with Pi(X) > Pi(q), a contradiction.
If q = (x, 0), then DW(q) = diag(lambda_-, lambda_+) with lambda_- = w'(x); lambda_- > 0 is impossible, since Pi_x = w
vanishes at q, Pi_xx = lambda_- > 0, and K contains a short horizontal side of q (the axis part of K is [-x_*, x_*]),
so q would be a strict local minimum of Pi on K along the axis. If lambda_- <= 0, the strong unstable manifold for
lambda_+ = 2 c_l - lambda_- > 1 is tangent to the vertical, its upper branch enters y > 0, and its points lie in K
with larger Pi, again a contradiction. Hence K = {0}, and (v) gives (H-dyn).

## A.3.32 Second far-field term

Inverse estimate (condensed). Let f be smooth off 0, odd in y and even in x, locally integrable, with |D^k f| <= C_k
|X|^{b-k} for |X| >= 1, -3 < b < 1, and bounded derivatives on compact sets away from 0. Then its canonical velocity
(A.3.1(ii)) satisfies the same bounds. At |X| = R >= 2 split the density into |Y| < R/4, R/4 <= |Y| <= 4R and |Y| >
4R. The kernel K has degree -2. Near part: K(X) int f = 0 by central oddness, |D^k K(X - Y) - D^k K(X)| <= C |Y|
R^{-3-k}, and int_{|Y|<R/4} |Y| |f| <= C (1 + R^{b+3}) since b > -3, giving C R^{b-k}. Far part: subtracting K(-Y),
|D^k_X (K(X - Y) - K(-Y))| <= C R^{1-k} |Y|^{-3} for k = 0 and C |Y|^{-2-k} for k >= 1, and b < 1 gives C R^{b-k}.
Middle part: after rescaling to the unit annulus it is an order-zero singular integral of a density with uniformly
bounded derivatives, so derivatives fall on the density and give C R^{b-k}. Also, the canonical velocity of a
homogeneous density r^s Theta(th) (-1 < s < 1, Theta smooth, odd in y and even in x) is r^s (-Phi', (s + 1) Phi) with
stream function r^{s+1} Phi(th): it is homogeneous of degree s by scaling and uniqueness (3.1(i)), and -Lap(r^{s+1}
Phi) = d_x(r^s Theta) reads -Phi'' - (s + 1)^2 Phi = s cos th Theta - sin th Theta'. Phi is a sine series in sin(2n
th), n >= 1, and is unique, since the homogeneous solutions sin((s + 1) th), cos((s + 1) th) are not of this form for
0 < s + 1 < 2.
First term. With p = 1/c_l and the equation, d/dt [t^{-p} rho(tX)] = t^{-p-1} [-p rho + p c_l Y . grad rho](tX) = -p
t^{-p-1} (U . grad rho)(tX), and t^{-p} rho(tX) -> r^p Theta0(th) (3.7), so rho(X) - r^p Theta0(th) = (1/c_l)
int_1^inf t^{-p-1} (U . grad rho)(tX) dt. By 3.23, U . grad rho has symbol bounds of degree 2p - 1, and D^k_X of the
integrand is O(t^{p-2} r^{2p-1-k}), integrable since p < 1; so rho - r^p Theta0 has symbol bounds of degree 2p - 1.
The inverse estimate (b = 2p - 1 in (-1, 1)) and the homogeneous formula (s = p) give U = r^p u_0 + O(r^{2p-1}) with
all derivatives.
Second term. Using grad(r^p Theta0) = r^{p-1} (p Theta0 e_r + Theta0' e_th), U . grad rho = r^{2p-1} (p u_{0,r}
Theta0 + u_{0,th} Theta0') + O(r^{3p-2}) with symbol bounds, and inserting this in the integral, with (1/c_l)
int_1^inf t^{p-2} dt = 1/(c_l (1 - p)) = 1/D and int_1^inf t^{2p-3} dt < inf, gives rho = r^p Theta0 + r^{2p-1}
Theta1 + O(r^{3p-2}) with all derivatives. The inverse estimate with b = 3p - 2 in (-2, 1) and the homogeneous formula
with s = 2p - 1 in (-1, 1) (s + 1 = 2p) give U = r^p u_0 + r^{2p-1} u_1 + O(r^{3p-2}) with all derivatives.
u_0 is not zero. If u_0 = 0, then curl(r^p u_0) = -d_x(r^p Theta0) gives d_x(r^p Theta0) = 0 on R^2 minus {0}, so r^p
Theta0 = K sgn(y) |y|^p with K = Theta0(pi/2) != 0 (A.3.6), i.e. Theta0 = K sgn(sin th) |sin th|^p, which is not
differentiable at th = 0 for 0 < p < 1, contradicting smoothness of Theta0 (3.23). Hence max_{|X|=r} |U| = r^p max
|u_0| + O(r^{2p-1}) is comparable to r^p. At a zero th* of Theta0 the second term is r^{2p-1} u_{0,th}(th*)
Theta0'(th*)/D, which gives the scope remark.

## A.3.33 Two-sided bound under (H-dyn)

Axis. By 3.22, (H-dyn) gives g/a0 > 0 on the x-axis and rho/(a0 y) > 0 off it, so q is smooth (q = G/a0 with rho = y
G) and positive. On the axis w g' = (w' - A) g (3.21(iv)), and by 3.23 w = c_l x + O(x^p), w' = c_l + O(x^{p-1}).
Since c_l - A = 1 - c_l = c_l (p - 1), g'/g = (w' - A)/w = (p - 1)/x + O(x^{p-2}); the error is integrable at
infinity, so g = G x^{p-1} (1 + O(x^{p-1})) with G != 0 and G/a0 > 0. With F_r(th) := r^{-p} rho(r cos th, r sin th),
rho_y(r, 0) = r^{p-1} F_r'(0), and ||F_r - Theta0||_{C^1} <= C0 r^{p-1} (3.23) gives G = Theta0'(0), so
Theta0'(0)/a0 > 0.
Angles. By A.3.30(vii), Theta0 has no zero in (0, pi), and Theta0(pi/2) = K has the sign of a0 (A.3.6), so Theta0/a0 >
0 on (0, pi). Theta0 is odd in th about 0 and symmetric about pi/2 (parity), so H := Theta0/(a0 sin th) extends
continuously to [0, pi] with H(0) = H(pi) = Theta0'(0)/a0 > 0, and min_{[0,pi]} H > 0.
Bound. F_r - Theta0 vanishes at th = 0 and pi, so |F_r - Theta0|(th) <= C0 r^{p-1} min(th, pi - th) <= C r^{p-1} sin
th. For y > 0 (and by parity y < 0), q = rho/(a0 y) = r^{p-1} F_r/(a0 sin th) = r^{p-1} (H + O(r^{p-1})) uniformly in
th. Choose R1 >= 1 with the error at most (1/2) min H for r >= R1; then (1/2) min H r^{p-1} <= q <= 2 max H r^{p-1}
off the axis for r >= R1, and on the axis by continuity of q (or directly from the asymptotics of g). Since p < 1, for
r >= R1 >= 1 one has (1 + r)^{p-1} <= r^{p-1} <= 2^{1-p} (1 + r)^{p-1}. On the disk r <= R1, q is continuous and
positive, so m1 := min q > 0 and m2 := max q < inf there, while (1 + R1)^{p-1} <= (1 + r)^{p-1} <= 1. Hence kappa_1
(1 + |X|)^{p-1} <= q(X) <= kappa_2 (1 + |X|)^{p-1} on R^2 with kappa_1 := min(m1, (1/2) min H) > 0 and kappa_2 :=
max(m2 (1 + R1)^{1-p}, 2^{2-p} max H) >= kappa_1. Conversely, the lower bound gives rho/(a0 y) > 0 for y != 0, which
is (H-dyn) by 3.22 ((2) implies (1)).

## A.3.34 Sign transfer and critical escaping nodes

Notation of A.3.30; x_* = b is the largest nonnegative root of w (b = 0 if w has no positive root; 3.34(d)), and Q is
the scattering map of 3.30(vi).
(a) For X outside K with y > 0, |Q(X)|^p > 0 and arg Q(X) is in (0, pi), so rho(X)/a0 and Theta0(arg Q(X))/a0 have the
same sign; every angle in (0, pi) is attained (Q maps each open quadrant onto itself and the y-axis escapes, A.3.6),
and rho = 0 on K. Both equivalences follow.
(b) Let (H-dyn) fail and let q maximize Pi on K (q != 0 by A.3.30(vii)). q is not a hyperbolic source: if all
eigenvalues of B = DW(q) have positive real part, M := int_0^inf e^{-B^T t} e^{-B t} dt is positive definite with B^T
M + M B = I, so a small sublevel set V of (X - q)^T M (X - q) is backward invariant with all backward orbits tending
to q; for X in V intersect K, X != q, Pi(X) - Pi(q) = int_{-inf}^0 |W(Phi_t X)|^2 dt > 0, contradicting maximality, so
q would be isolated in the connected set K != {q}, impossible. By A.3.30(iii), grad rho(q) != 0 would give eigenvalues
1 and A (a hyperbolic source), so grad rho(q) = 0, DW(q) is symmetric with trace 2 c_l, and its eigenvalues are
lambda_- <= 0 and lambda_+ = 2 c_l - lambda_- >= 2 c_l (both positive is excluded). By parity Pi is even in x and in
y, so we may take q in the closed first quadrant; q is not on the y-axis, where W has no zero other than 0 (v > 0 in
A.3.6). If q = (x_q, 0), then w'(x_q) <= 0 as in A.3.30(vii) and the fast unstable direction is vertical; its upper
branch lies in the open first quadrant. If q is off the axes, both halves of its fast unstable curve lie in its open
quadrant. As in A.3.30(vii) these branches are nodal with Pi > Pi(q), hence escape, and distinct halves give distinct
angles; reflection in the y-axis gives at least two interior zeros of Theta0 symmetric about pi/2, and four if q is
off the axis.
Critical nodes. Along a nonstationary nodal trajectory put Wn := |W|, T = W/Wn, N = J T (J the quarter turn) and h =
grad rho . N, so grad rho = h N. Differentiating transport, d/dt grad rho = (I - DW^T) grad rho; with N . N' = 0 and
Wn'/Wn = T^T DW T this gives h' = (1 - N^T DW N) h and (h/Wn)' = (1 - tr DW)(h/Wn) = -A (h/Wn), so (h/Wn)(t) =
(h/Wn)(t0) e^{-A(t - t0)}. On a fast branch of q, grad rho(q) = 0 gives |h| <= C |X - q|, and Wn >= c |X - q| near q
(the tangent eigenvalue lambda_+ is nonzero), so h/Wn is bounded as t -> -inf, which forces h = 0 on the whole branch.
Writing rho = F o Q with F(R, th) = R^p Theta0(th), grad rho = DQ^T grad F with DQ invertible, so at the escape angle
th_*, Theta0(th_*) = Theta0'(th_*) = 0.
(e) If every zero of Theta0 in (0, pi) is simple, no such th_* exists, so (H-dyn) holds; otherwise the zero can be
reflected into (0, pi/2], and it is not pi/2 since Theta0(pi/2) = K != 0.
(f) Straighten one fast branch: smooth coordinates (s, n) with q = (0, 0), the branch {n = 0, s > 0}, and s' = v(s) +
O(n), n' = beta_n(s) n + O(n^2) with v(s) = lambda_+ s + O(s^2), beta_n(s) = lambda_- + O(s). If th_* has finite order
k, the scattering diffeomorphism gives rho exactly order k across the nonstationary part of the branch; with b_i(s) :=
d_n^i rho(s, 0)/i!, b_i = 0 for i < k (also at s = 0 by smoothness) and the order-k Taylor coefficient of the equation
is v b_k' + k beta_n b_k = b_k, with no lower terms. Hence b_k = C s^e E(s) with C != 0, E smooth, E(0) > 0 and e =
(1 - k lambda_-)/lambda_+, since (1 - k beta_n)/v - e/s is smooth at 0. As lambda_- <= 0 and lambda_+ = 2 c_l -
lambda_-, 0 < e = k - (2 k c_l - 1)/lambda_+ < k, and smoothness of b_k forces e to be an integer l in [1, k - 1],
i.e. k lambda_- + l lambda_+ = 1. Then lambda_- = (1 - 2 l c_l)/(k - l) < 0, and k = 1 is impossible (consistent with
the critical-node identity). If lambda_- = 0, then e = 1/(2 c_l) is not an integer, so no finite k exists and the zero
is flat. At an axis maximizer the fast curve is x = x_q + chi_b(y) with chi_b smooth, even, chi_b(0) = chi_b'(0) = 0;
with s = y and n = x - x_q - chi_b(y), reflection y -> -y sends (s, n) to (-s, n) and rho is odd, so each b_i is odd
and l is odd. If g has finite order m at x_q, then lambda_- = -A/(m - 1) (A.3.30(iv)); for i < m the exponent (1 - i
lambda_-)/lambda_+ lies in (0, 1), so successively b_i = 0, while b_m'(0) = g^(m)(x_q)/m! != 0 (chi_b'(0) = 0), so k =
m and l = 1.
(c) At a simple root x1 with w'(x1) = -A/(m - 1) < 0, g = C |x - x1|^m E on each side (A.3.30(iv)) with smooth
matching, so g changes sign at x1 exactly when m is odd; then g/a0 < 0 just to the right of x1, and since rho(x, y)/y
-> g(x) as y -> 0, rho/a0 < 0 on an open set just above that interval; (a) transfers this to Theta0. The periodic
fields W = ((A/k) sin kx, (2 c_l - A cos kx) y), rho = A (1 + cos kx) y have div W = A cos kx + 2 c_l - A cos kx = 2
c_l, curl W = A k y sin kx = -rho_x, and W . grad rho = A y [-A sin^2 kx + (A + 1 - A cos kx)(1 + cos kx)] = A y (1 +
cos kx) = rho (2 c_l = A + 1); DW(0) = diag(A, 1), w'(pi/k) = -A, m = 1 - A/w' = 2, rho >= 0 on y > 0, and rho(0, y) =
2A y violates the growth class.
(d) On (x_*, inf), w > 0 and w g' = (w' - A) g, so g is identically 0 there or of one sign; by 3.23, (w' - A)/w = (p -
1)/x + O(x^{p-2}), so g = G x^{p-1} (1 + O(x^{p-1})) with G = 0 in the zero case, and d_th rho(x cos th, x sin th) at
th = 0 equals x g(x), so C^1 angular convergence gives x^{1-p} g(x) -> Theta0'(0) = G. Let G != 0 and x_* > 0, and put
alpha_w := w'(x_*) >= 0. The axis orbit x(t) > x_* tends to x_* as t -> -inf, and along it g_dot = (w'(x(t)) - A) g;
if alpha_w = 0 the coefficient tends to -A and nonzero g would grow backward, contradicting boundedness, so
alpha_w > 0. If g(x_*) = 0, g/w is bounded near x_* while d(g/w)/dt = -A (g/w), again a contradiction; so g(x_*) != 0,
and (w' - A) g = 0 at x_* gives w'(x_*) = A.
(g) Assume every zero of W is nondegenerate. Zeros lie in K (compact) and are isolated, so finitely many. If (H-dyn)
fails, w has positive roots, all simple, with w > 0 near 0 and near infinity, so they number 2J >= 2 and alternate
downward and upward crossings. At a downward root the exponent analysis of A.3.30(iv) gives eigenvalues (-A/(m_j - 1),
2 c_l + A/(m_j - 1)), m_j >= 2 and nonzero g on both sides; at an upward root w' > 0, the exponent 1 - A/w' < 1 must
be 0, so w' = A, g != 0, eigenvalues (A, 1). With the origin and the reflections there are at least five zeros. Each
nondegenerate zero is a source or a saddle (eigenvalues (1, A), or a symmetric matrix of positive trace). On a large
