circle W is homotopic through nonzero fields to c_l X, so the indices sum to 1; the origin has index 1, the axis
sources and saddles cancel, there are no zeros on the y-axis, and reflections group off-axis zeros in quadruples, so
each quadrant has equally many off-axis sources and saddles. g never vanishes off the axis saddles, and by the
matching of A.3.30(iv) its sign flips exactly at odd m_j, so beyond the last root it is (-1)^M sgn(a0), M = m_1 +
... + m_J. (h) If X . U >= -(c_l - eps) |X|^2, then X . W >= eps |X|^2 and d|X|^2/dt >= 2 eps |X|^2 along orbits, so W
has no zero other than 0 and every nonzero orbit tends to 0 backward and escapes forward; sup |DU|_op < c_l suffices
because U(0) = 0.
Non-profile test. Let a = +-1, c_l = 2 (so p = 1/2 and A = 3), tau = -2 + 5a/2, and

    rho = a y (1 + r^2)^{-1/4} (1 - 2 x^2/(1 + r^2)) + 4 tau x^2 y e^{-r^2},

with its canonical velocity U and stream function psi (A.3.1, which does not use exactness). rho is smooth, odd in y
and even in x. Since sin th cos^2 th = (sin th + sin 3th)/4, rho = g1(r) sin th + g3(r) sin 3th with g1 = a r (1 +
r^2)^{-1/4} (1 - r^2/(2 (1 + r^2))) + tau r^3 e^{-r^2} and g3 = -(a/2) r^3 (1 + r^2)^{-5/4} + tau r^3 e^{-r^2}.
Strain: a0 = a, int_0^inf s (1 + s^2)^{-5/4} ds = 2 and int_0^inf s e^{-s^2} ds = 1/2, so A.3.2 gives c = -a/4 - a +
tau/2 = -5a/4 + tau/2 = -1; hence 1 - c = 2 = c_l, and DW(0) = c_l I + diag(-c, c) = diag(3, 1) = diag(A, 1).
Far field: with u = r^{-2}, g1 = a r^{1/2} (1 + u)^{-1/4} (1 - 1/(2 (1 + u))) + tau r^3 e^{-r^2} and g3 = -(a/2)
r^{1/2} (1 + u)^{-5/4} + tau r^3 e^{-r^2}, so rho = r^{1/2} Theta0(th) + f with Theta0 = (a/2) (sin th - sin 3th) = a
sin th (1 - 2 cos^2 th) = -a sin th cos 2th and |D^k f| <= C_k r^{-3/2-k} for r >= 1. Thus rho is in the growth class
with gamma = 1/2, and Theta0 has exactly the zeros pi/4 and 3 pi/4 in (0, pi), both simple.
Velocity. With cos th sin 3th = (sin 4th + sin 2th)/2 and sin th cos 3th = (sin 4th - sin 2th)/2, d_x (r^{1/2} Theta0)
= r^{-1/2} (p cos th Theta0 - sin th Theta0') = a r^{-1/2} (-sin 2th + (5/8) sin 4th). Only the modes f_1, f_2 of
A.3.1(iv) are nonzero, they are bounded near 0, and f_n = A_n r^{-1/2} + e_n with A_1 = -a, A_2 = 5a/8 and e_n =
O(r^{-5/2}) for r >= 1 (also |e_n| <= C r^{-1/2} for r <= 1). In the formula of 3.1(iv) (m = 2n) and its derivative
psi_n' = (1/2) [ -r^{-m-1} int_0^r s^{m+1} f_n ds + r^{m-1} int_r^inf s^{1-m} f_n ds ], the part A_n s^{-1/2} gives
exactly A_n r^{3/2}/(m^2 - 9/4) and (3/2) A_n r^{1/2}/(m^2 - 9/4) (the integrals converge as m > 3/2), and the part
e_n gives O(r^{-1/2}) and O(r^{-3/2}) for r >= 1. With m^2 - 9/4 = 7/4 and 55/4,

    psi = r^{3/2} Phi0(th) + O(r^{-1/2}),   Phi0 = a (-(4/7) sin 2th + (1/22) sin 4th),

and -Phi0'' - (9/4) Phi0 = a (-sin 2th + (5/8) sin 4th) (the homogeneous formula of A.3.32 with s = 1/2). Hence U_th =
psi_r = (3/2) r^{1/2} Phi0 + O(r^{-3/2}) and U_r = -psi_th/r = -r^{1/2} Phi0' + O(r^{-3/2}).
The ray th = pi/4. There Theta0 = 0 and Theta0' = (a/2)(cos th - 3 cos 3th) = a sqrt(2), so d_r rho = O(r^{-5/2}) and
r^{-1} d_th rho = a sqrt(2) r^{-1/2} + O(r^{-5/2}). Therefore U . grad rho = U_r d_r rho + U_th r^{-1} d_th rho =
(3/2) Phi0(pi/4) a sqrt(2) + O(r^{-2}) = (3/2)(-4a/7)(a sqrt(2)) + O(r^{-2}) = -6 sqrt(2)/7 + O(r^{-2}), for both
signs since a^2 = 1. On the ray sin th = sin 3th = 1/sqrt(2), and since (1 + r^2) - r^2/2 - r^2/2 = 1, g1 + g3 = a r
(1 + r^2)^{-5/4} + 2 tau r^3 e^{-r^2}; so rho(r, pi/4) = (a/sqrt(2)) r^{-3/2} (1 + O(r^{-2})) up to a Gaussian term,
and as (2 r d_r - 1) r^{-3/2} = -4 r^{-3/2}, the linear part is c_l X . grad rho - rho = -2 sqrt(2) a r^{-3/2} +
O(r^{-7/2}). Hence R = (c_l X + U) . grad rho - rho = -6 sqrt(2)/7 + O(r^{-3/2}) on the ray: transport fails, and rho
is not a profile, for either sign. For the normalized residuals, |rho| and |X . grad rho| are O(r^{-3/2}), so N_v = 6
sqrt(2)/7 + O(r^{-3/2}) and |R|/N_v -> 1. Further grad rho = a r^{-1/2} (-1, 1) + O(r^{-5/2}) (e_th = (-1,
1)/sqrt(2)), c_l X = sqrt(2) r (1, 1) and U = O(r^{1/2}), so each of |(c_l x + U_1) rho_x| and |(c_l y + U_2) rho_y|
is sqrt(2) r^{1/2} + O(1), N_f = 2 sqrt(2) r^{1/2} + O(1) and |R|/N_f = O(r^{-1/2}) -> 0. (The two large terms cancel
in R because grad rho is nearly orthogonal to X on the ray.)
Role in (e). Together with A.3.30(vii), (e) says that Theta0 of an exact profile cannot have zeros in (0, pi) all of
which are simple (such zeros would make (H-dyn) fail by A.3.30(vii), while (e) would give (H-dyn)). The example has
the parities, the growth class, its canonical velocity and DW(0) = diag(A, 1), and its Theta0 has exactly such zeros;
so this consequence depends on transport, which the computation above shows to fail.
Local transport models. These are fields near a point q = (0, 0), in coordinates (s, n), with div W = 2 c_l and W .
grad rho = rho; they do not satisfy curl W = -rho_x and are not canonical velocities, so they show only that the local
analysis of (f) cannot by itself exclude the cases it leaves open. (1) Resonances: for integers k >= 2 and 1 <= l <=
k - 1 put lambda_- = (1 - 2 l c_l)/(k - l) < 0, lambda_+ = 2 c_l - lambda_-, W = (lambda_+ s, lambda_- n) and rho =
s^l n^k. Then div W = 2 c_l and W . grad rho = (l lambda_+ + k lambda_-) rho = ((k - l) lambda_- + 2 l c_l) rho = rho;
grad rho(q) = 0 since k + l >= 3; {n = 0, s > 0} is the fast unstable branch, rho vanishes to order exactly k across
it, and b_k(s) = s^l, so e = l and k lambda_- + l lambda_+ = 1. Every pair (k, l) allowed in (f) occurs. (2) Flat
zero: for C > 0 and an integer l >= 1 put W = ((2 c_l + 3 C n^2) s, -C n^3), and rho = s^l n^{3l} E(n) with E(n) =
exp(-(2 c_l l - 1)/(2 C n^2)) for n != 0, rho = 0 for n = 0. Since 2 c_l l - 1 > 0, rho is smooth and flat on {n =
0}. div W = 2 c_l + 3 C n^2 - 3 C n^2 = 2 c_l, and for n != 0, using E'/E = (2 c_l l - 1)/(C n^3), W . grad rho = rho
[l (2 c_l + 3 C n^2) - 3 l C n^2 - (2 c_l l - 1)] = rho, which also holds on n = 0. DW(q) = diag(2 c_l, 0), so
lambda_- = 0 and lambda_+ = 2 c_l, and rho vanishes to infinite order across the fast branch {n = 0, s > 0}: this is
the flat case of (f).

(i) In the setting of (f), grad Pi = W + rho e_2 gives DW = D^2 Pi - e_2 grad rho^T, so DW(q) = D^2 Pi(q) is symmetric
because grad rho(q) = 0, with eigenvalues lambda_- <= 0 and lambda_+ = 2 c_l - lambda_-. Hence DU(q) = DW(q) - c_l I
is symmetric with eigenvalues lambda_- - c_l and lambda_+ - c_l = c_l - lambda_-, so it is trace-free and |DU(q)|_op =
c_l - lambda_-. The resonance of (f), k lambda_- + l lambda_+ = 1 with 1 <= l <= k - 1, gives lambda_- = (1 - 2 l
c_l)/(k - l), so |DU(q)|_op = c_l + (2 c_l l - 1)/(k - l); this increases with l (numerator increasing and positive,
denominator decreasing and positive), so it is >= c_l + (2 c_l - 1)/(k - 1) = c_l + A/(k - 1). For k = 2 only l = 1 is
allowed and the value is 3 c_l - 1, while DU(0) = diag(c_l - 1, 1 - c_l) (3.2) has operator norm c_l - 1.
Consequence. Let M >= 2 be an integer (unrelated to the M of (g)), and assume that every zero of Theta0 in (0, pi) has
finite order at most M and that |DU|_op < c_l + A/(M - 1) at every nonzero zero of W where grad rho vanishes. If
(H-dyn) failed, (b) would give the maximizer q != 0 of Pi on K, with W(q) = 0 and grad rho(q) = 0, and the
critical-node identity would give an escape angle th_* in (0, pi) with Theta0(th_*) = Theta0'(th_*) = 0. By assumption
th_* has finite order k, so 2 <= k <= M, and (f) applies; then |DU(q)|_op >= c_l + A/(k - 1) >= c_l + A/(M - 1),
contradicting the assumed bound. Hence (H-dyn) holds. Both assumptions are needed for this argument: (f) gives nothing
for a flat zero, and for M = 1 all zeros are simple and (e) applies instead.

## A.3.35 Energy lower bound on gradients

Setup. Let rho be an exact profile of the primary class. By 3.23, |D^j rho| + |D^j U| <= C_j (1 + r)^{p-j}, so G_rho,
G_U < inf and D^j rho, D^j U are in L^2 for j >= 2 (2(p - j) + 2 < 0 as p < 1). Since grad rho_l(X) = (grad rho)(X/l)
and DU_l(X) = (DU)(X/l) (A.3.5), G_rho and G_U are dilation invariant. Norms of tensors are Frobenius norms over
ordered indices.

Identity. Fix k >= 2 and write f = D^k rho. Since [d_i, x_m d_m] = d_i, D^k(X . grad rho) = X . grad f + k f, and
D^k(U . grad rho) = U . grad f + C_k with C_k := [D^k, U . grad] rho = sum_{j=1}^k binom(k, j) D^j U_m D^{k-j} d_m rho
(symmetrized over the free indices). Hence the k-th derivative of c_l X . grad rho + U . grad rho = rho reads c_l X .
grad f + (k c_l - 1) f + U . grad f + C_k = 0. Pair with chi_R f, chi_R(X) = chi(X/R), chi = 1 on B_1, supported in
B_2. Integration by parts (div X = 2, div U = 0) gives int chi_R (X . grad f) . f = -int chi_R |f|^2 - (1/2) int (X .
grad chi_R) |f|^2 and int chi_R (U . grad f) . f = -(1/2) int (U . grad chi_R) |f|^2. As |X . grad chi_R| <= C and |U|
|grad chi_R| <= C R^{p-1} on the annulus R < r < 2R, both errors are bounded by C int_{R<r<2R} |f|^2 -> 0. The pairing
int chi_R C_k . f converges absolutely: C_k is a sum of products of bounded factors and one factor D^j U or D^{k-j+1}
rho of order >= 2, or of two L^4 factors as below. Letting R -> inf,

    ((k - 1) c_l - 1) ||D^k rho||_2^2 = - < D^k rho, [D^k, U . grad] rho >.

Multiplier bound. From div U = 0, curl U = -rho_x one has -Lap U = (-d_xy rho, d_xx rho), so for j >= 2 the Fourier
transforms of D^j U and m(xi) D^j rho, m = (xi1 xi2, -xi1^2)/|xi|^2, agree away from 0. Both are L^2 functions, so
their difference is a polynomial (Fourier support at 0) in L^2, hence zero. As |m_1|^2 + |m_2|^2 = xi1^2/|xi|^2 <= 1,
Plancherel gives ||D^j U||_2 <= ||D^j rho||_2 for j >= 2.

Interpolation. For a smooth (vector valued) v with |D^i v| <= C (1 + r)^{-i - theta}, i <= 2, theta > 0 (which holds
for v = grad rho and v = DU by 3.23, with theta = 1 - p), integrate by parts on B_R (the boundary term is O(R^{1 - 4
theta - 3}) -> 0): int |Dv|^4 = -int v_a (Lap v_a |Dv|^2 + d_i v_a d_i |Dv|^2). Pointwise |v_a Lap v_a| <= |v| sqrt(2)
|D^2 v| (in two dimensions (v_xx + v_yy)^2 <= 2 (v_xx^2 + v_yy^2)), and with w_i = v_a d_i v_a, |w| <= |v| |Dv|, |v_a
d_i v_a d_i |Dv|^2| = 2 |w_i d_j v_b d_ij v_b| <= 2 |v| |Dv|^2 |D^2 v| by Cauchy-Schwarz. So int |Dv|^4 <= (2 + sqrt
2) ||v||_inf int |Dv|^2 |D^2 v| <= (2 + sqrt 2) ||v||_inf ||Dv||_4^2 ||D^2 v||_2, i.e.

    ||D v||_4^2 <= (2 + sqrt 2) ||v||_inf ||D^2 v||_2.

Nonvanishing. If D^k rho = 0, rho is a polynomial; the growth bound with gamma < 1 makes it constant, and oddness in y
makes it 0, contradicting a0 != 0. So ||D^k rho||_2 > 0 and the identity may be divided by it.

k = 2. C_2 consists of two terms of the form d_i U_m d_jm rho, each bounded pointwise by |DU| |D^2 rho| <= G_U |D^2
rho|, and d_ij U_m d_m rho, bounded by |D^2 U| G_rho. Hence |<D^2 rho, C_2>| <= 2 G_U ||D^2 rho||_2^2 + G_rho ||D^2
U||_2 ||D^2 rho||_2 <= (2 G_U + G_rho) ||D^2 rho||_2^2, and the identity gives c_l - 1 <= 2 G_U + G_rho.

k = 3. C_3 has three terms bounded by G_U |D^3 rho|, three bounded by |D^2 U| |D^2 rho| and one bounded by |D^3 U|
G_rho. The first and last contribute <= (3 G_U + G_rho) ||D^3 rho||_2^2 (multiplier bound with j = 3). For the middle
terms, by Holder and the interpolation with v = DU and v = grad rho, 3 int |D^3 rho| |D^2 U| |D^2 rho| <= 3 ||D^3
rho||_2 ||D^2 U||_4 ||D^2 rho||_4 <= 3 (2 + sqrt 2) ||D^3 rho||_2 (G_U ||D^3 U||_2 G_rho ||D^3 rho||_2)^{1/2} <= 3
(2 + sqrt 2) sqrt(G_U G_rho) ||D^3 rho||_2^2. With (k - 1) c_l - 1 = 2 c_l - 1 this gives

    2 c_l - 1 <= 3 G_U + G_rho + 3 (2 + sqrt 2) sqrt(G_U G_rho).

Consequences. With S = G_rho + G_U, 3 G_U + G_rho <= 3 S and sqrt(G_U G_rho) <= S/2, so 2 c_l - 1 <= (6 + 3 sqrt(2)/2)
S = C_* S; as c_l > 1, S > 1/C_*. If S <= M (c_l - 1) along a family, then M (c_l - 1) >= (2 c_l - 1)/C_* > 1/C_*,
i.e. c_l - 1 > 1/(C_* M). Origin values: grad rho(0) = (0, a0) and DU(0) = DW(0) - c_l I = diag(c_l - 1, 1 - c_l)
(3.2), so G_rho >= |a0| and G_U >= sqrt(2) (c_l - 1). Then 2 G_U + G_rho >= 2 sqrt(2) (c_l - 1) > c_l - 1, so the k =
2 bound is implied by the origin values. The bound S >= (2 c_l - 1)/C_* improves on S >= |a0| + sqrt(2) (c_l - 1) only
if (2 c_l - 1)/C_* > |a0| + sqrt(2) (c_l - 1); this needs (2 c_l - 1) > sqrt(2) C_* (c_l - 1), i.e. c_l < (sqrt(2)
C_* - 1)/(sqrt(2) C_* - 2) = (6 sqrt 2 + 2)/(6 sqrt 2 + 1) < 1.106, and |a0| < (2 c_l - 1)/C_*. The bounds are lower
bounds on suprema only; they locate nothing and give no upper bound.

## A.3.36 Sharper energy constants and a conditional strain-cap exclusion

Conventions are those of Appendix A, with D = c_l - 1, A = 2 c_l - 1 = 1 + 2 D and B = A - 1.

Setup. As in A.3.35: rho is an exact profile of the primary class; G_rho and G_U are finite; D^j rho and D^j U are in
L^2 for j >= 2; f = D^k rho; E_k = ||D^k rho||_2^2 > 0 (Nonvanishing in A.3.35); and tensor norms are Frobenius norms
over ordered indices. For an ordered index I = (i_1, ..., i_k) and J a subset of {1, ..., k}, let I_J be the indices
in the slots of J. The Leibniz rule gives d_I (U_m d_m rho) = U . grad f_I + (C_k)_I with

    (C_k)_I = sum_{J nonempty} (d_{I_J} U_m) (d_{I \ J} d_m rho),

which is the commutator [D^k, U . grad] rho of A.3.35. The origin values are grad rho(0) = (0, a0) and DU(0) = S(0) =
diag(D, -D) (3.2). Hence sigma >= D and G_rho >= |a0|.

(i) Interpolation with constant 3. Let v be smooth (vector valued) with |D^i v| <= C (1 + r)^{-i-theta} for i <= 2 and
some theta > 0. For v = grad rho and v = DU this is 3.23 with theta = 1 - p. As in A.3.35, integration by parts on
B_R, with boundary term O(R^{-2-4 theta}), gives int |Dv|^4 = -int v_a (Lap v_a |Dv|^2 + d_i v_a d_i |Dv|^2).
Pointwise, |v_a Lap v_a| <= |v| |Lap v| with |Lap v|^2 = sum_a (Lap v_a)^2, and |v_a d_i v_a d_i |Dv|^2| <= 2 |v|
|Dv|^2 |D^2 v| (A.3.35). Hence

    ||Dv||_4^4 <= ||v||_inf ||Dv||_4^2 (||Lap v||_2 + 2 ||D^2 v||_2).

A.3.35 used the pointwise bound |Lap v| <= sqrt 2 |D^2 v|. The improvement replaces it by the identity ||Lap v_a||_2 =
||D^2 v_a||_2. On R^2 \ {0} the Fourier transforms of d_ij v_a and of (xi_i xi_j/|xi|^2) Lap v_a agree, since both
equal -xi_i xi_j hat v_a there. Both are L^2 functions (|xi_i xi_j| <= |xi|^2), so their difference is supported at 0
and lies in L^2, hence is 0. Since sum_{i,j} xi_i^2 xi_j^2/|xi|^4 = 1, Plancherel gives the identity. Dividing by
||Dv||_4^2 (the case Dv = 0 is trivial) gives

    ||Dv||_4^2 <= 3 ||v||_inf ||D^2 v||_2.

(ii) First-order terms and k = 3. The terms of C_k with |J| = 1 are those with J = {l}, l = 1, ..., k. Fix l and the
indices outside slot l, and put w_i = f_I with i in slot l. The contribution of these terms to the pointwise sum sum_I
f_I (C_k)_I is sum_{i,m} w_i (d_i U_m) w_m = w^T S w, because the antisymmetric part of DU does not contribute to a
quadratic form. It is therefore bounded by |S|_op |w|^2. Summing over the other indices and over l, the first-order
terms contribute at most k |S|_op |f|^2 pointwise, and at most k sigma E_k after integration.

For k = 3 there are three terms with |J| = 2. By Cauchy-Schwarz over m and the ordered indices, each is bounded
pointwise by |f| |D^2 U| |D^2 rho|. The term J = {1, 2, 3} is bounded by |f| |D^3 U| |grad rho|. Hence

    |< f, C_3 >| <= 3 sigma E_3 + 3 ||D^3 rho||_2 ||D^2 U||_4 ||D^2 rho||_4 + G_rho ||D^3 U||_2 ||D^3 rho||_2.

By (i) with v = DU and v = grad rho, ||D^2 U||_4^2 <= 3 G_U ||D^3 U||_2 and ||D^2 rho||_4^2 <= 3 G_rho ||D^3 rho||_2.
By the multiplier bound of A.3.35, ||D^3 U||_2 <= ||D^3 rho||_2. The middle term is therefore <= 9 sqrt(G_U G_rho) E_3
and the last <= G_rho E_3. In the identity of A.3.35, (k - 1) c_l - 1 = 2 c_l - 1, and dividing by E_3 > 0 gives

    2 c_l - 1 <= 3 sigma + G_rho + 9 sqrt(G_U G_rho).

Strain versus gradient. Write DU = S + Omega with Omega antisymmetric, so |DU|^2 = |S|^2 + |Omega|^2. S is trace free
(div U = 0), so its eigenvalues are +-lambda and |S|_op = |S|/sqrt 2. Hence sigma <= G_U/sqrt 2. With x = sqrt(G_rho)
and y = sqrt(G_U), the right side above is at most x^2 + 9 x y + (3/sqrt 2) y^2 = (x, y) M (x, y)^T, with M = [[1,
9/2], [9/2, 3/sqrt 2]]. This is <= Lambda (x^2 + y^2), where Lambda is the largest eigenvalue of M:

    Lambda = (1 + t)/2 + sqrt((1 - t)^2/4 + 81/4) = 6.0954523...,  t = 3/sqrt 2.

So G_rho + G_U >= (2 c_l - 1)/Lambda. Lambda is smaller than C_* = 6 + 3 sqrt(2)/2 = 8.12... of A.3.35. The gain comes
from (i) and from the bound sigma <= G_U/sqrt 2 in the first-order terms.

(iii) Strain cap. Assume sigma <= D. Since U(0) = 0,

    X . U(X) = int_0^1 X^T DU(t X) X dt = int_0^1 X^T S(t X) X dt >= -D |X|^2,

so X . W = c_l |X|^2 + X . U >= |X|^2. In particular W has no zero other than 0, which is (H-dyn). W is smooth with
|W| <= C (1 + |X|) (3.1(iii)), so the flow Phi_t is global. Along an orbit, d/dt |Phi_t X|^2 = 2 Phi_t X . W(Phi_t
X) >= 2 |Phi_t X|^2, so |Phi_t X| <= e^t |X| for t <= 0, and every backward orbit tends to 0.

Differentiating W . grad rho = rho gives W . grad g = (I - DW^T) g for g = grad rho (A.3.29). Since g . (DW^T g) = c_l
|g|^2 + g^T S g,

    W . grad (|g|^2/2) = -D |g|^2 - g^T S g <= (sigma - D) |g|^2 <= 0,

and |grad rho| is nonincreasing along forward orbits. For X != 0 and t <= 0, |grad rho(X)| <= |grad rho(Phi_t X)|,
which tends to |grad rho(0)| = |a0| as t -> -inf. So G_rho = |a0|. Finally, curl U = -rho_x, so |DU|^2 = |S|^2 +
rho_x^2/2 <= 2 sigma^2 + a0^2/2 <= 2 D^2 + a0^2/2, which is the stated bound on G_U.

Exclusion. Let 0 < D <= 1/2, 0 < a := |a0| <= 1/400 and sigma <= D (so sigma = D). By (ii), 1 + 2 D <= 3 D + a + 9
sqrt(a G_U), and with the bound on G_U,

    1 - D <= a + 9 sqrt(a G_U) <= a + 9 (a (2 D^2 + a^2/2)^{1/2})^{1/2}.

The right side increases in D and in a. At D = 1/2 and a = 1/400: 2 D^2 + a^2/2 = 1/2 + 1/320000 < (71/100)^2, and
(1/400)(71/100) = 71/40000 < (17/400)^2 = 289/160000. So the right side is < 1/400 + 9 (17/400) = 154/400 < 1/2 <= 1 -
D, a contradiction. The exact worst value is about 0.3809. Hence no exact profile has 1 < c_l <= 3/2, 0 < |a0| <=
1/400 and sigma <= c_l - 1. An exact symbolic and numerical check (accompanying artifacts) confirms the value of
Lambda, the positive semidefiniteness of Lambda I - M, the rational inequalities and a grid evaluation of the last
display.

Remark 2. Let C_k' denote the terms of C_k with |J| >= 2. Separating the first-order terms, the identity of A.3.35
gives ((k - 1) c_l - 1) E_k <= k sigma E_k + |< f, C_k' >|. If |< f, C_k' >| = o(k E_k) along a sequence k -> inf,
dividing by k E_k gives c_l - (c_l + 1)/k <= sigma + o(1), hence sigma >= c_l. This deduction rests on an unproved
hypothesis and is not a result.

Remark 3 (condensed). Base. Let rho* be a smooth density of the class with canonical velocity U* and W* = c_l X + U*,
such that c* = 1 - c_l, a0* = a0 != 0, G_rho* < inf and X . W* > 0 for X != 0. Then X . W* >= eps0 |X|^2 for some
eps0 > 0: near 0, U* = (D x, -D y) + O(r^3) by parity alone (as in A.3.2), so X . W* = A x^2 + y^2 + O(r^4); at infinity
|U*| <= C (1 + r)^gamma; in between use compactness.

Such a base exists unconditionally. Take F0 smooth, radial and nonincreasing, with F0 = 1 on [0, 1] and F0 = r^{p-1}
on [2, inf), and put rho_b = a y F0(r) with a = 4 D. Its only mode is rho_1 = a r F0. By 3.1(iv), psi_b = 2 H(r) x y
with H(r) = -(a/2) r^{-4} int_0^r s^3 F0(s) ds, and 0 < F0 <= 1 gives -a/8 <= H < 0. Since X . U = -d_th psi and d_th
psi_b = 2 r^2 H cos 2th, X . U_b >= -2 r^2 |H| >= -D r^2 and X . W_b >= |X|^2. Moreover c_b = -a/4 = 1 - c_l (3.2),
Theta0 = a sin th, G_rho,b < inf, and on B_1, U_b = (D x, -D y) and the residual of rho_b vanishes. If an exact
profile with outward flow exists, it may serve as rho* instead.

Perturbation. Fix 0 < r1 < r2, f in C_c^inf((r1, r2)) with f >= 0 and f != 0, an integer N >= 4, eps > 0 and delta_N =
eps/(1 + log N). Put

    h_N = delta_N f(r) sin th cos(2N th) = (delta_N/2) f(r) [sin((2N + 1) th) - sin((2N - 1) th)].

h_N is smooth, compactly supported, even in x and odd in y. So rho = rho* + h_N is in the class, with canonical
velocity U* + U[h_N] (linearity and 3.1(i)). By 3.1(iv), only the modes n = N - 1, N, N + 1 of psi[h_N] are nonzero.
For r < r1, psi_n = (1/2) r^{2n} int s^{-2n} rho_{2n+1} ds, so

    psi[h_N] = C_{N-1} Im (x + i y)^{2N-2} + C_N Im (x + i y)^{2N}  on B_{r1},
    C_{N-1} = -(delta_N/4) int_{r1}^{r2} s^{2-2N} f(s) ds != 0.

This function is harmonic on B_{r1}. Hence rho = rho* near 0 (all jets of rho at 0 agree), U - U* = O(r^{2N-3}) (the
jets of U agree to order 2N - 4), a0 and c are unchanged, and, as rho - rho* has compact support, Theta0 is unchanged.

Outward flow. The kernel form 3.1(ii) is split at |Z| = 1/N. On |Z| < 1/N, the zero circular mean of K gives the bound
||grad h_N||_inf/N. On |Z| >= 1/N, the bound |K| <= 1/(2pi |Z|^2) over a disk of radius r2 gives at most ||h_N||_inf
log(1 + N r2), and the local term -(h_N/2) e_2 is bounded by ||h_N||_inf/2. With ||grad h_N||_inf <= delta_N
(||f'||_inf + (2N + 1) ||f||_inf/r1), this yields ||U[h_N]||_inf <= C_f delta_N (1 + log N) = C_f eps. On B_{r1/2},
the gradient estimate for the harmonic field U[h_N] on B_{r1} and U[h_N](0) = 0 give |U[h_N](X)| <= (4/r1) C_f eps
|X|, and for |X| >= r1/2, |U[h_N](X)| <= C_f eps <= (2/r1) C_f eps |X|. So |U[h_N](X)| <= C1 eps |X| everywhere, with
C1 independent of N and eps, and X . W >= (eps0 - C1 eps) |X|^2 > 0 for eps < eps0/C1.

Size. Pick r0 with f(r0) > 0 and th_N = pi/2 + pi/(4N), so that cos(2N th_N) = 0 and |sin(2N th_N)| = 1. At X0 = r0
(cos th_N, sin th_N), d_r h_N = 0 and |d_x h_N| = 2N delta_N f(r0) sin^2(th_N)/r0 >= N delta_N f(r0)/r0, as
sin^2(th_N) = cos^2(pi/(4N)) > 1/2. Since |DU|^2 >= (curl U)^2/2 = rho_x^2/2,

    G_rho >= N delta_N f(r0)/r0 - G_rho*,  G_U >= (N delta_N f(r0)/r0 - G_rho*)/sqrt 2,

and N delta_N = eps N/(1 + log N) -> inf.

Not a profile. If rho were an exact profile with some speed c_l', the origin relation (3.2) with the unchanged c would
give c_l' = c_l. If rho* is exact, then on B_{r1} the residual of rho is U[h_N] . grad rho* = a0 C_{N-1} (2N - 2) Im
(x + i y)^{2N-3} + O(r^{2N-2}), which is not identically zero. If rho* is not exact, choose X1 with residual R*(X1) !=
0 and the annulus (r1, r2) not containing |X1|; then the residual of rho at X1 is R*(X1) + U[h_N](X1) . grad rho*(X1),
which is nonzero for eps small. In both cases rho is not an exact profile.

## A.3.37 The limit c_l -> 1

(i) By 3.23, |grad rho| <= C (1 + r)^{p-1} -> 0 at infinity. So for a != 0, sup |grad rho - a e_2| >= limsup_{r ->
inf} |grad rho - a e_2| = |a|. A dilate rho_l is an exact profile with the same c_l (A.3.5), so the bound applies to
it as well. Hence the global C^1 distance to a y is >= |a|. (The C^0 part is even infinite, since |rho| <= C (1 +
r)^p.)

(ii) By A.3.35, 2 c_l - 1 <= C_* (G_rho + G_U) <= C_* M |a0| <= C_* M K D. Since 2 c_l - 1 = 1 + 2 D, this is (C_* M
K - 2) D >= 1. If C_* M K <= 2, the left side is <= 0, a contradiction; otherwise D >= 1/(C_* M K - 2). With 3.36(ii) in
place of A.3.35, the same argument gives (Lambda M K - 2) D >= 1.

(iii) Modes. q_1 = a y chi(r) + b r sin(3 th) eta(r), with b = (a/4 - D)/J, is smooth, compactly supported, even in x
and odd in y. Its only modes are rho_1 = a r chi(r) and rho_3 = b r eta(r).

Mode sin 2th. In the derivative-free form of 3.1(iv) with m = 2, for r <= 1: int_0^r s^2 rho_1 ds = a r^4/4, and
int_r^inf s^{-2} rho_3 ds = b int eta(s) ds/s = b J, since eta is supported in (2, 3). Hence

    psi_1 = (1/2) [r^2 b J - a r^2/4] = (r^2/2)(b J - a/4) = -D r^2/2,

and psi_1 sin 2th = -D x y. The f_n form agrees. On [0, 1], f_1 = 0, because rho_1' - rho_1/r = 0 and rho_3 = 0.
Moreover s^{-1} f_1 = (1/2)(rho_1/s)' + (1/2)(rho_3/s)' + 2 s^{-2} rho_3, so int_r^inf s^{-1} f_1 = -a/2 + 2 b J and
psi_1 = (r^2/4)(-a/2 + 2 b J) = -D r^2/2.

Mode sin 4th. Here rho_5 = 0, so f_2 = (1/2)(rho_3' - 3 rho_3/r) and s^{-3} f_2 = (1/2)(s^{-3} rho_3)', a total
derivative. For r < 2, int_0^r s^5 f_2 ds = 0 and int_r^inf s^{-3} f_2 ds = -(1/2) r^{-3} rho_3(r) = 0, so psi_2 = 0.
(Equivalently, both integrals in the derivative-free form with m = 4 vanish for r < 2.)

Higher modes. f_n involves only rho_{2n-1} and rho_{2n+1}, which vanish for n >= 3.

Conclusion for q_1. psi = -D x y on B_1, and the canonical velocity is v_1 = (-psi_y, psi_x) = (D x, -D y) there. v_1
is smooth (3.1(ii)), and Dv_1 = O(|X|^{-3}) at infinity (kernel estimate), so Dv_1 is bounded.

Dilation. One checks directly that q_L(X) = L q_1(X/L). By A.3.5, v_L(X) = L v_1(X/L), grad q_L(X) = grad q_1(X/L) and
Dv_L(X) = Dv_1(X/L). So the gradient bounds do not depend on L, and v_L = (D x, -D y) on B_L. There q_L = a y, and

    (c_l X + v_L) . grad q_L - q_L = a y (c_l - D - 1) = 0.

q_L is compactly supported, so r^{-p} q_L -> 0 for every p, while an exact profile has Theta0(pi/2) = K != 0 (3.7).
Hence q_L is not an exact profile for any speed. The last sentence of (iii) restates what this example shows. Two
exact symbolic and numerical checks (accompanying artifacts) confirm psi_1 = -D r^2/2 and psi_2 = 0 on B_1 by
quadrature of both modal forms, and v_1 = (D x, -D y) at sample points of B_1 by the real-space kernel of 3.1(ii).

(iv) Compactness. By parity, rho_n(0) = 0 and U_n(0) = 0. Hence |rho_n(X)| <= G_rho,n |X| and |U_n(X)| <= G_U,n |X|,
so |rho_n| + |U_n| <= M |X|. By Arzela-Ascoli and a diagonal extraction, a subsequence converges locally uniformly to
(rho, U). By Banach-Alaoglu (L^inf = (L^1)^*, with L^1 separable), a further subsequence has grad rho_n -> g and DU_n
-> G weak-* in L^inf(R^2). Testing against derivatives of test functions gives g = grad rho and G = DU, so rho and U
are Lipschitz. The pointwise limits keep the parities, rho(0) = U(0) = 0 and |rho| + |U| <= M |X|.

Linear relations. The identities int U_n . grad phi = 0 and int (U_{n,1} d_y phi - U_{n,2} d_x phi) = int rho_n d_x
phi (that is, curl U_n = -d_x rho_n) pass to the limit by local uniform convergence.

Product. For phi in C_c^inf,

    int phi (c_n X + U_n) . grad rho_n = c_n int phi X . grad rho_n + int phi U . grad rho_n
                                         + int phi (U_n - U) . grad rho_n.

phi X and phi U are in L^1 and c_n -> 1, so by weak-* convergence the first two terms tend to int phi X . grad rho and
int phi U . grad rho. The last term is bounded by M ||phi||_1 sup_{supp phi} |U_n - U| -> 0. Since also int phi rho_n
-> int phi rho, the equations pass to the limit: int phi ((X + U) . grad rho - rho) = 0 for every phi. The bracket is
in L^inf_loc, so it vanishes a.e.

Lemma. Let Z be a field with |Z| <= C (1 + |X|), the parities of U, and div Z = curl Z = 0 in distributions. Then Z =
b (x, -y) for some real b. Proof: f = Z1 - i Z2 satisfies (d_x + i d_y) f = div Z - i curl Z = 0, so f is entire
(Weyl's lemma for 4 d_z d_zbar); |f| <= C (1 + |z|) and Cauchy's estimates make f affine, f = alpha + beta z; Z(0) = 0
by parity, so alpha = 0; and with beta = b + i b', Z = (b x - b' y, -b' x - b y), where evenness of Z1 in y forces b'
= 0.

Application. Let V have at most linear growth, the parities, div V = 0 and curl V = -rho_x. The lemma applied to Z =
V - U gives V = U + b (x, -y); conversely, every such field has these properties. The normalization U = o(|X|) of 3.1(i)
is not available at linear growth. If U + b (x, -y) also solves the transport equation, then b (x rho_x - y rho_y) = 0
a.e.

If rho = a y with a != 0, then curl U = 0, and the lemma with Z = U gives U = b (x, -y). The equation becomes a (y - b
y) = a y, so a b y = 0, b = 0 and U = 0.

What is not obtained. By A.3.5, rho_{n,l} = l rho_n(X/l) is an exact profile with the same c_{l,n}, G_rho,n and G_U,n.
Moreover |rho_{n,l}(X)| + |U_{n,l}(X)| <= C_n l^{1-gamma_n} (l + |X|)^{gamma_n} (growth bound of the class and
3.1(iii)). Choosing l_n with sup_{|X| <= n} (|rho_{n,l_n}| + |U_{n,l_n}|) <= 1/n gives the zero limit. Therefore a
nonzero limit, a nonzero slope and strictly sublinear growth are not conclusions. Weak-* convergence does not preserve continuity
of the gradients, so C^1 regularity is not obtained. That every limit is affine is not proved. This is the statement
of 3.37(iv).

## A.3.38 Sharpness of the regularity ceiling for homogeneous source modes

Notation. Write a = a0 > B = A - 1 > 0 and, as in A.3.11,

    u = (d - A)/B,  v = (a + 2 - A (d + 1))/B,  kappa_x = (A d - 1)/B,  p_y = kappa_y = (a - d + 1)/B.

Then p_y = d + v + 1, u + v - a/B = -d - 2 and kappa_x - d = (d - 1)/B > 0. "Class C^s", with s = m + alpha and 0 <
alpha < 1, means h in C^{m,alpha}_loc(R^2). F = hat h is tempered, homogeneous of degree -d - 2, even in xi1 and odd
in xi2.

Fourier equation. We have hat(x_j d_j g) = -(1 + xi_j d_{xi_j}) hat g. On R^2 \ {0}, |xi|^2 hat psi = i xi1 F, so
hat(psi_x) = -xi1^2 F/|xi|^2 there. Hence the mode equation is equivalent off 0 to

    [A xi1 d_{xi1} + xi2 d_{xi2} + A + 2 + a xi1^2/|xi|^2] F = 0  on R^2 \ {0}.

Step 1 (s <= d). Suppose s > d. Choose omega with h(omega) != 0, and let P = sum_{j <= m} P_j be the Taylor polynomial
of h at 0. Then t^d h(omega) - sum_{j <= m} t^j P_j(omega) = O(t^s) as t -> 0+. All exponents are < s and pairwise
distinct (d is not an integer), so all coefficients vanish, including h(omega). This is a contradiction, so s <= d. In
particular no nonzero mode is C^infinity at 0. Also, if d < m + 1, a C^{m+1} mode would be C^{s'} for noninteger s' in
(max(m, d), m + 1), which is impossible.

Step 2 (F on xi1 > 0). On Omega+ = {xi1 > 0} use the coordinates (xi1, q), q = xi2/xi1. Homogeneity means (xi1
d_{xi1})|_q F = -(d + 2) F, so xi1^{d+2} F has zero xi1-derivative, and F = xi1^{-d-2} f(q) with f a distribution on
R, odd since F is odd in xi2. Since A xi1 d_{xi1} + xi2 d_{xi2} = A xi1 d_{xi1}|_q - B q d_q and xi1^2/|xi|^2 = 1/(1 +
q^2), the equation becomes

    B q f' = [2 - A (d + 1) + a/(1 + q^2)] f,

and g = (1 + q^2)^{a/(2B)} f satisfies q g' = v g. So g is homogeneous of degree v and odd. The odd homogeneous
distributions of degree v on R form a line spanned by S_v (Hormander, The Analysis of Linear Partial Differential
Operators I, Section 3.2): S_v is the continuation of sgn(q) |q|^v if v is not in {-2, -4, ...}, and delta^{(-v-1)} if
it is. Hence, with m(tau) = (1 + tau^2)^{-a/(2B)},

    F = C xi1^{-d-2} (m S_v)(xi2/xi1)  on Omega+,

and on Omega- by evenness. The quadrant form of A.3.11 is the case S_v = sgn |q|^v, since xi1^{-d-2-v+a/B} = xi1^u.

Step 3 (C != 0 for h != 0). If C = 0, F is supported in {xi1 = 0}. A tempered distribution has finite order, so F =
sum_{k <= N0} delta^{(k)}(xi1) u_k(xi2) (tensor products; Hormander I, Section 2.3), and h = sum_k x^k t_k(y) with t_k
tempered. By uniqueness of the coefficients, t_k is homogeneous of degree d - k, so y t_k' = (d - k) t_k. Off 0, hat
psi = i xi1 F/|xi|^2 is supported in {xi1 = 0}, so in the same way psi = sum_k x^k s_k(y), with s_k homogeneous of
degree d + 1 - k. Let N be the top x-degree of h (t_N != 0) and N' that of psi. If N' >= N, the x^{N'} coefficient of
-Lap psi = h_x reads -s_{N'}'' = (N' + 1) t_{N'+1} = 0, so s_{N'} is a polynomial of degree <= 1, homogeneous of the
noninteger degree d + 1 - N', hence 0, contrary to the choice of N'. So N' < N, and the x^N coefficient of (A x d_x +
y d_y - 1) h + a psi_x = 0 is (A N + d - N - 1) t_N = (B N + d - 1) t_N = 0. Since B N + d - 1 > 0, t_N = 0, a
contradiction. Hence C != 0 for every nonzero mode.

Step 4 (s <= p_y). If p_y >= d, Step 1 suffices, so assume p_y < d, that is v < -1. For phi in C_c^inf((1, 2)) put
H_phi(x) = int h(x, y) phi(y) dy and w = F^{-1} phi.

H_phi is even and continuous, with |H_phi(x)| <= C (1 + |x|)^d. For chi in C_c^inf((1, inf)), <hat H_phi, chi> = <h,
hat chi(x) phi(y)> = <F, chi(xi1) w(xi2)>. Approximate w in S by compactly supported w_j, so that chi(xi1) w_j(xi2)
lies in C_c^inf(Omega+). Using Step 2 and the homogeneity S_v(eta/xi) = xi^{-v} S_v(eta), this gives, for xi > 1,

    hat H_phi(xi) = C xi^{-d-2-v} < S_v, m(./xi) w > = C xi^{-1-p_y} (c0 + O(xi^{-2})),  c0 = < S_v, w >.

For the error term, write m(tau) = 1 + tau^2 m1(tau) with m1 smooth and bounded with all derivatives. Then eta^2
m1(eta/xi) w(eta) is bounded in S for xi >= 1, and S_v is continuous on S.

phi can be chosen with c0 != 0. The map phi -> < S_v, F^{-1} phi > is a nonzero multiple of hat S_v, which is odd and
homogeneous. If it vanished on (1, 2), it would vanish on R \ {0}, so S_v would be a polynomial. That is impossible
for a nonzero distribution homogeneous of degree v < 0.

Let zeta be an even real Schwartz function with hat zeta in C_c^inf({1 < |xi| < 2}), hat zeta >= 0 and hat zeta != 0;
all moments of zeta vanish. For 0 < eps <= 1, by Parseval and evenness,

    I_eps := int H_phi(x) eps^{-1} zeta(x/eps) dx = (1/pi) int_{1/eps}^{2/eps} hat H_phi(xi) hat zeta(eps xi) dxi
           = eps^{p_y} (C c0 J + O(eps^2)),  J = (1/pi) int_1^2 t^{-1-p_y} hat zeta(t) dt > 0.

On the other hand, h is C^s near {0} x [1, 2], so H_phi = P + R on [-1, 1], with P a polynomial and |R| <= C |x|^s.
Subtracting P (vanishing moments) and using the growth bound and the decay of zeta for |x| > 1 gives I_eps = O(eps^s).
Since C c0 J != 0, s <= p_y.

Step 5 (supremum). By Steps 1 and 4, s <= min(d, p_y(d)). Here d is increasing and p_y(d) is decreasing in d, and they
are equal at d = (a + 1)/A, which is > 1 because a > B. So min(d, p_y(d)) <= (a + 1)/A = s_sup for every d. Also a/B -
(a + 1)/A = (a - B)/(A B) > 0, which gives the parenthetical identity. Conversely, Step 6 gives a mode of class C^s
for every noninteger s < s_sup. Hence the supremum of the attained s is s_sup. Attainment is not claimed.

Step 6 (existence). Fix a noninteger s = m + alpha < s_sup and a noninteger d in (max(1, s), a + 1 - B s) with kappa_x
and p_y not integers. The interval is nonempty because A s < a + 1 and s < s_sup < a/B. The excluded d are finitely
many. The condition d < a + 1 - B s means p_y > s, and kappa_x > d > s holds automatically.

Angular system. With h = r^d Theta(th), psi = r^{d+1} Phi(th), c = cos th, z = sin th and q = A c^2 + z^2, the two
equations are

    (d q - 1) Theta - B z c Theta' + a [(d + 1) c Phi - z Phi'] = 0,
    Phi'' = z Theta' - d c Theta - (d + 1)^2 Phi.

For Y = (Theta, Phi, Phi') this is a linear analytic first-order system on (0, pi/2) (divide by B z c).

At the x-axis. Put t = th; then t Y' = R(t) Y with R analytic for |t| < pi/2 and

    R(0) = R_x = [[kappa_x, a (d + 1)/B, 0], [0, 0, 0], [0, 0, 0]].

At the y-axis. Put s~ = pi/2 - th and Y~ = (Theta, Phi, d Phi/ds~); then s~ Y~' = R~(s~) Y~ with R~ analytic and

    R~(0) = R_y = [[-(d - 1)/B, 0, -a/B], [0, 0, 0], [(d - 1)/B, 0, a/B]].

Both residues have rank 1, eigenvalues {0, 0, kappa_x} and {0, 0, p_y} (the traces), and eigenvectors R_x e_1 =
kappa_x e_1 and R_y (1, 0, -1) = p_y (1, 0, -1). Their kernels are ker R_x = {kappa_x Theta + a (d + 1) Phi/B = 0},
which contains (0, 0, 1), and ker R_y = {(d - 1) Theta + a Phi_s~ = 0}, which contains (a, 0, -(d - 1)).

Frobenius solutions. Let lambda be an eigenvalue of R(0) with eigenvector Y_0, such that lambda + j - R(0) is
invertible for j = 1, 2, .... Then the recursion (lambda + j - R(0)) Y_j = sum_{i<j} R_{j-i} Y_i and the majorant
argument give a convergent solution t^lambda sum_j Y_j t^j (Coddington and Levinson, Theory of Ordinary Differential
Equations, Chapter 4). The hypothesis holds for lambda = 0 and for lambda = kappa, because kappa is not an integer. At
each axis this gives, for each Y_0 in the kernel, a unique analytic solution with Y(0) = Y_0, and a fractional
solution t^kappa (e + O(t)), e the eigenvector. These three solutions are independent, since a function analytic in t
is not t^kappa times an analytic function with nonzero value at 0.

Parities. The system is invariant under (Theta, Phi)(th) -> (-Theta, -Phi)(-th) and under (Theta, Phi)(th) -> (Theta,
-Phi)(pi - th) (direct substitution). The first reflection fixes Y_0 = (0, 0, 1) and the second fixes Y~_0 = (a, 0,
-(d - 1)). By uniqueness, the corresponding analytic solutions are odd at th = 0 (Theta, Phi odd) and have Theta even
and Phi odd at th = pi/2.

Matching. Let V_x be the span of the odd analytic solution and the fractional solution at the x-axis, and V_y the span
of the analytic solution with Y~_0 = (a, 0, -(d - 1)) and the fractional solution at the y-axis. Both are 2-planes in
the 3-dimensional solution space on (0, pi/2), so there is Y != 0 in V_x and V_y. Then Theta is not identically 0.
Otherwise the first equation gives Phi = K sin^{d+1} th, and the second gives 0 = Phi'' + (d + 1)^2 Phi = K d (d + 1)
sin^{d-1} th, so K = 0 and Y = 0.

Extension. Extend Theta and Phi to the circle by Theta(-th) = -Theta(th), Theta(pi - th) = Theta(th), Phi(-th) =
-Phi(th) and Phi(pi - th) = -Phi(th). By the two invariances, the equations hold on each open quadrant. For g
analytic, g(|t|) = g_e(t^2) + |t| g_o(t^2), so the odd extension of t^kappa g(t) is a sum of sgn(t) |t|^kappa and
sgn(t) |t|^{kappa+1} times analytic functions, hence of class C^kappa. At th = 0, pi the Phi component of the fractional branch is
O(t^{kappa+2}), since its derivative, the third component, is O(t^{kappa+1}); at th = +-pi/2 the corresponding
orders are O(t^{p_y+1}) and O(t^{p_y}). Hence Theta is C^{kappa_x} at th = 0, pi
and C^{p_y} at th = +-pi/2, Phi is C^{kappa_x + 2} and C^{p_y + 1} there, and both are analytic elsewhere. So Theta is
in C^s(S^1) and Phi in C^{s+1}(S^1).

Regularity of the mode. Put h = r^d Theta and psi = r^{d+1} Phi. Off 0, h is C^s and psi is C^{s+1}. At 0 they are C^s
and C^{s+1} because d > s, as follows. D^j h is homogeneous of degree d - j > 0 for j <= m, so it extends continuously
by 0. For the Holder quotient of D^m h at X, Y with |X| >= |Y|, split into two cases. If |X - Y| <= |X|/2, use the
C^alpha bound on a dyadic annulus, scaled by homogeneity, which contributes the factor |X|^{d-s} <= 1 for |X| <= 1;
otherwise use |D^m h(X)| + |D^m h(Y)| <= C |X|^{d-m} <= C' |X - Y|^alpha. psi is treated in the same way.

The equations. h is continuous, and on lines crossing the axes it is absolutely continuous with locally integrable
derivative, because Theta' = O(|s~|^{p_y - 1}) with p_y > 0. Likewise psi is C^1 with locally integrable second
derivatives. So the distributional derivatives are the pointwise ones, and both equations hold in D'(R^2 \ {0}). The
two defects are distributions supported at 0, homogeneous of degree d and d - 1, which are not integers <= -2. Hence
they vanish.

Conclusion. psi is homogeneous of degree d + 1. Two such inverses differ by a harmonic tempered homogeneous
distribution, which is a polynomial of noninteger degree, hence 0. So psi is the unique homogeneous inverse. h is
tempered (|h| <= C |X|^d), nonzero, even in x and odd in y, and is a mode of class C^{m,alpha} with stream of class
C^{m+1,alpha}.

For m = 1 and d < 2, this gives a second proof of the single-mode existence of 3.25(ii), which A.3.25(ii) proves
directly. The uniform rank argument and the superpositions of A.3.25(ii) are not treated here. If m >= 1, the interval contains degrees d <
m + 1, because s < m + 1 and s < a + 1 - B s; by Step 1 those modes are not C^{m+1}.

Example. h = y |x|^p and psi = -y x |x|^p/(p + 1), with a = A p and d = p + 1, solve both equations (exact symbolic
check, accompanying artifacts). Here v = -2, S_v = delta', F is carried by {xi2 = 0}, and p_y = p. For noninteger p >
B/A, h is C^p but not better at the y-axis, so the bound s <= p_y of Step 4 is attained. Here p_y = p < s_sup = p +
1/A, so this mode does not reach s_sup. Since F is carried by the axis {xi2 = 0}, the case S_v = delta^{(-v-1)} of
Step 2 cannot be omitted. The remaining checks (accompanying artifacts) confirm the exponent identities, the Fourier
form of the transport operator, the quadrant solution, the angular system and both residues with their eigenvectors.

The last three sentences of 3.38 delimit its scope and need no proof.

## A.3.39 Critical escaping nodes: conditional exclusions

Inputs: A.3.1(ii) (kernel formula), A.3.2 and 3.2 (rho = a0 y + O(r^3), DU(0) = diag(D, -D)), A.3.5 (scaling),
A.3.6 (v > 0 on the positive y-axis), 3.7 and 3.23 (Theta0(pi/2) = K != 0; |D^k rho| + |D^k U| <= C_k (1 + r)^{p-k}),
A.3.30, A.3.32, A.3.34.

Throughout, q is a zero of W with grad rho(q) = 0. Transport at q gives rho(q) = W(q) . grad rho(q) = 0, and q != 0
because grad rho(0) = (0, a0). By A.3.30(iii), DW(q) is symmetric with trace 2 c_l, so DU(q) = DW(q) - c_l I is
symmetric and trace-free. lambda_- <= lambda_+ are the eigenvalues of DW(q), and z = r (cos th, sin th) is the
variable of integration.

(a) Kernel derivative. With K1 = -z1 z2/(pi |z|^4) and K2 = (z1^2 - z2^2)/(2 pi |z|^4) (A.3.1(ii)), in complex notation
K2 + i K1 = 1/(2 pi z^2). So K and all its derivatives are harmonic off 0, and for z != 0

    d_j K_i(z) = M_ij(z)/(pi |z|^6),   M_11 = -M_22 = z2 (3 z1^2 - z2^2),   M_12 = M_21 = z1 (3 z2^2 - z1^2).

For example, d_1 K1 = -(z2/pi) (|z|^2 - 4 z1^2)/|z|^6 and d_1 K2 = (z1/pi) (|z|^2 - 2 z1^2 + 2 z2^2)/|z|^6 = d_2 K1.
From sin 3th = 3 sin th cos^2 th - sin^3 th and cos 3th = cos^3 th - 3 cos th sin^2 th,
(M_11, M_12) = r^3 (sin 3th, -cos 3th), so (M_11, M_12)/(pi |z|^6) = Q(z).

Kernel formula. Fix delta > 0 and a smooth zeta_0 with zeta_0 = 1 on B(0, 1) and support in B(0, 2). Put
zeta(Y) = zeta_0((Y - q)/delta), rho_1 = zeta rho, rho_2 = (1 - zeta) rho and R0 = 2 (|q| + 2 delta) + 2. The formula of
A.3.1(ii) is linear in the density.

- For rho_1 (smooth and compactly supported) it is the classical potential
  U^1_i(X) = PV int K_i(z) rho_1(X - z) dz - (1/2) delta_{i2} rho_1(X).
- rho_2 vanishes on B(q, delta) and equals rho on |Y| > R0. For |X - q| < delta/2 its velocity is

    U^2(X) = int_{|Y|<R0} K(X - Y) rho_2(Y) dY + int_{|Y|>R0} (K(X - Y) - K(-Y)) rho(Y) dY.

  This holds because K(-Y) rho(Y) is odd under Y -> -Y (K is even and rho is centrally odd), so it integrates to 0
  over centred annuli.

Both integrands of U^2 are smooth in X near q. Moreover D_X (K(X - Y) - K(-Y)) = DK(X - Y) is O(|Y|^{-3}) on |Y| > R0,
while |rho(Y)| <= C |Y|^p. So differentiation under the integral sign gives DU^2(q) = int DK(z) rho_2(q - z) dz,
absolutely convergent.

For U^1, the principal value commutes with translations, so
d_j U^1_i(q) = PV int K_i(z) (d_j rho_1)(q - z) dz - (1/2) delta_{i2} d_j rho_1(q), and d_j rho_1(q) = d_j rho(q) = 0.
Put f_1(z) = rho_1(q - z), so that (d_j rho_1)(q - z) = -d_j f_1(z). Integrating by parts on |z| > eps leaves
int_{|z|>eps} (d_j K_i) f_1 dz plus a boundary term on |z| = eps. That term is bounded by
2 pi eps sup_{|z|=eps} |K| |f_1| <= C eps, since |K| <= C eps^{-2} and f_1(z) = O(|z|^2) (f_1(0) = rho(q) = 0,
grad f_1(0) = -grad rho(q) = 0). As eps -> 0, DU^1(q) = int DK(z) rho_1(q - z) dz. Adding the two parts,

    DU(q) = int DK(z) rho(q - z) dz = (1/pi) int rho(q - z) |z|^{-6} M(z) dz.

The integrand is O(|z|^{-1}) near 0 (rho(q - z) = O(|z|^2)) and O(|z|^{p-3}) at infinity (3.23). Both are integrable in
two dimensions. In entries, DU(q) = [[m1, m2], [m2, -m1]] with

    m(q) = (m1, m2) = int rho(q - z) Q(z) dz,     m1 + i m2 = -(i/pi) int rho(q - z) r^{-3} e^{3 i th} dz.

A symmetric trace-free matrix with entries m1, m2 has eigenvalues +-|m|. So |DU(q)|_op = |m(q)|, the modulus of a
cubic-angle moment of rho about q.

Moment identity. Put f(z) = rho(q - z), dU(z) = U(q - z) - U(q) and V(z) = -W(q - z). Then:

- Since W(q) = 0, V(z) = c_l z - dU(z) and div V = 2 c_l (div U = 0).
- V(0) = 0, so |V(z)| <= C |z| near 0, and |V(z)| <= C (1 + |z|) everywhere.
- Transport at q - z gives V . grad f = W(q - z) . (grad rho)(q - z) = f.
- Q is homogeneous of degree -3, so z . grad Q = -3 Q and V . grad Q = -3 c_l Q - (dU . grad) Q.

Multiply V . grad f = f by Q and integrate by parts on A = {eps < |z| < L}:

    int_A f Q = int_{dA} f Q (V . n) - int_A f (2 c_l Q + V . grad Q)
              = int_{dA} f Q (V . n) + c_l int_A f Q + int_A f (dU . grad) Q.

On |z| = eps, |f| <= C eps^2, |V| <= C eps and |Q| = 1/(pi eps^3), so the boundary integral is O(eps). On |z| = L,
|f| <= C L^p, |V| <= C L and |Q| = 1/(pi L^3), so it is O(L^{p-1}).

The radial and normalized angular derivatives

    d_r Q = -3 (sin 3th, -cos 3th)/(pi r^4),     r^{-1} d_th Q = 3 (cos 3th, sin 3th)/(pi r^4)

are orthogonal and each has length 3/(pi r^4). So for every vector v,

    |v . grad Q| = |v_r d_r Q + v_th r^{-1} d_th Q| = 3 |v|/(pi r^4).

Hence |f (dU . grad) Q| <= 3 |f| |dU|/(pi r^4). This is O(r^{-1}) near 0 (|dU| <= C r) and O(r^{2p-4} + r^{p-4}) at
infinity, so it is integrable. Letting eps -> 0 and L -> inf gives (1 - c_l) m = int f (dU . grad) Q, that is

    D m(q) = - int rho(q - z) [(U(q - z) - U(q)) . grad] Q(z) dz,
    |DU(q)|_op = |m(q)| <= (3/(pi D)) int |rho(q - z)| |U(q - z) - U(q)| |z|^{-4} dz.

Scale invariance. For rho_l, U_l (A.3.5), q_l = l q satisfies W_l(q_l) = l W(q) = 0 and
grad rho_l(q_l) = (grad rho)(q) = 0. Substituting z = l w, the moment of rho_l about q_l is
int l rho(q - w) Q(l w) l^2 dw = m(q), because Q(l w) = l^{-3} Q(w). Likewise the right side of the bound acquires the
factor l . l . l^{-4} . l^2 = 1, and DU_l(q_l) = DU(q). So the identity and the bound are dilation invariant.

Double node. Take the setting of A.3.34(f) with k = 2. Then only l = 1 is allowed, lambda_- = 1 - 2 c_l = -A and
lambda_+ = 4 c_l - 1, and A.3.34(i) gives |DU(q)|_op = c_l - lambda_- = 3 c_l - 1. So the right side of the moment
bound is at least 3 c_l - 1 there, and a strict bound below 3 c_l - 1 at the maximizer excludes k = 2.

Next, DU(q) - DU(0) is symmetric and trace-free with entry vector m - (D, 0) (DU(0) = diag(D, -D), 3.2), so

    |DU(q) - DU(0)|_op = |m - (D, 0)| >= |m| - D = (3 c_l - 1) - (c_l - 1) = 2 c_l.

Equality holds exactly when m is a positive multiple of (1, 0), that is when DU(q) = diag(3 c_l - 1, 1 - 3 c_l), or
equivalently DW(q) = diag(4 c_l - 1, 1 - 2 c_l): the fast direction at q is horizontal. So
|DU(q) - DU(0)|_op < 2 c_l excludes k = 2. The non-strict bound 2 c_l would exclude it only if the horizontal case
were also excluded, and nothing known excludes that case off the x-axis. At an axis node
DW(q) = diag(lambda_-, lambda_+) (A.3.30(iv)), so m = (1 - 3 c_l, 0) and |m - (D, 0)| = 4 c_l - 2 > 2 c_l.

Local jet (remark, not needed for 3.39). Let lambda_- <= 0, and let (u, v) be the coordinates of X - q along unit
eigenvectors for lambda_-, lambda_+.

- Write rho = P_2 + P_3 + O(|X - q|^4) with P_j homogeneous of degree j, and W = DW(q) (X - q) + O(|X - q|^2).
- The degree-2 part of transport is (lambda_- u d_u + lambda_+ v d_v) P_2 = P_2. The weights of u^2, u v, v^2 are
  2 lambda_- <= 0, 2 c_l > 2 and 2 lambda_+ >= 4 c_l. None equals 1, so P_2 = 0.
- The degree-3 part is then (lambda_- u d_u + lambda_+ v d_v) P_3 = P_3. At a double node
  (lambda_- = 1 - 2 c_l, lambda_+ = 4 c_l - 1) the cubic weights are 3 - 6 c_l, 1, 6 c_l - 1, 12 c_l - 3, so
  P_3 = C u^2 v.
- In the coordinates (s, n) of A.3.34(f), n = gamma u + O(|X - q|^2) and s = alpha v + tau u + O(|X - q|^2) with
  alpha gamma != 0, since the branch is tangent to the v-axis. Then b_2(s) = (1/2) d_n^2 rho(s, 0)
  = C s/(alpha gamma^2) + O(s^2), whatever the tilt tau. The terms of degree >= 4 and the curvature of the branch
  contribute only O(s^2).
- Since b_2 = C_+ s E(s) with C_+ != 0 (A.3.34(f) with l = 1), C != 0.

At an axis double node u = +-(x - x_q) and v = +-y, so rho = C y (x - x_q)^2 + O(|X - q|^4) with C != 0. This is the
local shape prescribed in the countertest below.

Countertest (no bound from the kernel alone). Fix c_l > 1, a0 != 0, q = (2, 0), and a smooth nonnegative radial chi
with chi = 1 near 0 and support in B(0, 1/10). Let

    rho_b = a0 y [chi(X) + (x - 2)^2 chi(X - (2, 0)) + (x + 2)^2 chi(X + (2, 0))].

It is smooth, compactly supported, even in x and odd in y, with rho_b/a0 >= 0 on y > 0, rho_y(0) = a0, and
rho_b = a0 y (x - 2)^2 near q.

Let eta_1 be a smooth nonnegative radial bump of unit integral with support in B(0, 1/10). For a, b > 0 put

    B_{a,b}(X) = eta_1(x - a, y - b) + eta_1(x + a, y - b) - eta_1(x - a, y + b) - eta_1(x + a, y + b).

It is even in x, odd in y, and >= 0 on y > 0 when b > 1/10. For (a, b) = (3, 1) and (1, 1/2) the supports avoid q, 0
and the support of rho_b.

Since q lies outside the support and U1 has no local term, the canonical velocity of B_{a,b} has
U1(q) = int K1(q - Y) B_{a,b}(Y) dY and d_x U1(q) = int d_1 K1(q - Y) B_{a,b}(Y) dY. The maps Y -> K1(q - Y) and
Y -> d_1 K1(q - Y) are harmonic near each support disk, and eta_1 is radial of unit mass. So the mean value property
makes these values equal to the point-mass values

    U1(q) = (2/pi) sum_{s=+-1} (2 - s a) b/[(2 - s a)^2 + b^2]^2,
    d_x U1(q) = (2/pi) sum_{s=+-1} b [b^2 - 3 (2 - s a)^2]/[(2 - s a)^2 + b^2]^3.

These are:

- for (3, 1): u_R = (2/pi)(-41/169) < 0 and s_R = (2/pi)(-1117/4394) < 0;
- for (1, 1/2): u_L = (2/pi)(11552/34225) > 0 and s_L = (2/pi)(-4564464/6331625) < 0.

Let u_b, s_b be the corresponding values for rho_b. Put t_L = (-2 c_l - u_b - t u_R)/u_L and
rho_t = rho_b + t B_{3,1} + t_L B_{1,1/2}. Then:

- U2(q) = 0 by parity and U1(q) = u_b + t u_R + t_L u_L = -2 c_l, so W(q) = 0;
- grad rho_t(q) = 0, rho_t = a0 y (x - 2)^2 near q, and rho_y(0) = a0;
- the strain at q is

    d_x U1(q) = s_b + (-2 c_l - u_b) s_L/u_L + t (s_R - u_R s_L/u_L).

The t-coefficient is negative, since u_R s_L/u_L > 0. Let t -> +inf when a0 > 0 and t -> -inf when a0 < 0. Then t and
t_L have the sign of a0, so rho_t/a0 >= 0 on y > 0, and |DU(q)|_op >= |d_x U1(q)| -> inf.

These densities are not profiles:

- They are compactly supported, so Theta0 = 0, contrary to 3.7.
- For large |t| they do not satisfy transport near q. There DU(q) is symmetric (rho_x(q) = 0) and diagonal (U1 is
  even in y), so DW(q) = diag(c_l + d_x U1(q), c_l - d_x U1(q)). The cubic part of transport applied to
  a0 y (x - 2)^2 would then force 3 c_l + d_x U1(q) = 1, i.e. d_x U1(q) = 1 - 3 c_l.
- For large |t| they do not satisfy the origin strain. By the same mean value argument, d_x U1(0) is affine in t with
  t-coefficient (2/pi)(-13/250 - (41/169)(176/125)(34225/11552)) = -(2/pi)(8114296/7626125) != 0, while 3.2 requires
  d_x U1(0) = D.

So the moment formula and the sign of the density, without transport, give no bound on |DU(q)|.

(b) Sign subclass (proved). Let (H-dyn) fail, and let the maximizer q of Pi on K be off the x-axis, hence in an open
quadrant, with eigenvalues lambda_- <= 0 < lambda_+ = 2 c_l - lambda_- (A.3.34(b)). By A.3.34(b), both halves of the
fast unstable curve are nodal, lie in the open quadrant of q near q, and escape. Suppose one of them escapes at a zero
th_+ of Theta0 of finite order k.

By A.3.34(f), lambda_- < 0 and k lambda_- + l lambda_+ = 1 for an integer 1 <= l <= k - 1. So q is a hyperbolic
saddle and its unstable manifold is a smooth curve through q. Take smooth coordinates (s, n) on a neighbourhood
{|s|, |n| < s0} of q, as in A.3.34(f), such that:

- the curve is {n = 0} and the escaping half is {s > 0};
- W = (S, n beta) with S(s, 0) = v(s) = lambda_+ s + O(s^2) and beta(0, 0) = lambda_-;
- after shrinking s0, v(s)/s > 0 for 0 < |s| < s0.

Write rho = sum_i b_i(s) n^i, S = sum_j S_j(s) n^j and beta = sum_j beta_j(s) n^j for the Taylor expansions in n. The
coefficients are smooth, and S_0 = v. The coefficient of n^i in W . grad rho - rho = 0 is

    v b_i' + (i beta_0 - 1) b_i = - sum_{j=1}^{i} (S_j b_{i-j}' + (i - j) beta_j b_{i-j}).                    (1)

For each i, (1 - i beta_0)/v = e_i/s + h_i(s), with h_i smooth on |s| < s0 and e_i = (1 - i lambda_-)/lambda_+ > 0.
Where the right side of (1) vanishes, therefore, b_i = C_+ s^{e_i} E_i(s) for s > 0 and b_i = C_- |s|^{e_i} E_i(s)
for s < 0, with E_i(s) = exp(int_0^s h_i) and E_i(0) = 1. By A.3.34(f), on (0, s0) we have b_i = 0 for i < k and
b_k = C_+ s^l E_k with C_+ != 0 (e_k = l).

- Induction on i < k. Suppose b_j = 0 on (-s0, s0) for all j < i. Then (1) is homogeneous for b_i. Since b_i is smooth
  and vanishes on (0, s0), it is flat at 0. So C_- = 0, since otherwise |b_i| would be comparable to |s|^{e_i} as
  s -> 0-. Hence b_i = 0 on (-s0, s0).
- Order k. Now (1) is homogeneous for b_k, so b_k = C_- |s|^l E_k on (-s0, 0). The one-sided l-th derivatives of the
  smooth b_k at 0 are l! C_+ from the right and (-1)^l l! C_- from the left. Equating them gives C_- = (-1)^l C_+,
  that is

    b_k(s) = C_+ s^l E_k(s) on (-s0, s0),    C_+ != 0.

So on the half {s < 0} every derivative of rho of order < k vanishes, and d_n^k rho = k! b_k != 0: rho has order
exactly k at each of its points. Since rho o Phi_t = e^t rho, the order is constant along the trajectory. Where the
trajectory escapes, rho = F o Q with F = |Q|^p Theta0(arg Q) and Q a local diffeomorphism (A.3.30(vi)). So its escape
angle th_- is a zero of Theta0 of order exactly k. The exponent of this branch in A.3.34(f) is again
e_k = (1 - k lambda_-)/lambda_+ = l. This proves the first clause.

Sign. Let q lie in y > 0 and let rho/a0 >= 0 on y > 0. Shrink s0 so that the coordinate neighbourhood lies in y > 0.
At a point (s, 0) with 0 < |s| < s0, rho = b_k(s) n^k + O(n^{k+1}) with b_k(s) != 0.

- If k were odd, rho would change sign across the branch inside y > 0. So k is even.
- With k even, rho/a0 >= 0 near (s, 0) forces b_k(s)/a0 > 0 for 0 < |s| < s0. Hence C_+/a0 > 0 and (-1)^l C_+/a0 > 0,
  so l is even.

With 1 <= l <= k - 1 this gives l >= 2 and k >= 4. In particular k = 2 is impossible: there is no off-axis double node
with rho/a0 >= 0 on y > 0. (Pi is even in y, so the reflection X -> (x, -y) gives the same conclusion for a maximizer
in y < 0.)

Remark. About q, the proof uses only that grad rho(q) = 0, lambda_- <= 0, q is off the x-axis, and one fast branch
escapes at a zero of finite order; A.3.34(f) needs no more. For every such q:

- the other branch is nodal (as in A.3.30(vii)) and has transverse order exactly k, with b_k = C_+ s^l E_k;
- it escapes at a zero of order k with the same l, whenever it escapes;
- the parity conclusion holds.

What is not known in general is that the other branch escapes. At an axis node the two branches lie in opposite
half-planes and are exchanged by y -> -y, so the sign argument gives nothing there; see (e).

(c) Counting. On x = 0, W1 = 0 (U1 is odd in x), and W2(0, y) = v(y) is odd with v > 0 for y > 0 (A.3.6). So the
y-axis contains no zero of W other than 0.

Now let every zero be nondegenerate and let (H-dyn) fail.

- By A.3.34(g), the zeros are finitely many and the positive x-axis carries 2J >= 2 of them. W1 is odd in x, so the
  negative x-axis carries 2J more. With the origin, W has at least 1 + 4J >= 5 zeros.
- Let one zero s_0 be an off-axis saddle; it lies in an open quadrant. For R = diag(-1, 1) and R = diag(1, -1),
  W(R X) = R W(X), because W1 is odd in x and even in y while W2 is even in x and odd in y. So
  DW(R X) = R DW(X) R, and the four images of s_0 under the reflections are zeros with det DW < 0: there is one saddle
  in each open quadrant.
- By the index count of A.3.34(g), each open quadrant contains as many off-axis sources as saddles, hence at least one
  source.

So W has at least 1 + 4J + 8 >= 13 >= 9 zeros. The last sentence of (c) is the contrapositive of the first count.

(d) Second far-field term at a double zero. Let Theta0(th*) = Theta0'(th*) = 0 and T := Theta0''(th*) != 0, and put
b0 = u_{0,th}(th*). Theta0 is odd about 0 and about pi (rho is odd in y), so Theta0'' vanishes at 0 and pi, and th* is
neither. Differentiating Theta1 = (p u_{0,r} Theta0 + u_{0,th} Theta0')/D (3.32),

    Theta1' = (p u_{0,r}' Theta0 + p u_{0,r} Theta0' + u_{0,th}' Theta0' + u_{0,th} Theta0'')/D,

so Theta1(th*) = 0 and Theta1'(th*) = b0 T/D.

Nodal line. By A.3.30(vi), the preimage under Q of the ray arg = th* is an escaping trajectory on which
rho = |Q|^p Theta0(th*) = 0. In the exterior r' = c_l r + O(r^p) > 0. So along the trajectory th is a function of r,
th -> th* as r -> inf, and dth/dr = U_th/(r (c_l r + U_r)) = O(r^{p-2}) (A.3.30(vi), 3.23). Integrating from r to inf
gives th - th* = O(r^{p-1}). By 3.32, U_th = r^p u_{0,th}(th) + O(r^{2p-1}) = b0 r^p + O(r^{2p-1}) and U_r = O(r^p).
Hence dth/dr = (b0/c_l) r^{p-2} + O(r^{2p-3}), and since c_l (1 - p) = D,

    th(r) - th* = -(b0/D) r^{p-1} + O(r^{2p-2}).

So the physical nodal line is the ray th* displaced by an angle O(r^{p-1}).

Cancellation. Put eps := th - th* in the expansion of 3.32. Then Theta0(th) = (T/2) eps^2 + O(eps^3) and
Theta1(th) = (b0 T/D) eps + O(eps^2) give

    r^p Theta0(th) + r^{2p-1} Theta1(th) = (T b0^2/(2 D^2) - T b0^2/D^2) r^{3p-2} + O(r^{4p-3})
                                         = -(T b0^2/(2 D^2)) r^{3p-2} + O(r^{4p-3}).

This has the order r^{3p-2} of the remainder in 3.32. So the identity rho = 0 on the nodal trajectory is consistent
with the first two terms, and it gives no contradiction. By 3.68(b), with b < 3p - 2 close to 3p - 2, rho has a third
term r^{3p-2} Theta2(th), with Theta2 smooth, and a remainder o(r^{3p-2}) uniformly in th (its terms of degree p and
2p - 1 are those of 3.32, and no logarithm occurs at the degree 3p - 2: by 3.68(c) a logarithm is created only at a
degree -2m - 1 <= -3 and propagates only to lower degrees, while 3p - 2 > -2). With this term the same computation
gives Theta2(th*) = T b0^2/(2 D^2).

Exterior model. The cancellation is realized by exact transport on an exterior sector. For smooth F and a constant B,
the fields

    W = c_l r e_r + B D r^p e_th,    rho = r^p F(th + B r^{p-1})

satisfy div W = 2 c_l and W . grad rho = rho. Indeed, the r-derivative of the phase contributes
c_l (p - 1) B r^{2p-1} F', the angular part contributes B D r^{2p-1} F', and c_l (p - 1) + D = 0. The far-field
coefficients are F, B F' and B^2 F''/2, and u_{0,th} = B D. So Theta1 = B F' agrees with 3.32, and
Theta2(th*) = T b0^2/(2 D^2). These fields are not profile candidates, since curl U = B D (p + 1) r^{p-1} is in general
not -rho_x.

(e) Periodic non-profile. With wave number kappa > 0 (the k of 3.34(c)), the fields
W = ((A/kappa) sin kappa x, (2 c_l - A cos kappa x) y) and rho = A (1 + cos kappa x) y satisfy div W = 2 c_l,
curl W = -rho_x and W . grad rho = rho (A.3.34(c)). At q = (pi/kappa, 0):

- W(q) = 0 and rho(q) = 0;
- grad rho(q) = (-A kappa y sin kappa x, A (1 + cos kappa x)) at q, which is 0;
- the Jacobian is

    DW = [[A cos kappa x, 0], [A kappa y sin kappa x, 2 c_l - A cos kappa x]],
    DW(q) = diag(-A, 2 c_l + A) = diag(-A, 4 c_l - 1).

The line x = pi/kappa is invariant (W1 = 0 there), with y' = (4 c_l - 1) y, so it is the fast curve of q. With s = y
and n = x - pi/kappa, rho = A (1 - cos kappa n) s = (A kappa^2/2) s n^2 + O(n^4) s. So b_0 = b_1 = 0 and
b_2 = (A kappa^2/2) s, giving (k, l) = (2, 1); indeed 2 (-A) + (4 c_l - 1) = 1. Also rho >= 0 on y > 0, since A > 0.

The model has grad Pi = W + rho e_2 with Pi = (A/kappa^2)(1 - cos kappa x) + (2 c_l + A) y^2/2. Its forward-bounded set
is the x-axis, because y' = (2 c_l - A cos kappa x) y with 2 c_l - A cos kappa x >= 1, and q maximizes Pi there. So the
double order occurs at an axis maximizer with rho >= 0 on y > 0, and for the local identities the restriction of (b)
to off-axis nodes cannot be dropped. The model is not in the class: rho(0, y) = 2 A y grows linearly, and
U1(x, 0) = (A/kappa) sin kappa x - c_l x is not o(r).

Scope.

- The kernel formula uses only rho(q) = 0, grad rho(q) = 0 and the growth bound. The moment identity and the
  double-node values use W(q) = 0 and exact transport on the whole plane.
- The countertest satisfies neither transport nor the origin strain.
- (b) needs the global sign rho/a0 >= 0 on y > 0 and an off-axis maximizer; double nodes on the x-axis remain allowed.
- (c) counts nondegenerate zeros only.
- (d) concerns the first two far-field terms.

None of (a)-(e) proves (H-dyn) or excludes the double node in general.

## A.3.40 Scale-invariant derivative residual

Hypotheses and notation. rho is smooth, even in x and odd in y, and U is its canonical velocity (A.3.1(ii)). For some
q < 1 (unrelated to the point q of A.3.39),

    |D^j rho(X)| + |D^j U(X)| <= C_j (1 + |X|)^{q-j},    0 <= j <= 3.

No transport equation is assumed. Put W = c_l X + U, R = W . grad rho - rho, T = D^3 rho, G_rho = sup |grad rho| and
G_U = sup |DU|, with Frobenius norms over ordered indices as in A.3.35, and

    B = 3 G_U + G_rho + 3 (2 + sqrt 2) sqrt(G_U G_rho).

Assume D^3 rho != 0 and D^3 R in L^2.

(a) Finiteness. G_rho and G_U are finite, since q - 1 < 0. For j = 2, 3, D^j rho and D^j U are O((1 + r)^{q-j}) with
2 (q - j) + 2 < 0, so they are in L^2, and D^2 rho, D^2 U are in L^4. ||T||_2 > 0 because T is continuous and not
identically 0. So eta_3 = ||D^3 R||_2/||T||_2 is finite.

(b) Identity. As in A.3.35, D^3(X . grad rho) = X . grad T + 3 T and D^3(U . grad rho) = U . grad T + C_3 with
C_3 = [D^3, U . grad] rho. So

    D^3 R = W . grad T + (3 c_l - 1) T + C_3.

The seven Leibniz terms of C_3 (3 + 3 + 1) give pointwise

    |C_3| <= 3 |DU| |T| + 3 |D^2 U| |D^2 rho| + |D^3 U| |grad rho|,

so C_3 is in L^2; the middle term is O((1 + r)^{2q-4}). Pair with chi_L T, chi_L(X) = chi(X/L), as in A.3.35. Since
div W = 2 c_l,

    int chi_L (W . grad T) . T = -c_l int chi_L |T|^2 - (1/2) int (W . grad chi_L) |T|^2.

On the annulus L < r < 2L, |W . grad chi_L| <= C because |W| <= C (1 + r). So the last term is bounded by
C int_{L<r<2L} |T|^2, which tends to 0. D^3 R . T and C_3 . T are integrable, as products of L^2 functions. Letting
L -> inf,

    (2 c_l - 1) ||T||_2^2 + < T, C_3 > = < T, D^3 R >.

This is the identity of 3.35 for k = 3 with R kept; for R = 0 it is ((k - 1) c_l - 1) ||D^k rho||^2 = -<D^k rho, C_k>.

(c) Bound. The k = 3 estimates of A.3.35 use only the following about rho and U:

- div U = 0 and curl U = -rho_x (A.3.1(ii));
- D^3 rho and D^3 U are in L^2;
- the decay |D^i v| <= C (1 + r)^{-i-theta}, i <= 2, for v = grad rho and v = DU, which holds here with
  theta = 1 - q > 0.

So they apply verbatim. The multiplier bound gives ||D^3 U||_2 <= ||T||_2. The interpolation gives
||D^2 U||_4^2 <= (2 + sqrt 2) G_U ||D^3 U||_2 and ||D^2 rho||_4^2 <= (2 + sqrt 2) G_rho ||T||_2. By Minkowski and
Holder,

    ||C_3||_2 <= 3 G_U ||T||_2 + 3 ||D^2 U||_4 ||D^2 rho||_4 + G_rho ||D^3 U||_2 <= B ||T||_2.                (2)

Hence (2 c_l - 1) ||T||^2 <= ||T|| ||D^3 R|| + B ||T||^2. Dividing by ||T||^2 and using eta_3 >= 0,

    eta_3 >= [2 c_l - 1 - 3 G_U - G_rho - 3 (2 + sqrt 2) sqrt(G_U G_rho)]_+ .

(d) Dilations. For rho_l(X) = l rho(X/l), the canonical velocity is U_l(X) = l U(X/l) (A.3.5, by 3.1(i)), and
R_l(X) = l R(X/l). Then D^3 rho_l(X) = l^{-2} T(X/l) and D^3 R_l(X) = l^{-2} (D^3 R)(X/l). Both L^2 norms are therefore
multiplied by l^{-2} . l = l^{-1}, and eta_3 is invariant. So are G_rho and G_U (A.3.35), and the hypotheses hold with
new constants.

(e) Size. With S = G_rho + G_U, B <= C_* S (A.3.35), so eta_3 >= 2 c_l - 1 - C_* S. For small gradients eta_3 is thus
at least about 2 c_l - 1, but there is no upper bound of this kind.

Small multiples. Let rho_1 != 0 be smooth, compactly supported, even in x and odd in y, with canonical velocity U_1, and
put T_1 = D^3 rho_1. T_1 != 0, because a compactly supported polynomial of degree <= 2 is 0. Let rho = eps rho_1. The
hypotheses hold with q = 0 (U_1 and its derivatives decay at infinity), U = eps U_1, G_rho + G_U = O(eps), and

    D^3 R = eps (c_l X . grad T_1 + (3 c_l - 1) T_1) + eps^2 D^3(U_1 . grad rho_1)

is compactly supported. Since <X . grad T_1, T_1> = -||T_1||^2 (div X = 2),

    lim_{eps -> 0} eta_3^2 = ||c_l X . grad T_1 + (3 c_l - 1) T_1||^2/||T_1||^2
                           = c_l^2 ||X . grad T_1||^2/||T_1||^2 + (3 c_l - 1)(c_l - 1).

Cauchy-Schwarz gives ||X . grad T_1|| >= ||T_1||, so the limit is at least c_l^2 + (3 c_l - 1)(c_l - 1)
= (2 c_l - 1)^2, consistent with (c).

Oscillating example (condensed). Take rho_1 = y chi(r) cos(N r) with chi smooth, nonnegative, nonzero and supported in
[1, 2]. The derivatives falling on cos(N r) dominate. With e = X/r, uniformly,

    T_{1,abc} = N^3 y chi(r) sin(N r) e_a e_b e_c + O(N^2),
    (X . grad T_1)_{abc} = N^4 r y chi(r) cos(N r) e_a e_b e_c + O(N^3).

By the Riemann-Lebesgue lemma, ||T_1||^2 = (N^6/2) int y^2 chi^2 + o(N^6), and

    ||X . grad T_1||^2 = (N^8/2) int r^2 y^2 chi^2 + o(N^8) >= (N^8/2) int y^2 chi^2 + o(N^8),

since r >= 1 on the support. So ||X . grad T_1||/||T_1|| >= N (1 + o(1)), and the limit of eta_3 is at least
c_l N (1 + o(1)). Thus eta_3 can be arbitrarily large while G_rho + G_U is arbitrarily small.

(f) The vanishing family of 3.41. For 0 < D <= 1 let rho_D and U_D be as in 3.41: c_l = 1 + D, eta = D/(1 + D) <= 1/2,
a = 4D, f = (1 + r^2)^{-eta/2} and H = int_0^1 t^3 f(r t) dt. Put L := log(1 + r^2) and
g_eta(s) := (e^{-eta s/2} - 1)/eta, so that f = 1 + eta g_eta(L).

Uniform bounds. For k >= 1 and s >= 0, |g_eta^{(k)}(s)| = 2^{-k} eta^{k-1} e^{-eta s/2} <= 2^{-k}. Also
|D^m L| <= C_m (1 + r)^{-m} for m >= 1. The chain rule then gives, uniformly in D,

    |D^m g_eta(L)| <= C_m (1 + r)^{-m},     |D^m f| <= C_m eta (1 + r)^{-m}     (m >= 1).

From D^m H(X) = int_0^1 t^{3+m} (D^m f)(t X) dt and t/(1 + t r) <= 1/(1 + r) for 0 <= t <= 1, also
|D^m H| <= C_m eta (1 + r)^{-m} for m >= 1. Finally 0 < H <= 1/4 and |r H'| = |f - 4 H| <= 1.

Hypotheses. Fix D.

- y f is a symbol of order 1 - eta. H is a symbol of order -eta: at large r the integral for D^m H is bounded by
  C r^{-4-m} int_0^r s^{3+m} (1 + s)^{-eta-m} ds <= C r^{-eta-m}.
- So rho_D and U_D = a (x (H + y^2 H'/r), -y (H + x^2 H'/r)) (from psi_D = -a x y H) satisfy the symbol bounds with
  q = 1 - eta < 1.
- rho_D is O(r^{1-eta}), odd in y and nonzero, so it is not a polynomial, and D^3 rho_D != 0.
- Since c_l eta = D,

    c_l X . grad rho_D - rho_D = a D y f/(1 + r^2) = 4 D^2 y f/(1 + r^2),

  which is a symbol of order -1 - eta, while U_D . grad rho_D is a symbol of order 1 - 2 eta. Their third derivatives
  are O(r^{-4-eta}) and O(r^{-2-2 eta}), so D^3 R is in L^2.

Thus (a)-(e) apply for each D. The relative residuals are O(D) by 3.41(iii).

Lower bound. By 3.41(v), G_rho = 4D and G_U <= D (sqrt 2 + 4 eta + eta^2/2) < 4D, so S < 8D. By (c) and (e),
eta_3 >= [1 + 2D - 8 C_* D]_+, hence liminf_{D -> 0} eta_3 >= 1.

Upper bound. By (b),

    D^3 R = 4 D^2 D^3(y f/(1 + r^2)) + U_D . grad T + C_3.

- First term: y/(1 + r^2) is a symbol of order -1 and the derivatives of f are bounded as above, uniformly in D. So its
  L^2 norm is <= C D^2.
- Second term: T = D^3 rho_D = 4 D eta D^3(y g_eta(L)), since D^3(4 D y) = 0. Similarly
  D^4 rho_D = 4 D eta D^4(y g_eta(L)) is bounded by C D^2 (1 + r)^{-3}, while |U_D| <= (5/4) a r = 5 D r. So
  ||U_D . grad T||_2 <= C D^3.
- Third term: by (2), ||C_3||_2 <= B ||T||_2 <= 8 C_* D ||T||_2.

Hence, with C independent of D,

    eta_3 <= C D^2/||T||_2 + 8 C_* D.

Lower bound for ||T||. D^3(y g_eta(L)) involves only g_eta^{(k)}(L) with 1 <= k <= 3 (times derivatives of y and L).
It is bounded by C (1 + r)^{-2} uniformly in eta, and it converges pointwise to -(1/2) D^3(y L) as eta -> 0, because
g_eta' -> -1/2 and g_eta'', g_eta''' -> 0. As (1 + r)^{-2} is in L^2(R^2), dominated convergence gives
T/(4 D eta) -> -(1/2) D^3(y L) in L^2. Moreover D^3(y L) != 0, since y L is not a polynomial. With
4 D eta = 4 D^2/(1 + D), ||T||_2 >= c D^2 for small D, with c > 0. So limsup_{D -> 0} eta_3 < inf, and

    1 <= liminf_{D -> 0} eta_3 <= limsup_{D -> 0} eta_3 < inf.

eta_3 stays of order 1, although the relative residuals are O(D).

Remark (compare 3.41(v); not part of 3.40). The same dominated convergence gives, in L^2,

    D^3 rho_D/D^2 -> -2 D^3(y L),     D^3 R/D^2 -> 4 D^3(y/(1 + r^2)) = D^3(-4 y r^2/(1 + r^2)).

The other two terms of D^3 R are O(D^3) in L^2. Exact symbolic integration gives ||D^3(2 y L)||_2^2 = 512 pi/5 and
||D^3(4 y/(1 + r^2))||_2^2 = 6144 pi/35. So eta_3 -> sqrt((6144/35)/(512/5)) = sqrt(12/7) = 1.3093... .

Scope. eta_3 is built from global L^2 norms. A value computed on a finite box or a sampled grid is not eta_3 without a
tail bound, and the inequality gives no bound for sampled norms. By (e), the gradients do not control eta_3 from above.
The inequality is a necessary condition on candidates, not a distance or existence theorem. For an exact profile,
R = 0 and eta_3 = 0, and the inequality reduces to the k = 3 bound of 3.35.

## A.3.41 Vanishing approximate family

Notation as in 3.41: 0 < D <= 1, c_l = 1 + D, eta = D/(1 + D) in (0, 1/2], p = 1 - eta = 1/c_l, a = 4D,
f(r) = (1 + r^2)^{-eta/2}, H(r) = int_0^1 t^3 f(r t) dt, q = r^2/(1 + r^2), rho_D = a y f, psi_D = -a x y H, and the
transport residual R = (c_l X + U_D) . grad rho_D - rho_D. No exactness is assumed.

(i) Elliptic relation and canonical velocity. For r > 0, H(r) = r^{-4} int_0^r s^3 f(s) ds, so r H' = f - 4 H, and
differentiating once more gives H'' + (5/r) H' = f'/r. The integral form shows that H(|X|) is smooth at the origin.
With P = x y, Lap(P H) = P (H'' + 5 H'/r) (as Lap P = 0 and grad P . grad H = 2 P H'/r), so -Lap psi_D =
a x y f'/r = d_x rho_D. The velocity U_D = (-d_y psi_D, d_x psi_D) is
    U_1 = a x (H + y^2 H'/r),     U_2 = -a y (H + x^2 H'/r).
For 0 < t <= 1, f(r t)/f(r) = ((1 + r^2)/(1 + r^2 t^2))^{eta/2} lies in [1, t^{-eta}], hence tau := H/f lies in
[1/4, 1/(4 - eta)] and J := r H'/f = 1 - 4 tau lies in [-eta/(4 - eta), 0]. So H and r H' are O(r^{-eta}),
U_D = O(r^{1 - eta}) = o(r) and rho_D = O(r^p). Parities: rho_D is even in x and odd in y, psi_D is odd in x and in y.
Uniqueness of the canonical velocity in this class is 3.1(i), so U_D is the canonical velocity of rho_D.

(ii) Origin values. f(0) = 1 and H(0) = 1/4, so a0 = d_y rho_D(0) = a = 4D and c = d_xy psi_D(0) = -a/4 = -D;
hence c_l + c = 1.

(iii) Residual formula. Since r f'/f = -eta q, X . grad rho_D = rho_D (1 - eta q). Directly from the formulas in (i),
X . U_D = a H (x^2 - y^2) = a r^2 H cos(2 th), and
    U_D . grad rho_D = a^2 y [ (x^2 - y^2) H f'/r - H f - x^2 f H'/r ]
                     = -a rho_D f [ tau + cos^2(th) J + eta q tau cos(2 th) ]
(the terms in x^2 y^2 f' H'/r^2 cancel). With c_l eta = D and a = 4D,
    R/rho_D = c_l (1 - eta q) - 1 - a f (tau + cos^2(th) J + eta q tau cos(2 th))
            = D [ (1 - q) - 4 f (tau + cos^2(th) J + eta q tau cos(2 th)) ].
As eta <= 1/2: tau <= 2/7, |J| <= 1/7, eta q tau <= 1/7, f <= 1 and 0 <= 1 - q <= 1, so
|R| <= D (1 + 4 (4/7)) |rho_D| = (23/7) D |rho_D|. Since N_f >= |rho_D| and N_v >= |rho_D|, |R| <= 4D N_f and
|R| <= 4D N_v everywhere; on the x-axis all three vanish.

(iv) Non-profile. On the positive y-axis (cos^2 th = 0, cos 2 th = -1, 1 - q = 1/(1 + y^2)),
    R(0, y) = a y f(y) [ D/(1 + y^2) - a H(y) (1 - eta q) ].
By dominated convergence f(y) ~ y^{-eta} and H(y) ~ y^{-eta}/(4 - eta); the first term in the bracket is
O(y^{-2}) and 1 - eta q -> p, so R(0, y) ~ -a^2 p y^{1 - 2 eta}/(4 - eta), with 1 - 2 eta = (1 - D)/(1 + D) >= 0. For
0 < D < 1, R(0, y) -> -infinity; for D = 1 the limit is -16 (1/2)/(7/2) = -16/7. In either case R is not identically
zero. Cubic relations: expanding, rho_D = a y - (a eta/2)(x^2 y + y^3) + O(r^5) and
psi_D = -(a/4) x y + (a eta/12) x y (x^2 + y^2) + O(r^6), so in the notation of 3.3 b = e = -a eta/2 = -2D^2/(1 + D)
and the sin 4th coefficient of the quartic part of psi_D is 0. With A = 2 c_l - 1 = 1 + 2D, a0 - 2A = -2 and
a0 - 4A = -4(1 + D), so the defects are (a0 - 2A) b - 6 e = -8 b = 16 D^2/(1 + D) and (a0 - 4A) b - 0 = -4(1 + D) b
= 8 D^2. As a cross-check, the cubic part of R is -4 D^2 x^2 y - (4 D^2 (3 - D)/(3 (1 + D))) y^3.

(v) Derivative sizes. rho_x = -a f eta q sin(th) cos(th) and rho_y = a f (1 - eta q sin^2 th), so
|grad rho_D|^2 = a^2 f^2 [1 - eta q (2 - eta q) sin^2 th] <= a^2, with equality at the origin; sup |grad rho_D| = 4D.
For the velocity, |DU_D|_F = |D^2 psi_D|_F = a |D^2 (P H)|_F and
D^2 (P H) = H D^2 P + grad P (x) grad H + grad H (x) grad P + P D^2 H with |D^2 P|_F = sqrt 2, |grad P| = r,
|P| <= r^2/2 and |D^2 H|_F <= |H''| + |H'|/r, so |D^2 (P H)|_F <= sqrt(2) H + (5/2) r |H'| + (1/2) r^2 |H''|.
Differentiating under the integral, r H'(r) = int_0^1 t^3 (s f'(s))|_{s = r t} dt and
r^2 H''(r) = int_0^1 t^3 (s^2 f''(s))|_{s = r t} dt, with s f' = -eta q_s f and s^2 f'' = f (-eta q_s + eta (eta + 2) q_s^2),
q_s = s^2/(1 + s^2); hence 0 < H <= 1/4, r |H'| <= eta/4 and r^2 |H''| <= eta (eta + 1)/4 <= eta (eta + 3)/4. So
sup |DU_D|_F <= 4D (sqrt(2)/4 + 5 eta/8 + eta (eta + 3)/8) = D (sqrt 2 + 4 eta + eta^2/2). By 3.35 every exact profile
with this c_l has G_rho + G_U >= (2 c_l - 1)/C_* = (1 + 2D)/C_*, while for the family the same sum is at most
D (4 + sqrt 2 + 4 eta + eta^2/2) -> 0; the distance statement of 3.41(v) is the triangle inequality for the seminorm
sup |grad .| + sup |D U[.]| (U[.] is linear). The limit of eta_3 quoted in 3.41(v) is proved in the Remark at the end
of A.3.40.

(vi) Strain and weighted residual. Put z = r^2, b = eta/2 <= 1/4 and G(z) = H(r). Substituting u = t^2 in the
definition of H gives G(z) = (1/2) int_0^1 t (1 + z t)^{-b} dt, and f = (1 + z)^{-b}. Then G' <= 0 <= G'', and z^2
G(z) = (1/2) int_0^z u (1 + u)^{-b} du gives 2G + z G' = f/2. With psi_D = -a x y G(z) and s = sin(2 th), direct
differentiation gives psi_xy = -a (P + Q s^2) and (psi_xx - psi_yy)/2 = -a Q s cos(2 th), where P = G + 2 z G' and
Q = z^2 G'' >= 0. The symmetric part of DU_D has |S|_op^2 = psi_xy^2 + ((psi_xx - psi_yy)/2)^2 = a^2 [P^2 + s^2 (2 P Q
+ Q^2)], which is affine in s^2, so its maximum over th is a^2 max(P^2, (P + Q)^2). Now P + Q/2 = (1/2) d/dz [z (2G +
z G')] = (f + z f_z)/4 = (1 + z)^{-b-1} (1 + (1 - b) z)/4 > 0, so (P + Q)^2 >= P^2 and the angular maximum of |S|_op
is a (P + Q) = a (G + 2 z G' + z^2 G''). With w = z t/(1 + z t) in [0, 1), G + 2 z G' + z^2 G'' = (1/2) int_0^1 t (1 +
z t)^{-b} [1 - 2 b w + b (b + 1) w^2] dt. The bracket is a convex function of w with value 1 at w = 0 and 1 - b +
b^2 <= 1 at w = 1, so it lies in (0, 1] (its discriminant is -4b < 0), and (1 + z t)^{-b} <= 1. Hence the angular
maximum is at most a/4 = D, with equality at z = 0, so sigma = D. From (iii), -X . U_D/|X|^2 = -a G cos(2 th) <= a
G(z) <= a G(0) = D, with equality approached as z -> 0 on the y-axis, so M = D and X . W = c_l |X|^2 + X .
U_D >= |X|^2. By (iv) the cubic part of R contains -4 D^2 x^2 y, so d_xxy R(0) = -8 D^2. Weighted residual. As c_l +
c = 1, R and h_D = rho_D - a y are O(r^3) at 0 and O(r) at infinity, so ||R||_m and ||h_D||_m are finite for
2 < m < 4. Uniformly in 0 < D <= 1: 0 <= 1 - f <= (eta/2) log(1 + r^2) <= (D/2) log(1 + r^2), so |h_D|/D^2 <= 2 r
log(1 + r^2); and in the formula of (iii) for R/rho_D the bracket equals -q - (4H - 1) - 4 f cos^2(th) J - 4 f eta q
tau cos(2 th) (as f tau = H), where, using log(1 + r^2) <= r^2, |4H - 1| <= 4 int_0^1 t^3 (1 - f(r t)) dt <= D r^2/3,
f |J| = |f - 4H| <= |f - 1| + |4H - 1| <= 5 D r^2/6, q <= r^2 and 4 f eta q tau <= 8 D r^2/7. Hence the bracket is at
most 6 r^2 in modulus, and at most 23/7 by (iii), so |R|/D^2 = 4 |y| f |bracket| <= C min(r^3, r). So h_D/D^2 and
R/D^2 have majorants C r^3 near 0 and C r (1 + log(1 + r^2)) at infinity, which are in L^2(r^{-2m} dX) for 2 < m < 4.
Pointwise, (1 - f)/D -> (1/2) log(1 + r^2), f -> 1, tau -> 1/4, J -> 0 and eta -> 0, so h_D/D^2 -> -2 y log(1 + r^2)
and R/D^2 -> 4 y (-q) = -4 y r^2/(1 + r^2), and dominated convergence gives these limits in L^2(r^{-2m} dX). At m = 3,
with s = r^2 and int_0^inf log^2(1 + s) s^{-2} ds = 2 int_0^inf log(1 + s)/(s (1 + s)) ds = pi^2/3, ||-2 y log(1 +
r^2)||_3^2 = 4 pi int_0^inf log^2(1 + r^2) r^{-3} dr = 2 pi^3/3 and ||-4 y r^2/(1 + r^2)||_3^2 = 16 pi int_0^inf r (1
+ r^2)^{-2} dr = 8 pi, so the ratio ||R||_3/||h_D||_3 tends to (12/pi^2)^{1/2} = 2 sqrt(3)/pi.

## A.3.42 Weighted lower bound for h = rho - a0 y

Setup. rho is an exact profile of the primary class, W = c_l X + U, D = c_l - 1 and c = psi_xy(0) = 1 - c_l = -D
(3.2). As in 3.42, h = rho - a0 y, phi = psi - c x y, v = (-phi_y, phi_x) = U - (-c x, c y), w = r^{-2m}, ||g||_m^2 =
int |g|^2 w dX, S = (DU + DU^T)/2 and sigma = sup |S|_op. By 3.23, rho and U are O(r^p) with p = 1/c_l < 1, and G_rho
= sup |grad rho| and G_U = sup |DU| are finite.

(i) Transport identity. Proof. U_2 = psi_x = c y + phi_x = c y + v_2, so W_2 = (c_l + c) y + v_2 = y + v_2 by 3.2.
Since W . grad(a0 y) = a0 W_2 and W . grad rho = rho,

    W . grad h - h = (W . grad rho - rho) - a0 (W_2 - y) = -a0 v_2.

Only c_l + c = 1 was used; for any smooth pair with this relation the computation gives W . grad h - h + a0 v_2 = W .
grad rho - rho. Also -Lap phi = -Lap psi = d_x rho = d_x h, because Lap(x y) = 0 and d_x(a0 y) = 0.

(ii) Weighted identity. Proof. Orders at 0: rho is smooth, even in x and odd in y, so its Taylor monomials are x^{2i}
y^{2j+1}; none has degree 2, hence h = O(r^3). psi is smooth and odd in x and in y, so its monomials are x^{2i+1}
y^{2j+1}; none has degree 3 and the coefficient of x y is c, hence phi = O(r^4) and v = O(r^3). Orders at infinity:
|grad psi| = |U| and psi(0) = 0 give |psi(X)| <= int_0^1 |U(tX)| |X| dt = O(r^{1+p}); hence h = O(r), v = O(r) and phi
= O(r^2). So |h|^2 w and |v|^2 w are O(r^{6-2m}) at 0 and O(r^{2-2m}) at infinity, and with dX = r dr dth both are
integrable for 2 < m < 4. If h = 0 then rho = a0 y with a0 = rho_y(0) != 0, which does not have sublinear growth;
so 0 < ||h||_m < inf, and also ||v||_m < inf.
From div W = 2 c_l (div U = 0) and grad w = -2m r^{-2} X w,

    div(w W) = 2 (1 - m) c_l w - 2m (X . U/r^2) w,
    (W . grad h - h) h w = (1/2) div(h^2 w W) + ((m - 1) c_l - 1) h^2 w + m (X . U/r^2) h^2 w,

the second line because h w W . grad h = (1/2) div(h^2 w W) - (1/2) h^2 div(w W). Integrate over eps < r < R. On |X| =
eps, h^2 = O(eps^6), w = eps^{-2m} and |W| = O(eps), so the flux is O(eps^{8-2m}); on |X| = R, h^2 = O(R^2) and |W| =
O(R), so it is O(R^{4-2m}). Both tend to 0 for 2 < m < 4. The bulk terms are absolutely integrable: U(0) = 0 gives |X
. U|/r^2 <= |U|/r <= G_U, and |v_2 h| w <= (|v|^2 + |h|^2) w/2. Letting eps -> 0 and R -> inf and inserting (i) gives
the identity of 3.42(ii).

(iii) Mellin bound. Proof. Put s = log r, F = r^{1-m} h and G = r^{-m} phi, functions of (s, th). Since dX = r^2 ds
dth, r phi_r = r^m (d_s + m) G and phi_th = r^m G_th,

    ||h||_m^2 = int |F|^2 ds dth,   ||v||_m^2 = int (|(d_s + m) G|^2 + |d_th G|^2) ds dth,

and int |G|^2 ds dth < inf as well (phi = O(r^4) at 0 and O(r^2) at infinity). With r d_r = d_s, r^2 Lap phi = r^m
((d_s + m)^2 + d_th^2) G and r^2 d_x h = r (cos th r h_r - sin th h_th) = r^m (cos th (d_s + m - 1) F - sin th F_th).
Since d_th(-sin th F) = -cos th F - sin th F_th, the equation -Lap phi = d_x h on the punctured plane becomes

    -((d_s + m)^2 + d_th^2) G = (d_s + m) H_1 + d_th H_2,   H = (H_1, H_2) = (cos th F, -sin th F),   |H| = |F|.

Angular modes: phi is odd in x and in y, so phi(-th) = -phi(th) = phi(pi - th) and phi(th + pi) = phi(th); only even
frequencies occur (phi is a series in sin(2j th)). h is even in x and odd in y, so h(th + pi) = -h(th) and F has only
odd frequencies; hence cos th F and sin th F have only even frequencies. Expand in e^{i n th}, n even, and transform
in s with frequency xi; put z = m + i xi. All of G, (d_s + m) G, d_th G and H are in L^2, so

    (n^2 - z^2) hat G = z hat H_1 + i n hat H_2.

Here n^2 - z^2 = n^2 - m^2 + xi^2 - 2 i m xi vanishes only if xi = 0 and n^2 = m^2, which is impossible because m in
(2, 4) is not an even integer. So hat G = (z hat H_1 + i n hat H_2)/(n^2 - z^2) almost everywhere, and with a = (z, i
n),

    ((d_s + m) G, d_th G)^ = a (a^T hat H)/(n^2 - z^2).

The complex matrix a a^T has operator norm |a|^2 = xi^2 + m^2 + n^2 (a a^T u = (a^T u) a, and |a^T u| <= |a| |u| with
equality for u the complex conjugate of a), and |n^2 - z^2|^2 = (xi^2 + (n - m)^2)(xi^2 + (n + m)^2). So the auxiliary
map H -> ((d_s + m) G, d_th G), on two-component inputs H, is on the mode (n, xi) a rank-one matrix of norm
