    M_{m,n}(xi) = (xi^2 + m^2 + n^2)/((xi^2 + (n - m)^2)(xi^2 + (n + m)^2))^{1/2},

and Plancherel gives ||v||_m <= (sup_{n even, xi} M_{m,n}(xi)) ||H|| = (sup M_{m,n}) ||h||_m.
Maximization. With t = xi^2, M_{m,n}^2 = 1 + 4 m^2 n^2/((t + (n - m)^2)(t + (n + m)^2)), which is nonincreasing in t.
So the supremum over xi is attained at xi = 0, where M_{m,n}(0) = (m^2 + n^2)/|m^2 - n^2| (and M_{m,0} = 1). As a
function of u = n^2, (m^2 + u)/|m^2 - u| increases on (0, m^2) and decreases on (m^2, inf). Since 4 < m^2 < 16, the
even n with 0 < n^2 < m^2 are n = 2 and n = -2, and every even n with n^2 > m^2 has |n| >= 4. Hence sup M_{m,n} =
max((m^2 + 4)/(m^2 - 4), (m^2 + 16)/(16 - m^2)) = N_m, attained at |n| = 2 or |n| = 4. For m = 3 the two values are
13/5 and 25/7, so N_3 = 25/7; for m^2 = 8 both are 3, so N_{sqrt 8} = 3.
Scope of the constant. N_m is the norm of the auxiliary two-component map; the bound for v follows by restricting it
to inputs H = (cos th F, -sin th F), and N_m is not claimed to be the norm of h -> v. Normalization: v is the inverse
of the source d_x h in the weighted space (v = O(r^3) at 0, so it has finite ||.||_m). The canonical inverse (3.1) of
the same source d_x h = d_x rho is U = v + (-c x, c y) = v + (D x, -D y), so U_2 = v_2 - D y; the field (D x, -D y)
has infinite ||.||_m near 0 for m >= 2, so the bound is a statement about v and not about U.

(iv) Strain bound. Proof. U(0) = 0 gives U(X) = int_0^1 DU(tX) X dt, so X . U(X) = int_0^1 X^T S(tX) X dt >= -sigma
|X|^2. In (ii), m int (X . U/r^2) h^2 w >= -m sigma ||h||_m^2, and by Cauchy-Schwarz and (iii), |a0 int v_2 h w| <=
|a0| ||v||_m ||h||_m <= N_m |a0| ||h||_m^2. Dividing by ||h||_m^2 > 0 gives (m - 1) c_l - 1 <= m sigma + N_m |a0|, and
m = 3 gives 2 c_l - 1 <= 3 sigma + (25/7) |a0|. Since div U = 0, S is symmetric with trace 0, its eigenvalues are
lambda and -lambda, and |S|_op = lambda = |S|_F/sqrt 2; S is the orthogonal projection of DU onto the symmetric
matrices, so |S|_F <= |DU|_F and sigma <= G_U/sqrt 2. Also |a0| = |rho_y(0)| <= G_rho. Hence

    2 c_l - 1 <= (3/sqrt 2) G_U + (25/7) G_rho <= (25/7)(G_rho + G_U),

because 3/sqrt 2 = 2.121... < 25/7 = 3.571...; that is, G_rho + G_U >= 7 (2 c_l - 1)/25 = 0.28 (2 c_l - 1), compared
with (2 c_l - 1)/Lambda = 0.164... (2 c_l - 1) in 3.36(ii).

(v) Strain cap. Proof. If sigma <= c_l - 1, (iv) gives 2 c_l - 1 <= 3 (c_l - 1) + (25/7) |a0|, that is 2 - c_l <=
(25/7) |a0|. This is false when 1 < c_l < 2 and |a0| < 7 (2 - c_l)/25, which is the exclusion. For 1 < c_l <= 3/2 and
0 < |a0| <= 1/400 one has 7 (2 - c_l)/25 >= 7/50 > 1/400, so the exclusion of 3.36(iii) is contained. Since sigma >= D
always (3.36), the hypothesis sigma <= c_l - 1 means sigma = c_l - 1.

## A.3.43 Angular contrast, a positivity test and non-profiles with the integral identities

Setup. In (i) and (ii) rho is an exact profile of the primary class, D = c_l - 1 > 0, c = -D (3.2), q = rho/(a0 y) and
Q is the open first quadrant. q is smooth and even in x and in y with q(0) = 1, so q = 1 + O(r^2), q_r = O(r) and q_th
= x q_y - y q_x = O(r^2) at 0; by 3.23, q = O(r^{p-1}), q_r = O(r^{p-2}) and q_th = O(r^{p-1}) uniformly on the closed
quadrant. Sine coefficients are rho_j(r) = (1/pi) int_0^{2pi} rho sin(j th) dth.
Kernel. k(th) = sin^2 th (4 sin^2 th - 3) satisfies

    k = (cos 4th - cos 2th)/2 = -sin th sin 3th = -(cos th sin^3 th)',

the last since (cos th sin^3 th)' = 3 cos^2 th sin^2 th - sin^4 th. Hence int_0^{pi/2} k dth = 0 (cos th sin^3 th
vanishes at 0 and pi/2); k < 0 on (0, pi/3), k(pi/3) = 0 and k > 0 on (pi/3, pi/2]; int_{pi/3}^{pi/2} k dth =
cos(pi/3) sin^3(pi/3) = 3 sqrt 3/16, so the negative part has the same mass and int_0^{pi/2} |k| dth = 3 sqrt 3/8.

(i) Angular contrast formula. Proof. Put I(r) = int_0^{pi/2} k(th) q(r, th) dth. Since rho sin 3th = a0 r q sin th sin
3th is even under th -> -th and th -> pi - th (q is even in x and in y), rho_3(r) = (4 a0 r/pi) int_0^{pi/2} q sin th
sin 3th dth = -(4 a0 r/pi) I(r). Inserting this into c = -a0/4 + int_0^inf rho_3 s^{-2} ds (3.2), using c = -D and
dividing by -a0 gives

    D/a0 = 1/4 + (4/pi) int_0^inf I(r) dr/r.

Convergence with the angular integral taken first: int k = 0 gives I(r) = int_0^{pi/2} k (q - 1) dth = O(r^2) at 0,
and |I(r)| <= (3 sqrt 3/8) sup_th |q(r, th)| = O(r^{p-1}) at infinity, so int |I(r)| dr/r < inf. The double integral
is not absolutely convergent: q -> 1 uniformly as r -> 0, so int_0^{pi/2} |k q| dth -> 3 sqrt 3/8 > 0 and int_0^1
int_0^{pi/2} |k q| dth dr/r = inf. Hence the order of integration is part of the formula.
Passage from the q_x form. In Q, x y^2 r^{-4} dX = cos th sin^2 th dr dth and q_x = cos th q_r - r^{-1} sin th q_th,
so

    (4/pi) int_Q x y^2 r^{-4} q_x dX = (4/pi) int_0^{pi/2} cos^2 th sin^2 th (int_0^inf q_r dr) dth
                                       - (4/pi) int_0^inf r^{-1} (int_0^{pi/2} cos th sin^3 th q_th dth) dr.

The left side and both pieces are absolutely convergent, by q_r = O(r) at 0, O(r^{p-2}) at infinity, and r^{-1} q_th =
O(r) at 0, O(r^{p-2}) at infinity. Integration by parts in r gives int_0^inf q_r dr = q(inf) - q(0) = -1, and
int_0^{pi/2} cos^2 th sin^2 th dth = pi/16, so the first piece is -1/4. Integration by parts in th, with cos th sin^3
th = 0 at both ends and -(cos th sin^3 th)' = k, gives int cos th sin^3 th q_th dth = I(r). So the left side equals
-1/4 - (4/pi) int I(r) dr/r = -D/a0 = c/a0. Read backwards, this is the derivation of the formula from the q_x form of
3.24(i).

(ii) Oscillation bound. Lemma. For g continuous on [0, pi/2], |int_0^{pi/2} k g dth| <= (3 sqrt 3/16) osc g, with
strict inequality unless g is constant. Proof. Write k = k_+ - k_- with k_+, k_- >= 0 of equal mass kappa = 3 sqrt
3/16. Then int k g = int k_+ g - int k_- g lies between kappa (min g - max g) and kappa (max g - min g). Equality in
the upper bound forces g = max g on (pi/3, pi/2], where k_+ > 0, and g = min g on (0, pi/3), where k_- > 0; continuity
at pi/3 then gives max g = min g. The lower bound is the same with g replaced by -g.
Bound. Proof. By (i) and the lemma applied to g = q(r, .) for each r,

    |D/a0 - 1/4| <= (4/pi) int_0^inf |I(r)| dr/r <= (4/pi)(3 sqrt 3/16) A(q) = (3 sqrt 3/(4 pi)) A(q).

A(q) is finite: osc_th q(r, .) <= 2 sup_th |q - 1| = O(r^2) at 0 and <= 2 sup_th |q| = O(r^{p-1}) at infinity. It is
dilation invariant: the dilate rho_l(X) = l rho(X/l) of 3.5 has the same a0 and quotient q_l(X) = q(X/l), and r -> l r
preserves dr/r. Strictness: if A(q) > 0, then osc_th q(r0, .) > 0 for some r0, hence for r in an open interval (q is
continuous); there |I(r)| < (3 sqrt 3/16) osc_th q(r, .) by the lemma, and both sides are continuous in r, so the
integrated inequality is strict.
Consequences. Proof. Put z = 3 sqrt 3 A(q)/pi; the bound is |D/a0 - 1/4| <= z/4, strict if z > 0, and D > 0. If z = 0,
then a0 = 4D. If 0 < z < 1, then (1 - z)/4 < D/a0 < (1 + z)/4; so D/a0 > 0, a0 > 0 and 4/(1 + z) < a0/D < 4/(1 - z).
If A(q) <= pi/(3 sqrt 3), i.e. z <= 1, then either a0 = 4D, or 0 <= (1 - z)/4 < D/a0 < (1 + z)/4 <= 1/2; in both cases
a0 > 2D. If a0 < 0, then z > 0 (z = 0 would give a0 = 4D > 0) and 1/4 + D/|a0| = |D/a0 - 1/4| < z/4, that is A(q) >
(pi/(3 sqrt 3))(1 + 4D/|a0|). If 0 < a0 <= 2D, then D/a0 >= 1/2, so z > 0 and D/a0 - 1/4 < z/4, that is A(q) > (pi/(3
sqrt 3))(4D/a0 - 1).

(iii) Positivity test. Proof. For f in L^2, int f Tf dX = (2pi)^{-2} int (xi_1^2/|xi|^2) |hat f|^2 dxi >= 0. Let G =
e^{-r^2}, so g = y e^{-r^2} = -(1/2) G_y and Tg = -(1/2) d_y TG. The radial F with -(r F')'/r = e^{-r^2} and F'
regular at 0 has r F' = -int_0^r s e^{-s^2} ds, i.e. F'(r) = -(1 - e^{-r^2})/(2r) (F itself grows like -(1/2) log r,
but only F' and F'' are used). Then

    -d_x^2 F = -(F'' x^2/r^2 + F' y^2/r^3) = e^{-r^2} x^2/r^2 + (1 - e^{-r^2})(y^2 - x^2)/(2 r^4),

a smooth function (removable singularity at 0) that is O(r^{-2}) at infinity, hence in L^2. Since Lap(-d_x^2 F) =
d_x^2 G, its Fourier transform equals (xi_1^2/|xi|^2) hat G up to a distribution supported at xi = 0, that is up to
the transform of a polynomial; an L^2 polynomial is 0, so TG = -d_x^2 F. Differentiating in y at (2, 1), where r^2 =
5, gives d_y TG(2, 1) = 11/125 - (266/125) e^{-5}, so

    Tg(2, 1) = -11/250 + (133/125) e^{-5},

which is negative if and only if e^5 > 266/11 = 24.18...; and e^5 > 1 + 5 + 25/2 + 125/6 = 118/3 > 266/11. T commutes
with x -> -x and y -> -y, so Tg, like g, is even in x and odd in y, and g Tg is continuous, even in x and in y, with g
Tg(2, 1) = e^{-5} Tg(2, 1) < 0. Choose a smooth zeta >= 0, not identically 0, supported in a disk around (2, 1) inside
Q on which g Tg < 0, and let w0 be the sum of its four reflections in the axes; then int w0 g Tg = 4 int zeta g Tg
< 0. g Tg is bounded, so int e^{-r^2} |g Tg| < inf, and w = w0 + eta e^{-r^2} with 0 < eta int e^{-r^2} |g Tg| < |int
w0 g Tg| is smooth, positive, even in x and in y, with int w g Tg dX < 0. (The unweighted value is int g Tg =
(2pi)^{-2} (pi^2/4) int (xi_1^2 xi_2^2/|xi|^2) e^{-|xi|^2/2} dxi = pi/32, using hat g = -(i pi/2) xi_2 e^{-|xi|^2/4}.)

(iv) Non-profiles with the integral identities (condensed). Proof.
Functionals. For smooth v, even in x and odd in y, with v = y + O(r^3) at 0 and symbol bounds of degree p < 1 at
infinity, let V[v] be its canonical velocity (3.1) and psi_v its stream function, and put phi = r^{-3} sin 3th = (3
x^2 y - y^3)/r^6 (harmonic off 0),

    J(v) = (1/pi) lim_{eps -> 0} int_{r > eps} v phi dX = int_0^inf v_3 r^{-2} dr,   S(v) = 1/4 - J(v),
    B(v) = lim_{eps -> 0} int_{r > eps} v V[v] . grad phi dX.

The derivation of 3.2 uses only the elliptic relation, so d_xy psi_v(0) = -1/4 + J(v) = -S(v). For rho = a0 v and U =
a0 V[v], psi_xy(0) = -a0 S(v), so the strain identity c = 1 - c_l = -D is D = a0 S(v), and DU(0) = diag(D, -D), DW(0)
= diag(2 c_l - 1, 1) by the parities. The identity 3.4 reads -D pi a0 J(v) + a0^2 B(v) = -a0 pi D/2; with D = a0 S and
J = 1/4 - S it is equivalent to B(v) = C_s := -pi s (s + 1/4), s = S(v). For q = v/y with q -> 0 at infinity, (x y^2
q_x + y^3 q_y) r^{-4} dX = sin^2 th q_r dr dth gives (4/pi) int_Q (x y^2 q_x + y^3 q_y) r^{-4} dX = (4/pi)(pi/4)(-1) =
-1, and by (i) (an elliptic computation) S = (4/pi) int_Q x y^2 r^{-4} (-q_x) dX = D/a0; this is 1 = S + T of
3.24(ii). So the three identities hold once S(v) = s, D = a0 s and B(v) = C_s.
Radial reference. For 1/2 <= p < 1 let v_p = y F_p, F_p = (1 + r^2)^{(p-1)/2} and b_p(r) = int_0^1 t^3 F_p(r t) dt, so
that r^4 b_p = int_0^r t^3 F_p dt, r b_p' = F_p - 4 b_p, b_p(0) = 1/4, b_p' <= 0 and b_p -> 0. In polar form psi_p =
-x y b_p = -(r^2 b_p/2) sin 2th has -Lap psi_p = ((5/2) r b_p' + (r^2/2) b_p'') sin 2th = (r F_p'/2) sin 2th = d_x
v_p, using r b_p'' + 5 b_p' = F_p'. Its velocity V_p = (x b_p + x y^2 b_p'/r, -y b_p - x^2 y b_p'/r) is O(r^p), so it
is canonical (3.1(i)), and d_xy psi_p(0) = -1/4 gives S(v_p) = 1/4, J(v_p) = 0. From 0 < F_p <= 1, |r F_p'| <= 1 and
|r^2 F_p''| <= 3 one gets |b_p| <= 1/4, |r b_p'| <= 1/4 and |r^2 b_p''| <= 3/4. D(x b_p, -y b_p) has Frobenius norm <=
sqrt 2 |b_p| + r |b_p'| <= sqrt 2/4 + 1/4. For H = (x y^2, -x^2 y), |H| <= r^3/2 and |DH|_F^2 = r^4 + 6 x^2 y^2 <= 5
r^4/2, so D((b_p'/r) H) has norm <= sqrt(5/2) r |b_p'| + (r^2 |b_p''| + r |b_p'|)/2 <= sqrt 10/8 + 1/2. Hence
||DV_p||_inf < 2. In polar form V . grad phi = 3 r^{-4} (psi_r cos 3th + r^{-1} psi_th sin 3th) = -3 r^{-3} (b_p sin
5th + (r b_p'/2) sin 2th cos 3th) for V = V_p; with int_0^{2pi} sin th sin 5th dth = 0 (so the circular limit exists)
and int_0^{2pi} sin th sin 2th cos 3th dth = -pi/2,

    B(v_p) = (3 pi/4) int_0^inf F_p b_p' dr,   -3 pi/16 <= B(v_p) <= 0.

Bumps. Let eta be a smooth radial bump supported in the unit disk with int eta = 1, eta_delta(X) = delta^{-2}
eta(X/delta). For a point z of the unit circle in Q, at angle th_z, let g = sum_{sigma, tau = +-1} tau eta_delta(X -
(sigma x_z, tau y_z)) (delta small, so that the four supports are disjoint and avoid the axes). g is even in x, odd in
y and >= 0 for y > 0, and J(g) -> (4/pi) phi(z) = (4/pi) sin 3th_z. Fix s < 0 or s >= 1/2 and the centres th_- =
pi/12, th_+ = pi/4 if s < 0, th_- = 5 pi/12, th_+ = 17 pi/48 if s >= 1/2. In each case sin 3th_+- has the sign of
1/4 - s, so beta_+- = (1/4 - s)/J(g_+-) > 0 (with positive limits) and S(v_p + beta_+- g_+-) = s; and cos 4th_- > 0 >
cos 4th_+. Self term: for radial eta, Plancherel and the symbols xi_1 xi_2/|xi|^2, -xi_1^2/|xi|^2 of V (3.1(ii)) give
int eta V_1[eta] = 0 (odd symbol) and int eta V_2[eta] = -||eta||_2^2/2 (rotation average of xi_1^2/|xi|^2); the
symbols are homogeneous of degree 0, |grad phi(X) - grad phi(z')| <= C delta on a bump centred at z', and ||V[f]||_2
<= ||f||_2, so a bump at z' contributes -(1/2) delta^{-2} ||eta||_2^2 d_y phi(z') + O(delta^{-1}). With d_y phi = 3
r^{-4} cos 4th (even in x and in y) and O(1) interactions between distinct bumps (the kernel is smooth between their
supports, the masses are bounded),

    B(beta g) = -(6 beta^2/delta^2) ||eta||_2^2 cos 4th_z + O(delta^{-1}).

Cross terms: B(v_p + beta g) - B(v_p) - B(beta g) = beta int (v_p V[g] + g V_p) . grad phi. The g V_p term is O(1)
(|V_p| <= 2 |X|). On r > 1/2, |v_p grad phi| <= C r^{-3} is in L^2 uniformly in p and ||V[g]||_2 <= ||g||_2 =
O(delta^{-1}). On r < 1/2 (away from the bumps), V[g] = int K(X - Y) g(Y) dY is analytic with derivatives bounded
uniformly in delta, and by the parities V[g] = (h x, -h y) + O(r^3); with v_p = y + O(r^3) uniformly in p, the only
non-integrable term is y (h x, -h y) . grad phi = -3 h r^{-2} sin th sin 5th, of zero circular mean, and the rest is
O(1). So the cross terms are O(delta^{-1}) uniformly in p, the circular limits exist, and B(v_p + beta_+- g_+-) ->
+-inf as delta -> 0, uniformly in p in [1/2, 1).
Matching. Fix delta with B(v_p + beta_- g_-) < C_s < B(v_p + beta_+ g_+) for all p in [1/2, 1). For v_{p,t} = v_p +
(1 - t) beta_- g_- + t beta_+ g_+, 0 <= t <= 1, S(v_{p,t}) = s (J is linear and J(v_p) = 0), v_{p,t}/y > 0, and t ->
B(v_{p,t}) is a quadratic polynomial, so B(v_{p,t}) = C_s for some t in (0, 1). For smooth compactly supported f,
|DV[f]|_F <= (2pi)^{-2} int |xi| |hat f| dxi <= (1/32) ||(1 - Lap)^3 f||_1, since the symbol of DV has Frobenius norm
<= |xi|, |hat f| <= ||(1 - Lap)^3 f||_1 (1 + |xi|^2)^{-3} and (2pi)^{-2} int |xi| (1 + |xi|^2)^{-3} dxi = 1/32. So
||DV[v_{p,t}]||_inf <= M := 2 + (beta_- ||(1 - Lap)^3 g_-||_1 + beta_+ ||(1 - Lap)^3 g_+||_1)/32, independent of p and
t. Choose 0 < D < min(1, |s|/(4M)), c_l = 1 + D, p = 1/c_l in (1/2, 1) and a0 = D/s. For rho = a0 v_{p,t}, U = a0
V[v_{p,t}] one has ||DU||_inf < 1/4, |U(X)| <= |X|/4 and X . W >= (c_l - 1/4) |X|^2 >= (3/4) |X|^2; D = a0 s, so the
three identities hold; and rho = a0 y F_p outside a compact set, so r^{-p} rho -> Theta0 = a0 sin th.
Oscillation. Let chi be smooth, even in x and odd in y, supported in four reflected rectangles that avoid the axes and
the bump supports (for instance near (+-3, +-3)), with chi = 1 on a rectangle R_+ in Q. Put f_n = eps n^{-2} chi cos(n
x), d_n = -Lap f_n = eps chi cos nx + 2 eps n^{-1} chi_x sin nx - eps n^{-2} (Lap chi) cos nx and Z_n = (-d_x d_y f_n,
d_x^2 f_n). Since -Lap(d_x f_n) = d_x d_n and Z_n is compactly supported, Z_n = V[d_n] (3.1(i)); |d_n| + |Z_n| <=
C_chi eps uniformly in n; and J(d_n) = -(1/pi) int f_n Lap phi = 0. The change B(v_{p,t} + d_n) - B(v_{p,t}) = int
(d_n V[v_{p,t}] + v_{p,t} Z_n + d_n Z_n) . grad phi is an integral over supp chi and is O(eps + eps^2) uniformly in n
and t. For eps small, independent of n, the strict inequalities at t = 0 and t = 1 persist, so there is t_n in (0, 1)
with B(v_{p,t_n} + d_n) = C_s. Put rho_n = a0 (v_{p,t_n} + d_n) and U_n = a0 (V[v_{p,t_n}] + Z_n), the canonical
velocity. S = s is unchanged, so all three identities hold. On supp chi, v_{p,t} = v_p and v_p/y = F_p has a positive
minimum, while the bumps and chi avoid the axes; so for eps small, F_p/2 <= q_n <= C F_p with C independent of n. With
r_* the least radius on supp chi and eps so small that |a0| ||Z_n||_inf <= r_*/4, X . W_n >= (3/4) |X|^2 - |X| r_*/4
>= |X|^2/2 on supp chi, and X . W_n >= (3/4) |X|^2 elsewhere. On R_+, d_n = eps cos nx and Z_n = (0, -eps cos nx), so
d_x d_n = -eps n sin nx and d_x (Z_n)_2 = eps n sin nx, while the derivatives of v_{p,t} and V[v_{p,t}] are bounded
uniformly in t; for n large R_+ contains points with |sin nx| = 1, so sup |grad rho_n| and sup |DU_n| are >= |a0| eps
n - C, which is unbounded. The higher symbol constants of rho_n are not uniform in n.
Not profiles. Outside a compact set rho_n = a0 y F_p = a0 r^p sin th + a0 ((p - 1)/2) r^{p-2} sin th + O(r^{p-4}). If
rho_n, with c_l and U_n, solved the transport equation, it would be an exact profile of the primary class with Theta0
= a0 sin th, and 3.32 would give rho_n - r^p Theta0 - r^{2p-1} Theta1 = O(r^{3p-2}); with rho_n - r^p Theta0 =
O(r^{p-2}) and 2p - 1 > max(p - 2, 3p - 2) this forces Theta1 = 0. But for Theta0 = a0 sin th the equation of 3.32 is
-Phi0'' - (p + 1)^2 Phi0 = (p - 1)(a0/2) sin 2th; as 4 - (p + 1)^2 = (1 - p)(p + 3), Phi0 = -a0 sin 2th/(2 (p + 3)),
u_{0,r} = -Phi0' = a0 cos 2th/(p + 3), u_{0,th} = (p + 1) Phi0 = -a0 (p + 1) sin th cos th/(p + 3), and

    Theta1 = (p u_{0,r} Theta0 + u_{0,th} Theta0')/D = -a0^2 sin th (cos^2 th + p sin^2 th)/(D (p + 3)),

which is nonzero for 0 < th < pi. So no rho_n is an exact profile. Taking s < 0 gives a0 < 0, and s >= 1/2 gives 0 <
a0 <= 2D.

## A.3.44 Sharp weighted constants

Setup. In (i)-(v) rho is an exact profile of the primary class; (vi) concerns candidates. Notation of A.3.42: W = c_l
X + U, D = c_l - 1, c = psi_xy(0) = -D, h = rho - a0 y, phi = psi + D x y, v = (-phi_y, phi_x) = U - (D x, -D y), w =
r^{-2m} (w = r^{-2 mu} in (v)), S = (DU + DU^T)/2, sigma = sup |S|_op and M = sup_{X != 0} (-X . U/r^2). As in
A.3.42(iii), s = log r, F = r^{1-m} h, G = r^{-m} phi, xi is the frequency dual to s and z = m + i xi.
D <= M <= sigma. Proof. U(0) = 0 gives X . U(X) = int_0^1 X^T S(tX) X dt >= -sigma r^2, so M <= sigma. On the y-axis X
. U = y psi_x(0, y) = y (-D y + phi_x(0, y)) = -D y^2 + O(y^4), since phi = O(r^4); so -X . U/r^2 -> D as y -> 0, and
M >= D.
Jacobi matrices. Let d_1 = 1/4, d_j = 1/2 for j >= 2 and, for m not an even integer, b_j = b_j(m) = (m^2 + 4 j^2)/(4
|4 j^2 - m^2|). J^+ (resp. J^-) is the symmetric tridiagonal matrix on l^2(j >= 1) with diagonal entries d_j (resp.
-d_j) and entries b_j at (j, j + 1) and (j + 1, j); Q_m^- (resp. Q_m^+) is the top of its spectrum, the supremum of
its Rayleigh quotient. As a function of u = 4 j^2, b_j = (m^2 + u)/(4 |m^2 - u|) increases for u < m^2 and decreases
for u > m^2 (A.3.42(iii)), and b_j -> 1/4; so J^+ and J^- are bounded and, by 2 |u_j u_{j+1}| <= u_j^2 + u_{j+1}^2,
Q_m^-, Q_m^+ <= 1/2 + 2 max_j b_j(m) < inf. The off-diagonal entries are >= 0, so <J u, u> <= <J |u|, |u|> for J =
J^+, J^- and every real or complex u (|u| taken entrywise).
Lemma 1 (positive vector). Let J be a bounded symmetric tridiagonal matrix, on the half-line or on Z, with diagonal
a_j and off-diagonal entries b_j >= 0, and let s_j > 0 with (J s)_j <= L_0 s_j for every j. Then <J u, u> <= L_0
|u|^2. Proof. For finitely supported real u, 2 b_j u_j u_{j+1} <= b_j (s_{j+1}/s_j) u_j^2 + b_j (s_j/s_{j+1})
u_{j+1}^2; summing and collecting the coefficient of each u_j^2 gives <J u, u> <= sum_j ((J s)_j/s_j) u_j^2 <= L_0
|u|^2, and such u are dense.
Lemma 2 (elimination). Let J be as in Lemma 1 on the half-line, N >= 1 and tau real with <J u, u> <= tau |u|^2 for
every u supported in j >= N + 1. (a) Let Lambda > tau, p_1 = Lambda - a_1 and p_j = Lambda - a_j - b_{j-1}^2/p_{j-1}
for 2 <= j <= N, and then subtract b_N^2/(Lambda - tau) from p_N (from p_1 when N = 1). If p_1, ..., p_N > 0, the top
of the spectrum of J is < Lambda. (b) If the numbers q_j given by the same recursion at l, without the tail term,
satisfy q_1, ..., q_{n-1} > 0 > q_n for some n, the top of the spectrum of J is > l. Proof. (a) Write u = (u', u'')
with u' = (u_1, ..., u_N), J_N for the leading N x N block and J'' for the tail block. Then

    <(Lambda - J) u, u> = <(Lambda - J_N) u', u'> - 2 b_N u_N u_{N+1} + <(Lambda - J'') u'', u''>,

and the last term is >= (Lambda - tau) |u''|^2 >= (Lambda - tau) u_{N+1}^2. Minimizing over u_{N+1} gives <(Lambda -
J) u, u> >= <K u', u'>, where K is Lambda - J_N with its (N, N) entry decreased by b_N^2/(Lambda - tau). The p_j are
the pivots of Gaussian elimination of the tridiagonal matrix K in the natural order, K = E diag(p_1, ..., p_N) E^T
with E unit lower bidiagonal, so K is positive definite and Lambda - J >= 0. The pivots depend continuously on Lambda,
so they remain positive at some Lambda' < Lambda, and the top of the spectrum is <= Lambda' < Lambda. (b) The q_j are
the pivots of l - J_n; since q_1, ..., q_{n-1} != 0 the factorization exists, and by Sylvester's law of inertia l -
J_n has a negative eigenvalue. Its eigenvector u, extended by 0, has <J u, u> = <J_n u, u> > l |u|^2.
Tails. If a_j = a for j >= N + 1 and b_j is nonincreasing for j >= N + 1, then 2 b_j u_j u_{j+1} <= b_j (u_j^2 +
u_{j+1}^2) gives the tail bound tau = a + 2 b_{N+1}. In Lemma 1 with s_{j+1} = t s_j for j >= n, (J s)_j/s_j = a +
b_{j-1}/t + t b_j for j >= n + 1, which is nonincreasing in j under the same hypothesis; so finitely many rows decide.

(i) Bounds, sharpness and enclosures. Proof. Tridiagonal form. By A.3.42(ii)-(iii), F, G, (d_s + m) G and d_th G are
in L^2(ds dth), F has only the modes sin((2j - 1) th), G only the modes sin(2j th), and after the transform in s the
equation reads (n^2 - z^2) hat G_n = (source)_n with n^2 - z^2 != 0. For F = sin(k th), k odd, the source z cos th F -
d_th(sin th F) and the resulting G are

    source = ((z - k - 1)/2) sin((k + 1) th) + ((z + k - 1)/2) sin((k - 1) th),
    G = -sin((k + 1) th)/(2 (k + 1 + z)) + sin((k - 1) th)/(2 (k - 1 - z))   (second term absent for k = 1).

From r phi_r = r^m (d_s + m) G and phi_th = r^m d_th G, r^{1-m} v_2 = r^{1-m} (cos th phi_r - r^{-1} sin th phi_th) =
cos th (d_s + m) G - sin th d_th G, with transform V = (z cos th - sin th d_th) hat G, and

    (z cos th - sin th d_th) sin(n th) = ((z - n)/2) sin((n + 1) th) + ((z + n)/2) sin((n - 1) th).

Composing, in the orthonormal basis e_j = pi^{-1/2} sin((2j - 1) th) of the odd sine modes in L^2(0, 2pi) one gets V =
T(xi) c, c the coefficient vector of hat F, with

    T_jj = -d_j,   T_{j+1,j} = (2j - z)/(4 (2j + z)),   T_{j,j+1} = (2j + z)/(4 (2j - z))

(each of the two G-modes next to sin(k th) returns -1/4 to sin(k th); for k = 1 only one exists). For fixed m the
entries are bounded in j and xi (Re z > 0 and |2j - z| >= |2j - m| > 0). Since r^{-2m} dX = r^{2-2m} ds dth, int v_2 h
w dX = int (r^{1-m} v_2) F ds dth, and Plancherel in s gives

    int v_2 h w dX = (1/2pi) int Re <T(xi) c(xi), c(xi)> dxi,   ||h||_m^2 = (1/2pi) int |c(xi)|^2 dxi.

Hermitian part. Re <T c, c> = <H c, c> with H = (T + T^*)/2, which has diagonal -d_j and, with n = 2j,

    H_{j+1,j} = (T_{j+1,j} + conj(T_{j,j+1}))/2 = (n^2 + m^2 + xi^2)/(4 (n + z)(n - conj(z))).

As |n + z| |n - conj(z)| = |n^2 - z^2|, |H_{j+1,j}| = M_{m,n}(xi)/4 with M_{m,n} as in A.3.42(iii), where M_{m,n}(xi)
<= M_{m,n}(0) = (m^2 + n^2)/|n^2 - m^2| was shown; so |H_{j+1,j}| <= b_j(m), with equality at xi = 0, and H_{j+1,j}(0)
= sgn(2j - m) b_j(m). Hence -<J^+ |c|, |c|> <= <H c, c> <= <J^- |c|, |c|>, so -Q_m^- |c|^2 <= Re <T c, c> <= Q_m^+
|c|^2 for every xi, and integration in xi gives the two bounds.
Sharpness. Let eps > 0. As <J^+ u, u> <= <J^+ |u|, |u|> and finitely supported vectors are dense, there is omega =
(omega_1, ..., omega_N, 0, ...) with omega_j >= 0, |omega| = 1 and <J^+ omega, omega> > Q_m^- - eps. Choose signs sg_j
in {1, -1} with sg_j sg_{j+1} = -sgn(2j - m) and put u_j = sg_j omega_j; then <H(0) u, u> = -<J^+ omega, omega>. Let
chi be real and smooth, supported in [-1, 1], with int chi^2 ds = 1, and for L > 0 put

    F_L(s, th) = L^{-1/2} chi(s/L) sum_{j <= N} u_j e_j(th),   h_L(X) = r^{m-1} F_L(log r, th).

h_L is smooth, supported in e^{-L} <= r <= e^L, even in x and odd in y (odd sine modes), ||h_L||_m = 1, and v is its
weighted inverse (the solution with G in L^2, unique by A.3.42(iii)). Its coefficient vector is L^{1/2} hat chi(L xi)
u, so with the bounded continuous function q(xi) = Re <T(xi) u, u>,

    int v_2 h_L w dX = (1/2pi) int q(xi) L |hat chi(L xi)|^2 dxi -> q(0) = -<J^+ omega, omega> < -Q_m^- + eps

as L -> inf, because (1/2pi) L |hat chi(L xi)|^2 dxi is a probability measure that concentrates at xi = 0. So -Q_m^-
is the best constant in the lower bound. With sg_j sg_{j+1} = sgn(2j - m) instead, <H(0) u, u> = <J^- omega, omega>,
and the same construction shows that Q_m^+ is sharp. The test functions are not profiles; nothing is asserted for
profiles.
Enclosures at m = 3 (b_1 = 13/20, b_2 = 25/28, b_3 = 5/12, b_9 = 37/140). Two certificates; in each, every comparison
is between exact rational numbers, and both were recomputed in exact rational arithmetic for this appendix.
Certificate A (external analysis: Lemma 1 and Rayleigh quotients). For J^+ take s = (470100, 1000000, 926400, 375600,
118940, 33690, 8987, 2312, 582) for j = 1, ..., 9 and s_{j+1} = s_j/4 for j >= 9. The nine ratios (J^+ s)_j/s_j are
below 1633/1000, the closest being j = 8 with margin 793727/4854044000; for j >= 10 the ratio 1/2 + 4 b_{j-1} + b_j/4
is nonincreasing (b_j decreases for 2j > 3), equals 1.6225... at j = 10 and tends to 25/16. For J^- take s = (68130,
100000, 85260, 32120, 9472, 2502) and s_{j+1} = s_j/4 for j >= 6; the six ratios are below 71/100 (closest j = 6,
margin 251149/45536400), and for j >= 7 the ratio -1/2 + 4 b_{j-1} + b_j/4 is nonincreasing and equals 0.7018... at j
= 7. The finite vectors (the listed entries only) have Rayleigh quotients 1.632715... > 16327/10000 for J^+ and
0.704088... > 704/1000 for J^-.
Certificate B (checker: Lemma 2 with N = 8). The tail bound is tau = +-1/2 + 2 b_9(3), that is 36/35 for J^+ and 1/35
for J^-. All eight pivots are positive at Lambda = 1633/1000 for J^+ and at Lambda = 71/100 for J^-. For the lower
bounds, at l = 16327/10000 the pivots of J^+ are positive for j <= 6 and q_7 < 0, and at l = 88/125 those of J^- are
positive for j <= 5 and q_6 < 0.
Hence 1.6327 < Q_3^- < 1.633 and 0.704 < Q_3^+ < 0.710.

(ii) Profile inequalities. Proof. In the identity of 3.42(ii), X . U/r^2 >= -M gives m int (X . U/r^2) h^2 w >= -m M
||h||_m^2. By (i), -a0 int v_2 h w <= Q_m^- a0 ||h||_m^2 if a0 > 0, and -a0 int v_2 h w = |a0| int v_2 h w <= Q_m^+
|a0| ||h||_m^2 if a0 < 0. Dividing by ||h||_m^2 > 0 (A.3.42(ii)) gives the two inequalities; at m = 3, M <= sigma and
(i) give 2 c_l - 1 <= 3 sigma + 1.633 a0 and 2 c_l - 1 <= 3 sigma + 0.710 |a0|. In both cases 2 c_l - 1 <= 3 sigma +
1.633 |a0|, and with sigma <= G_U/sqrt 2 and |a0| <= G_rho (A.3.42(iv)),

    2 c_l - 1 <= (3/sqrt 2) G_U + 1.633 G_rho <= (3/sqrt 2)(G_rho + G_U),

because 1.633 < 3/sqrt 2 = 2.1213...; that is, G_rho + G_U >= (sqrt 2/3)(2 c_l - 1) = 0.4714... (2 c_l - 1).

(iii) Small slope. Proof. Fix c_l and a sequence of exact profiles with a0 -> 0. For each m in (2, 4), Q_m =
max(Q_m^-, Q_m^+) is finite (Setup), and (ii) with M <= sigma gives sigma >= c_l - (c_l + 1)/m - Q_m |a0|/m along the
sequence, so liminf sigma >= c_l - (c_l + 1)/m. The right side increases to (3 c_l - 1)/4 as m -> 4. Together with
sigma >= M >= c_l - 1 (Setup) this is the claim; the argument gives the same bound for liminf M.

(iv) Higher vanishing. Proof. Let h = O(r^{2k+1}) with k >= 1 (for k = 1 this holds by A.3.42(ii)). h is smooth, so
its Taylor polynomial of degree 2k vanishes and grad h = O(r^{2k}); W = O(r), so 3.42(i) gives a0 v_2 = h - W . grad h
= O(r^{2k+1}), and a0 != 0. phi is odd in x, so phi(0, y) = 0 and |phi(x, y)| <= |x| sup_{|t| <= |x|} |v_2(t, y)| =
O(r^{2k+2}); hence the Taylor polynomial of phi of degree 2k + 1 vanishes and v = O(r^{2k+1}). Then |h|^2 w, |v|^2 w
and |phi|^2 r^{-2m-2} (the density of |G|^2 ds dth with respect to dX) are O(r^{4k+2-2m}) at 0, integrable for m <
2k + 2, and the inner flux in A.3.42(ii) is O(eps^{4k+4-2m}); nothing changes at infinity. So the identity of 3.42(ii)
holds for 2 < m < 2k + 2. If moreover m is not an even integer, n^2 - z^2 != 0 for every even n and real xi, so the
transformed equation determines hat G: a solution with G in L^2 and zero source vanishes (in particular no harmonic
polynomial can be added), the actual phi is the weighted inverse, and every b_j(m) is finite. The proofs of (i) and
(ii) then apply verbatim.
Flat case. If h is flat, the above holds for every k, in particular for every odd m = 2J + 1 >= 3. By the monotonicity
in the Setup, max_j b_j(m) = max(b_J, b_{J+1}) with b_J = (2m^2 - 2m + 1)/(4 (2m - 1)) = m/4 - 1/8 + 1/(8 (2m - 1))
and b_{J+1} = (2m^2 + 2m + 1)/(4 (2m + 1)) = m/4 + 1/8 + 1/(8 (2m + 1)) > b_J. So Q_m^-, Q_m^+ <= 1/2 + 2 b_{J+1} =
m/2 + 3/4 + 1/(4 (2m + 1)), and (ii) divided by m gives

    c_l - (c_l + 1)/m <= M + (1/2 + 3/(4m) + 1/(4m (2m + 1))) |a0|.

Letting m -> inf, M >= c_l - |a0|/2, hence sigma >= c_l - |a0|/2. (A.3.46(ii) replaces 1/2 by lambda < 0.3635.)

(v) Derivative form. Proof. Let 1 < mu < 3, w = r^{-2 mu} and g = grad h. Differentiating 3.42(i) and using DW = c_l
I + DU,

    W . grad g + (c_l - 1) g + (DU)^T g = -a0 grad v_2.

Here g . (DU)^T g = g^T S g, and as in A.3.42(ii) with m replaced by mu, (W . grad g) . g w = (1/2) div(|g|^2 w W) +
(mu - 1) c_l |g|^2 w + mu (X . U/r^2) |g|^2 w. Since h, v = O(r^3) at 0 and grad rho, DU are bounded, g and Dv are
O(r^2) at 0 and O(1) at infinity; all terms are integrable for 1 < mu < 3, the fluxes on |X| = eps and |X| = R are
O(eps^{6-2mu}) and O(R^{2-2mu}), and

    (mu c_l - 1) ||g||_mu^2 + mu int (X . U/r^2) |g|^2 w dX + int g^T S g w dX = -a0 int grad v_2 . g w dX.   (*)

Potentials. phi_j = d_j phi (j = 1, 2) satisfies -Lap phi_j = d_x h_j with h_j = d_j h, and is O(r^3) at 0 and O(r) at
infinity; the rows of Dv are -grad phi_2 and grad phi_1, so |Dv|_F^2 = |grad phi_1|^2 + |grad phi_2|^2. As phi(-X) =
phi(X) and h(-X) = -h(X), the functions phi_j, cos th h_j and sin th h_j are odd under X -> -X: only odd angular
frequencies n occur. The argument of A.3.42(iii) with m replaced by mu and even n by odd n (G_j = r^{-mu} phi_j,
(d_s + mu) G_j and d_th G_j are in L^2 for 1 < mu < 3) gives ||grad phi_j||_mu <= (sup_{n odd, xi} M_{mu,n}(xi))
||h_j||_mu; here n^2 - z^2 != 0 because mu is not an odd integer, the supremum over xi is attained at xi = 0, and
since 1 < mu^2 < 9 the supremum over odd n is attained at |n| = 1 or |n| = 3 and equals N'_mu. Summing, ||Dv||_mu <=
N'_mu ||g||_mu. In (*) use X . U/r^2 >= -M, g^T S g >= -sigma |g|^2, |grad v_2| <= |Dv|_F and Cauchy-Schwarz, and
divide by ||g||_mu^2 > 0 (h(0) = 0 and h != 0, so h is not constant):

    mu c_l - 1 <= mu M + sigma + N'_mu |a0| <= (mu + 1) sigma + N'_mu |a0|.

At mu = 2 the two candidates are 5/3 and 13/5, so N'_2 = 13/5.

(vi) Residual form. Proof (after the checker). rho is a candidate as in 3.44(vi), with c, delta, R and F as defined
there, phi = psi - c x y and v = U - (-c x, c y). Identity: U_2 = psi_x = c y + v_2, so W_2 - y = delta y + v_2, and
since W . grad(a0 y) = a0 W_2,

    W . grad h - h = R - a0 (W_2 - y) = -a0 v_2 + F,   -Lap phi = d_x rho = d_x h.

Orders: by parity and smoothness h = O(r^3), phi = O(r^4) and v = O(r^3) at 0 (as in A.3.42(ii)); R is smooth, even in
x and odd in y, with R_y(0) = (d_y W_2(0) - 1) a0 = (c_l + c - 1) a0 = a0 delta, so R = a0 delta y + O(r^3) and F =
O(r^3). At infinity the symbol bounds give h, v, F = O(r), phi = O(r^2), and grad h, Dv, grad F = O(1). The
derivations of the identity of 3.42(ii), of (*) and of the potential bounds used only these orders, parity,
smoothness, div U = 0 and -Lap phi = d_x h; with the source F they give, for 2 < m < 4,

    ((m - 1) c_l - 1) ||h||_m^2 + m int (X . U/r^2) h^2 w dX + a0 int v_2 h w dX = int F h w dX <= ||F||_m ||h||_m,

and the steps of (ii) give ||F||_m/||h||_m >= (m - 1) c_l - 1 - m M - Q_m^-+ |a0| (h != 0, since rho = a0 y violates
the symbol bounds). For 1 < mu < 3, (*) acquires the term int grad F . g w <= ||grad F||_mu ||g||_mu on the right, and
the steps of (v) give the derivative inequality. M >= |c| and sigma >= |c|: by parity psi_xx(0) = psi_yy(0) = 0, so
DU(0) = diag(-c, c) and |S(0)|_op = |c|, while -X . U/r^2 tends to -c along the y-axis and to c along the x-axis.
Centre defect: if delta != 0, then |R| >= |a0 delta| r/4 on the sectors |sin th| >= 1/2 for r small, so ||R||_m^2 >= C
int_0^{r_0} r^{3-2m} dr = inf for m >= 2; likewise grad R = a0 delta e_2 + O(r^2) gives ||grad R||_mu^2 >= C
int_0^{r_0} r^{1-2mu} dr = inf for mu >= 1. Dilations: for rho_l(X) = l rho(X/l) the canonical velocity is U_l(X) = l
U(X/l) (psi_l(X) = l^2 psi(X/l)), so a0, c, delta, sigma and M are unchanged and h, R, F become l h(X/l), l R(X/l), l
F(X/l); every weighted norm of order m (resp. derivative norm of order mu) is multiplied by l^{2-m} (resp. l^{1-mu}),
so the ratios are invariant. For exact profiles R = 0 and delta = 0 (3.2), so F = 0 and (vi) reduces to (ii) and (v).
Scope. (i)-(v) are necessary conditions and (vi) is a diagnostic. No upper bound on sigma or M is proved, so none of
them excludes a parameter region by itself.

## A.3.45 Strain cap: the cubic jet and the weight m = 5

Setup. rho is an exact profile of the primary class with sigma <= D = c_l - 1, so sigma = D (A.3.42(v)); A = 2 c_l -
1 > 1. In the notation of 3.3, h = b x^2 y + e y^3 + O(r^5) and phi = psi + D x y = q1 x^3 y + q2 x y^3 + O(r^6). The
relations of 3.3 are the degree-3 part of 3.42(i), (A x d_x + y d_y - 1) h_3 = -a0 d_x phi_4, that is 2 A b = -3 a0 q1
and 2 e = -a0 q2, and the degree-2 part of -Lap phi = d_x h, that is q1 + q2 = -b/3; together they give 6 e = (a0 -
2A) b.

(i) Alternative. Proof. Strain route. S = [[S11, S12], [S12, -S11]] with S11 = -psi_xy = D - phi_xy and S12 =
(psi_xx - psi_yy)/2 = (phi_xx - phi_yy)/2, and |S|_op^2 = S11^2 + S12^2 (A.3.42(iv)). From phi_xy = 3 q1 x^2 + 3 q2
y^2 + O(r^4) and phi_xx - phi_yy = 6 (q1 - q2) x y + O(r^4),

    |S(X)|_op^2 = D^2 - 6 D (q1 x^2 + q2 y^2) + O(r^4).

The cap gives |S|_op^2 <= D^2 everywhere, with equality at 0. On the x-axis this reads -6 D q1 x^2 + O(x^4) <= 0 and
on the y-axis -6 D q2 y^2 + O(y^4) <= 0; as D > 0, q1 >= 0 and q2 >= 0, that is a0 b <= 0 and a0 e <= 0 (q1 = -2Ab/(3
a0), q2 = -2e/a0, A > 0). Gradient route. Under the cap |grad rho| <= |a0| (3.36(iii)), and rho_x = 2 b x y + O(r^4),
rho_y = a0 + b x^2 + 3 e y^2 + O(r^4) give

    |grad rho|^2 = a0^2 + 2 a0 (b x^2 + 3 e y^2) + O(r^4);

on the two axes this again gives a0 b <= 0 and a0 e <= 0. Alternative. If b != 0, then a0 b < 0, and 0 >= a0 e = (a0 -
2A) a0 b/6 forces a0 - 2A >= 0. If b = 0, then e = (a0 - 2A) b/6 = 0 and q1 = q2 = 0. If a0 < 0, a0 >= 2A > 0 is
impossible, so b = e = q1 = q2 = 0.

(ii) The weight m = 5. Proof. In the second alternative h = O(r^5), so 3.44(iv) with k = 2 admits every m in (2, 6)
that is not an even integer, in particular m = 5, and 3.44(ii) with M <= sigma = D gives 4 c_l - 1 <= 5 (c_l - 1) +
Q_5 |a0|, that is 4 - c_l <= Q_5^- a0 if a0 > 0 and 4 - c_l <= Q_5^+ |a0| if a0 < 0.
Enclosures (b_1 = 29/84, b_2 = 41/36, b_3 = 61/44, b_4 = 89/156, b_9 = 349/1196), by Lemmas 1 and 2 of A.3.44; every
comparison is between exact rational numbers, and all of them were recomputed in exact rational arithmetic for this
appendix.
Certificate A (external analysis). For J^+ take s = (103006148110, 630425246996, 1000000000000, 825876687427,
266782969625, 61992046393, 12191499542, 2173849306, 364028298, 58503079) for j = 1, ..., 10 and s_{j+1} = s_j/6 for j
>= 10: the ten ratios are below 2363/1000 (closest j = 9, margin 79014184391/1571441907160125), and for j >= 11 the
ratio 1/2 + 6 b_{j-1} + b_j/6 is nonincreasing and equals 2.2462... at j = 11. For J^- take s = (135728860001,
635390652548, 1000000000000, 824121246701, 265704112852, 61626228123, 12097266329, 2153109069, 359900321, 57737236)
with the same tail: the ratios are below 6831/5000 = 1.3662 (closest j = 10, margin 11227810703/388427255190000), and
the tail ratio -1/2 + 6 b_{j-1} + b_j/6 is nonincreasing and equals 1.2462... at j = 11. The finite vectors have
Rayleigh quotients 2.3629497... > 23629/10000 and 1.3661710... > 13661/10000.
Certificate B (checker). Lemma 2(a) with N = 8 and tau = +-1/2 + 2 b_9(5), that is 324/299 for J^+ and 25/299 for J^-:
all pivots are positive at Lambda = 2363/1000 and at Lambda = 1367/1000. Lemma 2(b), computed for this appendix: at l
= 23629/10000 (J^+) and at l = 13661/10000 (J^-) the pivots are positive for j <= 6 and q_7 < 0.
Hence 2.3629 < Q_5^- < 2.363 and 1.3661 < Q_5^+ < 1.3662 < 1.367.
Consequences. Let 1 < c_l < 4. If a0 > 0, either a0 >= 2A = 4 c_l - 2 (first alternative of (i)) or a0 >= (4 -
c_l)/Q_5^- > (4 - c_l)/2.363. If a0 < 0, the second alternative holds and |a0| >= (4 - c_l)/Q_5^+ > (4 - c_l)/1.367.
As c_l -> 1, min(4 c_l - 2, (4 - c_l)/2.363) -> 3/2.363 = 1.26957... and (4 - c_l)/1.367 -> 3/1.367 = 2.19458....

(iii) Scope. Proof of the remarks. On the y-axis X . U = y psi_x(0, y) = -D y^2 + q2 y^4 + O(y^6), so -X . U/r^2 = D -
q2 y^2 + O(y^4), and M <= D gives q2 >= 0, that is a0 e <= 0. In general X . v = -d_th phi, so

    -X . U/r^2 = D - 2 D cos^2 th + r^2 f(th) + O(r^4),   f(th) = d_th (q1 cos^3 th sin th + q2 cos th sin^3 th),

with f(+-pi/2) = -q2. If q2 > 0 the right side is < D for small r > 0 in every direction (near th = +-pi/2 because f <
0 there, elsewhere because 2 D cos^2 th has a positive lower bound), so at this order the radial cap imposes q2 >= 0
and nothing else. Example: c_l = 2 (A = 3), a0 = -1, h_3 = -x^2 y/2 + 7 y^3/12, phi_4 = -x^3 y + 7 x y^3/6 (b = -1/2,
e = 7/12, q1 = -1, q2 = 7/6) satisfies (A x d_x + y d_y - 1) h_3 = -a0 d_x phi_4 and -Lap phi_4 = d_x h_3, hence the
local relations of 3.3, and has q2 > 0, but violates the alternative of (i) (a0 < 0, b != 0); its q1 < 0 is excluded
by the strain route. So this argument does not give (i) from M <= D; whether an exact profile with M <= D can violate
(i) is not decided. The last two sentences of 3.45(iii) are statements of scope: (i)-(ii) presuppose the cap, and a
maximum over sample points is at most the supremum over the plane.

## A.3.46 Strain cap at every order

Setup. rho is an exact profile of the primary class with sigma <= D, A = 2 c_l - 1, B = A - 1 = 2D > 0, and h, phi, v
are as in A.3.44, so that U = (D x, -D y) + v and W = (A x, y) + v; a0 != 0. (x)_k = x (x + 1) ... (x + k - 1) is the
rising factorial, (x)_0 = 1, and C(p, q) is a binomial coefficient.

(i) Jet threshold. Proof. Step 1 (leading equations). h is odd under X -> -X, so its Taylor parts have odd degree; let
h_n, n = 2K + 1 >= 3, be the first nonzero one, so h = h_n + O(r^{n+2}). As in A.3.44(iv) with 2k + 1 = n, v_2 =
O(r^n), phi = O(r^{n+1}) and v = O(r^n); phi is even under X -> -X, so phi = phi_{n+1} + O(r^{n+3}) with phi_{n+1}
homogeneous of degree n + 1. In W . grad h - h = -a0 v_2 the term v . grad h is O(r^{2n-1}) = O(r^{n+2}), so the parts
of degree n of this equation and of degree n - 1 of -Lap phi = d_x h are

    (A x d_x + y d_y - 1) h_n = -a0 d_x phi_{n+1},   -Lap phi_{n+1} = d_x h_n.   (1)

Step 2 (coefficients). By parity h_n = sum_{k=0}^K al_k x^{2k} y^{n-2k} and phi_{n+1} = sum_{k=0}^K be_k x^{2k+1}
y^{n-2k}. With N = n - 1 = 2K and e_k = N + 2 B k > 0, A x d_x + y d_y - 1 multiplies x^{2k} y^{n-2k} by e_k, so the
first equation of (1) is al_k = -a0 (2k + 1) be_k/e_k. Inserting this in the coefficient of x^{2k+1} y^{n-2k-2} of the
second equation gives, for 0 <= k <= K - 1,

    (2k + 2)(2k + 3)(1 - a0/e_{k+1}) be_{k+1} = -(n - 2k)(n - 2k - 1) be_k,   (2)

and (1) is equivalent to the formula for al_k together with (2). Put g_k = (2k + 1)(n - 2k) be_k; then (phi_{n+1})_xy
= sum_k g_k x^{2k} y^{N-2k} = y^N P(x^2/y^2) with P(t) = sum_k g_k t^k, and h_n != 0 if and only if g != 0. With eta =
1 + K/B and chi = eta - a0/(2B) one has 1 - a0/e_{k+1} = (k + chi)/(k + eta), and multiplying (2), written in the g_k,
by (2k + 1)(N - 2k - 1)(k + eta) != 0 gives the equivalent recursion

    (2k + 1)(2k + 2)(k + chi) g_{k+1} = -(N - 2k)(N - 2k - 1)(k + eta) g_k,   0 <= k <= K - 1.   (3)

Step 3 (solution space). If k + chi != 0 for 0 <= k <= K - 1, (3) determines g from g_0. If chi = 1 - j0 with 1 <= j0
<= K (equivalently a0 = e_{j0}), the row k = j0 - 1 of (3) gives g_{j0-1} = 0 (its right coefficient is nonzero, eta >
0), the rows k < j0 - 1 then give g_{j0-2} = ... = g_0 = 0, g_{j0} is free and the rows k >= j0 determine the rest. So
for every real a0 the solutions of (1) form a one-dimensional space. The coefficients of

    F_chi(t) = sum_{k=0}^K (-1)^k C(2K, 2k) (eta)_k (chi + k)_{K-k} t^k

are polynomials in chi; when no k + chi vanishes, the ratio of consecutive coefficients is -(C(2K, 2k + 2)/C(2K,
2k))(k + eta)/(k + chi) = -(N - 2k)(N - 2k - 1)(k + eta)/((2k + 1)(2k + 2)(k + chi)), so they satisfy (3), and since
(3) is polynomial in chi it holds for every chi. The top coefficient (-1)^K (eta)_K is nonzero. Hence, for every a0, P
is a nonzero multiple of F_chi.
Step 4 (sign). phi_xy = psi_xy + D and |psi_xy| = |S11| <= |S|_op <= sigma <= D, so phi_xy >= 0 everywhere. As phi_xy
= (phi_{n+1})_xy + O(r^{n+1}) with (phi_{n+1})_xy homogeneous of degree N, (phi_{n+1})_xy(X) = lim_{t -> 0+} t^{-N}
phi_xy(t X) >= 0, and at X = (x, 1) this reads P(x^2) >= 0; so P >= 0 on [0, inf).
Step 5 (an integral that vanishes). Suppose a0 < N A. Then chi - (1 - K) = (N A - a0)/(2B) > 0. Put u = chi + K - 1 >
0 and let T and S be independent random variables, T with the beta-prime density t^{u-1} (1 + t)^{-u-K-1/2}/Beta(u,
K + 1/2) on (0, inf) and S with the beta density s^{-1/2} (1 - s)^{eta-3/2}/Beta(1/2, eta - 1/2) on (0, 1) (eta > 1;
Beta is Euler's beta function). For 0 <= k <= K the moments are finite (k < K + 1/2) and

    E T^k = Beta(u + k, K + 1/2 - k)/Beta(u, K + 1/2) = (-1)^k (u)_k/(1/2 - K)_k,   E S^k = (1/2)_k/(eta)_k,

where (1/2 - K)_k is a product of nonzero half-integers. Using C(2K, 2k) = (-K)_k (1/2 - K)_k/((1/2)_k k!) (from
(2K)!/(2K - 2k)! = 4^k (-K)_k (1/2 - K)_k and (2k)! = 4^k (1/2)_k k!) and (-K)_k/k! = (-1)^k C(K, k),

    E F_chi(T S) = sum_{k=0}^K (-1)^k C(K, k) (chi + k)_{K-k} (chi + K - 1)_k.

The product (chi + k)_{K-k} (chi + K - 1)_k consists of the factors chi + i for k <= i <= K + k - 2 together with a
second factor chi + K - 1, so it equals (chi + K - 1)(chi + k)_{K-1}, an identity of polynomials in chi. Hence E
F_chi(T S) = (chi + K - 1) sum_k (-1)^k C(K, k) p(k) with p(k) = (chi + k)_{K-1} a polynomial of degree K - 1 in k,
and this K-th finite difference vanishes: E F_chi(T S) = 0 for every chi > 1 - K. (With this auxiliary index, u =
chi + J with J = K - 1, no exceptional values of chi occur.)
Conclusion of (i). T S has the density z -> int_0^1 f_T(z/s) f_S(s) ds/s, positive on (0, inf). If kappa F_chi >= 0 on
[0, inf) with kappa != 0, then kappa F_chi(T S) >= 0 has expectation 0, so F_chi vanishes almost everywhere on (0,
inf), hence identically, contradicting (-1)^K (eta)_K != 0. Since P is a nonzero multiple of F_chi and P >= 0 (Step
4), a0 < N A is impossible: a0 >= (n - 1) A >= 2A.
Step 6 (jets at and above the threshold). At a0 = N A = e_K, chi = 1 - K, and by Step 3 only g_K is nonzero; g_K > 0
gives P = g_K t^K >= 0. For a0 > N A, k + chi < 0 for k <= K - 1, so by (3) all g_k have the sign of g_0, and g_0 > 0
gives P > 0 on [0, inf). In both cases the al_k of Step 2 complete a pair solving (1). So the threshold is sharp for
the leading jet equations with P >= 0; nothing follows for exact profiles.
Step 7 (gradient condition). By Step 2, (n - 2k) al_k = -a0 g_k/e_k, so a0 (h_n)_y = -a0^2 y^N Ptilde(x^2/y^2) with
Ptilde(t) = sum_k g_k t^k/e_k = int_0^1 s^{N-1} P(s^{2B} t) ds (as int_0^1 s^{N-1+2Bk} ds = 1/e_k). So P >= 0 implies
a0 (h_n)_y <= 0, the leading-order form of |grad rho| <= |a0|, because |grad rho|^2 = a0^2 + 2 a0 (h_n)_y +
O(r^{n+1}). The converse fails: for c_l = 19, a0 = -2 (A = 37, B = 36, n = 5, eta = 19/18, chi = 13/12 > 1 - K = -1)
the pair

    h_5 = y^5/10 - (2/39) x^2 y^3 + (38/2925) x^4 y,   phi_6 = x y^5/5 - (76/117) x^3 y^3 + (2812/14625) x^5 y

satisfies (1), P(t) = 1 - (76/13) t + (2812/2925) t^2 = (144/325) F_chi(t) has P(1) = -11363/2925 < 0, and Ptilde(t) =
1/4 - t/13 + (19/2925) t^2 has discriminant -22/38025 < 0 and positive leading coefficient, so a0 (h_5)_y = -(76 x^4 -
900 x^2 y^2 + 2925 y^4)/2925 < 0 for X != 0 (all checked in exact rational arithmetic). These polynomials satisfy only
(1); by Step 5 no capped profile has such a leading jet.

(ii) Flat case. Proof. If h is flat, 3.44(iv) gives 3.44(ii) for every odd m = 2J + 1 >= 3:

    (m - 1) c_l - 1 <= m M + Q_m |a0|,   Q_m = Q_m^- if a0 > 0,   Q_m = Q_m^+ if a0 < 0.   (4)

Comparison with L. Let L be the operator of 3.46(ii), the symmetric tridiagonal matrix on l^2(Z) with zero diagonal
and entry l_k = 1/(4 |2k - 1|) at (k, k + 1) and (k + 1, k), and lambda the top of its spectrum (L is bounded, l_k <=
1/4). Embed the half-line vertex j >= 1 as k = j - J in Z and extend J^+/m (resp. J^-/m) by 0 to the vertices k <= -J;
call the result Z_m. For an edge (j, j + 1), q = 2j satisfies q - m = 2k - 1, so 1/(4 |q - m|) = l_k, and

    b_j(m)/m - l_k = (m^2 + q^2 - m (q + m))/(4 m |q - m| (q + m)) = sgn(q - m) q/(4 m (q + m)),

of modulus < 1/(4m). The edges (k, k + 1) of L missing in Z_m have k <= -J and l_k = 1/(4 (2|k| + 1)) <= 1/(4m), and
the diagonal of Z_m has modulus <= 1/(2m). So L - Z_m is tridiagonal with absolute row sums <= 1/(2m) + 2/(4m) = 1/m,
and ||L - Z_m|| <= 1/m (Schur test). The top of the spectrum of Z_m is max(Q_m/m, 0) = Q_m/m, since Q_m > 0: Q_m^- >=
d_1 = 1/4 (test vector e_1), and for Q_m^+ the unit vector (e_j + e_{j+1})/sqrt 2 with 2j = m + 1 >= 4 has Rayleigh
quotient -1/2 + (2m^2 + 2m + 1)/(4 (2m + 1)) > 0 for m >= 3. The top of the spectrum changes by at most the norm of a
perturbation, so |Q_m/m - lambda| <= 1/m, and (4) divided by m gives

    c_l - (c_l + 1)/m <= M + (lambda + 1/m) |a0|.

Letting m -> inf through odd integers, M >= c_l - lambda |a0|, and sigma >= M (A.3.44).
Enclosures for lambda. In this indexing L is symmetric about the vertex 1 (l_0 = l_1 = 1/4), and on both arms the edge
from distance r to distance r + 1 has weight alpha_r = 1/(4 (2r + 1)). Every comparison below is between exact
rational numbers, and both certificates were recomputed in exact rational arithmetic for this appendix.
Certificate A (external analysis: Lemma 1 on Z and a Rayleigh quotient). Take s = (1, 727/1000, 17/100, 3/125, 3/1250,
1/5000) at distances r = 0, ..., 5 on both arms and s_{r+1} = s_r/8 for r >= 5. The ratio (L s)/s is 2 alpha_0 s_1/s_0
= 727/2000 = 4/11 - 3/22000 at the centre and (alpha_{r-1} s_{r-1} + alpha_r s_{r+1})/s_r at distance r >= 1; it is
below 4/11 for r <= 5 (smallest margin 23/112200, at r = 2), and for r >= 6 it equals 8 alpha_{r-1} + alpha_r/8, which
decreases and is 843/4576 at r = 6. So lambda < 4/11. The symmetric vector with the six listed values has Rayleigh
quotient 67289333/185151890 = 0.3634277... > 0.36342.
Certificate B (checker: elimination from both ends). On each arm the vertices at distance >= 9 form a tail with form
<= tau |u|^2, tau = 2 alpha_9 = 1/38. With Lambda = 363427799/10^9 > tau, the argument of Lemma 2(a), applied to both
tails, leaves the 17 x 17 matrix Lambda - L_17 (distances <= 8) with its two end diagonal entries decreased by
alpha_8^2/(Lambda - tau); Gaussian elimination from both ends towards the centre has the pivots

    p_8 = Lambda - alpha_8^2/(Lambda - tau),   p_r = Lambda - alpha_r^2/p_{r+1}   (1 <= r <= 7, on each arm),
    p_0 = Lambda - 2 alpha_0^2/p_1,

all positive (p_0 = 1.919...e-9), so lambda < Lambda. For l = 363427798/10^9 the pivots q_8 = l, q_r = l -
alpha_r^2/q_{r+1}, q_0 = l - 2 alpha_0^2/q_1 of l - L_17 are positive for r >= 1 and q_0 = -1.962...e-10 < 0, so by
inertia L_17, and hence L, has a Rayleigh quotient above l. So 0.363427798 < lambda < 0.363427799 (and 0.36342 <
lambda < 4/11 by Certificate A).

(iii) Conclusion. Proof. h is either flat at 0 or has a first nonzero homogeneous Taylor part (no analyticity is
used). In the second case (i) gives a0 >= (n - 1) A >= 2A = 2 (2 c_l - 1) > 2. In the first case (ii) and the cap give
c_l - 1 >= sigma >= c_l - lambda |a0|, so |a0| >= 1/lambda > 10^9/363427799 = 2.75157817... > 2.7515. So |a0| > 2 in
both cases, and a0 < 0 forces the flat case. This supersedes 3.45(i)-(ii): the first alternative of 3.45(i) is the
case n = 3 of (i), and the bounds of 3.45(ii) follow, since min(4 c_l - 2, (4 - c_l)/2.363) <= min(2A, 1/lambda) (as
(4 - c_l)/2.363 < 1.27 < 1/lambda) for a0 > 0 and (4 - c_l)/1.367 < 2.2 < 1/lambda for a0 < 0. Under the radial cap M
<= c_l - 1 alone, (ii) still gives |a0| >= 1/lambda when h is flat, but Step 4 of (i) uses sigma <= D and is not
available (3.45(iii)).
Scope. A conditional theorem: whether any exact profile satisfies sigma <= c_l - 1 is open, and nothing is claimed
about the existence of capped profiles. The flat alternative is excluded separately in 3.47.

## A.3.47 Strain cap or one-sided sign: no flat remainder

Setup. rho is an exact profile of the primary class with canonical velocity U = (-psi_y, psi_x). In (i)-(iii) it
satisfies the cap sigma <= D; in (iv) it satisfies y H >= 0 instead. Notation of 3.47: a = a0, D = c_l - 1, A = 2
c_l - 1, W = c_l X + U, h = rho - a y, H = y - rho/a = -h/a, phi = psi + D x y, V = U_2 + D y = phi_x and B = X .
W/r^2 (in this entry B is not A - 1 = 2D); S = (DU + DU^T)/2, and for m > 2, w0 = y r^{2-2m} and w = y r^{-2m}. A
function is flat at 0 if it and each of its derivatives are O(|X|^N) at 0 for every N.

Basic facts (every exact profile). (F1) Parity: rho is even in x and odd in y, so rho(x, 0) = 0, rho_x(0) = 0 and grad
rho(0) = (0, a); U_1 = -psi_y is odd in x and even in y and U_2 = psi_x is even in x and odd in y, so U(0) = 0, U_1(0,
y) = 0 and U_2(x, 0) = 0. (F2) Origin values: differentiating W . grad rho = rho in y and evaluating at 0, where W = 0
and rho_x = 0, gives (c_l + d_y U_2(0)) a = a, so psi_xy(0) = d_y U_2(0) = 1 - c_l = -D (the origin relation of 3.2);
psi_xx and psi_yy are odd in x, resp. in y, so they vanish at 0, and DU(0) = diag(D, -D). (F3) psi is odd in x and in
y, so its Taylor monomials are x^{odd} y^{odd}; hence psi = -D x y + O(r^4), phi = O(r^4), and near 0 U = (D x, -D
y) + O(r^3) and W = (A x, y) + O(r^3). (F4) V = W_2 - y, since W_2 = c_l y + U_2. (F5) Bounds at infinity: by
3.23, |rho| + |U| <= C (1 + r)^p and |grad rho| + |DU| <= C (1 + r)^{p-1} with p = 1/c_l < 1; hence for r >=
1, |H| + |V| + |W| <= C r and |grad H| + |grad V| <= C, with C depending on the profile.

Lemma 1 (identities). For every exact profile and every m > 2,

    W . grad H - H = V,   Lap V = a H_xx,                                                (1)
    Lap w0 = 4 (m - 1)(m - 2) y r^{-2m},   d_xx w0 = 2 (m - 1) y r^{-2m} (2m x^2/r^2 - 1),   (2)
    |w0| <= r^{3-2m},   |grad w0| <= (2m - 3) r^{2-2m},
    w (W . grad H - H) = div(H w W) + H y r^{-2m} (2m B - 2 c_l - 1) - H W_2 r^{-2m}.       (3)

Proof. W . grad y - y = W_2 - y = V by (F4), and W . grad rho - rho = 0 by transport; subtracting 1/a times the second
identity from the first gives the first part of (1). V = psi_x + D y and -Lap psi = rho_x give Lap V = d_x Lap psi =
-rho_xx = a H_xx. For (2) write w0 = y g with g = r^k, k = 2 - 2m: Lap g = k^2 r^{k-2} and g_y = k y r^{k-2}, so Lap
w0 = y Lap g + 2 g_y = k (k + 2) y r^{k-2} = 4 (m - 1)(m - 2) y r^{-2m}; d_x w0 = 2 (1 - m) x y r^{-2m} and d_xx w0 =
2 (1 - m) y r^{-2m} (1 - 2m x^2/r^2). Next, grad w0 = r^{2-2m} e_2 + (2 - 2m) y r^{-2m} X, so |grad w0|^2 r^{4m-4} =
1 + 4 (m - 1)(m - 2) sin^2 th <= 1 + 4 (m - 1)(m - 2) = (2m - 3)^2, and |w0| <= r . r^{2-2m}. For (3), grad w =
r^{-2m} e_2 - 2m y r^{-2m-2} X gives W . grad w = r^{-2m} (W_2 - 2m y B), and div W = 2 c_l gives div(H w W) = w W .
grad H + H W . grad w + 2 c_l H w; solving for w W . grad H and subtracting w H gives (3). Only (1) uses the
equations; (2) and (3) hold for any smooth H and W with div W = 2 c_l.

Lemma 2 (moments). Let m > 2 and let rho be an exact profile with h flat at 0. Then V is flat at 0, the integrals

    I_m = int H y r^{-2m} dX,   J_m = int V y r^{-2m} dX,   K_m = int H y r^{-2m} (2m x^2/r^2 - 1) dX,
    int H y B r^{-2m} dX,   int H W_2 r^{-2m} dX

converge absolutely, and

    J_m = (a/(2 (m - 2))) K_m,                                                           (4)
    J_m = 2m int H y B r^{-2m} dX - (2 c_l + 1) I_m - int H W_2 r^{-2m} dX.              (5)

Proof. H = -h/a is flat, and by (1) V = W . grad H - H with W smooth, so every derivative of V at 0 is a finite sum of
products of derivatives of W and of H, and V is flat. Absolute convergence: W(0) = 0 gives |W| <= C r near 0, so B is
bounded near 0, and |B| <= |W|/r <= C for r >= 1 by (F5); hence each integrand is bounded by C r^{2-2m} for r >= 1,
which is integrable since m > 2, and by C_N r^N near 0 by flatness. Let Omega = {eps < |X| < R}, with outer normal n.
Green's second identity, the divergence theorem applied to d_x(H d_x w0 - w0 H_x) = H d_xx w0 - w0 H_xx, and the
divergence theorem applied to (3) together with V = W . grad H - H give

    int_Omega (V Lap w0 - w0 Lap V) dX = int_{dOmega} (V d_n w0 - w0 d_n V) ds,
    int_Omega (H d_xx w0 - w0 H_xx) dX = int_{dOmega} (H d_x w0 - w0 H_x) n_1 ds,
    int_Omega w V dX = int_{dOmega} H w W . n ds + int_Omega (H y r^{-2m} (2m B - 2 c_l - 1) - H W_2 r^{-2m}) dX.

On |X| = R, by (F5) and (2), the boundary integrands are at most C R (2m - 3) R^{2-2m} + C R^{3-2m}, resp. C R .
R^{1-2m} . C R; after multiplication by the length 2 pi R the outer terms are O(R^{4-2m}) and tend to 0. On |X| = eps
the factors H, V, grad H, grad V are O(eps^N) by flatness, while w0, grad w0 and w W are O(eps^{3-2m}), O(eps^{2-2m})
and O(eps^{2-2m}); so the inner terms tend to 0. By Lap V = a H_xx the first two identities give int_Omega V Lap w0
dX = a int_Omega H d_xx w0 dX + (boundary terms). Letting eps -> 0 and R -> inf, the absolute convergence of V Lap
w0 = 4 (m - 1)(m - 2) V y r^{-2m} and of H d_xx w0 = 2 (m - 1) H y r^{-2m} (2m x^2/r^2 - 1) gives 4 (m - 1)(m - 2)
J_m = 2 (m - 1) a K_m, which is (4). The third identity gives (5) in the same way. Only first derivatives of H and V
enter the boundary terms, so no bound on second derivatives at infinity is used, and w0 Lap V = a w0 H_xx is never
required to be absolutely integrable. All functions are smooth on the closed annulus, so there is no boundary along
the axes.

(i) Consequences of the cap. Proof. Radial bound (cap and parity only). d/dt [X . U(tX)] = X^T DU(tX) X = X^T S(tX) X,
since the skew part of DU has zero quadratic form; integrating over 0 <= t <= 1 with U(0) = 0 gives X . U = int_0^1
X^T S(tX) X dt, so |X . U| <= sigma r^2 <= D r^2 and r^2 = (c_l - D) r^2 <= X . W <= (c_l + D) r^2 = A r^2; thus 1 <=
B <= A. Orbits. Along a solution of X' = W(X), d|X|^2/dt = 2 X . W lies in [2 |X|^2, 2A |X|^2], so |X(t)| lies in
[e^t |X(0)|, e^{At} |X(0)|] for t >= 0 and in [e^{At} |X(0)|, e^t |X(0)|] for t <= 0. No solution leaves a bounded set
in finite time, the flow is global, and every backward orbit tends to 0, with |X(t)| <= e^t |X(0)| for t <= 0.
Gradient (uses exact transport). Let g = grad rho. The gradient of W . grad rho - rho = 0 is (W . grad) g + DW^T g -
g = 0, and DW = c_l I + DU, so W . grad g = -D g - DU^T g and

    (1/2) W . grad |g|^2 = -D |g|^2 - g^T S g <= -D |g|^2 + sigma |g|^2 <= 0.

Thus |g(X(t))| is nonincreasing in t; as t -> -inf, X(t) -> 0 and g(X(t)) -> g(0) = (0, a) by (F1), so |grad rho(X)|
<= |a| for every X. Since rho(x, 0) = 0, integrating in y gives |rho(x, y)| <= |a| |y|, and y H = y^2 - y rho/a >=
y^2 - |y| |rho|/|a| >= 0. Axes (cap and parity only). By (F1), U_1(x, y) = U_1(0, y) + int_0^1 x d_x U_1(tx, y) dt = x
int_0^1 S_11(tx, y) dt and U_2(x, y) = y int_0^1 S_22(x, ty) dt, and |S_11|, |S_22| <= |S|_op <= D. Hence U_1/x and
U_2/y lie in [-D, D] (with continuous extensions to the axes), 1 <= W_1/x <= A, 1 <= W_2/y <= A, and V/y = U_2/y + D
lies in [0, 2D]. Further bounds. DU = S + (curl U/2) [[0, -1], [1, 0]] with curl U = -rho_x, so |DU|_op <= D + |a|/2;
hence |H| <= 2 |y|, |grad H| <= 1 + |grad rho|/|a| <= 2, |V| <= 2D |y|, |grad V| <= |grad U_2| + D <= 2D + |a|/2
and |W| <= (c_l + D + |a|/2) r. For capped profiles these give the bounds (F5) without 3.23. Remark (the bound 0 <
rho/(a y) quoted in the Scope; uses exact transport). q = rho/(a y) = (1/a) int_0^1 rho_y(x, ty) dt is smooth with
q(0) = 1, and G := V/y = int_0^1 V_y(x, ty) dt is smooth with G(0) = d_y U_2(0) + D = 0 by (F2), so |G| <= C |X|
on |X| <= 1. Substituting rho = a y q in W . grad rho = rho and using W . grad y = W_2 = y + V gives W . grad q = -G
q. Along a backward orbit, q(X) = q(X(t)) exp(-int_t^0 G(X(tau)) dtau); since |X(tau)| <= e^tau |X|, the integral
converges as t -> -inf and q(X(t)) -> 1, so q(X) = exp(-int_{-inf}^0 G(X(tau)) dtau), which lies in (0, 1] because
G >= 0.

(ii) h is not flat at 0. Proof. Suppose h is flat. Lemma 2 applies for every m > 2 (its bounds at infinity come from
3.23, or from the end of (i)). I_m > 0: y H >= 0 by (i), and y H is not identically 0, for otherwise H = 0 off the
x-axis, hence everywhere by continuity, and rho = a y, which violates |rho| <= C (1 + r)^gamma with gamma < 1 on the
y-axis; so y H > 0 on a nonempty open set. Upper bound from (4): the weight 2m x^2/r^2 - 1 lies in [-1, 2m - 1] and H
y r^{-2m} dX is a nonnegative measure, so -I_m <= K_m <= (2m - 1) I_m. For a > 0 this gives J_m <= a (2m - 1) I_m/(2
(m - 2)). For a < 0 the coefficient a/(2 (m - 2)) is negative, so the lower bound -I_m must be used, and J_m <= |a|
I_m/(2 (m - 2)). Lower bound from (5): B >= 1 by (i), and off the x-axis H W_2 = (H y)(W_2/y) <= A H y by (i); hence
J_m >= (2m - 2 c_l - 1 - A) I_m = (2m - 4 c_l) I_m. Choice of m. Let m = 3 + 2 c_l + 2 |a|. Then 2m - 4 c_l = 6 +
4 |a| and m - 2 = 1 + 2 c_l + 2 |a| > max(3, 2 |a|). If a > 0, a (2m - 1)/(2 (m - 2)) = a (1 + 3/(2 (m - 2))) < 3a/2 <
5a/2 < 6 + 4a. If a < 0, |a|/(2 (m - 2)) < 1/4 < 6 + 4 |a|. In both cases the upper and lower bounds for J_m/I_m are
incompatible (I_m > 0), so h is not flat.

(iii) Conclusion with 3.46(i). Proof. By (ii) h has a nonzero Taylor coefficient at 0. h is even in x and odd in y, so
its Taylor monomials are x^{2i} y^{2j+1}, of odd degree, and its degree-1 part is (grad rho(0) - (0, a)) . X = 0 by
(F1). So its first nonzero homogeneous part h_n has odd degree n >= 3, and 3.46(i), which assumes the same cap, gives
a0 >= (n - 1)(2 c_l - 1) >= 2 (2 c_l - 1) = 4 c_l - 2 > 0. If 2A <= a0 < 4A, then (n - 1) A <= a0 < 4A gives n < 5, so
n = 3. In particular a0 < 0 and a0 < 4 c_l - 2 are impossible.

(iv) The one-sided sign instead of the cap. Proof. Let rho be an exact profile with y H >= 0 (no cap) and suppose h is
flat. Lemmas 1 and 2 hold (they use only the equations, flatness and (F5)), and the upper bound in (ii) used only (4)
and y H >= 0; so J_m/I_m <= a (2m - 1)/(2 (m - 2)) if a > 0 and J_m/I_m <= |a|/(2 (m - 2)) if a < 0, for every m > 2
(I_m > 0 is shown below). In particular J_m/I_m stays bounded as m -> inf. As in (ii), y H is not identically 0, so
r_* = inf{|X| : H(X) y > 0} is finite. A disc where B >= 1/2. If r_* > 0, then H y <= 0 on the open disc |X| < r_* by
the definition of r_*, so H y = 0 there by the hypothesis y H >= 0, hence H = 0 there (continuity across y = 0), V = W
. grad H - H = 0 there by (1), and phi = 0 there, since phi_x = V, phi(0, y) = 0 (phi is odd in x) and the disc
contains the segment from (0, y) to (x, y). Then psi = -D x y, U = (D x, -D y), W = (A x, y) and B = 1 + 2D x^2/r^2 >=
1 on 0 < |X| < r_*. B is continuous on X != 0, so B >= 1 on the circle |X| = r_*, and by uniform continuity on a
compact annulus around this circle, B >= 1/2 on 0 < |X| < R for some R > r_*. If r_* = 0, then by (F3) X . W = A x^2 +
y^2 + O(r^4) and B = 1 + 2D x^2/r^2 + O(r^2) >= 1 - C r^2, so B >= 1/2 on 0 < |X| < R for some R > 0. Concentration.
Fix r0 with r_* < r0 < R. By the definition of r_* there is X1 = (x1, y1) with |X1| < r0 and H(X1) y1 > 0, so c0 :=
int_{|X| < r0} H y dX > 0 by continuity, and since H y >= 0, I_m >= int_{|X| < r0} H y r^{-2m} dX >= c0 r0^{-2m}.
Exterior. Let C_H and C_W be constants with |H| <= C_H r and |W| <= C_W r for r >= R (by (F5) for r >= 1, and for R <=
r <= 1 by H(0) = 0, W(0) = 0 and smoothness; then |B| <= C_W and |W_2| <= C_W r there). With int_{r >= R} r^{2-2m}
dX = 2 pi R^{4-2m}/(2m - 4),

    E_m := int_{r >= R} H y r^{-2m} dX <= 2 pi C_H R^{4-2m}/(2m - 4),
    int_{r >= R} |H y B| r^{-2m} dX <= C_W E_m,
    F_m := int_{r >= R} |H W_2| r^{-2m} dX <= 2 pi C_H C_W R^{4-2m}/(2m - 4).

Interior. On 0 < |X| < R, B >= 1/2 and H y >= 0, so int_{r < R} H y B r^{-2m} dX >= (1/2)(I_m - E_m); and with C_R =
sup_{|X| < R} |W_2/y|, which is finite because W_2/y = int_0^1 d_y W_2(x, ty) dt is continuous, int_{r < R} H W_2
r^{-2m} dX <= C_R I_m. Inserting these bounds in (5),

    J_m >= m (I_m - E_m) - 2m C_W E_m - (2 c_l + 1) I_m - C_R I_m - F_m.

Dividing by I_m >= c0 r0^{-2m} and putting K0 = 2 pi C_H R^4/c0,

    J_m/I_m >= m - (2 c_l + 1) - C_R - (m (1 + 2 C_W) + C_W) K0 (r0/R)^{2m}/(2m - 4).

Since r0 < R, the last term tends to 0, so J_m/I_m >= m - (2 c_l + 1) - C_R - o(1) -> inf as m -> inf, which
contradicts the bounded upper bound. Hence h is not flat. Equivalently, if h is flat then y H < 0 at some point with y
!= 0, that is rho/(a0 y) > 1 there (y H = y^2 (1 - rho/(a y)) for y != 0).

Scope. Proof of the remarks. The first sentence states that the hypotheses are open; it is not a claim. The sentence
on capped non-profiles cites 3.50(a), whose construction (at c_l = 2) is not reproduced here; it shows that these
inequalities can hold for a capped density whose transport fails. In the proofs above exact transport enters in (i)
through the gradient monotonicity, which gives |grad rho| <= |a| and y H >= 0 (and 0 < rho/(a y) in the Remark),
in (ii) and (iv) through the identity W . grad H - H = V of (1), and in (iii) through 3.46(i); the bounds on X . W, B,
W_1/x, W_2/y and V/y in (i) use only the cap and parity. The last sentence of the Scope restates (iv) and refers to
3.51.

The identities were checked by symbolic computation in the main analysis.

## A.3.48 Low-slope regime

Setup. rho is an exact profile of the primary class, with |rho| + (1 + |X|) |grad rho| <= C (1 + |X|)^gamma, gamma <
1, a0 = rho_y(0) != 0, D = c_l - 1 > 0 and A - 1 = 2D. Let rho_3(r) = (1/pi) int_0^{2 pi} rho(r, th) sin(3 th) dth and
J = int_0^inf rho_3 r^{-2} dr.

Convergence and the identity. Proof. rho is odd under X -> -X, so Taylor's theorem gives rho = a0 y + P_3(X) + R(X)
with P_3 a homogeneous cubic and |R| <= C' r^5 for r <= 1. Since int_0^{2 pi} sin th sin(3 th) dth = 0, the term a0
y = a0 r sin th does not contribute to rho_3, so |rho_3(r)| <= C'' r^3 for r <= 1. For r >= 1, |rho_3(r)| <= (1/pi)
int_0^{2 pi} |rho| dth <= 2 C (1 + r)^gamma <= 2^{1+gamma} C r^gamma. Hence |rho_3| r^{-2} is O(r) on (0, 1] and
O(r^{gamma-2}) on [1, inf), and J converges absolutely since gamma - 2 < -1. By 3.2, psi_xy(0) = -a0/4 + J, and for an
exact profile psi_xy(0) = 1 - c_l = -D (the origin relation of 3.2; A.3.47, (F2)). Hence J = a0/4 - D. The
two-dimensional integral (the parenthetical remark). In polar coordinates the absolute integrand of (1/pi) int rho
sin(3 th) r^{-3} dX is pi^{-1} |rho sin(3 th)| r^{-2} with respect to dr dth. For r <= 1, |rho sin(3 th)| >= |a0|
r |sin th sin(3 th)| - C_3 r^3 (with |P_3 + R| <= C_3 r^3 for r <= 1), and int_0^{2 pi} |sin th sin(3 th)| dth = 3
sqrt 3/2: sin th sin(3 th) = (cos(2 th) - cos(4 th))/2 has the antiderivative sin(2 th)/4 - sin(4 th)/8 and changes
sign at th = pi/3, 2 pi/3, 4 pi/3, 5 pi/3, which gives (3 + 6 + 6 + 6 + 3) sqrt 3/16 on the five intervals. So
int_0^{2 pi} |rho sin(3 th)| dth >= (3 sqrt 3/2) |a0| r - 2 pi C_3 r^3 >= |a0| r for 0 < r <= r1 with r1 small, and
int_0^{r1} |a0| r . r^{-2} dr = inf. Thus this integral never converges absolutely when a0 != 0.

(a) Proof. If 0 < a0 <= 2D, then J = a0/4 - D <= -D/2. Since (rho_3)_+ >= 0 and (rho_3)_- r^{-2} is integrable,
int_0^inf (rho_3)_- r^{-2} dr >= -J >= D/2 = (A - 1)/4.

(b) Proof. If a0 > 0 and |J| <= eps0 a0/4, then a0/4 - D = J >= -eps0 a0/4, so (1 + eps0) a0 >= 4D = 2 (A - 1) and
a0 >= 2 (A - 1)/(1 + eps0).

(c) Proof. Let |J| <= kappa |a0| with 0 <= kappa < 1/4. If a0 < 0, then J = -(|a0|/4 + D) and |J| = |a0|/4 + D >
kappa |a0| (as kappa < 1/4 and D > 0), a contradiction; since a0 != 0, a0 > 0. Then -kappa a0 <= a0/4 - D <= kappa a0,
that is (1 + 4 kappa) a0 >= 4D and (1 - 4 kappa) a0 <= 4D, which is 4D/(1 + 4 kappa) <= a0 <= 4D/(1 - 4 kappa).

Scope. A statement of status: no bound of the kind assumed in (b) or (c) is proved for exact profiles, and (a)-(c) are
conditional.

The identities were checked by symbolic computation in the main analysis.

## A.3.49 Endpoint regimes c_l -> 1 and c_l -> inf

Setup. Exact profiles of the primary class; D = c_l - 1, S = (DU + DU^T)/2, sigma = sup |S|_op, M = sup_{X != 0} (-X .
U/r^2), so M <= sigma (3.44); G_rho = sup |grad rho| and G_U = sup |DU| (Frobenius norm); b_j(m) = (m^2 + 4 j^2)/(4 |4
j^2 - m^2|).

(a) Proof. Gershgorin bound. Let 2 < m < 4. Then 4 - m^2 < 0 < 16 - m^2, so every b_j(m) is finite, and for j >= 2, 4
j^2 > m^2 and b_j = (1/4)(1 + 2 m^2/(4 j^2 - m^2)), which decreases in j. Let J be either Jacobi matrix of 3.44(i)
(diagonal entries d_j = +(1/4, 1/2, 1/2, ...) or -(1/4, 1/2, 1/2, ...), off-diagonal entries b_j). For a finitely
supported real sequence z, 2 |z_j z_{j+1}| <= z_j^2 + z_{j+1}^2 gives <J z, z> <= sum_j (|d_j| + b_{j-1} + b_j) z_j^2
with b_0 = 0. The coefficients are 1/4 + b_1 for j = 1, 1/2 + b_1 + b_2 for j = 2 and 1/2 + b_{j-1} + b_j <= 1/2 +
b_2 + b_3 for j >= 3, all at most B_m := 1/2 + b_2 + max(b_1, b_3). J is real and symmetric, so complex sequences
reduce to their real and imaginary parts, and by density Q_m^-, Q_m^+ <= B_m. At m = 11/3, m^2 = 121/9, b_1 = 157/340,
b_2 = 265/92 and b_3 = 445/812 > b_1, so B_m = 1/2 + 265/92 + 445/812 = 18342/4669 (about 3.9284). Exclusion. Fix K >
0 and 0 <= s < 1/2, let m = 2 + 1/(1 - s), which lies in [3, 4), and put beta = m (1 - s) - 2 = 1 - 2s > 0 and k_m = K
B_m - (m - 1). Let eps(K, s) = beta/k_m if k_m > 0 and eps(K, s) = 1 otherwise. Suppose an exact profile has 0 < D <
eps, |a0| <= K D and sigma <= s. By 3.44(ii) (with Q_m^- if a0 > 0 and Q_m^+ if a0 < 0), M <= sigma <= s and the
Gershgorin bound, (m - 1) c_l - 1 <= m M + B_m |a0| <= m s + K B_m D. The left side is m - 2 + (m - 1) D, so beta =
m - 2 - m s <= k_m D. If k_m <= 0 this contradicts beta > 0; otherwise it gives D >= eps, a contradiction. For K = 1
and s = 2/5: m = 11/3, beta = 1/5, k_m = 18342/4669 - 8/3 = 17674/14007 > 0 and eps(1, 2/5) = (1/5)(14007/17674) =
14007/88370 = 0.15850... > 0.158. Remarks. 3.44(iii) is the corresponding statement at fixed c_l. The argument needs m
(1 - s) > 2 with m < 4, which forces s < 1/2; for sigma >= 1/2 it gives nothing.

(b) Proof. Normalization. For an exact profile at c_l put q = rho/c_l and u = U/c_l. Dividing the equations by c_l^2,
resp. c_l, gives

    (X + u) . grad q = q/c_l,   div u = 0,   curl u = -q_x,   div((X + u) q) = (2 + 1/c_l) q,

the last since div X = 2 and div u = 0. Compactness. Let (rho_n, U_n) be exact profiles at c_n -> inf with sup |grad
q_n| + sup |D u_n| <= L. By parity q_n(0) = 0 and u_n(0) = 0, so |q_n(X)| <= L |X| and |u_n(X)| <= L |X|. By the
Arzela-Ascoli theorem on each disc |X| <= k and a diagonal extraction, a subsequence converges locally uniformly to
L-Lipschitz limits q and u with |q|, |u| <= L |X| (linear growth) and the same parities. Limit equations. For chi in
C_c^inf(R^2) the equations of q_n and u_n in weak form read

    int u_n . grad chi dX = 0,   int (u_{n,1} chi_y - u_{n,2} chi_x) dX = int q_n chi_x dX,
    int q_n (X + u_n) . grad chi dX = -(2 + 1/c_n) int q_n chi dX,

and they pass to the limit, with 1/c_n -> 0. The limits are Lipschitz, so their distributional first derivatives are
their a.e. derivatives: div u = 0 and curl u = -q_x a.e., and div((X + u) q) = (X + u) . grad q + 2 q a.e., so the
third identity gives (X + u) . grad q = 0 a.e. Nonzero solutions. For f smooth and odd with bounded derivative (for
instance f(y) = y or f = tanh), q = f(y) and u = (x, -y) satisfy (X + u) . grad q = (2x, 0) . (0, f'(y)) = 0, div u =
1 - 1 = 0 and curl u = d_x(-y) - d_y(x) = 0 = -q_x; they are smooth and Lipschitz, have the parities and vanish at 0.
So the class inherited by the limits (Lipschitz, the parities, linear growth) admits no Liouville theorem. Velocity
ambiguity (the parenthetical remark). If u and u' are two velocities in this class for the same q, then d = u - u' is
weakly div- and curl-free, so d_1 - i d_2 is holomorphic (Cauchy-Riemann and Weyl's lemma) and entire with bounded
derivative, hence affine; d(0) = 0 and the parities give d = b (x, -y) with b real. For each exact profile the law U =
o(r) of Section 2 removes this freedom, but the law is not uniform in n and does not survive locally uniform limits
(u = (x, -y) is not o(r)).

Non-profiles. Fix kappa != 0 and a smooth zeta >= 0, not identically 0, supported in (2, 3), and let J0 = int_0^inf
zeta(r) r^{-1} dr > 0. Let g3 = r sin(3 th) zeta(r) and f = r sin(5 th) zeta(r); they are smooth with compact support,
even in x and odd in y (r^k sin(k th) = Im (x + i y)^k with k odd). For n >= 2 put c_l = n, p_n = 1/n, D_n = n - 1,
a_n = kappa n, F_n(r) = (1 + r^2)^{-(1-p_n)/2}, k_n = (a_n/4 - D_n)/J0 and

    rho_n = a_n y F_n + k_n g3 + n^2 f.

Class and far field. rho_n is smooth with the parities, and rho_n = a_n y F_n for r < 2, so a0 = a_n and a0/c_l =
kappa. Since 0 < F_n <= min(1, r^{p_n - 1}) and r |F_n'| <= (1 - p_n) F_n, |y F_n| <= r^{p_n}, |grad(y F_n)| <= F_n +
r |F_n'| <= 2 F_n and (1 + r) F_n <= sqrt 2 (1 + r^2)^{p_n/2} <= sqrt 2 (1 + r)^{p_n}; so rho_n is in the primary
class with gamma = p_n = 1/c_l, and r^{-p_n} rho_n(r, th) -> a_n sin th != 0, a nonzero r^{1/c_l} far field. Velocity.
The canonical inverse is linear. For the radial part, psi = -a_n x y H_n(r) with H_n(r) = r^{-4} int_0^r t^3 F_n(t) dt
satisfies r H_n' + 4 H_n = F_n and -Lap psi = d_x(a_n y F_n), with velocity a_n (x (H_n + y^2 H_n'/r), -y (H_n + x^2
H_n'/r)). F_n is decreasing, so F_n/4 <= H_n <= 1/4 and -1 <= r H_n' = F_n - 4 H_n <= 0, and F_n(t) <= t^{p_n - 1}
gives H_n <= r^{p_n - 1}/(3 + p_n) and |r H_n'| <= 2 r^{p_n - 1}; so this velocity is O(r^{p_n}), has the parities and
is canonical, and |U[y F_n]| <= 2 r. The velocities U[g3] and U[f] of the compactly supported parts (Fourier
multipliers of 3.1(ii), with integrable transforms) are bounded, continuous and tend to 0 at infinity, so they are
canonical. Origin condition. 3.2 holds for every rho in P_inf (A.3.2). The term y F_n contributes only to rho_1 and f
only to rho_5, while g3 gives rho_3 = k_n r zeta(r); so int_0^inf rho_3 r^{-2} dr = k_n J0 = a_n/4 - D_n and
psi_xy(0) = -a_n/4 + k_n J0 = -D_n = 1 - c_l. Unbounded normalized gradient. rho_n/c_l = b_n + n f with b_n = kappa y
F_n + (k_n/n) g3, and |k_n/n| = |kappa/4 - 1 + 1/n|/J0 <= (|kappa|/4 + 1)/J0; so sup |grad b_n| <= C1 := 2
|kappa| + (|kappa|/4 + 1) sup |grad g3|/J0, independent of n, and sup |grad(rho_n/c_l)| >= n sup |grad f| - C1 -> inf;
since curl(U_n/c_l) = -d_x(rho_n/c_l) and f_x is not identically 0, also sup |D(U_n/c_l)|_F >= (n sup
|f_x| - C1)/sqrt2 -> inf. Not profiles. Let v = U[f] and w_n = U[b_n], so U_n = n w_n + n^2 v, and let R_n = (n
X + U_n) . grad rho_n - rho_n. Expanding,

    R_n/n^2 = n^2 v . grad f + n (v . grad b_n + (X + w_n) . grad f) + (X + w_n) . grad b_n - f - b_n/n.

Let chi = y eta(r) with eta smooth, eta = 1 on [1, 4] and eta = 0 on [5, inf). Since f is supported in 2 < r < 3, div
v = 0 and the transform of v_2 is -(xi1^2/|xi|^2) hat f,

    int chi v . grad f dX = int y v . grad f dX = -int f div(y v) dX = -int f v_2 dX
                          = (2 pi)^{-2} int (xi1^2/|xi|^2) |hat f|^2 dxi =: k_f,

and k_f > 0 because hat f is real analytic and not identically 0. On r <= 5 the functions b_n, grad b_n and w_n =
kappa U[y F_n] + (k_n/n) U[g3] are bounded independently of n, and v, f and grad f do not depend on n. Hence int chi
R_n dX = n^4 k_f + O(n^3), which is nonzero for n >= n0. So rho_n is not a profile at c_l = n, and since psi_xy(0) =
1 - n while every exact profile has psi_xy(0) = 1 - c_l, it is not a profile at any c_l. For n >= n0 the rho_n are the
stated non-profiles.

(c) Proof. Solutions (a y, 0): X . grad(a y) = a y, and U = 0 is div- and curl-free, with curl 0 = 0 = -d_x(a y).
Rigidity. Let rho and U be smooth with bounded first derivatives, U(0) = 0, grad rho(0) = 0, DU(0) = 0 (so rho(0) =
U(0) . grad rho(0) = 0 by the equation at 0) and sup |S|_op <= s < 1; no parity is used. Flatness: suppose rho =
rho_j + O(r^{j+1}) with rho_j homogeneous of degree j, where j >= 2 since the first jet vanishes. U = O(r^2) and grad
rho = O(r^{j-1}) give U . grad rho = O(r^{j+1}), and X . grad rho_j = j rho_j, so the degree-j part of the equation
reads j rho_j = rho_j; hence rho_j = 0, and by induction rho is flat at 0. Contraction: as in A.3.47(i), U(0) = 0
gives X . U = int_0^1 X^T S(tX) X dt >= -s |X|^2, so X . W >= (1 - s) |X|^2 for W = X + U, and |W| <= (1 +
sup |DU|) |X|; the flow of W is global and backward orbits satisfy |X(t)| <= e^{(1-s) t} |X| for t <= 0. Along orbits
d rho(X(t))/dt = rho(X(t)), so rho(X) = e^{-t} rho(X(t)). Choose N with N (1 - s) > 1; flatness gives |rho(Y)| <=
C_N |Y|^N for |Y| <= 1, so for t <= min(0, -log(|X|)/(1 - s)), |rho(X)| <= C_N e^{(N (1 - s) - 1) t} |X|^N, which
tends to 0 as t -> -inf. Hence rho = 0. Then div U = 0 and curl U = 0, so U_1 - i U_2 is entire (Cauchy-Riemann) with
bounded derivative, hence affine by Liouville's theorem, and U(0) = 0, DU(0) = 0 give U = 0. The last sentence of (c)
says that the compactness and the nondegeneracy needed to apply this to families are not proved; it is not a claim.

(d) Proof. Notation. Let the profile at c_l, with D = c_l - 1 <= 1/2, have the representation of 3.49(d) with constant
M. Write t = log r, so d_t = D d_s, and a_1(t) = D h(s), a_j(t) = D^2 H_j(s) for odd j >= 3, so that rho = sum_j r
a_j(t) sin(j th). Write ||.|| for ||.||_{C^3_b} (only sup |H^{(k)}| <= ||H|| for k <= 3 is used). The hypothesis
gives ||h|| + ||H_3||_{L^1} + sum_j (1 + j) ||H_j|| <= M, and for k <= 3, sup |d_t^k a_1| <= D^{1+k} ||h|| and
sup |d_t^k a_j| <= D^{2+k} ||H_j||. The bounds below are summable, so the series for grad rho and for the second
derivatives of psi converge uniformly on r > 0; termwise differentiation is justified and the bounds hold at every X
!= 0, hence everywhere by continuity. Density gradient. grad(r a(t) sin(j th)) = (a + d_t a) sin(j th) e_r + j a cos(j
th) e_th, so |grad(r a sin(j th))| <= (1 + j) |a| + |d_t a|. Hence, with D <= 1/2 and 1 + j >= 4 for j >= 3,

    G_rho <= (2D + D^2) ||h|| + sum_{j >= 3} ((1 + j) D^2 + D^3) ||H_j||
          <= 2.5 D ||h|| + (9/8) D^2 sum_j (1 + j) ||H_j|| <= 2.5 D M.

Stream function modes. By 3.1(iv) and A.3.1(iv), psi = sum_{n >= 1} psi_n(r) sin(2n th), where d_x rho = sum_n f_n
sin(2n th) and f_n = (1/2)(rho_{2n-1}' - (2n - 1) rho_{2n-1}/r + rho_{2n+1}' + (2n + 1) rho_{2n+1}/r). With rho_j = r
a_j(t), rho_j' = a_j + d_t a_j, so f_n = F_n(t) with

    F_n = (1/2) ((2 - 2n) a_{2n-1} + d_t a_{2n-1}) + (1/2) ((2n + 2) a_{2n+1} + d_t a_{2n+1}),

and, with psi_n = r^2 p_n(t), the formula of 3.1(iv) reads

    p_n(t) = (1/(4n)) [ int_{-inf}^t e^{-(2n+2)(t - tau)} F_n(tau) dtau
                        + int_t^inf e^{(2n-2)(t - tau)} F_n(tau) dtau ].

Hessian of a mode. For G = r^2 p(t) sin(N th) the Hessian in the polar frame (e_r, e_th) has the entries (2p + 3 p_t +
p_tt) sin(N th) and (2p + p_t - N^2 p) sin(N th) on the diagonal and N (p + p_t) cos(N th) off it; the Cartesian
Hessian is its conjugate by the rotation through th and has the same Frobenius norm. Hence, for N >= 2,

    |D^2 G|_F <= (N^2 + 2N) sup |p| + (2N + 4) sup |p_t| + sup |p_tt|,

and |DU|_F = |D^2 psi|_F, since DU = [[-psi_xy, -psi_yy], [psi_xx, psi_xy]]. Mode 2 (n = 1). F_1 = (1/2) d_t a_1 + 2
a_3 + (1/2) d_t a_3 = D^2 ((1/2) h' + 2 H_3 + (D/2) H_3')(s). The class bound rho = O(r^gamma), gamma < 1, applied to
rho_1 = r D h(s) and rho_3 = r D^2 H_3(s), gives h(s) -> 0 and H_3(s) -> 0 as s -> +inf, and H_3 is in L^1; so Q(t) :=
int_t^inf F_1 dtau = D B(s) (absolutely convergent: the growth bound |grad rho| = O(r^{gamma - 1}) gives a_j, d_t
a_j = O(e^{(gamma - 1) t}), hence F_1(t) = O(e^{(gamma - 1) t})) with B = -h/2 - (D/2) H_3 + 2 int_s^inf H_3. Since
F_1 = -d_t Q and Q is bounded, an
integration by parts in the first integral gives p_1(t) = int_0^inf e^{-4u} Q(t - u) du. From B' = -h'/2 - (D/2)
H_3' - 2 H_3 and B'' = -h''/2 - (D/2) H_3'' - 2 H_3', sup |B^{(k)}| <= 2M for k <= 2, so sup |d_t^k p_1| <= (1/4)
sup |d_t^k Q| = (1/4) D^{1+k} sup |B^{(k)}| <= D^{1+k} M/2, and the mode-2 Hessian is at most 8 sup |p_1| + 8 sup |d_t
p_1| + sup |d_t^2 p_1| <= (M/2)(8D + 8D^2 + D^3) <= 6.125 D M. Modes N = 2n >= 4. The kernel K_n(u) = e^{-(2n+2)
u}/(4n) for u > 0 and e^{(2n-2) u}/(4n) for u < 0 has L^1 norm (1/(4n))(1/(2n + 2) + 1/(2n - 2)) = 1/(N^2 - 4), and
d_t^k p_n = K_n * d_t^k F_n. For k <= 2 and D <= 1/2, sup |d_t^k F_n| <= (1/2)(2n - 2 + D) D^2 ||H_{2n-1}|| +
(1/2)(2n + 2 + D) D^2 ||H_{2n+1}|| <= D^2 (n + 3/2)(||H_{2n-1}|| + ||H_{2n+1}||). Since N^2 + 4N + 5 <= (37/12)(N^2 -
4) for N >= 4, the mode-N Hessian is at most (37/12) D^2 (n + 3/2)(||H_{2n-1}|| + ||H_{2n+1}||). Each H_j with j >= 3
occurs for n = (j + 1)/2 and, if j >= 5, for n = (j - 1)/2, with total factor at most (j + 4)/2 + (j + 2)/2 = j + 3 <=
(3/2)(1 + j); so the modes N >= 4 contribute at most (37/8) D^2 sum_j (1 + j) ||H_j|| <= (37/16) D M < 2.32 D M.
Conclusion. G_U < 6.125 D M + 2.32 D M < 8.45 D M, and G_rho + G_U < 11 D M for D <= 1/2. By 3.44(ii), G_rho + G_U >=
(sqrt 2/3)(2 c_l - 1) > sqrt 2/3 > 0.47, so D > 0.47/(11 M) > 1/(24 M). Hence no exact profile with c_l - 1 < min(1/2,
1/(24 M)) has the representation with constant M, and no exact family with c_l -> 1 has it with M independent of c_l.
The remaining sentences of (d) are statements of scope.

Scope. A statement of status: (a) assumes sigma <= s and |a0| <= K (c_l - 1), (b) and (c) assume uniform bounds or
compactness, and (d) assumes the representation; none of these is proved for exact profiles, so none of (a)-(d)
excludes a parameter interval without an extra hypothesis.

The identities were checked by symbolic computation in the main analysis.

## A.3.50 Capped non-profiles and capped local solutions

Setup. Notation of 3.47: D = c_l - 1, A = 2 c_l - 1, W = c_l X + U, S = (DU + DU^T)/2, sigma = sup |S|_op,
M = sup_{X != 0} (-X . U/r^2), q = rho/(a0 y), h = rho - a0 y, F = W . grad rho - rho. A symmetric trace-free 2 x 2
matrix [[S11, S12], [S12, -S11]] has operator norm (S11^2 + S12^2)^{1/2}.

Radial formulas. For a smooth radial f put H(r) = int_0^1 u^3 f(u r) du, so that 4H + r H' = f (differentiate r^4 H =
int_0^r v^3 f(v) dv), and psi = -a x y H(r). Then Lap(x y H) = x y (H'' + 5 H'/r), and differentiating 4H + rH' = f
gives r H'' + 5 H' = f', so -Lap psi = a x y f'/r = d_x(a y f). The velocity is U = a (x (H + y^2 H'/r), -y (H +
x^2 H'/r)). With K = 2f + r f' = 8H + 7rH' + r^2 H'' and Q = r f' + 24 H - 6 f = r^2 H'' - r H',

    S11 = (a/8)(K - Q cos 4th),   S12 = -(a/8) Q sin 4th,   max_th |S|_op = (|a|/8)(|K| + |Q|),          (R1)

the last because |S|^2 = (a/8)^2 (K^2 - 2KQ cos 4th + Q^2). Since K >= 0 in every case below, |K| + |Q| = max(K + Q,
