K - Q). In t = log r, K - Q = 8H + 8 H_t and K + Q = 8H + 4 H_t + 2 H_tt. The transport residual is

    F/(a y) = c_l r f' + D f - a H f - a r H f' + cos^2 th . a r (2 H f' - H' f).                          (R2)

Also |grad(y f)|^2 = cos^2 th f^2 + sin^2 th (f + r f')^2, and grad(y f) is the second row of D(X f(r)), whose
eigenvalues are f and f + r f'. These identities were checked by symbolic computation in the main analysis. If f is
smooth in r^2 (or constant near 0) and H = O(r^{-e}) with e > 0 at infinity, U = o(r), so U is the canonical velocity
of a y f (3.1(i)); the strain at 0 is diag(-psi_xy(0), psi_xy(0)) with psi_xy(0) = -a H(0) = -a f(0)/4.

(a) Proof. Fix c_l = 2, D = 1, B >= 9, C = 1179936, L = C B, delta = B/(L + 1)^2 and t = 1 - delta, so 0 < delta < 1/2
and t > 1/2; rho_B = t rho_b + rho_g with rho_b = 4 y f(r), f = (1 + s)^{-1/4}, s = r^2, and rho_g = B y E, E =
exp(-x^2/L^2 - y^2). Let c_* = 1/73746 = 1/(2 . 4097 . 9); then C = 16 . 73746 = 16/c_*, 4B/L = 4/C = c_*/4 =
1/294984.

Base cap. Write F(s) = (1 + s)^{-1/4}, positive, decreasing and convex, and H = (1/(2S^2)) int_0^S s F(s) ds with S =
r^2 (substitute s = u^2 S). The chord F(s) <= 1 - (1 - F(S)) s/S and the tangent F(s) >= F(S) + F'(S)(s - S) on [0, S]
give H <= 1/12 + F/6 and H >= F/4 - S F'(S)/12 = f/4 - r f'/24 (r f' = 2 S F'(S)). Here r f' = -(s/2)(1 + s)^{-5/4} <
0 and K = (1 + s)^{-5/4}(2 + 3s/2) > 0, and the tangent bound gives Q >= 0. With a = 4, (R1) gives max_th |S_b| = (K +
Q)/2 = 12 H - 2f + r f' <= 1 + r f' = 1 - r^2/(2 (1 + r^2)^{5/4}). For r <= 64, (1 + r^2)^{5/4} <= 4097 . 4097^{1/4} <
4097 . 9 (9^4 = 6561 > 4097), so the deficit is at least c_* r^2. For r >= 64, f(v) <= v^{-1/2} gives H <= (2/7)
r^{-1/2} <= 1/28, and 12H - 2f + r f' <= 12 H <= 3/7 <= 1 - c_*. Hence

    |S_b(X)|_op <= 1 - c_* min(r^2, 1),   S_b(0) = diag(1, -1)   (H(0) = 1/4).                              (A1)

Gaussian strain. With hat g(xi) = int e^{-i X . xi} g dX, hat rho_g = -i (B pi L/2) xi2 e^{-(L^2 xi1^2 + xi2^2)/4}.
The canonical multipliers of 3.1(ii) give hat psi_g = i xi1 hat rho_g/|xi|^2 = (B pi L/2) xi1 xi2 e^{-(...)}/|xi|^2,
hat S11 = xi1 xi2 hat psi_g and hat S12 = ((xi2^2 - xi1^2)/2) hat psi_g. Both are real and even under xi -> -xi, so
S_g(X) = (2 pi)^{-2} int cos(X . xi) hat S_g dxi, and the Euclidean norm of (hat S11, hat S12) is |xi|^2 |hat
psi_g|/2 = (B pi L/4) |xi1 xi2| e^{-(L^2 xi1^2 + xi2^2)/4}. With int |z| e^{-c z^2} dz = 1/c and int |z|^3 e^{-c z^2}
dz = 1/c^2 (c = L^2/4 and c = 1/4),

    |S_g(X)|_op <= (2 pi)^{-2} int |hat S_g| = B/(pi L),
    |S_g(X) - S_g(0)|_op <= (2 pi)^{-2} int (r^2 |xi|^2/2) |hat S_g| = (2B/(pi L))(1 + L^{-2}) r^2 <= (4B/L) r^2,

by |cos u - 1| <= u^2/2 and (X . xi)^2 <= r^2 |xi|^2. At 0, hat S12 is odd in xi1, so S_g,12(0) = 0, and with
1/|xi|^2 = int_0^inf e^{-u |xi|^2} du (Tonelli, positive integrand) and int z^2 e^{-c z^2} dz = pi^{1/2}/(2 c^{3/2}),

    S_g,11(0) = (2 pi)^{-2} (B pi L/2)(pi/4) int_0^inf (L^2/4 + u)^{-3/2} (1/4 + u)^{-3/2} du = B/(L + 1)^2 = delta,

using int_0^inf (al + u)^{-3/2} (be + u)^{-3/2} du = 2/((al be)^{1/2} (al^{1/2} + be^{1/2})^2), whose antiderivative
is -2 (2u + al + be)/((al - be)^2 ((al + u)(be + u))^{1/2}). So S_g(0) = delta diag(1, -1). For r >= 1, |S_g(X) -
S_g(0)| <= B/(pi L) + delta <= 2B/L. Hence |S_g(X) - S_g(0)|_op <= (4B/L) min(r^2, 1) = (c_*/4) min(r^2, 1).

Cap. The strain of rho_B is t S_b + S_g, and t + delta = 1, so by (A1)

    |S(X)|_op <= t (1 - c_* min(r^2, 1)) + delta + (c_*/4) min(r^2, 1) <= 1 - (c_*/4) min(r^2, 1),

since t c_* - c_*/4 >= c_*/4. This is |S(X)|_op <= 1 - min(r^2, 1)/294984. At 0, S(0) = (t + delta) diag(1, -1) =
diag(1, -1), so psi_xy(0) = -1 and sigma = 1 = D. X . U = int_0^1 X^T S(tau X) X dtau >= -r^2 gives M <= 1, and on the
y-axis -U_2(0, y)/y -> -psi_xy(0) = 1, so M = 1.

Slope, q and gradient. a0 = 4t f(0) + B = B + 4 (1 - delta), unbounded in B. q = (4t f + B E)/a0 lies in
(0, 1]. |grad(y f)| <= max(f, |f + r f'|) <= 1, since f + r f' = (1 + s)^{-5/4}(1 + s/2) and (1 + s/2)^4 <=
(1 + s)^5 coefficientwise. With Z = (x/L, y), y E = Z_2 e^{-|Z|^2}, whose Z-gradient has norm at most
max(e^{-w}, |1 - 2w| e^{-w}) <= 1 (w = |Z|^2; (2w - 1) e^{-w} has maximum 2 e^{-3/2} < 1), and grad_X =
diag(1/L, 1) grad_Z. Hence |grad rho_B| <= 4t + B = a0. The bounds on X . W, W_1/x, W_2/y and V/y of
3.47(i) follow from the cap and the parities alone (A.3.47(i), "Radial bound" and "Axes"), so they hold
here.

Class. rho_b is smooth, |rho_b| <= 4 r^{1/2}, |grad rho_b| <= C (1 + r)^{-1/2}; rho_g is a Schwartz function. So rho_B
is in P_inf with gamma = 1/2 = 1/c_l. The base velocity is O(r^{1/2}) by the radial formula (H <= C r^{-1/2}) and the
Gaussian velocity is bounded (integrable transform), so the velocity is canonical.

Not a profile. At (0, 1), rho_x = 0 (parity), rho_B(0, 1) > 0 and W_2(0, 1) >= 1 (W_2/y >= 1). By the formula for f +
r f', d_y rho_b(0, 1) = 4 (3/2) 2^{-5/4} = 6 . 2^{-5/4} < 3, while d_y rho_g(0, 1) = -B/e < -3 (B >= 9, e < 3). So d_y
rho_B(0, 1) < 0 and F(0, 1) = W_2 rho_y - rho < 0: transport fails at (0, 1). Since rho_y(0, 0) = a0 > 0 > rho_y(0, 1)
and rho_x = 0 on the y-axis, which is invariant with W_2 > 0 for y > 0, |grad rho| vanishes at some 0 < y1 < 1 and is
positive at y = 1: it increases along W beyond y1, so the monotonicity of 3.47(i) fails.

(b) Proof. Let a = 4D, beta = D/(2 (1 + D)) = D/(2 c_l), so 0 < beta < 1/2 and 1 - 2 beta = 1/c_l; put z = 1/r^2, g =
e^{-z} (g(0) = 0) and f = (1 - g)^beta, rho = a y f. Smoothness and flatness: g is smooth and flat at 0 with values in
[0, 1), and Phi(w) = (1 - w)^beta is smooth on (-inf, 1), so f = Phi(g) is smooth; a0 = a f(0) = 4D, and h = 4D y
(Phi(g) - 1) with Phi(g) - 1 = g Phi1(g), Phi1 smooth, so h is flat at 0; h != 0 since f < 1 for r > 0. Class and
velocity: 1 - e^{-z} <= z gives f <= min(1, r^{-2 beta}) and H <= r^{-2 beta}/(4 - 2 beta), so U = O(r^{1 - 2 beta}) =
o(r) is the canonical velocity; r f' = -2 beta z g (1 - g)^{beta - 1} = O(r^{-2 beta}) at infinity, so rho is in P_inf
with exponent 1 - 2 beta = 1/c_l.

Cap for the unit block. Let f1 = 1 - g and a > 0. Then H[f1] = 1/4 - H_g with H_g = int_0^1 u^3 e^{-z/u^2} du, and
0 <= H_g <= g/4. Here r f1' = -2 z g, so K = 2 (1 - (1 + z) g) >= 0 (e^z >= 1 + z) and Q = 6g - 2zg - 24 H_g; hence
K - Q = 2 - 8g + 24 H_g <= 2 - 2g <= 2 and K + Q = 2 + 4 (1 - z) g - 24 H_g. If z >= 1, K + Q <= 2. If z < 1,
e^{-w} >= 1 - w gives H_g/g = int_0^1 u^3 e^{-z (u^{-2} - 1)} du >= int_0^1 u^3 (1 - z (u^{-2} - 1)) du = (1 -
z)/4, so 24 H_g >= 6 (1 - z) g >= 4 (1 - z) g and K + Q <= 2. As K >= 0, |K| + |Q| = max(K + Q, K - Q) <= 2, and
(R1) gives |S[a y f1]|_op <= a/4 everywhere.

Convex combination. For 0 < beta < 1 the binomial series gives (1 - g)^beta = sum_{j >= 1} w_j (1 - g^j), with w_j =
(-1)^{j+1} binom(beta, j) = beta (1 - beta)(2 - beta) ... (j - 1 - beta)/j! > 0 and sum_{j >= 1} w_j = 1 - (1 -
1)^beta = 1 (the series converges at 1 since beta > 0). Here 1 - g^j = f1(r/sqrt j), and a y f1(r/l) = l (a (y/l)
f1(r/l)) is the dilate rho_l(X) = l rho(X/l) of a y f1, whose canonical strain is S(X/l). Since K, Q and H are linear
in f and the series for f, r f' and H converge for r > 0 (uniformly on compact subsets for f and r f', since w_j
j g^j is summable for g < 1; by monotone convergence for H), (R1) gives for r > 0

    max_th |S|_op = (a/8)(|K| + |Q|) <= sum_j w_j (a/8)(|K_j| + |Q_j|) <= a/4 = D,

and at r = 0 by continuity. At 0, psi_xy(0) = -a f(0)/4 = -D, so sigma = D, attained at 0; X . U >= -D r^2 and the
y-axis limit give M = D. So the density is capped.

Not a profile. This is a case of 3.24(v). Directly: if F = 0, the coefficient of cos^2 th in (R2) vanishes, so 2 H
f' = H' f, that is (H/f^2)' = 0 (f > 0), and H = f^2/4 (H(0) = 1/4, f(0) = 1). Then 4H + r H' = f gives f + r f'/2 =
1, so (r^2 (f - 1))' = 0 and f = 1, contradicting f -> 0. Since the density is capped, canonical, in the class and h
is flat and nonzero, the conclusion of 3.47(ii) (h not flat) fails without exact transport.

(c) Proof. Here psi_xx = A k y sin(k x) and psi_yy = 0, so -Lap psi = -A k y sin(k x) = rho_x. U = (-psi_y, psi_x) =
(-(c_l x - (A/k) sin(k x)), y (c_l - A cos(k x))), so W = c_l X + U is as stated, and with 2 c_l - A = 1,

    W . grad rho = A y [-A sin^2(k x) + (2 c_l - A cos(k x))(1 + cos(k x))] = A y (2 c_l - A)(1 + cos(k x)) = rho.

U(0) = 0, a0 = rho_y(0) = 2A, psi_xy = c_l - A cos(k x) gives psi_xy(0) = c_l - A = -D, and h = A y (cos(k x) - 1) =
-(A k^2/2) x^2 y + O(r^5), so n = 3 and a0 = 2A = (n - 1) A. Strain: S11 = -psi_xy = A cos(k x) - c_l = D - A w and
S12 = psi_xx/2 = (A k y/2) sin(k x), with sin^2(k x) = w (1 + cos(k x)); hence

    |S|_op^2 - D^2 = (D - A w)^2 - D^2 + (A^2 k^2 y^2/4) w (1 + cos(k x))
                   = A w [-2D + A w + (A k^2 y^2/4)(1 + cos(k x))].

Since 0 <= w <= k^2 x^2/2 and 1 + cos(k x) <= 2, the bracket is at most -2D + A k^2 r^2/2, which is <= 0 for r <=
(2/k) (D/A)^{1/2}; as A w >= 0 the cap |S|_op <= D holds there. rho(0, y) = 2A y grows linearly, so the pair is not in
the class. Both equations hold exactly on R^2, so any argument that uses only the two equations and the cap on a
neighbourhood of 0 (to every Taylor order) cannot exclude a0 = 2A = (n - 1) A. These identities, including the
factorization, were checked by symbolic computation in the main analysis.

(d) Proof. Fix c_l > 1, a0 > 4D, R > 0; put b = a0 - 4D > 0, alpha = D/c_l in (0, 1) (so 1 - alpha = 1/c_l), and
let eta(s) = Z^{-1} exp(-1/(s (1 - s))) on (0, 1), eta = 0 elsewhere, with Z chosen so that int eta = 1.

Base. In t = log r let H0(t) = 1 for t <= 0 and H0(t) = (e^{-alpha t} - alpha e^{-t})/(1 - alpha) for t > 0; H0 is C^1
(H0(0+) = 1, H0'(0+) = 0), and calH = eta * H0 (convolution in t) is smooth with calH = 1 for t <= 0. Put psi_0 = -D x
y calH(log r) and rho_0 = 4D y f, f = calH + calH'/4. This is the radial pair with a = 4D and H = calH/4 (then 4H + r
H' = f); for r <= 1, psi_0 = -D x y and rho_0 = 4D y. By (R1) and the t-forms of K - Q and K + Q,

    max_th |S_0|_op = D max(|calH + calH'|, |calH + calH'/2 + calH''/4|) = D max(|eta * (H0 + H0')|, |eta * G0|),

where G0 = H0 + H0'/2 + H0''/4 is a bounded function (H0' is continuous, so H0'' has no
point mass). For t > 0, H0 + H0' = e^{-alpha t} and G0 = ((1 - alpha/2 + alpha^2/4)
e^{-alpha t} - (3 alpha/4) e^{-t})/(1 - alpha), with G0(0+) = 1 - alpha/4; G0 is
decreasing since 1 - alpha/2 + alpha^2/4 = 3/4 + (1 - alpha)^2/4 >= 3/4 and e^{-t} <=
e^{-alpha t}, and positive since (1 - alpha) e^t G0(t) = (1 - alpha/2 + alpha^2/4) e^{(1 -
alpha) t} - 3 alpha/4 >= (1 - alpha)(1 - alpha/4) > 0. Both are 1 for t <= 0, so 0 < H0 +
H0' <= 1 and 0 < G0 <= 1 on R. As eta >= 0 has mass 1, |S_0|_op <= D everywhere. For t >=
1 (r >= e) the formulas for t > 0 apply under the convolution, e^{alpha} < 3 and 1/(1 -
alpha) = c_l give |S_0|_op <= 3 D c_l r^{-alpha}, so |S_0|_op <= D/2 for r >= R_* := (6
c_l)^{1/alpha} (> e). Also for r >= e, calH = (M_alpha r^{-alpha} - alpha M_1 r^{-1})/(1 -
alpha) with M_be = int eta(s) e^{be s} ds, so rho_0 = C_0 y r^{-alpha} + C_1 y r^{-1} with
C_0 = 4D (1 - alpha/4) M_alpha/(1 - alpha) > 0, and U_0 = O(r^{1 - alpha}): the far-field
class with exponent 1 - alpha = 1/c_l, canonical.

Remote pair. Let f_*(s) = eta(s - 1) for s > 0, extended oddly; f_* is smooth, odd and supported in 1 <= |s| <= 2.
K_*(s) = int_{-inf}^s f_* is even, equals -1 on [-1, 1] and 0 for |s| >= 2. With I(s) = int_{-inf}^s eta, chi(y) = 1 -
I(|y| - 1) is smooth (I(|y| - 1) = 0 for |y| <= 1), equals 1 on |y| <= 1 and 0 for |y| >= 2; g = y^3 chi/6 is odd with
g'' = y on |y| <= 1. Put

    psi_r = (b/L) f_*(x/L) g(y),   rho_r = -(b/L^2) f_*'(x/L) g(y) - b K_*(x/L) g''(y).

Both have the parities and compact support, and -Lap psi_r = -(b/L^3) f_*'' g - (b/L) f_* g'' = d_x rho_r, so U_r =
(-(b/L) f_* g', (b/L^2) f_*' g) is the canonical velocity of rho_r (compactly supported, so o(r); 3.1(i)). On |x| < L,
f_*(x/L) = f_*'(x/L) = 0, so U_r = 0 and rho_r = b g''(y), which is b y for |y| < 1. The strain is S_r,11 = -(b/L^2)
f_*' g' and S_r,12 = (b/(2L))(f_*'' g/L^2 - f_* g''), supported in L <= |x| <= 2L, |y| <= 2.

Constants. With v = 1/(s (1 - s)) >= 4, eta' = Z^{-1} e^{-v} (1 - 2s) v^2 (up to sign) and eta'' = Z^{-1} e^{-v}
((1 - 2s)^2 v^4 - 2 v^2 - 2 (1 - 2s)^2 v^3); with v^k e^{-v} <= k! and Z >= (1/3) e^{-9/2} > 1/729 (s (1 - s) >=
2/9 on [1/3, 2/3], e^{9/2} < 3^{9/2}), ||eta|| <= 729, ||eta'|| <= 2 . 729 = 1458, ||eta''|| <= 40 . 729 = 29160.
Since 0 <= chi <= 1, |chi'| <= 729, |chi''| <= 1458 and |y| <= 2 on the support: ||g|| <= 4/3, ||g'|| <= 2 + (4/3)
729 = 974, ||g''|| <= 2 + 4 . 729 + (4/3) 1458 = 4862. For L >= 1, |S_r|_op <= |S_r,11| + |S_r,12| <= (b/L)(1458 .
974 + (1/2) (29160 . (4/3) + 729 . 4862)) = 3211731 b/L < 4 . 10^6 b/L.

Assembly. Take L >= max(2, R_*, 8 . 10^6 b/D) and rho = rho_0 + rho_r, U = U_0 + U_r. Then |S_r|_op <= D/2; on the
support of S_r, r >= L >= R_*, so |S|_op <= D/2 + D/2 = D, and elsewhere S = S_0. So the global cap holds; rho is
smooth with the parities and the far-field class above (rho_r has compact support). On |X| < 1 (so |x| < L, |y| <
1): rho = (4D + b) y = a0 y, U = (D x, -D y), W = (A x, y), hence F = a0 y - a0 y = 0; also psi_xy(0) = -D. The
dilation rho_l(X) = l rho(X/l), U_l = l U(X/l) keeps rho_y(0) = a0, has strain S(X/l) (same sigma and cap) and
F_l(X) = l F(X/l); with l = R, F = 0 on |X| < R. Since h = rho - a0 y vanishes on that disc, h is flat and nonzero,
so by 3.47(ii) the pair is not an exact profile: F != 0 somewhere outside the disc. Sign: int_0^2 g'' = g'(2) -
g'(0) = 0 and int_0^1 g'' = 1/2, so g''(y1) < 0 for some y1 in (1, 2); as f_*'(0) = 0 and K_*(0) = -1, rho(0, y1) =
4D y1 f(y1) + b g''(y1), independent of L, is negative once b > 4D y1 f(y1)/|g''(y1)|; then rho/(a0 y) < 0 at (0,
y1) (and at (0, R y1) after the dilation). The base functions H0, G0 and the remote-pair identities were checked by
symbolic computation in the main analysis.

(e) Proof of the bound. On E_+ = {|x| <= 1, 1 <= y <= 6/5} we use the family of (a) (L >= 9C, so 1/L^2 < 1/16). x
rho_x <= 0 for y > 0: x d_x(4 t y f) = 4 t y f' x^2/r <= 0 and x d_x(B y E) = -2 B x^2 y E/L^2 <= 0. rho_y < 0: on
E_+, sin^2 th >= 1/2 and u = 1 + r^2 >= 2, and r f' < 0, so d_y(4 t y f) = 4t (f + sin^2 th . r f') <= 4 (f + r
f'/2) = 4 ((3/4) u^{-1/4} + (1/4) u^{-5/4}) <= 7 . 2^{-5/4} < 3 ((7/3)^4 = 2401/81 < 32); and d_y(B y E) = -B
e^{-x^2/L^2} (2 y^2 - 1) e^{-y^2} <= -B e^{-1 - 1/L^2}, since (2z - 1) e^{-z} is increasing on [1, 3/2] and y^2 <=
36/25 < 3/2; e^{1 + 1/L^2} < (11/4)(16/15) = 44/15 < 3 (e < 11/4, e^w <= 1/(1 - w)), so this is < -B/3 <= -3.
Velocity: U_1(0, y) = 0 and d_x U_1 = S11 with |S11| <= D give W_1/x in [c_l - D, c_l + D] = [1, A], and likewise
W_2/y in [1, A]; in particular |W| <= A r. Hence W . grad rho = (W_1/x)(x rho_x) + W_2 rho_y < 0 on E_+, and F = W
. grad rho - rho < -rho < 0, so |F_B| > rho_B. Size: rho_B >= B y E >= B e^{-1/L^2 - 36/25} > B/5, since 1/L^2 +
36/25 <= 25/16 and e^{25/8} < (11/4)^3 (16/15)^2 = 5324/225 < 25. F is odd in y (W_1 and rho_y even, W_2 and rho_x
odd), so |F_B| > |rho_B| > B/5 on the reflection E_- as well. E_+ and E_- have total area 4/5 and r^2 <= 61/25 <
5/2 there, so r^{-6} > 8/125 and ||F_B||_3^2 > (B^2/25)(4/5)(8/125) = 32 B^2/15625. On the other side h_B = 4t y
(f - 1) + B y (E - 1) with 0 <= 1 - f <= min(r^2/4, 1) and 0 <= 1 - E <= min(r^2, 1), so |h_B| <= (B + 4) |y|
min(r^2, 1) and ||h_B||_3^2 <= (B + 4)^2 int_0^{2pi} sin^2 th dth (int_0^1 r dr + int_1^inf r^{-3} dr) = pi (B +
4)^2. So the ratio is at least (B/(B + 4))(32/(15625 pi))^{1/2}, and for B >= 9 its square exceeds
(81/169)(32/62500) > 10^{-4} (pi < 4). These numbers were checked by symbolic computation in the main analysis.

Gaussian limit, 2 < m < 4. Uniform bounds: |W| <= 3r; |grad rho_B| <= a0 <= B + 4 gives |rho_B| <= (B + 4)|y|;
so |F_B|/B <= 8r. Near 0, h_B and V_B = W_2 - y are even in x, odd in y and vanish to second order (grad
h_B(0) = 0, psi_xy(0) = -1), so they are O(r^3) with constants given by sup |D^3 h_B|/B and sup |D^3 V_B|,
which are bounded uniformly in B (x-derivatives of y E carry factors 1/L, and the Fourier bound for D^3 U_g is
O(B/L)); hence F_B = a0 V_B + W . grad h_B - h_B gives |F_B|/B <= C r^3 for r <= 1. So F_B^2 r^{-2m}/B^2 and
h_B^2 r^{-2m}/B^2 are dominated by C min(r^{6-2m}, r^{2-2m}), integrable for 2 < m < 4. Pointwise limits: t ->
1, delta -> 0, and |U_g,1| <= delta |x|, |U_g,2| <= delta |y| (hat S_g,11 >= 0, so |S_g,11| <= S_g,11(0) =
delta); hence W -> W_b = 2X + U_b and

    h_B/B -> y (e^{-y^2} - 1),   F_B/B -> y e^{-y^2} (T (1 - 2 y^2) - 1),   T = W_b,2/y in [1, 3].

By dominated convergence ||F_B||_m/||h_B||_m -> R_m := ||F_inf||_m/||h_inf||_m, and R_m > 0 because for
y^2 > 1/2, T (1 - 2y^2) - 1 <= -2 y^2 < 0. Since |F_inf| >= 2 |y|^3 e^{-y^2} for y^2 >= 1/2, int (x^2 +
y^2)^{-m} dx = C_m |y|^{1-2m} (C_m > 0) and s = y^2 give ||F_inf||_m^2 >= 4 C_m int_{1/2}^inf s^{3-m}
e^{-2s} ds and ||h_inf||_m^2 = C_m J_m, so

    R_m^2 >= 4 int_{1/2}^inf s^{3-m} e^{-2s} ds / J_m,   J_m = int_0^inf s^{1-m} (1 - e^{-s})^2 ds.

At m = 3 the numerator is 2/e, and integrating by parts and then using (e^{-s} - e^{-2s})/s = int_1^2 e^{-us} du with
Tonelli, J_3 = 2 int_0^inf (e^{-s} - e^{-2s})/s ds = 2 log 2; so R_3 >= (e log 2)^{-1/2}.

Pairs of (d), L -> inf. The ratio is unchanged by the dilation (both norms scale by l^{2 - m}),
so take l = 1. For fixed X, once L > |x|, rho = rho_0 + b g''(y), U = U_0, hence F = F_0 + b G_c
and h = rho_0 - 4D y + b (g'' - y) exactly, with F_0 = (c_l X + U_0) . grad rho_0 - rho_0 and
G_c = (c_l y + U_0,2) g''' - g''. Uniformly in L >= 1, |grad rho_r| <= C b and |S| <= C
(constants above), so |W| <= C r, |rho| <= C |y| and |F| <= C r, while F = h = 0 on |X| < 1.
With b fixed, dominated convergence (majorant C r^{2-2m} on r >= 1) gives the limit ||F_0 + b
G_c||_m/||rho_0 - 4D y + b (g'' - y)||_m. With b = kappa L (capped for kappa <= D/(8 . 10^6)),
the same bounds hold for F/b and h/b, and the limit is ||G_c||_m/||g'' - y||_m. The denominators
are positive (g'' - y = -y for |y| >= 2, and rho_0 = o(r)). The numerators are positive: for 0 <
y < 1 fixed and x -> inf, g''' = 1, g'' = y, U_0,2 -> 0 and F_0 -> 0 by (R2) (f, r f', H, r H'
are O(r^{-alpha})), so G_c -> D y != 0 and F_0 + b G_c -> b D y != 0.

m -> 2 for a fixed member. In both families rho = O(r^p) at infinity with p = 1/c_l (p = 1/2 for (a)), so h^2 =
a0^2 y^2 + O(r^{1+p}) for r >= 1 and int_{r >= 1} a0^2 y^2 r^{-2m} dX = pi a0^2/(2 (m - 2)); the remainder and the
part r < 1 (h = O(r^3)) are bounded for 2 < m <= 3, so ||h||_m^2 = pi a0^2/(2 (m - 2)) + O(1). For F: near 0, F =
O(r^3) for (a) and F = 0 for (d); at infinity F = O(r^{b0}) with b0 = max(0, 2p - 1) < 1, so F is in L^2(r^{-4} dX)
on r >= 1 and ||F||_m^2 <= int_{r < 1} C r^{6-2m} dX + int_{r >= 1} F^2 r^{-4} dX stays bounded. For the bound at
infinity: the leading term of rho is homogeneous of degree p (4t y r^{-1/2} for (a); C_0 y r^{-alpha} for (d)), and
c_l p = 1, so it cancels in c_l X . grad rho - rho, leaving O(1); U . grad rho = O(r^p) O(r^{p-1}) = O(r^{2p-1}).
For (a) the Gaussian part is a Schwartz function and its velocity is bounded, so it contributes O(r^{-1/2}) (it is
not compactly supported, but this suffices); for (d) the remote pair has compact support. Hence the ratio tends to
0 as m -> 2.

## A.3.51 One-sided sign: local version, trajectory criterion, jets without the cap

Setup. rho is an exact profile; notation of A.3.47: a = a0 != 0, H = y - rho/a = -h/a, phi = psi + D x y, V = U_2 +
D y = phi_x, B = X . W/r^2 (in (a)); facts (F1)-(F5), Lemma 1 (identity (1): W . grad H - H = V, Lap V = a H_xx) and
Lemma 2 (identities (4), (5)) of A.3.47. H is odd in y, V is even in x and odd in y. Since y H = y^2 (1 - q) for y !=
0, y H >= 0 is q <= 1 off the x-axis.

(a) Proof. Let h be flat, r_d = inf{|X| : H(X) != 0} < R, and suppose that H y does not take both signs on |X| < R;
then there is s in {1, -1} with s H y >= 0 on |X| < R. Lemma 2 of A.3.47 (which uses only the equations, flatness
and (F5), not the sign) gives the absolute convergence of I_m, J_m, K_m and of the B- and W_2-moments and the
identities (4), (5) for every m > 2. A disc where B >= 1/2. If r_d > 0, H = 0 on |X| < r_d, so V = 0 there by (1),
phi = 0 there (phi_x = V, phi(0, y) = 0), W = (A x, y) and B = 1 + 2D x^2/r^2 >= 1 on 0 < |X| < r_d; by continuity
of B on X != 0 and compactness of the circle |X| = r_d there is R1 in (r_d, R] with B >= 1/2 on 0 < |X| < R1. If
r_d = 0, (F3) gives B >= 1 - C r^2, so B >= 1/2 on 0 < |X| < R1 for some R1 in (0, R]. Concentration. Fix r0 in
(r_d, R1). There is X1 = (x1, y1) with |X1| < r0 and H(X1) != 0; since H(x, 0) = 0, y1 != 0, so s H(X1) y1 > 0, and
c0 := s int_{|X| < r0} H y dX > 0. Put P_m = s int_{|X| < R1} H y r^{-2m} dX >= c0 r0^{-2m}. Exterior. With |H| <=
C_H r and |W| <= C_W r for r >= R1 ((F5) for r >= 1, smoothness and H(0) = W(0) = 0 for R1 <= r <= 1) and int_{r >=
R1} r^{2-2m} dX = 2 pi R1^{4-2m}/(2m - 4), put E_m = 2 pi C_H R1^{4-2m}/(2m - 4); then the integrals over r >= R1
of |H y| r^{-2m}, |H y B| r^{-2m} and |H W_2| r^{-2m} are at most E_m, C_W E_m and C_W E_m (|B| <= C_W, |W_2| <=
C_W r there).

Upper bound from (4). The weight 2m x^2/r^2 - 1 lies in [-1, 2m - 1] and s H y >= 0 on |X| < R1, so -P_m - (2m - 1)
E_m <= s K_m <= (2m - 1)(P_m + E_m). Hence s J_m <= a (2m - 1)(P_m + E_m)/(2 (m - 2)) if a > 0, and s J_m <= |a|
(P_m + (2m - 1) E_m)/(2 (m - 2)) if a < 0. Lower bound from (5). On 0 < |X| < R1, B >= 1/2 and s H y >= 0, so the
inner part of s int H y B r^{-2m} is >= P_m/2; s I_m <= P_m + E_m; and with C_R = sup_{|X| < R1} |W_2/y| (finite,
W_2/y = int_0^1 d_y W_2(x, t y) dt), s H W_2 = (s H y)(W_2/y) <= C_R s H y inside. Hence

    s J_m >= m P_m - 2m C_W E_m - (2 c_l + 1)(P_m + E_m) - C_R P_m - C_W E_m.

Conclusion. E_m/P_m <= K0 (r0/R1)^{2m}/(2m - 4) with K0 = 2 pi C_H R1^4/c0, which tends to 0 exponentially in m since
r0 < R1. Dividing by P_m, the upper bound gives s J_m/P_m <= C (independent of m >= 3), and the lower bound gives s
J_m/P_m >= m - (2 c_l + 1) - C_R - o(1). This is a contradiction for large m. So H y takes both signs on |X| < R.

(b) Proof. rho is smooth and odd in y, so rho = y int_0^1 rho_y(x, t y) dt and q = a0^{-1} int_0^1 rho_y(x, t y) dt
is smooth, even in x and in y, with q(0) = rho_y(0)/a0 = 1. Likewise G = V/y = int_0^1 V_y(x, t y) dt is smooth and
even in x and in y, and G(0) = d_y U_2(0) + D = 0 by (F2), so G = O(r^2) at 0. Since W_2 = c_l y + U_2 = y + V, W .
grad y = y + V; with rho = a0 y q, transport gives a0 (y + V) q + a0 y W . grad q = a0 y q, so y W . grad q = -q V,
that is W . grad q = -q G off y = 0 and, by continuity, everywhere; and G = W_2/y - 1. Trajectories. W is smooth
with |W| <= C (1 + r) ((F5)), so the flow X(t; X) exists for all t. Along an orbit d/dt q(X(t)) = -G(X(t)) q(X(t)),
so for t < 0, q(X) = q(X(t)) exp(-int_t^0 G(X(tau)) dtau). Suppose X(t) -> 0 as t -> -inf. By (F3), X . W = A x^2 +
y^2 + O(r^4) >= r^2 (1 - C r^2), so on a disc |X| <= r1 (r1 small) d/dtau log |X(tau)| >= 1/2; once the backward
orbit stays in this disc for tau <= T, |X(tau)| <= r1 e^{(tau - T)/2}, so |G(X(tau))| <= C e^{tau - T} is integrable
on (-inf, T]. Letting t -> -inf, q(X(t)) -> q(0) = 1 and q(X) = exp(-int_{-inf}^0 G(X(t; X)) dt) > 0. Hence, if
every backward orbit tends to 0, q <= 1 everywhere (equivalently y H >= 0, using continuity across the x-axis) holds
exactly when all the backward integrals are >= 0. If W_2/y >= 1 off the x-axis then G >= 0 there, hence everywhere
by continuity, so 0 < q <= 1. Finally W_2/y = c_l + U_2/y, so W_2/y >= 1 is U_2/y >= -D.

(c) Leading equations. As in A.3.24(iii), the first nonzero homogeneous part h_n of h has odd degree n = 2K + 1 >= 3
(rho is even in x and odd in y and grad h(0) = 0), and below degree n the homogeneous parts of h and of phi_x vanish:
if H_m = 0 for m < n, then the degree-m part of (1) gives V_m = 0 for m < n, because W = (A x, y) + O(r^3) by (F3) and
the O(r^3) part of W applied to grad H only produces degrees >= n + 2. At degree n, with L = A x d_x + y d_y - 1, the
parts of (1) are

    V_n = L H_n,   Lap V_n = a (H_n)_xx,

the leading equations (phi_{n+1} = int_0^x V_n). Conversely, if a homogeneous H_n (even in x, odd in y, degree n)
satisfies Lap L H_n = a (H_n)_xx, then V_n := L H_n and phi_{n+1} := int_0^x V_n satisfy both, and Lap phi_{n+1} -
a (H_n)_x has zero x-derivative and is odd in x, hence is 0 (the degree n - 1 part of -Lap phi = rho_x). Recurrence.
Lap (A x f_x) = A x d_x Lap f + 2A f_xx and Lap (y f_y) = y d_y Lap f + 2 f_yy give Lap L = L Lap + 2A d_xx + 2 d_yy,
so the condition is

    (L + 2) Lap H_n + (2 (A - 1) - a) (H_n)_xx = 0.

L + 2 multiplies x^{2j} y^{n-2-2j} by 2jA + n - 2 - 2j + 1 = n - 1 + 2j (A - 1) = e_j, and e_j + 2 (A - 1) = e_{j+1}.
The coefficient of x^{2j} y^{n-2-2j} (0 <= j < K) in Lap H_n is (2j + 2)(2j + 1) c_{j+1} + (n - 2j)(n - 2j - 1) c_j
and in (H_n)_xx it is (2j + 2)(2j + 1) c_{j+1}; so the condition is exactly

    (n - 2j)(n - 2j - 1) e_j c_j + (2j + 2)(2j + 1)(e_{j+1} - a) c_{j+1} = 0   (0 <= j < K).                (C1)

Since A > 1, e_j > 0, and n - 2j >= 3 for j < K, the coefficient of c_j in row j is nonzero; so c_K determines all
c_j, the solutions form a line, and c_K = 0 forces H_n = 0. Solving downwards, with prod_{j<K} (2j+2)(2j+1) = (2K)!
and prod_{j<K} (n - 2j)(n - 2j - 1) = (2K + 1)!,

    c_0 = c_K prod_{i=1}^K (a - e_i) / ((2K + 1) prod_{j=0}^{K-1} e_j).                                    (C2)

Sign. If y H >= 0 near 0, then at X = (lam t^{1/2}, lam), lam > 0, y H = lam^{n+1} (H_n(t^{1/2}, 1) + O(lam^2)) >= 0;
letting lam -> 0, P(t) = H_n(t^{1/2}, 1) = sum_j c_j t^j >= 0 for t >= 0. Here c_K != 0 (as H_n != 0), so P has
degree K, and P >= 0 on [0, inf) forces c_K > 0; c_0 = P(0) >= 0 gives prod_{i=1}^K (a - e_i) >= 0 by (C2). If K is
odd and a < e_1, all K factors are negative (e_i increases in i); so a >= e_1 = n - 1 + 2 (A - 1).

The case A <= n. Suppose A <= n and a < (n - 1) A; note e_K = n - 1 + 2K (A - 1) = (n - 1) A. Put eta = K/(A - 1) >=
1/2 and chi = 1 + (2K - a)/(2 (A - 1)), so that e_j = 2 (A - 1)(eta + j) and e_{j+1} - a = 2 (A - 1)(chi + j). Then
(C1) is (n - 2j)(n - 2j - 1)(eta + j) c_j + (2j + 2)(2j + 1)(chi + j) c_{j+1} = 0, and

    F_j = (-1)^j binom(n, 2j) (eta)_j (chi + j)_{K-j}

((x)_j the rising factorial) solves it, by binom(n, 2j + 2)(2j + 2)(2j + 1) = binom(n, 2j)(n - 2j)(n - 2j - 1)
and (eta)_{j+1} = (eta)_j (eta + j), (chi + j)(chi + j + 1)_{K-j-1} = (chi + j)_{K-j}. F_K = (-1)^K n (eta)_K !=
0, so P = lambda F_chi with F_chi(t) = sum_j F_j t^j and lambda != 0. The law: u := chi + K - 1 = ((n - 1) A -
a)/(2 (A - 1)) > 0. Let T have the beta-prime law with density x^{u-1} (1 + x)^{-u-K-3/2}/B(u, K + 3/2) on (0,
inf), so E T^j = (u)_j (3/2)_{K-j}/(3/2)_K for 0 <= j <= K; if A < n (eta > 1/2) let S be independent of T with
the Beta(1/2, eta - 1/2) law, E S^j = (1/2)_j/(eta)_j; if A = n (eta = 1/2) let S = 1, which has the same
moments. The law of T S has a positive density on (0, inf). With (1/2)_j = (2j)!/(4^j j!) and (3/2)_m = (2m +
1)!/(4^m m!),

    binom(2K + 1, 2j) (1/2)_j (3/2)_{K-j}/(3/2)_K = binom(K, j),
    (chi + j)_{K-j} (u)_j = (chi + K - 1)(chi + j)_{K-1},

the second because the two products cover chi + j, ..., chi + K + j - 2 with chi + K - 1 counted twice. Hence

    E F_chi(T S) = (chi + K - 1) sum_{j=0}^K (-1)^j binom(K, j) (chi + j)_{K-1} = 0,

a K-th difference of a polynomial of degree K - 1 in j. But P(T S) >= 0 and P is a nonzero polynomial, so E P(T S) >
0 for a law with positive density: a contradiction. So a >= (n - 1) A. Sharpness: at a = e_K, row K - 1 of (C1) gives
c_{K-1} = 0 and then c_j = 0 for all j < K, so H_n = c_K x^{2K} y with y H_n = c_K x^{2K} y^2 >= 0.

The quintic. For n = 5, e = (4, 2A + 2, 4A), and (C1) with c_2 = 1 gives P(t) = t^2 + 2 (a - e_2) t/e_1 + (a -
e_1)(a - e_2)/(20 e_1). If a >= e_2 all coefficients are >= 0. If e_1 <= a < e_2, P(0) <= 0 and P'(0) < 0, so P < 0
for small t > 0. If a < e_1, P(0) > 0 and P'(0) < 0, so P >= 0 on [0, inf) iff the discriminant is <= 0; it equals
-4 (e_2 - a) beta(a)/(20 e_1^2) with beta(a) := (20 - e_1) a + e_1^2 - 20 e_2 = (18 - 2A) a + 4A^2 - 72A + 4, so the
condition is beta(a) >= 0. beta is affine with beta(e_1) = 20 (e_1 - e_2) < 0 (and beta(e_2) = e_1 (e_1 - e_2) < 0).
If A <= 9 its slope is >= 0, so beta < 0 on a < e_1 and only a >= 4A remains. If A > 9 the slope is negative and
beta(a) >= 0 iff a <= a_* = 2 (A^2 - 18A + 1)/(A - 9), with e_1 - a_* = 20 (A - 1)/(A - 9) > 0. Corollaries. By
3.47(iv), y H >= 0 forces h not flat, so a first degree n exists. If 1 < c_l <= 3 (A <= 5): n = 3 has K = 1 odd, so
a >= e_1 = 2A; n >= 5 has A <= n, so a >= (n - 1) A. If 1 < c_l <= 5 (A <= 9): n = 3 gives a >= 2A; n = 5 gives a >=
4A; n = 7 (K = 3 odd) gives a >= e_1 = 2A + 4; n >= 9 gives a >= (n - 1) A >= 8A; so a >= 2A > 0. The recurrence,
the solution F_j, the two identities, the vanishing differences for K <= 6, the moments and the quintic thresholds
were checked by symbolic computation in the main analysis.

(d) Proof. For A = 11, a = -76, n = 5: e_1 = 24, e_2 = 44, and the quintic formulas give c_1/c_2 = 2 (-120)/24 = -10,
c_0/c_2 = (-100)(-120)/480 = 25, so H_5 = (1/25)(25 y^5 - 10 x^2 y^3 + x^4 y) = y (y^2 - x^2/5)^2 and P = (1 - t/5)^2,
with y H_5 = y^2 (y^2 - x^2/5)^2 >= 0. Explicitly V_5 = L H_5 = 4 y^5 - (48/5) x^2 y^3 + (44/25) x^4 y, phi_6 = 4 x
y^5 - (16/5) x^3 y^3 + (44/125) x^5 y, and Lap V_5 = (304/5) y^3 - (912/25) x^2 y = -76 (H_5)_xx, Lap phi_6 = (304/5)
x y^3 - (304/25) x^3 y = a (H_5)_x. Here a_*(11) = 2 (121 - 198 + 1)/2 = -76, so by (c) every a <= -76 gives a
sign-compatible solution of the leading equations (y H_5 = y^6 P(x^2/y^2) for y != 0). For every A > 9, any a <=
min(a_*(A), -1) < 0 works in the same way; for example A = 11, a = -100 gives (c_0, c_1, c_2) proportional to (1,
-10/31, 5/186) with discriminant -10/2883 < 0. These were checked by symbolic computation in the main analysis.

## A.3.52 Composition of 3.27 and 3.28

Proof. 3.27 defines E as the weighted Sobolev space of 3.28 (H^s near 0, r^nu H^s_b at infinity, with the parities),
P0 h = W* . grad h - h, X0 = {h in E : P0 h in E} with its graph norm ||h||_E + ||P0 h||_E, and L(h, delta) = P0 h +
U[h] . grad rho* + delta X . grad rho*; 3.28 uses the same E, P0, graph domain and L = L0 + delta X . grad rho with
L0 = P0 + M, M h = U[h] . grad rho. So, for the same nu and s, the operator of the hypothesis of 3.27 is the
augmented map of 3.28 on the same spaces. The parameters are compatible: given 1/c_l < nu < 1, choose q with 1/c_l <
q < nu for 3.27 and an even s = 2m >= 4 above the threshold max(1 + c_l, (1 + c_l + max(a0, 0))/A) of 3.28 (such s
also satisfy s > 2). The graph domain is the domain used in the Fredholm proof: by A.3.28, Step 2, X0 = J^{-1} D(T)
with an equivalent graph norm, so the Fredholm statement of 3.28 is for X0 with the graph norm of 3.27. Hence, for
rho* of the primary class with (H-dyn), L : X0 x R -> E is Fredholm of index 1 with (e_sc, 0) in its kernel. The
remaining part of the hypothesis of 3.27 is that the kernel is exactly span{(e_sc, 0)}; then dim ker L = 1 and index
1 give that L is onto, so the hypothesis of 3.27 holds and 3.27 gives local uniqueness modulo scaling in its Holder
neighbourhood. 3.28 is stated for profiles of the primary class (it uses the far-field bounds of 3.23), so the
composition requires rho* in that class.

## A.3.53 Angular monotonicity under the one-sided sign

Proof. Let rho be an exact profile of the primary class with q <= 1 everywhere and q_th >= 0 on the open first
quadrant. Since y H = y^2 (1 - q) for y != 0, y H >= 0, so h is not flat at 0 by 3.47(iv). q is smooth and even in x
and in y with q(0) = 1 (A.3.43, Setup), and q - 1 = h/(a0 y) is not flat, so q - 1 has a first nonzero homogeneous
Taylor part Q_{2k} = sum_{j=0}^k t_j x^{2j} y^{2k-2j}, k >= 1, and rho^(m) = 0 for 3 <= m < n = 2k + 1, with rho^(n) =
a0 y Q_{2k}.

Integration by parts. In A.3.43(i), D/a0 = 1/4 + (4/pi) int_0^inf I(r) dr/r with I(r) = int_0^{pi/2} k(th) q(r, th)
dth, the angular integral taken first, and int_0^inf |I(r)| dr/r < inf (both proved there). Its weight is k = -(cos th
sin^3 th)'. For each r > 0, q(r, .) is smooth on [0, pi/2] and w = cos th sin^3 th vanishes at th = 0 and th = pi/2,
so integration by parts in th has no boundary terms and gives I(r) = int_0^{pi/2} w q_th dth (this step is also in
A.3.43(i), "Passage from the q_x form"). Since w >= 0 and q_th >= 0 on the open quadrant, I(r) >= 0 for every r > 0,
so D/a0 >= 1/4. No change of the order of integration is used. (The double integral is in fact absolutely convergent
for dth dr/r: w q_th = O(r^2) at 0, and |w q_th| <= (|grad rho| + |rho|/r)/|a0| = O(r^{gamma-1}) at infinity uniformly
in th, as in A.3.54, Step 0.) As D > 0, 0 < a0 <= 4D.

Leading part of q_th. From q <= 1, Q_{2k}(X) = lim_{lam -> 0} lam^{-2k} (q(lam X) - 1) <= 0, so t_0 = Q_{2k}(0,
1) <= 0. In polar coordinates q_th = x q_y - y q_x, and

    (x d_y - y d_x) Q_{2k} = sum_j t_j [(2k - 2j) x^{2j+1} y^{2k-2j-1} - 2j x^{2j-1} y^{2k-2j+1}],

whose x y^{2k-1} coefficient is 2k t_0 - 2 t_1 and whose other terms contain x^3; since q - 1 - Q_{2k} = O(r^{2k+2})
is smooth, its angular derivative is O(r^{2k+2}). At X = (lam s, lam) with s, lam > 0 small, q_th = lam^{2k} (2 (k
t_0 - t_1) s + O(s^3)) + O(lam^{2k+2}) >= 0; dividing by lam^{2k} s and letting lam -> 0, then s -> 0, gives t_1 <= k
t_0 <= 0.

Recursion. A.3.24(iii) uses only the leading transport and Poisson equations at degree n (with the harmonic datum
unrestricted; no monotonicity), and gives, for 1 <= j <= k,

    2j (a0 - d_j) t_j = [(2k - 2j + 3)(2k - 2j + 2)/(2j - 1)] d_{j-1} t_{j-1},
    d_j = 2jA + 2 (k - j) = 2j (A - 1) + 2k,

checked by symbolic computation in the main analysis for k = 1, ..., 4. At j = 1, 2 (a0 - d_1) t_1 = 2k (2k + 1) d_0
t_0 with d_0 = 2k > 0 and d_1 = 2 (A - 1) + 2k = 4D + 2k > 4D >= a0. The left side is >= 0 (a0 - d_1 < 0, t_1 <= 0)
and the right side is <= 0 (t_0 <= 0), so both vanish: t_1 = 0 and then t_0 = 0. Since d_j increases in j, a0 - d_j <
0 for every j >= 1, and the recursion gives t_j = 0 inductively; so Q_{2k} = 0, a contradiction.

The remark. If |grad rho| <= |a0|, then since rho(x, 0) = 0, |rho(x, y)| <= |a0| |y|, so |q| <= 1; and |grad
rho(0)| = |a0| by (F1) of A.3.47, so "the gradient maximum is attained at the origin" is |grad rho| <= |a0|, and
the theorem applies. The coefficients d_j and t_j agree with 3.51(c) (e_j = d_j for n = 2k + 1 and c_j = -t_j), as
they must.

## A.3.54 Angular variation under the one-sided sign

Setup. rho is a density of the primary class (an exact profile where stated), q = rho/(a0 y) extended to y = 0 by q(x,
0) = rho_y(x, 0)/a0, w(th) = cos th sin^3 th and k = -w' = sin^2 th (4 sin^2 th - 3) on [0, pi/2],
H = y - rho/a0 = -h/a0, and P, N, A(q) are as in 3.54 and 3.43(ii). M = max w = w(pi/3) = 3 sqrt3/16.

Step 0 (finiteness and the identity). q is smooth and even in x and in y with q(0) = 1, so grad q = O(r) and q_th = (x
d_y - y d_x) q = O(r^2) uniformly in th near 0. For r >= 1 differentiation of q = rho/(a0 r sin th) gives

    q_th = (-sin th rho_x + cos th rho_y)/(a0 sin th) - rho cos th/(a0 r sin^2 th),
    w q_th = cos th sin^2 th (-sin th rho_x + cos th rho_y)/a0 - rho cos^2 th sin th/(a0 r),

so |w q_th| <= (|grad rho| + |rho|/r)/|a0| = O(r^{gamma-1}) uniformly in th by the growth bound. Hence int_0^inf
int_0^{pi/2} |w q_th| dth dr/r < inf, and P, N are finite. The same bounds give A(q) < inf: osc q(r, .) = O(r^2) at 0,
and at infinity q = O(r^{gamma-1}) uniformly in th (off the strip |y| < r/2 divide the growth bound by |a0 y|; in the
strip |x| > sqrt3 r/2 and integration of rho_y on the vertical segment gives |rho| <= C |y| r^{gamma-1}). For each r,
w(0) = w(pi/2) = 0 and integration by parts give int_0^{pi/2} k q dth = int_0^{pi/2} w q_th dth. Inserting this in
3.43(i) and splitting w q_th = w (q_th)_+ - w (-q_th)_+ (w >= 0; both parts are absolutely integrable for dth dr/r)
gives D/a0 = 1/4 + (4/pi)(P - N) for every exact profile.

(a) Proof. Let rho be an exact profile with q <= 1, that is y H >= 0. By 3.47(iv) h is not flat, so it has a first
nonzero homogeneous part h_n, n = 2K + 1 >= 3, and H_n = -h_n/a0 = sum_j c_j x^{2j} y^{n-2j} satisfies the recurrence
of 3.51(c),

    (n - 2j)(n - 2j - 1) e_j c_j + (2j + 2)(2j + 1)(e_{j+1} - a0) c_{j+1} = 0  (0 <= j < K),
    e_j = n - 1 + 2j (A - 1),

with c_K > 0. Threshold. Suppose a0 >= (n - 1) A. Since 4D = 2A - 2,

    N - P = (pi/4)(1/4 - D/a0) >= (pi/4)(1/4 - D/((n - 1) A)) = pi ((n - 3) A + 2)/(16 (n - 1) A).

If a0 > (n - 1) A the inequality is strict and N >= N - P gives the claim. If a0 = (n - 1) A = e_K, the row j = K - 1
of the recurrence gives 6 e_{K-1} c_{K-1} = 0, so c_{K-1} = 0, and the rows j < K - 1 then give c_j = 0 for every
j < K (each e_j > 0). So H_n = c_K x^{n-1} y with c_K > 0, q = 1 - H/y = 1 - c_K r^{n-1} cos^{n-1} th + O(r^{n+1})
with a remainder whose th-derivative is O(r^{n+1}) uniformly (q is smooth in Cartesian coordinates), and

    q_th = (n - 1) c_K r^{n-1} cos^{n-2} th sin th + O(r^{n+1}).

On the sector pi/6 <= th <= pi/3 the leading term is at least (n - 1) c_K 2^{1-n} r^{n-1}, so there is delta > 0 with
q_th > 0 on {r < delta, pi/6 <= th <= pi/3}, where w >= w(pi/6) > 0; hence P > 0 and N > N - P, which again gives the
strict claim. Range. Let 1 < c_l <= 5 (A <= 9). By 3.51(c): for n = 3, K = 1 is odd and a0 >= e_1 = 2A; for n = 5,
A <= 9 gives a0 >= 4A; for n = 7, K = 3 is odd and a0 >= e_1 = 2A + 4; for n >= 9, A <= n gives a0 >= (n - 1) A >= 8A.
So a0 >= 2A, with equality only if n = 3. If a0 > 2A, then N - P = (pi/4)(1/4 - D/a0) > (pi/4)(1/4 - D/(2A)) = pi/(16
A) directly (A - 2D = 1), so N > pi/(16 A). If a0 = 2A, then n = 3 and a0 = (n - 1) A, and the endpoint argument of
the threshold statement gives P > 0, so again N > pi/(16 A). For 1 < c_l <= 3, and for A <= n at any c_l, 3.51(c)
gives a0 >= (n - 1) A for the first degree n, and the threshold statement applies.

Contrast. If A(q) = 0 then 3.43(ii) gives a0 = 4D = 2A - 2 < 2A, contrary to the range just proved; so A(q) > 0 and
3.43(ii) gives N - P = (pi/4)(1/4 - D/a0) < (pi/4)(3 sqrt3/(4 pi)) A(q) = M A(q). With N - P >= pi/(16 A) this gives
A(q) > pi/(16 A M) = pi/(3 sqrt3 A). (The constant: k < 0 on (0, pi/3), k > 0 on (pi/3, pi/2), int k = 0 and int
k_+ = int k_- = w(pi/3) = M, so |int k f| <= M osc f for continuous f, with equality only for constant f.)

(b) Proof. For a0 > 0, Step 0 and P >= 0 give D/a0 >= 1/4 - 4N/pi, which is positive when N < pi/16; rearranging gives
a0 <= 4D/(1 - 16 N/pi). Equality holds for the non-profiles of (d) (P = 0 there).

(c) Proof. eps = 1/(2A) < 1/2 and 0 <= y^2/(1 + r^2) < 1, so q_eps is smooth, even in x and in y, and 0 < q_eps <= 1.
At fixed r, (q_eps)_th = -2 eps exp(-r^2) r^2 sin th cos th/(1 + r^2) < 0 on (0, pi/2), so P(q_eps) = 0 and, with
int_0^{pi/2} cos^2 th sin^4 th dth = pi/32,

    N(q_eps) = (eps pi/16) int_0^inf r exp(-r^2)/(1 + r^2) dr < eps pi/32 = pi/(64 A).

The density-only form of Step 0 (it uses only the canonical inverse, not transport: c/a = -1/4 - (4/pi)(P - N) for the
canonical c of a y q) gives psi_xy(0) = a_eps (-1/4 + 4 N(q_eps)/pi) = -D for a_eps = D/(1/4 - 4 N(q_eps)/pi), and
1/4 - 4 N(q_eps)/pi > 1/4 - 1/(16 A) = D/(2A) + 3/(16 A) gives 0 < a_eps < 2A. The density a_eps y q_eps is rapidly
decreasing, so it lies in the growth class, and its cubic part is h_3 = -a_eps (x^2 y + (1 + eps) y^3), that is
b = -a_eps and e = -(1 + eps) a_eps in (T1) of 3.3; (T1) 6e = (a0 - 2A) b would require 6 (1 + eps) = a_eps - 2A < 0.
So it is not a profile.

(d) Proof. Put B = sqrt beta >= 1 and t = x^2 + beta y^2, s = beta y^2. q = exp(-t) lies in (0, 1]. The absolutely
convergent form c = (1/pi) int x y r^{-4} rho_x dX of the canonical strain (3.2) with rho_x = -2 a_beta x y exp(-t)
gives, after the radial integration,

    c = -(4 a_beta/pi) int_0^{pi/2} cos^2 th sin^2 th/(cos^2 th + B^2 sin^2 th) dth = -a_beta/(1 + B)^2 = -D;

the angular integral equals pi/(4 (1 + B)^2) (substitute u = tan th and use partial fractions for B != 1; at B = 1 it
is pi/16). For the gradient, |grad rho_beta|^2/a_beta^2 = exp(-2t) [(1 - 2s)^2 + 4 x^2 s/beta] <= exp(-2t) [1 + 4s
(t - 1)] since beta >= 1; for t <= 1 this is at most 1, and for t >= 1, s <= t bounds it by exp(-2t) (2t - 1)^2, whose
maximum on [1, inf) is 4 e^{-3} < 1 (at t = 3/2). So |grad rho_beta| <= a_beta, with equality only at 0. At x = 0,
y^2 = 1/(2 beta) the gradient vanishes while rho_beta > 0, so (c_l X + U) . grad rho - rho = -rho != 0 there for every
velocity. Also q_th = -2 (beta - 1) r^2 sin th cos th q <= 0, so P = 0 and the bound of (b) holds with equality.

(e) Proof. At c_l = 2 (A = 3, D = 1, a0 = 13) put H_3 = x^2 y + (7/6) y^3, V_3 = 6 x^2 y + (7/3) y^3 and phi_4 = 2 x^3
y + (7/3) x y^3. Then (3 x d_x + y d_y - 1) H_3 = V_3 = d_x phi_4 and Lap phi_4 = 26 x y = 13 d_x H_3, which are the
leading equations of 3.51(c) (with h_3 = -13 H_3); y H_3 = y^2 (x^2 + (7/6) y^2) >= 0, and q = 1 - r^2 (cos^2
th + (7/6) sin^2 th) + ... has q_th = -(1/3) r^2 sin th cos th + O(r^4); for rho = 13 (y - H_3), |grad
rho|^2/169 = 1 - 2 (H_3)_y + |grad H_3|^2 with (H_3)_y = x^2 + (7/2) y^2 >= r^2 and |grad H_3|^2 = x^4 + 11 x^2
y^2 + (49/4) y^4 <= (49/4) r^4, so |grad rho| < 13 for 0 < r < 2 sqrt2/7. At c_l = 19 (A = 37, D = 18, a0 = 2) put

    H_5 = x^4 y - (73/19) x^2 y^3 + (2701/380) y^5,   V_5 = 148 x^4 y - 292 x^2 y^3 + (2701/95) y^5,
    phi_6 = (148/5) x^5 y - (292/3) x^3 y^3 + (2701/95) x y^5.

Then (37 x d_x + y d_y - 1) H_5 = V_5 = d_x phi_6 and Lap phi_6 = 8 x^3 y - (292/19) x y^3 = 2 d_x H_5.
(H_5)_y = x^4 - (219/19) x^2 y^2 + (2701/76) y^4 has, as a quadratic in x^2/y^2, discriminant -3358/361 < 0, so
(H_5)_y > 0 off 0, (H_5)_y >= c r^4 with c > 0 by compactness of the circle, and y H_5 >= 0. For rho = 2 (y - H_5),
|grad rho|^2/4 = 1 - 2 (H_5)_y + |grad H_5|^2 < 1 on a punctured disc, since |grad H_5|^2 = O(r^8). With
psi = -18 x y + phi_6, S_22 = d_y U_2 = -18 + (V_5)_y and (V_5)_y(t, t) = -(11131/19) t^4 < 0, so |S|_op > D on the
diagonal near 0. For both pairs Poisson holds exactly while the full transport residual -a0 v . grad H_n (v = (-phi_y,
phi_x)) is a nonzero polynomial; the pairs are local jet solutions only (they have neither sublinear growth nor a
canonical velocity), so they refute the stated local implications and say nothing about global profiles.

Scope. (a) is a subclass theorem (the hypothesis q <= 1 is not known for exact profiles); (b) is conditional on a
bound on N; (c)-(e) are non-profiles or jets. The identities were checked by symbolic computation in the main
analysis.

## A.3.55 Compactness and the strain cap

Setup. K and the centred truncation are those of A.3.1(ii), U(X) = -rho(X) e_2/2 + PV int K(X - Y) rho(Y) dY, and (G)
denotes the common bound |rho_n| + (1 + r) |grad rho_n| <= C (1 + r)^gamma, 0 < gamma < 1. Since rho_n -> rho in C^1
on compact sets, rho satisfies (G). The construction, regularity and growth estimates of A.3.1 use only smoothness,
parity and the growth bound, so they apply also when rho_y(0) = 0.

(a) Proof. Fix M >= 1, |X| <= M, 0 < delta < 1 and T >= 2M + 2, and put g_n = rho_n - rho. As in A.3.1(ii), on |Y| > T
the kernel K(X - Y) may be replaced by K(X - Y) - K(-Y), since rho_n(-Y) = -rho_n(Y), K(-Y) = K(Y) and the truncation
is by centred discs; with |K(X - Y) - K(-Y)| <= C_K |X| |Y|^{-3} and (G) the exterior part is at most C M
T^{gamma-1}/(1 - gamma) for every n and for rho. On |Y - X| < delta, the zero circular mean of K allows the
subtraction of g_n(X), and this part is at most C delta sup_{B_{M+1}} |grad g_n|. The remaining bounded region is
nonsingular and contributes at most C(delta, T) sup_{B_T} |g_n|, and the contact term is |g_n(X)|/2. Hence limsup_n
sup_{|X| <= M} |U_n - U| <= C M T^{gamma-1}/(1 - gamma) for every T, so U_n -> U locally uniformly. The bound
|U| <= C' (1 + r)^gamma is A.3.1(iii) applied to rho. For the derivatives, d_j U = -d_j rho e_2/2 + PV int K(X - Y)
d_j rho(Y) dY: multiply rho by a smooth radial cutoff chi_T (equal to 1 on |Y| < T, 0 on |Y| > 2T, |grad
chi_T| <= 2/T); the commutator (PV K) * ((d_j chi_T) rho) is O(T^{gamma-1}) on compact sets, and the difference
between the truncated and full derivative integrals is bounded by C int_T^inf s^{gamma-2} ds, since |grad rho| <= C
r^{gamma-1} and |K| <= C r^{-2}. Near X subtract d_j rho_n(X); a common Dini modulus omega on B_{M+1} bounds this
inner part by C int_0^delta omega(s) ds/s uniformly in n, and the limit gradient has the same modulus. The bounded
annulus converges by C^1 convergence. Choosing delta and T first and then n gives DU_n -> DU locally uniformly.

(b) Proof. For a fixed unit vector v, v^T S v = v^T (DU) v = d_v (v . U). For phi >= 0 smooth with compact support,
integration by parts gives int phi v^T S_n v dX = -int (v . U_n)(v . grad phi) dX, which converges by (a) to the same
expression for U, that is to int phi v^T S v dX; no convergence of DU_n is used. The cap gives |int phi v^T S_n
v| <= (c_{l,n} - 1 + eps_n) int phi, hence |int phi v^T S v| <= (c_l - 1) int phi for every such phi. S is continuous
(rho is smooth, so U is smooth by A.3.1(ii)), so |v^T S(X) v| <= D at every X: a violation at one point would persist
on a neighbourhood and contradict a test function supported there. Taking v in a countable dense subset of the circle
and using continuity in v, |S(X)|_op = sup_{|v| = 1} |v^T S(X) v| <= D, since S(X) is symmetric. Both signs of the cap
are used. By (a) and C^1 convergence, R_n = (c_{l,n} X + U_n) . grad rho_n - rho_n -> (c_l X + U) . grad rho - rho
locally uniformly, so R_n -> 0 locally uniformly gives the exact equation; and rho_{n,y}(0) -> rho_y(0).

(c) Proof. Fix a nonnegative even C^inf function eta supported in [-b, b], b = 1/4, with int eta = 1. For L >= 1 put
f_L(t) = int_{-L}^0 eta(t - s) ds and q_L(r, th) = r sin(3 th) f_L(log(r/R0)), R0 = 1/8. Then 0 <= f_L <= 1,
f_L' = eta(t + L) - eta(t), q_L is smooth, even in x and odd in y, and supported in R0 e^{-L-b} <= r <= h0 := R0 e^b,
so it vanishes near 0. From d_r q_L = sin(3 th)(f_L + f_L') and r^{-1} d_th q_L = 3 cos(3 th) f_L its global C^1 norm
is bounded independently of L, and ||q_L||_{L^1} <= 4 h0^3/3. Since q_L vanishes near 0, the centre formula of 3.2
gives psi_xy(0) for q_L as c[q_L] = int_0^inf (q_L)_3(r) r^{-2} dr with (q_L)_3(r) = r f_L(log(r/R0)), so by Tonelli

    c[q_L] = int_R f_L(t) dt = int_{-L}^0 int_R eta(t - s) dt ds = L.

Put F_n(x, y) = (1/n) sum_{sigma, tau = +-1} tau q_{n^2}(sigma x - 3, tau y - 3). Relabelling sigma and tau shows that
F_n is even in x and odd in y; its four supports are disjoint discs of radius h0 < 1/5 centred at (+-3, +-3);
||F_n||_{C^1} = O(1/n) and ||F_n||_{L^1} <= 16 h0^3/(3n). The centre strain of a density vanishing near 0 is int H rho
dX with H = sin(3 th)/(pi r^3) (equivalent to the formula of 3.2 after the angular integration), so d_n := c[F_n]
satisfies |d_n| <= ||F_n||_{L^1}/(pi (3 sqrt2 - h0)^3) = O(1/n). Let J = r sin(3 th) eta(log r), supported in
e^{-b} <= r <= e^b, disjoint from the patches, with c[J] = int eta = 1, and let rho_0 = 4D y exp(-r^2), which has only
the sine mode 1, so c[rho_0] = -rho_{0,y}(0)/4 = -D. Then rho_n = rho_0 + F_n - d_n J has c[rho_n] = -D, agrees with
rho_0 on |X| < e^{-b} (so a0 = 4D and all its Taylor coefficients are those of rho_0), converges to rho_0 in global
C^1 at rate O(1/n), and satisfies (G) with constants independent of n for every gamma in (0, 1) (the perturbations are
bounded in C^1 with fixed compact support).

At P = (3, 3), S_22 = d_y U_2. Each patch is compactly supported, so its velocity is a classical convolution and
commutes with translations; the patch centred at P contributes (1/n) c[q_{n^2}] = n to d_y U_2(P). The other three
patches lie at distance at least 6 - h0 from P and the correction d_n J at distance at least 3 sqrt2 - e^b, where the
kernel of d_y U_2 is bounded; their L^1 norms are O(1/n), so they contribute O(1/n). Hence

    d_y U_2[rho_n](P) = d_y U_2[rho_0](P) + n + O(1/n),   |S_n(P)|_op >= |S_{n,22}(P)| -> inf.

The cubic coefficients are those of rho_0, b = e = -4D, with a0 = 4D and a0 - 2A = -2, so 6e - (a0 - 2A)
b = -24D - 8D = -32D != 0 and (T1) of 3.3 fails: no rho_n is a profile. (Common local C^2 bounds would give a common
Dini modulus, so by (a) they fail for this sequence.)

(d) Proof. Suppose a sequence of such pairs had d_R + E_S -> 0. The C^{k+1} bounds on B_{j+1} give equicontinuity of
all derivatives of order <= k on B_j, so Arzela-Ascoli and a diagonal extraction over k and j give rho_n -> rho in
C^inf_loc; extract also c_{l,n} -> c_l in [c_min, c_max]. The parities, (G), |a0| >= a_min and a0 <= 2A - eta pass to
the limit (a_n -> a0 by C^1 convergence). For each j, min(1, sup_{B_j} |R_n|) <= 2^j d_R -> 0, so R_n -> 0 uniformly
on B_j; and sigma_n <= c_{l,n} - 1 + E_S. By (a) and (b) the limit pair, with the canonical velocity, solves the
profile equation and has sigma <= c_l - 1. It lies in the primary class (smooth, the parities, rho_y(0) = a0 != 0, the
growth bound (G), canonical velocity with |U| <= C' (1 + r)^gamma), so 3.46 and 3.47(ii) give a0 >= 2A, contradicting
a0 <= 2A - eta. The constant depends on all the fixed bounds and no value is obtained; the statement is vacuous if the
class is empty.

Scope. (a)-(b) are statements about convergence of canonical pairs; (c) consists of non-profiles and fixes the density
on a neighbourhood of 0, not the velocity jets; (d) needs common bounds on every derivative, which no computation in
Section 4 supplies. The kernel identities and the cubic defect were checked by exact symbolic computation in the
external audit.

## A.3.56 First moment at the first degree under the one-sided sign

Setup. Notation of 3.47: a = a0, H = y - rho/a = -h/a, V = U_2 + D y = phi_x, W = c_l X + U and B = X . W/r^2. By
3.47(ii), exact transport and the Poisson equation give W . grad H - H = V and Lap V = a H_xx. Let n >= 3 be the first
degree of h (odd by parity; finite by 3.47(iv)) and H_n the first part of H.

Step 1 (behaviour at 0 and at infinity). By parity and the origin relation phi = psi + D x y = O(r^4), so W = (A x,
y) + O(r^3), W_2 = y + O(r^3) and B = 1 + (A - 1) x^2/r^2 + O(r^2). On r <= 1, H = H_n + O(r^{n+2}), and V = W . grad
H - H = V_n + O(r^{n+2}) with V_n = (A x d_x + y d_y - 1) H_n. For r >= 1, |H| <= |y| + |rho|/|a| <= C r and
|V| <= |U| + D r <= C r (U = o(r)); also |W| <= C r and |B| <= C.

Step 2 (convergence). Fix m with 2 < m < (n + 3)/2. Each of the integrands H y r^{-2m}, V y r^{-2m}, H y (x^2/r^2)
r^{-2m}, H y B r^{-2m} and H W_2 r^{-2m} is bounded by C r^{n+1-2m} on r <= 1 and by C r^{2-2m} on r >= 1; both
majorants are integrable in the plane exactly in this range of m. So I_m = int H y r^{-2m} dX and J_m = int V y
r^{-2m} dX converge absolutely, as do the integrals below. Since y H >= 0 is continuous and not identically 0 (h != 0,
because a y is not sublinear), I_m > 0.

Step 3 (Poisson test). Put F_m = y r^{2-2m}/(4 (m - 1)(m - 2)). For p = 2 - 2m, Lap(y r^p) = p (p + 2) y r^{p-2} and
d_xx(y r^p) = p y r^{p-2} (1 + (p - 2) x^2/r^2), so

    Lap F_m = y r^{-2m},   (F_m)_xx = y r^{-2m} (2m x^2/r^2 - 1)/(2 (m - 2)).

Let chi(X) = zeta(r/eps)(1 - zeta(r/R)), with zeta smooth, zeta = 0 on [0, 1] and zeta = 1 on [2, inf), 0 < 2 eps < R.
Then chi F_m is smooth with compact support away from 0, and int V Lap(chi F_m) = a int H d_xx(chi F_m). The terms in
which no derivative falls on chi are int chi V y r^{-2m} and (a/(2 (m - 2))) int chi H y r^{-2m} (2m x^2/r^2 - 1). In
the remaining terms, |grad chi| <= C/eps and |D^2 chi| <= C/eps^2 on eps < r < 2 eps, and the same with R on
R < r < 2R; F_m and grad F_m are homogeneous of degrees 3 - 2m and 2 - 2m. With |H|, |V| <= C r^n near 0 and <= C r
for r >= 1, these terms are bounded by C eps^{n+3-2m} + C R^{4-2m}, which tend to 0 as eps -> 0 and R -> inf. By
dominated convergence (Step 2)

    J_m = (a/(2 (m - 2))) int H y r^{-2m} (2m x^2/r^2 - 1) dX.                        (1)

Step 4 (transport test). Multiply W . grad H = H + V by chi y r^{-2m} and integrate by parts. Since div W = 2 c_l and
W . grad(y r^{-2m}) = W_2 r^{-2m} - 2m y B r^{-2m},

    -int chi H (2 c_l y + W_2 - 2m y B) r^{-2m} - int H y r^{-2m} W . grad chi
        = int chi (H + V) y r^{-2m}.

The term with grad chi is bounded by C eps^{n+3-2m} + C R^{4-2m} (|H| <= C r^n, |W| <= C r near 0; |H|, |W| <= C r at
infinity). Letting eps -> 0 and R -> inf,

    J_m = 2m int H y B r^{-2m} dX - (2 c_l + 1) I_m - int H W_2 r^{-2m} dX.             (2)

Step 5 (the endpoint m -> (n + 3)/2). Put delta = n + 3 - 2m and let m increase to (n + 3)/2 (so m >= (n + 2)/2 > 2
eventually). For a continuous function G on the circle, int_{r <= 1} G(om) r^{n+1-2m} dX = delta^{-1} int_0^{2 pi} G
dth. By Step 1, each integrand of Step 2 differs on r <= 1 from its leading part G(om) r^{n+1-2m} by at most C
r^{n+3-2m}, whose integral over r <= 1 is bounded uniformly in m; on r >= 1 the integrals are bounded uniformly for
m >= (n + 2)/2. Hence, with C_n and T_n as in 3.56,

    delta I_m -> C_n,   delta int H y (x^2/r^2) r^{-2m} dX -> C_n T_n,
    delta int H y B r^{-2m} dX -> C_n (1 + (A - 1) T_n),   delta int H W_2 r^{-2m} dX -> C_n.

Multiplying (1) and (2) by delta and passing to the limit (2 (m - 2) -> n - 1, 2m -> n + 3, 2 c_l + 2 = A + 3):

    lim delta J_m = a C_n ((n + 3) T_n - 1)/(n - 1),
    lim delta J_m = C_n [(n + 3)(1 + (A - 1) T_n) - (A + 3)] = C_n [n - A + (n + 3)(A - 1) T_n].

Step 6 (sign and conclusion). Dividing y H(r om) >= 0 by r^{n+1} and letting r -> 0 gives sin th H_n(om) >= 0. The
restriction of H_n to the circle is a nonzero trigonometric polynomial, so it has finitely many zeros, and sin th
H_n(om) is positive on an open arc that avoids the axes. Hence C_n > 0, and cos^2 th sin th H_n(om) and sin^2 th sin
th H_n(om) both have positive integrals, so 0 < T_n < 1. Dividing the two limits of Step 5 by C_n and putting
z = (n + 3) T_n - 1, the second becomes n - 1 + (A - 1) z, and equality gives

    [a - (n - 1)(A - 1)] z = (n - 1)^2,   -1 < z < n + 2.

If a - (n - 1)(A - 1) < 0 then z < 0, and z > -1 gives a - (n - 1)(A - 1) < -(n - 1)^2, that is a < (n - 1)(A - n). If
a - (n - 1)(A - 1) > 0 then z > 0, and z < n + 2 gives a - (n - 1)(A - 1) > (n - 1)^2/(n + 2). The value
a = (n - 1)(A - 1) is impossible. This proves 3.56.

Remarks. (i) The limits in Step 5 involve only H_n and V_n, and the identity holds for
every homogeneous solution of the leading equations V_n = (A x d_x + y d_y - 1) H_n, Lap V_n = a d_xx H_n, with no
sign assumption. Put f = H_n(om), g = V_n(om), C = int f sin th dth, M = int f cos^2 th sin th dth and L = int g sin
th dth (integrals over the circle). Polar differentiation gives g = [n - 1 + n (A - 1) cos^2 th] f - (A - 1) cos th
sin th f', and one integration by parts, with (cos th sin^2 th)' = 3 cos^2 th sin th - sin th, gives L = (n - A)
C + (n + 3)(A - 1) M. By homogeneity (Lap V_n)(om) = n^2 g + g'', so int (Lap V_n)(om) sin th dth = (n^2 - 1) L; and
(H_n)_xx(om) = n [(n - 1) cos^2 th + sin^2 th] f - 2 (n - 1) cos th sin th f' + sin^2 th f'', so one and two
integrations by parts, with (sin^3 th)'' = 9 cos^2 th sin th - 3 sin th, give int (H_n)_xx(om) sin th
dth = (n + 1)((n + 3) M - C). The Poisson equation therefore gives (n - 1) L = a ((n + 3) M - C), and comparison with
the first expression for L gives [a - (n - 1)(A - 1)]((n + 3) M - C) = (n - 1)^2 C, also when C = 0. (This argument
was proposed in an external audit; the formula for int (H_n)_xx(om) sin th dth was checked exactly on all monomials
x^{n-k} y^k of degrees 3 to 9.) So Steps 3-5 give a second, global proof, and the sign enters only through C_n > 0 and
0 < T_n < 1; since the sign condition P >= 0 of 3.51(c) implies these, the dichotomy follows from the leading
equations and P >= 0. For n = 3 with h_3 = b x^2 y + e y^3, C_3 = -(pi/(4a))(b + 3e) and (n + 3)
M_3 - C_3 = -(pi/(4a)) 2b, and the undivided identity reduces to 6e = (a0 - 2A) b, which is (T1) of 3.3. (ii) For
n = 7 and A = 10 (K = 3 in 3.51(c)), e_j = 6 + 18 j, and the inequalities a0 >= e_1 and prod_j (a0 - e_j) >= 0 listed
in 3.51(c) give 24 <= a0 <= 42 or a0 >= 60; the dichotomy requires a0 < 18 or a0 > 58, which removes [24, 42]. The
full condition P >= 0 is stronger than the listed inequalities: the normalized solution of the recurrence is
P(t) = t^3 + (5 (a0 - 60)/42) t^2 + ((a0 - 42)(a0 - 60)/336) t + (a0 - 24)(a0 - 42)(a0 - 60)/42336, and at a0 = 30 it
has P(1) = -71/49 < 0. (iii) No step uses a bound on derivatives of U beyond U = o(r) and the smoothness of rho; the
sign y H >= 0 is a hypothesis, not a property established for the primary class.

## A.3.57 The first sine projection of transport

Setup. rho is smooth with the parities and the growth bound |rho| + (1 + r)|grad rho| <= C (1 + r)^gamma,
0 < gamma < 1, of the primary class, U is its canonical velocity, a = a0 = rho_y(0) != 0 and psi_xy(0) = -D. Transport
is not assumed in (a). Put H = y - rho/a, phi = psi + D x y, v = (-phi_y, phi_x), V = v_2 = phi_x, mu = y H, G = V/y,
om = X/r, B = X . W/r^2, beta = X . v/r^2, R = W . grad rho - rho and R_1(r) = int_0^{2 pi} R(r, th) sin th dth. Since
psi is odd in x and in y, its Taylor series has only monomials x^{2i+1} y^{2j+1}, so phi = O(r^4) and V = O(r^3);
H = O(r^3) because rho is odd in y with rho_y(0) = a. So H, V = O(r^n) at 0 holds with n = 3, and we fix any integer
n >= 3 for which it holds. At infinity H, V, W = O(r) because U = o(r). G is smooth because V is odd in y.

Step 1 (three identities). Since U = (-psi_y, psi_x) = v + (D x, -D y), W_2 = c_l y + V - D y = y + V, and rho = a
(y - H) gives

    R = a (W_2 - W . grad H - y + H) = -a (W . grad H - H - V).

Next Lap phi = Lap psi = -rho_x = a H_x, so Lap V = a H_xx. Finally X . U = X . v + D (x^2 - y^2), so B = c_l + D (2
om_x^2 - 1) + beta = 1 + (A - 1) om_x^2 + beta, since c_l - D = 1 and 2D = A - 1.

Step 2 (the identity of (a)). Fix 2 < m < (n + 3)/2. The integrands mu r^{-2m}, mu om_x^2 r^{-2m}, mu B r^{-2m}, mu G
r^{-2m} = H V r^{-2m}, V y r^{-2m} and R y r^{-2m} are bounded by C r^{n+1-2m} on r <= 1 (R = O(r^n) there by Step 1)
and by C r^{2-2m} on r >= 1 (for R use |R| <= |W| |grad rho| + |rho| <= C r^gamma); both majorants are integrable in
the plane in this range of m. Step 3 of A.3.56 uses only Lap V = a H_xx and the bounds on H, V; it gives

    J_m := int V y r^{-2m} dX = (a/(2 (m - 2))) int mu r^{-2m} (2m om_x^2 - 1) dX.

Step 4 of A.3.56, applied to W . grad H - H - V = -R/a instead of W . grad H - H - V = 0, uses div W = 2 c_l and W .
grad(y r^{-2m}) = (W_2 - 2m y B) r^{-2m} and the same cutoffs (their errors are again O(eps^{n+3-2m} + R^{4-2m}),
using only value bounds on H and W). With W_2 = y + V and H V = mu G it gives

    -int mu r^{-2m} (2 c_l + 2 + G - 2m B) dX - J_m = -(1/a) int R y r^{-2m} dX.

Adding the two displays, and using 2 c_l + 2 = A + 3,

    int mu r^{-2m} Phi_m dX = (1/a) int R y r^{-2m} dX,
    Phi_m = a (2m om_x^2 - 1)/(2 (m - 2)) + A + 3 + G - 2m B.

In polar coordinates int R y r^{-2m} dX = int_0^inf R_1(r) r^{2-2m} dr.

Step 3 (equivalence with R_1 = 0). If R_1 = 0 identically the right side vanishes for every m. Conversely,
R_1 = O(r^n) at 0 and O(r^gamma) at infinity, so the Mellin transform M(z) = int_0^inf R_1(r) r^{z-1} dr converges
absolutely and is holomorphic on the strip -n < Re z < -gamma (differentiate under the integral; on a compact substrip
the logarithmic factors are bounded by nearby powers). The values z = 3 - 2m, 2 < m < (n + 3)/2, fill the interval
(-n, -1) of the real axis, so if they all vanish then M = 0 on the strip by the identity theorem. Fix a real z0 in the
strip. Then g(t) = R_1(e^t) e^{z0 t} is in L^1(R) and its Fourier transform, M(z0 - i xi), vanishes. Convolving g with
a centred Gaussian approximate identity gives 0 for every width (Fubini and Fourier inversion for the Gaussian), and
these convolutions converge to g in L^1, so g = 0 almost everywhere; R_1 is continuous on r > 0, hence R_1 = 0 at
every radius.

Step 4 (proof of (b)). Expanding B by Step 1, Phi_m = C(m) om_x^2 + d(m) + G - 2m beta with C(m) = a m/(m - 2) - 2m
(A - 1) and d(m) = -a/(2 (m - 2)) + A + 3 - 2m. If 0 < a < (n - 1)(A - 1), then m_* = 2 + a/(2 (A - 1)) satisfies
2 < m_* < (n + 3)/2; a/(m_* - 2) = 2 (A - 1) gives C(m_*) = 0, and
d(m_*) = -(A - 1) + (A - 1) - a/(A - 1) = -a/(A - 1). For an exact profile R = 0, so the identity of Step 2 at m = m_*
is the identity stated in (b).

Step 5 (proof of (c): the radial inverse). Let rho = y f(r). Restricting rho to the y-axis and dividing the odd smooth
restriction by y gives f(r) = a + O(r^2) and f'(r) = O(r) near 0; at infinity the growth bound gives
f = O(r^{gamma - 1}) and r f' = O(r^{gamma - 1}). Put J(r) = r^{-4} int_0^r t^3 f(t) dt = int_0^1 s^3 f(r s) ds; J is
smooth and radial, J(0) = a/4, r J' = f - 4J and J = O(r^{gamma - 1}) at infinity. Since rho_x = y f'(r) x/r = (r
f'/2) sin 2th and, for K = r^2 J = r^{-2} int_0^r t^3 f dt, K'' + K'/r - 4K/r^2 = r f' (direct differentiation), the
function psi = -(1/2) r^2 J sin 2th solves -Lap psi = rho_x. It is smooth, odd in x and in y, and its velocity
U_r = -psi_th/r = r J cos 2th, U_th = psi_r = r (J - f/2) sin 2th is O(r^gamma) = o(r); by uniqueness of the canonical
velocity (3.1) it is the canonical one. Near 0, psi = -J(0) x y + O(r^4), so psi_xy(0) = -a/4 and the normalization
psi_xy(0) = -D forces a = 4D > 0.

Step 6 (proof of (c): the projection and the ODE). With rho_r = (f + r f') sin th and rho_th/r = f cos th,

    R = c_l r (f + r f') sin th + r J cos 2th (f + r f') sin th + r (J - f/2) f sin 2th cos th - r f sin th,

and int sin^2 th = pi, int cos 2th sin^2 th = -pi/2, int sin 2th cos th sin th = pi/2 (over [0, 2 pi]) give

    R_1(r)/(pi r) = (c_l - J/2) r f' + D f - f^2/4.

Suppose R_1 = 0 for every r > 0 and write t = log r and a dot for d/dt. As t -> -inf, (f, J) -> (4D, D) and 4
c_l - 2J -> 2 c_l + 2 > 0, so on a half-line t <= t1

    f-dot = f (f - 4D)/(4 c_l - 2J),   J-dot = f - 4J.

Let k = 4D - f; then k = O(e^{2t}) as t -> -inf and k-dot = lambda(t) k with lambda(t) = f/(4
c_l - 2J) -> 2D/(c_l + 1) < 2. Choose 2D/(c_l + 1) < b < 2 and t0 <= t1 with lambda <= b on t <= t0. If k(t0) != 0,
then for t <= t0, |k(t)| = |k(t0)| exp(-int_t^{t0} lambda) >= |k(t0)| e^{b (t - t0)}, which contradicts k = O(e^{2t}).
So k(t0) = 0 and, by uniqueness for the scalar linear equation, f = 4D on t <= t0; then J-dot = 4D - 4J and
boundedness of J at -inf give J = D there. The right side of the system is smooth near (4D, D), where the denominator
is 2 c_l + 2 > 0; so the set of t where (f, J) = (4D, D) is open (local uniqueness) and closed (continuity), hence all
of R. Thus rho = 4D y, which is not sublinear. This contradiction shows that R_1 is not identically 0; by Step 3 the
family of (a) fails, and since an exact profile has R = 0, no density y f(r) is a profile.

Step 7 (proof of (d)). Let c_l = 2 (D = 1, A = 3, p = 1/2), 0 < eta < 1, f(r) = (1 + r^2)^{-1/4}, chi = r^2/(1 + r^2)
and rho = a y f (1 - eta y^2/(1 + r^2)). Then rho is smooth with the parities, and q = rho/(a y) = f (1 - eta
y^2/(1 + r^2)) satisfies 0 < (1 - eta) f <= q <= f <= 1. Its sine modes are b_1 = a r f (1 - 3 eta chi/4) and b_3 = a
eta r f chi/4 (from sin^3 th = (3 sin th - sin 3th)/4), so by the strain formula of 3.2,
c = psi_xy(0) = -a/4 + int_0^inf b_3 r^{-2} dr = -a/4 + (a eta/4) int_0^inf r (1 + r^2)^{-5/4} dr = -a/4 + a eta/2.
The first part of H is H_3 = y ((1/4) x^2 + (1/4 + eta) y^2), so (T1) of 3.3, 6 (1/4 + eta) = (a - 2A)/4, reads
a = 12 + 24 eta, and c = -D reads a = 4/(1 - 2 eta). Both hold for eta = 1/sqrt6 and a = 12 + 4 sqrt6
(4/(1 - 2/sqrt6) = 2 sqrt6 (sqrt6 + 2)). At infinity rho = a r^{1/2} Theta(th) + O(r^{-3/2}) with Theta = sin th
(1 - eta sin^2 th), and the canonical stream is psi = a r^{3/2} Phi(th) + O(r^{-1/2}) with Phi = P sin 2th + Q sin
4th, P = (5 eta - 2)/14, Q = -eta/44 (the homogeneous solution of -Lap psi = rho_x of degree 3/2 is unique, since R^2
minus the origin carries no nonzero harmonic function homogeneous of noninteger degree; the remainder bound comes from
the convergent mode-by-mode Green integrals of 3.1). Hence the polar velocity is a r^{1/2} (-Phi', (3/2)
Phi) + O(r^{-3/2}), the dilation part 2 r rho_r - rho of R is O(r^{-3/2}), and

    lim_{r -> inf} R_1(r) = a^2 int_0^{2 pi} (-(1/2) Phi' Theta + (3/2) Phi Theta') sin th dth
                          = -pi a^2 (2951 eta^2 - 3344 eta + 880)/4928.

At eta = 1/sqrt6 this is pi a^2 (3344 sqrt6 - 8231)/29568, which is negative because 8231^2 - 6 * 3344^2 = 655345 > 0.
The angular integral is a trigonometric polynomial integral; it was evaluated exactly in two ways (directly, and as a
polynomial in u = sin^2 th with int_0^{2 pi} u^k dth = 2 pi binom(2k, k)/4^k).

Scope. (a) holds for every canonical pair with the stated normalization and (b) whenever R_1 = 0, in particular for
exact profiles; (c) excludes the radial subclass rho = y f(r) only; at 0 its proof uses smoothness only through
f - a = O(r^sigma) for some sigma > 2D/(c_l + 1) (together with the regularity needed for the formulas of Steps 5 and
6); (d) shows that the one-sided sign, the centre normalization and (T1) do not imply R_1 = 0. None of these
statements bounds a0 for the primary class.

## A.3.58 Radial densities of finite regularity

Setup. rho = y f(r), J(r) = r^{-4} int_0^r s^3 f(s) ds, psi = -x y J, U = (-psi_y, psi_x), t = log r, a dot denotes r
d/dr = d/dt, so J-dot = f - 4J. Write R = (c_l X + U) . grad rho - rho.

Step 1 (inverse and residual, valid when f is C^1 on r > 0). Direct differentiation gives Lap psi + rho_x = -x y
(J'' + 5 J'/r - f'/r), which vanishes because r J' = f - 4J; so -Lap psi = rho_x on r > 0. The polar velocity is
U_r/r = J cos 2th, U_th/r = (J - f/2) sin 2th, and with rho_r = (f + f-dot) sin th, rho_th/r = f cos th,

    R/r = C1 sin th + C3 sin 3th,   C1 = (c_l - J/2) f-dot + D f - f^2/4,   C3 = J f + (J/2) f-dot - f^2/4

exactly (all other Fourier coefficients vanish), and R_1 = pi r C1. If rho is C^1 on the plane with f(0) = a, then
rho_y(0, r) = f + f-dot -> a forces f-dot -> 0, hence J -> a/4, J-dot -> 0 and (r d/dr)^2 J -> 0 as r -> 0. The second
derivatives of psi on r > 0 are combinations of J, J-dot and (r d/dr)^2 J with bounded angular coefficients and tend
to those of -(a/4) x y; since psi = O(r^2) and grad psi = O(r), psi is C^2 on the plane (a C^1 function that is C^2
off a point and whose second derivatives have limits there is C^2), U is C^1 with DU(0) = diag(a/4, -a/4), and the
Poisson equation holds at 0 by continuity. At infinity the growth bound on the y-axis gives f = O(r^{gamma - 1}),
hence J, J-dot = O(r^{gamma - 1}) and U = O(r^gamma). Two velocities with these parities, divergence and curl differ
by a harmonic field of sublinear growth, which is constant by interior gradient estimates and zero by parity; so U is
the canonical velocity. Dividing the transport equation on the y-axis by y and letting y -> 0 gives c_l - a/4 = 1, so
a = 4D and J(0) = D (this uses transport at the centre only and is the centre relation of 3.2).

Step 2 (proof of (i)). Under full transport C1 = C3 = 0 for every r > 0. On a small interval (0, r1), f > 0, J > 0 and
v := c_l - J > 0 (v -> 1). Subtracting C3 = 0 from C1 = 0 gives v f-dot + (D - J) f = 0, that is f-dot/f = (1 - v)/v
since J - D = 1 - v. The equation C3 = 0 gives f-dot/f = f/(2J) - 2; comparing, f = g(J) := 2J + 2J/(c_l - J), and
then J-dot = f - 4J = 2J (1 - v)/v. Differentiating f = g(J), with g'(J) = 2 + 2 c_l/v^2, gives f-dot = g'(J) J-dot,
and inserting f-dot = f (1 - v)/v and J-dot = 2J (1 - v)/v yields

    0 = ((1 - v)/v) (2 J g'(J) - f),   2 J g'(J) - f = 2J (v^2 - v + 2 c_l)/v^2 > 0,

since v^2 - v + 2 c_l = (v - 1/2)^2 + 2 c_l - 1/4 > 0. Hence v = 1, J = D and f = 4D on (0, r1). The equation C1 = 0
reads f-dot = f (f - 4D)/(4 c_l - 2J), J-dot = f - 4J wherever 4 c_l - 2J != 0; its right side is smooth near the
equilibrium (4D, D), where the denominator is 2 c_l + 2 > 0. The set of t where (f, J) = (4D, D) is nonempty, closed,
and open by local uniqueness, so it is all of R. Then rho = 4D y, which violates the growth bound with gamma < 1. Only
C^1 regularity of rho and of f on r > 0 was used.

Step 3 (construction for (ii)). Write a = 4D, d0 = 2 c_l + 2, so lambda = a/d0. With f = a - h and J = D - j the
system C1 = 0, J-dot = f - 4J becomes

    h-dot = lambda h + N(h, j),   j-dot = h - 4j,   N(h, j) = -h (h + 2 lambda j)/(d0 + 2j).

For t <= t0 put (Kh)(t) = int_{-inf}^t e^{-4(t - s)} h(s) ds and (Ph)(t) = C e^{lambda t} + int_{-inf}^t e^{lambda
(t - s)} N(h(s), (Kh)(s)) ds, on the closed set {h continuous : sup_{t <= t0} e^{-lambda t} |h - C e^{lambda
t}| <= C/2}. There h > 0 and Kh > 0, so d0 + 2Kh >= d0, and |N(h, Kh)| <= K1 C^2 e^{2 lambda t}, |N(h1, Kh1) - N(h2,
Kh2)| <= K1 C e^{2 lambda t} sup e^{-lambda t}|h1 - h2| with K1 depending only on c_l once C e^{lambda t0} <= 1.
Choosing t0 with K1 C e^{lambda t0}/lambda < 1/2, P maps the set into itself and is a contraction; its fixed point
solves the system (differentiate the integral equation), is smooth in t, and satisfies h = C e^{lambda t} + O(e^{2
lambda t}), j = C e^{lambda t}/(lambda + 4) + O(e^{2 lambda t}), with the same expansions after any fixed number of
t-derivatives (each nonlinear remainder has two factors of order e^{lambda t}). Uniqueness of the fixed point and the
scaling rho -> s rho(X/s), which maps f(r) to f(r/s) and C to C s^{-lambda}, show that the branches for different
C > 0 form one scale orbit.

Step 4 (global continuation and decay). For t near -inf the branch lies in the open triangle T = {0 < f < a,
f/4 < J < f/3, J < D}: J - f/4 = h/4 - j has positive leading term, J - f/3 -> -D/3 and j > 0. The vector field points
into T on its boundary: on J = f/4 the derivative of J - f/4 is -f-dot/4 > 0 (f-dot < 0 there since 0 < f < a); on
J = D, J-dot = f - a < 0; on J = f/3 put k = (a - f)/(4 c_l - 2J), so f-dot = -k f; there k < 1 (since a - f < 4
c_l - 2f/3 is equivalent to f/3 + 4 > 0) and the derivative of J - f/3 is f (k - 1)/3 < 0. In the closure of T, 4
c_l - 2J >= 2 c_l + 2 > 0, and f-dot = -k f keeps f > 0. So the solution exists for all t and stays in T; f and J
decrease, and f -> 0 (a positive limit below a would give a limiting f-dot < 0), hence J -> 0. Put q = J/f (a ratio of
this proof only), so 1/4 < q < 1/3, and

    q-dot = 1 - (4 - k) q,   k-dot = k (3f - 8J)/(4 c_l - 2J) > 0,   k_inf - k = f (c_l - 2Dq)/(c_l (4 c_l - 2J)) > 0,

with k_inf = D/c_l = 1 - p (in particular 0 < k < 1). Since k is eventually bounded below, f decays exponentially in
t, k_inf - k = O(f) is integrable, and integrating f-dot/f = -k gives f(t) e^{k_inf t} -> K in (0, inf) and f = K
r^{p - 1}(1 + O(r^{p - 1})). Boundedness of J at -inf gives J = int_{-inf}^t e^{-4(t - s)} f(s) ds, which is the
canonical integral, and f(t - u)/f(t) <= e^{k_inf u} with dominated convergence gives q -> 1/(3 + p). The equations
give the corresponding derivative bounds, so |rho| + (1 + r)|grad rho| <= C' (1 + r)^p, and Step 1 (applied with the
regularity of Step 6) identifies U as the canonical velocity, with psi_xy(0) = -J(0) = -D.

Step 5 (the sign of C3). C1 = 0 by construction, and C3 = f^2 (q (1 - k/2) - 1/4). Let E = 1/(4 - k) - q. Then
E-dot + (4 - k) E = k-dot/(4 - k)^2 > 0, E is bounded at -inf (q -> 1/4, k -> 0), and variation of constants from -inf
gives E(t) = int_{-inf}^t exp(-int_s^t (4 - k)) k-dot(s)/(4 - k(s))^2 ds > 0. Hence q < 1/(4 - k) and, as 0 < k < 1,

    C3/f^2 < (1 - k/2)/(4 - k) - 1/4 = -k/(4 (4 - k)) < 0

for every r > 0. Near 0, C3 = -D lambda (1 + lambda/2) C r^lambda/(4 + lambda) + O(r^{2 lambda}); at infinity
C3/f^2 -> (p - 1)/(4 (p + 3)).

Step 6 (regularity). The leading non-polynomial part of rho at 0 is -C y r^lambda, homogeneous of degree 1 + lambda
with smooth angular factor; its k-th derivatives are O(r^{1 + lambda - k}), which gives the stated Holder classes, and
the remainder is at least as regular by the derivative expansions of Step 3. On the y-axis rho(0, y) = a y - C y
|y|^lambda + O(|y|^{1 + 2 lambda}) and U_2(0, y) = -D y + (C/(lambda + 4)) y |y|^lambda + O(|y|^{1 + 2 lambda}), so
for lambda < 1 the second derivatives are unbounded, for lambda = 1 the one-sided second derivatives differ, and for
1 < lambda < 2 the third derivatives are unbounded, for rho and for U. Note lambda < 1 if and only if c_l < 3.

Step 7 (bounds). With k = -f-dot/f and q = J/f as above, |grad rho|^2 = f^2 ((1 - k)^2 sin^2 th + cos^2
th) <= f^2 < a^2 for r > 0. In the polar frame S = sym DU has S_rr = -S_thth = f (1 - 3q) cos 2th and S_rth = f
((2 + k)/4 - 3q) sin 2th (from S_rr = (J + J-dot) cos 2th and 2 S_rth = (-2J + J-dot - f-dot/2) sin 2th). With
s1 = 1 - 3q and s2 = 3q - 1/2 - k/4 one has 0 < s1 < 1/4 and (1 - k)/4 < s2 < 3/(4 - k) - 1/2 - k/4 < 1/4 (the last
difference from 1/4 is k (k - 1)/(4 (4 - k)) < 0), so ||S||_op^2 = f^2 (s1^2 cos^2 2th + s2^2 sin^2
2th) < f^2/16 < D^2 for r > 0, and S(0) = diag(D, -D). Since U is C^1, integrating sym DW = c_l I + S along segments
gives (W(X) - W(Y)) . (X - Y) >= (c_l - D)|X - Y|^2 = |X - Y|^2. Finally q_rho = rho/(a y) = f/a lies in (0, 1) for
r > 0.

Step 8 (the moment identities). H = y - rho/a and V = U_2 + D y are O(r^{1 + lambda}) with gradients O(r^lambda) at 0
and are smooth off 0; at infinity H, V, W = O(r) and grad H = O(1). With w_m = y r^{-2m}, R/a = V + H - W . grad H and
div W = 2 c_l, integration over eps < r < L and one integration by parts give

    int [w_m V + (2 c_l + 1) w_m H + H W . grad w_m] dX = (1/a) int w_m R dX
                                                         = (1/a) int_0^inf R_1(r) r^{2 - 2m} dr = 0

for 2 < m < 2 + lambda/2: every volume integrand is O(r^{2 + lambda - 2m}) near 0 and O(r^{2 - 2m}) at infinity, and
the boundary terms are O(eps^{4 + lambda - 2m}) and O(L^{4 - 2m}). Steps 2-3 of A.3.57 apply in the same way with n
replaced by 1 + lambda (they use only these bounds and the smoothness off 0), so the identities of 3.57(a) hold on
this interval. A boundary-free radial form: with A0 = c_l - J/2 and h = a - f, C1 = 0 gives A0 h-dot = f h/4, and
A0-dot = -(f - 4J)/2, so d/dt (e^{(4 - 2m) t} A0 h) = e^{(4 - 2m) t} h ((4 - 2m) c_l + m J - f/4); the differentiated
quantity tends to 0 at both ends exactly for 2 < m < 2 + lambda/2 (by the asymptotics of Steps 3-4), which gives
int_0^inf r^{3 - 2m} h ((4 - 2m) c_l + m J - f/4) dr = 0 there (at m = 2 + lambda/2 the inner boundary value is C
(c_l + 1)/2 != 0, at m = 2 the outer one is a c_l != 0).

Scope. (i) needs full transport; (ii) gives non-profiles with R_1 = 0 at every radius and R_3 != 0 at every radius.
Neither statement concerns nonradial densities, whose higher angular modes couple into every projection.

## A.3.59 One-sided projected equations

Setup. rho is smooth with the parities, a = a0 = rho_y(0) != 0 and the growth bound |rho| + (1 + r)|grad rho| <= C
(1 + r)^gamma, 0 < gamma < 1; U is its canonical velocity and psi_xy(0) = -D. Put h = rho - a y, H = -h/a, mu = y H,
phi = psi + D x y, V = phi_x = U_2 + D y, W = c_l X + U = (A x - phi_y, y + V), R = W . grad rho - rho, B = X . W/r^2,
G = V/y, om = X/r, beta = X . (-phi_y, V)/r^2, so that B = 1 + (A - 1) om_x^2 + beta. As in A.3.57, phi = O(r^4),
V = O(r^3), G, beta = O(r^2) at 0, and H, V, W = O(r), beta = O(1) at infinity. The one-sided sign is mu >= 0. Density
modes are b_k(r) = (1/pi) int_0^{2 pi} rho sin k th dth (odd k), and R_k(r) = int_0^{2 pi} R sin k th dth. Transport
is not assumed.

Step 1 (the canonical first mode of V). By 3.1(iv) the stream mode of even frequency k is P_k(r) sin k th with

    P_k(r) = (1/2) [r^k int_r^inf b_{k+1}(s) s^{-k} ds - r^{-k} int_0^r b_{k-1}(s) s^k ds],

which gives psi_xy(0) = -a/4 + int_0^inf b_3 s^{-2} ds (3.2). Only k = 2 contributes to v_1(r) = (1/pi) int V sin th
dth, and differentiation gives

    v_1(r) = r int_r^inf b_3(s) s^{-2} ds - (b_1(r) + b_3(r))/4 + D r.

The normalization cancels the linear term at 0. Hence, if h = O(r^n) with the corresponding Taylor bounds on its
derivatives (n >= 3, the first degree of h), then v_1 = O(r^n) and v_1' = O(r^{n-1}); if h is flat at 0, so is v_1; at
infinity v_1 = O(r) and v_1' = O(1). This does not say that V itself is O(r^n): interior harmonic stream terms r^{2j}
sin 2j th (j >= 2) may remain.

Step 2 (the two moment tests under R_1 = 0). Let n be the first degree of h and 2 < m < (n + 3)/2. Put I_m = int mu
r^{-2m} dX, L_m = int mu om_x^2 r^{-2m} dX (absolutely convergent: mu = O(r^{n+1}) at 0, O(r^2) at infinity) and
J_m = pi int_0^inf v_1(r) r^{2-2m} dr (absolutely convergent by Step 1). With f = y r^{2-2m} one has Lap f = 4
(m - 1)(m - 2) y r^{-2m} and f_xx = 2 (m - 1) y r^{-2m} (2m om_x^2 - 1). Testing Lap V = a H_xx (A.3.57 Step 1)
against f on eps < r < L and integrating by parts twice gives

    J_m = a (2m L_m - I_m)/(2 (m - 2)).

On each circle the boundary terms involving V pair V and V_r with sin th only, so they are pi (3 - 2m) r^{3-2m} v_1
and -pi r^{3-2m} r v_1' at r = eps, L, which are O(eps^{n+3-2m}) and O(L^{4-2m}) by Step 1; those involving H, H_x
have the same orders by Taylor expansion and the growth bound. Testing W . grad H - H - V = -R/a against w = y
r^{-2m}, with div W = 2 c_l and W . grad w = (W_2 - 2m y B) r^{-2m}, and using int R w dX = int_0^inf R_1 r^{2-2m}
dr = 0, gives (boundary terms O(eps^{n+3-2m} + L^{4-2m}) from H w W . n)

    J_m = 2m int mu B r^{-2m} dX - (2 c_l + 1) I_m - int H W_2 r^{-2m} dX,

where int V w dX is taken with angular integration first, which is J_m. Since W_2 = y + V and H V = mu G, and the
integral of H V r^{-2m} converges absolutely (H V = O(r^{n+3}) at 0, O(r^2) at infinity), adding the two displays
gives

    int mu r^{-2m} [a (2m om_x^2 - 1)/(2 (m - 2)) + A + 3 + G - 2m B] dX = 0.

This is the identity of 3.57(a) with R_1 = 0, now justified up to m < (n + 3)/2 without any assumption on the order of
V beyond V = O(r^3).

Step 3 (the endpoint). Write H_n for the first nonzero Taylor term of H, C_n = int_0^{2 pi} H_n(om) sin th dth and
T_n = C_n^{-1} int_0^{2 pi} cos^2 th H_n(om) sin th dth. The leading term of mu is r^{n+1} H_n(om) sin th, so H_n(om)
sin th >= 0, and it is positive on an open set (H_n is a nonzero polynomial); hence C_n > 0 and 0 < T_n < 1. Splitting
the radial integrals at r = 1 gives (n + 3 - 2m) I_m -> C_n and L_m/I_m -> T_n as m increases to m_n = (n + 3)/2,
while int mu G r^{-2m} and int mu beta r^{-2m} stay bounded (two extra powers of r at 0, integrable tails).
Multiplying the identity of Step 2 by n + 3 - 2m, inserting B = 1 + (A - 1) om_x^2 + beta and letting m -> m_n gives a
((n + 3) T_n - 1)/(n - 1) + A + 3 - (n + 3) - (n + 3)(A - 1) T_n = 0, that is, with z = (n + 3) T_n - 1 in (-1,
n + 2),

    [a - (n - 1)(A - 1)] z = (n - 1)^2.

This is the relation of 3.56, here obtained from R_1 = 0 alone.

Step 4 (proof of (i)). Put N = n - 1 >= 2, so a = N (A - 1) + N^2/z and z != 0. If n = 3, H_3 = y (alpha x^2 + beta'
y^2) with alpha, beta' >= 0 not both 0 (mu = y^2 (alpha x^2 + beta' y^2) + O(r^6) >= 0), and the circle integrals int
sin^2 cos^2 = pi/4, int sin^4 = 3 pi/4, int sin^2 cos^4 = int sin^4 cos^2 = pi/8 give T_3 = (alpha + beta')/(2
(alpha + 3 beta')) and z = 2 alpha/(alpha + 3 beta'); z != 0 forces alpha > 0, so 0 < z <= 2 and a >= 2
(A - 1) + 2 = 2A, with equality exactly when beta' = 0. (This case uses neither a > 0 nor c_l <= 5.) Let n >= 5. If
z > 0, then z < n + 2 = N + 3 and a > N (A - 1) + N^2/(N + 3); since A > 1 and N >= 4, N (A - 1) - 2A = (N - 2)
