A - N > -2, so a - 2A > N^2/(N + 3) - 2 >= 16/7 - 2 > 0. If z < 0, then z > -1 gives a < N (A - 1) - N^2 = N (A - n);
for n >= 9 this is < 0, because c_l <= 5 gives A <= 9 <= n, contradicting a > 0. For n = 5, 7 write H_n(om) sin
th = sin^2 th P(cos^2 th), where P has degree at most K = (n - 1)/2 <= 3 and P >= 0 on [0, 1] (H_n = y Q(x^2, y^2)
with Q homogeneous). With u = cos^2 th = (1 + cos phi)/2, phi = 2 th, and g(phi) = (1 - u) P(u), one has T_n = int u g
dphi/int g dphi over a period, and g, u g are trigonometric polynomials in phi of degree at most K + 1 <= 4 and
K + 2 <= 5. The six-point rule at phi_j = (2j + 1) pi/6, j = 0, ..., 5, integrates trigonometric polynomials of
degree <= 5 exactly (the sums of e^{i k phi_j} vanish for 1 <= |k| <= 5), so T_n = sum u_j g_j/sum g_j with g_j >= 0,
a weighted average of the values u_j in {(2 - sqrt3)/4, 1/2, (2 + sqrt3)/4}. Hence T_n >= (2 - sqrt3)/4 > 1/16
(squaring 7 > 4 sqrt3 gives 49 > 48). For n = 5, z = 8 T_5 - 1 in (-1/2, 0) and a < 4 (A - 1) - 32 = 4A - 36 <= 0; for
n = 7, z = 10 T_7 - 1 in (-3/8, 0) and a < 6 (A - 1) - 96 = 6A - 102 < 0. Both contradict a > 0.

Step 5 (proof of (ii)). If mu = 0 everywhere, then rho = a y, which is not sublinear; so r_* < inf. Flatness of h and
Step 1 make all inner boundary terms of Step 2 vanish for every m > 2, so the two displays of Step 2 hold for every
m > 2. Since mu >= 0 and 0 <= om_x^2 <= 1, 0 < L_m < I_m, hence J_m/I_m <= a (2m - 1)/(2 (m - 2)) if a > 0 and
J_m/I_m <= |a|/(2 (m - 2)) if a < 0; in both cases J_m/I_m is bounded above as m -> inf. Suppose there are R > r_* and
b0 > 0 with B >= b0 on the support of mu in r < R. Choose r_* < r0 < R with c0 = int_{r < r0} mu dX > 0, so I_m >= c0
r0^{-2m}. On r < R, W_2/y is smooth (W_2 is odd in y) and bounded by some C_R, so int_{r<R} H W_2 r^{-2m} = int_{r<R}
mu (W_2/y) r^{-2m} <= C_R I_m. On r >= R, mu, mu B and H W_2 are O(r^2), so their weighted integrals are
O(R^{4-2m}/(2m - 4)), which divided by I_m and multiplied by 2m tend to 0 because r0 < R. The transport display then
gives J_m/I_m >= 2m b0 - (2 c_l + 1) - C_R - o(1) -> inf, a contradiction. If r_* = 0 this situation occurs with any
small R, since B = 1 + (A - 1) om_x^2 + O(r^2) >= 1/2 near 0; hence r_* > 0. If B > 0 on the circle r = r_*,
compactness gives B >= b0 > 0 on r_* <= r < R for some R > r_*, and mu = 0 on r < r_*; this is the same situation.
Hence min over r = r_* of B is <= 0, and since B = c_l + X . U/r^2, sup (-X . U/r^2) >= c_l. In r < r_*, mu = 0 gives
H = 0 off y = 0 and so everywhere by continuity: rho = a y there. Finally U(0) = 0 by parity, so -X . U(X) = -int_0^1
X . DU(t X) X dt <= sigma r^2 with sigma = sup ||sym DU||_op (the antisymmetric part has zero quadratic form);
sigma <= D < c_l would contradict sup (-X . U/r^2) >= c_l.

Step 6 (proof of (iii)). If h were flat, Step 5 would give rho = a y on r < r_*, so b_1 = a r and b_k = 0 (k >= 3)
there. In the formula of Step 1, for r < r_*: P_k = 0 for k >= 2N + 2 (both b_{k-1}, b_{k+1} vanish identically for
k >= 2N + 4, and b_{2N+1} = 0 on the disc for k = 2N + 2); for 4 <= k <= 2N, P_k = p_k r^k with p_k = (1/2)
int_{r_*}^inf b_{k+1} s^{-k} ds; and P_2 = (r^2/2)(int_0^inf b_3 s^{-2} ds - a/4) = -D r^2/2. So
psi = -D x y + sum_{j=2}^N p_{2j} r^{2j} sin 2j th on the disc. There R = a W_2 - a y = a V, and since d_x Im
z^{2j} = 2j Im z^{2j-1}, R = a sum_{j=2}^N 2j p_{2j} r^{2j-1} sin (2j - 1) th, so R_{2j-1} = 2 pi a j p_{2j} r^{2j-1}
on the disc. The hypotheses R_3 = ... = R_{2N-1} = 0 give p_{2j} = 0 for 2 <= j <= N, so W = (A x, y) and
B = 1 + (A - 1) om_x^2 >= 1 on the disc, hence on its boundary by continuity, contradicting Step 5. For N = 1 the sum
is empty and only R_1 = 0 is used.

Step 7 (proof of (iv)). By (iii), h is not flat; let n = N + 1 (N >= 2 even) be its first degree and b_1 = a r + alpha
r^{N+1} + O(r^{N+3}), b_3 = beta r^{N+1} + O(r^{N+3}). Then C_n = -pi alpha/a > 0, so alpha/a < 0, and with
lambda = beta/alpha the leading term of mu is a positive multiple of r^{N+2} sin^2 th (1 + lambda (4 cos^2 th - 1))
(from sin 3th = sin th (4 cos^2 th - 1)), so -1/3 <= lambda <= 1. The formula of Step 1 gives

    P_2 = -(D/2) r^2 - (1/2)(alpha/(N + 4) + beta/N) r^{N+2} + O(r^{N+4}),
    P_4 = -beta r^{N+2}/(2 (N + 6)) + O(r^{N+4}),

and P_k = 0 for k >= 6. With U_r = -psi_th/r and U_th = psi_r, the coefficients of r^{N+1} in R_1/pi and R_3/pi,
multiplied by 4, are the two rows of

    [ N (A + 3) - a              (N + 4)(A - 1 - a/N)   ] [alpha]
    [ N (A - 1 - a/(N + 4))      2 ((N + 1) A + N - 1 - a) ] [beta ]  = 0

(products of two remainders are of higher order). Put E = A - 1 > 0 and d = 1 + (N + 4) lambda/N, so
(2N - 4)/(3N) <= d <= 2 + 4/N. The first row divided by N alpha reads (E - a/N) d + 4 = 0; so d != 0, hence d > 0, and
a = N (E + 4/d) > 0. Substituting a and lambda = N (d - 1)/(N + 4) into the second row divided by alpha gives
(2N/(N + 4)) [E (d + 1) + 2N (d - 3 + 1/d)] = 0, that is E/N = F(d) := 2 (-d^2 + 3d - 1)/(d (d + 1)). As E > 0,
delta < d < (3 + sqrt5)/2 with delta = (3 - sqrt5)/2. If N <= 6, a < 6E + 24/delta = 6E + 36 + 12
sqrt5 < 6E + 64 < (3E + 8)(E + 8) (sqrt5 < 7/3). If N >= 8, F' = -2 (4d^2 - 2d - 1)/(d^2 (d + 1)^2) has the single
positive zero (1 + sqrt5)/4, a maximum, and the allowed interval [L_N, T_N], L_N = (2N - 4)/(3N) in [1/2, 2/3),
T_N = 2 + 4/N in (2, 5/2], contains it; F(L_N) >= F(1/2) = 2/3 and F(T_N) <= F(2) = 1/3, so F(d) >= F(T_N) and E >= N
F(T_N) = N (N^2 - 4N - 16)/((N + 2)(3N + 4)) = N/3 - 22/9 + 4 (13N + 44)/(9 (N + 2)(3N + 4)) > N/3 - 22/9. Thus
N < 3E + 22/3 and, as d >= 1/2, a <= N (E + 8) < (3E + 22/3)(E + 8) < (3E + 8)(E + 8). Since 3E + 8 = 3A + 5 = 2 (3
c_l + 1) and E + 8 = A + 7 = 2 (c_l + 3), a < 4 (3 c_l + 1)(c_l + 3). The matrix, the reduction of the second row and
the values of F were checked symbolically (the matrix for N = 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 from the angular products directly).

Scope. All four statements are necessary conditions on projected equations under the one-sided sign, and the theorem
makes no existence assertion; the densities of 3.61 satisfy the hypotheses of (i) when 1 < c_l <= 5, and of (iii) with
N = 1. (iv) is restricted to densities with the two modes 1 and 3 on the whole plane and is not uniform in c_l; adding
the mode 5 changes the second row and the elimination fails, and with the mode 5 present only outside a disc,
R_1 = R_3 = 0 on the disc and the one-sided sign do not bound a0 (3.63). Interior harmonic stream terms r^{2j} sin 2j
th, j >= 2, which a single projection does not remove, are why (iii) needs finitely many modes. Nothing here bounds a0
from above for densities with unrestricted angular content or excludes the full primary class.

## A.3.60 No elliptical profiles

Setting. Let rho = a0 y F(alpha x^2 + beta y^2) be an exact profile of the primary class with exponent gamma, where
alpha, beta > 0, F is in C^inf([0, inf)) and F(0) = 1, so rho_y(0) = a0 != 0. Put delta = (1 - gamma)/2, which lies in
(0, 1/2), and k = a0 alpha/2; D = c_l - 1 and A = 2D + 1 as in Section 2. In this entry w, nu, lam, J and M are local
notation, and C, c denote constants that may depend on the profile, alpha and beta.

Step 1 (decay of F). On the positive y-axis, with s = beta y^2, rho(0, y) = a0 y F(s) and rho_y(0, y) = a0 (F(s) + 2 s
F'(s)). For y >= 1 the growth bound gives |a0| y |F(s)| <= C y^gamma and |a0| |F(s) + 2 s F'(s)| <= C y^{gamma - 1},
so |F(s)| + |F(s) + 2 s F'(s)| <= C s^{-delta} for s >= beta. With smoothness on [0, beta],
    |F(s)| + s |F'(s)| <= C (1 + s)^{-delta}   (s >= 0),   (1)
and in particular F(s) -> 0 as s -> inf.

Step 2 (the canonical stream). For t >= 0 let a_t = alpha/(1 + alpha t), b_t = beta/(1 + beta t), s_t = a_t x^2 + b_t
y^2 and omega(t) = (1 + alpha t)^{-3/2} (1 + beta t)^{-3/2}, and define
    psi(x, y) = -k x y int_0^inf F(s_t) omega(t) dt.   (2)
On each compact set of X the numbers s_t lie in a fixed compact interval and omega = O((1 + t)^{-3}), so (2) and all
its Cartesian derivatives converge locally uniformly; psi is smooth and odd in x and in y. Direct differentiation
gives Lap[x y F(s_t)] = x y [6 (a_t + b_t) F'(s_t) + 4 (a_t^2 x^2 + b_t^2 y^2) F''(s_t)], and since d_t a_t = -a_t^2,
d_t b_t = -b_t^2 and d_t omega = -(3/2)(a_t + b_t) omega,
    omega Lap[x y F(s_t)] = -4 x y d_t[F'(s_t) omega].
As t -> inf, s_t -> 0 and omega -> 0, so F'(s_t) omega -> 0, while at t = 0 it equals F'(alpha x^2 + beta y^2). Hence
Lap psi = -4 k x y F'(alpha x^2 + beta y^2) = -2 a0 alpha x y F'(alpha x^2 + beta y^2) = -rho_x. Growth: there are c,
C > 0 with c r^2/(1 + t) <= s_t <= C r^2/(1 + t), omega <= C (1 + t)^{-3} and |grad s_t| <= C r/(1 + t). By (1),
|grad(x y)| |F(s_t)| <= C r (1 + s_t)^{-delta} and |x y F'(s_t) grad s_t| <= C r s_t |F'(s_t)| <= C r
(1 + s_t)^{-delta}, so
    |grad psi| <= C r int_0^inf (1 + t)^{-3} (1 + c r^2/(1 + t))^{-delta} dt.
For r >= 1 split at 1 + t = r^2: the part 1 + t <= r^2 is at most C r^{1 - 2 delta} int_1^{r^2} u^{delta - 3} du <= C
r^{1 - 2 delta}, and the rest is at most C r int_{r^2}^inf u^{-3} du = O(r^{-3}). So |U| <= C r^{1 - 2 delta} = C
r^gamma = o(r); U = (-psi_y, psi_x) has the parities of Section 2, and by the uniqueness in 3.1(i) it is the canonical
velocity.

Step 3 (centre normalization; the non-flat case). Let I_K = int_0^inf (1 + alpha t)^{-K} omega(t) dt for K >= 0; then
I_0 > 0 and 0 < I_K < I_0 for K >= 1. From (2), c = psi_xy(0) = -k I_0, and by 3.2 (a0 != 0) c_l + c = 1, so
    k I_0 = D;   in particular k > 0 and a0 > 0.   (3)
Suppose that F - 1 is not flat at 0: F(s) = 1 + f_K s^K + O(s^{K + 1}) with f_K != 0 and an integer K >= 1. Then
h = rho - a0 y = a0 f_K y (alpha x^2 + beta y^2)^K + O(r^{2K + 3}), whose coefficient of x^{2K} y is a0 f_K alpha^K.
On bounded sets of X, |F(s_t) - 1 - f_K s_t^K| <= C r^{2K + 2} uniformly in t (since s_t <= C r^2), so
psi - c x y = -k f_K x y int_0^inf s_t^K omega dt + O(r^{2K + 4}), and its homogeneous part P of degree 2K + 2 has the
coefficient -k f_K alpha^K I_K at x^{2K + 1} y. By 3.2 the linear part of W is (A x, y), and the products of nonlinear
velocity terms with nonlinear density terms have degree >= 4K + 1, so the degree-(2K + 1) part of transport is
    (A x d_x + y d_y - 1) h_{2K+1} + a0 d_x P = 0.
The coefficient of x^{2K} y gives 2KA a0 f_K alpha^K - (2K + 1) a0 k f_K alpha^K I_K = 0, so by (3)
    2KA = k (2K + 1) I_K = D (2K + 1) I_K/I_0 < D (2K + 1).
But 2KA - D (2K + 1) = (2K - 1) D + 2K > 0, a contradiction; the sign of f_K is not used. Hence F - 1 is flat at 0.

Step 4 (the axis equation). Put z = alpha x^2 and substitute u = (1 + alpha t)^{-1} in (2). With
lam(u) = beta + (alpha - beta) u, which is positive on [0, 1], let
    w(u) = sqrt(alpha) u lam(u)^{-3/2},     J(z) = int_0^1 F(z u) w(u) du.
Then omega dt = w(u) du, s_t = z u on y = 0, w >= 0 is smooth on [0, 1], w(0) = 0, w(1) = 1/alpha and int_0^1 w
du = I_0. Differentiating (2), U_1(x, 0) = -psi_y(x, 0) = k x J(z) and d_y U_2(x, 0) = psi_xy(x, 0) = -k (J(z) + 2 z
J'(z)). Differentiate transport W . grad rho = rho in y and restrict to y = 0, where rho_x = 0 and W_2 = 0: W_1
rho_xy + (d_y W_2 - 1) rho_y = 0. With rho_y(x, 0) = a0 F(z), rho_xy(x, 0) = 2 a0 alpha x F'(z), W_1(x,
0) = x (c_l + k J) and d_y W_2(x, 0) = c_l - k (J + 2 z J'), this is, for z > 0,
    2 z (c_l + k J) F' + (D - k J - 2 k z J') F = 0.
Let g = F - 1 and J_g(z) = int_0^1 g(z u) w(u) du, so that J = I_0 + J_g. By (3), c_l + k J = A + k J_g and D - k
J - 2 k z J' = -k (J_g + 2 z J_g'), hence
    2 z (A + k J_g) g' = k (1 + g)(J_g + 2 z J_g').   (4)
Since 2 z J_g'(z) = 2 int_0^1 u w(u) d_u[g(z u)] du and u w(u) = O(u^2) at 0, integration by parts gives
    J_g + 2 z J_g' = 2 w(1) g(z) + int_0^1 nu(u) g(z u) du,   (5)
    nu = w - 2 (u w)' = -3 sqrt(alpha) beta u lam(u)^{-5/2}.
Put C_w = 2 w(1) + int_0^1 |nu| du, which is finite.

Step 5 (the flat case). Choose r0 > 0 with |g| <= 1 on [0, r0]. Then |k J_g| <= k I_0 = D there, so |A + k
J_g| >= A - D = D + 1 > A/2, and (4), (5) give, with M(z) = sup_{[0, z]} |g| and C = 2 k C_w/A,
    |g'(z)| <= C M(z)/z   (0 < z <= r0).   (6)
Fix an integer N > C. Since g is flat at 0, B_N = sup_{0 < z <= r0} |g(z)| z^{-N} is finite (Taylor's formula with
integral remainder), and M(s) <= B_N s^N. Integrating (6) from 0 (g(0) = 0) gives |g(z)| <= C B_N int_0^z s^{N - 1}
ds = (C/N) B_N z^N, so B_N <= (C/N) B_N and B_N = 0: g = 0 on [0, r0]. Propagation: let Z = sup{z : g = 0 on [0,
z]} >= r0 and suppose Z < inf. By continuity there is eps > 0 with |g| <= 1 on [0, Z + eps], so again |A + k
J_g| > A/2 there. For Z <= z <= Z + eps, g(z u) = 0 when z u <= Z, so by (5) |J_g + 2 z J_g'| <= C_w M_Z(z) with
M_Z(z) = sup_{[Z, z]} |g|, and (4) gives |g'(z)| <= (C/Z) M_Z(z). Integrating from Z and taking the supremum,
M_Z(z) <= (C/Z) P(z) with P(z) = int_Z^z M_Z(s) ds. P is C^1 (M_Z is continuous), P(Z) = 0, P >= 0 and P' <= (C/Z) P,
so (exp(-C (z - Z)/Z) P)' <= 0 and P = 0 on [Z, Z + eps]. Then g = 0 on [0, Z + eps], contradicting the choice of Z.
Hence g = 0 on [0, inf) and F = 1, which contradicts F(s) -> 0 from (1). Both cases are impossible.

Scope. The excluded class is the family of shapes with q = rho/(a0 y) = F(alpha x^2 + beta y^2); alpha = beta is the
radial case of 3.57(c). The proof uses the explicit inverse (2) and does not extend to general angular content; it
does not exclude the full primary class.

## A.3.61 The first projection and the one-sided sign do not bound the slope

Setting. Fix c_l > 1 and an integer n >= 0, and put nu = 2n + 3/2, a0 = 4 (c_l + 1) nu = (8n + 6)(c_l + 1),
D = c_l - 1, A = 2 c_l - 1, M = a0/4 - D and L0 = (c_l + 1)/2; then M - L0 = 2 + 2n (c_l + 1) > 0. Let 0 < eps <= 1/4.
Write t = log r, z = r^2, and a dot for d/dt = r d/dr. In this entry f, g, T, J, K, L, N, S, w, Z, Y, d, F1 and the
constants below are local notation; R = (c_l X + U) . grad rho - rho and R_k(r) = int_0^{2 pi} R sin k th dth.

Step 1 (the ansatz, the stream and the projection). Let
    T = M (1 + z)^{-eps},   g = -T-dot = 2 eps M z (1 + z)^{-eps - 1},   K = r^{-6} int_0^r s^5 g(s) ds,
and, for a function f still to be chosen with f(0) = a0, let J = r^{-4} int_0^r s^3 f(s) ds and
    rho = r f sin th + r g sin 3th,   psi = (1/2) r^2 (T - J) sin 2th - (1/2) r^2 K sin 4th.
Then T-dot = -g, J-dot = f - 4 J and K-dot = g - 6 K. With rho_x = (1/2)(f-dot + g-dot + 4 g) sin
2th + (1/2)(g-dot - 2 g) sin 4th and -Lap(r^2 V sin m th) = -(V-dot-dot + 4 V-dot + (4 - m^2) V) sin m th, these three
identities give -Lap psi = rho_x mode by mode. At the origin T - J = M - a0/4 = -D and K = O(r^2), so
psi = -D x y + O(r^4) and psi_xy(0) = -D. Once Step 5 gives f, J, T, K = O(r^{-2 eps}) with their dots, U = (-psi_y,
psi_x) is O(r^{1 - 2 eps}) = o(r) and has the parities of Section 2, so by the uniqueness in 3.1(i) it is the
canonical velocity. (Only these identities are used; no general Green formula is needed.) With U_r = -psi_th/r and
U_th = psi_r, R = c_l r rho_r - (psi_th r rho_r - r psi_r rho_th)/r^2 - rho, and the products of the modes give
    R_1/(pi r) = L f-dot - N,   L = c_l + (T - J)/2,
    N = f^2/4 - (D + T) f - f g/2 + (2 T + J - 2 K) g + ((T - J)/2 + K) g-dot.   (1)
(This identity was also checked symbolically.) So R_1 = 0 at every radius if and only if L f-dot = N, which together
with J-dot = f - 4 J is a two-dimensional ODE system in t whose coefficients are explicit functions of t.

Step 2 (an analytic branch at the origin). At eps = 0, f = a0, J = a0/4, T = M and g = K = 0 solve the system, with
L = L0 and N = a0 (a0/4 - D - M) = 0. In z, and with u = (f - a0, J - a0/4), the linearization is z u' = [[nu, 0],
[1/2, -2]] u: the f-equation has dN/df = a0/2 - (D + M) = a0/4 and f-dot = 2 z f', so z u_1' = a0 u_1/(8 L0) = nu u_1.
Neither nu nor -2 is a positive integer, so z d/dz minus this matrix is invertible on power series without constant
term, with an inverse bounded in the norm sum |u_j| R^j uniformly in R, because sup_{j >= 1} max(|j - nu|^{-1},
(j + 2)^{-1}) is finite. The remaining terms are at least quadratic in u or carry a factor eps z (T - M, g, g-dot and
K are analytic in z, with a factor eps, and vanish at z = 0), and the analytic algebra estimate gives a contraction on
a small ball for R and eps small. This gives a solution analytic in z near 0 with f(0) = a0, J(0) = a0/4, depending
analytically on eps, and ODE continuation extends it to every fixed compact z-interval for eps small, with derivatives
in eps given by the variational equations about the constant solution.

Step 3 (the first variation). Let F1 = d f/d eps at eps = 0. Since dT/d eps = -M log(1 + z), dg/d eps = 2 M z/(1 + z)
and d(g-dot)/d eps = 4 M z/(1 + z)^2, differentiating L f-dot = N gives
    z F1' - nu F1 = (M/(c_l + 1)) [a0 log(1 + z) + (a0/2 - 4D) z/(1 + z) - 2 D z/(1 + z)^2],
whose solution analytic at 0 is
    F1 = (M/(c_l + 1)) [4 (nu + 2) Y - 4 (c_l + 1) log(1 + z) - 2 D z/(1 + z)],
    Y = sum_{j >= 1} (-1)^{j-1} z^j/(j - nu),
since z Y' - nu Y = z/(1 + z), and the operator z d/dz - nu maps log(1 + z) to z/(1 + z) - nu log(1 + z) and z/(1 + z)
to z/(1 + z)^2 - nu z/(1 + z). Since (z^{-nu} Y)' = z^{-nu}/(1 + z) is integrable at infinity, Y = z^nu [C - int_z^inf
s^{-nu}/(1 + s) ds] on z > 0 for a constant C, and z^{-nu} Y -> C as z -> inf. To find C, let Y_mu be the same series
with nu replaced by a half-integer mu > 0, continued along z > 0 by z Y_mu' - mu Y_mu = z/(1 + z). Then Y_{1/2} = 2
sqrt z arctan sqrt z, so z^{-1/2} Y_{1/2} -> pi, and Y_{mu+1} = -z/mu - z Y_mu (separate the term j = 1 and shift the
index; the identity holds near 0 and then on z > 0 by analytic continuation), so z^{-mu-1}
Y_{mu+1} = -z^{-mu}/mu - z^{-mu} Y_mu and the limit changes sign at each of the 2n + 1 steps from 1/2 to
nu = 2n + 3/2. Hence C = -pi and
    Y = z^nu [-pi - int_z^inf s^{-nu}/(1 + s) ds] <= -z/(nu (1 + z)),
the last step by s = z u and 1 + z u <= u (1 + z) for u >= 1. With log(1 + z) >= z/(1 + z) and
6 - (4 + 2D)/(c_l + 1) = 4,
    d(f + 3g)/d eps at eps = 0 is F1 + 6 M z/(1 + z) <= -8 M z/(nu (c_l + 1)(1 + z)).
Since f + 3g - a0 vanishes at z = 0 for every eps and is analytic in (z, eps) near (0, 0), the second-order remainder
in eps is at most C eps^2 z/(1 + z) on each fixed compact z-interval (near 0 by analyticity, elsewhere by the
continuation of Step 2). Hence for eps small, f > 0 and f + 3g <= a0 on that interval. Also w = f - 4 (D + T) has
first variation (M/(c_l + 1)) [4 (nu + 2) Y - 2 D z/(1 + z)], which tends to -inf as z -> inf.

Step 4 (departure). Put Lmax = c_l + M/2, kappa = D/(2 Lmax), CS = M (2 a0 + 14 M), CB = 2 CS/L0 + 8 M and K0 = max(4
CB/kappa, 12 M, 1). For 0 < eps <= 1/4, with d = g-dot/g = 2 - 2 (1 + eps) z/(1 + z),
    0 < g <= 2 eps T,   -2 eps <= d <= 2,   |g-dot| <= 4 eps T,   0 <= K <= g/(6 - 2 eps) <= eps T/(3 - eps);
the bound on K follows from g(s) <= g(t) exp(2 eps (t - s)) for s < t and K = int_{-inf}^t exp(-6 (t - s)) g(s) ds.
Fix t1 >= 0 such that the first variation of w at t1 is < -2 K0; by Step 3, for eps small, w(t1) <= -K0 eps,
f(t1) > 2D, and 0 < f <= a0, 0 <= J <= a0/4 on t <= t1. Consider t >= t1 while f >= 2D, w <= -K0 eps and T >= M - L0.
There f = 4 (D + T) + w <= a0, J stays in [0, a0/4] by J-dot = f - 4 J, and L0/2 <= L <= Lmax. Write N = f w/4 + S;
term by term, |f g/2| <= a0 eps T, |(2 T + J - 2 K) g| <= (8 M + a0/2) eps T and |((T - J)/2 + K) g-dot| <= (6
M + a0/2) eps T, so |S| <= eps (2 a0 + 14 M) T <= CS eps. Since w < 0, f >= 2D and L <= Lmax,
    w-dot = f w/(4 L) + S/L + 4 g <= kappa w + CB eps <= (kappa/2) w < 0.
Take eps smaller so that K0 eps < a0 and eps M [log 2 + 2 t1 + (4/kappa) log(a0/(K0 eps))] < L0/2, which is possible
since eps log(1/eps) -> 0. If f stayed >= 2D on [t1, t1 + tau], tau = (2/kappa) log(a0/(K0 eps)), then -w would reach
a0, while f >= 2D gives w >= 2D - 4 (D + M) = 2D - a0 > -a0. On this interval M - T <= eps M log(1 + z) <= eps M (log
2 + 2 t) < L0/2, so the conditions on T and L cannot fail first. Hence there is a first t2 > t1 with f(t2) = 2D.

Step 5 (trapping, the sign and decay). At t2, with Z = J - T,
    0 <= f <= 2D,   0 <= J <= a0/4,   Z <= D + L0/2,
and in this box L = c_l - Z/2 >= 3 L0/4. The box is invariant for t >= t2. At f = 2D, N <= -D^2 - 2 D T + CS eps < 0
once CS eps < D^2/2. At f = 0, N = g [(2 + d/2) T + (1 - d/2) J + (d - 2) K] >= g T (6 - 7 eps - eps^2)/(3 - eps) > 0.
At J = 0, J-dot = f >= 0, and at J = a0/4, J-dot = f - a0 < 0. At Z = D + L0/2, Z-dot = f - 4 Z - 4 T + g <= 2D - 4
Z < 0. The coefficients stay bounded and L stays positive, so the solution exists for all t. Sign: for t <= t1,
f + 3g <= a0 by Step 3; during departure f + 3g <= a0 - K0 eps + 6 M eps <= a0; in the box f + 3g <= 2D + 6 M eps < a0
for eps small. Since sin 3th = sin th (4 cos^2 th - 1) and g >= 0, q = [f + g (4 cos^2 th - 1)]/a0 <= (f + 3g)/a0 <= 1
for y != 0; with g = z G(z), G = 2 eps M (1 + z)^{-eps - 1}, q = [f + G (3 x^2 - y^2)]/a0 is smooth on the plane,
q(0) = 1, and q <= 1 everywhere. Decay: in the box, f^2/4 - D f <= -D f/2 and |S| <= C T, so f-dot <= -kappa f + C T;
with 2 eps < kappa and T <= M exp(-2 eps t), f = O(exp(-2 eps t)), and then J, g, K, T and the dots of f and g are
O(r^{-2 eps}). Hence rho = O(r^{1 - 2 eps}), grad rho = O(r^{-2 eps}) and U = O(r^{1 - 2 eps}). Smoothness: f is
analytic in z near 0 and g/z is analytic, so rho = y f + (3 x^2 y - y^3) g/z is smooth at 0; elsewhere the solution of
the ODE is smooth. Finitely many smallness conditions on eps were used, which leaves an interval 0 < eps < eps_*.

Step 6 (the third projection). Write rho = a0 y + b x^2 y + e y^3 + O(r^5) and g = g2 z + O(z^2), g2 = 2 eps M. From r
g sin 3th = g (3 x^2 y - y^3)/z, b - e = 4 g2. With no density mode 5, the canonical quartic stream coefficients are
psi = -D x y + q1 x^3 y + q2 x y^3 + O(r^6) with q1 = (3 e - 11 b)/48 and q2 = -(5 b + 3 e)/48 (q1 + q2 = -b/3 from
-Lap psi = rho_x, and the sin 4th part equals -(1/2) r^2 K = -g2 r^4/16 + O(r^6)). The cubic part of R is r21 x^2
y + r03 y^3 with r21 = 2 A b + 3 a0 q1 and r03 = 2 e + a0 q2, and x^2 y = r^3 (sin th + sin 3th)/4, y^3 = r^3 (3 sin
th - sin 3th)/4. R_1 = 0 gives r21 + 3 r03 = 0, that is 6 e = (a0 - 2A) b, so b = 24 g2/(4 (c_l + 1) - a0) and e = 4
g2 (a0 - 2A)/(4 (c_l + 1) - a0), and
    lim_{r -> 0} R_3/(pi r^3) = (r21 - r03)/4 = g2 [a0^2 - (4 c_l + 20) a0 + 64 A]/[4 (4 (c_l + 1) - a0)].
The denominator is nonzero since a0 = 4 (c_l + 1) nu with nu != 1. For n >= 1, a0 >= 14 (c_l + 1), which exceeds the
vertex 2 c_l + 10 of the bracket, and at a0 = 14 (c_l + 1) the bracket equals 140 c_l^2 + 184 c_l - 148 > 0, while the
denominator is negative; so the limit is negative, R_3 < 0 for small r > 0, and R_3 is not identically 0. For n = 0
the bracket is 4 (3 c_l^2 + 14 c_l - 37), which vanishes at c_l = (-7 + 4 sqrt 10)/3.

Step 7 (the seventh projection). The stream has the angular modes 2 and 4 (so U_r and U_th have the angular
frequencies 2 and 4), rho the modes 1 and 3, and c_l X . grad rho - rho only the modes 1 and 3, so R_7 comes only from
the part psi_4 = -(1/2) r^2 K sin 4th of the stream acting on r g sin 3th. With U_r = -r^{-1} psi_th, U_th = psi_r and
K-dot = g - 6K, this part of U is U_r = 2 r K cos 4th, U_th = r (2K - g/2) sin 4th, and its product with the polar
components ((g + g-dot) sin 3th, 3 g cos 3th) of grad(r g sin 3th) has the sin 7th coefficient r [K (g-dot + 4g) - 3
g^2/4], so
    R_7 = pi r [K (g-dot + 4 g) - (3/4) g^2].
Let d = g-dot/g = 2 - 2 (1 + eps) r^2/(1 + r^2); it is strictly decreasing in t = log r and below 2 for r > 0. By
K(t) = int_0^inf e^{-6u} g(t - u) du and g(t - u) = g(t) exp(-int_{t-u}^t d) < g(t) e^{-d(t) u} for u > 0,
K < g/(6 + d) at every radius where 6 + d > 0. If d + 4 > 0, then R_7/(pi r g^2) < (d + 4)/(d + 6) - 3/4 = (d - 2)/(4
(d + 6)) < 0; if d + 4 <= 0, then R_7/(pi r g^2) <= -3/4. Hence R_7 < 0 at every r > 0, for every n >= 0 and every
eps > 0, whatever f is; at the origin R_7/(pi r^7) -> -(1 + eps) g2^2/10.

Scope. Only R_1 = 0 is imposed; these densities are not profiles (for n >= 1 by Step 6, and for every n by Step 7 and
by 3.10, since they have two angular modes), q >= 0 is not asserted, the exponent 1 - 2 eps depends on the member, and
nothing is claimed about R_1 = R_3 = 0 with more than two modes.

## A.3.62 No profile of finite Cartesian separation rank

Setting. rho is an exact profile of the primary class and p = 1/c_l is in (0, 1) (3.6). By 3.7, r^{-p} rho(r,
.) -> Theta0 uniformly on S^1, Theta0 is Holder continuous of every order below 1, and Theta0(pi/2) = K != 0. Hence
rho_inf(X) = |X|^p Theta0(arg X) is homogeneous of degree p, |rho_inf(X)| <= C |X|^p, R^{-p} rho(R X) -> rho_inf(X)
for every X != 0, and rho_inf is Holder continuous of every order below 1 on each compact subset of R^2 \ {0}. Fix
alpha with p < alpha < 1. In this entry N, F_j, G_j, Omega, E, V, W, T_s, Z, C1, the points x_i, y_k, z_i and the norm
||.|| are local notation. Statement (i) follows from (ii) with Omega = {y > 0}: if rho_inf = sum_{j <= N} F_j(x)
G_j(y) on y > 0, then E = rho - rho_inf there and R^{-p} E(R X) = R^{-p} rho(R X) - rho_inf(X) -> 0. So assume the
representation of (ii).

Step 1 (dimension). Fix x_0, ..., x_N in R and y_0, ..., y_N > 0. For R large every point (R x_i, R y_k) lies in
Omega, and the matrix with entries R^{-p} [rho(R x_i, R y_k) - E(R x_i, R y_k)] = sum_{j <= N} R^{-p} F_j(R x_i) G_j(R
y_k) has rank at most N, so its determinant is 0. As R -> inf the entries tend to rho_inf(x_i, y_k); the determinant
is a polynomial in the entries, so det[rho_inf(x_i, y_k)] = 0. If V = span{rho_inf(., y) : y > 0} had dimension at
least N + 1, there would be y_0, ..., y_N with rho_inf(., y_k) linearly independent, and then points x_0, ..., x_N
with det[rho_inf(x_i, y_k)] != 0 (for linearly independent functions f_0, ..., f_m on a set, the vectors (f_0(x), ...,
f_m(x)) span R^{m + 1}, since a vector orthogonal to all of them would give a linear relation). Hence V has dimension
at most N.

Step 2 (a dilation lemma). For s > 0 let T_s f(x) = f(s x). Let W be a finite-dimensional space of real functions on R
with T_s W contained in W for every s > 0, and suppose that every g in W satisfies g(0) = 0, |g(x)| <= C_g |x|^alpha
for |x| <= 1 and |g(x)| <= C_g (1 + |x|)^p for all x, where alpha > p. Then W = 0. Indeed, if W has dimension d >= 1,
choose a basis g_1, ..., g_d and, by the argument of Step 1, points z_1, ..., z_d with det[g_j(z_i)] != 0; then
||g|| = max_i |g(z_i)| is a norm on W, the coefficients of g in the basis are bounded by a constant times ||g||, and
so |g(x)| <= C1 ||g|| |x|^alpha for |x| <= 1 and |g(x)| <= C1 ||g|| (1 + |x|)^p for all x, with C1 independent of g.
Put Z = max_i |z_i|; Z > 0, since every g in W vanishes at 0. For 0 < s <= min(1, 1/Z) this gives ||T_s g|| <= C1
Z^alpha s^alpha ||g|| and ||T_{1/s} g|| <= C1 (1 + Z/s)^p ||g|| <= C1 (1 + Z)^p s^{-p} ||g||. Since T_s T_{1/s} is the
identity on W, applying the two bounds to g != 0 gives 1 <= C1^2 Z^alpha (1 + Z)^p s^{alpha - p}, which fails as
s -> 0.

Step 3 (the sections are constant). For s > 0, homogeneity gives rho_inf(s x, y) = s^p rho_inf(x, y/s), so T_s V is
contained in V. Let W = {f - f(0) : f in V}; since (T_s f)(0) = f(0), T_s W is contained in W, and W has finite
dimension. For y > 0, f = rho_inf(., y) satisfies |f(x) - f(0)| <= C_y |x|^alpha for |x| <= 1, by the Holder
continuity of rho_inf on the segment [-1, 1] x {y}, and |f(x) - f(0)| <= 2 C (x^2 + y^2)^{p/2} <= C_y (1 + |x|)^p;
both bounds pass to finite linear combinations, so Step 2 applies and W = 0. Hence every element of V is constant, and
rho_inf(x, y) = rho_inf(0, y) = y^p Theta0(pi/2) = K y^p for x in R and y > 0.

Step 4 (contradiction). rho_inf is Holder continuous of order alpha on a neighbourhood of (1, 0). By Step 3,
rho_inf(1, y) = K y^p for y > 0, so rho_inf(1, 0) = 0 and |K| y^p = |rho_inf(1, y) - rho_inf(1, 0)| <= C y^alpha for
small y > 0, which is impossible since K != 0 and alpha > p. In polar form, Theta0(th) = K (sin th)^p on (0, pi),
which is not Holder of order alpha at th = 0.

Remark (a second proof of Step 3 when Theta0 is C^inf, 3.23). Then V consists of smooth functions and is closed under
pointwise limits (by the point evaluations of Step 2), so x d/dx, the limit of (f(s .) - f)/(s - 1) as s -> 1, maps V
into V, and P(x d/dx) = 0 on V for its characteristic polynomial P. For f in V, the Taylor coefficients of f at 0
vanish in every degree k with P(k) != 0; subtracting the finitely many remaining Taylor terms leaves a flat solution h
of P(x d/dx) h = 0, and on each half-line the vector Z(t) of the first deg P derivatives of h(+-e^t) satisfies Z' = B
Z for a companion matrix B, so ||Z(t0)|| <= e^{||B|| (t0 - t)} ||Z(t)|| for t < t0, and flatness forces Z = 0. The
elements of V are therefore polynomials, hence constant by the growth bound.

Remark (linear coordinates; proposed in an external audit, proved here, confirmed by the checker and in an external
audit). Let M be a fixed invertible real 2 x 2 matrix and suppose rho(M Y) = sum_{j <= N} F_j(u) G_j(v) + E(M Y) for
Y = (u, v) with v > 0 outside a disc, with R^{-p} E(R M Y) -> 0 for every such Y. Put F~(Y) = rho_inf(M Y). It is
C^inf on R^2 \ {0}, homogeneous of degree p, and |F~(Y)| <= C |Y|^p, since |M Y| is comparable to |Y|; the determinant
argument of Step 1 (the scaling X -> R X is Y -> R Y, and R Y lies outside the disc for R large) gives dim span{F~(.,
v) : v > 0} <= N. Every section u -> F~(u, v), v > 0, is smooth (it does not pass through 0) and O((1 + |u|)^p), so
the dilation lemma of Step 2 (with any alpha in (p, 1)) makes every element of this span constant, and F~(u,
v) = F~(0, v) = C v^p for v > 0. At the point (1, 0), F~(1, 0) = lim_{v -> 0+} C v^p = 0 and F~ is C^1 near (1, 0), so
|C| v^p <= L v for small v > 0, which forces C = 0 since p < 1. Thus F~ = 0 on v > 0. Since rho is even in x and odd
in y, rho_inf(-X) = -rho_inf(X), hence F~(-Y) = -F~(Y) and F~ = 0 on v < 0, and by continuity on v = 0, Y != 0. Hence
rho_inf = 0, contradicting K != 0. Central oddness is needed in the last step: without it a nonzero homogeneous
function could vanish on v > 0.

Scope. Exact transport enters only through 3.6 and 3.7: the convergence of R^{-p} rho(R X) to the homogeneous far
field rho_inf of degree p in (0, 1), its axis coefficient K != 0 and the Holder continuity of Theta0 of some order
above p. The argument applies to every density with such a far field, which the non-profiles of 3.61 need not have. It
excludes finite sums of Cartesian separated functions on Omega, also up to errors o(R^p) along each ray, and hence
every density whose quotient rho/(a0 y) is such a finite sum on Omega (division by a0 y does not change the rank on
y > 0). It does not exclude profiles of infinite separation rank, nor finite rank in nonlinear coordinates: in
u = x/y, v = y (a change of variables singular at y = 0), homogeneity gives rho_inf(u v, v) = v^p rho_inf(u, 1), of
rank one; this concerns the far field only and says nothing about the rank of rho in these coordinates.

## A.3.63 Two projections with the one-sided sign on a disc do not bound the slope

Setting. Fix c_l > 1, put c = c_l, D = c - 1, write a for a0, t = log r, z = r^2 and a dot for r d/dr. In this entry
f, g, k, T, S, J, K, L, u, v, w, B, C, E1, E3, E5, F1, F3, H, I, F, G, P, Y and the constants are local notation;
R = (c X + U) . grad rho - rho and R_k(r) = int_0^{2 pi} R sin k th dth.

Step 1 (radial system). For smooth f, g, k on [0, inf) with f(0) = a, g = O(z), k = O(z^2) at 0, vanishing for large
r, let rho = r (f sin th + g sin 3th + k sin 5th) and
    T = int_r^inf g(s)/s ds,   S = r^2 int_r^inf k(s) s^{-3} ds,   J = r^{-4} int_0^r s^3 f(s) ds,
    K = r^{-6} int_0^r s^5 g(s) ds,   L = r^{-8} int_0^r s^7 k(s) ds,
    u = (T - J)/2,   v = (S - K)/2,   w = -L/2,   psi = r^2 (u sin 2th + v sin 4th + w sin 6th).
Then T-dot = -g, S-dot = 2 S - k, J-dot = f - 4 J, K-dot = g - 6 K and L-dot = k - 8 L. The sin m th coefficient of
rho_x (m even) is (1/2) (F_{m-1}-dot - (m - 2) F_{m-1} + F_{m+1}-dot + (m + 2) F_{m+1}) with F_1 = f, F_3 = g, F_5 = k
and F_j = 0 otherwise, and -Lap(r^2 V sin m th) = -(V-dot-dot + 4 V-dot + (4 - m^2) V) sin m th; with the five
identities this gives -Lap psi = rho_x mode by mode for m = 2, 4, 6. The density is smooth when f, g/z and k/z^2 are
smooth in z, since rho = y f + (3 x^2 y - y^3) g/z + (r^5 sin 5th) k/z^2, and then so is psi, since u, v/z and w/z^2
are smooth in z and r^2 sin 2th, r^4 sin 4th, r^6 sin 6th are polynomials. Outside the support T = S = 0 and J, K, L
are constant multiples of r^{-4}, r^{-6}, r^{-8}, so U = O(r^{-3}); U has the parities of Section 2, so by the
uniqueness in 3.1(i) it is the canonical velocity. At 0, T(0) - J(0) = T(0) - a/4, so psi_xy(0) = -D if and only if
T(0) = M := a/4 - D. A density mode r F_j sin j th and a stream mode r^2 h_m sin m th contribute -m h_m
(F_j + F_j-dot) cos m th sin j th + j (2 h_m + h_m-dot) F_j sin m th cos j th to (U . grad rho)/r (U_r = -psi_th/r,
U_th = psi_r); expanding the products and using the five identities, with B = -u - K + S and C = K - 3L/2 - S,
    E1 := R_1/(pi r) = (c + u) f-dot + B g-dot + C k-dot + F1,
    E3 := R_3/(pi r) = B f-dot + (c - 3L/2) g-dot - u k-dot + F3,
    E5 := R_5/(pi r) = c k-dot + D k + C f-dot - u g-dot + (2 J + T) g + 2 K f - f g - f k/2 - 3 g^2/4,
    F1 = (D + T) f - f^2/4 + f g/2 + (-J + 2K + 4S - 2T) g + (-4K + 6L - 6S) k + g k/2,
    F3 = (J + 2S) f - f^2/4 - f g/2 + (D + 3L) g + (-2J - 3T + f + g/2) k.
(These identities are algebraic; they were derived independently by the checker and checked symbolically.)

Step 2 (local analytic solution). Fix H > 0. Near 0 take k = 0, so L = 0 and S = H z there, and seek f, g with
T = M - int_0^r g/s ds (so T-dot = -g and T(0) = M), J, K as in Step 1, and E1 = E3 = 0. With Y = (f, g, T, J, K) this
is a system z Y' = Phi(z, Y): the T, J, K rows are z T' = -g/2, z J' = (f - 4J)/2, z K' = (g - 6K)/2, and the f, g
rows are z (f', g')^T = -(1/2) Mat^{-1} (F1, F3)^T with Mat = [[c + u, B], [B, c]]; Mat is invertible near (0, Y0),
since at z = 0 and Y = Y0 = (a, 0, M, a/4, 0) one has u = -D/2, B = D/2 and det Mat = c
(c + 1)/2 - D^2/4 = (c^2 + 4c - 1)/4 > 0. Phi is analytic near (0, Y0) and Phi(0, Y0) = 0 (at Y0, F1 = (D + M)
a - a^2/4 = 0 and F3 = J f - f^2/4 = 0). At order z^j (j >= 1) put lam = 2j; the scalar rows give T_j = -g_j/lam,
J_j = f_j/(lam + 4), K_j = g_j/(lam + 6), and the f, g rows, multiplied by 2 Mat at Y0 (equivalently, E1 = E3 = 0 in
the dot form), become
    A(lam) (f_j, g_j)^T = (terms of lower order),
    A(lam) = [[(c + 1) lam/2 - a/4, D lam/2 + 2D - a/4 - a/lam], [D lam/2 - a/4 + a/(lam + 4), c lam + D - a/2]],
with 16 det A(lam) = I(a, lam); moreover det(j I - DPhi_Y(0, Y0)) = j (j + 2) (j + 3) I(a, 2j)/(16 (c^2 + 4c - 1))
(checked symbolically), so the moment rows add no resonance. So for a not in E_c, j I - DPhi_Y(0, Y0) is invertible
for every integer j >= 1, with inverse O(1/j), and the operator z d/dz - DPhi_Y(0, Y0) is invertible on power series
without constant term, with an inverse bounded uniformly in rho0 in the norm sum_j |V_j| rho0^j. Writing Y = Y0 + V,
the remainder Phi(z, Y0 + V) - DPhi_Y(0, Y0) V is O(z) + O(z |V|) + O(|V|^2), so the analytic algebra estimate gives a
contraction on a small ball for rho0 small, and a unique solution analytic in z near 0, real since the data are real.
The order-1 equations are
    A(2) (f_1, g_1)^T + (0, 2 a H)^T = 0,
the term 2 a H coming from 2 S f in F3. With F(a) := I(a, 2) = 16 det A(2) = a^2 - (4c + 20) a + 128 c - 64,
    f_1 = -24 H a (a - 4c + 4)/F(a),   g_1 = 8 H a (a - 4c - 4)/F(a).
In Cartesian form rho = a y + b x^2 y + e y^3 + O(r^5) with b = f_1 + 3 g_1 = -192 H a/F(a) and e = f_1 - g_1 = -32 H
a (a - 4c + 2)/F(a). For a >= 100 (c + 1) one has a > 4c + 20, so F(a) > 128 c - 64 > 0, and b < 0, e < 0. Since
q = 1 + (b x^2 + e y^2)/a + O(r^4) is smooth, q < 1 on a punctured disc 0 < r < r1, including its points on y = 0. If
H = 0 the order-1 system is homogeneous, so f_1 = g_1 = 0 unless F(a) = 0.

Step 3 (fifth projection). On the disc of Step 2, k = 0 and E5 = C f-dot - u g-dot + (2J + T) g + 2 K f - f g - 3
g^2/4 with C = K - S. Its z coefficient vanishes and its z^2 coefficient is C5 = -2 H f_1 + (D - a/20) g_2 - 3
g_1^2/4, where the order-2 equations are
    A(4) (f_2, g_2)^T + (6 H g_1 - 5 f_1^2/12 - f_1 g_1/2 + 3 g_1^2/2, 4 H f_1 + f_1^2/12 - f_1 g_1/4)^T = 0.
Solving and substituting f_1, g_1 gives the identity of rational functions
    C5 = -384 H^2 a P(a)/(5 F(a)^2 G(a)),   G(a) = a^2 - (12c + 36) a + 32 c^2 + 384 c - 160,
    P(a) = 15 a^4 + (200 - 560 c) a^3 + (6704 c^2 - 2320 c - 2816) a^2 + (-29056 c^3 - 8512 c^2 + 63616 c - 26048) a
           + 40960 c^4 + 61440 c^3 - 245760 c^2 + 184320 c - 40960
(checked symbolically, also directly from the Cartesian polynomials of rho and psi). For c > 1 the coefficient of a^2
in P is at least 1568 c^2 > 0, the coefficient of a is at least -63616 c^3, and the constant term is at least -286720
c^4. For a >= 100 (c + 1) > 100 c, dividing by a^4, 560 c/a + 63616 c^3/a^3 + 286720 c^4/a^4 < 5.6 + 0.07 + 0.003 < 6,
so P(a) > 9 a^4 > 0; also G(a) > 0 since a > 12 c + 36 and 32 c^2 + 384 c - 160 > 0. Hence C5 < 0, and R_5 = pi C5
r^5 + O(r^7) is not identically 0 near 0.

Step 4 (extension). Let 0 < r2 < r3 < r1 with the solution of Step 2 defined on r < r1, and a smooth radial cutoff chi
with 0 <= chi <= 1, chi = 1 on r <= r2 and chi = 0 for r >= r3. Put f0 = chi f, g0 = chi g. Where q >= 0,
multiplication by chi does not increase q, and where q < 0 the new quotient is <= 0; so q < 1 off 0 for the density of
(f0, g0, 0). Choose smooth nonnegative functions phi3, phi5, not identically zero, with compact support in an annulus
r4 < r < r5 with r4 > r3, and constants A3, A5 with
    int_0^inf (g0(s) + A3 phi3(s))/s ds = M,   int_0^inf A5 phi5(s) s^{-3} ds = H,
and a smooth function 0 <= zeta <= 1 with compact support in r > r3 and zeta = 1 on r4 <= r <= r5. Set
    f1* = f0 - B0 zeta,   g1* = g0 + A3 phi3,   k1* = A5 phi5,   B0 > 3 |A3| max phi3 + 5 |A5| max phi5.
Since |sin 3th/sin th| <= 3 and |sin 5th/sin th| <= 5, rho/y = f1* + g1* sin 3th/sin th + k1* sin 5th/sin
th <= f1* + 3 |g1*| + 5 |k1*| < 0 on r4 <= r <= r5, and rho/y = -B0 zeta <= 0 elsewhere on the support of zeta; so
q < 1 off 0 (a > 0). For r <= r2 the upper integrals of Step 1 for (f1*, g1*, k1*) are T = M - int_0^r g/s ds and
S = H r^2, and the lower integrals involve only s < r; so the density and the stream coincide there with those of Step
2. Hence psi_xy(0) = -D, R_1 = R_3 = 0 on r <= r2, and R_5 = pi C5 r^5 + O(r^7). The density is smooth, compactly
supported, with the parities, satisfies the growth bound of Section 2 for every gamma in (0, 1), has only the modes 1,
3, 5, and its fifth mode vanishes on r <= r2, with int_0^inf k1* s^{-3} ds = H.

Step 5 (dilation). For l > 0 put rho_l(X) = l rho(X/l). Its canonical stream is l^2 psi(X/l) and its velocity l
U(X/l), so R[rho_l](X) = l R[rho](X/l), (R[rho_l])_k(r) = l R_k(r/l), the slope, psi_xy(0) and q(X/l) are unchanged, H
becomes H/l^2 and C5 becomes C5/l^4. With l = R/r2 the projections vanish on r <= R.

Step 6 (the exceptional set). For a in a bounded interval, I(a, 2j) >= 16 (c^2 + 4c - 1) j^2 - C (1 + j) > 0 for all
large j, so only finitely many j contribute, each with at most two roots; so E_c is finite on bounded intervals. For
c = 2 or 3, I(a, 2j) = a^2 - 4 b a + 4 d with integers b, d; if a = n + sqrt 2 with n an integer, I = 0 forces n = 2b
(irrational part) and then 2 - 4 b^2 + 4 d = 0, impossible modulo 4. Since 1000 > 100 (c + 1) for c <= 3, every
a = 1000 + m + sqrt 2 is admissible.

Scope. Only R_1 and R_3 are imposed, and only on a disc. If H = 0 (as for densities with only the modes 1 and 3 on the
whole plane, since H = int_0^inf k s^{-3} ds) the cubic part of h = rho - a y vanishes unless F(a) = 0 (Step 2); the
bound of 3.59(iv) uses this. With exterior higher modes permitted, imposing R_1 = R_3 = 0 on a prescribed disc
therefore gives no upper bound on a, even with q < 1 off 0, and for fixed R none depending only on c and R, since E_c
is finite on bounded intervals. The construction does not decide whether imposing both projections at every radius
bounds a, says nothing about exact transport, and gives no existence or nonexistence conclusion for exact profiles of
the primary class. For fixed a, dilation sends H and C5 to 0, so |C5| has no positive lower bound without a
normalization of length; on compact sets rho_l tends to a y and its stream to -D x y, a strain that is not sublinear,
and the limit has q = 1, so no profile arises in this limit.

## A.3.64 No profile satisfies an exterior linear equation with constant coefficients

Notation: F = rho_inf, D'(V) the distributions on an open set V, <u, phi> the bilinear pairing, and
phi_s(X) = phi(X/s). A distribution u on V, with V invariant under dilations, is homogeneous of degree lambda if <u,
phi_s> = s^{lambda + 2} <u, phi> for all s > 0 and test functions phi on V. Pointwise conditions on sigma refer to the
fixed measurable function sigma of the statement.

Step 1 (inputs). By 3.7 and 3.23, F(X) = |X|^p Theta0(arg X) is C^inf on R^2 \ {0}, homogeneous of degree p in (0, 1),
|F(X)| <= C |X|^p, and R^{-p} rho(R X) -> F uniformly on compact subsets of R^2 \ {0}; by 3.6, F(0, 1) = K != 0.

Step 2 (convergence of the rescalings). Let sigma_R(X) = R^{-p} sigma(R X), defined for R X outside B. Fix a compact
set Q in R^2 \ {0} with 0 < a1 <= |X| <= b1 on Q; for R large, R Q does not meet B. In case (a), with eps(t) = t^{-p}
sup_{|Y| = t} |sigma(Y) - rho(Y)|, sup_Q |R^{-p} (sigma - rho)(R X)| <= b1^p sup_{t >= R a1} eps(t) -> 0, and sup_Q
|R^{-p} rho(R X) - F| -> 0, so sigma_R -> F uniformly on Q. In case (b), R^{-p} |rho - sigma|(R X) <= C R^{-p} (1 + R
|X|)^p = C (R^{-1} + |X|)^p <= C (1 + b1)^p on Q for R >= 1, and it tends to 0 for almost every X, so it tends to 0 in
L^1(Q) by dominated convergence. In both cases sigma_R -> F in L^1_loc(R^2 \ {0}), hence in D'(R^2 \ {0}).

Step 3 (the part of lowest order annihilates F off 0). For a test function phi supported in a compact Q in R^2 \ {0}
and R large, the change of variables Y = R X in <P(d) sigma, phi(./R)> = 0 and d^alpha [sigma(R .)] = R^{|alpha|}
(d^alpha sigma)(R .) give sum_j R^{p + 2 - j} <P_j(d) sigma_R, phi> = 0. Dividing by R^{p + 2 - m}, with P_j(-d) the
transpose of P_j(d) for the bilinear pairing (complex coefficients need no conjugation),

    <P_m(d) sigma_R, phi> = - sum_{j > m} R^{m - j} <sigma_R, P_j(-d) phi>.

By Step 2, <sigma_R, P_j(-d) phi> -> <F, P_j(-d) phi>, which is bounded in R, and R^{m - j} -> 0 for j > m, so the
right side tends to 0 while the left side tends to <F, P_m(-d) phi> = <P_m(d) F, phi>. Hence P_m(d) F = 0 in D'(R^2 \
{0}). The large-scale limit selects the part of lowest order: normalizing by the highest order d0 instead would
produce the factors R^{d0 - j}, which diverge for j < d0. The part of highest order would be selected by a small-scale
limit at a point where the equation holds, which is not available for an equation holding only outside a compact set.

Step 4 (no mass at 0). F is locally integrable on R^2 (|F| <= C |X|^p, p > -2) and defines a distribution on R^2,
homogeneous of degree p: <F, phi_s> = s^2 int F(s Y) phi(Y) dY = s^{p + 2} <F, phi>. Each derivative lowers the degree
by 1, so u = P_m(d) F is homogeneous of degree p - m, and by Step 3 its support is contained in {0}. A distribution
supported at 0 is a finite sum u = sum_{|alpha| <= N} c_alpha d^alpha delta. Since <d^alpha delta,
phi_s> = s^{-|alpha|} <d^alpha delta, phi>, homogeneity of degree p - m gives sum_alpha c_alpha
(s^{-|alpha|} - s^{p - m + 2}) <d^alpha delta, phi> = 0 for all s > 0 and phi; the d^alpha delta are linearly
independent and p - m + 2 is not an integer, so every c_alpha = 0. Thus P_m(d) F = 0 in D'(R^2).

Step 5 (Fourier transform). F is tempered (locally integrable and polynomially bounded), and P_m(i xi) F^(xi) = 0 in
S'(R^2). The restriction of F^ to R^2 \ {0} is a C^inf function: write 1 = sum_{l in Z} chi(2^{-l} X) on X != 0 with
chi smooth and supported in an annulus; then F = sum_l 2^{l p} (chi F)(2^{-l} X) with chi F in C_c^inf, and for a
Schwartz function phi the l-th pairing is bounded by C_phi 2^{l (p + 2)} for l <= 0 and by C_{phi, M} 2^{l
(p + 2 - M)} for l >= 0 (any M), so the series converges in S'. Hence F^(xi) = sum_l 2^{l (p + 2)} a(2^l xi), a = (chi
F)^ a Schwartz function. On a compact set of xi with 0 < r1 <= |xi| <= r2, the derivative d^beta of the term l is
bounded by 2^{l (p + 2 + |beta|)} sup |d^beta a| for l -> -inf and by C_M 2^{l (p + 2 + |beta| - M)} for l -> +inf, so
every differentiated series converges uniformly there. Let Z = {xi : P_m(i xi) = 0}. P_m(i xi) is a nonzero
polynomial; its real part or its imaginary part is a nonzero real polynomial, which cannot vanish on a nonempty open
set, so Z has empty interior. On the open set R^2 \ (Z u {0}) the function 1/P_m(i xi) is smooth, so F^ = 0 there. F^
is continuous on R^2 \ {0} and vanishes on a dense subset of it, so F^ = 0 on R^2 \ {0}. Hence supp F^ is contained in
{0}, and F is a polynomial. A polynomial with F(s X) = s^p F(X) for all s > 0 and p in (0, 1) is 0 (compare
homogeneous parts), contradicting F(0, 1) = K != 0.

Step 6 (ridge sums). For sigma = sum_{j <= N} h_j(l_j . X + b_j) with h_j in L^1_loc(R) and l_j != 0, choose v_j != 0
with v_j . l_j = 0. Each term is locally integrable (integrate in the orthogonal coordinates along l_j and v_j over
bounded intervals), and for a test function phi, int h_j(l_j . X + b_j) (v_j . grad) phi dX = 0 (Fubini in the same
coordinates: for fixed l_j . X the integral of the derivative of phi along v_j vanishes), so (v_j . grad) annihilates
the j-th term without differentiating h_j. The product P(d) = prod_j (v_j . grad) of commuting operators annihilates
sigma on R^2; it is homogeneous of order N, and its symbol is a product of nonzero linear forms, hence nonzero. Case
(a) with sigma the ridge sum gives the statement.

Scope. Steps 2-5 use only that F is a nonzero homogeneous function of degree p in (0, 1), C^inf off 0, with the stated
convergence; the profile enters only through 3.6, 3.7 and 3.23. Uniform (or dominated) convergence is used in Step 2;
the purely raywise error condition of 3.62(ii) is not enough here. The smoothness of F off 0 is used in Step 5 and
cannot be dropped: K sign(y) |y|^p is homogeneous of degree p and annihilated by d_x. The class excluded is one fixed
equation outside a compact set; it overlaps with, but does not contain, the classes of 3.10 and 3.62. Conversely, it
is not contained in them, as the following test density shows (proposed in an external audit; confirmed by the checker
by an independent proof; hand-checked in the main analysis). In this paragraph Q, H, h, h_0, h_+, h_-, mu, zeta, c_*,
kappa and S are local notation. In coordinates (s, t) let Q = d_s^4 - d_t^6 and let H be the inverse Fourier transform
of (i eta)^3/(xi^4 + eta^6), defined at 0 by pairing with the part of the test function odd in eta (absolutely
convergent there). Then Q H = d_t^3 delta and H(lam^3 s, lam^2 t) = lam H(s, t); H is smooth off 0 (by a dyadic
decomposition in these anisotropic dilations: the low-frequency shells are summable with all derivatives because H is
odd in t, the high-frequency shells by rapid decay), and H(0, t) = kappa sign(t) |t|^{1/2} with kappa = 1/(2 sqrt pi)
(from int_R e^{i s xi} (xi^4 + b^4)^{-1} d xi = pi (sqrt2 b^3)^{-1} e^{-z} (cos z + sin z), z = b |s|/sqrt2, and
int_0^inf u^{-3/2} sin u du = sqrt(2 pi)). Let h = H * mu with mu a radial mollifier, h_0(X) = h(x, y),
h_+(X) = h((x - y)/sqrt2, (x + y)/sqrt2), h_-(X) = h((x + y)/sqrt2, (y - x)/sqrt2), zeta a radial cutoff equal to 1
near 0, and c_* a constant with rho_y(0) != 0 for rho = h_0 + h_+ + h_- + c_* y zeta. Then rho is smooth, even
in x and odd in y (x -> -x exchanges h_+ and h_-, y -> -y exchanges them with a change of sign), |rho| + (1 + r) |grad
rho| <= C (1 + r)^{2/3}, rho is annihilated outside a compact set by the product of the three operators Q written in
the coordinates of h_0, h_+ and h_-, and R^{-1/2} rho(R X) -> kappa [S(y) + S((x + y)/sqrt2) + S((y - x)/sqrt2)]
locally uniformly, S(t) = sign(t) |t|^{1/2}. The limit has a square-root cusp on each of three distinct lines, with
nonzero coefficients; so it is not a trigonometric polynomial in th on the unit circle, which excludes finite angular
support of rho outside every disc, and in linear coordinates (u, v) at least one cusp line meets the sections
v = const at a point u = tau v with tau != 0, so finitely many sections with distinct moving cusps are linearly
independent and the separation rank is infinite, which by the argument of A.3.62 excludes finite separation rank of
rho outside every disc. Its far field is not smooth off 0, so rho violates 3.23 and is not a profile. Nothing is said
about operators with variable coefficients: a far field with finite angular spectrum, r^p sum_{k <= K} c_k sin(k th),
is annihilated by prod_k (d_th^2 + k^2), and r^p sin th is annihilated by d_r^2 - (p/r) d_r - (p/r^2) d_th^2, whose
Cartesian coefficients are homogeneous of degree 0; neither is excluded by this argument. Nothing is said about
general profiles.

## A.3.65 Finitely many projections, or exact transport, on a disc with the one-sided sign do not bound the slope

Setting. Fix c_l > 1 and put c = c_l, D = c - 1, A = 2c - 1, and write a for a0 > 0. N is an integer >= 2, or N = inf
for part (b). In this entry h, P, P0, L, Pi, Gamma, S_{n,p}, V_n, w, v, omega_k, u_k, u'_k, s_k, K, alpha, beta,
gamma, t, S, H, M_m, F_k, f_1, g_1, b, e, m, F, Z, chi, phi, zeta, C_k, I_k, B and the radii r1, ..., r5 are local
notation, i is the imaginary unit, and j, k, mu are indices; R = (c X + U) . grad rho - rho and R_k(r) = int_0^{2 pi}
R sin k th dth. Write w = x + i y and v = x - i y, treated as independent complex variables in Step 4, and for odd
n >= 1 and odd 1 <= p <= n put S_{n,p} = r^n sin p th = (w^{(n+p)/2} v^{(n-p)/2} - w^{(n-p)/2} v^{(n+p)/2})/(2i), and
S_{n,-p} = -S_{n,p}. For odd n = 2j + 1 the real homogeneous polynomials of degree n that are even in x and odd in y
form the space V_n with basis S_{n,1}, S_{n,3}, ..., S_{n,n} (j + 1 elements). For a density rho = r sum_{k >= 0}
F_k(r) sin (2k + 1) th with the parities of Section 2 the upper moments are M_m = int_0^inf F_m(s) s^{1-2m} ds
(m >= 1), when they converge.

Step 1 (the stream in modes, and its local form). Let rho be smooth with compact support and the parities, and F_k as
above. By 3.1(iv) the canonical stream is psi = sum_{m >= 1} psi_m(r) sin 2m th with psi_m = (1/(4m)) [r^{-2m} int_0^r
s^{2m+1} f_m ds + r^{2m} int_r^inf s^{1-2m} f_m ds], where f_m = (1/2) [(s F_{m-1})' - (2m - 1) F_{m-1} + (s
F_m)' + (2m + 1) F_m] is the sin 2m th coefficient of rho_x (F_{-1} = 0; for the mode sin k th of rho with coefficient
b_k(s), the coefficient of sin m th in rho_x is (1/2) [b_{m-1}' - (m - 1) b_{m-1}/s + b_{m+1}' + (m + 1) b_{m+1}/s]).
With b = s (F_{m-1} + F_m), s^{2m+1} f_m = (1/2) (s^{2m+1} b)' - 2m s^{2m+1} F_{m-1} and s^{1-2m} f_m = (1/2)
(s^{1-2m} b)' + 2m s^{1-2m} F_m; the boundary terms at s = r cancel and those at 0 and at infinity vanish, so
    psi_m(r) = (r^2/2) [ r^{2m-2} int_r^inf F_m(s) s^{1-2m} ds - r^{-2m-2} int_0^r s^{2m+1} F_{m-1}(s) ds ].   (1)
Now suppose that on a disc r < r0 the density is rho = a y + sum_{j >= 1} h_{2j+1} with h_n in V_n, the series
converging with all derivatives; then F_0 = a + O(r^2) and F_k = O(r^{2k}), so M_m is finite. On that disc write
int_r^inf F_m s^{1-2m} ds = M_m - int_0^r F_m s^{1-2m} ds in (1) and integrate termwise. The term a y gives -(a/8) r^2
sin 2th = -(a/4) x y, and the constants M_m give (M_m/2) S_{2m,2m}. For h_n = S_{n,p} (p = 2k + 1, so F_k = r^{n-1})
the two integrals give
    P S_{n,p} = - S_{n+1,p+1}/(2 (n + p + 2)) - [p > 1] S_{n+1,p-1}/(2 (n - p + 2)),   (2)
since int_0^r s^{2k+3} s^{n-1} ds = r^{n+p+2}/(n + p + 2) and int_0^r s^{n-1} s^{1-2k} ds = r^{n-p+2}/(n - p + 2).
Hence on r < r0
    psi = (M_1 - a/4) x y + sum_{m >= 2} (M_m/2) S_{2m,2m} + P h,   h = sum_j h_{2j+1},   (3)
with P extended linearly. The operator P is a local inverse: d_x S_{n,p} = ((n - p)/2) S_{n-1,p+1} + ((n + p)/2)
S_{n-1,p-1} (with S_{n-1,0} = 0) and Lap S_{m,k} = (m^2 - k^2) S_{m-2,k}, and
(n + 1)^2 - (p + 1)^2 = (n - p)(n + p + 2), (n + 1)^2 - (p - 1)^2 = (n + p)(n - p + 2), give -Lap P h = d_x h. For
p = n the first term of (2) is harmonic; it is part of the canonical stream and must be kept. In the construction
M_1 = a/4 - D, M_2 = H > 0 and M_m = 0 for m >= 3, so that psi = -D x y + (H/2) S_{4,4} + P h near 0 and
psi_xy(0) = -D.

Step 2 (the linear operator). Since c X + grad^perp(-D x y) = (A x, y) and R[a y] = 0 for the stream -D x y, for
rho = a y + h and psi = -D x y + psi_H + P h with psi_H = (H/2) S_{4,4} one has
    R = L h + a d_x psi_H + U_H . grad h + U[h] . grad h,   L h = (A x d_x + y d_y - 1) h + a d_x P h,   (4)
with U_H = grad^perp psi_H and U[h] = grad^perp P h (grad^perp = (-d_y, d_x)). L maps V_n to V_n. From A x d_x + y
d_y = c (x d_x + y d_y) + D (x d_x - y d_y), (x d_x - y d_y) S_{n,p} = ((n - p)/2) S_{n,p+2} + ((n + p)/2) S_{n,p-2},
and d_x P S_{n,p} = -S_{n,p}/4 - (n - p) S_{n,p+2}/(4 (n + p + 2)) - [p > 1] (S_{n,p}/4 + (n + p) S_{n,p-2}/(4
(n - p + 2))), the matrix of L on V_n in the basis S_{n,2k+1} (k = 0, ..., j) is, with lam = n - 1 = 2j, tridiagonal
with diagonal
    d_0 = (c + 1) lam/2 - a/4,   d_k = c lam + D - a/2   (k >= 1),
and, for k >= 0, entries u_k (row k, column k + 1) and u'_k (row k + 1, column k)
    u_k = (lam + 2k + 4) [2D (lam - 2k) - a]/(4 (lam - 2k)),
    u'_k = (lam - 2k) [2D (lam + 2k + 4) - a]/(4 (lam + 2k + 4)).   (5)
For d <= j + 1 let A_d(lam) be its leading d x d block (rows and columns k = 0, ..., d - 1): it is the matrix of Pi L
restricted to span{S_{n,1}, ..., S_{n,2d-1}}, where Pi deletes the modes above 2d - 1 (for d = j + 1 it is the whole
matrix). For d = 2 it is the matrix A(lam) of A.3.63, Step 2.

Step 3 (determinant, weighted dominance and the exceptional sets). Expanding along the last row, det A_d = P_d with
P_d as in 3.65: u_k u'_k = [2D (lam - 2k) - a][2D (lam + 2k + 4) - a]/16 = Q_k, since the two factors are 2D
(lam + 2) - a -+ 4D (k + 1). The leading coefficients of P_0, P_1, P_k in a are 1, -1/4 and -1/2 times that of P_{k-1}
minus 1/16 times that of P_{k-2}, so that of P_k is (-1/4)^k, and every P_d(lam, .) is a nonzero polynomial of degree
d. For lam = 2j put W = diag(omega_k) with omega_k = binom(2j + 1, j - k) and A~_d = W^{-1} A_d W. Since
omega_{k+1}/omega_k = (lam - 2k)/(lam + 2k + 4), the off-diagonal entries of A~_d are [2D (lam - 2k) - a]/4 (row k,
column k + 1) and [2D (lam + 2k + 4) - a]/4 (row k + 1, column k). At a = 0 these are >= 0 (lam - 2k >= 2 for
k <= d - 2), and the diagonal entry minus the off-diagonal row sum is lam in every row (first row: (c + 1) lam/2 - D
lam/2; interior row k: c lam + D - D (lam - 2k)/2 - D (lam + 2k + 2)/2), except in a last row with d < j + 1, where it
is lam + D (lam - 2d + 2)/2 >= lam. The coefficient of a in A~_d has absolute row sums at most 1 (entries -1/4 on the
first diagonal entry, -1/2 on the others, -1/4 off the diagonal). So for real a and every x, ||A~_d
x||_inf >= (lam - |a|) ||x||_inf, and if 2j > |a|,
    ||A~_d(2j)^{-1}||_inf <= 1/(2j - |a|)   (maximum absolute row sum).   (6)
For finite N put d_j = min(N, j + 1), and for N = inf put d_j = j + 1; then E^N (E^inf) is the set of a with
P_{d_j}(2j, a) = 0 for some j >= 1. On [-B0, B0], by (6) only j <= B0/2 can contribute, each with at most d_j roots;
so E^N and E^inf are finite on bounded intervals. For N = 2, d_j = 2 for all j, and 16 P_2(lam, a) = I(a, lam) of
3.63, so E^2 = E_c. If c is an integer >= 2, then for lam = 2j the polynomials 4 P_1 = 2 (c + 1) lam - a, 4 (c
lam + D - a/2) = 4 c lam + 4 D - 2 a and 16 Q_k = [2D (lam + 2) - a]^2 - 16 D^2 (k + 1)^2 have integer coefficients,
so by the recursion 4^d P_d(2j, a) is a polynomial in a with integer coefficients, and its leading coefficient is 4^d
(-1/4)^d = (-1)^d; by the rational root theorem its rational roots are integers. Hence every rational element of E^N
and of E^inf is an integer (the irrational real roots are not controlled), and every rational a that is not an integer
lies outside all of these sets.

Step 4 (a norm). For a homogeneous polynomial g of degree n in (w, v), g = sum_mu g_mu w^mu v^{n-mu}, put
||g||_n = max_mu |g_mu|/binom(n, mu). By Vandermonde's identity ||f g||_{p+q} <= ||f||_p ||g||_q. Since (mu + 1)
binom(n, mu + 1) = (n - mu) binom(n, mu) = n binom(n - 1, mu), ||d_w g||, ||d_v g|| <= n ||g||_n, and with
d_x = d_w + d_v, d_y = i (d_w - d_v), ||d_x g||_{n-1}, ||d_y g||_{n-1} <= 2n ||g||_n. For g = sum_k s_k S_{n,2k+1} in
V_n (n = 2j + 1), the coefficient of w^{j+1+k} v^{j-k} is s_k/(2i) and binom(n, j + 1 + k) = omega_k, so
||g||_n = max_k |s_k|/(2 omega_k): it is the weighted norm of Step 3 up to the common factor 1/2, deleting modes does
not increase it, and the operator norm of A_d^{-1} in it equals ||A~_d^{-1}||_inf. For the stream, let P0
g = sum_{mu=1}^{n} g'_mu w^mu v^{n+1-mu} with g'_mu = -(1/4) (g_mu/(n - mu + 1) + g_{mu-1}/mu); then -4 d_w d_v P0
g = (d_w + d_v) g, that is -Lap P0 g = d_x g, and since binom(n + 1, mu) (n - mu + 1) = (n + 1) binom(n, mu) and mu
binom(n + 1, mu) = (n + 1) binom(n, mu - 1), ||P0 g||_{n+1} <= ||g||_n/(2 (n + 1)). For g in V_n, P g - P0 g is
harmonic of degree n + 1 with only the pure powers w^{n+1}, v^{n+1}, which occur in (2) only for p = n; so P g - P0
g = -s_j S_{n+1,n+1}/(4 (n + 1)) (s_j the coefficient of S_{n,n}) with |s_j| <= 2 ||g||_n and
||S_{n+1,n+1}||_{n+1} = 1/2. Hence ||P g||_{n+1} <= ||g||_n/(n + 1) and
    ||d_x P g||_n, ||d_y P g||_n <= (3/2) ||g||_n <= 2 ||g||_n.   (7)
Also |g(w, v)| <= ||g||_n (|w| + |v|)^n.

Step 5 (the local solution). Fix H > 0, N (finite, or inf) and a >= 4c + 20 not in E^N (E^inf); in fact the argument
of this step needs only a > 0 not in the exceptional set. Let Pi_N be the projection deleting the sine modes above
2N - 1 (Pi_inf = identity), and on V_{2j+1} let L^N be the compressed operator Pi_N L restricted to the span of the
modes 1, ..., 2 d_j - 1; its matrix is A_{d_j}(2j), which is invertible since a is not exceptional. Seek
h = sum_{j >= 1} h_{2j+1} with h_{2j+1} in that span. By (4), Pi_N R = 0 degree by degree is equivalent to h = Gamma
h,
    Gamma h = -(L^N)^{-1} Pi_N { a d_x psi_H + U_H . grad h + U[h] . grad h },   (8)
where the right side is computed degree by degree (at degree 2j + 1 it involves only h_3, ..., h_{2j-1}, since U_H has
degree 3 and U[h_p] degree p). Put
    K = max { 2, max_{1 <= j <= ceil(a)} 2j ||A~_{d_j}(2j)^{-1}||_inf };
by (6), 2j ||A~_{d_j}(2j)^{-1}||_inf <= 2j/(2j - a) < 2 for j > ceil(a), so ||(L^N)^{-1}|| <= K/(2j) on V_{2j+1} for
every j >= 1. Now a d_x psi_H = 2 a H S_{3,3} has norm a H, and both components of U_H = (-H (w^3 + v^3), 2 H S_{3,3})
have norm H. With the norm ||h||_t = sum_{j >= 1} ||h_{2j+1}|| t^j (0 < t <= 1) and the estimates of Step 4: the
source gives (K/2) a H t; U_H . grad h_{2j+1} has degree 2j + 3 and norm <= 2 H 2 (2j + 1) ||h_{2j+1}||, multiplied by
K/(2j + 2), at most 4 K H ||h_{2j+1}||; U[h_p] . grad h_q (p, q >= 3, degree n = p + q - 1) has norm <= 2 (2
||h_p||)(2q ||h_q||), multiplied by K/(n - 1) with q/(n - 1) <= 1, at most 8 K ||h_p|| ||h_q||. Hence, with alpha = K
a H/2, beta = 4 K H, gamma = 8 K,
    ||Gamma h||_t <= alpha t + beta t ||h||_t + gamma ||h||_t^2,
    ||Gamma h - Gamma h'||_t <= (beta t + gamma (||h||_t + ||h'||_t)) ||h - h'||_t.
Take t = min{1, 1/(4 beta), 1/(16 gamma alpha)} and S = 2 alpha t; then alpha t = S/2, beta t <= 1/4 and gamma
S <= 1/8, so Gamma maps the ball ||h||_t <= S of the Banach space of such series into itself (at most 7S/8) with
Lipschitz constant at most 1/2, and has a unique fixed point there. Its coefficients are real (the data and Gamma
preserve real polynomials). From ||h_{2j+1}|| <= S t^{-j} and |h_{2j+1}| <= ||h_{2j+1}|| (2r)^{2j+1} on the real
plane, the series for h, and by Step 4 the series for P h, converge with all derivatives on r < sqrt(t)/2, to real
analytic functions; there rho = a y + h and psi = -D x y + psi_H + P h satisfy -Lap psi = rho_x and Pi_N R = 0, that
is R_1 = ... = R_{2N-1} = 0 for finite N and R = 0 for N = inf.

Step 6 (cubic jet and sign near 0). At degree 3, d_1 = 2 for every N >= 2, and (8) reads A_2(2) (f_1, g_1)^T + (0, 2 a
H)^T = 0 for h_3 = f_1 S_{3,1} + g_1 S_{3,3}. As in A.3.63, Step 2, with F(a) = 16 P_2(2, a) = a^2 - (4c + 20)
a + 128c - 64,
    f_1 = -24 H a (a - 4c + 4)/F(a),   g_1 = 8 H a (a - 4c - 4)/F(a),
and h_3 = b x^2 y + e y^3 with b = f_1 + 3 g_1 = -192 H a/F(a), e = f_1 - g_1 = -32 H a (a - 4c + 2)/F(a). For
a >= 4c + 20, F(a) = a (a - 4c - 20) + 128c - 64 > 0 and a - 4c + 2 >= 22, so b < 0 and e < 0; let m = min(-b,
-e) > 0. Each h_n is odd in y, so |h_n(x, y)/y| <= sup |d_y h_n| on the segment from (x, 0) to (x, y), which is at
most 2n ||h_n|| (2r)^{n-1}; with ||h_{2j+1}|| <= S t^{-j},
    |(h - h_3)/y| <= 2S sum_{j >= 2} (2j + 1) (4r^2/t)^j <= 640 S r^4/t^2   for 4r^2/t <= 1/2,
since sum_{j >= 2} (2j + 1) s^j = s^2 (5 - 3s)/(1 - s)^2 <= 20 s^2 for s <= 1/2. Put r1^2 = min{t/16, m t^2/(1280 S)}.
Then on 0 < r <= r1, with q = rho/(a y) extended smoothly to y = 0,
    q = 1 + (b x^2 + e y^2)/a + (h - h_3)/(a y) <= 1 - m r^2/(2a) < 1.   (9)

Step 7 (extension). Put r2 = r1/8, r3 = r1/4, r4 = r1/2, r5 = 3 r1/4. Let Z(u) = e^{-1/u} for u > 0 and 0 otherwise,
sigma(u) = Z(u)/(Z(u) + Z(1 - u)), chi(r) = 1 - sigma((r - r2)/(r3 - r2)), zeta(r) = sigma((r - r3)/(r4 - r3))
[1 - sigma((r - r5)/(r1 - r5))], eta(u) = e^{-1/(u (1 - u))} for 0 < u < 1 and 0 otherwise, and
phi(r) = eta((r - r4)/(r5 - r4)). Let F_k be the angular coefficients of the local solution (F_k = 0 for k >= N when N
is finite). For k >= 1 put
    I_k = int_0^inf phi(s) s^{1-2k} ds > 0,   C_k = (M_k - int_0^inf chi(s) F_k(s) s^{1-2k} ds)/I_k,
with M_1 = a/4 - D, M_2 = H, M_k = 0 (k >= 3); for finite N, C_k = 0 for k > max(N - 1, 2). For N = inf the C_k decay
geometrically: for k >= 1 and s <= r3, the coefficient of S_{n,2k+1} in h_n (n = 2j + 1 >= 2k + 1) has modulus at most
2 omega_k ||h_n|| <= 2^{n+1} S t^{-j}, so |F_k(s)| <= 4S sum_{j >= k} (4 s^2/t)^j <= 8S (4/t)^k s^{2k} (here 4
s^2/t <= 1/64); the estimate is used only for k >= 1 (F_0(0) = a). So for k >= 3 the numerator of C_k is at most 4S
(4/t)^k r3^2. On the middle third [7 r1/12, 2 r1/3] of the support of phi, phi >= e^{-9/2}, so I_k >= e^{-9/2} (r1/12)
(2 r1/3)^{1-2k}, and
    |C_k| <= C* b*^k   (k >= 3),   C* = (9/2) e^{9/2} S,   b* = 16 r1^2/(9t) <= 1/9.   (10)
Put B = 1 + 3 |C_1| + 5 |C_2| + C* b*^3 (7 - 5 b*)/(1 - b*)^2 (the last term bounds sum_{k >= 3} (2k + 1) |C_k|, since
sum_{k >= 3} (2k + 1) b^k = b^3 (7 - 5b)/(1 - b)^2) and define
    rho_ext = chi rho - B r zeta(r) sin th + r phi(r) sum_{k >= 1} C_k sin (2k + 1) th.   (11)
By (10) the series and all its derivatives converge uniformly on the annulus r4 <= r <= r5, which is bounded away from
0 (angular derivatives give factors polynomial in k); so rho_ext is smooth, compactly supported, has the parities, and
has only the modes 1, 3, ..., max(2N - 1, 5) for finite N. Sign: on r <= r3 only chi rho is present, and chi
q <= max(q, 0) < 1 off 0 by (9); on r3 < r < r1 the first term vanishes, rho_ext/y = -B zeta <= 0 off the support of
phi, and on the support of phi (where zeta = 1), since |sin (2k + 1) th/sin th| <= 2k + 1 and phi <= 1,
rho_ext/y <= -B + sum_{k >= 1} (2k + 1) |C_k| <= -1; elsewhere rho_ext = 0. So q = rho_ext/(a y) < 1 off 0, and
q(0) = 1. Moments: for k >= 1 the coefficient of rho_ext is F_k^ext = chi F_k + C_k phi, so int_0^inf F_k^ext s^{1-2k}
ds = M_k exactly; the first-mode bump changes only F_0^ext, which enters (1) only through lower integrals, at radii
r > r3. Hence for r <= r2 every lower integral in (1) and every int_0^r F_m s^{1-2m} ds is that of the local solution,
and the upper integrals are M_m - int_0^r F_m s^{1-2m} ds: by (1) and (3) the canonical stream of rho_ext equals
-D x y + psi_H + P h on r <= r2 (for N = inf, (1) applies because rho_ext is smooth with compact support, and the
termwise integration of Step 1 is justified on r <= r2 by the convergence of Step 5). The velocity is that of 3.1(i):
it is the Green-function velocity of a smooth compactly supported density, has the parities, and is O(1/r) at
infinity. So psi_xy(0) = -D, rho_y(0) = a, the cubic part is b x^2 y + e y^3, and on r <= r2 the conclusions of Step 5
hold: R_1 = ... = R_{2N-1} = 0 (finite N), R = 0 (N = inf).

Step 8 (dilation and nonprofile). For l > 0 put rho_l(X) = l rho_ext(X/l). Its canonical stream is l^2 psi(X/l) and
its velocity l U(X/l), so R[rho_l](X) = l R[rho_ext](X/l), (R[rho_l])_k(r) = l R_k(r/l); the slope, psi_xy(0), the
parities, the modes and q(X/l) are unchanged, while H becomes H/l^2 and (b, e) becomes (b, e)/l^2 (the signs are
kept). Given R0 > 0, take l = R0/r2; the conclusions hold on r <= R0. A nonzero smooth compactly supported density odd
in y has a positive maximum at some X0; there grad rho = 0 and R(X0) = -rho(X0) < 0, so rho_l is not a profile.

Scope. Only the projections R_1, ..., R_{2N-1}, or the full equation, are imposed, and only on a disc; the densities
are smooth and compactly supported, their canonical velocities have the parities of Section 2 and are O(1/r) at
infinity, q(0) = 1 and q < 1 elsewhere, and they are not profiles. The moments M_m enter as fixed data, not as
unknowns: in the radial system of A.3.63, Step 2, extended to the modes 1, 3, ..., 2N - 1 with the upper integrals as
unknowns, integer resonances occur for every a when N >= 3 (for N = 3 the characteristic polynomial of the
linearization at 0 has the factor j (j - 1) (j + 2) (j + 3) (j + 4), checked symbolically), and excluding slopes does
not remove them; Steps 5-7 avoid them because the stream is given by (3). For N = 1 the construction gives no cubic
jet (Pi_1 (a d_x psi_H) = 0, so h = 0); the density for N = 2 satisfies R_1 = 0 as well. Existence at the excluded
slopes is not decided, the radius of the local solution and the constants are not uniform in a, and nothing is said
about exact profiles of the primary class.

## A.3.66 No exact profile has finite angular support outside a disc

Setting. rho is an exact profile of the primary class, c = c_l, p = 1/c, delta = 1 - p and D = c - 1 = c delta.
Suppose, for a contradiction, that rho(r, th) = sum_{j odd, j <= N} f_j(r) sin j th for r > R0. In this entry N, N',
R0, R1, R2, B, T, Phi, Phi', Phi_U, H, E, E', E_U, F, f, g, g_m, J_m, chi, Q, P, alpha, beta, beta_i, b, b', b0,
gamma', t, t1, t2, f1, f2, Lambda, C, n, a, n_k, s_k, sigma_i, M_i, A_k, b_k, c_ij, u, v, e1, e2, L, w, z, M are local
notation and i, j, k, l, m, d, q are indices or exponents. For a real b, S^b is the set of functions (or vector
fields) defined outside some disc whose Cartesian derivatives of order k are O(r^{b - k}) for every k >= 0; this
follows from |(r d_r)^k d_th^l f| <= C_{k, l} r^b for all k, l, since d_x and d_y are r^{-1} times combinations of r
d_r and d_th with smooth angular coefficients. An expression is a finite sum of terms r^s (log r)^d G(th) with d >= 0
an integer and G a trigonometric polynomial; its degrees are the exponents s that carry a nonzero term. A term of
degree s lies in S^{s'} for every s' > s. Velocities are written in polar components U_r = -psi_th/r, U_th = psi_r;
for a stream r^{s + 1} Q(log r) sin 2m th both components are terms of degree s and frequency 2m. Density terms have
odd sine frequencies and stream terms the frequencies 2m, m >= 1 (Section 2). Inputs: by 3.23, rho and U lie in S^p
and r^{-p} rho(r, .) -> Theta0 uniformly; by 3.7, Theta0(pi/2) = K != 0. Projecting on sin j th for r > R0 and letting
r -> inf shows that Theta0 is a trigonometric polynomial with odd sine frequencies at most N; let n be its highest
frequency and a != 0 the coefficient of sin n th.

Step 1 (radial transport). Put B = U . grad rho; by 3.23, B is in S^{2p - 1}. For r > R1 the equation (c X + U) . grad
rho = rho reads c r d_r rho = rho - B, that is d_r (r^{-p} rho) = -(1/c) r^{-p - 1} B. The right side is O(r^{p - 2}),
so integration along the ray from X to infinity, with r^{-p} rho -> Theta0, gives
    rho(X) = r^p Theta0(th) + (T B)(X),   (T f)(X) = (1/c) int_1^inf t^{-p-1} f(t X) dt   (|X| > R1).   (1)
If f is in S^b with b < p, then T f is in S^b: for a Cartesian derivative d^k of order k, d^k (T f)(X) = (1/c)
int_1^inf t^{k - p - 1} (d^k f)(t X) dt is bounded by C r^{b - k} int_1^inf t^{b - p - 1} dt. For s < p and an integer
d >= 0, from log(t r) = log r + log t and int_1^inf t^{-q-1} (log t)^i dt = i!/q^{i+1} (q > 0),
    T[r^s (log r)^d G(th)] = (r^s G(th)/c) sum_{i = 0}^{d} binom(d, i) i! (log r)^{d - i}/(p - s)^{i + 1}.   (2)
So T maps an expression with degrees below p to an expression with the same degrees and frequencies and no larger
logarithmic degrees.

Step 2 (exterior inverse lemma). Let f be a smooth density on R^2 with the parities of Section 2 and |f| <= C
(1 + r)^{gamma'} for some gamma' < 1, with only finitely many nonzero angular modes on r > R1. Suppose f = Phi + E on
r > R1, where Phi is an expression with degrees below 1 and E is in S^b, with b < 1 and b != -2m - 1 for every integer
m >= 1. Then for large r the canonical velocity of f is Phi_U + H + E_U, where E_U is in S^b, H is the velocity of a
finite sum of harmonic streams beta_m r^{-2m} sin 2m th with -2m - 1 > b, and Phi_U is an expression each of whose
terms is induced by a term r^s (log r)^d sin j th of Phi: it has degree s, frequency j - 1 or j + 1, and logarithmic
degree at most d, or at most d + 1 when s = -2m - 1 with 2m = j +- 1. Proof. Let chi be smooth and radial with chi = 0
for r <= R1 and chi = 1 for r >= 2 R1. Then f = chi Phi + F with F smooth, with the parities, sublinear growth,
finitely many modes for large r and F in S^b there. Each term of chi Phi and F has the parities and sublinear growth,
and the canonical inverse of 3.1 is linear, with the stream modes given by 3.1(iv): psi_m = (1/(4m)) [r^{-2m} int_0^r
s^{2m+1} g_m ds + r^{2m} int_r^inf s^{1-2m} g_m ds], where g_m is the sin 2m th coefficient of the x derivative of the
density. (a) A term chi r^s (log r)^d sin j th: for r >= 2 R1 the x derivative of r^s (log r)^d sin j th is r^{s-1}
times polynomials in z = log r in the modes j +- 1 (its sin (j + 1) th coefficient is r^{s-1} [(s - j) z^d + d
z^{d-1}]/2). For a source r^{s-1} P(z) sin 2m th the stream r^{s+1} Q(z) sin 2m th solves -Lap psi = source iff
-[Q'' + 2 (s + 1) Q' + ((s + 1)^2 - 4 m^2) Q] = P. If (s + 1)^2 != 4 m^2 the map Q -> left side is triangular with
nonzero diagonal on polynomials of degree at most deg P, so it has a solution of degree deg P. The case s + 1 = 2m is
impossible, since s < 1 <= 2m - 1. If s + 1 = -2m the equation reads -Q'' + 4 m Q' = P, which has a polynomial
solution of degree deg P + 1. On r > 2 R1 the canonical mode minus this solution solves the homogeneous mode equation,
so it is alpha r^{2m} + beta r^{-2m}; by 3.1(iv) the canonical mode is O(r^{s+1} (1 + log r)^{d+1} + r^{-2m}), and so
is the particular solution, while s + 1 < 2 <= 2m, so alpha = 0. The velocity of r^{s+1} Q(z) sin 2m th has degree s
and frequency 2m, and the harmonic part beta r^{-2m} sin 2m th has velocity degree -2m - 1; if -2m - 1 < b it lies in
S^b. (b) The remainder F: let F have only the frequencies up to N' on r > R2 (R2 >= 2 R1); then g = F_x has only the
stream frequencies up to N' + 1 there, and |(r d_r)^k g_m(r)| <= C_k r^{b - 1} for r > R2. For 2m <= N' + 1: the outer
integral is O(r^{b - 2m + 1}) because b - 2m < -1, so r^{2m} times it is O(r^{b + 1}); if 2m + b + 1 > 0 the inner
integral is O(r^{2m + b + 1}), and r^{-2m} times it is O(r^{b + 1}); if 2m + b + 1 < 0 the inner integral converges at
infinity to some J_m and equals J_m + O(r^{2m + b + 1}), and J_m gives the harmonic stream (J_m/(4m)) r^{-2m} sin 2m
th, with velocity degree -2m - 1 > b. Applying r d_r to the integrals reproduces g_m, so the same bounds hold for (r
d_r)^k of each remainder, and with finitely many modes the stream remainder is in S^{b + 1} and its velocity in S^b.
For 2m > N' + 1, g_m vanishes for s > R2, so psi_m = (J_m/(4m)) r^{-2m} with J_m = int_0^{R2} s^{2m+1} g_m ds and
|J_m| <= 2 R2^{2m+2} sup_{r <= R2} |g|. Each application of r d_r or d_th to r^{-2m} sin 2m th multiplies its size by
at most 2m, so for r >= 2 R2 the sum of these modes over 2m > M, with any fixed number of such derivatives, is bounded
by C (R2/r)^{M} with C depending on M and on the number of derivatives; for M large (M + 1 > -b) its velocity lies in
S^b, and the finitely many remaining modes with N' + 1 < 2m <= M are harmonic terms, in S^b when -2m - 1 < b. End of
proof.

Step 3 (finite expansions to every depth). Claim: for every b0 there are b < b0 and expressions Phi, Phi_U, H as in
Step 2 with rho - Phi in S^b and U - Phi_U - H in S^b. Choose b in (2p - 1, p) with b != -2m - 1; by (1), rho = r^p
Theta0 + T B with T B in S^{2p - 1}, so Phi = r^p Theta0 works for rho. Given rho = Phi + E with E in S^b, b < p, b
not a degree of Phi and b != -2m - 1, Step 2 applies to f = rho (rho has the frequencies up to N on r > R0, so E has
finitely many modes for large r) and gives U = Phi_U + H + E_U. The terms of Phi and Phi_U + H of degree p carry no
logarithm (the degree-p terms come from r^p Theta0, and p != -2m - 1), so Phi_U + H is in S^p and grad Phi in
S^{p - 1}. Hence B = (Phi_U + H) . grad Phi + E', with E' = (Phi_U + H) . grad E + E_U . grad Phi + E_U . grad E in
S^{p + b - 1} = S^{b - delta} (using 2b - 1 < p + b - 1). The product (Phi_U + H) . grad Phi = U_r rho_r + U_th
rho_th/r is an expression with degrees at most 2p - 1 < p, so by (1), (2) and Step 1, rho = r^p Theta0 + T[(Phi_U + H)
. grad Phi] + T E' is an expression plus a remainder in S^{b - delta}. Choose b' in (b - delta, b - delta/2) that is
not a degree of this expression and not of the form -2m - 1, and drop the terms of degree below b', which lie in
S^{b'} since the inequality of degrees is strict. This gives rho = Phi' + S^{b'} with b' < b - delta/2; finitely many
steps reach any b0. Uniqueness: an expression all of whose degrees exceed b and which is O(r^b) on r > R1 is zero, for
otherwise, with s its largest degree and d the largest logarithmic degree at s, r^{-s} (log r)^{-d} times it would
converge uniformly to a nonzero trigonometric polynomial while it tends to 0. Hence, after collecting equal degrees,
logarithmic powers and frequencies, the coefficients of the expansions of rho and of the total velocity U are
determined by rho and U and do not depend on the choices (the split of the velocity expansion into induced and
harmonic parts need not be unique at a resonance, where a constant can move between the two; nothing below uses that
split); the same argument applied to the projection on sin j th, which vanishes for r > R0 when j > N, shows that the
density expansion has no term of frequency j > N.

Step 4 (costs). Write the degree of a density or velocity term as p - t and call t its cost; let Lambda = {k
delta + 2l : k, l >= 0 integers}, which has finitely many elements below any bound. Induced velocity terms have the
cost of their density terms; the harmonic velocity of r^{-2m} sin 2m th has degree -2m - 1, so cost p + 2m + 1. In the
product (Phi_U + H) . grad Phi, an induced velocity term of cost t1 and a density term of cost t2 give degree
(p - t1) + (p - t2 - 1), so cost delta + t1 + t2, and a harmonic term and a density term of cost t2 give cost
delta + p + 2m + 1 + t2 = 2m + 2 + t2; T keeps degrees. The only term of cost 0 is r^p Theta0. Hence every density
cost lies in Lambda, and a density term of cost t > 0 is the image under T of the part of cost t of the product, whose
factors have costs at most t - delta (density, induced velocity) or are harmonic with t2 = t - 2m - 2.

Step 5 (frequencies). Put C = (n + 1)/delta, so C delta = n + 1 and C > 2. Claim: every density term of cost t has
frequency at most n + C t, and every induced velocity term of cost t has frequency at most n + 1 + C t. By induction
on t in Lambda: at t = 0 the density frequencies are at most n, and an induced velocity has frequency j +- 1. For
t > 0, the frequencies of a product of terms with frequencies f1, f2 are at most f1 + f2 (and are f1 + f2 or
|f1 - f2|); an induced velocity of cost t1 and a density term of cost t2 with delta + t1 + t2 = t give at most
(n + 1 + C t1) + (n + C t2) = n + C t, and a harmonic term of frequency 2m and a density term of cost t2 = t - 2m - 2
give at most 2m + n + C (t - 2m - 2) < n + C t, since 2m < C (2m + 2). The bound for induced velocities follows from
Step 2. Equality: a density term of cost t and frequency n + C t can only arise from an induced velocity term
attaining its bound times a density term attaining its bound, through the sum frequency, and an induced velocity term
attains its bound only when its density term does and the frequency is j + 1. By induction, equality occurs only at
the costs t = k delta (k >= 0) and the frequencies n_k := n + C k delta = (k + 1)(n + 1) - 1, and the sin n_k th
coefficient at cost k delta is the image under T of the sum, over i + j = k - 1, of the sin n_k th parts of the
products of the stream mode of frequency n_i + 1 induced at cost i delta with the density mode of frequency n_j at
cost j delta. Every contribution at cost k delta other than these maximal-frequency induced sum interactions, in
particular every interaction involving a harmonic term, has frequency at most n_k - 2 (a cost with several
representations in Lambda carries no additional terms; only the actual interactions count); the stream mode of
frequency n_i + 1 at cost i delta is induced only by the density mode of frequency n_i (there is no density mode
n_i + 2 at that cost), and no harmonic term reaches it (2m < n + 1 + C (p + 2m + 1)); harmonic terms enter the
products only through the strict bound above.

Step 6 (the top coefficients). Put s_k = p - k delta = (k + 1) p - k, and let A_k(z), a polynomial in z = log r, be
the coefficient of r^{s_k} sin n_k th in the density expansion; A_0 = a. Suppose A_0, ..., A_{k - 1} are constants
(k >= 1). For i < k, the sin (n_i + 1) th coefficient of the x derivative of A_i r^{s_i} sin n_i th is A_i (s_i - n_i)
r^{s_i - 1}/2, and -Lap (r^{s_i + 1} sin (n_i + 1) th) = [(n_i + 1)^2 - (s_i + 1)^2] r^{s_i - 1} sin (n_i + 1) th;
since n_i + s_i + 2 = (i + 1)(n + p) + 2 > 0 and n_i - s_i > 0, there is no resonance and the induced stream is beta_i
r^{sigma_i} sin M_i th with sigma_i = s_i + 1, M_i = n_i + 1 and beta_i = -A_i/(2 (n_i + s_i + 2)), a constant. Its
velocity is U_r = -beta_i M_i r^{sigma_i - 1} cos M_i th, U_th = beta_i sigma_i r^{sigma_i - 1} sin M_i th; with
rho_r = A_j s_j r^{s_j - 1} sin n_j th and rho_th/r = A_j n_j r^{s_j - 1} cos n_j th, and cos M th sin n th, sin M th
cos n th both having the coefficient 1/2 at sin (M + n) th, the sin n_k th coefficient of the product is (beta_i
A_j/2)(sigma_i n_j - M_i s_j) r^{s_k}, using sigma_i + s_j - 2 = s_k and M_i + n_j = n_k. All these are free of log r,
so by (2) with d = 0 and c (p - s_k) = c k delta = k D, A_k is a constant and
    k D A_k = sum_{i + j = k - 1} c_ij A_i A_j,   c_ij = (1/4) [1 - 2 (j + 1)(n + 1)/((i + 1)(n + p) + 2)].   (3)
Indeed, with u = i + 1 and v = j + 1, n_i = u (n + 1) - 1, s_i = 1 - u delta, and sigma_i n_j - M_i s_j = 2 v
(n + 1) - [u (n + p) + 2], while n_i + s_i + 2 = u (n + p) + 2. Sign: put e1 = u + v >= 2, e2 = u v, L = n + p and
