w = n + 1. Then c_ij + c_ji = 1/2 - (w/2) [v/(u L + 2) + u/(v L + 2)], and the bracket equals [L (e1^2 - 2 e2) + 2
e1]/[L^2 e2 + 2 L e1 + 4], which decreases in e2; at its largest value e2 = e1^2/4 it equals 2 e1/(L e1 + 4). Since e1
(2 w - L) = e1 (n + 2 - p) > 4, 2 e1/(L e1 + 4) > 1/w, so c_ij + c_ji < 0 for all i, j (including i = j, so c_ii < 0).
If A_i = (-1)^i a^{i + 1} b_i with b_i > 0 for i < k, then A_i A_j = (-1)^{k - 1} a^{k + 1} b_i b_j for i + j = k - 1,
and grouping the terms (i, j) and (j, i) in (3) gives k D A_k = (-1)^k a^{k + 1} times a positive number; as k D > 0,
A_k = (-1)^k a^{k + 1} b_k with b_k > 0.

Conclusion. Choose k with n_k > N. Step 3 with b0 < s_k gives the expansion through degree s_k, its coefficient of
r^{s_k} sin n_k th is A_k != 0 by Steps 5 and 6, and by Step 3 it is 0 since n_k > N. This contradiction proves the
statement. (If n = N, k = 1 suffices: n_1 = 2n + 1 and A_1 = c_00 a^2/D = (p - n) a^2/(4 D (n + p + 2)) != 0.)

Scope. Given the symbol bounds of 3.23 and Theta0 != 0 (3.7), the proof uses c > 1, the canonical velocity and its
parities, the smoothness and growth bound needed for the interior moments J_m, and the equation only for r > R1; this
does not assert that 3.7 and 3.23 themselves need only exterior information. Only finite angular support with one N on
the region r > R0 is excluded; densities whose angular frequencies have no uniform bound outside every disc are not
covered by this argument. Result 3.67 shows that in every exact profile the number of nonzero modes on the circle of
radius r tends to infinity, and gives asymptotic lower bounds for finite-mode approximations; finitely many modes on
each circle, with a number growing with r, are not excluded by what is proved here. The expansions of Step 3 are
finite at each depth; no convergence of an infinite expansion is asserted. For R0 = 0 the statement is 3.10, whose
proof in A.3.10 uses only the top mode of the equation and the growth bound.

## A.3.67 A finite leading trace forces infinitely many angular modes, and the number of modes tends to infinity

Setting. Notation as in A.3.66, except that no assumption on the angular support of rho is made. Theta0 is a
trigonometric polynomial; it has odd sine frequencies by the parities; n is its highest frequency and a != 0 the
coefficient of sin n th. In this entry H_m, lambda, mu, v, psi_rem, eps_k, Pi_N, P, rho_j, theta_j, C(r), E_M, J, M,
R_M, V_M, N_0, M_1, K, f, chi, R_k, E, chi_0, kappa, f_kappa, Psi and eta are further local notation.

Step 2' (canonical inverse without a support assumption). Let f be smooth on R^2 with the parities of Section 2 and f
in S^b outside a disc, with b < 1 and b != -2m - 1 for every integer m >= 1, and let g_m be the sin 2m th coefficient
of f_x. Claim: the canonical stream of f is psi = sum_{m >= 1, -2m - 1 > b} (J_m/(4m)) r^{-2m} sin 2m th + psi_rem,
where J_m = int_0^inf s^{2m+1} g_m(s) ds (finitely many convergent integrals) and psi_rem is in S^{b + 1}; so the
velocity is that of these harmonic terms plus a remainder in S^b. Proof. The canonical inverse of 3.1 applies to f,
which is smooth, has the parities and satisfies |f| + (1 + r)|grad f| <= C (1 + r)^{gamma'} for some gamma' < 1; so
the canonical stream exists, is unique, and by 3.1(iv) its modes are psi_m(r) = (1/(4m)) [r^{-2m} int_0^r s^{2m+1} g_m
ds + r^{2m} int_r^inf s^{1-2m} g_m ds]; the outer integral converges since g_m = O(r^{b - 1}) and b < 1 <= 2m - 1. Put
t = log r and H_m(t) = e^{(1 - b) t} g_m(e^t). For all integers j, L >= 0, sup over real t of |d_t^j H_m(t)| <= C_{j,
L} m^{-L}: d_t = r d_r, so d_t^j H_m is r^{1 - b} times a combination of (r d_r)^i g_m with i <= j; for large r, L
integrations by parts in th in the Fourier coefficient and f_x in S^{b - 1} give |(r d_r)^i g_m| <= C (2m)^{-L}
r^{b - 1}; on bounded annuli the bound follows from smoothness, and near r = 0 from the boundedness of (r d_r)^i
d_th^L f_x there (r d_r and d_th are smooth vector fields) together with r^{1 - b} -> 0. Put lambda = 2m + b + 1 and
mu = 2m - b - 1 > 0. The substitutions s = r e^{-v} in the inner and s = r e^{v} in the outer integral give, when
lambda > 0,
    r^{-b-1} psi_m(r) = (1/(4m)) [int_0^inf e^{-lambda v} H_m(t - v) dv + int_0^inf e^{-mu v} H_m(t + v) dv],   (4)
and, when lambda < 0, where J_m converges because 2m + b < -1, writing the inner integral as J_m - int_r^inf s^{2m+1}
g_m ds,
    r^{-b-1} [psi_m(r) - (J_m/(4m)) r^{-2m}] = (1/(4m)) [int_0^inf e^{-mu v} H_m(t + v) dv - int_0^inf e^{lambda v} H_m(t + v) dv].   (5)
Hence every t-derivative of the left sides of (4) and (5) is bounded, uniformly in t, by C_{j, L} m^{-L}
(1/|lambda| + 1/mu)/(4m); lambda != 0 by the assumption on b, and lambda < 0 only for the finitely many m with
2m < -b - 1. Since (r d_r)^i (r^{b + 1} F(t)) = r^{b + 1} (b + 1 + d_t)^i F(t) and d_th^l multiplies a mode by at most
(2m)^l, taking L > l + 1 shows that the series of the remainder modes, after any fixed number of applications of r d_r
and d_th, converges absolutely and is O(r^{b + 1}) uniformly in r; so psi_rem is in S^{b + 1}. Since this series and
the Fourier series of the canonical stream have the same modes, they agree; the series is not used near r = 0, where
the canonical stream is smooth by 3.1. End of proof. The exclusion b != -2m - 1 is necessary: f = y/(1 + r^2)^2 is in
S^{-3}, its canonical stream is psi_1(r) sin 2 th with psi_1(r) = -(1/(4 r^2))
[log(1 + r^2) + (1 + r^2)^{-1} - 1] = -(1/2) r^{-2} log r + O(r^{-2}) (checked symbolically, together with -Lap
psi = f_x and psi_1 = -r^2/8 + O(r^4) at 0), and its velocity is not in S^{-3}.

Step 2 without the support assumption. In Step 2 of A.3.66 drop the hypothesis of finitely many modes. Part (a) is
unchanged, since each term of chi Phi has finitely many modes; part (b) is replaced by Step 2' applied to F, which is
smooth on R^2, has the parities and lies in S^b for large r. The conclusion of Step 2 holds as stated, with H a finite
sum of harmonic terms from part (a) and from Step 2'.

Steps 3 to 6. Step 3 of A.3.66, with Step 2 as just modified, applies to f = rho without a support assumption and
gives expansions of rho and U to every depth, unique after collecting equal degrees, logarithmic powers and
frequencies; its last clause (no frequency above N) is not used. Steps 4, 5 and 6 use only these expansions and hold
verbatim: the coefficient of r^{s_k} sin n_k th in the density expansion is the constant A_k != 0 of (3) of A.3.66,
and every density term of cost t has frequency at most n + C t (Step 5).

Conclusion. Fix k and take, by Step 3, an expansion rho = Phi + E with E in S^b and b < s_k. On projecting on sin n_k
th, the terms of Phi of cost t < k delta do not contribute, since their frequencies are at most n + C t < n_k; the
terms of cost k delta contribute exactly A_k r^{s_k}, since every other term of that cost has frequency at most
n_k - 2; the remaining terms of Phi have degrees below s_k, are finitely many and carry powers of log r; and E
contributes O(r^b), with each r-derivative lowering the order by one. Choosing eps_k > 0 smaller than s_k - b and than
the gaps between s_k and the lower degrees of Phi gives rho_{n_k}(r) = A_k r^{s_k} + O(r^{s_k - eps_k}) and the stated
derivative bounds. For N >= n odd, the first k with n_k > N, and any P whose modes are sin j th with j <= N, the
coefficient rho_{n_k} of rho equals that of g = rho - P; since int_0^{2 pi} |sin n_k th| dth = 4,
|rho_{n_k}(r)| <= (4/pi) sup_th |g(r, th)|, and by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality |rho_{n_k}(r)| <= pi^{-1/2} (int_0^{2
pi} |g(r, th)|^2 dth)^{1/2}. Dividing by r^{s_k} and letting r -> inf gives the two lower bounds of (b).

Part (c). For a function g of th and an odd j put g_j = (1/pi) int_0^{2 pi} g sin j th dth; as above |g_j| <= (4/pi)
sup |g| and |g_j| <= pi^{-1/2} ||g||, with ||.|| the L^2(0, 2 pi) norm. Let J be a set of M + 1 odd frequencies and P
a sum of at most M sine modes. Some j in J is not a frequency of P, so (rho(r, .) - P)_j = rho_j(r), and therefore
sup_th |rho(r, .) - P| >= (pi/4) min_{j in J} |rho_j(r)| and ||rho(r, .) - P|| >= sqrt(pi) min_{j in J} |rho_j(r)|.
The right sides do not depend on P, so they bound E_M(r) from below; no minimizer is needed, and the missing frequency
may depend on r and on P. If theta_j != 0 for every j in J, uniform convergence of r^{-p} rho(r, .) to Theta0 gives
r^{-p} rho_j(r) -> theta_j for each of the finitely many j in J, which gives the first pair of bounds. Moreover, the
set V_M of sums of at most M sine modes is invariant under multiplication by scalars, so r^{-p} E_M(r) is the distance
from r^{-p} rho(r, .) to V_M in the chosen norm; a distance to a set is 1-Lipschitz, so uniform convergence gives
r^{-p} E_M(r) -> dist(Theta0, V_M) in either norm, with no closedness of V_M or minimizer needed. Under the hypothesis
of (a), let Theta0 have N_0 nonzero coefficients, let M >= N_0 and M_1 = M + 1 - N_0 >= 1, and take for J the N_0
frequencies of Theta0 together with n_1, ..., n_{M_1}, which exceed n and are distinct odd frequencies. For j in the
support of Theta0, r^{-s_{M_1}} |rho_j(r)| -> inf, since p - s_{M_1} = M_1 delta > 0; by (a), r^{-s_{M_1}}
|rho_{n_k}(r)| -> inf for 1 <= k < M_1, since s_k - s_{M_1} = (M_1 - k) delta > 0, and r^{-s_{M_1}}
|rho_{n_{M_1}}(r)| -> |A_{M_1}|; this gives the second pair. In both cases every rho_j with j in J is nonzero for all
large r, so C(r) > M there. If Theta0 has at least M + 1 nonzero coefficients the first case applies; otherwise Theta0
is a trigonometric polynomial with N_0 <= M nonzero coefficients and the second applies.

Example for the scope. Fix p in (0, 1), a positive odd n and the numbers A_k of (a). Let chi be smooth on [0, inf),
equal to 0 on [0, 1] and to 1 on [2, inf), choose R_0 >= 2 and R_{k+1} > 2 R_k as below, and put f = sum_{k >= 0} A_k
chi(r/R_k) r^{s_k} sin n_k th (f = 0 for r <= R_0). With E = r d_r, every E^i chi(r/R) is bounded independently of R,
since chi' is supported in [1, 2]; so each product of at most j factors E and d_th applied to the k-th term is bounded
by C_j |A_k| (1 + |s_k| + n_k)^j r^{s_k} on r >= R_k, with C_j depending only on chi and j. For k >= 1 choose R_k so
large that C_j |A_k| (1 + |s_k| + n_k)^j R_k^{-k delta/2} <= 2^{-k} for every j <= k (no condition of this kind is
imposed on R_0, since for k = 0 the radius factor is 1); then for k >= 1 and j <= k those derivatives of the k-th term
are at most 2^{-k} r^{p - k delta/2}. Fix K and j: the terms with k >= max(j, 2K + 2) are bounded by 2^{-k}
r^{s_{K+1}} for r >= 1 (as p - k delta/2 <= s_{K+1}) and sum geometrically, each of the finitely many terms with
K < k < max(j, 2K + 2) is bounded, by the estimate before the choice of R_k, by C_j |A_k| (1 + |s_k| + n_k)^j
r^{s_k} <= C_j |A_k| (1 + |s_k| + n_k)^j r^{s_{K+1}} for r >= 1, and the first K + 1 cutoffs equal 1 for r >= 2 R_K;
so f - sum_{k <= K} A_k r^{s_k} sin n_k th is in S^{s_{K+1}}. The sum is locally finite, so f is smooth, has the
parities of Section 2 (n_k is odd) and finitely many modes on every circle; f is in S^p, r^{-p} f -> A_0 sin n th
uniformly, f_{n_k}(r) = A_k r^{s_k} for r >= 2 R_k, and by Step 2' with b = p (no harmonic term is retained) its
canonical velocity is in S^p. The function f vanishes near the origin. Let chi_0 be smooth and radial, equal to 1 near
0 and to 0 for r >= R_0, and put f_kappa = f + kappa y chi_0(r) with kappa != 0. Then f_kappa has the slope kappa at
the origin and all the properties just listed: y chi_0(r) has only the mode sin th, and by (iv) of 3.1 its canonical
stream is -(1/2) (int_0^inf s^3 chi_0(s) ds) r^{-2} sin 2 th for r >= R_0, whose velocity is in S^{-3}. Near 0 that
stream is -x y/4 (its sin 2 th mode is (r^2/4) int_0^inf s^{-1} (s chi_0'(s)/2) ds = -r^2/8 there), so psi_xy(0) for
f_kappa is that of f minus kappa/4. The origin relation psi_xy(0) = 1 - c_l of 3.2, which every solution with nonzero
slope satisfies, therefore holds for at most one value of kappa; for every other kappa != 0, f_kappa is smooth, has
the parities, a nonzero slope, the growth bound of the primary class, finitely many modes on every circle and all the
asymptotics above, and is not a profile. No transport equation is claimed for f or f_kappa. So the conclusions of
(a)-(c) cannot by themselves give infinitely many modes on one circle; that would need a further use of the equation.

Scope. Parts (a) and (b) give necessary conditions on exact profiles whose trace is a trigonometric polynomial, and
(c) on all exact profiles; they do not decide whether such profiles exist, and they allow an infinite tail of
lower-order angular terms; (a) and (b) say nothing when Theta0 has infinitely many modes, since the argument needs a
highest frequency of the trace. Only the coefficients at the top frequencies n_k are controlled: for instance, for
p = 1/2 and Theta0 = a sin th + eta sin 5 th, the coefficient of r^0 sin 3 th in the density expansion comes only from
the first correction r^{2p - 1} D^{-1} [-p Psi' Theta0 + (p + 1) Psi Theta0'], where r^{p + 1} Psi(th) is the leading
term of the stream, and it equals -a^2/28 + 67 a eta/70, which vanishes at eta = 5a/134 (checked symbolically). For
each k the mode n_k is nonzero only beyond a radius that may depend on k. The lower bounds concern r -> inf and do not
restrict approximations on bounded regions. The expansions are finite at each depth; no convergence of an infinite
expansion is asserted. The inputs are those of A.3.66: the symbol bounds of 3.23, which give rho, U in S^p and r^{-p}
rho(r, .) -> Theta0 uniformly, the canonical velocity and its parities, smoothness, and the equation for large r;
finiteness of Theta0 is the only additional hypothesis in (a) and (b), and (c) uses in addition only the uniform
convergence of r^{-p} rho. If rho has finite angular support outside a disc, Theta0 is a trigonometric polynomial and
rho_{n_k} = 0 for large r once n_k > N, so 3.66 follows.

## A.3.68 Far-field expansions for an arbitrary smooth trace

Setting. Notation as in A.3.66 and A.3.67. rho is smooth on R^2 with the parities of Section 2, its canonical velocity
U satisfies (c X + U) . grad rho = rho for r > R1, rho and U lie in S^p, and r^{-p} rho(r, .) -> Theta0 uniformly; for
an exact profile of the primary class these hypotheses hold by 3.23. No assumption is made on the angular content of
Theta0 or of rho, and Theta0 = 0 is allowed. In this entry an expression is a finite sum of terms r^s (log r)^d G(th)
with d >= 0 an integer and G smooth and 2 pi-periodic, with odd sine modes for density terms and the modes sin 2m th
(m >= 1) for stream terms; degrees, the classes S^b and the polar velocity components are as in A.3.66. Sigma_rho and
Sigma_H are as in 3.68, and a_r, G, P, Q, q_j, g_j, G_m, Q_m, V_m, chi, f, psi_0, h, Phi, h_m, beta_m, C_L, J, u, v
are local notation.

Step 0 (the trace). Put a_r(th) = r^{-p} rho(r, th). Since rho is in S^p, every d_th^j rho is O(r^p), so for r > R1
the a_r are bounded in C^{j+1} uniformly in r, for every j. By the Arzela-Ascoli theorem every sequence r_n -> inf has
a subsequence along which a_r converges in C^j, and the limit is Theta0 by the uniform convergence. Hence
a_r -> Theta0 in every C^j (otherwise a sequence staying at a fixed C^j distance from Theta0 would contradict this),
and Theta0 is smooth. In particular r^p Theta0 is a term of an expression in the present sense.

Step 1 is that of A.3.66; (1) and (2) hold for smooth G with the same proofs.

Step 2'' (one term with a smooth angular coefficient). Let s < 1, let P(z, th) be a polynomial in z of degree d whose
coefficients are smooth with odd sine modes, let chi be smooth and radial with chi = 0 for r <= R1 and chi = 1 for
r >= 2 R1, and put f = chi r^s P(log r, th). For r >= 2 R1, with z = log r and d_x = cos th d_r - (sin th/r) d_th,
    f_x = r^{s - 1} G(z, th),   G = cos th (s + d_z) P - sin th d_th P,   (1)
whose coefficients have the modes sin 2m th, m >= 1, and for a stream r^{s+1} Q(z, th),
    -Lap (r^{s+1} Q) = r^{s - 1} [-d_th^2 - (s + 1)^2 - 2 (s + 1) d_z - d_z^2] Q.   (2)
On sin 2m th the operator -d_th^2 - (s + 1)^2 is multiplication by 4m^2 - (s + 1)^2, which vanishes only if
s + 1 = -2m; s + 1 = 2m is impossible since s < 1 <= 2m - 1. Write G = sum_{j <= d} g_j(th) z^j. Off the resonant mode
(all modes if s + 1 is not of the form -2m), set q_j = 0 for j > d and solve downward [-d_th^2 - (s + 1)^2]
q_j = g_j + 2 (s + 1)(j + 1) q_{j+1} + (j + 2)(j + 1) q_{j+2}, which is (2) = G coefficient by coefficient in z; the
Fourier coefficients are divided by numbers 4m^2 - (s + 1)^2 of absolute value at least 2m^2 for all large m, so the
rapid decay of the Fourier coefficients is preserved and the q_j are smooth. In the resonant mode, s + 1 = -2m, the
equation for the coefficient Q_m(z) is -Q_m'' + 4m Q_m' = G_m(z); it is solved by Q_m(z) = int_0^z V_m with
V_m = sum_{i <= d} G_m^{(i)}/(4m)^{i+1}, since 4m V_m - V_m' = G_m, and Q_m has degree at most d + 1 (one more than
the degree of G_m if G_m != 0, and Q_m = 0 if G_m = 0). Put psi_0 = chi r^{s+1} Q(log r, th) and h = f_x + Lap psi_0.
Then h is smooth, odd in x and in y, and vanishes for r <= R1 and, by (1) and (2), for r >= 2 R1. Let Phi be the
canonical stream of h, that is the solution of -Lap Phi = h given by 3.1(iv) with h in place of the x derivative of
the density (the formula applies to any smooth compactly supported odd-odd source). For r >= 2 R1 it is
Phi = sum_{m >= 1} beta_m r^{-2m} sin 2m th with beta_m = (1/(4m)) int_0^{2 R1} t^{2m+1} h_m(t) dt, h_m the sin 2m th
coefficient of h. Integration by parts in th gives |h_m| <= C_L m^{-L} for every L, uniformly in t, so |beta_m| <= C_L
m^{-L} (2 R1)^{2m+2}/(4m (2m + 2)). Each application of r d_r or d_th to r^{-2m} sin 2m th multiplies its size by at
most 2m, so on r >= 4 R1 the series of the terms with 2m > M, with any fixed number of such derivatives, is bounded by
a constant times (2 R1/r)^{M}; for every b, retaining the finitely many harmonic terms with -2m - 1 > b leaves a
velocity in S^b. The stream psi_0 + Phi solves -Lap psi = f_x on R^2, has the parities of Section 2, and its velocity
is o(r) because s < 1, Q is polynomial in log r and Phi decays; by the uniqueness in 3.1 it is the canonical stream of
f. Conclusion: for large r the canonical velocity of f is an expression of degree s, with logarithmic degree at most d
except in the single mode 2m when s = -2m - 1 (degree at most d + 1 there), plus finitely many harmonic terms of
degrees -2m - 1 > b with constant coefficients, plus a remainder in S^b. The coefficients beta_m are moments of h,
that is of the cutoff decomposition, not moments of the noncompact source.

Step 3' (expansions to every depth). As Step 3 of A.3.66, with these changes. Given rho = Phi + E for r > R1, with Phi
an expression with degrees below 1 and E in S^b, where b < p is neither a degree of Phi nor in Sigma_H, write
rho = chi Phi + F; F is smooth with the parities and lies in S^b outside a disc, so Step 2' of A.3.67 applies to F,
and Step 2'' to each of the finitely many terms of chi Phi; by linearity of the canonical inverse, U = Phi_U + H + E_U
with Phi_U an expression of the degrees of Phi, H a finite sum of harmonic terms of degrees in Sigma_H above b, and
E_U in S^b. The degrees of Phi_U + H are at most p, and its terms of degree p, if any, carry no logarithm, since they
are induced by r^p Theta0 and p is not in Sigma_H; so Phi_U + H is in S^p (it need not have a nonzero term of degree
p: for Theta0 = 0 the leading velocity term can be harmonic). The remaining steps of the induction, the choice of b'
in (b - delta, b - delta/2) outside Sigma_H and the degrees of the current expression, and the uniqueness argument
(r^{-s} (log r)^{-d} times a nonzero difference would converge uniformly to a nonzero smooth function) are unchanged.
For b < p outside Sigma_rho and Sigma_H, descend below b and drop the terms of degree below b; the expansions so
obtained for different b agree on common degrees by uniqueness.

Step 4' (degrees). As in Step 4 of A.3.66: costs lie in Lambda = {k delta + 2l}, so the density degrees lie in
Sigma_rho and the velocity degrees in Sigma_rho or Sigma_H. Step 5 of A.3.66 (frequency bounds) is not used.

Step 5' (logarithms). A logarithm can be created only in the resonant mode of Step 2'': formula (2) of A.3.66 does not
raise logarithmic degrees, products of expressions free of log r are free of log r, the off-resonant inversion in Step
2'' preserves the degree in z, and the harmonic coefficients of Step 2'' and of Step 2' of A.3.67 are constants. A
density degree s = p - k delta - 2l = 1 - (k + 1) delta - 2l equals -2m - 1 if and only if (k + 1) delta = 2
(m + 1 - l). If delta is irrational the left side is irrational and the right side an integer, so this never happens;
starting from r^p Theta0, which carries no logarithm, every expression of the induction is then free of log r. Also k
delta + 2l = k' delta + 2l' forces k = k' and l = l', and a velocity term induced by a density degree never has a
degree in Sigma_H. If delta = u/v in lowest terms, the equation requires (k + 1) u = 2 v J with J = m + 1 - l, an
integer, and J >= 1 since the left side is positive; then m = J + l - 1, which must be at least 1. For example,
delta = 1/2, k = 3, l = 0 satisfies the divisibility with J = 1 but gives m = 0, which is not a stream frequency.
These conditions are necessary only: the projection of the source on the resonant mode can vanish (for s = -3 the
density term r^{-3} sin 3 th has a source with no sin 2 th part, while r^{-3} sin th gives the particular stream
-(1/2) r^{-2} log r sin 2 th). These conditions concern the creation of a logarithm. Once created, it propagates: off
resonance the inversion of Step 2'' divides a highest logarithmic coefficient by 4m^2 - (s + 1)^2 != 0, the operator T
multiplies it by 1/(c_l (p - s)) (formula (2) of A.3.66), and products move it to other degrees, so logarithmic terms
of rho and U can have degrees not of the form -2m - 1 (A.3.69, Step 4).

Scope. 3.68 gives necessary conditions on the far field of every exact profile. It does not say which coefficients are
nonzero (the top-frequency argument of A.3.66 and A.3.67 needs a highest frequency of Theta0), it does not determine
the harmonic coefficients, which are global data of rho, it asserts no convergence of the infinite expansion and no
control of the constants as the depth grows, and it does not decide existence.

## A.3.69 Forced logarithms for a pure first-mode trace

Setting. Hypotheses and notation of A.3.68, with Theta0 = A sin th, A != 0; c = c_l, s_k = p - k delta, and the
deficit of a density degree s is p - s. P_k, H_k, B, g_*, k_*, n, j, sigma, q are local notation.

Step 1 (deficits). By Step 4' of A.3.68, an induced interaction of density terms of deficits t1 and t2 produces
deficit delta + t1 + t2, and a harmonic velocity term of degree -2m - 1 (m >= 1) acting on a density term of deficit t
produces deficit 2m + 2 + t; the operator T and the induced part of the canonical inverse preserve degrees. The set {k
delta + 2l : k >= 0, l = 0 or l >= 2} contains 0 and is closed under both operations, since 2m + 2 >= 4, so every
density deficit lies in it. A deficit k delta can be reached without a harmonic factor only by chains of induced
interactions starting at r^p Theta0.

Step 2 (the pure recurrence). For n odd, with the sin 0 th term dropped,
    d_x (r^s sin n th) = r^{s-1} [((s - n)/2) sin (n + 1) th + ((s + n)/2) sin (n - 1) th].   (1)
If (s + 1)^2 != 4m^2 for every m >= 1, the source r^{s-1} G(th), G = sum_m G_m sin 2m th, has the particular stream
r^{s+1} H(th) with H_m = G_m/(4m^2 - (s + 1)^2), by (2) of A.3.68. With U_r = -r^{-1} psi_th and U_th = psi_r, a
stream term h r^sigma sin j th and a density term P r^s sin n th give
    U . grad = (h P/2) r^{sigma + s - 2} [(sigma n - j s) sin (n + j) th - (sigma n + j s) sin (n - j) th],   (2)
with sin (-i th) = -sin i th. Put P_0 = A sin th and, while s_i is not of the form -2m - 1, let H_i be the particular
stream polynomial of r^{s_i} P_i (stream exponent s_i + 1). Since (s_i + 1) + s_j - 2 = s_{i+j+1} and (c r d_r - 1)
r^{s_k} = -c k delta r^{s_k}, the equation c r rho_r - rho = -U . grad rho gives, for the coefficient of r^{s_k} when
no other term has that degree,
    P_k = (1/(c k delta)) sum_{i+j=k-1} B(H_i, P_j),   (3)
where B(H_i, P_j) is (2) summed over the modes of H_i and P_j, with sigma = s_i + 1, s = s_j and the radial power
removed. P_k is homogeneous of degree k + 1 in A. For k = 1: H_0 = -(A/(2 (p + 3))) sin 2 th and P_1 = -((3p + 1)
A^2/(4 c delta (p + 3))) sin th - (A^2/(4 c (p + 3))) sin 3 th (for c = 3, P_1 = -(3/40) A^2 sin th - (1/40) A^2 sin 3
th); the sin 3 th coefficient is A_1 of 3.67 for n = 1.

Step 3 (the two cases). For c = 3, delta = 2/3 and s_5 = -3 = -2m - 1 with m = 1. Every deficit with l >= 2 is at
least 4 > 5 delta, and k delta = k' delta + 2l with l >= 2 would need k - k' = 3l >= 6; no s_k with k <= 4 has the
form -2m - 1. For c = 5/2, delta = 3/5 and s_9 = -5 = -2m - 1 with m = 2; s_k = -3 has no integral solution, and k
delta = k' delta + 2l with l >= 2 would need 3 (k - k') = 10 l, so k - k' >= 10. In both cases, for k <= k_*, the only
density term of degree s_k is r^{s_k} P_k with P_k given by (3), the streams H_0, ..., H_{k_*-1} are nonresonant, and
P_{k_*} depends on A and c alone. Define g_* as the coefficient of r^{-2m-2} sin 2m th in d_x (r^{s_{k_*}} P_{k_*}),
computed from (1). Exact rational evaluation of (1)-(3) with A = 1 gives the values in 3.69(b) (checker, two
implementations, one with real sine products and one with signed Fourier coefficients and Cartesian derivatives; the
main analysis recomputed both values from (1)-(3) with its own code and obtained the same rationals).

Step 4 (the forced logarithms). In the mode sin 2m th at s = -2m - 1, (2) of A.3.68 with Q(z) = q z gives -Lap (q
r^{-2m} log r sin 2m th) = 4m q r^{-2m-2} sin 2m th. By Step 3 and since no earlier term carries a logarithm, the
source of the canonical stream at degree -2m - 2 in this mode is g_* r^{-2m-2} sin 2m th, so by the uniqueness of the
collected coefficients in 3.68(b) the coefficient of r^{-2m} log r sin 2m th in the stream is q = g_*/(4m); a harmonic
term beta r^{-2m} sin 2m th carries no logarithm and cannot cancel it. The highest logarithmic part of the velocity is
U_r = -(g_*/2) r^{-2m-1} log r cos 2m th, U_th = -(g_*/2) r^{-2m-1} log r sin 2m th; acting on grad (A r^p sin th) it
gives
    -(A g_*/4) r^{p-2m-2} log r [delta sin (2m - 1) th + (1 + p) sin (2m + 1) th].   (4)
No other term has a logarithm at the density degree t = p - 2m - 2. Indeed, arguing by decreasing degree, a
logarithmic term of U . grad rho needs a logarithmic factor, since products of terms free of log r are free of log r.
The logarithmic velocity terms have degree at most -2m - 1, the only one of degree -2m - 1 being the term above, and
the density gradient has degree at most p - 1, so their products have degree at most t, with equality only for (4).
The operator T keeps degrees and does not create logarithms, so every logarithmic density term has degree at most t,
and its products with the velocity, of degree at most p, have degree at most t - delta. The highest logarithmic part
of (c r d_r - 1) on r^t log r is c (t - p) = -2c (m + 1), so the density contains (4) divided by 2c (m + 1), the term
of 3.69(c). It is nonzero because A g_* != 0, delta > 0 and 1 + p > 0. For c = 3 there is no resonant density degree
above -3, and for c = 5/2 the only candidate above -5, the degree -3, does not occur; so these are the first
logarithmic terms.

Scope. The result uses the exact trace A sin th; traces with other angular content are treated in 3.71. Logarithms at
infinity are compatible with smoothness on R^2, so 3.69 excludes no profile; it shows that the logarithms permitted by
3.68(c) are not vacuous, and that a far-field expansion free of logarithms is impossible for these traces and these
values of c_l.

## A.3.70 Transport identities with weights depending on (r, rho)

Setting. Hypotheses and notation of 3.70; d_th denotes the angular derivative, and S_beta = int_0^{2 pi} |sin th|^beta
dth.

Step 1 (identity (1)). For Phi in C_c^inf((0, inf) x R), Phi(r, rho(X)) is smooth with compact support in R^2 \ {0}.
Since div W = 2 c_l, W . grad r = c_l r + U_r and W . grad rho = rho + E, the chain rule gives div(W Phi(r, rho)) = 2
c_l Phi + (c_l r + U_r) Phi_r + (rho + E) Phi_s, whose integral over the plane is 0. This is (1).

Step 2 (equivalence). If the left side of (1) vanishes for every Phi, then int E Phi_s(r, rho) dX = 0 for all Phi, so
the image measure nu_E of E dX under X -> (r, rho(X)) satisfies d_s nu_E = 0 as a distribution on (0, inf) x R. On
(r1, r2) x R with 0 < r1 < r2, nu_E is supported in |s| <= max of |rho| on the annulus, and a distribution on such a
strip with d_s nu_E = 0 and bounded s-support vanishes. Conversely nu_E = 0 gives int E Phi_s dX = 0. Testing nu_E = 0
against eta(r) chi(s), with eta in C_c^inf((0, inf)) and chi in C_c^inf(R), gives int r F_chi(r) eta(r) dr = 0, where
F_chi(r) = int_0^{2 pi} E(r, th) chi(rho(r, th)) dth is continuous in r; so F_chi = 0 for every r and every chi, that
is, on every circle the image of E(r, th) dth under th -> rho(r, th) vanishes, including its part on critical levels.
At a regular value s of rho(r, .), the coarea formula on the circle gives the density G(r, s) = r sum E/|rho_th| of
nu_E with respect to dr ds, the sum over the points with rho(r, th) = s. Near a regular pair (r, s) the finitely many
preimages are smooth inverse branches, so G is smooth there, and nu_E = 0 forces G = 0 pointwise on the set of regular
pairs. This does not assert that nu_E is absolutely continuous: a part carried by critical levels is not described by
G.

Step 3 (near 0). By parity rho_x = x g with g smooth, and rho_th = -y rho_x + x rho_y = x (rho_y - y
g) = x (a0 + O(r^2)). Choose r0 > 0 with |rho_y - y g - a0| < |a0|/2 on r < r0. For r < r0, rho(r, .) is strictly
monotone on each of the two arcs x > 0 and x < 0, with extrema at x = 0, and rho is even in x; so each s strictly
between the extrema is attained exactly at two mirror points, and it is a regular value. W_1 is odd in x and W_2,
rho_x/x and rho_y are even in x, so W . grad rho, and hence E, is even in x. By Step 2 the density G vanishes at each
such level, and there it equals 2 r E/|rho_th|, so E = 0 on the disc r < r0 off the y-axis, and by continuity on the
whole disc.

Step 4 (power weights). Off the zero set of rho, div(W r^alpha |rho|^beta) = [(2 + alpha) c_l + beta] r^alpha
|rho|^beta + alpha r^{alpha - 2} (U . X) |rho|^beta for an exact profile, from W . grad r^alpha = alpha c_l
r^alpha + alpha r^{alpha - 2} U . X and W . grad |rho|^beta = beta |rho|^beta. For every beta > 0 it holds in the
sense of distributions: on a compact annulus the chain rule applied to h_eps = (rho^2 + eps^2)^{beta/2} gives div(W
r^alpha h_eps) = [(2 + alpha) c_l + beta] r^alpha h_eps + alpha r^{alpha - 2} (U . X) h_eps - beta r^alpha eps^2
(rho^2 + eps^2)^{beta/2 - 1}; the last term is bounded by C eps^beta for 0 < beta <= 2 and by C eps^2 for beta > 2,
and the other terms converge uniformly on the annulus as eps -> 0. No assumption on the zero set is needed. Near 0,
|rho| <= C r and |U . X| <= C r^2, so both integrands are O(r^{alpha + beta + 1}) after the factor r dr; at infinity,
by 3.23, int |rho(r, th)|^beta dth = r^{beta p} (int |Theta0|^beta dth + o(1)), with a positive limit, and |U .
X| <= C r^{p + 1}. Hence M and V converge absolutely for -2 - beta < alpha < -2 - beta p, and V also at
alpha = -2 - beta p. The flux through the circle of radius R is R^{alpha + 2} int |rho|^beta (c_l + U_r/R) dth, which
is O(R^{alpha + beta + 2}) as R -> 0 and O(R^{alpha + beta p + 2}) as R -> inf; it vanishes at both ends inside the
strip, which gives 0 = [(2 + alpha) c_l + beta] M + alpha V. Here alpha < 0, and (2 + alpha) c_l + beta < -beta p
c_l + beta = 0, so V < 0. At alpha = -2 - beta p the coefficient of M vanishes, the flux tends to 0 at 0 and to c_l
int |Theta0|^beta dth at infinity, and integration over annuli gives alpha V = c_l int |Theta0|^beta dth.

Step 5 (the family rho_t). With A = A_t and I(r) = int_0^r s^2 A(s) ds, rho_x = (1/2)(A' - A/r) sin 2 th, and
B = -I/(2 r^2) satisfies -(B'' + B'/r - 4B/r^2) = (1/2)(A' - A/r) (direct differentiation with I' = r^2 A). The stream
B(r) sin 2 th is smooth (B/r^2 is a smooth function of r^2 near 0), odd in x and in y, and has velocity O(r^p) at
infinity, so it is the canonical stream. Near 0, A = a r + b r^3 + O(r^5) with b = a (p - 1)/2 (f vanishes on r < 1),
so I = a r^4/4 + O(r^6), psi = -(a/8) r^2 sin 2 th + O(r^4), psi_xy(0) = -a/4 = 1 - c_l. Since U_r = I r^{-3} cos 2 th
and int_0^{2 pi} cos 2 th |sin th|^beta dth = -(beta/(beta + 2)) S_beta (from S_{beta + 2} = ((beta + 1)/(beta + 2))
S_beta),
    V(alpha, beta) = -(beta/(beta + 2)) S_beta int_0^inf r^{alpha - 3} I(r) |A(r)|^beta dr.
Write A_t = A_0 + t f and I_t = I_0 + t I_f, with I_f(r) = int_0^r s^2 f(s) ds. The part of the integral over r < 1
does not depend on t. On 1 <= r <= 2, I_t |A_t|^beta/(t |t|^beta) = (I_f + I_0/t) |f + A_0/t|^beta tends to I_f f^beta
for either sign of t and is bounded by (I_f + I_0)(f + A_0)^beta for |t| >= 1. On r > 2, A_t = A_0 and I_t = I_0 + t
int_1^2 s^2 f ds, so that part is affine in t with finite coefficients (the integrands are O(r^{alpha + (beta + 1) p})
and O(r^{alpha - 3 + beta p}), integrable also at alpha = -2 - beta p), hence O(1 + |t|). So V/(t |t|^beta) tends to
-(beta/(beta + 2)) S_beta int_1^2 r^{alpha - 3} I_f f^beta dr < 0, also at alpha = -2 - beta p. Inside the strip
M = S_beta int_0^inf r^{alpha + 1} |A_t|^beta dr = O(|t|^beta), while at the endpoint M is infinite for every t; int
|Theta0|^beta dth does not depend on t, and V and, inside the strip, M are continuous in t by domination on bounded
t-intervals. Hence V has the sign of -t for |t| large, and V - ((2 + alpha) c_l + beta) M/(-alpha), which is
continuous in t, takes both signs, so it vanishes for some t; the same holds for alpha V - c_l int |Theta0|^beta dth
at alpha = -2 - beta p. Finally, for rho = A sin th and psi = B sin 2 th,
    W . grad rho - rho = sin th [c_l r A' - A + A B'/r + ((A B' - 2 B A')/r) cos 2 th],
with (A B' - 2 B A')/r = (a b/3) r^3 + O(r^5) and, using a = 4 (c_l - 1), c_l r A' - A + A B'/r = (2 b (c_l + 2)/3)
r^3 + O(r^5). Since sin th cos 2 th = (sin 3 th - sin th)/2, this gives E = r^3 [a (p - 1) sin th + (a^2 (p - 1)/12)
sin 3 th] + O(r^5), and the coefficient of r^3 sin 3 th is nonzero, so no rho_t is a profile.

## A.3.71 The resonant coefficient for traces with other angular content

Setting. Hypotheses and notation of 3.71; M = 2m, s_i = p - i delta, q_i = |s_i + 1|, and s_K = -M - 1. The inherited
parities, Theta(-th) = -Theta(th) and Theta(pi - th) = Theta(th), leave only sin n th with n >= 1 odd, so the stream
frequencies in the recurrence are positive even integers. The definition of g by a coefficient of P_K is used because
P_K[Theta] in X_0 need not have a classical derivative.

Step 1 (the coefficients). 3.68(b) gives finite expansions of rho and U with smooth angular coefficients. The degree
bookkeeping of A.3.69 involves only radial degrees, so it holds for every trace: density deficits are k delta + 2l
with l = 0 or l >= 2, and k delta + 2l with l >= 2 never equals k' delta with k' <= K; the harmonic velocity degrees
-M' - 1 (M' >= 2 even) differ from s_i for i < K; and m'^2 != (s_i + 1)^2 for every even m' >= 2 and i < K. Hence the
coefficient of r^{s_k} is P_k = (c_l k delta)^{-1} sum_{i + j = k - 1} B_ij(P_i, P_j) for 1 <= k <= K, with B_ij(f,
h) = s_j (V_i[f])_r h + (V_i[f])_th h', where V_i[f] is the particular velocity of the density r^{s_i} f: a density
mode a_n sin n th gives the stream source (s_i - n) a_n/2 at sin (n + 1) th and (s_i + n) a_n/2 at sin (n - 1) th, the
stream mode H_{m'} = G_{m'}/(m'^2 - (s_i + 1)^2), and the polar velocity components -m' H_{m'} r^{s_i} cos m' th and
(s_i + 1) H_{m'} r^{s_i} sin m' th. At s_K the source coefficient of sin M th is -M times the coefficient of sin
(M - 1) th in P_K, since the contribution of sin (M + 1) th has the factor (s_K + M + 1)/2 = 0; this is g[Theta].

Step 2 (high modes). For Theta = sin th + eps sin N th, every contribution to the coefficient of eps^e in P_k has a
signed frequency a N + b with |a| <= e, a = e mod 2 and |b| <= 2k + 1 - e: the term has k + 1 trace factors, e of
which supply frequencies +-N, and the other trace factors and the k velocity shifts supply b. Reflected frequencies
are collected with sin(-x) = -sin x and zero frequencies are discarded. For N > 4K + 4, two pairs give the same
absolute frequency only if they are equal or (a, b) and (-a, -b), so all decisions of reflection, shifting and
collection are independent of N, and every collected coefficient is a rational function of N; the inversion
denominators m'^2 - (s_i + 1)^2 (i < K, m' even) do not vanish. For e = 1, a = +-1, so every frequency is at least
N - 2k > M - 1, and the coefficient of eps in g vanishes. The coefficient of eps^2 at N = 101 was computed in exact
rational arithmetic by two independent programs of the checker and independently in the external audit; its residues
modulo 1000003 are 668607 for c_l = 3 and 159236 for c_l = 5/2, and the denominators are nonzero modulo that prime. A
rational function of N that is nonzero at N = 101 has finitely many zeros, and for such N, g[sin th + eps sin N
th] - g[sin th] = eps^2 (a_2(N) + O(eps)) with a_2(N) != 0, which gives (a). Positivity: |sin N th| <= N |sin th| for
every integer N, so sin th + eps sin N th >= (1 - N |eps|) sin th > 0 on 0 < th < pi when |eps| < 1/N.

Step 3 (Lipschitz bound). For i < K, q_i is not a positive even integer, so B_i = sup over even m' >= 2 of
(m' + q_i)/|m' - q_i| is finite and is attained at one of the even neighbours of q_i (or at 2); put L_i = B_i
[(3/2)^K + 1]/2. For one input mode a_n, the weighted sum of the absolute output amplitudes of the two velocity
components is at most sum over m' = n + 1, n - 1 (m' > 0) of [(1 + m')/(1 + n)]^j (m' + q_i) |s_i -+ n|/(2
|m'^2 - q_i^2|); since |s_i - n| = |s_i + 1 - m'| <= m' + q_i for m' = n + 1 and
|s_i + n| = |s_i + 1 + m'| <= m' + q_i for m' = n - 1, each term is at most B_i/2 times the weight ratio, which is at
most (3/2)^j for the upper shift and at most 1 for the lower shift. So ||(V_i[f])_r||_j + ||(V_i[f])_th||_j <= L_i
||f||_j for 0 <= j <= K; for cosine series, including the constant term, ||sum_{n >= 0} b_n cos n th||_j = sum_n
(1 + n)^j |b_n|. Product-to-sum and 1 + |n +- n'| <= (1 + n)(1 + n') give ||f h||_j <= ||f||_j ||h||_j for sine and
cosine series, and ||f'||_j <= ||f||_{j + 1}. With t = K - k, i + j = k - 1,
    ||B_ij(P_i, P_j)||_t <= L_i (|s_j| + 1) ||P_i||_{K - i} ||P_j||_{K - j}.
These estimates hold first for trigonometric polynomials; since t <= K - i and t + 1 <= K - j, each bilinear operation
extends continuously to the weighted spaces, so by density of finite Fourier sums the recurrence is defined on X_K
with P_k in X_{K-k}, and the estimates hold there. Put C_0 = 1 and C_k = (c_l k delta)^{-1} sum_{i + j = k - 1} L_i
(|s_j| + 1) C_i C_j. Induction gives ||P_k[Theta]||_{K - k} <= C_k ||Theta||_K^{k + 1} and, writing each bilinear
difference as B_ij(P_i[Theta] - P_i[Phi], P_j[Theta]) + B_ij(P_i[Phi], P_j[Theta] - P_j[Phi]),
||P_k[Theta] - P_k[Phi]||_{K - k} <= (k + 1) C_k R^k ||Theta - Phi||_K with R = max(||Theta||_K, ||Phi||_K). By Step
1, |g[Theta] - g[Phi]| <= M (K + 1) C_K R^K ||Theta - Phi||_K. With g0 = g[sin th] (3.69(b)) and eps0 = min(1, |g0|/[2
M (K + 1) C_K (2^K + 1)^K]): if ||Theta - A sin th||_K <= eps0 |A|, then R <= (2^K + 1)|A|, since ||A sin th||_K = 2^K
|A|, and |g[Theta] - g0 A^{K + 1}| <= |g0| |A|^{K + 1}/2. The constants are exact rationals; the main analysis
recomputed eps0 = 2.1767e-21 for c_l = 3 and 3.0386e-53 for c_l = 5/2.

Step 4 (two modes). For Theta_eps, the recurrence shows that P_k is a polynomial in eps of degree at most k + 1, so g
is a polynomial of degree at most K + 1; exact evaluation gives the nonzero leading coefficients
-336578601/34112798720 for c_l = 3 and
2015039783110863755187469084657027535765859080056159847867/131994320935573283182140658195673253147294638726888325906432
for c_l = 5/2, so the degree is K + 1. For c_l = 3 the displayed integer polynomial is exactly 17909219328000000
g[Theta_eps]. Its coefficients were computed in exact rational arithmetic by the main analysis and by the checker (two
independent recurrences, real sine and Cartesian Laurent); the root counts in (0, 1) follow from exact Sturm
sequences, with rational isolating intervals (7/25, 29/100) and (16/25, 13/20) for c_l = 3; the external audit
isolated all six roots in intervals of length 2e-5 and found deg gcd(g, g') = 0 in both cases. Positivity: sin
th + eps sin 3 th = sin th [1 + eps (3 - 4 sin^2 th)] >= (1 - eps) sin th > 0 on 0 < th < pi for 0 <= eps < 1.

Step 5 (the density logarithm). As in A.3.69, the resonant inversion gives the stream term (g/(2M)) r^{-M} log r sin M
th, whose velocity has U_r = -(g/2) r^{-M-1} log r cos M th and logarithmic part of U_th equal to -(g/2) r^{-M-1} log
r sin M th. Acting on r^p Theta this gives the forcing -(g/2) r^{p - M - 2} log r [p cos M th Theta + sin M th
Theta'], and no other term reaches this degree with a logarithm (the decreasing-degree argument of A.3.69 uses only
radial degrees). Transport inversion divides by c_l (M + 2), which gives the term in (d). If the bracket vanished
identically, then on each interval between consecutive zeros of sin M th, Theta would solve a linear first-order
equation whose solutions are C |sin M th|^{-p/M}; boundedness at the end points forces C = 0, so Theta = 0 on each
interval and, by continuity, everywhere.

## A.3.72 Exact anisotropic rescaling and the large-slope limit of the inverse

(a) With x = h xi, d_x = h^{-1} d_xi, so rho_x = (a0/h) g_xi, rho_y = a0 g_y, U_1 = -psi_y = h V_1 and
U_2 = psi_x = V_2. The transport operator becomes (c_l h xi + h V_1)(a0/h) g_xi + (c_l y + V_2) a0 g_y = a0 [(c_l
xi + V_1) g_xi + (c_l y + V_2) g_y] and rho = a0 g. The Poisson equation -psi_xx - psi_yy = rho_x becomes -h^{-1}
Phi_xixi - h Phi_yy = (a0/h) g_xi; division by h and a0/h^2 = s give the second equation of (1). For fixed a0 the
norms |(x, y)| and |(xi, y)| are comparable, so smoothness, the parities, the growth bounds and the condition o(r)
correspond (with constants depending on a0). Uniqueness: a difference of two velocities comes from an odd potential
with Phi_yy + eps Phi_xixi = 0; in z = xi/sqrt(eps) it is harmonic, so its velocity components are harmonic functions
of sublinear growth, hence constants (Liouville), and the parities make them zero. The centre: psi_xy = h^{-1} h
Phi_xiy. The jets: g = rho(h xi, y)/a0 = y + (b h^2/a0) xi^2 y + (e/a0) y^3 + ..., and h^2/a0 = s. By (T1),
6E = 6e/a0 = (1 - 2A/a0) b = (1 - 2 A s eps) s B = (s - 2A eps) B. The axis statement is 3.6 divided by a0, and the
representative with L_K = 1 is that of 3.6.

(b) For y > 0, c_l y d_y(K y^p) = c_l p K y^p = K y^p, and the same holds for y < 0. Since rho is continuous and
absolutely continuous in y, its distributional derivative is K p |y|^{p - 1}, which is locally integrable, so y
rho_y = rho/c_l holds in distributions and there is no singular part on y = 0. Since rho_x = 0, the canonical velocity
is 0. At fixed y != 0, |grad rho| = |K| p |y|^{p - 1} does not tend to 0 as x -> inf, while the class requires |grad
rho| <= C (1 + r)^{gamma - 1}.

(c) Partial Fourier transform in xi: for q = sqrt(eps) |k| > 0 the odd-in-y solution of -Phi_yy + eps k^2 Phi = (ik)
ghat is Phihat(k, y) = ik int_0^inf D_q(y, t) ghat(k, t) dt with D_q(y, t) = [exp(-q |y - t|) - exp(-q (y + t))]/(2q)
(the odd reflection of the Green function of -d_y^2 + q^2), and d_y D_q(0, t) = exp(-q t). For the product inputs
g = H(xi) f(y) used below, f is bounded and Hhat is integrable; since int_0^inf D_q(y, t) dt <= q^{-2} and int_0^inf
|d_y D_q(y, t)| dt = (1 - exp(-q y) + exp(-2 q y))/q <= q^{-1}, Fourier inversion shows that both velocity components
are bounded for each fixed eps > 0 (by constants of order eps^{-1} and eps^{-1/2}), so by their parities and the
uniqueness in (a) this is the canonical inverse. For g = H(xi) f(y) this gives Phi_xiy(0) = -(2 pi)^{-1} int k^2
Hhat(k) L(sqrt(eps) |k|) dk with L(q) = int_0^inf exp(-q t) f(t) dt. For H = exp(-xi^2) and f_tau(y) = y exp(-tau y^2)
(tau > 0) the integral is elementary and Phi_xiy(0) = -(sqrt(tau) + sqrt(eps))^{-2}. With nu = 1 - gamma/2, f(y) = y
(1 + y^2)^{-nu} = Gamma(nu)^{-1} int_0^inf tau^{nu - 1} exp(-tau) f_tau(y) dtau, and Tonelli (all integrands have one
sign) gives Phi_xiy(0) = -Gamma(nu)^{-1} int_0^inf tau^{nu - 1} exp(-tau) (sqrt(tau) + sqrt(eps))^{-2} dtau. The
substitution tau = eps v^2 gives eps^{gamma/2} Phi_xiy(0) = -(2/Gamma(nu)) int_0^inf v^{1 - gamma} exp(-eps v^2)
(1 + v)^{-2} dv, which tends by monotone convergence to -(2/Gamma(nu)) B(2 - gamma, gamma) = -2 Gamma(2 - gamma)
Gamma(gamma)/Gamma(1 - gamma/2). Numerical check (main analysis): at gamma = 1/2 the closed form and direct quadrature
of the Fourier formula agree to 1e-11 at eps = 1e-2 and 1e-3, and the scaled strain is -2.17, -2.44, -2.52, -2.55 at
eps = 1e-4, 1e-6, 1e-8, 1e-10, against the limit -2.5637; the Gaussian formula was checked at (tau, eps) = (1, 0.3)
and (2, 0.05) to 1e-15. Bounds of the class: H and its derivatives decay faster than any power, |f| <= C
(1 + |y|)^{gamma - 1} and |f'| <= C (1 + |y|)^{gamma - 2}, and 1 + r <= (1 + |xi|)(1 + |y|). Hydrostatic velocity:
every potential odd in y with -Phi_yy = H'(xi) f(y) is y beta(xi) - H'(xi) int_0^y (y - t) f(t) dt, so V_2(0, y) = y
beta'(0) + 2 int_0^y (y - t) f(t) dt (H''(0) = -2), and the integral is asymptotic to
y^{gamma + 1}/(gamma (gamma + 1)), which no term y beta'(0) cancels.

(d) For y, t >= 0, D_q(y, t) = (1/2) int_{|y - t|}^{y + t} exp(-q tau) dtau, and exp(-sqrt(eps) |k| tau) is the
Fourier multiplier of convolution with the Poisson kernel P_{sqrt(eps) tau}, a positive even kernel of mass one with
P_a * P_b = P_{a + b}. Hence, for g of compact support (for which the Fourier formula gives a bounded velocity, as in
(c), and so the canonical inverse), with P_0 * F = F, the canonical velocity derives from the potential Phi_eps(xi,
y) = (1/2) int_0^inf int_{|y - t|}^{y + t} (P_{sqrt(eps) tau} * g_xi(., t))(xi) dtau dt, that is, V_eps,1(xi,
y) = -(1/2) int_0^inf [sgn(t - y) (P_{sqrt(eps) |y - t|} * f_t)(xi) + (P_{sqrt(eps) (y + t)} * f_t)(xi)] dt and
V_eps,2(xi, y) = (1/2) int_0^inf int_{|y - t|}^{y + t} (P_{sqrt(eps) tau} * f_t')(xi) dtau dt, where f_t = g_xi(., t),
which is odd, with |f_t| <= C (1 + t)^{gamma - 1} and |f_t'| <= C (1 + t)^{gamma - 2}. Convolution with P_a preserves
these sup bounds and oddness, so |P_a * f_t (xi)| <= C min((1 + t)^{gamma - 1}, |xi| (1 + t)^{gamma - 2}) and |P_a *
f_t'| <= C (1 + t)^{gamma - 2}. Splitting the t integral at t = |xi| gives |V_eps,1| <= C' (1 + |xi|)^gamma, and
int_0^inf min(y, t) (1 + t)^{gamma - 2} dt = ((1 + y)^gamma - 1)/(gamma (1 - gamma)) gives the bound on V_eps,2; these
majorants do not depend on eps. For general g choose smooth radial cutoffs chi_R equal to 1 on the disc of radius R
and to 0 outside the disc of radius 2R. For R >= 1, chi_R g has the parities and the three bounds with constants
independent of R, since the derivatives of chi_R are supported where r is comparable to R. The majorants give locally
uniform convergence, as R -> inf, of the potentials and velocities given by the formulas for chi_R g to those for g;
the elliptic equation passes to the limit in distributions, local elliptic regularity for fixed eps > 0 makes the
limit smooth, and the growth bound and the uniqueness in (a) identify it as the canonical inverse of g. As eps -> 0,
P_{sqrt(eps) tau} * F -> F locally uniformly for bounded continuous F, and dominated convergence gives (2), locally
uniformly, together with the locally uniform convergence of Phi_eps to Phi_0(xi, y) = int_0^inf min(y, t) g_xi(xi, t)
dt. The function Phi_0 has the continuous derivatives Phi_0,y = int_y^inf g_xi dt, Phi_0,xi = int_0^inf min(y, t)
g_xixi dt and Phi_0,yy = -g_xi; the hypotheses do not give d_xi V_0,2, so no regularity of the full velocity gradient
is claimed. Uniqueness of the hydrostatic velocity: two odd potentials with the same -Phi_yy differ by y beta(xi),
whose velocity (-beta, y beta') is sublinear on each vertical line only if beta' = 0, and beta is odd, so beta = 0.
Setting y = 0 in V_eps,1 and differentiating once in xi (majorant C (1 + t)^{gamma - 2}) gives the strain formula and
its limit. For varying inputs the same majorants hold, and C^2 convergence on compact sets with the uniform sup bounds
controls the Poisson tails; truncating the vertical integrals then gives the convergence on compact sets, so every
step is unchanged.

(e) For each n, g_n solves (1) with eps_n = 1/a0,n -> 0, s = 1 and c_l,n, and c_l,n >= 1/gamma by 3.6, since g_n(0, y)
~ (K_n/a0,n) y^{1/c_l,n} with K_n/a0,n > 0 and |g_n| <= C (1 + r)^gamma. By (d) for varying inputs, V_n -> V_0[g_lim]
locally uniformly, and g_n -> g_lim in C^1 on compact sets, so the transport equation, g_y(0) = 1 and the three bounds
pass to the limit, and Phi_n,xiy(0) = 1 - c_l,n converges to int_0^inf g_lim,xixi(0, t) dt. For the second statement,
suppose that profiles with c_l,n in J and a0,n -> inf have representatives obeying the bounds with C, gamma and (C_R).
For X in the disc of radius R, Taylor's formula for d_i g_n along a unit coordinate segment gives |d_ij g_n(X)| <= 2
sup |d_i g_n| + (1/2) sup |d_ijj g_n|, the suprema taken over the disc of radius R + 1, so the second derivatives are
bounded on compact sets and, by the bounds on D^3 g_n, equicontinuous there. By Arzela-Ascoli and a diagonal argument
a subsequence has c_l,n -> c_lim in J and g_n -> g_lim in C^2 on compact sets, and then g_lim is a C^2 density solving
(3) with the velocity (2) and the three bounds, which was excluded. For a0 < 0, (1) has s = -1; the velocity is linear
in the right-hand side, so V_n -> -V_0[g_lim], the centre condition becomes -int_0^inf g_lim,xixi(0, t)
dt = 1 - c_lim, and the argument is otherwise unchanged.

## A.3.73 The hydrostatic problem on the axis

(a) Since g is even in xi, g_xi(0, y) = 0 and V_1(0, y) = -int_y^inf g_xi(0, t) dt = 0, so (3) on the axis reads v
G' = G. By |g_xixi| <= C (1 + r)^{gamma - 2} the integral int_y^inf g_xixi(0, t) dt converges, and differentiating
V_2(0, y) = int_0^y t g_xixi(0, t) dt + y int_y^inf g_xixi(0, t) dt gives v' = c + int_y^inf g_xixi(0, t) dt and
v'' = -g_xixi(0, y), continuous since g is C^2. V_2 is odd in y, so v(0) = 0, and |V| <= C' (1 + r)^gamma (3.72(d))
gives v(y)/y -> c. As y -> 0, G(y)/y -> G'(0) = 1 and v(y)/y -> v'(0), so v G' = G gives v'(0) = 1; in particular v, G
and G' are positive on some interval (0, delta). On any interval (0, y1) on which v is positive, the linear equation
G' = G/v gives G(y) = G(y0) exp(int_{y0}^y dt/v(t)) > 0 for y0 in (0, min(delta, y1)), and hence G' > 0. A first
positive zero y1 of v would therefore have G(y1) >= G(y0) > 0, contradicting v(y1) G'(y1) = G(y1). So v, G and G' are
positive on (0, inf). For (2), integration by parts gives int_0^R (1 - t/R) (-v''(t)) dt = [-(1 - t/R)
v'(t)]_0^R - R^{-1} int_0^R v'(t) dt = v'(0) - v(R)/R = 1 - v(R)/R. If g_xixi(0, .) >= 0 on (0, inf), the left side of
(2) is nonnegative for every R, while the right side tends to 1 - c < 0. By |g_xixi(0, t)| <= C (1 + t)^{gamma - 2},
both terms of V_2(0, y) are O(y^gamma), so v(t) - c t = O(t^gamma) and 1/v(t) - 1/(c t) = O(t^{gamma - 2}) is
integrable on [1, inf). Hence log G(y) - p log y = log K - int_y^inf (1/v(t) - 1/(c t)) dt with a finite K > 0, and
G(y) = K y^p (1 + O(y^{gamma - 1})). The density bound |G(y)| <= C (1 + y)^gamma then gives p <= gamma. If g is C^3
near 0 with the stated expansion, then g_xixi(0, y) = 2 B y + o(y), so v'' = -2 B y + o(y) and, with v(0) = 0 and
v'(0) = 1, v = y - (B/3) y^3 + o(y^3); on the other hand G = y + E y^3 + o(y^3), G' = 1 + 3 E y^2 + o(y^2) and
v = G/G' = y - 2 E y^3 + o(y^3). Hence B = 6E.

(b) On [0, inf), v' = c - D/(1 + y^2) >= 1, v(y) - y = D (y - arctan y) >= 0, v <= c y and v'' = 2 D y/(1 + y^2)^2 > 0
for y > 0. The function 1/v(t) - 1/t = -D (t - arctan t)/(t v(t)) is odd and real analytic on R, since t - arctan
t = t^3 w(t^2) with w analytic and v(t)/t = 1 + D (t - arctan t)/t >= 1; so G is odd and real analytic, G'/G = 1/v by
differentiation, G' > 0, and G <= y on (0, inf) because 1/v <= 1/t there. Since v(t) - c t = -D arctan t is bounded, G
~ K y^p with 0 < K < inf as in (a). From v = y + D y^3/3 + O(y^5), 1/v(t) - 1/t = -D t/3 + O(t^3), so G = y (1 - D
y^2/6 + O(y^4)). If phi is odd and smooth with support in [-y2, -y1] u [y1, y2], 0 < y1 < y2, let m = min over y in
[y1, y2] of min(v(y) - y, v''(y)), which is positive, and suppose ||phi||_{C^2} = max_{0 <= j <= 2} sup |phi^(j)| < m.
Then v_phi = v + phi has v_phi > y and v_phi'' > 0 on [y1, y2] and coincides with v elsewhere, so v_phi'' > 0 on (0,
inf); with v_phi'(0) = 1 and v_phi' -> c this gives 1 <= v_phi' <= c and y <= v_phi <= c y. Define G_phi by the
formula of (b) with v_phi in place of v; it is smooth and odd, G_phi'/G_phi = 1/v_phi, G_phi' > 0 and 0 < G_phi <= y.
G_phi = G on [0, y1], and on [y2, inf) G_phi is a positive constant multiple of G, so G_phi(y) ~ K_phi y^p with a
finite K_phi > 0 that may differ from K. Real analyticity is not asserted for the perturbed pair. These phi form an
infinite-dimensional set.

(c) The identity h_y = g_xi is -Phi_yy = g_xi; b_y = c - h_xi is d_xi V_1 + d_y V_2 = 0, which holds classically for
the velocity (2) of 3.72 (both derivatives are int_y^inf g_xixi dt up to sign); a g_xi + b g_y = g is (3).
Substituting the expansions: order xi^0 of b_y = c - h_xi gives v' = c - h_1; order xi of h_y = g_xi gives h_1' = 2
g_2, so g_2 = -v''/2; order xi^2 of the transport equation gives 2 (c + h_1) g_2 + v g_2' + G' b_2 = g_2, which is the
stated formula for b_2 after inserting h_1 and g_2; order xi^2 of b_y = c - h_xi gives b_2' = -3 h_3, and order xi^3
of h_y = g_xi gives h_3' = 4 g_4. In general the order xi^{2k} of the transport equation is linear in b_{2k} with
coefficient G' and otherwise involves only coefficients already determined, and the orders xi^{2k} of b_y = c - h_xi
and xi^{2k+1} of h_y = g_xi give b_{2k}' = -(2k + 1) h_{2k+1} and h_{2k+1}' = (2k + 2) g_{2k+2}; the parities are
preserved. This is a formal calculation for smooth data; it does not assume or show that a C^2 solution has such an
expansion, and it does not use the velocity formula beyond the three identities. Where q = g_y > 0, the transport
equation gives b = (g - a h_y)/q, and b_y = c - h_xi gives h_xi = c - d_y((g - a h_y)/q). Replacing (g, h) by (g + u,
h + z) and keeping first-order terms, with a replaced by a + z and b = (g - a h_y)/q, gives u_xi = z_y and
z_xi = -d_y((u - h_y z - a z_y - b u_y)/q). At an axis point a = 0 and h_y = g_xi = 0 by parity, so a_y = h_y = 0 and
h_yy = g_xiy = 0 there, q = G'(y0) and b = v(y0). Expanded, z_xi = (b/q) u_yy + ((b/q)_y - 1/q) u_y + (q_y/q^2)
u + (a/q) z_yy + (h_y/q + (a/q)_y) z_y + (h_y/q)_y z, and on the axis a = a_y = h_y = h_yy = 0, so the three
coefficients of z, z_y and z_yy vanish there; at (0, y0), with q = G'(y0) and every coefficient evaluated there, the
frozen system is u_xi = z_y, z_xi = (v/q) u_yy + ((v/q)' - 1/q) u_y + (q'/q^2) u, where (v/q)' - 1/q = 2 (v' - 1)/q by
differentiation of v q = G. For the modes exp(lambda xi + i eta y) its characteristic equation is lambda^2 + i (v/q)
eta^3 + ((v/q)' - 1/q) eta^2 - i (q'/q^2) eta = 0, so lambda^2 = -i (v/q) eta^3 (1 + O(1/|eta|)). The square roots of
-i eta^3 have real parts +-|eta|^{3/2}/sqrt(2) for both signs of eta, which gives the stated real parts with remainder
O(|eta|^{1/2}). The frozen matrix has trace zero, so its roots are lambda_0(eta) and -lambda_0(eta), and data u = u_0,
z = 0 at xi = 0 give u_hat(xi, eta) = u_hat_0(eta) cosh(lambda_0(eta) xi). Take smooth data u_0 with Fourier transform
supported in [N, N + 1] (and its reflection, for real data), normalized in H^s. For fixed xi > 0 the H^{s - m} norm of
the solution is at least a positive constant times N^{-m} exp(k N^{3/2} xi), k > 0, which is unbounded as N -> inf; so
no estimate with a fixed finite loss of derivatives holds for the frozen system, also with z = 0 on the axis.

(d) (i) For s > 0, F(s) = G(sqrt(s/beta))/sqrt(s/beta), so F is C^2 on (0, inf) and tends to g_y(0) = 1 as s decreases
to 0; the value at 0 does not affect g, and we set F(0) = 1. Then F(alpha xi^2) = g_y(xi, 0) is C^1 in xi. On the axis
g(0, y) = y F(beta y^2) = O(y^gamma), so F(s) -> 0 as s -> inf. Since g_xi = 2 alpha xi y F'(alpha xi^2 + beta
y^2) = (alpha/beta) xi d_y(F(alpha xi^2 + beta y^2)), formula (2) of 3.72 gives h = V_1 = (alpha/beta) xi F(s),
s = alpha xi^2 + beta y^2. The centre condition (a) gives d_xi V_1(0) = -int_0^inf g_xixi(0, t) dt = c - 1 = D, so
alpha/beta = D. Differentiate (3) in y and set y = 0, where g = g_xi = g_yy = 0, b = 0, g_y = F(s), g_xiy = 2 alpha xi
F'(s) and b_y = c - h_xi = c - D F(s) - 2 D s F'(s), s = alpha xi^2: (c xi + D xi F)(2 alpha xi F') + (c - D F - 2 D s
F') F = F, that is 2 c s F'(s) = D F(s) (F(s) - 1) for all s > 0. Near 0, where F > 0, Z = (F - 1)/F satisfies s
Z' = nu Z with nu = D/(2c) in (0, 1/2), so Z = k s^nu and F(alpha xi^2) = 1/(1 - k alpha^nu |xi|^{2 nu}). Since
F(alpha xi^2) = g_y(xi, 0) is C^1 in xi and 2 nu < 1, k = 0, so F = 1 near 0, and uniqueness for this ODE on s > 0
(locally Lipschitz there) gives F = 1 on [0, inf), contradicting F(s) -> 0. (ii) g_y(0) = f(0) G_0'(0) = 1, so
f(0) != 0; hence G_0 = G/f(0) is C^2, and for y_* with G_0(y_*) != 0, f(xi) = g(xi, y_*)/G_0(y_*) is C^2. G_0 is
unbounded because G(y) = f(0) G_0(y) = y^{p + o(1)} by (a). The bound |g_xi| = |f'(xi) G_0(y)| <= C
(1 + r)^{gamma - 1} at fixed xi and y -> inf forces f'(xi) = 0 for every xi, so g = f(0) G_0(y), and |g_y| = |f(0)
G_0'(y)| <= C (1 + r)^{gamma - 1} at fixed y and xi -> inf forces G_0' = 0, contradicting G_0'(0) != 0. (iii)
Iterating, g(X) = l^{-n} g(l^n X) for all integers n; letting l^n -> 0 and using differentiability at 0 gives
g(X) = grad g(0) . X = y (parities and g_y(0) = 1), which violates |g| <= C (1 + r)^gamma. For the scalings with
lambda, mu > 0: if g~(xi, y) = (lambda^2/mu) g(xi/lambda, y/mu), then the velocity (2) of g~ is (lambda V_1, mu V_2)
evaluated at (xi/lambda, y/mu), so (3) is preserved, and g~_y(0) = (lambda/mu)^2 g_y(0); invariance g~ = g with
g_y(0) = 1 forces lambda = mu, and then g~(X) = lambda g(X/lambda).

## A.3.74 The hydrostatic problem: isopycnal form, far field, and the case c = 1

Preliminaries. By 3.72(d), |V| <= C' (1 + r)^gamma. Since g_xi(0, t) = 0 and 1 + r >= (1 + |xi| + t)/2, the bound on
g_xixi gives |g_xi(xi, t)| <= C |xi| (1 + t)^{gamma - 2}, |g(xi, y) - G(y)| <= C xi^2 (1 + y)^{gamma - 2} and
|h_xi(xi, y)| = |int_y^inf g_xixi(xi, t) dt| <= C'' (1 + |xi| + y)^{gamma - 1}. The functions h and b are C^1 in y and
h is C^1 (h_y = g_xi, h_xi = -int_y^inf g_xixi dt, b_y = c - h_xi); no derivative of V_2 in xi is used below.

(a) Differentiate a g_xi + b g_y = g in y at y = 0, where g = g_xi = g_yy = 0 (g is odd in y), b = 0 (V_2 is odd in
y), a_y = h_y = g_xi = 0 and b_y = c - h_xi: a_0 k' + (c - h_xi(xi, 0)) k = k, which is the first identity of (1)
since a_0' = c + h_xi(xi, 0) and A = 2c - 1. Hence (a_0/k)' = (a_0' k - a_0 k')/k^2 = A/k, and a_0(0) = 0 gives the
second identity; for xi > 0 it gives a_0 > 0. Then k'/k = (1 - c + h_xi)/(c xi + h) at y = 0, and with h(xi,
0) = O(xi^gamma) and h_xi(xi, 0) = O(xi^{gamma - 1}), k'/k - (p - 1)/xi = (c xi h_xi - (1 - c) h)/(c xi (c
xi + h)) = O(xi^{gamma - 2}), which is integrable on [1, inf). So log(xi^{1 - p} k(xi)) tends to a finite limit log L
with error O(xi^{gamma - 1}), and evenness of k gives (1). Now let g_y > 0 on {y >= 0}. For fixed xi, g(xi, 0) = 0 and
g(xi, y) - G(y) -> 0 with G(y) -> inf (3.73(a)), so g(xi, .) is an increasing bijection of [0, inf) onto itself; its
inverse Y is C^2 in (xi, sigma) by the inverse function theorem, with Z = 1/g_y(xi, Y) > 0, and differentiating g(xi,
Y(xi, sigma)) = sigma gives g_xi = -Y_xi/Z at y = Y. Hence H_sigma = h_y Z = g_xi Z = -Y_xi, and the substitution
t = Y(xi, s) in the absolutely convergent integral h = -int_y^inf g_xi(xi, t) dt gives H = int_sigma^inf Y_xi(xi, s)
ds. Put a~(xi, sigma) = a(xi, Y) = c xi + H and b~(xi, sigma) = b(xi, Y). The transport equation at y = Y reads -a~
Y_xi/Z + b~/Z = sigma, that is b~ = a~ Y_xi + sigma Z. By the chain rule a_xi = d_xi a~ - a_y Y_xi = d_xi
a~ + Y_xi^2/Z, d_sigma a~ = a_y Z = -Y_xi and b_y = Z^{-1} d_sigma b~ = Z^{-1}(-Y_xi^2 + a~ Z_xi + Z + sigma Z_sigma),
using Y_xisigma = Z_xi. Inserting these in a_xi + b_y = (c + h_xi) + (c - h_xi) = 2c and multiplying by Z gives
d_xi(a~ Z) + Z + sigma Z_sigma = 2c Z, which is the first equation of (2). The conditions at sigma = 0: Y(xi, 0) = 0
since g(xi, 0) = 0; Z(xi, 0) = 1/k(xi) and Z(0, 0) = 1/g_y(0) = 1; H_sigma(xi, 0) = -Y_xi(xi, 0) = 0; Z_sigma = -g_yy
Z^3 vanishes at sigma = 0 since g_yy(xi, 0) = 0. At fixed xi, g(xi, y) = G(y) + O(y^{gamma - 2}) = K y^p (1 + o(1)),
so Y ~ (sigma/K)^c; by transport g_y = (g - a g_xi)/b with |a g_xi| = O(y^{2 gamma - 2}) = o(y^p) and b = c
y + O(y^gamma), so g_y ~ p K y^{p - 1} and Z ~ c K^{-1} Y^{1 - p} ~ c K^{-c} sigma^{c - 1}; and H -> 0 since h(xi,
y) -> 0 as y -> inf. For (3): differentiating Y(xi, g(xi, y)) = y twice in xi at xi = 0, where g_xi = 0, gives
Y_xixi(0, G(y)) = -Z g_xixi(0, y) = v''(y)/G'(y) by 3.73(a); the substitution sigma = G(y) gives int_0^inf Y_xixi(0,
sigma) dsigma = int_0^inf v''(y) dy = c - v'(0) = c - 1, the integral being absolutely convergent since |v''| <= C
(1 + y)^{gamma - 2}. Integrating the first equation of (2) over (0, sigma_1), with int_0^{sigma_1} sigma Z_sigma
dsigma = sigma_1 Z(xi, sigma_1) - Y(xi, sigma_1) and int_0^{sigma_1} Z dsigma = Y(xi, sigma_1), and differentiating
under the integral over the compact interval, gives the second identity, since A + 1 = 2c. The integrands G - g, g_xi
and g_xixi of M, M' and M'' are bounded by C xi^2 (1 + y)^{gamma - 2}, C |xi| (1 + y)^{gamma - 2} and C
(1 + y)^{gamma - 2}, so M is C^2 with M' = -int_0^inf g_xi(xi, y) dy = h(xi, 0) and M'' = -int_0^inf g_xixi(xi, y) dy,
and M''(0) = c - 1 by 3.73(a). Finally d_xi(a~ Z) = (c + H_xi) Z + a~ Z_xi, so (2) gives a~ Z_xi + sigma
Z_sigma = (A - c - H_xi) Z = (D - H_xi) Z, with H_xi taken at fixed sigma.

(b) Write W = c X + V = (a, b), w_r = W . e_r and w_t = W . e_th. Since |V| <= C' (1 + r)^gamma, there is R > 1 with
w_r >= c r/2 for r >= R, and w_r = c r + O(r^gamma), w_t = O(r^gamma). The field W is continuous and a_xi + b_y = 2c
with both terms continuous, so its mollifications W_eps = W * phi_eps satisfy div W_eps = 2c; the divergence theorem
for W_eps on the sector {R_0 < |X| < r, 0 < arg X < th}, in the limit eps -> 0 (uniform convergence on compact sets)
and with w_t(rho, 0) = 0 (the xi-axis is invariant: b(xi, 0) = 0), gives for I(r, th) = int_0^th r w_r(r, s) ds (th in
R, w_r extended periodically) I(r, th) = I(R_0, th) + c th (r^2 - R_0^2) - int_{R_0}^r w_t(rho, th) drho. Hence I is
C^1 for r > R with I_r = 2 c r th - w_t and I_th = r w_r > 0. For r >= R the trajectories of X' = W, parametrized by
r, are the solutions of th' = w_t/(r w_r), and along a C^1 solution z(r) = I(r, th(r)) satisfies z' = I_r + I_th
th' = 2 c r th = f(r, z), where f(r, z) = 2 c r I^{-1}(r, z) with I^{-1}(r, .) the inverse of th -> I(r, th). By the
implicit function theorem I^{-1} is C^1, and d_z f = 2c/w_r(r, I^{-1}(r, z)) is continuous; so solutions with
z(R) = I(R, omega) exist for all r >= R, are unique and are C^1 in omega, and conversely th = I^{-1}(r, z) solves
th' = w_t/(r w_r). Write th(r, omega) for the solution with th(R, omega) = omega. The variational equation (d_omega
z)' = (2c/w_r) d_omega z with d_omega z(R) = R w_r(R, omega) gives d_omega z = R w_r(R, omega) e^{2c tau}, tau(r,
omega) = int_R^r ds/w_r(s, th(s, omega)), and d_omega z = r w_r(r, th) J with J = d_omega th; with delta = tau - p
log(r/R) and e^{2c tau} = e^{2c delta} (r/R)^2 this is J = r w_r(R, omega) e^{2c delta}/(R w_r(r, th)). Since
|th'| <= C r^{gamma - 2} and |delta'| = |1/w_r - p/r| <= C r^{gamma - 2}, th(r, omega) and delta(r, omega) converge as
r -> inf uniformly in omega, with errors O(r^{gamma - 1}), to limits Omega(omega) and delta_inf(omega), continuous in
omega; and J converges uniformly to w_r(R, omega) e^{2c delta_inf(omega)}/(c R) > 0. So Omega is C^1 with Omega' = lim
J > 0, Omega(omega + 2 pi) = Omega(omega) + 2 pi (as for each th(r, .), which is a bijection of the circle since
backward solutions exist down to r = R), and Omega is a C^1 diffeomorphism of the circle; Omega(0) = 0 and
Omega(pi/2) = pi/2 because the axes are invariant (V_1(0, y) = 0 by parity). Along a trajectory d_tau g = g, so r^{-p}
g(r, th(r, omega)) = R^{-p} e^{delta(r, omega)} g(R, omega), which converges uniformly to Phi(omega) = R^{-p}
e^{delta_inf(omega)} g(R, omega). Put Theta = Phi o Omega^{-1}. Given th, let omega_r be defined by th(r,
omega_r) = th; since th(r, .) -> Omega uniformly and d_omega th(r, .) is bounded below by a positive constant for
large r, omega_r -> Omega^{-1}(th) uniformly in th, and the uniform continuity of Phi and the uniform convergence
above give sup_th |r^{-p} g(r, th) - Theta(th)| -> 0, which is (4); in particular r^{-p} g is bounded. Parities of
Theta follow from those of g. On the invariant ray th = pi/2, r^{-p} G(r) -> K (3.73(a)), so Theta(pi/2) = K. Since
g(R, .) is C^1 and vanishes at omega = 0 and omega = pi, and Omega^{-1} is C^1 and fixes 0 and pi, |Theta(th)| <= C''
|sin th|. If g_y > 0 on {y >= 0}, then g(R, omega) > 0 for 0 < omega < pi and Omega maps (0, pi) onto itself, so
Theta > 0 on (0, pi); moreover d_omega g(R, 0) = R k(R), so Phi(omega) = R^{1 - p} k(R) e^{delta_inf(0)}
omega + o(omega) by continuity of delta_inf, and Omega^{-1}(th) = th/Omega'(0) + o(th) with Omega'(0) = a_0(R) e^{2c
delta_inf(0)}/(c R) (w_r = a_0 on the xi-axis); so Theta(th) = L' th + o(th) with L' = c R^{2 - p} k(R) e^{-A
delta_inf(0)}/a_0(R). On the xi-axis the trajectory is xi(tau) with xi' = a_0(xi), and integrating (log k)' = (log
a_0)' - A/a_0 from R to r gives k(r) = k(R) (a_0(r)/a_0(R)) e^{-A delta(r, 0)} (r/R)^{-A p}, with A p = 2 - p; since
a_0(r)/r -> c, r^{1 - p} k(r) -> c R^{2 - p} k(R) e^{-A delta_inf(0)}/a_0(R) = L', so L' = L. For the remark on
derivatives: d_xi^2 (R^{-p} g(R X)) = R^{2 - p} g_xixi(R X) = O(R^{gamma - p}) on a fixed annulus, and gamma >= p
(3.73(a)). The function K sgn(sin th) |sin th|^p is not O(|sin th|) as th -> 0 since p < 1.

(c) Insert g_D = y + D u + O(D^2) (in C^1 on compact sets) and V[g_D] = D V[u] + O(D^2) (uniformly on compact sets;
V[y] = 0) in (c X + V[g_D]) . grad g_D = g_D with c = 1 + D; the terms of order D give X . grad u + y + V_2[u] = u,
which is (5). Suppose u is as stated. All terms of (5) are odd in y, so with V_2[u] extended oddly (5) holds on R^2.
For fixed xi, V_2[u](xi, .) is C^1 on R with d_y V_2[u] = int_y^inf u_xixi(xi, t) dt for y > 0 (even in y, continuous
at y = 0) and d_y^2 V_2[u] = -u_xixi on y != 0; V_2[u] = -y - (X . grad - 1) u is continuous on R^2 (and so is d_y
V_2[u](xi, y) = V_2[u](xi, 1) + int_0^1 (1 - t) u_xixi(xi, t) dt - int_0^y u_xixi(xi, t) dt for y >= 0); so d_y^2
V_2[u] = -u_xixi in the sense of distributions on R^2 (integration by parts in y on each line). With d_y^2 (X . grad
u) = (X . grad + 2) d_y^2 u for distributions, applying d_y^2 to (5) gives
    u_xixi = (X . grad + 1) u_yy   in the sense of distributions on R^2.   (L)
The function y satisfies (L), the parity and growth conditions and the tail-integrability condition (it does not
satisfy (5)); consequently w = u - u_y(0) y also satisfies (L) and these conditions; w(0) = 0, grad w(0) = 0 (w_xi(xi,
0) = 0 by oddness), so |w| <= C r^2 for r <= 1 and, as q < 2, |w(X)| <= C |X|^2 and |w(X)| <= C (1 + |X|)^q on R^2
after enlarging C. With w^ the Fourier transform (variables (kappa, eta)), X . grad -> -(kappa d_kappa + eta
d_eta + 2) and d_xi -> i kappa, d_y -> i eta give, for Lambda = kappa d_kappa + eta d_eta,
    eta^2 (Lambda + 3) w^ + kappa^2 w^ = 0.
On the open set {eta != 0} use the coordinates alpha = kappa/eta, beta = eta, in which Lambda = beta d_beta: the
equation is beta d_beta w^ = -(3 + alpha^2) w^, so d_beta(|beta|^{3 + alpha^2} w^) = 0 and w^ = |beta|^{-3 - alpha^2}
S_+(alpha) on beta > 0 and |beta|^{-3 - alpha^2} S_-(alpha) on beta < 0 with distributions S_+-; hence for lambda > 0
the dilate w^(lambda .) equals lambda^{-3 - alpha^2} w^ on {eta != 0}. For a Schwartz function phi, <w^(lambda .),
phi> = lambda^{-2} int w(Y/lambda) phi^(Y) dY, so |<w^(lambda .), phi>| <= C lambda^{-2 - q} int (1 + |Y|)^q |phi^(Y)|
dY for lambda <= 1 and |<w^(lambda .), phi>| <= C lambda^{-4} int |Y|^2 |phi^(Y)| dY for all lambda, bounds by a fixed
seminorm of phi. On {eta != 0} this says that e^{t (alpha^2 - (q - 1))} w^ (lambda = e^{-t}) and e^{t (1 - alpha^2)}
w^ (lambda = e^t) are bounded by a fixed seminorm, uniformly for t >= 0. If chi is a test function supported in a
compact subset of {eta != 0} on which f = alpha^2 - (q - 1) >= f_0 > 0, then |<w^, chi>| = |<e^{t f} w^, e^{-t f}
chi>| <= C ||e^{-t f} chi||_{C^N} -> 0 as t -> inf; so w^ vanishes on {alpha^2 > q - 1}, and in the same way on
{alpha^2 < 1}. Since q - 1 < 1 these sets cover {eta != 0}, so w^ is supported in {eta = 0}. A tempered distribution
supported in this line is a finite sum of terms T_j(kappa) delta^(j)(eta), so w = sum_{j <= N} y^j t_j(xi); pairing
w(xi, .) with N + 1 smooth compactly supported functions of y whose moment matrix is invertible shows that the t_j are
continuous, and |w| <= C (1 + |X|)^q with q < 2 forces t_j = 0 for j >= 2. Oddness in y gives t_0 = 0, so w = y
t_1(xi); (L) gives t_1'' = 0, evenness gives t_1 constant, and w_y(0) = 0 gives t_1 = 0. So u = u_y(0) y, for which
the left side of (5) is u_y(0) (y - y) + 0 = 0, not -y: a contradiction. A function with |u| <= C (1 + r) log(2 + r)
satisfies the growth bound for every q in (1, 2). For the comparison functions: c y d_y (K_D y^{1/c}) = K_D y^{1/c}
with c = 1 + D, and K_D y^{1/(1 + D)} = y + D y (kappa_1 - log y) + O(D^2) at fixed y > 0.

(d) With f_p of degree p and V[f_p] of degree p, the terms of degree 2p - 1 of (c X + V[g]) . grad g = g are (c
(2p - 1) - 1) f_{2p-1} + V[f_p] . grad f_p = 0, and c (2p - 1) - 1 = 1 - c = -D. At th = pi/2, d_xi^2 = r^{-1}
d_r + r^{-2} d_th^2 on functions of (r, th), so (f_p)_xixi(0, y) = (p K + Theta''(pi/2)) y^{p - 2}; then V_2[f_p](0,
y) = Q (int_0^y t^{p - 1} dt + y int_y^inf t^{p - 2} dt) = Q y^p (1/p + 1/(1 - p)), and since V_1[f_p](0, y) = 0 and
d_y f_p(0, y) = p K y^{p - 1}, (6) follows. Degrees: products of terms of degrees d_m and d_m' - 1 have degree
d_m + d_m' - 1, and d_n = 1 - n (1 - p) gives c d_n - 1 = c - 1 - n (c - 1) = -(n - 1) D. A term of degree d with axis
curvature Q_d y^{d - 2} gives int_0^y Q_d t^{d - 1} dt in V_2(0, y), divergent at 0 when d <= 0 and Q_d != 0; at
d = 0, with the lower end replaced by a regular core (for example, the integral taken from t = 1), the first part of
V_2(0, y) is Q_0 log y plus a constant and the second is y int_y^inf Q_0 t^{-2} dt = Q_0. For the moment:
V_2(0, y) = int_0^y t g_xixi(0, t) dt + y int_y^inf g_xixi(0, t) dt; with e(t) = g_xixi(0, t) - Q t^{p - 2}, the parts
Q t^{p - 2} give Q y^p/(p (1 - p)), int_0^y t e(t) dt -> m_0, and |y int_y^inf e(t) dt| <= int_y^inf t |e(t)| dt -> 0;
equivalently the remainder is exactly -int_y^inf (t - y) e(t) dt. Formally, v = c y + Q y^p/(p (1 - p)) + m_0 + ... in
G'/G = 1/v gives the term -m_0/(c^2 y^2) in 1/v and the factor 1 + m_0/(c^2 y) in G. For the cusp: f_p(xi, y) = |xi|^p
F(y/|xi|) gives (f_p)_xixi(xi, t) = |xi|^{p - 2} q(t/|xi|), and q(s) = s^{p - 2} f''(1/s) with
f(u) = f_p(u, 1) = K + Q u^2/2 + O(u^4) (Theta smooth and even about pi/2), so q(s) = Q s^{p - 2} + O(s^{p - 4}) as
s -> inf, while q(s) = O(s) as s -> 0 because Theta(th) = O(th) and Theta is smooth; so C_p(Theta) is finite (p > 0).
With x = |xi| and S = y/x, V_2[f_p](xi, y) = x^p int_0^S s q(s) ds + y x^{p - 1} int_S^inf q(s) ds; subtracting Q
s^{p - 2} in both integrals gives x^p (C_p(Theta) + Q S^p/p + Q S^p/(1 - p) + O(S^{p - 2})) = Q
y^p/(p (1 - p)) + C_p(Theta) |xi|^p + O(xi^2 y^{p - 2}). In V[f_p] . grad f_p, the term V_1[f_p] d_xi f_p is O(xi^2)
near the vertical axis, so the term with |xi|^p is C_p(Theta) |xi|^p d_y f_p(0, y) = p K C_p(Theta) |xi|^p y^{p - 1}.

(e) If g solves (3) of 3.72, then g_l(X) = l g(X/l) has V[g_l](X) = l V[g](X/l) (substitute t = l s in (2) of 3.72)
and d_y g_l(0) = 1, so it solves (3) with the same c; d/dl at l = 1 gives g - X . grad g, which is nonzero since
otherwise g would be homogeneous of degree 1, excluded by 3.73(d)(iii). The formal linearization in (g, c) of (c
X + V[g]) . grad g - g is L_g u + c_1 X . grad g, and d/dc r^{1/c} = -p^2 r^p log r. Compactness: D^2 g_n(0) = 0 by
the parities (g_n(xi, 0) = 0 and d_xi g_n(0, y) = 0), so |D^3 g_n| <= C_R gives bounds of g_n in C^3 on each disc; by
the Arzela-Ascoli theorem and a diagonal argument a subsequence converges in C^2 on compact sets to a C^2 function g,
which inherits the parities, d_y g(0) = 1 and the three bounds with the same C and gamma. The integrands of V_1[g_n]
and V_2[g_n] are dominated by C |xi| (1 + t)^{gamma - 2} and C (1 + t)^{gamma - 2} (and the integral int_0^y t d_xi^2
g_n dt is over a compact interval), so V[g_n] -> V[g] uniformly on compact subsets of {y >= 0}; passing to the limit
in the residual gives (3) of 3.72 for g with c_lim = c, and c >= 1/gamma by 3.73(a).

## A.3.75 The hydrostatic problem: local analytic solutions from the bottom, divergence from the axis, the source representation, and the cusp coefficient

Preliminaries. As in A.3.74, evenness and the bound on g_xixi give |g_xi(xi, t)| <= C |xi| (1 + t)^{gamma - 2} and
|h_xi(xi, y)| <= C'' (1 + |xi| + y)^{gamma - 1} whenever h = V_1. Throughout, I^2 f(sigma) = int_0^sigma (sigma - s)
f(s) ds, so that I^2 sigma^j = sigma^{j + 2}/((j + 1)(j + 2)).

(a)(i) Since g_xi(xi, .) is absolutely integrable on [0, inf), integrating h_y = g_xi from y to inf and using h(xi,
y) -> 0 gives h = -int_y^inf g_xi(xi, t) dt = V_1. The bound on g_xixi, locally uniform in xi, justifies
h_xi = -int_y^inf g_xixi(xi, t) dt. Integrating b_y = c - h_xi from 0 with b(xi, 0) = 0 and exchanging the order of
integration gives b = c y + int_0^y t g_xixi(xi, t) dt + y int_y^inf g_xixi(xi, t) dt = c y + V_2. The converse is the
identity h_y = g_xi, b_y = c - h_xi of 3.73(c) together with V_2(xi, 0) = 0 and V_1(xi, y) -> 0. The canonical h is
C^1, and the canonical b is continuous with continuous b_y; no derivative b_xi is needed or asserted.

(a)(ii) Coefficients. Write g = sum g_{2n+1} y^{2n+1}, h = sum h_{2n} y^{2n} and b = sum b_{2n+1} y^{2n+1}, with
g_1 = k and h_0 as stated. The first two equations of (1) give h_{2n} = g_{2n-1}'/(2n) and
b_{2n+1} = -h_{2n}'/(2n + 1) for n >= 1, and b_1 = c - h_0' = 2c - a_0' = 1 - a_0 k'/k by (1) of 3.74. The coefficient
of y^{2n+1} in the transport equation is sum_{i+j=n} (a_{2i} g_{2j+1}' + (2j + 1) b_{2i+1} g_{2j+1}) = g_{2n+1}, with
a_0 as stated and a_{2i} = h_{2i} for i >= 1; the terms containing g_{2n+1} are a_0 g_{2n+1}' + (2n + 1) b_1 g_{2n+1},
and all other terms are polynomials in g_1, ..., g_{2n-1} and their derivatives, since a_{2i} and b_{2i+1} for
1 <= i <= n involve only g_{2i-1}. For n = 1 the other terms are h_2 k' + b_3 k = k'^2/2 - k k''/6. Put
u = g_{2n+1} = k^{2n+1} w(zeta). Since zeta' = 1/k and a_0 = A k zeta, a_0 u' = k^{2n+1}(A zeta w' + (2n + 1) a_0
(k'/k) w), and with b_1 = 1 - a_0 k'/k the equation becomes
    (A zeta d_zeta + 2n) w = f_n,   f_n(zeta) = F_n/k^{2n+1}.   (A1)
For E_m = A zeta d_zeta + m one has A zeta d_zeta [f(t^A zeta)] = t d_t [f(t^A zeta)], so E_m int_0^1 t^{m-1} f(t^A
zeta) dt = int_0^1 d_t (t^m f(t^A zeta)) dt = f(zeta), and w = int_0^1 t^{2n-1} f_n(t^A zeta) dt solves (A1); it is
smooth (real analytic) when f_n is, and even when f_n is even. Every other solution on zeta > 0 or zeta < 0 differs
from it by a multiple of |zeta|^{-2n/A}, which is unbounded at 0, and k is bounded and positive near 0. This proves
the recursion and the uniqueness of bounded coefficients. For a C^inf solution of (3) of 3.72 with k > 0, a_0 = A k
zeta is C^inf by (1) of 3.74, so h = h_0 + int_0^y g_xi and b = int_0^y (c - h_xi) are C^inf near the bottom, and
their Taylor coefficients in y, which are continuous, satisfy the recursion; this gives the statement on jets.

Isopycnal form near the bottom. Near the bottom g_y > 0, and for a local solution of (1) with g(xi, 0) = 0, g_y(xi,
0) = k(xi) and b(xi, 0) = 0, the computation of A.3.74(a) (which uses only the local equations) gives, for the local
inverse Y(xi, sigma) of y -> g(xi, y), Z = Y_sigma and H = h(xi, Y): H_sigma = -Y_xi and d_xi((c xi + H) Z) + sigma
Z_sigma = A Z, with Y(xi, 0) = 0, Z(xi, 0) = 1/k and H(xi, 0) = h_0. Hence H = h_0 - d_xi I^2 Z, c xi + H = a_0 - d_xi
I^2 Z, and
    a_0 Z_xi + sigma Z_sigma + (a_0' - A) Z = d_xi (Z d_xi I^2 Z).   (A2)
Conversely, let Z be real analytic near [-R, R] x {0} in the variables (xi, sigma), even in sigma and in xi, with
Z(xi, 0) = 1/k, solving (A2). Put Y = int_0^sigma Z, H = h_0 - d_xi I^2 Z, let g be the inverse of sigma -> Y(xi,
sigma) (possible since Y_sigma(xi, 0) = 1/k != 0), and put h(xi, y) = H(xi, g) and b(xi, y) = ((c xi + H) Y_xi + sigma
Z) at sigma = g. Then g_xi = -Y_xi/Z, h_y = H_sigma g_y = -Y_xi/Z = g_xi, a g_xi + b g_y = (c xi + H)(-Y_xi/Z) + ((c
xi + H) Y_xi + sigma Z)/Z = sigma = g, and by the same chain-rule computation a_xi + b_y = 2c, i.e. b_y = c - h_xi;
the parities follow from those of Z, and g(xi, 0) = 0, g_y(xi, 0) = k, h(xi, 0) = h_0, b(xi, 0) = 0.

Majorant. Let kappa(zeta) = k(xi(zeta)) and W = kappa Z. Since d_xi = kappa^{-1} d_zeta and a_0' - A = a_0 k'/k, (A2)
becomes
    (A zeta d_zeta + sigma d_sigma) W = d_zeta [ (W/kappa^2) d_zeta (I^2 W/kappa) ],   W(zeta, 0) = 1.   (A3)
The map xi -> zeta is real analytic with derivative 1/k > 0 on [-R, R], hence injective there; after extending the
real interval slightly, compactness and the inverse function theorem give a centred rectangle Omega = {|Re
zeta| < X_0, |Im zeta| < Y_0} containing zeta([-R, R]) such that xi(zeta) and kappa are holomorphic, and kappa is
nonvanishing, on a neighbourhood of its closure; kappa is even, and M and N_0 below are finite. Let d(zeta) be the
distance to the boundary of Omega, M = sup_Omega |1/kappa| and N_0 = sup_Omega |kappa|, and ||f||_j = sup_Omega |f|
d^j. Cauchy's estimate on the disc of radius d/(j + 1) for j >= 1, and d/2 for j = 0, gives ||f'||_{j+1} <= e (j + 1)
||f||_j, and ||f g||_{i+j} <= ||f||_i ||g||_j. Since t^A zeta stays in Omega with d(t^A zeta) >= d(zeta) for
0 < t <= 1, E_m^{-1} f = int_0^1 t^{m-1} f(t^A zeta) dt satisfies ||E_m^{-1} f||_m <= ||f||_m/m. Write W = sum_m W_m
sigma^m. Then W_0 = 1 and E_m W_m = sum_{i+j=m-2} d_zeta[(W_i/kappa^2) d_zeta(W_j/kappa)]/((j + 1)(j + 2)), so the odd
coefficients vanish, each W_m is holomorphic on Omega, and with U_m = ||W_m||_m the two estimates give
||d_zeta[(W_i/kappa^2) d_zeta(W_j/kappa)]||_m <= e^2 m (j + 1) M^3 U_i U_j, hence U_m <= e^2 M^3 sum_{i+j=m-2} U_i
U_j. By induction U_{2l} <= C_1^l Cat_l <= (4 C_1)^l with C_1 = e^2 M^3 and Cat_l the Catalan numbers, so sum W_m
