sigma^m converges normally for |sigma| < d(zeta)/(2 e M^{3/2}) and defines there a holomorphic solution of (A3); the
coefficient equations are equivalent to (A3) for convergent series. For |sigma| <= rho = d/(4 e M^{3/2}) one has
|W - 1| <= sum_{l >= 1} 4^{-l} < 1/2, so Re(kappa Y_sigma) > 1/2 and sigma -> Y is injective on this disc, and since
|kappa Y - sigma| < |sigma|/2 on its boundary, Rouche's theorem shows that its image contains the disc of radius
rho/(2 N_0). If d >= d_0 on zeta([-R, R]), the triple is therefore defined and real analytic for xi in [-R, R] and
|y| < d_0/(8 e M^{3/2} N_0). These constants depend on Omega, so on the complex extension of k near the interval;
strip analyticity of k alone does not control them (for k = 1 + m xi^2 the complex zeros of k approach the real axis
as m grows).

Uniqueness. A real-analytic triple as in (ii) has h(xi, 0) = h_0 (by (1) of 3.74 and oddness of h) and Taylor
coefficients in y that are real analytic, hence bounded near 0, so they are the coefficients above. Two such triples
thus have the same Taylor series at every point of [-R, R] x {0}, agree near this segment, and agree on the stated
component by the identity theorem.

(b) For n = 1, g_2 = -v''/2 and v'' = -Q_G G''' + (terms in G, G', G''). Assume g_{2n} = Q_G^n G^{(3n)}/(2n)! + (terms
of derivative order at most 3n - 1). The coefficient of xi^{2n} in a g_xi + b g_y = g gives b_{2n} G' = g_{2n} - v
g_{2n}' - sum_{i>=1, j>=1, i+j=n} (2j a_{2i+1} g_{2j} + b_{2i} g_{2j}') - 2n a_1 g_{2n}, with a_1 = 2c - v' and
a_{2i+1} = h_{2i+1} = -b_{2i}'/(2i + 1); by induction b_{2i} has derivative order 3i + 1, so the only term of order
3n + 1 in b_{2n} is -v g_{2n}'/G'. Then g_{2n+2} = -b_{2n}''/((2n + 1)(2n + 2)) has the single top term (v/G') Q_G^n
G^{(3n+3)}/(2n + 2)! = Q_G^{n+1} G^{(3n+3)}/(2n + 2)!. Preservation of the axis properties: B is complete; by Cauchy
estimates on a smaller strip each derivative satisfies |phi^{(j)}(y)| <= C_j ||phi|| exp(-alpha y^2/2) on R. For G_*,
G_*'(y) >= c_1 (1 + |y|)^{p-1} on R, v_* - c y = -D arctan y, and v_*'' = 2 D y/(1 + y^2)^2, with v_*'''(0) = 2D > 0.
Hence for ||phi|| small, G' > 0 on R, G'(0) = 1 (phi'(0) = 0), v - c y = O(1), and v'' > 0 on (0, inf): near 0 since
v'' is odd with v'''(0) close to 2D, on compact subsets of (0, inf) by continuity, and at infinity since the
perturbation of v'' decays faster than any power while v_*'' ~ 2D y^{-3}. Then G = K_G y^p (1 + O(y^{-1})) as in
3.73(a). Genericity: g_{2n}(y_0) is a continuous function of G on G_* + N (it is a polynomial in finitely many
derivatives at y_0 divided by a power of G'(y_0)), so, for integers m >= 1, the set S_m = {G in G_* + N :
|g_{2n}(y_0)| <= m^{2n} for every integer n >= 1} is closed in G_* + N, and every G with limsup
|g_{2n}(y_0)|^{1/(2n)} < inf lies in some S_m. The functions P_n(z) = z^3 (z^2 - y_0^2)^{3n} exp(-(alpha + beta n)
z^2), beta > 0, lie in B, vanish to order 3n at y_0, and satisfy ||P_n|| <= C_2 C_3^n and P_n^{(3n)}(y_0) = (3n)!
y_0^3 (2 y_0)^{3n} exp(-(alpha + beta n) y_0^2). Adding +-eps P_n/||P_n|| leaves G, ..., G^{(3n-1)} at y_0, hence
Q_G(y_0) and R_n(y_0), unchanged and changes g_{2n}(y_0) by at least eps C_4 C_5^n (3n)!/(2n)!, which exceeds 2 m^{2n}
for n large; so one of the two signs leaves S_m, S_m has empty interior, and the complement of the union of the S_m is
a countable intersection of dense open sets (Baire). If a triple solving (1) were real analytic near (0, y_0) with
g(0, .) = G, its xi-Taylor coefficients would solve the recursion of 3.73(c) and would be the g_{2n}, so the series
would converge.

(c) Integrating the bound on h_xi from xi = 0, where h = 0, gives |h(xi, y)| <= C'' int_0^{|xi|} (1 + s)^{gamma - 1}
ds = (C''/gamma)((1 + |xi|)^gamma - 1), uniformly in y, which gives the bounds of (c) with C' = max(C'', C''/gamma);
hence |H(xi, sigma)| <= C' ((1 + |xi|)^gamma - 1), uniformly for sigma >= 0 (no corresponding bound for H_xi is used).
Since g is C^2 with g_y > 0, Y is C^2 and H = h(xi, Y) is C^1, so T has C^1 coefficients and unique trajectories.
Along a backward trajectory sigma(tau) = sigma_0 e^tau -> 0; the bound on H gives |c xi + H| >= c |xi| - C'
(1 + |xi|)^gamma, so the trajectory stays bounded backward; on bounded xi-intervals c xi + H(xi, sigma) -> a_0(xi)
uniformly as sigma -> 0, and a_0 has the sign of xi by (1) of 3.74, so outside any interval (-eps, eps) the eventual
backward velocity points strictly inward and the trajectory is eventually trapped in it; trajectories on sigma = 0
behave in the same way. Hence P_tau -> (0, 0). Since DT(0, 0) = diag(A, 1), continuity gives P . T(P) >= |P|^2/2 near
the origin, so d_tau |P_tau|^2 >= |P_tau|^2 once the trajectory is near the origin, and the convergence just proved
gives |P_tau| <= C(P) e^{tau/2} for tau <= 0. Next, h_xi(xi, 0) - D = a_0' - A = a_0 k'/k = O(|xi|), h_xi(xi,
Y) - h_xi(xi, 0) = int_0^Y g_xixi dt = O(sigma) and g_xi^2/g_y = O(xi^2) near 0, so H_xi - D = O(|xi| + sigma) and the
integral in (2) converges absolutely. By (2) of 3.74, T Z = (D - H_xi) Z (expand d_xi((c xi + H) Z) = (c xi + H)
Z_xi + (c + H_xi) Z and use A - c = D), so d_tau log Z(P_tau) = (D - H_xi)(P_tau), and Z(P_tau) -> Z(0, 0) = 1 as
tau -> -inf gives (2). The fixed-point property is H = int_sigma^inf Y_xi ds of 3.74(a). The dilation g_l(X) = l
g(X/l) has V[g_l](X) = l V[g](X/l) (A.3.74(e)), so its inverse is Y_l(xi, sigma) = l Y(xi/l, sigma/l) and H_l(xi,
sigma) = l H(xi/l, sigma/l).

(d) For (1) frozen at a point, perturbations (u, z, w) of (g, h, b) satisfy b u_y + a u_xi - u + g_xi z + g_y w = 0,
z_y = u_xi and w_y = -z_xi. For exp(lambda y + i eta xi) this gives z = i eta u/lambda, w = eta^2 u/lambda^2 and (b
lambda + i a eta - 1 + i g_xi eta/lambda + g_y eta^2/lambda^2) u = 0, which is (3) after multiplication by lambda^2;
equivalently, (3) is the determinant of the frozen 3 x 3 system for the amplitudes of (u, z, w), so no mode with
lambda = 0 is lost. At a positive axis point (v > 0, G' > 0) (3) reads v lambda^3 - lambda^2 + G' eta^2 = 0, whose
roots as |eta| -> inf are (G'/v)^{1/3} |eta|^{2/3} omega (1 + O(|eta|^{-2/3})) with omega^3 = -1, of real parts
-(G'/v)^{1/3} |eta|^{2/3} and (1/2)(G'/v)^{1/3} |eta|^{2/3} (twice), up to O(1). Where a != 0, the balances i a eta
lambda^2 + g_y eta^2 = 0 and b lambda^3 + i a eta lambda^2 = 0 give the stated roots. The Gevrey orders and the count
are heuristic readings of these formulas, as stated.

(e) Direct differentiation gives f_xi = C_0 (p - 1) xi y r^{p-5} (3 xi^2 + p y^2), f_y = C_0 r^{p-5} (3 xi^4 + 6p xi^2
y^2 + p (p + 2) y^4), d_y V_1[f] = f_xi, d_y^2 V_2[f] = -f_xixi, and X . grad f = p f. At fixed xi the expressions (4)
satisfy V_1 -> 0 and d_y V_2 -> 0 as y -> inf and V_2(xi, 0) = 0, while the formulas (2) of 3.72 converge (f_xi and
f_xixi are O(y^{p-2}) at fixed xi, and f_xixi(0, t) = -C_0 p (1 - p) t^{p-2} is integrable against t at 0); the
differences therefore vanish, the case xi = 0 being checked directly: V_2(0, y) = Q y^p/(p (1 - p)) = -C_0 y^p with
Q = -C_0 p (1 - p). The trace identity is sin th (3 cos^2 th + (p + 2) sin^2 th) = (3 (p + 3)/4)(sin th + ((1 - p)/(3
(p + 3))) sin 3th), and Theta' = 3 C_0 cos th (cos^2 th + p sin^2 th) > 0 on (0, pi/2). As xi/y -> 0, V_2[f] = -C_0
y^p (1 + O(xi^2/y^2)) = Q y^p/(p (1 - p)) + O(xi^2 y^{p-2}); comparing with the expansion of 3.74(d) and using p < 2
gives C_p(Theta) = 0. For the perturbation, Q is unchanged and q changes by eps (p (p - 1) chi - 2 (p - 1) s
chi' + s^2 chi''); since int s^2 chi' ds = -2 int s chi ds and int s^3 chi'' ds = 6 int s chi ds, C_p changes by eps
(p (p - 1) + 4 (p - 1) + 6) int s chi ds = eps (p + 1)(p + 2) int s chi ds. The perturbation is supported in the cone
1 <= y/xi <= 2 of the first quadrant and its parity reflections. On the compact arc arctan(1) <= th <= arctan(2) of
the unit circle, Theta, Theta', f_y and -f_xi have positive minima, and their perturbations there are uniformly small
when |eps| is small; homogeneity and parity propagate the strict signs, and outside these cones the functions are
unchanged. Finally V[f] . grad f is a direct computation from (4) (checked symbolically), and its quartic factor is
positive for 0 < p < 1.

## A.3.76 The second compatibility condition of the far field when 1 < c < 2

Preliminaries. For u as in 3.76, smoothness near the vertical axis and the parities give F_u(s) = K_u s^q + (Q_u/2)
s^{q - 2} + O(s^{q - 4}) as s -> inf, with K_u = u(0, 1), so q_u(s) = Q_u s^{q - 2} + O(s^{q - 4}), and smoothness and
oddness at the horizontal axis give F_u(s) = O(s) and q_u(s) = O(s) as s -> 0; hence the integral defining C_q(u)
converges at both ends (0 < q < 2). Finite-part identity: two integrations by parts on [0, S] give int_0^S s q_u
ds = S^3 F_u'(S) - (2q + 1) S^2 F_u(S) + (q + 1)(q + 2) int_0^S s F_u ds; inserting the expansion of F_u at S, the
terms in S^{q + 2} and S^q cancel against those of the last integral, and
    C_q(u) = (q + 1)(q + 2) FP int_0^inf s F_u(s) ds,   (A1)
where FP int_0^inf s F_u ds is the limit as S -> inf of int_0^S s F_u ds - K_u S^{q + 2}/(q + 2) - Q_u S^q/(2q).
C_q(u) is linear in u.

Velocity of f_d and (1). f_d is smooth on R^2 minus the origin as a product of smooth functions; its parities follow
from those of f (V_1[f] odd in xi and even in y, V_2[f] even in xi and odd in y), and f_d(xi, 0) = 0. At fixed xi,
d_xi f_d(xi, t) = O(|xi| t^{d - 2}) and d_xi^k f_d(xi, t) = O(t^{d - k}) for k >= 2 as t -> inf, uniformly for xi near
any point, so the tails in (2) of 3.72 converge, and t d_xi^2 f_d(0, t) = Q_{f_d} t^{d - 1} is integrable at 0 since
d > 0. Near a point (0, y_0) with y_0 > 0 the same bounds for all xi-derivatives show that V_1[f_d] = -int_y^inf d_xi
f_d dt is smooth and odd in xi, so V_1[f_d] d_xi f = O(xi^2) and is smooth. The computation of A.3.74(d) applies with
p replaced by d (it uses only 0 < d < 1, smoothness and the parities; Q_{f_d} replaces Q): V_2[f_d](xi, y) = Q_{f_d}
y^d/(d (1 - d)) + C_d(f_d) |xi|^d + O(xi^2 y^{d - 2}) as xi -> 0. Also V[f] . grad f_d is smooth near (0, y_0), and
d_y f(xi, y) = p K y^{p - 1} + O(xi^2). In (3) of 3.72 the terms of degree 3p - 2 are (c X . grad - 1) f_{3p-2} + V[f]
. grad f_d + V[f_d] . grad f, and X . grad f_{3p-2} = (3p - 2) f_{3p-2}, which gives (1). By (1), 2D f_{3p-2} = V[f] .
grad f_d + V_1[f_d] d_xi f + V_2[f_d] d_y f, whose first two terms are smooth and even in xi near (0, y_0), hence
equal to their values at xi = 0 up to O(xi^2); writing V_2[f_d](xi, y) d_y f(xi, y) - V_2[f_d](0, y) d_y f(0,
y) = (V_2[f_d](xi, y) - V_2[f_d](0, y)) d_y f(xi, y) + V_2[f_d](0, y)(d_y f(xi, y) - d_y f(0, y)) gives, at fixed
y > 0, f_{3p-2}(xi, y) - f_{3p-2}(0, y) = (p K C_d(f_d)/(2D)) |xi|^d y^{p - 1} + O(xi^2), so the quotient in 3.76 has
the stated limit; for a function that is even and C^1 in xi the quotient tends to 0, since d < 1.

(a) For f of (4) of 3.75, V[f] is given there and is smooth on R^2 minus the origin, and with beta = p (p + 2) the
formula for V[f] . grad f in 3.75(e) gives f_d(1, s) = -(C_0^2/D) s (1 + s^2)^{p - 3} (3 + 2 beta s^2 + beta
s^4) = -(C_0^2/D)(beta phi_0(s) + (3 - beta) phi_2(s)), with phi_0(s) = s (1 + s^2)^{(d - 1)/2} and phi_2(s) = s
(1 + s^2)^{(d - 5)/2} (since beta (1 + s^2)^2 + 3 - beta = 3 + 2 beta s^2 + beta s^4). Here phi_0 and phi_2 are the
values at (1, s) of y r^{d - 1} and xi^4 y r^{d - 5}, both of degree d. For phi_0, K_u = 1 and Q_u = d - 1. From d_s[s
(1 + s^2)^{(d + 1)/2}] = (1 + s^2)^{(d - 1)/2} + (d + 2) s^2 (1 + s^2)^{(d - 1)/2} and d_s[s
(1 + s^2)^{(d - 1)/2}] = d (1 + s^2)^{(d - 1)/2} + (1 - d)(1 + s^2)^{(d - 3)/2} one finds FP int_0^inf s phi_0
ds = (1 - d) J_d/(d (d + 2)), so C_d(phi_0) = (1 - d^2) J_d/d by (A1). For phi_2, K_u = Q_u = 0, int_0^inf s phi_2
ds = int_0^inf s^2 (1 + s^2)^{(d - 5)/2} ds = J_d/(3 - d) (from d_s[s
(1 + s^2)^{(d - 3)/2}] = (1 + s^2)^{(d - 3)/2} + (d - 3) s^2 (1 + s^2)^{(d - 5)/2}), so C_d(phi_2) = (d + 1)(d + 2)
J_d/(3 - d). Linearity gives C_d(f_d) = -(C_0^2/D) J_d (beta (1 - d^2)/d + (3 - beta)(d + 1)(d + 2)/(3 - d)), a
negative number since 0 < beta < 3 for 1/2 < p < 1; with C_0 = 1/(p + 2), D = (1 - p)/p and d = 2p - 1 this is (2).
Direct quadrature of the defining integral at p = 0.6, 0.75 and 0.9 agrees with (2) with relative discrepancies below
1e-9; this is a numerical check of the analytic formula.

(b) Stream representation. For the smooth streams constructed below (W_e, W_0 and their linear combinations; the chart
W_* is used only through (A2) and (A3)), put s = y/x, Psi = -x^{p+1} W(s) and f = x^p F(s) for x > 0; each W has a
smooth odd extension through s = 0, satisfies W(0) = 0, and obeys W^{(j)}(s) = O(s^{p - j}) as s -> inf for j = 1, 2,
3 (a bound on W' alone would not suffice). Then -Psi_yy = d_x f is
    W'' = p F - s F',   F(s) = -s^p int_0^s t^{-p-1} W''(t) dt,   (A2)
the second formula being the solution of the first with F = O(s) at 0 when W'' = O(s); V_1 = -Psi_y = x^p W'(s) and
V_2 = Psi_x = x^p (s W' - (p + 1) W) satisfy d_y V_1 = d_x f, V_1 -> 0 as y -> inf and V_2(x, 0) = 0, d_y^2
V_2 = -d_x^2 f, and d_y V_2 -> 0 as y -> inf, so they are the velocity of (2) of 3.72 (as in A.3.75(e)). For the
streams used below, Psi, extended by Psi(-x, y) = -Psi(x, y) and Psi(x, -y) = -Psi(x, y), is smooth on R^2 minus the
origin (near the vertical axis it is -C_0 x y r^{p - 1} for W_0 below and -x y^p for the smoothed charts, and near the
positive horizontal axis -C_0 x y r^{p - 1}, respectively -A_e x^p y), so V and f are smooth there with the parities
of 3.76. Every stream used below has W(s) = w_1 s^p + w_2 s^{p - 2} + O(s^{p - 4}) as s -> inf, with the corresponding
differentiated expansion and no constant term; hence V_2 = -w_1 y^p + O(x^2 y^{p - 2}) near each positive
vertical-axis point, and comparison with the cusp formula of A.3.74(d) gives C_p(f) = 0. Smoothness of V follows from
the explicit local stream formulas above and is preserved by the linear combinations below. By Euler's identity, T(s)
:= (V[f] . grad f)(1, s) = p W' F - (p + 1) W F', and integration by parts gives int_0^S s T ds = (2p + 1) int_0^S s
W' F ds + (p + 1) int_0^S W F ds - (p + 1) S W(S) F(S). If W'' < 0 and F > 0 on (0, inf), then (A2) gives F' > p
F/s > 0 and p F - s F' < 0, so f_y = x^{p - 1} F' > 0, f_x = x^{p - 1}(p F - s F') < 0 in the open first quadrant, and
the trace derivative, which has the sign of (1 + s^2) F' - p s F, is positive; for the final densities constructed
below the positive axis limits follow from the W_0 component and the normalization f(0, 1) = 1, and the parities then
give f_y > 0 on R^2 minus the origin.

A positive limiting value. For the concave continuous chart W_*(s) = s on [0, 1] and s^p on [1, inf), (A2) (with the
jump p - 1 of W_*' at 1) gives F_* = 0 on [0, 1) and F_* = K_* s^p + b_* s^{p - 2} on (1, inf) with
K_* = (1 - p)(p + 2)/2 and b_* = -p (1 - p)/2, so F_* jumps by 1 - p at 1. Then T_* = 0 on (0, 1) and T_* = -p K_*
s^d + (p + 2) b_* s^{d - 2} on (1, inf), and by the integrated form above the jump contributes -(p + 1)(1 - p); hence
    M_* := FP int_0^inf s T_* ds = -(p + 1)(1 - p) + p K_*/(2p + 1) - (p + 2) b_*/(2p - 1) = (1 - p)^2 (2p^2 + 2p + 1)/(4p^2 - 1) > 0.   (A3)
Smoothing. Let eta >= 0 be smooth with support [-1, 1], positive inside, of integral 1, eta_e(a) = eta(a/e)/e, and
W_e(s) = int exp(p a) W_*(s exp(-a)) eta_e(a) da. W_e is smooth on (0, inf), concave, equal to A_e s for s < exp(-e)
(A_e > 0) and to s^p for s > exp(e); by (A2) and the substitution t = exp(a) u, F_e(s) = int exp((p - 2) a) F_*(s
exp(-a)) eta_e(a) da, which is smooth, 0 for s < exp(-e), positive for s > exp(-e), and equal to K_e s^p + b_*
s^{p - 2} for s > exp(e) with K_e = K_* int exp(-2a) eta_e(a) da. For e < log 2 the integrand of FP int s T_e is given
exactly by the exterior formula on (2, inf), while on [0, 2] W_e -> W_* uniformly and W_e', F_e converge boundedly
almost everywhere as e -> 0; by the integrated form of int_0^2 s T_e ds and dominated convergence, M_e := FP int s T_e
ds -> M_* > 0. Fix such an e with M_e > 0.

Strict signs and interpolation. Let W_0 = s (1 + s^2)^{(p - 1)/2}/(p + 2), the stream of the density f_0 of (4) of
3.75 (then (A2) gives F_0 = f_0(1, s), with W_0'' < 0 and F_0 > 0). For delta > 0 small put W = (W_e + delta
W_0)/(K_e + delta); then W'' < 0, F > 0, f(0, 1) = 1, there is no constant term at infinity, and, by continuity in
delta (on [0, 2] directly, on (2, inf) from the expansions in powers s^{p - 2j}, with s O(s^{d - 4}) integrable), the
second coefficient of the corresponding density f_+ is positive. For f_t = (1 - t) f_0 + t f_+, 0 <= t <= 1, the
inverse is linear, C_p(f_t) = 0, the strict signs and f_t(0, 1) = 1 persist, and t -> C_d((f_t)_d) is a quadratic
polynomial (bilinearity of V[f] . grad f and linearity of C_d), negative at t = 0 by (a) and positive at t = 1, so it
vanishes at some t in (0, 1). The density f_+ gives C_d > 0 and f_t gives C_d = 0. All these densities are smooth on
R^2 minus the origin, and, being homogeneous of degree p < 1 with f(0, 1) = 1, not C^1 at the origin.

## A.3.77 The core constant of the vertical velocity, and necessary far-field conditions

Bounds on a vertical line. In the class of 3.73, r >= y gives |g_xixi(xi, y)| <= C (1 + y)^{gamma - 2}, and g_xi(0,
y) = 0 by evenness, so |g_xi(xi, y)| <= C |xi| (1 + y)^{gamma - 2} and |g(xi, y) - G(y)| <= C xi^2
(1 + y)^{gamma - 2}/2. Integrating, |V_1(xi, y)| <= C |xi| (1 + y)^{gamma - 1}/(1 - gamma), and |V_2(xi, y)| <= C
int_0^y t (1 + t)^{gamma - 2} dt + C y int_y^inf (1 + t)^{gamma - 2} dt <= C_1 (1 + y)^gamma with C_1 independent of
xi. Hence there is y_0 >= 1, independent of xi, with b(xi, t) >= c t/2 for t >= y_0, and |a(xi, t)| <= C_2 |xi| with
a = c xi + V_1.

(a) For t >= y_0, (3) of 3.72 gives g_y = (g - a g_xi)/b, and 3.73 gives G' = G/v with v > 0 and G > 0 on (0, inf).
Since v - b = -Delta,
    g_y(xi, t) - G'(t) = (g - G)/b - a g_xi/b - G Delta/(b v),   (A1)
and by the bounds the first two terms on the right are at most C_4 xi^2 t^{gamma - 3} in absolute value, with C_4
independent of xi. Integrate (A1) over [y, Y] and let Y -> inf: (g - G)(xi, Y) -> 0, and the first two terms are
absolutely integrable, so the integral of the last term converges and
    I(xi, y) = (g - G)(xi, y) + int_y^inf ((g - G)/b - a g_xi/b) dt,
whence |I(xi, y)| <= (C/2 + C_4/(2 - gamma)) xi^2 y^{gamma - 2}. By 3.73 and the bound on V_2, G(t)/(b(xi, t)
v(t)) = (K/c^2) t^{p - 2} (1 + O(t^{gamma - 1})) > 0 for large t. If Delta(xi, t) = A t^alpha (1 + o(1)) with A != 0,
the integrand of (1) has eventually the sign of A and absolute value at least |A| K t^{p - 2 + alpha}/(2 c^2). If
p - 1 + alpha >= 0 the integral diverges; otherwise |I(xi, y)| >= |A| K y^{p - 1 + alpha}/(2 c^2 (1 - p - alpha)) for
large y, which contradicts the bound when p - 1 + alpha > gamma - 2. A nonzero limit is the case alpha = 0, admissible
since gamma - 1 - p < 0. Moments: as in A.3.74(d), if int_0^inf t |g_xixi(xi, t) - Q(xi) t^{p - 2}| dt < inf, then
V_2(xi, y) = Q(xi) y^p/(p (1 - p)) + m(xi) + o(1). Under the two hypotheses, Delta(xi_1, y) = (Q_1 - Q) y^p/(p
(1 - p)) + m(xi_1) - m_0 + o(1); if Q_1 != Q this has the form A y^p (1 + o(1)) with A != 0, which is excluded
(alpha = p > gamma - 1 - p), and if Q_1 = Q it tends to m(xi_1) - m_0, which is therefore 0.

(b) chi f is smooth on R^2 and d_xi^2 (chi f) = O(r^{p - 2}) as r -> inf, so the integrals (2) of 3.72 for chi f
converge on every vertical line, V_2[R] is defined, and V_2 = V_2[chi f] + V_2[R]. For |xi| >= 2, chi f = f near the
vertical line through (xi, 0), so V_2[chi f](xi, y) = V_2[f](xi, y), and the computation of A.3.74(d) gives, for fixed
xi != 0 and y -> inf, V_2[f](xi, y) = Q y^p/(p (1 - p)) + C_p(Theta) |xi|^p + O(xi^2 y^{p - 2}), Q = p
K + Theta''(pi/2). On the axis, d_xi^2 (chi f)(0, t) = Q t^{p - 2} for t >= 1, so for y >= 1, V_2[chi f](0, y) = Q
y^p/(p (1 - p)) + kappa with kappa = int_0^1 t d_xi^2 (chi f)(0, t) dt - Q/p. Hence for |xi| >= 2, Delta(xi,
y) -> C_p(Theta) |xi|^p - kappa + v_R(xi) as y -> inf, and by (a) this limit is 0. Dividing by |xi|^p and letting
|xi| -> inf gives C_p(Theta) = 0.

(c) Since r >= (|xi| + t)/sqrt 2, int_0^inf t |d_xi^2 R(xi, t)| dt <= C' int_0^inf t (1 + (|xi| + t)/sqrt
2)^{-2 - eps} dt <= C'' (1 + |xi|)^{-eps}, so w(xi) = int_0^inf t d_xi^2 R(xi, t) dt exists and tends to 0 as
|xi| -> inf, and V_2[R](xi, y) = w(xi) - int_y^inf (t - y) d_xi^2 R(xi, t) dt -> w(xi) as y -> inf, the last integral
being bounded by int_y^inf t |d_xi^2 R(xi, t)| dt. So the hypothesis of (b) holds with v_R = w - w(0), C_p(Theta) = 0,
and the limit in the proof of (b) gives -kappa + w(xi) - w(0) = 0 for |xi| >= 2; letting |xi| -> inf,
kappa + w(0) = 0. On every vertical line g_xixi - Q t^{p - 2} = (d_xi^2 (chi f) - Q t^{p - 2}) + d_xi^2 R; t times the
bracket is integrable near t = 0 (d_xi^2 (chi f) is bounded on compact sets and t^{p - 1} is integrable since p > 0),
and the bracket is O(xi^2 t^{p - 4}) as t -> inf (from d_xi^2 f(xi, t) = |xi|^{p - 2} q(t/|xi|) and q(s) = Q
s^{p - 2} + O(s^{p - 4}), exactly 0 on the axis for t >= 1), so the hypothesis of 3.74(d) holds on every line; on the
axis V_2(0, y) - Q y^p/(p (1 - p)) = kappa + V_2[R](0, y) -> kappa + w(0) = 0, that is m_0 = 0, and more precisely
E(y) = V_2(0, y) - Q y^p/(p (1 - p)) = -int_y^inf (t - y) d_xi^2 R(0, t) dt = O(y^{-eps}). Write a_Q = Q/(p (1 - p)),
so v(y) = c y + a_Q y^p + E(y). By 3.73, log(G(y)/(K y^p)) = -int_y^inf (1/v(t) - p/t) dt, and 1/v - p/t = -(a_Q
t^p + E(t))/(c t v(t)) = -a_Q t^{p - 2}/c^2 + O(t^{2p - 3}) + O(t^{-2 - eps}). Integrating, log(G(y)/(K y^p)) = a_Q
y^{p - 1}/(c^2 (1 - p)) + O(y^{2p - 2}) + O(y^{-1 - eps}), and 2p - 2 < -1 since p < 1/2; exponentiating gives (2)
with A_2 = K a_Q p^2/(1 - p) = K Q p/(1 - p)^2 = K Q/((1 - p) D), since D = (1 - p)/p. For the second statement: chi
f_d is smooth on R^2 and has d_xi^2 (chi f_d) = O(r^{d - 2}) and d - 2 = -2 - (1 - 2p), and e < d, so |d_xi^2
R| <= C'' (1 + r)^{d - 2} and the first hypothesis holds with eps = 1 - 2p. For |xi| >= 2, d_xi^2 f_d(xi,
t) = |xi|^{d - 2} q_{f_d}(t/|xi|), where q_{f_d}(s) = O(s) as s -> 0 (smoothness and oddness at the horizontal axis)
and q_{f_d}(s) = Q_{f_d} s^{d - 2} + O(s^{d - 4}) as s -> inf, so s q_{f_d} is integrable (d < 0) and int_0^inf t
d_xi^2 f_d(xi, t) dt = C_d^-(f_d) |xi|^d; and int_0^inf t (1 + r)^{e - 2} dt = O(|xi|^e) (substitute t = |xi| u; the
integral in u converges since e < 0). Hence w(xi) = C_d^-(f_d) |xi|^d + O(|xi|^e) for |xi| >= 2. By the previous
paragraph w is constant on |xi| >= 2 and tends to 0, so w = 0 there, and C_d^-(f_d) |xi|^d = O(|xi|^e) with e < d
forces C_d^-(f_d) = 0.

(d) Here p = 1/2, Q y^p/(p (1 - p)) = 4 Q y^{1/2}, and the computation in (b) for chi f applies unchanged. For
|xi| >= 2, d_xi^2 f_0(xi, t) = xi^{-2} q_{f_0}(t/|xi|) with q_{f_0} the expression of 3.76 at q = 0; as s -> inf,
F_0(s) = f_0(1/s, 1) = F_inf + (B/2) s^{-2} + O(s^{-4}) by homogeneity and smoothness at the vertical axis, so
q_{f_0}(s) = B s^{-2} + O(s^{-4}), and q_{f_0}(s) = O(s) as s -> 0. Hence int_0^S s q_{f_0} ds = B log
S + C_0(f_0) + O(S^{-2}) and S int_S^inf q_{f_0} ds = B + O(S^{-2}), so with S = y/|xi|, V_2[f_0](xi, y) = B log y - B
log |xi| + C_0(f_0) + B + o(1) as y -> inf. On the axis d_xi^2 (chi f_0)(0, t) = B t^{-2} for t >= 1, so for y >= 1,
V_2[chi f_0](0, y) = kappa_0 + B log y + B with kappa_0 = int_0^1 t d_xi^2 (chi f_0)(0, t) dt. As in (c), V_2[R_2](xi,
y) -> w_2(xi) = int_0^inf t d_xi^2 R_2(xi, t) dt with |w_2(xi)| <= C'' (1 + |xi|)^e. Hence for |xi| >= 2,
    Delta(xi, y) -> C_p(Theta) |xi|^{1/2} - B log |xi| + C_0(f_0) - kappa - kappa_0 + w_2(xi) - w_2(0),
and by (a) this limit is 0 for every |xi| >= 2. Dividing by |xi|^{1/2}, then by log |xi|, and letting |xi| -> inf
gives C_p(Theta) = 0, then B = 0, and then C_0(f_0) = kappa + kappa_0 + w_2(0). On the axis, with B = 0, V_2(0, y) = 4
Q y^{1/2} + kappa + kappa_0 + V_2[R_2](0, y) = 4 Q y^{1/2} + C_0(f_0) + O(y^e). Then v = 2 y (1 + u) with u = 2 Q
y^{-1/2} + C_0(f_0)/(2 y) + O(y^{e - 1}), 1/v - 1/(2 t) = (1/(2 t)) (-u + u^2 + O(u^3)) = -Q t^{-3/2} + (4
Q^2 - C_0(f_0)/2)/(2 t^2) + O(t^{-5/2}) + O(t^{e - 2}), so log(G(y)/(K y^{1/2})) = 2 Q y^{-1/2} - (2
Q^2 - C_0(f_0)/4)/y + o(1/y), and exponentiating gives (3).

## A.3.78 A near-axis layer of the hydrostatic far field (formal)

Derivation of (1). For u = y^q h(z), xi u_xi = y^q z h' and y u_y = y^q (q h - mu z h'), so (c X . grad - 1) u = y^q
(c (1 - mu) z h' + (c q - 1) h), and c q - 1 = mu + 1 - c - 1 = mu - c because c mu p = mu and c (p - 1) = 1 - c. The
velocity correction multiplies d_y f_p = p K y^{p - 1} + O(xi^2 y^{p - 3}), giving p K y^{n + p - 1} w = p K y^q w.
The remaining products are, at fixed z: Q y^p d_y u/(p (1 - p)) = O(y^{q + p - 1}); V_1[f_p] u_xi with
V_1[f_p] = O(|xi| y^{p - 1}) and u_xi = y^{q - mu} h', of order y^{q + p - 1}; y^n w O(xi^2 y^{p - 3}) = O(y^{q + 2
mu - 2}) = O(y^{q + p - 1}); the products with f_s and V_s, smaller by O(y^{p - 1}) for the same reason; and the
quadratic terms in the layer, y^n w d_y u = O(y^{q + n - 1}) and V_1^l d_xi(f_p + u), where V_1^l is the horizontal
velocity of the layer, O(y^{q - mu + 1}) by (A0) below, so that V_1^l d_xi f_p = O(y^{q + p - 1}). Since n < p, all
are O(y^{q + p - 1}). These orders count the local interactions at fixed z only (see (a)); they assume that f_s
contains all smooth outer terms balanced by their own equations (if f_s contained only f_{2p-1}, the unbalanced smooth
residual of degree 3p - 2 would enter at the relative order y^{-(1 - p)(2 - p)/2}, earlier than y^{p - 1}, since
q - (3p - 2) = (1 - p)(2 - p)/2). For the velocity, V_{2,yy} = -g_xixi is exact; with y d_y acting on y^n w(z) as y^n
(n - mu th) w, y^2 d_y^2 = (y d_y)(y d_y - 1) gives y^n (n - mu th)(n - mu th - 1) w = (mu th - n)(mu th - n + 1) w
y^n, while -d_xi^2 (y^q h) = -y^{q - 2 mu} h'' and q - 2 mu = n - 2. The term Q y^p/(p (1 - p)) balances the axis
curvature Q y^{p - 2} of f_p, V_s balances the remaining curvature of f_p and f_s, and C_p(Theta) |xi|^p, which is
part of y^n w, is annihilated by d_y^2.

The inverse (2). Let xi > 0. For u = y^q h(xi/y^mu), u_xixi(xi, t) = t^{n - 2} h''(xi t^{-mu}). The substitution
tau = xi t^{-mu} gives t^{n - 1} dt = -(1/mu) xi^p tau^{-p - 1} d tau and t^{n - 2} dt = -(1/mu) xi^s tau^{-s - 1} d
tau (n/mu = p, (n - 1)/mu = s), and with xi^p = y^n z^p and y xi^s = y^n z^s (mu s = n - 1) the canonical vertical
velocity int_0^y t u_xixi dt + y int_y^inf u_xixi dt of the layer becomes y^n times the bracket in (2) divided by mu.
The integrals converge, since h'' is bounded, -s - 1 > -1, h'' = O(z^{p - 2}) as z -> inf and
p - s - 3 = 1/mu - 3 < -1. Adding C_p(Theta) |xi|^p = y^n C_p(Theta) z^p from V_2[f_p] gives (2); it solves the second
equation of (1) because the canonical V_2 satisfies V_{2,yy} = -g_xixi. At fixed xi the layer part y^n times the
bracket tends to 0 as y -> 0 (it is A y |xi|^s + O(y^{p + 1} |xi|^{p - 2}) there), while C_p(Theta) |xi|^p is part of
V_2[f_p], which vanishes at y = 0 only in full; the condition V_2(xi, 0) = 0 is to be checked on the complete outer
inverse. In the same way the horizontal velocity of the layer is
    V_1^l = -int_y^inf u_xi dt = -(1/mu) y^{n + mu - 1} z^{s + 1} int_0^z tau^{-s-2} h'(tau) d tau,   (A0)
and n + mu - 1 = q - mu + 1 (at s = -1 the integral is to be kept as it stands). Two solutions of the second equation
of (1) with the same h differ by a combination of z^p and z^s, because (mu m - n)(mu m - n + 1) = 0 exactly for m = p
and m = s; boundedness at z = 0 excludes z^s, as s < 0. As z -> inf, z^p int_z^inf tau^{-p-1} h'' d tau = O(z^{p - 2})
and z^s int_0^z tau^{-s-1} h'' d tau = mu A z^s + O(z^{p - 2}), so the bracket in (2) has no z^p term and the
coefficient C_p(Theta) of z^p fixes the solution; this gives the uniqueness statement and the expansion of w. As
z -> 0+, the second integral term of (2) is an even power series in z (asymptotically) beginning with h''(0)/(-s), and
z^p int_z^inf tau^{-p-1} h'' d tau = h''(0)/p + F z^p + O(z^2) with a constant F and an even remainder series. Hence
(2) is smooth at z = 0 exactly when F = -mu C_p(Theta), and then w(0) = (h''(0)/mu)(1/p - 1/s) = h''(0)/(n (1 - n)).
For the solution of (c), w obtained from the first equation of (1) is smooth, bounded and has coefficient C_p(Theta)
of z^p at infinity, so it equals (2) and F = -mu C_p(Theta) holds.

Matching. In the overlap |xi| << y << |xi|^{1/mu} (z -> inf), V_2 consists of the outer expansion Q y^p/(p
(1 - p)) + C_p(Theta) |xi|^p + O(xi^2 y^{p - 2}) and, by (2), of the term y^n A z^s = A y |xi|^s, which comes from y
int_y^inf g_xixi dt over the part of the vertical line inside the layer; it is a term of the overlap, not of the
expansion at fixed xi as y -> inf. On the density side the cusp of f_{2p-1} equals (p K C_p(Theta)/D) y^q z^p; this is
the coefficient of z^p in h forced by the first equation of (1) when w ~ C_p(Theta) z^p, since (mu - c) + c (1 - mu)
p = 1 - c = -D. A component z^m of h with w of lower order needs (mu - c) + c (1 - mu) m = 0, that is m = (c - mu)/(c
(1 - mu)) = p + 2; in outer variables y^q z^{p + 2} = |xi|^{p + 2} y^{-2} because q - mu (p + 2) = -2, a homogeneous
function of degree p behaving like |cos th|^{p + 2} at the axis, excluded when Theta is smooth.

Reduction. The first equation of (1) gives w = -(c (1 - mu)/(p K)) (th - p - 2) h. With h'' = z^{-2} th (th - 1) h the
second becomes
    p K th (th - 1) h = c (1 - mu) z^2 (mu th - n)(mu th - n + 1)(th - p - 2) h,   (A1)
that is (th - p)(th - s)(th - p - 2) h = 2 lambda h'', since mu th - n = mu (th - p), mu th - n + 1 = mu (th - s) and
p K/(mu^2 c (1 - mu)) = 2 lambda. Put t = z^{-2}, T = t d/dt and h = t^{-p/2} u. Then th acts on h as t^{-p/2} (-2
T + p) on u, so th (th - 1) -> 4 (T - p/2)(T - (p - 1)/2), mu th - n -> -2 mu T (as mu p = n), mu th - n + 1 -> -2 mu
(T - 1/(2 mu)) and th - p - 2 -> -2 (T + 1). Multiplying (A1) by t and dividing by -8 mu^2 c (1 - mu)/(p K) gives
    [T (T + b_1 - 1)(T + b_2 - 1) - X (T + a_1)(T + a_2)] u = 0,   X = -lambda t,   (A2)
with b_1 - 1 = -1/(2 mu), b_2 - 1 = 1, a_1 = -p/2, a_2 = (1 - p)/2 and lambda = p K/(2 mu^2 c (1 - mu)) = 4 p^2
K/((p + 1)^2 (1 - p)); T = X d/dX. This is the equation of 2F2(a_1, a_2; b_1, b_2; X). At X = 0 its local exponents
are 0, 1 - b_1 = 1/(p + 1) and 1 - b_2 = -1, giving h ~ z^p, z^{p - 2/(p + 1)} = z^s and z^{p + 2}; the first two
solutions are u = 2F2(a_1, a_2; b_1, b_2; X) and u = (-X)^{1 - b_1} 2F2(a_1 - b_1 + 1, a_2 - b_1 + 1; 2 - b_1,
b_2 - b_1 + 1; X) (b_1 is not an integer). The third contains a logarithm: inserting h = z^{p + 2} + k z^p log z + ...
in (th - p)(th - s)(th - p - 2) h = 2 lambda h'' and comparing the coefficients of z^p gives -2 k (p - s) = 2 lambda
(p + 1)(p + 2), that is k = -mu lambda (p + 1)(p + 2). The solutions that are O(z^p) as z -> inf are exactly span(h_1,
h_2).

Behaviour at z = 0. As X -> -inf, every solution of (A2) is a combination of (-X)^{-a_1} (1 + O(1/X)), (-X)^{-a_2}
(1 + O(1/X)), each with a full asymptotic series in powers of 1/X, and of a recessive solution e^X
(-X)^{a_1 + a_2 - b_1 - b_2} (1 + O(1/X)) (for example DLMF 16.11); for h the recessive solution is z^{5 + 2p + s}
exp(-lambda/z^2) (1 + O(z^2)), because p - 2 (a_1 + a_2 - b_1 - b_2) = 3 + 3p + 2p/(p + 1) = 5 + 2p + s, and it is
flat at z = 0. For h_1 and h_2 the expansions follow from the Mellin-Barnes representation (DLMF 16.5.1) of 2F2(a_1,
a_2; b_1, b_2; X) as Gamma(b_1) Gamma(b_2)/(Gamma(a_1) Gamma(a_2)) times (1/(2 pi i)) times the contour integral of
Gamma(a_1 + sigma) Gamma(a_2 + sigma) Gamma(-sigma) (-X)^sigma/(Gamma(b_1 + sigma) Gamma(b_2 + sigma)), over a contour
separating the poles of Gamma(-sigma) from those of Gamma(a_1 + sigma) Gamma(a_2 + sigma) (for h_1 the contour is not
a vertical line: since a_1 = -p/2 < 0, the pole sigma = p/2 of Gamma(a_1 + sigma) lies to the right of the pole
sigma = 0 of Gamma(-sigma), and the contour is deformed so that p/2 lies on its left and 0 on its right). Moving the
contour to the left across the poles sigma = -a_1 - k and -a_2 - k gives the expansions: the residues give the
connection coefficients below, the remainder after finitely many poles is O(|X|^{-M}) on the negative axis, and
differentiation under the integral shows that the expansions may be differentiated termwise. (A pointwise even
expansion alone would not give smoothness at z = 0.) Since a_1 - a_2 = -1/2 is not an integer, the two algebraic
series involve disjoint sets of powers. In terms of h, (-X)^{-a_1} = lambda^{p/2} z^{-p} gives z^p z^{-p} = 1 times a
series in z^2 and (-X)^{-a_2} = lambda^{-a_2} z^{1 - p} gives z times a series in z^2. Hence a combination of h_1 and
h_2 with zero odd coefficient has an even extension of class C^inf at z = 0, and one with nonzero odd coefficient has
h'(0+) != 0, so its even extension is not C^1. For h_1 the coefficient of z is Gamma(b_1) Gamma(b_2) Gamma(a_1 - a_2)
lambda^{-a_2}/(Gamma(a_1) Gamma(b_1 - a_2) Gamma(b_2 - a_2)); here a_1 = -p/2 is not a pole,
Gamma(a_1 - a_2) = Gamma(-1/2) != 0, b_2 - a_2 = (3 + p)/2 > 0, and 1/Gamma(b_1 - a_2) = 0 exactly when
b_1 - a_2 = (p^2 + 2p - 1)/(2 (p + 1)), which lies in (-1/2, 1/2), is 0, that is p = sqrt(2) - 1. For h_2 the
parameters are a_1' = a_1 - b_1 + 1 = (1 - p)(2 + p)/(2 (p + 1)) > 0, a_2' = a_2 - b_1 + 1, b_1' = 2 - b_1,
b_2' = 3 - b_1, with a_1' - a_2' = -1/2, b_1' - a_2' = 1 - a_2 = (1 + p)/2 > 0 and
b_2' - a_2' = 2 - a_2 = (3 + p)/2 > 0, so its coefficient is a product of finite nonzero factors, negative because
Gamma(-1/2) < 0 and all other arguments are positive. The coefficient of 1 (even coefficient) of h_1 is Gamma(b_1)
Gamma(b_2) Gamma(a_2 - a_1) lambda^{-a_1}/(Gamma(a_2) Gamma(b_1 - a_1) Gamma(b_2 - a_1)), and that of h_2 is the same
expression in the shifted parameters.

Count. Let O be the odd-coefficient functional; O(h_2) != 0, so S_inf = span(h_1, h_2) and the kernel S_0 of O on the
solution space are different planes. Their intersection consists of a h_1 + b h_2 with a O(h_1) + b O(h_2) = 0, the
line spanned by h_* = h_1 - (O(h_1)/O(h_2)) h_2, whose coefficient of z^p is 1 (the series of h_2 contains only the
powers z^{s - 2k}). The solutions with h even and smooth at z = 0 and no z^{p + 2} component are therefore the
multiples of h_*, and the coefficient of z^p in h is fixed by matching to p K C_p(Theta)/D; this gives exactly one
solution, zero when C_p(Theta) = 0. Its value at z = 0 is (p K C_p(Theta)/D) times the combination E(h_1) - (O(h_1)/
O(h_2)) E(h_2) of the even coefficients, which equals the closed form (3) (the simplification was obtained in an
external analysis and is checked below); all Gamma functions in (3) have positive arguments, so h(0) has the sign of
C_p(Theta). The recessive solution R lies in S_0; it is not in S_inf, since otherwise R would be a multiple of h_*,
while R is flat at z = 0 and h_*(0) != 0. So adding a multiple of R to h_* introduces a z^{p + 2} component: the
recessive part of the solution is fixed. At z = 0 the equations (1) give (mu - c) h(0) + p K w(0) = 0 and h''(0) + n
(n - 1) w(0) = 0, so w(0) = (c - mu) h(0)/(p K) = (1 - n) h(0)/(p^2 K) and h''(0) = n (1 - n) w(0), in agreement with
the value of (2) at z = 0. At p = sqrt(2) - 1, O(h_1) = 0, h_* = h_1 and A = 0, in agreement with A = (1/mu)
(h'(inf) - h'(0)) = 0 at s = -1; the horizontal velocity of the layer does not vanish with A (see Consistency).

Consistency. The layer contributes y^{n - 2} h''(z) to g_xixi, with h'' bounded; at fixed xi it contributes O(xi^2
y^{n - 2}) to g(xi, y) - G(y), smaller than the term Q xi^2 y^{p - 2}/2 of f_p, and O(xi^2 y^{n - 2 mu}) to V_2(xi,
y) - V_2(0, y), with n - 2 mu = n - p - 1 < 0; the latter is larger than the contribution O(xi^2 y^{p - 2}) of the
smooth outer terms, as n - 2 mu - (p - 2) = (1 - p)(2 - p)/2 > 0. With a = Q/(p (1 - p)), int_0^y t (g_xixi - Q
t^{p - 2}) dt = (V_2 - a y^p) - y d_y (V_2 - a y^p), and the layer part y^n w(z) contributes y^n ((1 - n) w + mu th
w) = (1 - n) w(0) y^n + O(xi^2 y^{n - 2 mu}) on each vertical line (w is smooth and even); this is where the term
C_p(Theta) |xi|^p of V_2[f_p], which is part of y^n w, is cancelled. On the axis g_xixi(0, y) - Q y^{p - 2} contains
h''(0) y^{n - 2} with h''(0) = n (1 - n) w(0) != 0 when C_p(Theta) != 0, so int t |g_xixi - Q t^{p - 2}| dt diverges
(n > 0). The outer velocity y A |xi|^s has degree 1 + s = (p^2 + 2p - 1)/(p + 1), and 1 + s - p = (p - 1)/(p + 1) < 0,
1 + s - (2p - 1) = p (1 - p)/(p + 1) > 0; by (A0), as z -> inf, V_1^l = B xi |xi|^s + o(|xi|^{1 + s}) with B = -(1/mu)
int_0^inf tau^{-s-2} h'(tau) d tau (convergent, since h' = O(tau) at 0 and p - s - 3 < -1), and integration by parts
gives A = -(s + 1) B; at p = sqrt(2) - 1 (s = -1) the vertical component vanishes and the horizontal one, B sgn(xi),
remains. The transport of this velocity against d f_p gives density of degree p + s, with c (p + s) - 1 = c s != 0 (no
transport resonance), p + s - (2p - 1) = 1 + s - p < 0 and p + s - (3p - 2) = p (1 - p)/(p + 1) > 0.

Next orders (the remarks in (e); from the external analysis, rederived here, and for p = sqrt(5) - 2 also found
independently by the checker). For a density correction y^{nu + p - 1} H(z) with velocity y^nu W(z), the homogeneous
inner equations are c (1 - mu) (th - r) H + p K W = 0 and H'' + mu^2 (th - m)(th - l) W = 0, with m = nu/mu,
l = (nu - 1)/mu and r = 2 (1 - nu)/(1 - p) (for nu = n these are p, s and p + 2), so (th - m)(th - l)(th - r) H = 2
lambda H'' with the same lambda. The z^r branch changes the degree-p trace and is excluded, and the coefficient of z^m
is matching data; a homogeneous solution is then a multiple of z^l 2F2(-l/2, (1 - l)/2; 1 + 1/(2 mu), 1 + (r - l)/2;
-lambda/z^2), and its coefficient of z at z = 0 is Gamma(1 + 1/(2 mu)) Gamma(1 + (r - l)/2) Gamma(-1/2)
lambda^{-(1 - l)/2}/(Gamma(-l/2) Gamma((1 + m)/2) Gamma((1 + r)/2)), by the formula above. The local interactions of
the leading layer enter at nu = q (relative order y^{p - 1}) and the quadratic terms at nu = 2n - 1 (relative order
y^{n - 1}). At c = 2 (p = 1/2, mu = 3/4) these give nu = -1/8 with (m, l, r) = (-1/6, -3/2, 9/2) and nu = -1/4 with
(m, l, r) = (-1/3, -5/3, 5); the arguments (-l/2, (1 + m)/2, (1 + r)/2) are (3/4, 5/12, 11/4) and (5/6, 1/3, 3) and
the numerator is finite, so the coefficient is nonzero and there is no homogeneous solution. The coefficient vanishes
when m = -1, that is nu = -mu: for nu = q this is p^2 + 4p - 1 = 0, p = sqrt(5) - 2, and for nu = 2n - 1 it is
2p^2 + 3p - 1 = 0, p = (sqrt(17) - 3)/4. The sources at these orders, the conditions they may have to satisfy at these
values of p, the nonlocal terms of relative order y^{mu (p - 1)} and the logarithms are not computed.

Checks. A symbolic computation reproduces the two equations (1) from the inserted expansion (the reduction to (A1) and
(A2) was checked by hand, by the checker and in an external audit). A multiprecision evaluation (40 digits) at
p = 0.75, 0.5, sqrt(2) - 1, 1/3 and 0.25 shows that h_1 and h_2 solve (A1) with normalized residuals of about 1e-41,
and that the even and odd coefficients obtained by cubic fits of h_1 and h_2 on 0.02 <= z <= 0.05 agree with the
connection formulas to within 4.1e-7 for the even and 5.4e-5 for the odd coefficients (absolute); at the decimal
approximation of sqrt(2) - 1 used, the formula gives -4.2e-21 for the odd coefficient of h_1 and the fit -7.5e-6 (the
exact zero follows from the Gamma formula). An external audit found ODE residuals below 1.2e-55 and agreement of the
canonical integrals below 1.4e-30 at the same five values of p. The closed form (3) agrees with (p K
C_p(Theta)/D)(E(h_1) - (O(h_1)/O(h_2)) E(h_2)) to a relative 7e-41 at p = 0.1, 0.25, sqrt(2) - 1, 0.5, 0.6, 0.75 and
0.9 (K = C_p(Theta) = 1, 40 digits), and with a fit of h near z = 0 to about 1e-8 at p = 0.25, 0.5, 0.75; the
relations for w(0) and h''(0) agree with the fit to about 1e-4 relative. At p = 1/2, K = C_p(Theta) = 1:
h(0) = 0.465462139 and A = 0.140564477, and the value of (z^p int_z^inf t^{-p-1} h'' dt - h''(0)/p)/(mu z^p) at
z = 0.1, 0.07, 0.05 is -0.99539, -0.99731, -0.99838, approaching -C_p(Theta) = -1 at the rate z^{2 - p} (similarly at
p = 0.25 and 0.75). The external analysis checked (2) against direct quadrature of the canonical inverse at 45 digits
(agreement 7e-42) and the checker rederived (1), (A1), the connection coefficients, the count and (2) independently.
These checks concern the formal inner problem only.

## A.3.79 The near-axis layer of the signed problem (formal, except the parts stated as proved in 3.79)

Inner equations. The derivation of A.3.78 applies with the velocity -V: the velocity correction now enters the
transport equation as -p K y^q w, while V_{2,yy} = -g_xixi for the inner part w of V_2, the inverse (2) of 3.78, its
uniqueness statement and the exclusion of the z^{p + 2} branch are unchanged (that branch needs (mu - c) + c (1 - mu)
m = 0, m = p + 2, independently of the velocity). With h ~ H z^p and w ~ C_p(Theta) z^p as z -> inf, the first
equation of (1) gives -D H - p K C_p(Theta) = 0, since (mu - c) + c (1 - mu) p = -D; this is the cusp of
f_{2p-1} = -(V[f_p] . grad f_p)/D, because d_y f_p = p K y^{p - 1} + O(xi^2 y^{p - 3}) and V_2[f_p] contains
C_p(Theta) |xi|^p. The first equation gives w = (c (1 - mu)/(p K)) (th - p - 2) h, and the second becomes (A1) of
A.3.78 with K replaced by -K, that is (th - p)(th - s)(th - p - 2) h = -2 lambda h''; the substitution t = z^{-2},
h = t^{-p/2} u of A.3.78 gives (A2) of A.3.78 with X = lambda t. A symbolic computation inserting the expansion with
either sign of the velocity reproduces (th - p)(th - s)(th - p - 2) h = 2 e lambda h'' (e = 1 for (3) of 3.72, e = -1
for the signed problem) after elimination, up to the common nonzero factor (p + 1)^2 (p - 1)/(8 K p^2).

Sign of K. The proof of 3.73(a) uses only the axis equation v G' = G, which holds because V_1(0, y) = 0 by parity, the
formula for V_2(0, y) and its derivative, g_y(0) = 1 and the bounds of 3.72(d). For the signed problem the axis
equation is v G' = G with v(y) = c y - V_2(0, y), so v' = c - int_y^inf g_xixi(0, t) dt, v(0) = 0 and v(y)/y -> c; v
G' = G forces v'(0) = 1 (the centre condition int_0^inf g_xixi(0, t) dt = c - 1 of 3.72(e)), and the steps of
A.3.73(a) that give the positivity and the far field apply word for word: v, G and G' are positive on (0, inf), and
since v(t) - c t = O(t^gamma), G(y) = K y^p (1 + O(y^{gamma - 1})) with 0 < K < inf. (The other identities of 3.73(a),
(2) and the cubic relation, change sign for the signed problem, since v'' = g_xixi(0, .) here; they are not used.)
Far-field terms. As c (2p - 1) - 1 = -D and c (3p - 2) - 1 = -2D, the terms of degrees 2p - 1 and 3p - 2 in the
transport equation of the signed problem give D f_{2p-1} + V[f_p] . grad f_p = 0 and 2 D f_{3p-2} + V[f_p] . grad
f_{2p-1} + V[f_{2p-1}] . grad f_p = 0; the first gives f_{2p-1} = -f_d, and, V being linear, the second becomes (1) of
3.76. The symmetry is the identity (c X + V[-g]) . grad (-g) = -(c X - V[g]) . grad g.

Behaviour at z = 0. As X -> +inf every solution of (A2) is a combination of X^{-a_1} (1 + O(1/X)), X^{-a_2}
(1 + O(1/X)), each with a full asymptotic series in powers of 1/X, and of e^X X^{a_1 + a_2 - b_1 - b_2} (1 + O(1/X))
(DLMF 16.11); for h these are lambda^{p/2} times an asymptotic series in z^2, lambda^{-a_2} z times an asymptotic
series in z^2, and z^{5 + 2p + s} exp(lambda/z^2) (1 + O(z^2)) (the exponent as in A.3.78), unbounded as z -> 0+. So
the solutions bounded near z = 0 are those without the exponential part, a plane S_b. Since a_1 = -p/2 and
a_2 = (1 - p)/2 are not poles of Gamma, DLMF 16.11.7 (with kappa = 1) gives 2F2(a_1, a_2; b_1, b_2; X) ~ Gamma(b_1)
Gamma(b_2) e^X X^{a_1 + a_2 - b_1 - b_2}/(Gamma(a_1) Gamma(a_2)) as X -> +inf, a nonzero multiple; hence h_1 is not in
S_b and S_b differs from S_inf = span(h_1, h_2).

The Meijer function. Let u_G(X) = (1/(2 pi i)) int Gamma(-sigma) Gamma(1 - b_1 - sigma) Gamma(a_1 + sigma)
Gamma(a_2 + sigma) X^sigma/Gamma(b_2 + sigma) dsigma (DLMF 16.17.1, G^{2,2}_{2,3}(X | 1 - a_1, 1 - a_2; 0, 1 - b_1 |
1 - b_2)), over a contour from -i inf to +i inf separating the poles sigma = k and 1 - b_1 + k (k = 0, 1, ...) of the
first two factors from the poles sigma = -a_1 - k and -a_2 - k of the next two. The two sets are disjoint (the second
lies in (-inf, p/2], the first in [0, inf), and p/2 is neither an integer nor 1 - b_1 + k, since p/2 = 1/(p + 1) only
for p = 1); as -a_1 = p/2 > 0 the contour is deformed so that p/2 lies on its left and 0 on its right, as in A.3.78.
By Stirling's formula the integrand is O(|sigma|^k exp(-3 pi |Im sigma|/2)) on the contour for some k, so the integral
converges for |arg X| < 3 pi/2, in particular for X > 0, and u_G solves X (T + a_1)(T + a_2) u = T
(T + b_1 - 1)(T + b_2 - 1) u, T = X d/dX, which is (A2) with X = lambda t (DLMF 16.21.1 with the upper parameters
1 - a_1, 1 - a_2 and the lower parameters 0, 1 - b_1, 1 - b_2). Closing to the right gives the convergent expansion at
X = 0 as minus the sum of the residues at sigma = k and 1 - b_1 + k, simple because 1 - b_1 = 1/(p + 1) is not an
integer: u_G is a power series in X plus X^{1 - b_1} times a power series, without the exponent 1 - b_2 = -1, so
h_G = z^p u_G(lambda/z^2) is in S_inf. Moving the contour to the left across the poles sigma = -a_1 - k and -a_2 - k
gives, for X -> +inf, the expansion of u_G as the sum of these residues with remainder O(X^{-M}) after finitely many
poles, and differentiation under the integral shows that it may be differentiated termwise; there is no exponential
part. The residue of Gamma(a_2 + sigma) at sigma = -a_2 is 1, which gives c_O; that of Gamma(a_1 + sigma) at -a_1
gives c_E. In (2), 1 - b_1 + a_2 = (3 - p^2)/(2 (p + 1)) > 0, a_2 > 0, b_2 - a_2 = (3 + p)/2 > 0 and
Gamma(a_1 - a_2) = Gamma(-1/2) = -2 sqrt(pi), so c_O < 0. Since a_1 - a_2 = -1/2, the two algebraic series involve
disjoint powers; in h, X^{-a_2} = lambda^{-a_2} z^{1 - p} gives the odd term c_O lambda^{-a_2} z, so h_G'(0+) = c_O
lambda^{-a_2} != 0. (Also c_E < 0, as Gamma(-p/2) < 0 and the other arguments are positive, and
u_G(0) = Gamma(1 - b_1) Gamma(a_1) Gamma(a_2)/Gamma(b_2) < 0, minus the residue at sigma = 0, since the upward contour
closes clockwise to the right.) In particular h_G is not zero, so h_G is in S_b and in S_inf.

Count. Two different planes in the three-dimensional solution space meet in a line, so S_b and S_inf meet exactly in
span(h_G). A solution whose even extension is C^1 at z = 0 is bounded near 0, hence in S_b; if it has no z^{p + 2}
component it is in S_inf, so it is a multiple of h_G, and its derivative at 0+ is that multiple of c_O lambda^{-a_2},
so the multiple is 0. Then the coefficient of z^p of h is 0, and matching to -p K C_p(Theta)/D forces C_p(Theta) = 0.
Equivalently, the even algebraic solution, which spans the solutions with C^1 even extension, has a nonzero z^{p + 2}
component. In 3.78, by contrast, the exponential solution is recessive at z = 0 and the solutions with C^1 even
extension form a plane S_0, which meets S_inf in a line with nonzero coefficient of z^p.

Checks. A symbolic computation reproduces (1) and the eliminated third-order equation for both signs (above). A
multiprecision evaluation (40 digits) at p = 0.25, 1/3, sqrt(2) - 1, 0.5 and 0.75 (K = 1) shows that u_G solves (A2)
with X = lambda t with normalized residuals below 1e-40 at X = 0.3, 3 and 30, that u_G at X = 200 and 800 equals the
sum of its two algebraic residue series, six terms each, to relative 1.5e-15 and 3.4e-19 or better, and that |X
u_G(X)| is at most 4.5e-5 and 4.5e-8 at X = 1e-6 and 1e-9, consistent with the absence of the exponent -1. The closed
form in (2) agrees with the Gamma quotient to relative 3e-41 at p = 0.1, 0.25, sqrt(2) - 1, 0.5, 0.75 and 0.9, and the
ratio of 2F2(a_1, a_2; b_1, b_2; X) to e^X X^{a_1 + a_2 - b_1 - b_2} at X = 100, 400 and 1600 approaches the predicted
constant at the rate 1/X (at p = 0.5: -0.155546, -0.151909, -0.151032 against -0.150743). Independently of the Meijer
function, the even and odd algebraic solutions, normalized by u = X^{-a_1} (1 + O(1/X)) and u = X^{-a_2} (1 + O(1/X)),
were computed from their optimally truncated asymptotic series at z = 0.12 and integrated outward (implicit Radau
method, relative tolerance 1e-11, absolute tolerance 1e-14) to z = 200; the combination without a z^{p + 2} component,
estimated from h''/((p + 2)(p + 1) z^p) at z = 200, has odd to even ratio 0.443898, 0.904805, 0.743366 and 1.406988 at
p = 0.25, 0.5, sqrt(2) - 1 and 0.75, against c_O/c_E = 0.443896, 0.904794, 0.743360 and 1.406913 (the estimates of the
z^{p + 2} coefficients at z = 100 and 200 differ by relative amounts up to 2e-4, which limits the accuracy of these
ratios). A second proof of the last statement of the count, without the Meijer function. Let F(tau, z) = 2F1(-p/2,
-(p + 2)/2; 1/2; -tau z^2/lambda) and E(z) = Gamma(-s/2)^{-1} int_0^inf e^{-tau} tau^{-s/2 - 1} F(tau, z) dtau (here
-s/2 > 0). On F, th = 2 tau d/dtau, and with Phi = (tau d/dtau - p/2)(tau d/dtau - (p + 2)/2) F the Gauss equation
gives (th - p)(th - s)(th - p - 2) F + 2 lambda F_zz = 8 (tau d/dtau - s/2 - tau) Phi; since e^{-tau} tau^{-s/2 - 1}
(tau d/dtau - s/2 - tau) Phi = d/dtau (e^{-tau} tau^{-s/2} Phi) and Phi grows polynomially in tau, the integral of the
right side vanishes, so E solves the third-order equation. E is even and smooth in z with E(0) = 1, and Watson's lemma
gives at z = 0 the asymptotic series 1 + sum_k e_k z^{2k}, e_k = (-p/2)_k (-(p + 2)/2)_k (-s/2)_k
(-1/lambda)^k/((1/2)_k k!), so E is the even algebraic solution with h(0) = 1. As (-p/2) - (-(p + 2)/2) = 1, 2F1(-p/2,
-(p + 2)/2; 1/2; -x) = sqrt(pi) x^{(p + 2)/2} (1 + O(x^{-1} log x))/(Gamma(-p/2) Gamma((p + 3)/2)) as x -> inf (DLMF
15.8(ii)), and dominated convergence gives E = A_E z^{p + 2} (1 + o(1)) as z -> inf, with A_E = sqrt(pi)
Gamma((p + 2 - s)/2) lambda^{-(p + 2)/2}/(Gamma(-s/2) Gamma(-p/2) Gamma((p + 3)/2)) < 0. Hence the solutions with C^1
even extension, the multiples of E, have a nonzero z^{p + 2} component unless they vanish. That these are all the
solutions with C^1 even extension also follows without the expansions at z = 0 used above. Let F_1 = 2F1((1 - p)/2,
-(1 + p)/2; 3/2; -tau z^2/lambda) and E_1(z) = z Gamma((1 - s)/2)^{-1} int_0^inf e^{-tau} tau^{-(1 + s)/2} F_1 dtau;
the same computation, with the weight e^{-tau} tau^{(1 - s)/2 - 1} and Phi replaced by (tau d/dtau + (1 - p)/2)(tau
d/dtau - (1 + p)/2) F_1, shows that E_1 solves the equation, and E_1 is odd and smooth with E_1'(0) = 1, so that
W_2 = E E_1' - E_1 E' tends to 1 as z -> 0+. Solved for h''', the equation has the coefficient -(1 - 2p - s)/z - 2
lambda/z^3 of h'', so by Abel's identity the Wronskian of E, E_1 and any solution h is W_0 z^{2p + s - 1}
exp(lambda/z^2) with a constant W_0; expanded along h, this reads W_2 h'' = W_0 z^{2p + s - 1} exp(lambda/z^2) plus a
combination of h and h' whose coefficients are 2 by 2 minors in E, E_1 and their first two derivatives, bounded near
0. If h and h' are bounded near 0+ and W_0 != 0, then near 0 the function h'' has a fixed sign and modulus at least a
positive multiple of z^{2p + s - 1} exp(lambda/z^2), which is not integrable at 0, so h' is unbounded. Hence W_0 = 0;
near 0 the identity is then a regular second-order equation for h with the independent solutions E and E_1, so
h = h(0+) E + h'(0+) E_1 on z > 0 by uniqueness, and h is a multiple of E when h'(0+) = 0. A numerical evaluation of
the integral (20 digits, K = 1) gives A_E = -0.896637, -0.193424 and -0.0210086 at p = 0.25, 0.5 and 0.75, equal to 12
digits to the z^{p + 2} coefficients obtained by integrating the equation outward from the truncated series at z = 0,
and E(z)/(A_E z^{p + 2}) = 1 to 1e-6 at z = 1e4; with the derivatives in z computed from the Gauss derivative formula,
E and E_1 satisfy the equation with relative residuals below 1e-20 at z = 0.3, 0.7 and 3 (p = 0.25, 0.5 and 0.75).
These checks concern the formal inner problem only.

## A.3.80 Finite polynomial axis data

Notation. As in 3.80. A prime denotes the derivative in the displayed independent variable: G' and V' are derivatives
in y, H' is a derivative in w, F', A' and B' are derivatives in t, and in the proof of (b) Psi', W', R' and Q_1' are
derivatives in x, while pi', pi_1' and pi_2' are derivatives in v (so pi'(z) is the derivative of pi at v = z). F, D,
A, B, I, J, h, n, d, q, a, b, l, s, mu and alpha are local, and so are x, sigma, kappa, Q_1, beta, e, delta, u, u_*,
u_j, u_-, u_+, v, v_j, z, pi, pi_1, pi_2, phi, Psi, R, W, T, A_0, A_j, mu_j, M_l, b_1, b_2, b_3, b_4, f_l, gamma_l,
tau, nu, p, omega, chi, theta_1, theta_2, L_0, L_1, L_2, K, eta, zeta_j, m, S, b_5, b_6, C_0, C_1, N_0, N_1, N_2, r_0,
r_1, r_2, r_3, b_7, b_8, Q_3, Q_4, Q_5, Q_6, R_12, R_13, R_23, R_34, R_35, R_45, R_46, R_56 and Lambda in the proof of
(b).

Reduction. Write H(w) = w^n h(w) with n >= 1 and h(0) != 0, F(t) = C t h(1 - t^2) and D = w F' + 2 (P - n) t F. F is a
nonzero odd polynomial of odd degree d >= 1 with F(0) = 0 and F(1) = -F(-1) = C h(0) != 0, so F and w have no common
complex root. From y = C t w^{-P}, G = y H(w) = F w^{n - P}, dG/dt = D w^{n - P - 1} and dy/dt = C Q w^{-P - 1}, so
G' = dG/dy = D w^n/(C Q). D is not the zero polynomial: if P != n, D(1) = 2 (P - n) F(1) != 0, and if P = n, D = w F'
with F nonconstant.

Suppose that (c y + V) G' = G on a nonempty open interval I of y > 0; shrinking I, D != 0 on I (a nonzero polynomial
has finitely many roots). Then c y + V = G/G' = C w^{-P} F Q/D, that is
    V = C w^{-P} A(t),   A = F Q/D - c t,   (A1)
with A a rational function of t (P need not be rational; the powers of w are differentiated only where w > 0).
Differentiate (A1) in t on I: dV/dt = k(w) dy/dt = C k(w) Q w^{-P - 1}, and d(w^{-P})/dt = 2 P t w^{-P - 1};
multiplying by w^{P + 1}/C gives
    w A' + 2 P t A = k(w) Q.   (A2)
Both sides of (A2) are rational functions of t that agree on an interval, so (A2) is an identity of rational
functions.

A is a polynomial. At a pole alpha of A with alpha != +-1, of order l >= 1 and leading Laurent coefficient a != 0, the
term w A' has a pole of order l + 1 with leading coefficient -l w(alpha) a != 0, and 2 P t A has a pole of order at
most l, so the left side of (A2) has a pole while the right side is a polynomial. At alpha = 1 the coefficient of
(t - 1)^{-l} on the left side of (A2) is 2 (l + P) a != 0, and at alpha = -1 the coefficient of (t + 1)^{-l} is -2
(l + P) a != 0 (the other terms of the Laurent series of A contribute only higher powers), again a contradiction. A
rational function without poles is a polynomial, so B = F Q/D = A + c t is a polynomial, and as w + 2 P t^2 = Q, (A2)
gives w B' + 2 P t B = (k(w) + c) Q. Hence
    D divides F Q, and Q divides w B' + 2 P t B.   (A3)
If P = n, then D(1) = 0 while F(1) Q(1) = 2 P F(1) != 0, contrary to (A3). So P != n, and D(1) = D(-1) = 2 (P - n)
F(1) != 0.

Multiplicities. At a root alpha of F of multiplicity mu, F' has multiplicity mu - 1 and w(alpha) != 0, while t F has
multiplicity at least mu, so D has multiplicity exactly mu - 1 there. Hence the monic greatest common divisor J of F
and D is the monic greatest common divisor of F and F', of degree d - s with s the number of distinct complex roots of
F, and F/J and D/J are coprime. By (A3), D/J divides (F/J) Q, hence divides Q.

Proof of (a). Case d != 2 (P - n). The leading coefficient of D is 2 (P - n) - d times that of F, so deg D = d + 1 and
deg(D/J) = s + 1 <= 2. Since F(0) = 0, s >= 1, so s = 1 and F = a t^d with a != 0. Then D = a t^{d - 1} (d + (2
(P - n) - d) t^2), J = t^{d - 1}, and D/J, of degree 2, divides Q and is therefore a constant multiple of Q: 2
(P - n) - d = d (2P - 1), that is d = (P - n)/P < 1, which is not a positive integer. Hence d = 2 (P - n), that is
P = n + d/2. Put q = 2P - 1 = 2n + d - 1 > 0, so Q = 1 + q t^2, and let alpha be a root of Q: alpha^2 = -1/q,
w(alpha) = (q + 1)/q and Q'(alpha) = 2 q alpha. If d = 1, then F = a t, D = a and B = t Q, so (w B' + 2 P t
B)(alpha) = w(alpha) alpha Q'(alpha) = -2 (q + 1)/q != 0, contrary to (A3). If d = 3, then F = a t^3 + b t with a != 0
and a + b != 0, D = b + (3a + 2b) t^2 and q = 2n + 2 >= 4. If b = 0, D = 3a t^2 and B = t Q/3, so (w B' + 2 P t
B)(alpha) = -2 (q + 1)/(3q) != 0. If b != 0, F has three simple roots, J = 1, and D, an even polynomial of degree at
most 2 with D(0) = b, divides Q: either 3a + 2b = 0, D = b and B = t (1 - 2 t^2/3) Q, so (w B' + 2 P t B)(alpha) = -2
(q + 1)(1 + 2/(3q))/q != 0, or D = b Q, a/b = (q - 2)/3 and B = t (1 + (q - 2) t^2/3), so (w B' + 2 P t B)(alpha) = -2
(q - 2)(q + 1)/(3 q^2) != 0. Each case contradicts (A3), so d >= 5, which proves (a).

Proof of (b). Polynomial coordinates. By (a), P = n + d/2, so kappa = P - 1/2 = n + (d - 1)/2 is an integer,
kappa >= 3. Put x = t w^{-1/2}, an increasing bijection of (0, 1) onto (0, inf), and sigma = 1 + x^2, so that
w = 1/sigma and t^2 = x^2/sigma. Then y = C x sigma^kappa and dy/dx = C sigma^{kappa - 1} Q_1 with Q_1 = 1 + 2P x^2.
Writing F(t) = sum_l f_l t^{2l + 1} (0 <= l <= (d - 1)/2), one finds G = F w^{n - P} = Psi(x) with
    Psi(x) = x sum_l f_l x^{2l} sigma^{(d - 1)/2 - l},
a real odd polynomial of degree d (its leading coefficient is sum_l f_l = F(1) != 0) with Psi(+-i) = f_{(d - 1)/2}
(+-i)^d != 0, since only the term l = (d - 1)/2 survives at sigma = 0. A factor t^2 - tau of F (tau != 1 because
F(1) != 0) becomes ((1 - tau) x^2 - tau)/sigma, and tau -> tau/(1 - tau) is injective, so F and Psi have the same
number of distinct roots, the root 0 with the same multiplicity A_0 (odd), and the nonzero roots in pairs +-alpha
whose multiplicities correspond.

Put W = c y + V. On a subinterval where Psi' != 0, W = Psi (dy/dx)/Psi', and dV/dy = k(w) gives
W'/(dy/dx) - c = k(1/sigma); as in (A2) this is an identity of rational functions of x, so W'/(sigma^{kappa - 1}
Q_1) = C (c + k(1/sigma)) has no poles other than possibly +-i. Let beta = i (2P)^{-1/2}, so that Q_1(+-beta) = 0, and
u_* = beta^2 = -1/(2P), which lies in (-1, 0). If alpha is a root of Psi' that is not a root of Psi and not one of
+-i, +-beta, then W has a pole at alpha and so has W'/(sigma^{kappa - 1} Q_1), which is impossible; if alpha = +-beta
is a root of Psi' of multiplicity at least two that is not a root of Psi, W has a pole there, and
W'/(sigma^{kappa - 1} Q_1) has a pole of order at least three, again impossible. Since Psi' has multiplicity exactly
mu - 1 at a root of Psi of multiplicity mu, and Psi' is even and real,
    Psi'/Psi = d sigma^e (x^2 - u_*)^delta/R,   (A4)
where R = x prod_j (x^2 - u_j) is the monic product of the distinct linear factors of Psi (the u_j distinct and
nonzero, none equal to -1 since Psi(+-i) != 0), e >= 0 is the multiplicity of +-i as roots of Psi', delta is 0 or 1,
deg R = 2e + 2 delta + 1 (compare with Psi'/Psi ~ d/x at infinity), and if delta = 1 no u_j equals u_*. With u = x^2,
(A4) says
    phi(u) := d (1 + u)^e (u - u_*)^delta/(u prod_j (u - u_j)) = A_0/u + sum_j A_j/(u - u_j),   (A5)
where A_j = 2 mu_j and mu_j is the multiplicity of the roots +-u_j^{1/2} of Psi; nonreal u_j occur in conjugate pairs
with equal A_j, and A_0 + sum_j A_j = d.

Case delta = 0. Here W = (C/d) R Q_1 sigma^{kappa - 1 - e} and W'/(sigma^{kappa - 1} Q_1) = (C/d) [(R Q_1)' sigma + 2
(kappa - 1 - e) x R Q_1]/(sigma^{e + 1} Q_1). At x = beta the bracket equals R(beta) Q_1'(beta) sigma(beta) with
Q_1'(beta) sigma(beta) != 0, so R(beta) = 0 and u_* is one of the u_j. Then 0 and u_* are real poles of phi with
positive residues. If u_- < u_+ are consecutive real poles of phi in [u_*, 0], phi is real and continuous on (u_-,
u_+), tends to +inf as u decreases to u_- and to -inf as u increases to u_+, and so vanishes in (u_-, u_+), while by
(A5) its only possible zero is u = -1 < u_*. So delta = 1.

Case delta = 1. Now there are e + 1 values u_j, R(beta) != 0, Q_1 = 2P (x^2 - u_*), W = (2P C/d) R
sigma^{kappa - 1 - e} and
    W'/(sigma^{kappa - 1} Q_1) = (C/d) [R' sigma + 2 (kappa - 1 - e) x R]/((x^2 - u_*) sigma^{e + 1}),
so the bracket vanishes at beta. Multiplying by beta/R(beta) and using x R'/R = 1 + sum_j 2 x^2/(x^2 - u_j) and (2
kappa + 1) u_* = -1, this becomes
    sum_j (1 + u_j)/(u_* - u_j) = 0.   (A6)
Put v = 1/(1 + u), v_j = 1/(1 + u_j), z = 1/(1 + u_*) = 2P/(2P - 1) > 1 and pi(v) = prod_j (v - v_j); the v_j are
distinct and different from 0, 1 and z. Since (1 + u_j)/(u_* - u_j) = -z/(z - v_j), (A6) says pi'(z) = 0. Expanding
(A5) at u = -1 with 1/(u - u_j) = -v_j sum_{l >= 0} v_j^l (u + 1)^l (and v_0 = 1 for the pole u = 0), the coefficient
of (u + 1)^{l - 1} in phi is -M_l, where
    M_l = A_0 + sum_j A_j v_j^l,
so the zero of order e of phi at u = -1 gives M_l = 0 for 1 <= l <= e. In the variable v, phi = v (A_0/(1 - v) + sum_j
A_j v_j/(v_j - v)) is v times a rational function with denominator (v - 1) pi(v) of degree e + 2, and phi = -M_{e + 1}
v^{-e} + O(v^{-e - 1}) at v = inf and phi = d v + O(v^2) at v = 0; so phi = v (d (-1)^e prod_j v_j - M_{e + 1}
v)/((v - 1) pi(v)), and the zero of phi at u = u_*, that is at v = z, gives
    M_{e + 1} z = (-1)^e d prod_j v_j.   (A7)
If e = 0, pi'(z) = 1, a contradiction. If e = 1, pi'(z) = 0 gives v_1 + v_2 = 2z, and M_1 = 0 gives A_0 + A_1
v_1 + A_2 v_2 = 0. If A_1 = A_2 these give A_0 = -2 A_1 z < 0, a contradiction. Otherwise they determine v_1 and v_2,
and substitution into (A7), M_2 z = -d v_1 v_2, gives after multiplication by (A_1 - A_2)^2
    (A_0 + (A_1 + A_2) z)(A_0 d - 4 A_1 A_2 z (z - 1)) = 0.
The first factor is positive. As z (z - 1) = 2P/(2P - 1)^2 decreases in P and 2P = 2n + d >= d + 2, and 4 A_1
A_2 <= (d - A_0)^2 < d^2, this gives A_0 d < d^2 (d + 2)/(d + 1)^2, that is A_0 < d (d + 2)/(d + 1)^2 < 1, a
contradiction. If all A_j (j >= 1) equal one value b > 0 (for any e), the conditions M_l = 0 say sum_j v_j^l = -A_0/b
for 1 <= l <= e, so as formal power series in tau, prod_j (1 - v_j tau) = exp(-sum_{l >= 1} (sum_j v_j^l)
tau^l/l) = (1 - tau)^{-A_0/b} + O(tau^{e + 1}); hence pi(v) = sum_{l=0}^{e + 1} gamma_l v^{e + 1 - l} with
gamma_l = (A_0/b)(A_0/b + 1)...(A_0/b + l - 1)/l! > 0 for l <= e, and pi'(z) = sum_{l=0}^{e} (e + 1 - l) gamma_l
z^{e - l} > 0, a contradiction. If e = 2 and the three v_j are real, M_2 > 0, a contradiction; otherwise one of them,
v_1, is real and v_2, v_3 are nonreal conjugates with A_2 = A_3. Then M_1 = M_2 = 0 give b_1 = v_2 + v_3 = -(A_0 + A_1
v_1)/A_2 and b_2 = v_2 v_3 = (A_0 + A_1 v_1^2 + A_2 b_1^2)/(2 A_2), and for pi(v) = (v - v_1)(v^2 - b_1 v + b_2)
    pi'(z) = A_1 (A_1 - A_2)/(2 A_2^2) (v_1 + (A_0 + 2 A_2 z)/A_1)^2
             + (1 + 2 A_2/A_1) z^2 + 2 A_0 z/A_1 + A_0/(2 A_2) + A_0^2/(2 A_1 A_2).
If A_1 > A_2 the right side is positive, a contradiction; A_1 = A_2 is the case of equal values. So e >= 2, the
nonzero roots of Psi do not all have the same multiplicity, and A_1 < A_2 if e = 2.

One exceptional value. Suppose that the A_j (j >= 1) all equal one value b except one, A_1 != b. Then v_1 is real,
since otherwise its conjugate would be a second node with the value A_1. No real u_j lies in (u_*, 0) or in (0, inf):
otherwise, among the real poles of phi in the closed interval between u_j and 0, two consecutive ones u_- < u_+ would
lie in (u_*, inf), and as in the case delta = 0, phi would vanish in (u_-, u_+), which contains neither -1 nor u_*. So
every real u_j is less than u_* and different from -1, and as v = 1/(1 + u) decreases on (-1, inf) with value z at
u_*, every real v_j is negative or greater than z. Since u_* - u_j = (v_j - z)/(z v_j) and u_* = (1 - z)/z,
phi(u_*) = 0 and sum_j A_j = d - A_0 give
    A_0/(z - 1) + sum_j A_j/(z - v_j) = d/z.   (A8)
As pi(z) != 0 and pi'(z) = 0, sum_j 1/(z - v_j) = 0, so the sum in (A8) is (A_1 - b)/(z - v_1). Multiplying (A8) by z
and using z/(z - 1) = 2P gives v_1 = z (1 + (A_1 - b)/T) with T = 2P A_0 - d = (A_0 - 1) d + 2 A_0 n >= 2n > 0. If
A_1 > b, then v_1 > z > 0, and M_l = 0 gives sum_j v_j^l = -(A_0 + (A_1 - b) v_1^l)/b for 1 <= l <= e, so as formal
power series prod_j (1 - v_j tau) = (1 - tau)^{-A_0/b} (1 - v_1 tau)^{-(A_1 - b)/b} + O(tau^{e + 1}), a product of two
series with positive coefficients; as in the case of equal values pi'(z) > 0, a contradiction. If A_1 < b, then
v_1 < z, so v_1 < 0, that is T < b - A_1 < b < d; as A_0 >= 3 would give T >= 2d + 6n, A_0 = 1, T = 2n and
b - A_1 > 2n. With A_j = 2 mu_j, this proves the last statement of (b). In particular, if e = 2, three real v_j being
excluded, A_0 = 1, A_2 = A_3 = b and b - A_1 > 2n, so b >= A_1 + 2n + 2 >= 6 and d = 1 + A_1 + 2b >= 15.

Degrees. Since deg R = 2e + 3 <= d, A_0 >= 1 is odd and the e + 1 values A_j are even, at least 2 and of sum d - A_0.
Let p be the number of conjugate pairs of nonreal v_j. If 2p + 2 <= e, there is a nonzero real polynomial omega of
degree at most p such that v_j omega(v_j) is real for one node v_j of each of these pairs (p real linear conditions on
p + 1 real coefficients); then chi(v) = v omega(v) is real at every v_j, chi^2 is a real linear combination of v^2,
..., v^{2p + 2}, and A_0 chi(1)^2 + sum_j A_j chi(v_j)^2 is the same combination of M_2, ..., M_{2p + 2}, which vanish
as 2p + 2 <= e. Every term of this sum is nonnegative, so chi vanishes at 0, at 1 and at the e + 1 distinct v_j, which
is impossible for a nonzero polynomial of degree at most p + 1 < e + 3. Hence 2p >= e - 1, that is, at most two of the
v_j are real. In particular the A_j are not pairwise distinct, since a nonreal v_j and its conjugate have the same
value.

Two relations. Multiplying (A8) by z and using z/(z - 1) = 2P gives sum_j A_j/(z - v_j) = -T/z with T = 2P
A_0 - d >= 2n as above, and pi'(z) = 0 with pi(z) != 0 gives sum_j 1/(z - v_j) = 0. If the A_j take exactly two values
theta_1 != theta_2, let pi_1 and pi_2 be the monic polynomials whose roots are the v_j of value theta_1 and of value
theta_2; they have real coefficients, as conjugation preserves the values, and pi = pi_1 pi_2. With
L_i = pi_i'(z)/pi_i(z), the two sums read L_1 + L_2 = 0 and theta_1 L_1 + theta_2 L_2 = -T/z, so
    (theta_1 - theta_2) z pi_1'(z) + T pi_1(z) = 0,   (theta_1 - theta_2) z pi_2'(z) - T pi_2(z) = 0.   (A9)
If instead exactly two of the v_j, say v_1 and v_2, have values taken by no other v_j (so that v_1 and v_2 are real)
and all others have one value b, subtracting b times the second sum from the first gives
    (A_1 - b)/(z - v_1) + (A_2 - b)/(z - v_2) = -T/z.   (A10)

Two pairs. Suppose that e = 3, A_1 = A_2 != A_3 = A_4 and T (A_1 + A_3) > A_1 A_3; the last condition holds if
min(A_1, A_3) = 2, as T >= 2n >= 2 > A_1 A_3/(A_1 + A_3), and if A_0 >= 3, as then T >= 2d + 6n > d > A_1
A_3/(A_1 + A_3). Write pi_1(v) = (v - v_1)(v - v_2) = v^2 - b_1 v + b_2 and pi_2(v) = (v - v_3)(v - v_4) = v^2 - b_3
v + b_4. By (A9) with theta_1 = A_1 and theta_2 = A_3,
    b_2 = ((T + A_1 - A_3) b_1 z - (T + 2 A_1 - 2 A_3) z^2)/T,
    b_4 = ((T - A_1 + A_3) b_3 z - (T - 2 A_1 + 2 A_3) z^2)/T,
and M_1 = A_0 + A_1 b_1 + A_3 b_3 = 0 gives b_3 = -(A_0 + A_1 b_1)/A_3. Substituting into M_2 = A_0 + A_1 (b_1^2 - 2
b_2) + A_3 (b_3^2 - 2 b_4) = 0 and multiplying by A_3 T gives a quadratic equation for b_1 with leading coefficient
A_1 (A_1 + A_3) T and discriminant -4 A_1 A_3 K, where
    K = A_0^2 T^2 + A_0 (A_1 + A_3)(1 + 2z) T^2 + 2 A_0 (A_1 - A_3)^2 z T + 2 (A_1 + A_3)^2 z^2 T^2
        + 4 (A_1 - A_3)^2 z^2 (T (A_1 + A_3) - A_1 A_3) > 0,
so b_1 = v_1 + v_2 is not real, a contradiction (neither M_3 nor (A7) is used).

Elimination. In the remaining cases put eta = 2P = 2n + d >= d + 2, so that z = eta/(eta - 1) and T = A_0 eta - d, and
replace each v_j by zeta_j = (eta - 1) v_j, the polynomials pi, pi_1 and pi_2 by the monic polynomials with the
corresponding roots zeta_j, and M_l by A_0 (eta - 1)^l + sum_j A_j zeta_j^l (keeping the names). The conditions used
below keep their form, with z replaced by eta and v_1, v_2 by zeta_1, zeta_2 in pi'(z) = 0, the two sums, (A9) and
(A10), and the fixed node 1 replaced by eta - 1 in M_l (the relation (A7), which is not used, changes form). Type (I):
two values theta_1 != theta_2, pi_1(v) = v^2 - b_1 v + b_2 and pi_2 of degree m = e - 1. The first relation of (A9)
gives b_2 as a polynomial in b_1 and eta divided by T; the equations M_1 = 0, ..., M_{m - 1} = 0 then give the
coefficients of v^{m - 1}, ..., v of pi_2 in turn, the one determined by M_l entering M_l linearly with coefficient -l
theta_2 (Newton's identities); and the second relation of (A9) gives the constant term of pi_2, which enters it with
coefficient -T. Let N_1 and N_2 be the numerators of M_m and M_{m + 1}, polynomials in b_1 and eta (the denominators
are nonzero integers times powers of T), and eliminate b_1. Type (II): v_1 and v_2 as in (A10), and the other e - 1
nodes of one value b, with pi_2 their monic polynomial (pi_2(v) = v^2 - b_3 v + b_4 if e = 3). (A10), multiplied by
eta (eta - zeta_1)(eta - zeta_2), is linear in zeta_2 with coefficient -S, where S = (T + A_1 - b) eta - T zeta_1, and
S != 0, since for S = 0 the relation would reduce to (A_1 - b)(A_2 - b) eta^2/T = 0. So zeta_2 is a rational function
of zeta_1 and eta, M_1 = 0, ..., M_{e - 1} = 0 give the coefficients of pi_2 in turn as in type (I), with b in place
of theta_2 (for e = 3, b_3 and b_4, entering with coefficients b and -2 b), and N_1 and N_2 are the numerators of M_e
and of pi'(eta), polynomials in zeta_1 and eta (the denominators are nonzero integers times powers of S and T);
eliminate zeta_1. Type (III): two values theta_1 != theta_2, each taken by three nodes (so e = 5), with
pi_1(v) = v^3 - b_1 v^2 + b_2 v - b_3 and pi_2(v) = v^3 - b_4 v^2 + b_5 v - b_6. The first relation of (A9) gives b_3
(entering with coefficient -T), M_1 = 0 and M_2 = 0 give b_4 and b_5 (entering with coefficients theta_2 and -2
theta_2), and the second relation of (A9) gives b_6 (entering with coefficient T); the numerator of M_3 is then C_1
b_2 + C_0 with polynomials C_0 and C_1 in b_1 and eta. If C_1 != 0, substituting b_2 = -C_0/C_1 into M_4 and M_5 gives
the numerators N_1 and N_2, polynomials in b_1 and eta (the denominators are nonzero integers times powers of T and
C_1); eliminate b_1. If C_1 = 0, then C_0 = 0, and the resultant of C_1 and C_0 with respect to b_1 vanishes at eta.
Type (IV): one node v_1 of a value A_1 taken by no other node, and two pairs of values theta_1 != theta_2, with
pi_1(v) = v^2 - b_1 v + b_2 and pi_2(v) = v^2 - b_3 v + b_4 (so e = 4). With L_0 = 1/(eta - zeta_1) and
L_i = pi_i'(eta)/pi_i(eta), the two sums read L_0 + L_1 + L_2 = 0 and A_1 L_0 + theta_1 L_1 + theta_2 L_2 = -T/eta,
which give L_1 and L_2 as rational functions of zeta_1 and eta. If L_1 L_2 != 0, the relations pi_i'(eta) = L_i
pi_i(eta) give b_2 and b_4 (entering with coefficients -L_1 and -L_2), M_1 = 0 gives b_3, and the numerator N_0 of M_2
is quadratic in b_1, with leading coefficient a nonzero integer times the product of the numerators of L_1 and L_2.
The pseudo-remainders of the numerators of M_3 and M_4 modulo N_0 with respect to b_1, r_1 b_1 + r_0 and r_3
b_1 + r_2, vanish at a solution, and hence so do N_1 = r_1 r_2 - r_0 r_3 and N_2, the resultant of N_0 and r_1
b_1 + r_0 with respect to b_1; these are polynomials in zeta_1 and eta. Divide them by the powers of the numerators of
L_1 and L_2 that they contain, and eliminate zeta_1. If L_1 = 0, then b_1 = 2 eta and L_0 = -T/((A_1 - theta_2) eta),
and M_1 = 0, the relation for pi_2 and M_2 = 0 give b_3, b_4 and b_2 in turn, so that M_3 and M_4 are rational
functions of eta; the case L_2 = 0 is the same with the two pairs exchanged. Type (V): two values theta_1 != theta_2,
taken by three and by four nodes (so e = 6), with pi_1(v) = v^3 - b_1 v^2 + b_2 v - b_3 and pi_2(v) = v^4 - b_4
v^3 + b_5 v^2 - b_6 v + b_7. The first relation of (A9) gives b_3 (entering with coefficient -T), M_1 = 0, M_2 = 0 and
M_3 = 0 give b_4, b_5 and b_6 (entering with coefficients theta_2, -2 theta_2 and 3 theta_2), and the second relation
of (A9) gives b_7 (entering with coefficient -T); the numerators of M_4, M_5 and M_6 are then polynomials in b_1, b_2
and eta (the denominators are nonzero integers times powers of T). Let Q_5 and Q_6 be the pseudo-remainders, with
respect to b_2, of the numerators of M_5 and M_6 by the numerator of M_4, of degree at most 1 in b_2, let R_56 be the
resultant of Q_5 and Q_6 with respect to b_2 (taken with formal degree 1 in b_2, that is, the determinant of their
coefficients), and let R_45 and R_46 be the resultants with respect to b_2 of the numerator of M_4 with Q_5 and with
Q_6. Divide each of the three polynomials R_56, R_45 and R_46 by the powers of eta and T that it contains (both
nonzero at a solution), which leaves polynomials in b_1 and eta, and then eliminate b_1 from the divided R_56 and R_45
and from the divided R_56 and R_46. A pseudo-remainder vanishes at a common root of the two polynomials even where the
leading coefficient of the divisor vanishes, since lc(g)^k f = h g + prem(f, g) is an identity of polynomials. Type
(VI): one node v_1 of a value A_1 taken by no other node, a pair of value theta_1 and three nodes of value theta_2,
with pi_1(v) = v^2 - b_1 v + b_2 and pi_2(v) = v^3 - b_3 v^2 + b_4 v - b_5 (so e = 5). As in type (IV), the two sums
give L_1 and L_2 as rational functions of zeta_1 and eta. If L_1 L_2 != 0, the relations pi_i'(eta) = L_i pi_i(eta)
give b_2 and b_5 (entering with coefficients -L_1 and L_2), M_1 = 0 and M_2 = 0 give b_3 and b_4 (entering with
coefficients theta_2 and -2 theta_2), and the numerators of M_3, M_4 and M_5 are polynomials in b_1, zeta_1 and eta
(the denominators are nonzero integers times powers of the numerators of L_1 and L_2). Let R_34 and R_35 be the
resultants with respect to b_1 of the numerator of M_3 with the numerators of M_4 and of M_5; let Q_4 and Q_5 be the
pseudo-remainders, with respect to b_1, of the numerators of M_4 and M_5 by the numerator of M_3, Q_3 the
pseudo-remainder of the numerator of M_3 by Q_4, and R_45 the resultant of Q_5 and Q_3 with respect to b_1. Divide
R_34, R_35 and R_45 by the powers of eta, T, eta - zeta_1 and the numerators of L_1 and L_2 that they contain (all
nonzero at a solution), which leaves polynomials in zeta_1 and eta, and eliminate zeta_1 from R_34 and R_35 and from
R_34 and R_45. If L_1 = 0, then b_1 = 2 eta and L_0 = -T/((A_1 - theta_2) eta), which gives zeta_1; M_1 = 0, M_2 = 0
and the relation for pi_2 give b_3, b_4 and b_5, and the numerators of M_3, M_4 and M_5 are polynomials in b_2 and

matrix is formed with the formal degrees r and s (also at values of eta where leading coefficients vanish), its
determinant is a polynomial of degree at most s a + r b in eta, and its exact values at eta = 0, 1, ..., s a + r b
determine it (by integer forward differences and exact division by factorials). In types (I) to (IV), with N_1 and N_2
taken with coprime integer coefficients, a solution gives a common root of N_1 and N_2 at the value eta, so their
resultant with respect to the eliminated variable vanishes at eta (the vector of powers of a common root is a nonzero
null vector of the Sylvester matrix, also when leading coefficients vanish at eta). Let Lambda be this resultant
divided by the greatest common divisor of its integer coefficients, with positive leading coefficient, a polynomial in
eta. In types (V) and (VI), and in the pairwise construction, each resultant formed above vanishes at a solution for
the same reason, so the two final resultants, polynomials in eta, vanish at eta; let Lambda be their greatest common
divisor divided by the powers of eta and T that it contains, with coprime integer coefficients and positive leading
coefficient.
